Commentator: Bhāskararāya Editor: Abhyaṅkara K.V. Description: Transcribed from volume 56 of the Ānandāśrama-saṃskṛtagranthāvaliḥ (Ananda Ashram Sanskrit Series).

Oṃ tatsad brahmaṇe namaḥ.
The Ocean of the Sixteen Nityās, contained within the Vāmakeśvara Tantra,
together with the commentary titled Setubandha composed by Śrī Bhāskararāya.
Therein, the first rest (viśrāma).
He who was born from the womb of Konamā, the mother of the illustrious Gambhīravipaścit his father;
he who became a knower of the essential points of the eighteen branches of learning from the preceptor Śrī Nṛsiṃha;
and he who was consecrated with the full initiation by the venerable Śivadattaśukla—[he is this one].
He considers that very triad of Lords to be the Tretā age, Tripura, and the Triple Veda.
The wise Bhāskara explains the two four-hundred-verse sections, the Pūrva- and Uttara-catuḥśatī, contained within the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava* of the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*.

In this Tantra named the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*, which is solely dependent upon Śiva and is exceedingly profound, what human is capable of even stirring within the coils of the serpent [of its verses]? (3)

Even though this is so, nevertheless, I have been compelled by my devotion to the Guru to proceed with the task of rescuing [beings] by means of the bridge demonstrated by the ancient masters, using firm bonds.
Those who desire to reach the further shore of the ocean of the eternal Ṣoḍaśī should resort to this bridge-construction, which is provided with eight resting places.
From Kāmarūpa in the east, washed by the river of the Son of Druhiṇa (the Gaṅgā), to Gāndhāra in the west, moist with the Indus and fashioned by the Rāpuvara;
and from the Setu in the south to the Tuṣāragahana (Himalayas) in the north— there exist assemblies of the learned.
May this effort of mine please all those [who are wise]; for who is able to cause wonder in those who already know?

In this world, indeed, happiness alone—desirable to all people—is the human goal (puruṣārtha). That [happiness] is of two kinds, artificial and non-artificial, which are designated respectively by the terms *kāma* (pleasure) and *mokṣa* (liberation). Dharma is the means for attaining both of these.

Since it is a means for accomplishing Dharma, Artha (wealth) is also desired by all; thus, although they differ from one another in degree, all four are indeed *puruṣārthas* (aims of human life), because there is no difference in their being sought after by persons. As for the statement in the *Kalpasūtra* that "self-investigation (*svavimarśa*) is the aim of man," [it refers to this].
This is not contradictory, as it is intended to show that liberation alone is primary because it consists of unconditioned bliss.

Those [liberations] are to be accomplished through such knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*vijñāna*), and those [knowledges and realizations] are to be accomplished solely by means of such and such states of mind (*citta*). As for the "suchness" (*tādṛśatva*) in those states of mind:

Because of the gradations of purity; and therefore, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, who is supremely compassionate and desires to favor those people who possess various states of mind dependent upon the ripening of diverse karmas,
[teaches] even those things that are mutually distinct, whether directly or indirectly.
He set forth the sciences (vidyās) which have as their sole purpose the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha). And so says the Śruti:
"The Lord of all sciences, who first created Brahmā and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him. Here, by the word "and" (ca), there is an inclusion of other sciences.
"He gave the Vedas and Purāṇas to that foremost of the twice-born"—from seeing such corroborative statements (upabṛṃhaṇa).
There is also a Smṛti: "Of these eighteen sciences which follow diverse paths..."
The Śruti declares that the original author is the poet [Brahmā] himself, the wielder of the trident.

Consequently, since there is no difference in the fact that all these sciences were composed by the supreme Śiva, who is the authoritative source for the world, their validity is established according to the differences among qualified practitioners; this is clear from the Sūtasaṃhitā and other texts.

Just as eligibility (*adhikāra*) is established according to the distinction of persons— such that it belongs only to atheists in the systems of the Arhats and others, and only to those of the three higher castes in the Vedic paths— likewise, even for a single person, it is established according to the degree of purity of the mind.
Since the establishment of dharma is observed to occur through the distinction of *āśrama*s just as it does through the distinction of *varṇa*s,
those statements which praise particular sciences are intended to incite only those who are qualified for them,
while those which disparage them are intended for those who are not so qualified.
They are prohibitive; they do not, however, praise the enjoined act by means of the "maxim of indirect censure" (*na hi nindā nyāya*),

because we observe that even parents and others who engage their children in playthings during extreme childhood subsequently administer beatings for such play when the child reaches the stage of eligibility for Vedic study.

Thus, this is the summarized meaning: for a person of the three higher castes immediately upon birth, once the period for play has passed, there is the practice of letters; thereafter, for the sake of knowing the meters and the language, there is the faultless engagement in the study of poetry.

Statements such as "poetry is possessed of qualities" are from the *Agnipurāṇa*. However, for one who is already proficient, there is the prohibition: "one should avoid talk of poetry. Since the purpose arising from the study of poetry has already been achieved, one has the right only to the subsequent stage; therefore, having left that [initial stage] behind...
The meaning is that it becomes undesirable for one who exhausts their lifespan while still remaining on the previous stage [of life].

Therefore, there is an injunction for the study of the Nyāya-śāstra in order to know the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, such as "seek the Self by means of the *śuṅga*," and so on. *Śuṅga*...
The meaning is that *nyāya* consists of a syllogism (*avayava*) composed of a collection of reasons (*hetu*).

However, once the self is known as distinct from the body and so forth, and as capable of traversing the journey to the next world, one becomes entitled to perform actions that yield such results; thus, one becomes devoted to *ānvīkṣikī*, the science of logic (*tarka-vidyā*).
Prohibitions such as "it is useless" and so forth negate the preceding stage; injunctions such as "the wise man should practice dharma alone" direct one toward the subsequent stage.
For its utility, there is the study of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā and the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) of the Veda.

When virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) have been accomplished by him, there arises a disparagement of action (*karman*) based on the thought, "There is nothing unaccomplished through what has been done," out of a desire to attain the fourth human goal (*puruṣārtha*) and to abandon the preceding stages. All these are called the stages of ignorance (*ajñāna-bhūmikā*). Through mutual inclusion, these are seven in number.

Vasiṣṭha says: These [preceding stages] are the stages of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmikā*). Now, for the sake of realizing that, one should approach a teacher alone; "the Self, indeed, should be seen," and so forth—these injunctions regarding the knowledge of Brahman are the initiators of the subsequent stages. Some maintain that the subsequent stages are many.
"Wise ones speak of the stages of yoga (*yogabhūmikā*) in many different ways," according to this statement.

However, the venerable Vasiṣṭha maintains that there are exactly seven, as it is said: "They know realization to be *jñāna*, and this consists of seven stages. Their names are: *vividiṣā* (the desire to know), *vicāraṇā* (investigation), and *tanumānasā* (the thinned mind).

The fourth state (*turyagā*) is non-attachment to the ocean of sentient beings, wherein objective entities do not exist; its characteristics, however, are to be seen in the *Jñānaśāstra* of the *Vāsiṣṭha*. For its utility, one should study the Upaniṣadic portion of the Veda and the Uttaramīmāṃsā.
Furthermore, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*) is twofold: that which is verbal (*śābda*) and that which consists of immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*).

As indicated by such scriptural authorities as: "The vision of the scriptures, the word of the Guru, and thirdly, self-conviction; verbal cognition alone is not capable of cutting away the darkness residing within."

Therefore, following the attainment of the stage of verbal knowledge (*śābdabhūmikā*), there are such injunctions as "having become disillusioned through scholarship, one should abide in simplicity," for the purpose of prohibiting the exhaustion of one's lifespan therein.
Furthermore, between the second and third stages within the seven stages, there is one great stage consisting of devotion (*bhakti*).

The preliminary stage (*bhūmikā*) consists of the study of *Bhaktimīmāṃsā* as a means to that end. And devotion (*bhakti*) persists until the conclusion of the fifth stage. Following its attainment, there is the acquisition of the sixth stage, which consists of direct experience (*aparokṣānubhava*). And that very [sixth stage]...

Liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); and immediately following that, liberation after death (*videhakaivalya*). This is because, in the statement "liberation comes from knowledge alone" (*jñānādeva tu kaivalyam*), the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to direct experience (*anubhava*). As for the descriptions in the *Nyāya* and other systems of philosophy regarding the attainment of liberation merely by reaching their respective stages (*bhūmikā*), [they refer to a relative state].

[This is] precisely by means of the negation of each successive higher stage. For, since that [negation] is not a fault—because it removes the absence of engagement due to the fear of delay in attaining the goal of human life (puruṣārtha)—and as for those [scriptural passages] such as "By action alone, indeed, is perfection attained" and "Whomever he... [the same applies].

Regarding such statements as "He chooses [it], by that it is to be attained," the restrictive particle *eva* serves to exclude other means with respect to the fruit consisting of the qualification for a higher stage— which is to be accomplished within one's own respective stage— and does not, however, indicate the non-existence of the higher stages.

However, in the passage "only from knowledge" (*jñānādeva tu*), because there is no stage consisting of other means subsequent to direct experience, it serves only to indicate the absence of such [means]; thus, there is no mutual contradiction among all the sages who are the originators of those respective sciences. And of these...

Within each of these stages, there are indeed many intermediate sub-stages; they are so numerous that they cannot be delimited by measure, being perceivable only through experience by those possessed of intelligence.
Thus it has been said: "O Rāghava, these seven states of ignorance have been described by me."
"Each one here consists of a hundred [sub-stages], possessing various forms of manifestation.
Thus, even within these many stages (*bhūmikā*), each single stage is accomplished only through many births.
Therefore, by means of immeasurable births and with great effort, [one attains] the Supreme Brahman.
For one who has gradually and properly ascended to the culmination of the stage of ascertaining the reality of the Word (*śābda-tattva-niścaya-bhūmikā*),

there arises a unique purification of the mind characterized by neither extreme attachment to *saṃsāra* nor firm world-weariness (*nirveda*). Such a person is the qualified candidate for the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*).
"Neither dispassionate nor attached—devotional yoga (bhaktiyoga) bestows success upon him," according to this statement.
And that devotion is of two kinds: secondary (gauṇī) and supreme (parā). Of these, the former [is directed] toward Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahman).

The first form of supreme devotion (*parabhakti*) consists of the possible combination of meditation, worship, chanting, glorification, and so forth; however, the [second] form consists of a particular kind of attachment (*anurāga*) generated by those [practices]. There are also many intermediate stages within the former; among them, the first is [the stage of] "the woman as fire" (*yoṣām agnim*).

The first is the accomplishment of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), as indicated by such passages as "one should meditate" (*dhyāyīta*). The second is the worship (*upāsti*) prescribed in such passages as "one should worship the mind as Brahman" (*mano brahmety upāsīta*). The third, however, is the worship of the Lord (*īśvara*);
and even the Lord is divided into the distinctions of Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Paraśiva, and Śakti.

Due to their manifold nature, the various forms of worship for each of them also constitute distinct stages (*bhūmikās*). Furthermore, *Śakti* herself is of infinite kinds, distinguished as *Chāyā*, *Vallabhā*, *Lakṣmī*, and so forth. By this sequence, for one who has ascended these stages over countless births, [the goal is subsequently attained] in Tripurasundarī.

The established position is that the arising of secondary devotion (gauṇabhakti) occurs there [in the initial stage], and for one who is properly established therein, the arising of supreme devotion (parabhakti) follows;
this occurs sequentially through the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Daurga, Ārka, Gāṇapatya, and other paths.
For one whose mind is purified by mantras, the knowledge of Kaula shines forth.
(5) The Vedas are supreme among all [scriptures], and the Vaiṣṇava is supreme among the Vedas;
the Śaiva is superior to the Vaiṣṇava, and the Dakṣiṇa is superior to the Śaiva.
"From the Dakṣiṇa, the Vāma is supreme; from the Vāma, the Siddhānta is supreme;
from the Siddhānta, the Kaula is supreme; there is nothing higher than the Kaula"—so says the scriptural statement.

Many other fundamental statements regarding such a sequence of stages (*bhūmikākrama*) should also be written down, but they have not been recorded here for fear of prolixity; however, a few have been presented by us in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara*. Furthermore, [we shall discuss] the secondary devotion (*gauṇī bhakti*) toward the venerable Mahātripurasundarī.

In order to definitively determine the specific duties [to be performed], the concluding portions of the Vedas— namely the *Sundarī*, *Tāpanī*, *Pañcaka*, *Bhāvanopaniṣad*, *Kaulopaniṣad*, *Guhyopaniṣad*, *Mahopaniṣad*, and so forth—
were composed. And within the Veda, regarding the first section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*)...
Just as the *Kalpasūtras* of Āśvalāyana and others, as well as the *Smṛtis* of Manu and others, have come into being as supplements (*śeṣa*) to the remaining portions of the Veda,

so too have the *Kalpasūtras* of Paraśurāma and others, as well as the *Tantras* such as the *Yāmalas*, arisen as supplements to the Upaniṣad section (*kāṇḍa*). As for the Purāṇas, however, they consist of two sections (*kāṇḍa*).

Furthermore, their application occurs by way of being subsidiary (śeṣatva). Consequently, the authority of the Smṛtis, Tantras, and Purāṇas is established solely on the basis of their having the Veda as their source.
As for those portions of them that contradict direct Śruti, they are [to be treated] according to the principle of the section on contradiction (virodhādhikaraṇa-nyāya).
Invalidity is characterized by the non-performance [of injunctions] due to hearing and seeing their very roots [to be contrary to the Veda]. However,
as for certain systems such as specific Pāśupata and specific Pāñcarātra traditions which are in every respect indeed opposed to the Veda, they do not possess such [validity].

[This applies] to one who has ascended to the stage [of eligibility]. However, only those who are qualified for the stages of Śrauta and Smārta rituals, having fallen from them due to some sin, have the qualification for those [Pāñcarātra and other systems].
For this very reason: "The Pāñcarātra, the Bhāgavata, and likewise that called Vaikhānasa..."
The Lord of Kamalā spoke with reference to those who have fallen away from the Vedas.

By such statements, the enumeration of only a few [cases] is justified. Therefore: "One who has fallen from the Śruti, having become afraid of the expiatory rites prescribed by the Śruti, should resort to the Tantra in order to gradually achieve the goal of the Śruti."
In this context, the term "Tantra" in general refers to such specific [Tantric] systems.
The *adhikaraṇa* (section) beginning with "Because of the lack of consistency in the case of the Lord" (*patyurasāmañjasyāt*) also refers precisely to such Tantras.
As for those [texts] by Agastya and others that enjoin the worship of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Rudra, Paraśiva, Sundarī, and so forth—
Since the Tantras are directly perceived as being rooted in the Rāmatāpanīya and other Upaniṣads,
there is no room for the stain of doubt regarding their lack of authority. In that regard:

The worship of Sundarī is twofold, distinguished by the outer sacrifice (bahir-yāga) and the inner sacrifice (antar-yāga). The inner sacrifice, moreover, is threefold: with parts (sakala), both with and without parts (sakala-niṣkala), and without parts (niṣkala). Thus, there are these four stages (bhūmikās).
Only one who has ascended to each preceding stage is qualified for the subsequent stage.

As before: those five divisions of the external sacrifice which were mentioned—namely, the *kevala*, *yāmala*, *miśra*, *cakrayug*, and *vīrasaṃkara*—and the five [limbs] beginning with *abhigamana* and the five beginning with *daurvodhya* as taught according to the different *tantras*; by these divisions it is distinguished.

The entire external sacrifice is but a single stage (*bhūmikā*); their differentiation is due solely to differences in place, time, capacity, and so forth, and not due to a difference in the purity of the mind (*citta-śuddhi*). This is because, in the distinction of stages, it is precisely the gradation of mental purity that serves as the determining factor. And thus, even in the *Sundarī-tantras*, [this is the case].

In the Kulārṇava, Jñānārṇava, Svacchanda, Parānanda, Bhairavī, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and other such texts, there is generally an extensive elaboration of the fire-sacrifice (vahniryāga) alone, while that of the internal sacrifice is meager;
however, in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra, it is precisely the opposite.
Because it is the supreme among all tantras, the qualification for this [work] belongs only to the foremost of worshippers who are habituated to internal worship.
This very point was stated by the venerable Ācārya Bhagavatpāda:
"Having encompassed the entire world through the sixty-four tantras..."
"Paśupati remained dependent upon various bonds of worldly success (siddhi) and the fetters of the bound souls (paśu);
yet, due to your persistent request, he brought down to the surface of the earth this Tantra of yours, which is independent and the sole means for accomplishing all human goals. Thus [it is said].
Having enumerated the sixty-four tantras by way of their names,

and because the question posed by the Goddess is seen again in this very tantra, it is inferred that this tantra alone is intended as the sixty-fifth in this verse, based on such indicative marks (*liṅga*).
The Beloved of Gaurī, however, maintains that the "Supreme Ocean of Knowledge" is the *Svatantra-pada*. Others, on the other hand,
hold that the sixty-fifth [tantra] is indeed the *Tantrarāja-tantra*, because the qualifying term *svatantra* mentioned here is seen in that very [text], serving as a sign.
And so it is recorded in the Smṛti: "From their mutual dependence, a confusion of understanding arises;
therefore, O Lord, tell me that independent system for them."

Thus they say. In reality, however, although liberation does not depend on the rituals mentioned in other tantras even for its external means— the external sacrifice— it is this [system] alone that is independent regarding its internal means— the internal sacrifice— precisely because such an extensive elaboration of the internal sacrifice is absent in other tantras.
On the contrary, even the *Tantrarāja* is seen to depend upon this very [work].
As it is said in that very [text]: "One should meditate by means of the clear method proclaimed in the *Nityāhṛdaya*.
The term *Nityāhṛdaya* is the name for the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, which constitutes the latter half of the Tantra. In this regard...

Even when only a few external sacrificial components are mentioned, it can be assumed that for those whose practice is characterized by firmness in internal worship, fulfillment is achieved through that alone; nor is there any dependence on other [components] in the *Tantrarāja*.

It should not be asked how fulfillment is achieved by that alone, given that the synthesis of qualities is necessary according to the principle of "the identity of all Vedāntas" (sarvavedāntapratyaya).
For such a conclusion is reached precisely because it is impossible to synthesize every single school of thought. It is for this very reason that—
Precisely because it is impossible to incorporate all the tantras—
[as stated: "Whether much or little is prescribed for someone in their own *gṛhya* tradition, when that much of the meaning of the scripture has been performed, everything has been performed."
Thus, the statement established by logic is justified. As for the statement regarding dependence:

for those initiated according to another *tantra*, there is an abundance of results when they incorporate as many auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) as possible from other *tantras*; however, for those who have received initiation according to the *Tantrarāja*, [the result is attained] by that alone.

The statement that "the mention of the fruit and the stages [of practice] is for the purpose of concluding with something else" is intended solely to show that those auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) which must necessarily be relied upon should be taken from the *Kalpasūtras* themselves;
for the *Kalpasūtras* exist precisely for the purpose of providing the matters required by each respective Vedic branch (*śākhā*).

Because of the established principle of *praṇayana* (the leading forth of the ritual procedure). For this very reason, the objection that "if these two [Tantras] were dependent on other sources for the sake of not mentioning the mantra-initiation (*mantradīkṣā*), the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), and so forth, their independence (*svātantrya*) would be compromised," is refuted. In reality, however:

Initiations and other such matters are also alluded to in this very Tantra, as we shall explain in various places. For the mere fact that the categories mentioned in the *Nityāhṛdaya* are alluded to does not constitute a violation [of the principles] for those who maintain the independence (*svātantrya*) of the *Tantrarāja*.
Because, according to the principle of the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*), the very act of adopting elements belonging to another [text] is itself of the nature of being dependent;

and since the meaning has already been virtually stated as it was voiced directly by the author himself, its adoption from elsewhere does not undermine its independence. However, in the case of the *Kalpasūtra*...
Since, among the fifteen branches beginning with Kaṇva, the single branch of Kātyāyana— just as the branch of Paraśurāma—
is a constituent part of all the Sundarī-tantras, it follows that there is no obstacle to accepting the meanings taught therein even in the Tantrarāja and other such works.

Since independence [of this tantra] is established merely by the absence of dependence on other tantras that are of equal primary importance, it remains unrefuted that one may accept, as far as necessary, the meanings stated in that [other] tantra provided they are not contradictory. Otherwise, even [the objection] regarding dependence on the etymological derivation of word-meanings would apply.

Because it would result in the destruction of independence [of the ritual procedure]. Therefore, the conclusion is that the twilight bath (*saṃdhyā-snāna*) and other such rites are not to be adopted from the *Kalpasūtras*; this is the direction [of the argument]. Furthermore, they consider this *Vāmakeśvaratantra* to consist precisely of the pair of four hundred verses known as the *Pūrva-catuḥśatī* and the *Uttara-catuḥśatī*.
This is because the opening and concluding sections display the signs of the commencement and completion of a tantra; however, in the *Tantrasāra* (p.
8), it is stated that the procedure for the consecration of the *cakra* is taught in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*. Furthermore, there are hymns (*stotra*s).

Some [verses] are found under the very name of this Tantra; furthermore, the six hundred verses recorded in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara* and the statements written in the *Lalitārcanacandrikā* and other works also exist under the name of this same Tantra.
Since they are not seen in the *Aṣṭaśatī*, it must be considered where their placement should be. Therefore...
Thus it is stated in the *Ṛjuvimarśinī* out of a sense of dissatisfaction [with other views]:
"The scripture named the venerable *Vāmakeśvara*, a Tantra, is revealed;
in the midst of that scripture lies the *Nityaṣoḍaśikārṇava*."
And in that regard, there are two [works] of four hundred [verses each].
However, in the *Manoramā*, on the occasion of commenting on the verse: "The nine tantras of the sixteen Nityās are complete," it is stated:
The *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*, *Sundarīhṛdaya*, and *Vāmakeśvaratantra* are counted as separate [texts];
however, within this *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, which is indeed the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, there are numerous points whose meaning remains unknown.
This contradicts the natural sense of the exposition. However, the unity of the two preceding and following *Catuḥśatīs* is beyond dispute, owing to the force of their respective titles.
This is because the nyāsas such as *karaśuddhi* mentioned in the former tantra are not mentioned in the latter tantra; therefore, [the reference] extracted from that [former tantra]...

Furthermore, because of the mutual expectancy [of the two texts], as indicated by the fact that the *Mūrtividyā* is not extracted in the *Pūrvatantra*, both *Catuḥśatis* have indeed been commented upon by many ancient scholars; however,
those commentaries are overly prolix in irrelevant places.

In some places they are overly restrictive; in some cases they contradict logic, in others they contradict tradition, in others they contradict the inherent spirit of the original source, in others they omit the root verses,
in others they contradict other tantras, and in others they are defiled by partiality.

Let the connoisseurs discern that this effort to provide a concise commentary— having set aside certain portions and extracted the others with extreme precision, following the very direction indicated therein— is fruitful. Thus concludes the exposition of the four ancillaries (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*).
Now, in this context, there are three forms of the Supreme Goddess to be meditated upon that are suitable for worship:

the gross, the subtle, and the supreme. Among these, the first possesses limbs such as hands and feet, and is accessible to the eyes and the sense of touch of those who have attained perfection through mantra.

Then, [the description] beginning with "the goddess lotus-like, red as the rays of the rising sun" and so forth will be stated; this second [form], consisting of mantra, is suitable for the ears and the faculty of speech of those who possess merit.
(p. 9) With the words "O you whose lotus-face is the singular essence of the glorious Vāgbhava-kūṭa," and so forth,
[is recited] the hymn of secret names (*rahasyanāmasūkta*), which is the root of all mantras and consists of Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī and the rest.

For this very reason, he will state at the end of the fifth chapter: "But when this [state] is established, the Mātṛkā becomes established," and so forth; and in the sixth chapter, with the words beginning "The third is the nature of latent impressions (vāsanā), the consciousness suitable for the minds of the meritorious, which is the form of the Self."

That which is about to be described is the undivided form that transcends these three, beyond speech and mind, and is experienced as the "I" (ahantā) by the liberated ones. Therein, Paramaśiva, desiring to commence the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*, [performs] its obstacle-free...

For the sake of completing the work, and because even the primary [deity]— being of an indivisible nature— is impossible to praise directly due to its transcendence of speech, he performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) consisting of the worship of that [deity] by means of its subtle form, according to the maxim of the "large Arundhatī," beginning with the words "Gaṇeśa, planets, constellations... and so forth.

With twelve verses ending with "I bow to the glorious Tripurā," [the author begins]. Since this hymn, which consists of the worship of the Goddess, is itself a collection of many verses, it is necessary to include another auspicious invocation for the sake of its completion without obstacle; with this intention, first—

The remembrance of Gaṇeśa has been performed. Nor does this lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā), because the word "Gaṇeśa" is not excluded from the twelve verses; thus, it does not apply [to itself]. Indeed, its exclusion from the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*—as opposed to the twelve verses—is precisely what is intended.

Because it is easily stated that the commencement [of the section] begins precisely with the words "The Goddess said," and so forth; for it cannot be said that the commencement of the verse begins precisely with the words "Planets, constellations," and so forth. By this, it is established that the worship of Mahāgaṇapati serves as an auxiliary to the worship of Vidyā by means of the removal of obstacles.
The meaning stated in the Kvalpasūtra is thus echoed:

"I bow to the Goddess Mātṛkā, who consists of mantra, who takes the form of Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, and the zodiac signs, and who is the embodiment of the sacred seats (pīṭhas). (1)
The Gaṇeśas are the fifty-one forms of Vināyaka, beginning with Vighneśvara and ending with Gaṇeśvara. The planets, lunar mansions, and zodiac signs are well known.
The Yoginīs are the seven deities beginning with Ḍākinī. The Pīṭhas—

There are fifty-one [deities] beginning with Kāmarūpa and ending with Icchāchatra; thus, there are one hundred and seven deities. The projection of these very [deities] upon one's own body, known as the "Brief Sixfold Installation" (laghu-ṣoḍhā-nyāsa), which brings about the state of the Supreme Lord, will be described by the Gaṇeśas in the eighth chapter.

From the passage beginning with "The first nyāsa" and ending with "he himself is the Supreme Lord," [it is described as] having the form of such a collection of deities; [referring to] the Goddess in her aspect of worldly manifestation (*vyavahāra-rūpā*). The terms "consisting of mantra" (*mantramayī*) and "abounding in mantra" (*mantrapracurām*) are adjectives qualifying the *mātṛkā*.

(p. 10) This is because Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī herself, whose form consists of the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* in the form of *vaikharī*, constitutes the seven crores of great mantras; and because she also constitutes the worldly and Vedic conventions.
Likewise, Gaṇeśa and the others, as well as the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) and so forth, each consist of a single syllable. Among the planets...

The Sun, however, is the form of the sixteen vowels. Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn are the forms of the five groups of consonants beginning with *ka*. The Moon and Rāhu are the forms of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) and sibilants (*ūṣman*), while the single letter *kṣa* is the form of Ketu. According to the tradition, the letter *la* is already accounted for by the letter *la* itself.
Among the lunar mansions, there is a pair, then one, three, four, one, and then two.
One pair, a pair, one pair, a pair, and a pair, in sequence.
"One pair, three, one, three, one by one, one, a pair,
one, a pair, three, a pair, joined with *bindu* and *visarga*. Thus,
in the sequence beginning with Aśvinī, the letters starting from *a* correspond respectively to "a pair," "one," and so forth.
[This] is to be applied. The meaning is as follows: Aśvinī consists of the two syllables *aṃ* and *āṃ*; Bharaṇī is in the form of the syllable *i*;

Kṛttikā consists of the three syllables *īṃ*, *uṃ*, and *ūṃ*, and so forth. However, the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the visarga (*visarga*), which are vowels, should be joined at the end of the letter *kṣa*. Thus: *laṃ*, *kṣaṃ*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*.

Thus, Revatī is accomplished as the form of four syllables. The Yoginīs, however, are seven, known by the names beginning with *ḍa*, *ra*, *la*, *ka*, *sa*, *ha*, and *ya*. Their essential nature consists of the sixteen vowels, twelve beginning with *ka*, ten beginning with *ḍa*, six beginning with *va*, and four beginning with *va*.
The letter *ha*, the letter *kṣa*, and their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) arise in this manner in sequence. The letter *la* is as before.
Among the heaps (*rāśi*), they are respectively four, three, three, two, two, and two.
Five, five, five, five, and then five.
"In Pisces there are four [letters] beginning with *meru*, and in Virgo five beginning with *śa*.
This means that the Pisces sign consists of the letter *kṣa* (meru) and the four letters beginning with *ya*;
the Virgo sign consists of the five letters beginning with *śa*, along with the *bindu* and *visarga*. The rest is clear.

In this regard, one should not be perplexed by the fact that each [deity] consists of multiple forms, nor by the non-difference even among forms that are mutually contradictory; for the majesty of the deity is beyond ratiocination, and because the *Kalpasūtras* state that the power of mantras is inconceivable.
And it is said in the *Mahābhārata* as well:
"Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable—one should not attempt to apply logic to them. The *Śruti* also says: "This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning."

Therefore, the meaning of the verse is: "I praise Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī, who is non-different from the assembly of deities whose nature consists of this entire phenomenal world. Here, since Mātṛkā alone is the substantive (viśeṣya), the fact that she possesses the qualification of being the sixfold form consisting of the assembly of deities such as Gaṇeśa and others is also an indicative mark (liṅga).

For it is possible for that [to occur] within that very [state] according to the manner already stated. Furthermore, in the following verse, the qualification of Mātṛkā as being the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*), because the *laghu-ṣoḍhā-nyāsa* brings about the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord. As for those deities, the universe (*prapañca*), and the world-spheres (*bhuvana*)...
When it is said that the *mūrtis*, mantras, deities, and *mātṛkās* are to be installed in the *mahāṣoḍhānyāsa*,

since all of them consist of the phonemes of the *mātṛkā*, the terms "Devi," "mantra," and "*mātṛkā*" in the present verse refer to them by way of synecdoche (*upalakṣaṇa*), as indicated by the grammatical gender (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, one should also keep in mind the non-difference [of this deity] from those mentioned in another scriptural passage as "served by the entire host of deities proclaimed in the Mahāṣoḍhā rite. As for what the ancients [say]: "The groups of Rudras here, such as Śrīkaṇṭha and others, who are mentioned in the Śruti as 'the thousands upon thousands of Rudras,' are fifty [in number]."

They explained that [the term] is designated by the word *gaṇeśa*. Others, however, explain that the forty-nine groups of Maruts mentioned in the Śruti as "the Marut-groups with Indra as their eldest" (*indrajyeṣṭhā marudgaṇāḥ*) are understood by the word *gaṇeśa*. Both of these views are to be considered, for in those two Śrutis...

Even though the Rudra-gaṇas and Marut-gaṇas possess reality and authority, there is no evidence for their inclusion here under the term "Gaṇeśa" as it pertains to the present context. Nor can they be included here on the grounds that they consist of the nature of the Mātṛkā vowels beginning with 'A'.

Because the nature of being the *mātṛkā* is common to the groups beginning with Keśava as well as to the groups of Tripuras such as Kāminī and others, it would follow that those [latter] too would be referred to by the term "Gaṇeśa. Nor can it be argued that the word "gaṇa" forms a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word "īśa," which denotes Rudra.

It is established that this [term] refers specifically to Śrīkaṇṭha and the other Gaṇas. However, it should not be argued that if it referred to Vighneśvara and others, it would result in a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, thereby contradicting the *Niṣādasthapati-ādhikaraṇa*;
for the word *gaṇeśa* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) applied to Vighneśvara and the like, according to the principle of the *Rathakāra-ādhikaraṇa*.

For it is appropriate to refer to those very [entities]; moreover, because the term *niṣādasthapati* is etymological (*yaugika*) in both positions, there is a disparity [between it and other terms]. Furthermore, even in the case of words such as *graha*, by the etymologies "they seize" (*gṛhṇanti*) or "they are seized" (*gṛhyante*), they would result in referring only to objects, sense organs, and so forth, and not otherwise.

Even by you who accept that the Sun and others are indeed the primary referents in those [passages], how can another meaning be asserted by disregarding their frequent occurrence in that context and the recognition of them as the deities of the *Laghu-ṣoḍhā*, all on the grounds of arbitrariness?
It is described as a marvel;
moreover, there would be a violation of the natural emphasis on the removal of obstacles to the propitiation of the Goddess.
Even though there are many other removers of obstacles, [the text specifies] that it is only through the propitiation of Gaṇeśa.

Because it is necessary to emphasize that the rule "one should dispel obstacles to the worship of Śrīvidyā" is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), there is a statement in the *Kalpasūtra* to this effect: "One who has received initiation from a true Guru [should perform] the rite of Gāṇanāyakī in order to remove obstacles to the worship of Mahāvidyā."

"One should contemplate the manual" (paddhati). Thus, having worshipped Gaṇapati and thereby shaken off the entire accumulation of obstacles, one should begin the ritual sequence (krama) of the venerable Lalitā, the sole sovereign of the wheel of powers (śakticakra);
this is indicated by the suffix -tvā in the statement of the Kalpasūtra.

This is because, as in the case of "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," the relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin) is clearly understood; furthermore, by stating that the sequence of Gaṇeśa is an auxiliary to the Lalitākrama and by asserting that the Lalitākrama alone possesses the fruit, any suspicion of a reversed relationship between the primary and the subordinate is dispelled.

This is because it is rejected by the principle of "the fruitful and the fruitless," just as in the case of the injunction: "Having performed the Vāravantīya as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman on the Revatī verses, one desiring cattle should sacrifice with this. However, there is this distinction: the worship of Lalitā must be performed throughout one's entire life.

Since it is impossible to perform other forms of worship due to mutual conflict with the duties such as rising during the *brāhmamuhūrta*, one should, for several days prior to the commencement of the *Lalitākrama*, perform recitations (*japa*) according to one's capacity.

The worship of Mahāgaṇapati should be performed only once, just like the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice; for this very reason, in the aforementioned statement, the mention of "one should begin the sequence" (*kramam ārabheta*) is appropriate as referring specifically to the commencement.
Nor does this contradict another statement which says, "In this way, the contemplation of the Śyāmā-krama should always be performed."

It might be argued: "Since the worship of Rājaśyāmalā is also prescribed in the *Lalitākramaprakaraṇa*, it is a constituent part [of the Lalitā worship]; therefore, according to the stated reasoning, how can their combination be justified given the contradiction?
To this it must be said: one who performs the daily service (*nityasaparyā*) in this manner at the very end of the internal section of Śyāmalā—

Since the commencement with the words "having recited," etc., by prescribing the recitation of exactly one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) [times], it necessarily follows that the word "always" (*sadā*) found at the beginning refers merely to that specific duration; therefore, according to the understanding of the sequence of the text, it is more appropriate to perform the worship of Śyāmala before the worship of Lalitā. For this very reason...

For the statement, "It is indeed proper to seek the king's favor through his chief minister," makes it logical that the worship of the chief minister is shown prior to the worship of the king; for here, by the word "hi" (for/indeed), the Blessed Paraśurāma follows common worldly usage.

Since in the world one frequently observes that people follow a king even without approaching his primary minister, it is indicated that the worship of that [minister] may be performed or not; however, when the worship of the king is preceded by the worship of him [the minister], there is an abundance of fruit according to worldly logic.

Just as the position regarding the inclusion of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is established even by Vedic logic, so too the worship of Daṇḍanātha, which is enjoined by the rule "having worshipped Saṅgītamātṛkā, one should duly choose Kolamukhī," is also [accomplished] through the worship of Śyāmālā, provided it is performed for a measure of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).

It should be understood that [the term *gaṇeśa*] is used here as a conceptual construction (*vikalpita*) precisely because it follows the sequence of expansion; for there is no such conceptual construction regarding the worship of Gaṇeśa, since that worship is a mandatory subsidiary (*nityāṅga*) with respect to the commencement of the primary rite.
Therefore, even due to the lack of contradiction in indicating such a necessary subsidiary, the word *gaṇeśa* [is not used here].

The description of Śrīkaṇṭha and others as being supreme is thus justified; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Alternatively, in the *Uttaratantra*, it will be stated in the root text itself that both the primary deity and the root-vidyā each consist of five aspects, beginning with Gaṇeśa (p. 13). And in the verse under discussion:

Since, among the six groups of deities mentioned in the *Laghuṣoḍhā*, only the first five are specifically enumerated separately from the deities of the *pīṭhas*, it is easy to state that [the word] "Devī" (in the phrase *devīṃ*) or "mantramayīm" (in the phrase *mantramayīm*) serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*). In that regard:
In the context of praising a particular deity, it should be explained as follows: "The Mother of the World (Jaganmātṛkā) consists of mantra, meaning she is primarily composed of mantra.
Furthermore, [she is so called] because she is the essence of one hundred and eleven deities.
The state of Gaṇeśa belongs to the Great Goddess.

By means of these six and a half verses, beginning with "The state of Gaṇeśa" and ending with "the one whose nature consists of the [five] groups," [one should understand] the mantra as being fivefold, consisting of Gaṇeśa and the others, according to the method that will be explained.

In the view where she is the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*), she is the Goddess who shines forth. She is the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) who is Gaṇeśa, consisting of the three rows beginning with the unutterable (*akathādi*), and following the sequence beginning with the third.

By these three verses beginning with "ityādibhiḥ" and ending with "rāśitvaṃ cāntyavarjitaiḥ," the meaning is that [the deity] consists of five aspects, such as Gaṇeśa and others, according to the direction that will be explained.
Furthermore, in these two positions, there is no [contradiction] regarding the terms "Gaṇeśa" and so forth.

It must be asked: if the abandonment of the conventional meaning is necessary, what fault has been committed by the interpretation that [the term] refers to Śrīkaṇṭha and others? For there is no defect in abandoning the conventional meaning when it is done in accordance with the aforementioned corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*). This is because the corroborative texts themselves support the interpretation as referring to Śrīkaṇṭha and others.
Because they too do not write [it]. Regarding the phrase "having the form of the *pīṭhas*":

in the case of the Goddess (*devī*), it means that her own nature resides in the *pīṭhas* known as Oḍḍiyāṇa, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa; however, in the case of the Mantra, the meaning should be described through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as "having the form of the *kūṭas*. Alternatively, it may mean that her form resides in the *pīṭha*, which is the Śrīcakra.

Or rather, this is the meaning: thus, there are exactly three meanings that are authoritative. As for what the ancients [said]—that the word *pīṭha* refers to the support of the universe, the word *yoginī* refers to Brāhmī and the other goddesses, the word *gaṇeśa* refers to Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, and the rest is just as it is commonly known.
Having stated that this is one commentary according to the tradition of the *sakīlaka* (with the kila),

and having made the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) that other fivefold commentaries will also be explained according to the tradition of the *niṣkīlaka* (without the kila), [the author] explains this verse with reference to the categories of phoneme (*varṇa*), mantra, consciousness (*saṃvit*), wheel (*cakra*), and abode (*dhāman*).
They explain it in five ways, but all of that is merely a deception of fools. For instance:
will, knowledge, action, and the quiescent—these four;
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā—these four; their two collective unities; thus, there are two pentads.

Since [the two] arise sequentially from the letters *a* and *ha*, the union (*sāmarasya*) of the letters *a* and *ha* constitutes the number one; thus, the number eleven is expressed by the term "Gaṇeśa.
As it has been said: "The letter *a* is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme light, the Great Śiva."
The final letter, Ha, is of the nature of Kalā and is proclaimed as being called Vimarśa (reflective awareness).

In this manner, having established the mere count of the syllables within the verse, the extraction of the syllables (*varṇoddhāra*) is performed as follows: *Gaṇeśa* is the syllable *ha*; *Graha* is the syllable *sa*. In the word *nakṣatra*, the single letter *ka* is intended [as the actual syllable], while the other letters are for the purpose of pronunciation. *Yoginī* is the syllable *la*; *Rāśi* is the syllable *ha*.

In the phrase *rūpiṇīm*, only the letters *re* and *phaṃ* are intended; in this manner, the extraction of the *Hādividyā* is established. The word *devīm* alone is intended [as significant], while everything else is for the purpose of pronunciation; its meaning is "the radiant one. By that—

The extraction of consciousness (*saṃvit*) takes the form of the column of light (*teja-daṇḍa*) situated within the *suṣumṇā*. By the word "Goddess" (*devī*) alone, the triad of lights is indicated; thus, there is the extraction of the three abodes (*dhāma*). By the word "seat" (*pīṭha*) alone, the extraction of the wheels (*cakra*) is indicated; in order to demonstrate everywhere these and other such methods as you have described.
Because it is possible [to assign arbitrary meanings]: since there is no lexicon (kośa) for words such as *gaṇeśa* and others when they follow letters such as *ha*,

one might imagine that any word whatsoever could have any desired meaning— even one that is useless to oneself— since all [such usage] would merely be for the sake of pronunciation and thus the meaning would not be intended (*avivakṣita*).
Because it is utterly devoid of any authoritative basis, even the recording of any random, incoherent statement as being "consensus" therein serves only to delude the ignorant. For this very reason,
the persistent effort to refute such a claim is improper, as its only result would be the unnecessary expansion of the treatise.

Although such [explanations] are seen many times throughout the subsequent [sections], we do not see any such commentary here; for it follows from the logic of the *lokavedādhikaraṇa* that one must conform to the etymological derivation of words and their meanings.

This is because the knowledge of the meaning brings about prosperity (*abhyudaya*). One must observe that even a meaning elevated by the power of scholarship and capable of causing wonder to all learned men may not be such [in reality]; whereas a meaning shown to be laughable is to be disregarded according to the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) principle.

The Kashmiris, however, say that Gaṇeśa is Kālarūpī Vināyaka and that the Yoginīs are Vaśinyā and the others; this is the distinction. In this verse, the praise of the Goddess is promised, and that consists in the description of qualities residing in one who possesses those qualities (guṇin). This applies to the entire Tantra.

Furthermore, because it consists of the expression of qualities, the meaning is also that "I shall expound the Tantra. In this context, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) is indicated by the two words "the Goddess" and "consisting of mantra"; that is to say, the subject matter here is the extraction of the deity and the extraction of the mantra. The purposes (*prayojana*) are found in the subsequent verses.
They will be explained in detail. || 1 ||
I bow to the Great Goddess, the Mother, the Supreme Sovereign,
who brings an end to the turbulent agitation of the surging waves of Time.

The "turbulent surge" (*hallohalo-vega*) of time is its surging motion; its "restlessness" (*lolatva*) is the act of overturning things from below to above; and its "calculation" (*kalanā*) is the binding performed by that [motion]. Alternatively, "turbulent calculation" refers to the connection between preceding and succeeding words; it is so called because it brings about their "subsidence," meaning their destruction.

The traditional commentators [explain as follows]: In reality, that which makes something struck (*hata*) is *hata*. From the word *hata*, with the causative suffix *ṇic*—according to the rule "one who performs that action" (*tatkaroti*) or "one who describes that" (*tadācaṣṭe*)—the suffix *kvip* is applied. That [being] is also *lohala*;
according to Amara, *lohala* means one whose speech is indistinct. This *lohala* is also *ullola*. Now, regarding the waves:
According to Amara, "mahatsu" means "in great waves. By this, the interpretation of *kalanā* as "seizing" is also well-explained;

for since the entire universe is swallowed by Time (*kāla*), the bestowing of the state of being beyond its reach culminates in the nature of Śiva, who transcends Time (*kālātīta*). Therefore, [Śiva]...

The teachers have stated that even the calculation of agent, time, and object occurs solely through the power of the Goddess: "O Mother, for Śambhu who has swallowed the terrible poison, there is no reckoning of time; the root of that is the majesty of Your earrings."
The word *ullola* is used to indicate that even the slap of Time (*kālacapeṭā*) is like that, because it is impossible to turn back a massive wave as it rushes with force upon the ocean;
[this occurs] merely by the wave's onset.

The qualification "it causes [the victim] to be struck" is used because one who is skilled in crossing [a river] does not perceive what is undesirable [until it is too late]. Even if the killer speaks clearly, the means of avoiding that [act] might be conceivable through prior warning;
therefore, to exclude that possibility, the word "iron" (*lohala*) is used. Here, as in the previous verse, there are three types of objects to be qualified. By this—

The term *mahādevī* refers to the *Mahāvidyā*, as indicated by the application [of this term] in the fourth chapter: "Now one should explain the practice for each individual syllable of the Mahādevī. When the three words beginning with *mahādevī* function as a single qualified subject (*viśeṣya*), the other two should be construed as its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). || 2 ||
If a man competes with the Sun, Garuḍa, the Moon, Kāmadeva, Śiva, Agni, and Viṣṇu even when only a single syllable has been mastered, [he is a fool]. (3)
When even a single syllable of that Mātṛkā-vidyā is perfectly mastered,

a person rivals the seven [planets] beginning with the Sun, due to attaining the extraordinary qualities inherent in its perfection. This is because even a single syllable [of the Mātṛkā], as explained in the *Mātṛkā-viveka* and other texts, [possesses such power].
This is because the methods of practice have been stated separately,

and because the practice of each individual syllable within the Vidyā will be explained in the fourth [chapter]. Furthermore, the qualities of the Sun (Ravi) include its excellence of radiance, its nature as the locus of the object of meditation, and its role as the initiator of ritual action.

In the case of Tārkṣya, [the qualities are] his capacity to bear the burden of Viṣṇu, his removal of poison, and his excessive speed; in the case of the Moon, his causing satisfaction to the gods, his reviving all medicinal herbs, and his quality of being delightful; and in the case of Kandarpa, his agitating the mind, his invisibility, and his beauty.

[The attributes] of Śaṅkara are his lordship over all ignorance, his supremacy over the universe, his being the object of service for the entire world, and so forth; those of Anala (Fire) are his residing within the bellies of living beings, his being the carrier of oblations, his being the destroyer of all, and so forth;
those of Viṣṇu are his being the protector of the universe, his being the husband of Lakṣmī, his being the wielder of Māyā, and so forth. Thus, by means of the fruits of these individual parts...

This is a praise of the whole by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) principle. [Objection: But if this is so, then since Śiva and Viṣṇu have been appointed to the governance of the world, it would be improper for their worshippers to obtain the governance of the world as a fruit of their merit (*dharma*).
If it is argued that this contradicts the Sūtra of Vyāsa, "excluding the activity of the world," we say no;

for although those who worship the *vidyās* such as the *Dahara* do not obtain the activity of the world, it is easily attained even by those who worship Tripurasundarī. And this [is stated] regarding her, the venerable Lalitā...
That "the Goddess bestows her own sovereignty" was established by us with supporting arguments in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara* during the commentary on this verse; however, in the *Manoramā*,
it is stated that the meaning of the phrase "in just a single syllable" is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.

The venerable Nāthacaraṇas, however, teach the syllable of Trimūrtīśa as being of that very nature, because it will be explained later that it is the transformation of that [syllable] itself into the form of the Goddess and its dissolution therein. In the context of the Goddess, the meaning is:
"upon the accomplishment of even a single syllable of whichever Goddess, such as Vāgbhava," and so forth.

By the word *mātra* (only/simply), it is suggested that even in the absence of the status of a seed-syllable (*bīja*) due to the lack of the nasal drop (*bindu*) and so forth, [the result still follows]. For this very reason, Satyavacas attained mastery over speech simply by uttering the single syllable *ai*, out of fear;
and [the sage] attained [his goal] simply by uttering the first syllable out of astonishment upon hearing the word "eunuch" (*klība*).
This is well known from the third book of the Devībhāgavata, where it is stated that the name of Sudarśana was Devīprasāda. || 3 ||
I salute the Goddess Mahāśrīsiddhamātṛkā, the Sovereign of All, by whose syllables the three worlds are adorned with the moonlight of the digits of the moon. 4.

At the beginning of creation, it proceeds forth in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.

And so forth. These [four powers] are "sheaths" (*kośa*), meaning they serve as the support or the means of realization, like the sheath of a sword. The term *yasyāḥ sā* (of which she is the sheath) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
thus, the meaning is that Brahman is its essence, being indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). She is the sheath of the four commands (*ājñās*).

Or, it means "that which gives birth to the Vedas. Indeed, both of these are the unique marks (liṅga) of the Supreme Brahman, as established in the two expositions (*varṇaka*) of the *Śāstrayonitva* section. Alternatively, "four commands" refers to the four scriptural traditions (*āmnāya*).

The directions known as east, south, west, and north are mentioned here primarily because they are the most excellent among them. Consequently, by stating that this tantra expounds the essence of the traditional teachings (āmnāya), it follows that this [tantra] is not in conflict with the *Kalpasūtra* which conforms to those established doctrines; therefore, regarding the portions required therein, one should rely on that very [sūtra].
It is implied that this [work] is not for the inclusion of any other tantra; and thus it is recorded at the beginning of the Kalpasūtra that he composed five Āmnāyas,
which constitute the essence of the ultimate truth, through his five mouths, among which this Siddhānta is one.

And so forth. The "four-footed" (*catuṣpāda*) is also an elliptical designation for the *ūrdhvāmnāya*. The meaning is: "I bow to such a Tripurā. Here, because all the Vedāntas have their purport (*tātparya*) in non-dual Brahman, the *āmnāyas* that follow them also [point toward] indivisible bliss.
Brahman alone is the primary subject matter. This has been indicated by the statement that it is the "essence of the sacred tradition" (āmnāya-sāra).

By the term "sheath" (kośa) as well, through wordplay (śleṣa), it is stated that [the deity] is within the five sheaths and transcends the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa). The meaning of the word "Tripurā" is also the same; as it has been said by the learned:

"Because she existed prior to the creation of the three forms (Trimūrti), because she consists of the three Vedas (Trayī), and because she generally fills even the three worlds at the time of dissolution, the name of Ambikā is 'Tripurā'. (p.
23) Thus, it is implied in this hymn that the attributeless Brahman itself is praised by means of its attributes.
For this very reason, it is recited in the *Tantrarāja* following the twelve verses:
"Thus, praise with these twelve verses brings about all accomplishments; for that [praise] is yours, O Goddess, whose form is indivisible."

What more need be said? It is also implied that throughout this entire tantra, Brahman alone—the goal to be reached by the liberated—is introduced as the object of worship by means of meditations on the qualified [Brahman] and so forth.
This very point, indicated in the first verse, is here concluded not by saying "I bow to Tripura," but rather by saying "I praise."

The term "Śrī Tripurā" has been mentioned. Furthermore, the word "I" (ahaṃ) denotes the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), as evidenced by the usage: "The ego is threefold—vaikārika, taijasa, and tāmasa. And that ego-sense is twofold: the higher (para) and the lower (apara).

The other [ego] is that which is expressed by living beings with respect to the body and so forth. The supreme [ego] is the "I-consciousness" (aham-abhimāna) that arises regarding the Supreme Brahman— pertaining to the entirety of the universe at its inception— with respect to the knowledge, will, and effort conducive to the creation of the world consisting of the thirty-six principles.

Furthermore, by merely postulating a relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) based on the fact that Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, has such supreme *ahaṃtā* (I-ness) as its object, that attribute is here designated by the term "Tripurasundarī" and the substrate,
which is non-different from it, by the term "Kāmeśvara. This too [is the case].

This is implied by the use of the word "I" (*ahaṃ*) in grammatical apposition with the word "Tripurā. Otherwise, as in the first verse, the agent would already be obtained by the mere word "I bow" (*naumi*); thus, if it were intended to convey that same meaning here, the word "I" would be redundant. Nor can it be argued [that the word "I" serves another purpose]...
This is the second objection: since *svarādi* is accepted as an *avyaya* (indeclinable) due to its being an *ākṛtigaṇa*, [the suffix] *tal* is elided.
As for usages such as *ahargi pralayaṃ kurvan*, these refer to the word itself—just like the expression *namāṃsi kurmaḥ*—intending the non-difference between the word and its meaning.
Thus it should be noted. || 12 ||

Thus, having described the subject matter, purpose, and so forth of the treatise by way of the opening benediction, [the author proceeds] to exclude other means such as books, etc., in accordance with what is implied by the word "alone" (*eva*) in Vedic passages such as, "To know that, one should approach a guru alone."

To demonstrate the necessity of a teacher, Paramaśiva, though himself non-dual, assumes two forms through the distinction of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness); having accepted the state of the questioner through the aspect of *vimarśa* and the state of the speaker through the aspect of *prakāśa*, he begins to bring down the Tantra.
The Śrīdevī said: Thus it is stated in the Svacchandatantra (p.
24): "Abiding in the roles of both teacher and disciple, Sadāśiva himself [acts]."
"He brought down the Tantra through dialogues consisting of questions and answers.

Here, the augment *āṭ* has not been applied because the rules of the *Āgama-śāstra* are not mandatory. In the *Kalpasūtra* as well, the Lord Paramaśiva-bhaṭṭāraka [taught] all eighteen sciences, beginning with the Śruti...

Having effortlessly composed various philosophical systems (*darśanas*) while assuming their respective states, he was questioned by the Goddess Bhairavī— who consists of pure consciousness and is non-different from his own self— and thus, through his five faces,
he brought forth the five *Āmnāyas*. Therefore, Paramaśiva himself [is the author].

The meaning is that [the Lord] questions His own self through the aspect of reflection (*vimarśa*). Likewise, regarding the phrase "Śrī Bhairava said," the meaning is that He Himself provides the answer to His own self through the aspect of luminosity (*prakāśa*).
As for the past tense indicated by the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix in the present context, it is because that which is to be spoken is eternal. For this very reason:

Although the meaning to be explained in the subsequent chapters of the *Tantrarāja* has already been taught in the preceding chapters, it is indicated here and there by means of words in the past tense (*bhūtārthaka*) alone. However, the state of being non-recent (*anadyatanatva*) is due to its being unconditioned by time, while the state of being beyond perception (*parokṣatva*) is established because it is not within the range of the sense organs.
The traditionalists [hold this view]. This should be applied everywhere in the same manner.
Now, the question of the Goddess is presented in thirteen verses:
"O Blessed One, all mantras have been revealed to me by you."
And there are sixty-four tantras, which are the most excellent among those of the Mothers.
All the mantras number seventy million; they belong to the Mothers, the Śaktis.
They are supreme because they bestow all human goals (puruṣārtha). 13.
Now, with seven and a half [verses], he enumerates the names of the tantras:
Mahāmāyā, Śambara, Yoginījālaśambara, Tattvaśambaraka, and likewise Bhairavāṣṭaka. (14)

In this regard, the *Ṛjuvimaśinī* explains that this refers to two tantras, namely the *Mahāmāyātantra* and the *Śambaratantra*; however, Lakṣmaṇa states that it is a single tantra called the *Mahāmāyāśambara*. In the *Artharatnāvalī*, on the other hand...

Neither of these two has been mentioned. Some have omitted the two verses beginning with "O God, the doctrine of Mahālakṣmī," which are to be cited hereafter; others, however, have accepted them. Nevertheless, for all [these views], it is difficult to justify the attainment of the number sixty-four. In reality, however:
For the sake of attaining that very [state], there are four tantras in the first half of this verse:
the *Tattvaśambaram* as one, and the *Bhairavāṣṭaka* as another; thus, there are six tantras. However, some [maintain]: "Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmatta..."
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas.

41) As for the four corners and the triad of whorls in the form of the left [channel], all of that which will be described in the sixth chapter is accomplished solely by the merging of the two circles of the pericarp.
Many commentators explain this as being intended to convey the number three; however, in reality, it will be stated later in the context of drawing the Śrīcakra by another method:
"One should draw two lotuses on the outside, with eight and sixteen petals respectively."
Then one should draw the line for the qualities (guṇa), and outside of that, a square.

In this statement, by the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word *tataḥ* (from there), it is understood that the three circles are indeed outside the two lotuses; therefore, in accordance with that, it is appropriate to regard even the singular term *pariveṣam* (the surrounding circle) found here as having an unintended meaning (*avivakṣitārthaka*), just as in the case of [the phrase] "he cleanses the cup" (*graṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). And thus...

In the *Vāsanāpaṭala*, by the phrase "the triad of circles," although it refers to the two lotuses through the merging of the pericarp-circles as previously stated, because the *Yāmala* shows the two lotuses are counted separately, the term "triad of circles" refers to [the three circles] excluding the pericarp itself.
It is appropriate to explain that [mandala] as consisting of exactly five circles. Therefore, it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Great Goddess, outside of this, there is a circle resembling the full moon;
O Fish-eyed One, make it beautiful with eight petals."
Likewise, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should draw a sixteen-petaled [lotus].
"Outside of that, O Goddess of the gods, is a triple circle endowed with the Mātṛkās.

Here, by the phrase "outside of that," three circles are clearly stated to exist without the pair of circles for the pericarp. Regarding this, some commentators have said that the meaning of the verse [ends] with the word "outside of that."

Because the method of writing the letters as inscribed upon one's own manuscript is established in other tantras, yet is not mentioned in any of the wheels (*cakra*) of this present tantra; because it would be inconsistent for it to be stated here all of a sudden that it is endowed with the *mātṛkā*; and because it is not found in many manuscripts.
It is determined that [the fifth] has indeed been interpolated; therefore, even according to the Jñānārṇava school, there are only three functions (vṛtti) and not five.
That is incorrect; for if that [fifth] were interpolated, then in the absence of any other statement indicating an external function, it would follow that there are only two functions. Not so.

Since the writing of the syllables (*akṣara*) is not mentioned [in this context], it is logical to conclude that it is an interpolation; for we see its mention in the subsequent text: "A square adorned with the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*) for the sake of attaining success. Nor is there sixty-four [crores] of it, because...
"O Dear One, it shall belong to the Yoginīs," and so forth— because these are statements read in a passage consisting mostly of explanatory eulogies (*arthavāda*),
they possess the status of an *arthavāda* according to the principle of the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*.

One should not be deluded into thinking that its justification is logical; for in the long *soma* sacrifice, even the word "steadfastness" (*dhṛti*)—which is part of a primary injunction found within a context of similar items (*prāyapāṭha*) and is otherwise disconnected—is seen to function as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). This will be shown further on.
Furthermore, since the writing of the phonemes was explicitly mentioned by direct statement on the occasion of describing the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*), [the objection is invalid].

If it is argued that [the sequence] in my manuscript is fabricated because it is written above [the main text], we reply: let it be unfabricated, for in our manuscript it is written right in the middle; thus, this argument amounts to nothing. This is clear in other Tantras such as the *Saṃhitā*.
If it is argued that only three circles are perceived and not that pentad, let it be so; this too is one position according to conceptual distinction.
For this very reason, in the *Viśuddheśvara-tantra* it is said:
"Outside of this, one should draw a single circle provided with eight petals."
Outside of that, there should also be a single circle provided with sixteen petals.
Outside of that, the practitioner should perform one square for the purpose of the boundary;
he should construct the earthly mandala consisting of three [sections] joined with doors.
"One should construct twelve doors in the four directions with a concentrated mind"—such statements as these are thus justified.
However, in the *Kādimata*, it says: "Outside [the central lotus] is an eight-petalled lotus, and outside of that, one with double the number of petals."

By the passage beginning with "vidhāya ṣaḍbhirvṛttaiśca," a set of six circles has been described. However, therein, having erroneously produced a circle, [the author] states "susame caturasrake" and so forth for the purpose of drawing a wheel with fourteen spokes. One—
It is stated in the *Manoramā* that there are six circles (*vṛtta*) including the one already mentioned;

their division is as follows: one boundary circle outside the fourteen-spoked [wheel], then the pericarp circle of the eight-petaled [lotus], and outside the eight petals, the pericarp circle of the sixteen spokes.
"Outside of that are three circles. Others, however, say: outside the fourteen-spoked wheel there is one circle for the boundary (*maryādā-vṛtta*);
attached to that is a circle for the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the eight petals; then a circle within the eight petals for the filaments (*kesara*);
and outside the eight-petaled lotus, a circle for the pericarp of the sixteen petals.

They describe that within the interior of the sixteen petals there is a circle for the filaments (*kesara*), and above the sixteen petals there is a boundary circle (*maryādāvṛtta*). However, in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*,
it is stated that there are exactly six circles, excluding the boundary circle of the fourteen spokes.
With the intent of explaining the meaning of the *Tantrarāja*, seven verses have been stated.
Regarding the circle situated immediately within the fourteen-spoked [mandala], there are three positions:
[the circle] touching all corners, not touching any of the corners, or touching only six while not touching the others.
In this manner, regarding the drawing of the circle (*vṛtta*), when there is a difference of opinion, the arrangement is according to tradition.
As it is said: "Because the Tantras possess many forms, that which is approved by the Guru must be performed.
Now, regarding the drawing of the square enclosure (*bhūgṛha*), there are differences of opinion: a square enclosure is called *caturasra*.

And that [mandala] consists of a single line and is indeed one, because of the singular number used in the phrase "at the base is the city of the earth" (mūle bhūpuram). Furthermore, this is confirmed by the *Jñānārṇava*, which states, "In the quadrangle with four gates, the Yoginīs are the bestowers of success," and by the *Saṃhitā*, which says, "The quadrangles are manifest in the sequence beginning from the West."
According to one view, the "form of the earth" (*bhūbimba*) consists of a single line in each direction,
provided with a single door per side; however, in the *Kādima-tantra*,
it consists of two lines in each direction, with two doors facing east and west, and three lines each on the south and north sides.

This second alternative is described as follows: having marked two points on the corners, one should divide it into four squares using four horizontal and vertical threads; this [mandala] is provided with three lines in each direction and lacks the common features of doorways.

The third [position] is supported by the *Yāmala-tantra*, the *Kalpasūtra*, the *Paddhati* of Śiṅgabhūpāla, the *Prapañcasārasaṃgraha*, the *Vidyāraṇyapaddhati*, and the exposition of the *Saundaryalaharī*; among these, they are favorable to this very view. In them—

Since no specific mention of drawing doors is made [in the root text], they say that the fourth position is that there are three earth-cells (*bhūgṛha*) each with four doors, as stated in the *Viśuddheśvaratantra*;
thus, the earth-cell has twelve doors and three lines. However, in the root text, all these positions are indicated.

By the singular number in the word "caturasram" (quadrangular), the position of a single line is indicated; and by the mention of three lines in the context of the *cakranyāsa* (the ritual placement of the wheel), the position of three lines is indicated—thus two positions are suggested.
Furthermore, since in the section on worship only the powers beginning with *aṇimā* and those beginning with *brāhmī* are mentioned as objects of worship, [one should worship] *aṇimā*.

By the mention of "the western gate" and so forth, as well as "Brahmāṇī at the western gate" and so forth, there is a reiteration of only the western and eastern gates; since the worship of the mudrās situated on the third line is not mentioned, the two-line alternative is also indicated. In reality, however, that which is stated in the *Tantrarāja*...
In the view that there are two doors, one is redundant; since the other three are mutually inclusive, they constitute only a single category, and thus a two-pronged alternative alone is appropriate.
For properties such as squareness and being a reflection reside collectively (*vyāsajjya*) in the whole (*avayavin*) consisting of three lines.

The three lines are indeed the constituent parts (*vṛtti*). For this very reason, the conventional usage found in the *cakranyāsa*—namely, "Obeisance to the first line of the square," "Obeisance to the middle line of the square," and "Obeisance to the final line of the square"—is logically justified; for the meaning of "the first line of the square" and so forth is evident by its own nature.

If a *karmadhāraya* compound were accepted [in the term *caturaśra-āya*], it would result in the improper usage of "to the first square" (*prathama-caturaśrāya*). Furthermore, in the statement from the *Viśuddheśvara*, "One should draw a circle (*maṇḍala*), a triad, joined with doors," the use of the singular number in the word "circle" (*maṇḍalam*) [supports this].
Furthermore, by means of the specific qualification of the three words denoting the three parts, the status of being an "earth-house" (bhūgṛha) is established for the whole (avayavin) alone.
Consequently, in statements such as "four-cornered" and "four-doored," the qualifications of the doors— namely the plural forms "four" and so on—
as well as the singular-terminating words such as "four-cornered," are also justified with reference to the whole.

If plural forms are observed in certain instances, they can indeed be justified by referring to the multiplicity of constituent parts, according to the principle established in the *pāśādhikaraṇa*; thus, what contradiction could there be? By this [the objection is answered].

The statement of Viśuddheśvara, which prescribes twelve doors, has been explained; for [otherwise] there would be a contradiction between the singular form "the earthly mandala" (*pārthivaṃ maṇḍalam*) heard in that very tantra and the state of having twelve doors.

Mutual contradiction can be resolved only by resorting to the relationship of part and whole; otherwise, there would be the contingency of twelve doors in a single line, which is not desired by anyone. Therefore, as stated by Śaṅkarānanda in the *Sundarīmahodaya*:

The expansion [of this teaching] consists of the reconciliation of the statements from the *Jñānārṇava*, *Vāmakeśvara*, and other scriptures composed in the singular number with the statement from the *Viśuddheśvarī* composed in the plural number.

There is no synthesis [of the mantras] according to the principle of synthesizing elements from different recensional branches (śākhāntaropasaṃhāra-nyāya), as in the case of the injunction "one performs the Āgneya oblation four times"; for those statements are unambiguous and thus require no further specification.
A general rule that is unclear should be restricted by means of a specific one.
"But for a rule that is clearly stated, there can be no subsumption by others," according to the *Tantravārtika*. Furthermore:
"Shaving the head and fasting—this is the rule at all sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."

Furthermore, it is accepted by those learned in the Dharmaśāstras that there is no sublation (*upasaṃhāra*) of an injunction formulated in the plural— such as "one should perform the shaving at Prayāga"— by a sentence formulated in the singular.
And because it would be impossible even for Brahman to establish syntactic unity between two mutually contradictory sentences composed of four and twelve words respectively—
this [objection] should not be taken seriously, according to the method already stated.

Since there is no contradiction, it is possible to apply the rule [of option] by subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*), as there would otherwise be the fallacy of an eightfold defect (*aṣṭadoṣa*) inherent in a disjunctive alternative (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the singular and plural forms in the injunctions "at all holy places" (*sarvatīrtheṣu*) and "at Prayāga" (*prayāge*);
