rather, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the two injunctions: "one should perform the purificatory rite again" (*punaḥ saṃskāram ācaret*) and "one should perform the purificatory rites again" (*saṃskārān ācaret punaḥ*).

Because it is desired; and because the *Saubhāgyaratnākara* states in its concluding summary that "having stayed there, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times," and further specifies,
"having muttered this one hundred thousand times."

This is because there is a synthesis of the statement from the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā* with the aforementioned statement from the *Jñānārṇava*. Moreover, it is established by the fact that all specific particulars are subsumed under the general term "all" (*sarva*) contained within the word "all" (*sarva*). For this very reason, [the rule] "one should not harm any living beings" is not [redundant] when compared with "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa."
That there is no such summary [of the subject] has been explained by us at length in the *Mīmāṃsāvādakautūhala*.
Therefore, it is not the case that the singular and plural numbers residing in the four-cornered words refer to having four doors and twelve doors [respectively].
And there is not even a trace of contradiction between the two qualifiers. As for the position that there is an absence of the door in general,

it [cannot be established] merely by the non-mention of a door in works such as the Yāmalas and Kalpasūtras, without either a prohibitive negation (*pratiṣedha*) or an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*) regarding the door.
(p. 45) To assume [this] would be mere rashness,

because there is no obstacle to the sublation of the injunction regarding the twin [shrines] and so forth— which consists merely of four square units— by means of the injunction for the six-doored quadrangle,
just as the injunction for the red turban sublates the injunction for the turban.
We consider this appropriate.

Having thus indicated the drawing of the Śrīcakra, he teaches its nature as consisting of nine wheels through their internal subdivisions in the three and a half verses beginning with "the center is a triangle" (*madhyaṃ tryasram*).
The middle [lotus] is triangular, as well as eight-spoked; there are two ten-spoked [lotuses] and one fourteen-spoked. || 43 ||
Outside of that is an eight-petaled lotus and a sixteen-spoked city of the earth;
it consists entirely of bliss and is supreme, bestowing all spiritual accomplishments.
Furthermore, this other wheel removes all diseases, likewise provides all protection, accomplishes all goals, and bestows all good fortune. || 45 ||
The All-Agitation, the Fulfiller of All Hopes, and the Enchanter of the Three Worlds—thus, through nine [mantras], there shall be ninefold [forms]. (46)
The center is the middle place, the *bindu*. "Fourteen" refers to the fourteen-spoked [wheel].
The three circles (*trivṛtta*) are not counted because each lacks the nature of being a wheel (*cakratva*).
"Consisting entirely of bliss" and so forth refer, in order, to the nine wheels beginning with the *bindu*.
These are the names; their etymologies, however, will become clear in the section on *vāsanā*.
Thus, the meaning is that one wheel (*cakra*) becomes ninefold by means of nine intermediate wheels (*avāntaracakra*). These three and a half verses are not seen in some commentaries.
But they are found in books. || 43 || 44 || 45 || 46 ||
Then, by means of one [verse], he teaches its very threefold nature:
"Thereafter, the great wheel of emanation is the third, while fire is situated in the middle; the second is indeed withdrawal, and that which is the first [is maintenance]. (47)

In this context, the nine [cakras] beginning with Bindu and ending with Bhūgṛha are designated by the terms "first," "second," and "third" after being divided into three groups; this results in the unification of each set of three cakras, according to the maxim that "when no specific distinction is heard, they should be equal."

Likewise, by the same logic, even within a single triple-wheel (*tricakrī*), an internal threefold division is established. Thus, the triad of wheels consisting of the *bindu*, the triangle, and the eight-spoked wheel is called the Wheel of Withdrawal (*saṃhāracakra*).

The two ten-spoked wheels and the fourteen-spoked wheel constitute the Wheel of Maintenance (*sthiticakra*). The two— [the sixteen-spoked and the thirty-two-spoked wheels]—constitute the Wheel of Creation (*sṛṣṭicakra*).
The lotus and the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha) constitute the wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra). Likewise, the subterranean chamber is the emanation of emanation;

the sixteen-spoked [wheel] is the emanation and maintenance (sthiti); the eight-spoked [wheel] is the emanation and withdrawal (saṃhāra); the fourteen-spoked [wheel] is the maintenance of emanation; the outer ten-spoked [wheel] is the maintenance of maintenance; and the inner ten-spoked [wheel]...
The destruction of persistence; the eight-cornered [figure] is the creation of destruction; the triangle is the persistence of destruction;

and the point (bindu) is the destruction of destruction. However, in another tantra, it is stated that the three triads beginning with the point consist respectively of the nature of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire. That too is our own accepted view.
This is intimated by the word *hutāśana* (fire). It should be understood that these designations serve a specific purpose at the time of describing their latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 47 ||
Now, he teaches the great majesty of the worship of the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) through seventeen verses beginning with "evam":
"Thus is this Great Wheel, consisting of the Great Śrī Tripurā."
Moistening, liquefying, agitating, and likewise deluding. || 48 ||
O Great Goddess, it effects attraction, yawning, and likewise paralysis;
it pacifies the affliction of disease and destroys all misconduct. (49)
It is supreme for performing pacification, nourishment, and the attainment of mantras through wealth and health;
it bestows both enjoyment and liberation, and brings about the power of moving through the sky.
O Goddess, it bestows all protection, likewise brings all joy, performs all rites, and accomplishes the purpose of every undertaking. || 51 ||
O Goddess, it brings all under control; O Goddess, it is supreme in piercing through all;
it consists of all principles (tattvas), and likewise, it bestows all knowledge. || 52 ||
It bestows all accomplishments and is the supreme bringer of all welfare;
O Goddess, it consists of all mantras and embodies all the lords of yoga.
O Goddess, it consists of all sacred seats; O Beloved, it consists of all knowledge;
O Goddess, it removes all defects and furthermore consists of all holy fords.
It consists entirely of all vows and likewise consists entirely of all nectar;
it is the pacifier of all suffering and the dispeller of all sorrow. || 55 ||
O Goddess, it causes universal exhilaration, brings about all-encompassing delight, pacifies all misfortune, and wards off all obstacles. || 56 ||
The wheel that bestows all accomplishments and fulfills all hopes;
it is the bow for fierce sorcery and the devourer of the floods of supreme mantras. (57)
It attracts the accomplishments of others and likewise draws in the commands of others;
it causes the paralysis of enemy armies and deludes the higher knowledge of adversaries. || 58 ||
It causes the paralysis of enemy armies and likewise the paralysis of weapons;
it produces great wonder and brings forth great intelligence. || 59 ||
O Goddess, it bestows great eloquence; O Goddess, it grants great happiness;
O Goddess, it effects great subjugation; and it bestows great good fortune. (60)
O Goddess, it removes great fevers, likewise removes great poisons, pacifies great death, and wards off great fears. || 61 ||
O Goddess, it brings about great mastery, it is the city that effects great penetration, it causes the great agitation of the cities, and it bestows great bliss and auspiciousness. || 62 ||
O Goddess, it consists of Mahālakṣmī, bestows great auspiciousness, is endowed with great power, and destroys great sins. || 63 ||
Thus has the power of this wheel been described by me;
it cannot be fully told, O Great Goddess, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.

The phrase "the great wheel is worshipped" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Alternatively, based on the verbal root *maha* meaning "to worship," its meaning is simply "the wheel is to be worshipped. However, the ultimate sense is "the worship of the wheel.
The subsequent portion of the text is an elaboration of the fruits resulting from the ritual action consisting of that worship. [It describes] that which consists of Tripura.
It is the locus of the Goddess’s manifestation;
it produces moisture even for that which is by nature dry, and it effects liquefaction even for that which is by nature solid,
like clarified butter.

*Kṣobhaṇa* generates an intense longing for the desire [for union]. *Mohana* causes the non-appearance of the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. *Jṛmbhaṇa* brings about the expansion of the limited individual soul (*aṇu*). *Stambhana* renders one motionless.
It effects all types of possession (*āveśa*), being the generator of the *āṇava*, *śākta*, and *śāmbhava* forms of possession.
And its characteristics are stated in the Mādhavīvijaya-tantra:

"That immersion (*samāveśa*) which occurs through the recitation (*uccāra*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), the phonemes (*varṇa*), and the mental construction of the locations (*sthāna-prakalpanā*), is called *āṇava* by the wise."
One who, contemplating an object with the mind alone, free from vocal utterance,
attains a state of immersion— that is here designated as the Śākta.
(As stated on p. 48: "That immersion (*āveśa*) which arises for one who is thinking of nothing at all, having been awakened by the Guru, is declared to be *Śāmbhava*.
[The term] *vedha* means piercing; it is that which effects [this] piercing, which colors [the soul] by cutting through all its constituent parts.

It bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*) and grants the powers such as *maṇi* and the rest. It consists entirely of nectar and brings about the fivefold liberation; some say that "death" (*mṛta*) refers to the undesirable, and it is the warder-off of that.
It causes universal intoxication (*unmāda*), producing mental disturbances born from possession by spirits and the like. It bestows all accomplishments.

The term "wheel" (*cakra*) is, however, a designation for the triangular wheel (*trikoṇacakra*), due to its grammatical coreferentiality with the word "wheel" and because it occurs in a context primarily concerned with fulfilling all desires. Its fruit, moreover,
is the praise of the whole by means of its parts, just as in the case of [the praise of] the sacrificial cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth.

Regarding the twelve-pot-sherd [offering]: by that, there is no room for the suspicion of redundancy with the previously mentioned qualification. It causes the paralysis of enemy armies and brings about the futility of machines constructed by enemies; it is a great performer of powerful subjugation (*vaśya*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that which takes [it] from that [state] necessarily. Therefore, there is no tautology.
It effects a great piercing (*mahāvedha*), even shattering the ageless;
it causes a great agitation of the city (*mahāpurakṣobha*), agitating even Vaikuṇṭha and other realms. The rest is clear. Here—
The injunction matures as follows: "One should bring about these fruits through the worship of the Wheel-King.

Nor does a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) arise from the multiplicity of the results to be brought about, because there is no such split here; for by means of the single word "accomplisher of all effects" (*sarvakāryārthasādhaka*), all the fruits are stated together. As for the words "moistening" (*kledana*) and so forth, however—
Since these [passages] consist of explanations of the meaning of the word "all," they are not purposeless; for it is accepted that the word "all" in the sentence,
"The Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed] for the sake of all desires," serves to explain that very word,
just as the supplementary passage, "Indeed, other sacrificial rites are undertaken for the sake of specific desires," does likewise.
Because the division of sentences has been refuted by the experts in the Tantras. 48 || 49 || 50 || 51 || 52 || 53 || 54 || 55 ||
Now, he teaches the practice of the Śrīcakra by means of another method, an easy path, through seventeen verses beginning with "atha ataḥ":
"Next, therefore, I shall explain the Tripurā-cakra in another way."
For that purpose, O Goddess, one should prepare an excellent mandala measuring three cubits.
With the third [part], a pericarp marked with a wheel should be made for this;
with the second, two lotuses; and the remainder, a square.

(p. 49) Now, immediately following this: because the previously mentioned method is difficult to comprehend, [the author proceeds] otherwise, that is, by way of a distinction from the previously mentioned method. Regarding the term "three cubits" (*trihasta*), the word *hasta* here denotes twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); such a number of parts—

The word "mātra" (measure) is an illustration; therefore, the meaning is that one should take possession of a level ground portion in the shape of a square, consisting of seventy-two equal parts, which constitutes the best of mandalas. By the third part of this mandala...
The pericarp should be marked with a wheel having fourteen spokes.
Having placed the tip of a compass at the center, one should then produce a circle for the pericarp by drawing a line twelve finger-breadths away and rotating it.

Therefore, by excluding one cubit each from the upper and lower portions, there is a pericarp (*karṇikā*) measuring one cubit in the middle portion; this is the third part. Then, taking twelve finger-breadths above the pericarp and twelve finger-breadths below it, making a total of...

With the hand that has been formed, one should fashion an eight-petalled and a sixteen-petalled lotus. And therein, according to the maxim "it should be equal because it is not heard otherwise," the eight-petalled lotus is [drawn] on a ground-space of six-six (twelve) finger-breadths, which is touched above and below by the pericarp and is immediately adjacent to it.
On that same extent of ground touched by both parts, there is a sixteen-petaled [lotus];

this is the second part. From the remainder—the first hand that was left over—a square must be made on the twelve-finger portion of ground attached to the upper and lower parts of the sixteen-spoked [circle].
The form of the earth arises. Therein, according to the principle that "it should be equal," there is the third line of the square at four finger-breadths on all sides;
immediately adjacent to that, at four finger-breadths, is the second line; and at four finger-breadths on the outermost edge is the [line] of the earth-dwelling (*bhūgṛha*).

The first line: where a square consisting of three combined parts occurs, that is this first section. Here, by not saying "the first square" but rather using the expression "from the remainder," it is indicated that the drawing of the three circles must be at the very end, specifically within the middle of the first section.

Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of the second part," the meaning follows from the natural sense of the text: once the drawing of the circle of qualities (*guṇavṛtta*) has been completed, whatever remains there is precisely where the three squares are to be drawn according to their respective divisions.
Here, starting from the outer portion and proceeding inward until the inner portion, it is done in sequence.

By means of the first, second, and third words [of the mantra], because the lines forming the parts of the *bhūgṛha* (the square enclosure) are also designated during the ritual placement (*cakranyāsa*) according to this very sequence, he has indicated that this alone is the primary order for the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) and so forth; however, in another Tantra, regarding the mandala—
Even though there is a division into seventy-two parts, an intermediate subdivision is perceived by another method:
on a ground area of forty-five finger-breadths (aṅgula), there is the central pericarp;
outside of that, measuring four and a half finger-breadths each separately for above and below, [making] eight and a half finger-breadths in total.

Within [the circle] nine finger-breadths [in diameter], there is an eight-petalled [lotus]. Outside of that, at intervals of four finger-breadths each, there is a sixteen-spoked [wheel] measuring eight finger-breadths; the remainder is for the earth-mansion (bhūgṛha). This very method is followed in the *Prapañcasārasaṃgraha*. || 65 || 66 ||
(p. 50) Now, with two and a half verses, he arranges eight divisions within the circle of the pericarp (karṇikā):

"Having first laid down the Brahma-thread from the center of the pericarp’s circumference, one should lay down a thread extending south to north; then, seven threads situated therein [should be laid]. (67)

Having placed a single thread from east to west across the middle of the square, one should draw a line; that is called the Brahma-thread (*brahmasūtra*). Its purpose, however, is [to mark] the corners of Śakti in the west and the corners of Vahni in the east.
The sequence is established by determining the locations. "Yāmyā" is the southern direction; "saumyā" is the northern.

The result is that one should draw seven horizontal lines across the middle of that circle. This being so, there is one part exceeding the space of the pericarp (karṇikā) to the east of the first line.
To the west of the seventh line, there is another section extending as far as the edge of the pericarp (karṇikā).

There are six sections formed by the junctions of the seven lines, thus resulting in eight paths (vīthīs). According to the principle that these should be equal, each of them becomes three finger-breadths (aṅgulas) wide.
In another tantra, however, it is stated that although the circle of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) measures forty-five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
one should divide that space again into forty-eight parts and draw nine lines within them. It is shown that the *Devīstuti* is the *Omaṅgāvallīstuti*.

In this system, numbers are indicated by the letters of the *ka*, *ṭa*, *pa*, and *ya* groups, together with the final letters of each group; however, the letter *ña* (and its substitute *ṇa*) should be known as zero, as should a vowel when it is uttered alone.
Thus, by the well-known technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) of Vararuci, the syllables beginning with *devī* [are used]. By that word *devī*, forty-eight parts (*aṃśa*) are expressed.
Among those, they indicate the measurement of the ten divisions produced by the nine horizontal lines.

The ten syllables beginning with *stutoma* [constitute the first part]. The meaning is that there are ten sections of the path (*vīthyaṃśa*) according to the sequence of the eastern directions: six, six, five, three, three, four, three, six, six, and six.
In this tantra as well, when a circle of one cubit (*hastamātra*) is divided into forty-eight parts...
In this way, each individual part becomes half a finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgula*) in measure.

Such six parts occur in the first and second *vīthīs*, as well as in the eight and the following three; thus, regarding that extent, the agreement with other tantras is quite clear. There is also agreement regarding the remaining portion.
It will become clear from the root [text]. || 67 ||
Then one should remove the *tūrya* thread; the middle portion shall consist of two parts.
The third and fifth [portions] are eight and sixteen parts respectively, turned by two parts each. (68)

By that measurement, there are exactly seven paths (*vīthi*) in the tantras; one should omit—that is, erase—the fourth line. By that, exactly seven paths are produced. However, among them, the fourth path is double the size in comparison to the other paths.

He says "by two parts" [to explain] how this occurs; the meaning is that one middle section consists of two parts, which amounts to a fourth path (*vīthi*) of six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). This is an elliptical expression for the partial erasure of the other lines. In another tantra:
The middle portion between the third and fifth lines is called the Gaṅgāvallī; while it was previously stated to consist of thirteen parts, here it consists of twelve parts.
Therefore, he teaches the lack of contradiction in this matter by means of the expansion of the middle portion.

Regarding "the third and fifth": having divided the third row into eight parts consisting of three *nāgas* (twelve *yavas*) each, and the fifth row into sixteen parts consisting of one and a half *bhūpas* (one and a half *yavas*) each.

Having divided [the width] into eight parts, one part is [one-sixteenth]; thus, one should make these two parts diminished by two portions. One should decrease the third row by its own eighth part, and one should decrease the fifth row by its own sixteenth part; this is the final meaning. || 68 ||

The reduction of the third lane by its own eighth part can be conceived in two ways: by shifting the second thread eastward and by shifting the third thread westward; likewise, the reduction of the fifth lane is also twofold.

He states, "by that measure," that the second alternative alone should be followed. That which was removed from the third path—namely, the fifth path—is four and a half *yavas*; thus, by a measure consisting of four and a half *yavas*, the middle portion, which consists of six *aṅgulas*, [is established].

The meaning is that one should increase it once again; that is to say, one should shift [the lines] eastward and westward along the third and fifth lines. Among the forty-eight divisions associated with the circle of the pericarp (karṇikā)—
In another tantra, the middle section consists of thirteen parts; here, however, it consists of thirteen parts plus half a *yava*, so that the difference is very slight.
In that other tantra, the reduction by one part occurs specifically in the third path (*vīthī*); but in this tantra, [it applies] as follows:
The difference— namely, that there is a deficiency when the third and fifth rows are combined—

is not a fault, as it arises from the distinction between different *tantras*. As for the fact that two parts each are treated separately within the eight parts situated in the third row and the sixteen parts situated in the fifth row...
The interpretation that one should "make it deficient" is disregarded because it results in numerous contradictions with other tantras. Here, this should be understood:
having divided the first sūtra into forty-eight parts, in both of those sections...
One should erase six parts of it by erasing three parts each individually;
the same applies to the seventh line as well. On both sides of the second line, one should erase ten parts, that is, five parts on each side. On the sixth line, however—
One should erase eight parts, namely four parts from each of the two [sides] at the corners. As it has been said:
"In the first, second, sixth, and seventh [sections], one should erase them in due order; however, one should not erase the three and five at the end of the *guṇa* and *bhoga*."
(52) It is well explained that "this very meaning [of the center] would be the middle portion (madhyāṃśa), consisting of two parts," as stated by [the author of the] *Caraṇa*. Furthermore,

one should omit the portion between the lines situated at the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) according to the division known as the "enjoyment of qualities" (*guṇabhoga*) mentioned in other tantras.
It should be understood that the word *syāt* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "somewhat" or "in a restricted sense";

for it is to be observed that since the state of having two parts in the middle section is already established by implication through the omission of the fourth thread (*tūryasūtra*), its explicit mention is not necessary.
At the end of the third, the second, and the first sūtra. || 69 ||
Then one should extend two pairs of threads downward from below,
meeting at the seventh thread on the ground and at the station of Brahmā.
Thus, among the seven lines, starting from the two end portions at the extremities of the third line— which touch the circle of the pericarp—
one should extend two lines toward the western direction as far as the earth.

It should be positioned lower and lower, in accordance with the triangle of the *śakti*. That which is called the "earth" (*bhauma*) is the circle surrounding the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Likewise, there is a second line that does not touch the pericarp and has five-fifths (five parts each) erased on both sides.
Starting from its two ends, one should draw two lines toward the western direction, extending as far as the middle portion of the seventh thread. Then,
starting from the two ends of that first thread— which does not touch the pericarp and has three parts erased on both sides—

In the western direction, one should draw two lines below the point where the fourth line has been wiped away, such that they meet at the Brahma-line (the north-south axis). This corner lies slightly more than three barley-corns to the east of the central portion of the fifth line.

It should be understood that [the word *anta*] means "falling down. Others, however, claim that when the word *anta* is construed with the phrase "of the third," it refers to the "end" (*prānta*), whereas when it is construed with the second and subsequent [lines], it refers to the "proximity" (*samīpa*).
This is incorrect; for previously, the first line and so forth...

Because, according to our own view, it is impossible to abandon the principle of uniformity—which is established by taking the root meaning [of the suffix] as having a marginal sense everywhere through the process of "root-climbing" (*mūlārūḍhīkaraṇa*)—as found in the case of *maṃśatomaṛjana*. || 69 || 70 ||

Thus, having generated the triad of powers by means of the first three sūtras, he generates the triad of fires by means of the latter one with the words "up to the fifth" (āpañcamāt); that is, by means of two [sūtras],
he should lead the three situated below up to the end of the fifth.
It rests upon the first syllable of the word *bhauma* and upon the third.
And two other threads; thus there are six triangles.
O Goddess of the Gods, the fourteen-spoked and the ten-spoked [mandalas] are accomplished here. (72)

p. 53) Just as two side-lines are drawn downward from the three ends of the eastern horizontal lines, so too one should draw another two lines each from the ends of the three horizontal lines situated below the fifth row, leading them upward. Then, that which is the sixth—
The thread, not touching the *karṇikā* and with four parts smoothed out on both sides,
should have its two end-lines drawn from the ends of that [thread] and joined at the middle point of the first transverse thread in the east. Then, as for the seventh...
The cord, divided into three parts on both sides, should be pulled with its two ends to draw two lines;
these should be joined at the middle point of the third transverse cord in the eastern direction. In this manner, six pairs of side-lines are formed. In reality, they thus become triangles.

The reading "ṣaḍitya" is indeed correct as stated in the *Ṛjuvimarśinī*. In this manner, by means of the triad of powers (*śaktitraya*) and the triad of fires (*vahnitraya*), two wheels arise, known as the "Mantra" and the "Outer Ten-Spoked" wheels. (71–72)
Then, with two [verses], he describes the inner nine-spoked [lotus]:
"From the second and sixth [lines] from the central axis, on both sides of the Brahma-thread, two pairs of lines should be drawn, following the sequence of downward and upward. (73)
Thereafter, one should extend a pair of threads joined at that point;
O Goddess, this third wheel is thus established as having ten spokes.

Since two lines have already been drawn downward from the two ends of the second sūtra, it is impossible to begin new lines from those points again; therefore, the middle portion alone is implied. Consequently, [the two lines] start from the middle portion of the second sūtra and extend downward.

Two lines should be drawn facing the southwest (the direction of the Rākṣasa) and northwest (the direction of Vāyu). Regarding their limit, he says "of the Brahma-sūtra": this means that they have as their limit the two sides—that is, the two lateral parts—of the Brahma-sūtra which extends from east to west. Now, regarding the three Śaktis already drawn:
That which is the middle power refers to the extent of the two side-lines; likewise,

because the two lines have been drawn upwards from the two ends of the sixth sūtra, two lines should be drawn starting precisely from their middle portion and directed toward the northeast (Īśa) and southeast (Agni) corners.

One should draw [the lines]. As for the limit of those two, it is precisely on the two sides of that middle fire among the three fires currently drawn. To indicate these two limits simultaneously, it is stated as "on the two sides of the Brahma-thread. As for the *ṛk-ava-stu*, it belongs to the second thread.

And they explain that because the middle portion of the sixth sūtra is touched by the Brahma-sūtra, the mention of "on both sides of it" (*tatpārśvayoḥ*)— by means of this elliptical expression (*tantra*)—
indicates the location specifically for the south-eastern corner-śakti and the western corner. Thus...
Having laid down two pairs of threads, immediately thereafter, one should extend and draw a pair of transverse threads across the pair of threads;
[the second thread] should begin from the center and touch the tips of the lines on both sides of the fire-altar.
(p. 54) Having drawn a horizontal line (*tiryaksūtra*) such that it extends over a distance measuring three *yavas* above the fifth line, one should establish the fire (*vahni*).
[This line] begins from the center of the sixth line and touches the tips of the two side-lines of the power (*śakti*).

Having drawn a horizontal line such that it extends across a space measuring three *yavas* below the third sūtra, one should thereby accomplish the *śakti*; this is the intended meaning. When this has been done, although only a hexagon results, there are nevertheless four [triangles] in the four intermediate directions (*vidik*) of that hexagon.
The three triangles were previously only half-formed; they became complete solely through the side-lines of the hexagon.
With this intention, it is stated that the third wheel, the inner ten-spoked one (*antardaśāra*), is perfectly accomplished in relation to the eight-spoked one (*manvasra*). || 73 || 74 ||
Now, regarding the eight-petaled and three-cornered wheels, he says with two verses:
From the fifth line from the center, one should lead two other lines upward and downward, reaching as far as the two vital points (*marman*) of the triangle situated in the middle. (75)
One should lay down the third thread so that it intersects those two;
likewise, the fourth is the eight-spoked [mandala], and the fifth is the central womb.

Starting from the middle portion of the fifth sūtra, one should draw two lines facing the northeast and southeast. Just as in expressions such as "falling from a tree" or "falling from the top," there is the status of an ablative (*apādāna*) even for the repetition of an action; likewise, when there is no repetition, it applies to that which is related to it, just as in the case of the word "tree."

[This refers to] *lakṣaṇā*. He states the limit of those two with the word "above" (*ūrdhva*). By the words "upward" and "downward," the hexagon currently being drawn is denoted. That triangle situated in its center, which is the form of the first *śakti*, [is defined by] the two side-lines.
Due to the connection with the two side-lines of the first fire, there are two junctions;

furthermore, due to their conjunction with the two side-lines of the second fire and also with the line denoting the third power, there are two vital points (*marmas*). The region immediately below those two such vital points—

It is indicated by way of secondary implication (lakṣaṇā). The meaning is that one should draw [the line] up to that limit. In reality, however, it is the junction itself that is indicated by the term "marmapada" (vital point), because it is precisely that which will become a vital point in the future; this is logical. Then, a thread [should be drawn] in such a way that it connects those two side-lines with one another.
One should draw the horizontal line; and that becomes the third with respect to the two side lines.
This being so, when counting starting from the fourteen-spoked [wheel], there is the fourth wheel consisting of eight corners (vasukoṇa) and the fifth consisting of the central womb (madhyayoni).
The word "is accomplished" (sidhyati) is to be construed by being drawn down [from the subsequent verse]. || 75 || 76 ||
Thus, O Goddess of gods, the entire enchanting wheel is accomplished;
its fivefold power [is established] through emanation, and the four fires through dissolution.
(p. 55) The arising of the *cakra* occurs through the conjunction of the five powers (*pañcaśakti*) and the four fires (*caturvahnī*).
Everything is contained within the pericarp (*karṇikā*), beginning with the fourteen-spoked wheel and ending with the point (*bindu*).
This is because [the *cakra*] is already established at the very moment the circle of the pericarp is fashioned by the stalk (*karkāṭaka*) of the point.
Alternatively, the bindu is joined to the triangle; the eight-petalled lotus is in the eight-spoked [wheel];
the sixteen-spoked [wheel] is in the two ten-spoked [wheels]; and the earth-house is in the world-spoked [wheel].

According to the method stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, with the intention that the four wheels (*cakras*) are included within the five wheels, there is the designation "all wheels" (*sarvacakra*) for just this many. By this,
the designations in the root text as the second and third enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) for the outer and inner ten-spoked wheels [are explained].

The two [groups] meet as they are about to be performed. According to some, the word "all" (sarva) excludes only what is deficient and not what is additional. Facing toward oneself is *sṛṣṭi*, with such a tip, being the fivefold power (*śaktipañcaka*); facing away from oneself is *lapa*, with such a tip, being the fourfold fire (*vahnicatuṣṭaya*). || 77 ||
Thus, through the correct union of the nine [deities] in the manner described, the arising of the wheel occurs.
Therein, O Goddess, there is one group of eight, two decagons, and fourteen [triangles]. (78)
O Maheśvarī, there are fourteen, ten, two, eight, and one [sites] respectively,
according to the sequence of the yoga of emanation and withdrawal, which are the locations of the Śaktis.
These reside in the wheel of Tripurā, and through the awakening of which one becomes Bhairava.
By the words "one" and so forth, there is a counting of forty-three triangles according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*);
however, the phrase "fourteen" and so forth follows the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). The triangles are the locations of the powers (*śaktisthāna*). As for that which...
In the *Saundaryalaharī*,

the enumeration beginning with "fourty-four, eight, petals, digits, three circles," and so forth, is intended to include the *bindu* (the dot). Alternatively, the reading there may simply be "forty-three."
Thus, there is no contradiction. || 78 || 79 ||
Through the awakening of this wheel, even the practitioner becomes Bhairava, who is none other than Paramaśiva.
Regarding the omission of the *bindu* by explicit verbal statement in both these types of wheel-extractions (*cakroddhāra*),
it is because in certain specific rites for desired ends (*kāmyaprayoga*), either the complete wheel or merely the nine-yoni wheel is required.

The application (viniyoga) will be explained in the second and fourth chapters; in those cases, whether there is an injunction for a portion to be written or a portion to be meditated upon in the center,
[the term is used] for the sake of presenting that which is devoid of the bindu, whereas if such an injunction is absent, the bindu is obtained by implication.
Because the all-empty itself has the form of the *bindu*, one should draw two lotuses outside, with eight and sixteen petals respectively. (80)
Then one should draw the line of qualities (guṇavṛtta), and outside of that, a square;
provided with four gates, thus shall be the supreme wheel. (81)
On the outer middle third, on a ground area of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) on each side; then, on the second part, which measures one cubit (*hasta*), on the appropriate side all around;
and outside that, beyond the three circles, a small forest [or similar feature].

On a ground area of eleven fingers; this being so, the meaning is that, compared to the previously mentioned method beginning with "power by power," the resulting *cakra* is superior and easy to draw. [This refers to] whatever the numerical value of the area (kṣetraphala) of the central pericarp-circle may be.

From that [total], having subtracted the numerical value of the area of the ground occupied by the forty-three triangles— ranging from a barley-corn (*yava*) up to an atom (*paramāṇu*)— the remainder, when divided by forty-three, is that which...
The meaning is that once the number has been obtained, it is measured by that many barley-corns and so forth;
for the first power’s manifestation is achievable only by the foremost among the most skillful calculators, as the other methods are difficult to master. And these are seventeen.
In some manuscript these verses are not seen, while in others they are seen. 80.

Having thus taught the extraction of the wheel (*cakroddhāra*), he teaches the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) by means of forty-four verses beginning with "Established here" (*saṃsthitātra*) and ending with "the subjugator of the three worlds" (*trailokyavaśakāriṇī*), as an introduction to the worship (*pūjā*) that is about to be described.
The Great Tripurasundarī is established here within this great wheel;
listen, O Goddess, how she is worshipped here by the most excellent practitioners.

For it is the established rule that the presence of Śiva’s splendor (*śivatejas*) in a *bāṇaliṅga* and the like is perpetual, whereas in an earthen *liṅga* (*pārthivaliṅga*) and the like, it lasts only for the duration of the worship. However, in the present context, the term "here" (*atra*) is mentioned twice to indicate that both cases apply. By this—

The presence of the Goddess on earth is perpetual when [the wheel] is fashioned from gold and other such materials, but it lasts only for as long as the worship continues when it is drawn upon the ground. Thus, although it will be stated later that "one should first draw the wheel," this implies that the worship is not performed there [on the drawing], but rather on one made of gold and so forth.

It should be understood that even though differences in time for the presence [of the deity] due to the distinction between supports such as gold and so forth are observed in other tantras, they are indeed permitted. By this, it is shown that the Great King of Mandalas (Mahācakrarāja) is to be drawn with vermilion and saffron.
Or, having caused it to be engraved with gold, silver, the five metals, gems, crystal, and so forth, the Kalpasūtra is applicable. || 82 ||
Therein, he first extracts the mantras of the eight goddesses of speech, beginning with Vaśinī:
"O Goddess, by means of the sequential order of the classes [of consonants], the first class is joined with the eight deities;
therein, O Goddess, the first class (the *avarga*) has Vaśinī as its presiding deity. (83)

(57) It is connected with the aforementioned group of eight speech-deities, such as Vaśinī and the rest, which are characterized by their sequential association with the classes [of consonants] beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*; this is to be construed with what precedes. The *a*-class consists of the sixteen vowels, each accompanied by a nasal drop (*bindu*); without the addition of the *bindu*, [the mantra would be incomplete].
Because it would be illogical for it to be a seed-syllable (*bīja*). For this very reason, in the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* of the pure [vowels], each is joined with a single *bindu*;

however, in the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* with *bindus*, each is joined with two *bindus*. This is a tradition to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru. Likewise, hereafter, even when only the *kavarga* and other consonant groups are indicated, they should be understood as including the *bindu*.

For this very reason, in the section on the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Vaśinī and the others, the Kalpasūtra states: "In all cases, there is the addition of the bindu to the groups [of consonants]. Even in the extraction of the seed-syllables such as Vāgbhava and Pāśacāpa which are about to be performed, the addition of the bindu should be understood in exactly the same way. || 83 ||
This guttural group (ka-varga) is devoted to that [Śakti], and Kāmeśvarī resides therein;
Modinī is situated in the palatal group (ca-varga), while Vimalā is remembered as being in the retroflex group (ṭa-varga).
Aruṇā resides in the *tavarga* (the dental class), while Jayinī likewise resides in the *pavarga* (the labial class).
Sarveśvarī resides in the *yavarga* (the palatal class), and Kaulinī resides in the *śavarga* (the sibilants). || 85 ||
Indeed, these eight deities alone, when properly worshipped within the eight groups, quickly bring the entire world under the control of a person. (86)
The five groups beginning with *ka* consist of five letters each; the *ya*-group consists of four letters;

and the *śa*-group consists of six letters. For this very reason, the *Kalpasūtra*’s statement that "the four beginning with *ya* and the six beginning with *śa*" is appropriate. This applies to both the *ya*-group and the *ṣa*-group as well.
Some, however, maintain that [the goddess] consists of five times five colors;

this view should be disregarded because it contradicts the *Arṇavasaṃhitā* and other tantras, as well as many treatises such as the *Mahodadhi*. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the subsequent text which states, "The goddess is the fifth of the Kaulinīs."
This will be refuted in that very same [section]. || 84 || 85 || 86 ||
Now, he extracts the uncommon seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Vaśinī and the others in sequence:
"One should extract the letter *ra* first; below that, the final letter of *kuṭilā* (the letter *la*);
and that [letter] should be joined with the sixth vowel residing in the seed-syllable of the earth (the letter *la*). (87)
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause it to be enriched above with a crescent moon and a bindu;
this is the seed-syllable of Vaśinī, which resides in the mouths of the Yoginīs. (88)
First is the letter *repha* (the sound *ra*), and then the "end of the crooked" (*kuṭilāntaka*). "Crooked" (*kuṭila*) refers to the second letter of the labial class (*pavarga*), the letter *pha*.
This is confirmed by the *Mātṛkākośa*, which states: "The crest-bearing [letter] is *pha*; the crooked is *dhūmrā*; Janārdana is on the left side.
At the end of that [is the following].

The letter *va* exists; the suffix *kan* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). Although it was previously stated [in the commentary] that "what has been described below will be explained above," and so forth, the words "above" (*ūrdhva*) and "below" (*adhas*) are well known for denoting what is to be uttered subsequently and what was uttered previously, respectively.
Nevertheless, in the present context, the word "below" (*adhas*) does not refer to that which is uttered first; for that would contradict other tantras.

Rather, since it is established by the tradition of writing (*lipi-sampradāya*) that the second letter is written below the first letter, it refers exclusively to that which is uttered later. Furthermore, this applies to both the letter *ra* and the letter *ba*.

The earth-syllable resides in the letter *pṛthvī*. Although the aggregate *laṃ* constitutes the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of earth, in this context, according to tradition, only the consonant in the form of the letter *la* is to be taken. By the phrase "situated therein" (*tatstham*), the writing of the letter *la* beneath the letter *ba* is indicated. *Lo* means flesh.

According to the lexicon, *pūtanā*, *pṛthvī*, *mādhavī*, and *śakranāmaka* [are synonyms for the earth element]. From that [comes] the sixth vowel, the letter *ū*. Following that is the *bindu*, which is the *anusvāra*. After that is the *ardhacandra*, which is the *nāda*.
The definition of the *ardhacandra* will be explained in the sixth chapter. For here—

Regarding the transcription of the syllable accompanied by *nāda* and *bindu*, the tradition of script dictates that one should draw a crescent moon (*ardhendu*) at the head of the syllable and write the *bindu* above it. With this intention, the mention of *bindu* and *ardhendu* in reverse order occurs in the root text; for this very reason, the word "above" (*ūrdhva*) refers to what is to be articulated subsequently.

Even if it were possible [to interpret it otherwise], it must be explained as referring specifically to the upper portion of the *akṣara*. For this very reason, he will clearly state in the extraction of the seed-syllable of Modinī: "surmounted by the head of the half-moon and adorned above with the *bindu*"; or else, it means "the *bindu* following the half-moon," using a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī*).

[This is] a compound. In reality, however, when the term *avanibījastha* (situated in the seed-syllable of the earth) prescribes a collection consisting of the letter *la*, the vowel *ā*, the bindu, and the nāda, this [sūtra] serves merely as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the bindu and the nāda, since the latter portion [the *ā*] has been set aside by the rule prescribing the sixth vowel (*ū*).

The phrase "it is performed" (*kriyate*) indicates that the purpose of this re-enactment is solely for that which has already been established, and not even with respect to the sequence; thus, there is no fault. Consequently, by means of the *repha* (r), *ba* (b), *la* (l), *ukāra* (u), *anusvāra* (ṃ), and *nāda* (ḥ) joined together in succession, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Vaśinī, consisting of the form *rb-lūṃ*, comes into being. This very [seed-syllable]...
The word *vaśinī*, which denotes those Yoginīs, should be employed at the beginning, situated at the start [of the mantra].

This is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the fact that the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Kāmeśvarī and the others should also be employed at the beginning of their respective denotative words. It is precisely with this intention that the plural number is used even for the Yoginīs.

And by the force of this very [rule], it is established that after each respective seed-syllable (*bīja*), its corresponding name must also be uttered. Furthermore, that name should follow the word for the goddess of speech (*vāgdevatā*), in accordance with the *Kalpasūtra*. Thus, there is a sequential utterance of the groups, seed-syllables, and names, such that each group, each seed-syllable, and each name occurs one by one.

Siddham. Some say that [the syllable] stands at the mouth of the eight seed-syllables of the Yoginīs, beginning with Vaśinī; that is, it is the first among them. Others say it means "recited by the Yoginīs.
Likewise, through the sequence beginning with "Śiva, Agni, and Bindu are the Goddess," there is the union of the two *tāra*s (the *praṇava*s) consisting of *Hṛllekhā* and *Ramā*.

(p. 59) It will be stated that the application of the *śakti* must be performed in all [mantras]. Since it is impossible to insert it into the middle of the groups (*varga*) and so forth, whose sequence is already fixed, and since another statement prescribes the application of the seven-syllable mantra at the end, it must be performed at the very beginning. For this very reason—

In the context of describing the worship of the deities situated on the outer ten spokes, the mention of the "first vidyā" appropriately refers to the second *tārā*. At the end, however, the seven-syllable *pādukā* mantra—"I worship the *pādukā*" (*pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*)—should be employed. This has been stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "Thus the seven-syllable [mantra] has been proclaimed."

"Beginning with 'Success is attained through the Śakti-tantras,' one should employ [the mantra] preceded by the names of all the Śaktis and deities for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, it is common to all. Thus it is said.
As for that which is recorded in the twenty-seventh chapter of the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā: "Having understood this very secret instruction, one should worship the Cakra;
or there may be a salutation [expressed] as 'I worship the Pādukā'."

"One should remember 'svāhā' in the homa and 'tarpayāmi' in the tarpaṇa. Thus, although there is an option between the word "namaḥ" and [other mantras] regarding the *pādukā-mantra*, according to the *Kalpasūtra*, the word "namaḥ" is used for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the seven-syllabled mantra for the worship (*arcana*).
The "established option" (vyavasthitavikalpa) is to be understood as follows: likewise, the Sūtra states, "In the place of *namaḥ*, there is the salutation (*saṃnāma*) of the worship mantra.
However, in the *Kādima-tantra*, it says: "But in a tantra that stands outside the *Śakti-tantras*, the state [of the mantra] is with *namaḥ*."
The arrangement has been stated. Therefore: *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ rblūṃ*, [I worship] the sandals of the speech-goddess Vaśinī.
The thirty-three-syllable mantra for the worship of Vaśinī, consisting of the form "pūjayāmi," is thus established.

As for the addition of the word *namaḥ* at the end of this, it should not be adopted, because there is no authority for such a combination among the authors of the ritual manuals (*paddhati*), and because it would contradict the optional alternatives prescribed in the *Saṃhitās* and other sources.
Thus it should be understood in the subsequent cases as well. || 87 || 88 ||
O Maheśvarī, one should extract the first [syllable] of the second group, which is mounted by Indra;
below it, one should extract the seed-syllable of the ether situated in the fire.
Joined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the dot (bindu) and the crescent moon (khaṇḍendu),
this is the seed-syllable (bīja) of Kāmeśvarī, which causes the agitation of the three worlds.

In the second class of consonants (the *ka*-group), the first is the letter *ka*. It is neuter by virtue of its general gender, or it may be intended as a syllable (*akṣara*). Alternatively, because of its syntactical connection with the word "one should extract" (*uddharet*), it ends in the accusative case. That letter *ka* [represents] Indra.

It is mounted upon the letter *la*. Below and following the letter *la* is the aggregate *haṃ*, which is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) pertaining to the sky (*nābhasa*), that is, related to space (*gagana*).

"Haḥ is Śiva, the sky, the swan, the world of the Nagas, and the Lord of Ambikā"—according to the lexicon. That seed-syllable (Ha) resides within the fiery element; "Ra" resides within the seed-syllable of fire. "Ra is Astra, Krodhinī, the letter Ra, Pāvaka, Taijasa, and Mahas"—according to the lexicon.

Agni is the deity of this [mantra], thus it is *Āgneya*. [The suffix] *ḍhak* [is applied] after *agni*. Here, by the statement "it stands in the *Āgneya*," the conjunction of the two seed-syllables is expressed; and since that [conjunction] is impossible for two independent [syllables] accompanied by their vowels, it is established that the vowel *a*, the bindu, and the nāda constitute the tantra (the underlying structure) of both. For injunctions and prohibitions apply to the qualified subject when they are accompanied by qualifiers.

This is according to the maxim: "When there is an obstruction, one moves on to the qualification. Some also hold that the words *nābhasa*, *bīja*, and *āgneya* refer merely to the consonants (*vyañjana*). Their intention is based on the maxim: "Words observed in a whole are also seen in its parts. This same logic and variety of explanations apply to what follows as well.
Or it may be transposed. Here, the word "fourth" sets aside the mere first vowel.
The fourth vowel is *ī*. Thus, *klhrīṃ* becomes the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of the *kūṭa* (consonant-cluster). Consequently, [the mantra becomes]:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ klhrīṃ*.
"I worship the sandals of Kāmeśvarī, the goddess of speech"— this is the twenty-three-syllable mantra of Kāmeśvarī. Herein, the mantras of Vaśinī and the others function as ancillary parts (*aṅga*),
while the fifteen-syllable Vidyā alone possesses primacy.

Therefore, this Tripurā Parameśvarī is the primary knowledge (*pradhāna-vidyā*), because it will be stated in the fourth chapter [of the text]: "Thus... And consequently, by the maxim that "the mention of results regarding the ancillaries (*aṅga*) must be an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*")...
Although the passage beginning with "the agitator of the three worlds" is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), nevertheless,

since those [powers] alone are predominant in the practice of the mantras of Vaśinī and the others, it is possible that the declaration of results (*phalaśruti*)— even if its primary intent is [merely] for the sake of praise— is also intended as a literal statement of its own meaning.
For this very reason, another scripture states: "Even if there may be a relationship of principal and subordinate among mantras that are each devoted to a single [deity],
nevertheless, these mantras shall grant all accomplishments."
Even for those meditations that are practiced as ancillaries (*aṅga*), there is indeed a fruit,

because the maxim "the mention of a fruit in the context of ancillaries" pertains only to dry (non-spiritual) ritual acts. This is confirmed by the fact that the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* sūtra "The fruit belongs to the master [of the rite], so says Ātreya" was composed specifically as an exception to that rule.

The authors of the *Mantradevatāprakāśikā* state, however, that the application of the aforementioned rule— "those [mantras] which are intent upon one [deity]"— is solely for the purpose of setting aside the primacy established by logic, which would otherwise apply even when the *Māsāgnihotra* and other such rites are performed independently, despite their being subsidiary to the *Kauṇḍapāyināmayana*.
(61) Below the fifth [syllable], Aruṇā, one should apply the Vāruṇa [seed-syllable].
Below that, however, is the seed-syllable of Indra; O Dear One, it is followed by the letter *i* above all.
This is the seed-syllable of Tanmodinī, which brings all beings under control; it is marked by a crescent moon at its head and adorned above with a bindu.
The group of *aruṇā* is the *tavarga*. This is because it is stated that "the *aruṇā*, however, resides in the *tavarga*. Therein, the fifth is the letter *na*. *Vāruṇa* is the letter *va*.
According to the statement: "Va is speech, vāruṇa is fat (*medas*), utkārīśa is Aniruddha."

The seed-syllable of Indra is the letter *la*. Immediately after the entire aforementioned collection of syllables, following the letter *i* (the vowel *i*), is the fourth vowel (*ī*). Thus, the seed-syllable is *nvlīmi*. These are the five [syllables] beginning with Modinī and ending with Sarveśvarī.
Each of the mantras should be understood to consist of twenty-two syllables. || 91 || 92 ||
The [seed-syllable] of Vāyu is situated upon the seed-syllable of Indra, joined with the sixth vowel, topped by a crescent moon, and adorned above by a bindu. || 93 ||
This has been told to you, O Goddess, the form of the seed-syllable of Vimalā;
it causes the destruction of all sins and the eradication of all calamities. || 94 ||

Its deity is Vāyu; its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *vāyavyam*. According to the lexicon [beginning with] "That which belongs to the wind, the seasons, the ancestors, and the dawn," and "Ya, vāṇī, vasudhā, vāyu, vikṛti, and Puruṣottama," the letter is *ya*.
The seed-syllable is *ylūm*. Regarding the term *vigraha*, it is neuter in the general sense, or it may simply be a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The letter *ja* mounted upon the letter *ka*, with the letter of fire (*ra*) below it, joined with the fourth vowel and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*. (95)
This is that red seed-syllable of qualities (*guṇabīja*), which deludes all;
*kāla* is the letter *ma*.
According to the lexicon: "Ma is Kālī; Kāla is afflicted; Mahākāla is Yama, the Ender."

The letter of fire is the *repha* (the letter *r*). By that, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *jmrīṃ*. In this mantra, there is no euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) between the seed-syllable and the word *aruṇā*. || 95 ||
The seed-syllable of Śiva is situated at its beginning, and below it are Indra and Varuṇa.
O Supreme Goddess, having joined the [syllable] of Vāyu which is split above, this very seed-syllable of Jayinī is adorned with the digit and the bindu. (97)
The seed-syllable of Śiva is the letter *ha*. Its beginning is the letter *sa*, which resides therein.
Below the two *ha*s is Indra, the letter *la*; below that is Vāruṇa, the letter *va*. Then follows Vāyavya, the letter *ya*.

This [seed-syllable] is pierced by the vowel *u*, which is the sixth vowel, and is joined with the digit (*kalā*), the resonance (*nāda*), and the point (*bindu*). Having combined this with the seven syllables beginning with the name [of the deity], ending with the victorious seed-syllable (*jayinī-bīja*), [one should recite it].
The word "should say" is to be supplied. By that, the seed-syllable *hslvyūm* is formed. || 96 || 97 ||
O Supreme Goddess, one should extract the fourth [letter] from the group beginning with Modinī;
then, one should sequentially apply those [letters] below, starting with Kālāgni and Vāyu.
One should unite, in their proper sequence, the long vowels together with the seed-syllables, ending with the Lord-bindu (visarga), all placed together in one place. 99.

This is the seed-syllable of Sarveśvarī, which is invincible everywhere. [The letters] "mo" and "ca" constitute the *modinī* group, because it is said that *modinī* resides within the group [of consonants]. Having extracted the fourth letter therein, namely *jha*, one places [the following] beneath it in sequence:

One should join together— that is, unify— the letters *ma*, *ra*, and *ya* from the words *kālāgni* and *vāyavya*, combined above with the sixth vowel as the seed-syllable for longevity (*dīrghāyus*), and those which have the Lord (*īśvara*), the resonance (*nāda*), and the point (*bindu*) at their end.
"Ū is Dīpikā, Rati, Śānti, Krodhana, Madhusūdana;
Ardheśa, Kāmacāra, and Dīrghāyus are [the names] of the left ear"—so says the lexicon (*kośa*).
Furthermore: "The Nāda is the Lord of the half-measure (ardhamātrā), the Kalā, the Half-moon, and Sadāśiva."

The meaning is that this seed-syllable of the Sovereign of All (Sarveśvarī), characterized by its sequential application— without deviating from the order of the *pādukā* mantras and the names of the *ya*-group consonants— should be employed in worship. By that [method], the mantra consists of twenty-two syllables, distinguished by the seed-syllable *jhanyūm*.
It comes to be. || 98 || 99 ||
O Goddess, the fifth [syllable] is Kaulinī, situated above the seed-syllable of Time (Kāla). || 100 ||
Likewise, one should place the seed-syllable of fire at the very bottom;
it should be joined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the *nāda* and the moon (*indu*). (101)
O auspicious one, in this most excellent seed-syllable, the form of Kaulinī is established.

The group of Kaulinī consists of the six syllables beginning with *śa*; for although the letter *la* is the fifth in that series, because it is non-different from *la*, it is included as a constituent of the seed-syllable.

Furthermore, since the independent mention of the letter *la* is generally not found in the Tantras, when that [letter] is excluded from the count, Meru—consisting of the letter *kṣa*—becomes the fifth.
Alternatively, "Kaulinī" is a partial name for the letter *śa*; among the names of the letter *śa*...

This is because of the recitation of the term *kulakaulinī*. Therefore, in the analysis (*vigraha*) "the fifth from that," the ablative case is used in the sense of eliding the suffix *lyap* (i.e., "having passed beyond"). The meaning is: "that which is the fifth when counting while excluding the letter *śa*. This amounts to saying it is the sixth including that [letter]. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "the fifth starting from Kaulinī and so forth," there is the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).

This is a compound in which the middle term is elided (*madhyamapadalopa*). However, in the word *kaulinī* and others, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities of the members do not apply to the whole (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). The meaning is as follows: those whose beginning is the letter *śa*—namely, those beginning with *ṣa* and so on—are the "kaulinī-beginnings," which refers to the five letters beginning with *ṣa*. Among these, the fifth is the letter *kṣa*. Alternatively, [it may refer to] *kaulinī*.

The term *saṃbuddhi* is an epithet for the Goddess. The analysis of the compound *īpañcama* is as follows: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which the letter *ī* is the fifth. Since, in the *mātṛkā-cakra*, when counting again starting from the letter *a* after the letter *kṣa*, the letter *ī* is indeed the fifth (the sequence being *kṣa-a-ā-i-ī*), the letter *kṣa* is intended here.

The fifth group is easily grasped with slight effort. As for the explanation given by the authors of the *Artharatnāvalī*, who interpret the "Kaulinī-group" as the "Ṣa-group" (the sibilants) with reference to the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) class and so forth, that contradicts the preceding text which states, "Kaulinī is in the Śa-group. In reality, however, [it is stated] in the *Tantrarāja*:

Because the conjunction of five and five syllables beginning with *ya* and *ṣa* respectively for Sarveśvarī and Kaulinī is accepted, there is merely a designation of the letter *kṣa* by means of the fifth word of Kaulinī according to that method.
However, in the case of those two mantras, the conjunction of the four letters beginning with *yā* and the six letters beginning with *śā* must indeed be performed; otherwise—

Because it would result in a contradiction with the preceding text, which has as its sole fruit the prescription of yoga; and from this very indicative instruction, it is also easy to say that the performance of the *Tantrarāja* system is likewise permitted as an alternative. Therefore, first—

Then there is the letter *kṣa*, which is the seed-syllable of Time (*kāla*); then the letter *ma*, which is the seed-syllable of Fire (*vahni*); then the letter *ra*, the fourth vowel *ī*, and the Moon (*indu*), which is the *anusvāra*. The *bindu* is the void (*śūnya*), the fifteenth [element], the *anusvāra* named "Moon"—according to the lexicon (*kośa*).
And likewise, *kṣmrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). The *Kaulinī* mantra consists of twenty-three syllables;
however, in that version where it consists of twenty-two syllables, the preceding mantra should be understood as having twenty-three syllables.
Thus, having concluded the eight mantras of the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā), he introduces the mantras of the Sovereigns of the Wheels (Cakreśvarīs) beginning with Trailokyamohanā:
"O Great Goddess, these are the eight seed-syllables (bījas) in their proper sequence. (102)
I have now spoken; listen to those whose forms are the limbs of the Vidyā:
the Vidyā that effects purification of the hands, as well as that which takes the form of the ritual placement upon the limbs (aṅganyāsa). 103.
She is seated upon the seat of the Self, likewise stationed upon the seat of the wheel;
she is seated upon the seats of all mantras, and stationed upon the seats of the sādhya and the siddha. || 104 ||
O beloved, listen now to the root-vidyā, which is also the vidyā for the invocation of the Goddess.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Listen to the eight vidyās which are constituent parts (aṅga) of the mantra of the principal deity of the fifteen-fold vidyā; listen to the ninth, the root-vidyā, and the principal vidyā. This refers to the word "eight" (aṣṭau).

This is because they are connected [to the main mantra] by way of the "crow's eye" principle (*kākākṣinyāya*). For it is stated in scripture: "Thus, these eight vidyās are said to be the limbs (*aṅga*) of the goddess Mahāmāyā. By the phrase "having the form of limbs," it is implied that the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) should also be recited at the conclusion of the primary recitation.
*Karaśuddhikarī* and so forth are the names of the mantras in their respective order.

By the phrase *aṅganyāsarūpiṇī*, it is indicated that the application (*viniyoga*) of that [mantra] is in the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the root-vidyā (*mūlavidyā*). Among these nine, the seventh vidyā is called the *mūrtividyā*. And that is right here.

It should be understood that although it ought to be mentioned, because it is independent, or for the sake of suggesting another purpose, it will be discussed in the subsequent tantra; therefore, it has neither been included in this enumeration nor extracted here. || 102 || 103 || 104 ||
O Goddess, the Vāgbhava is the first, and the Kāmarāja is the second.

Joined with the end of *śānta* (the letter *sa*) and the *ka*-group, and conjoined with the end of that which ends in *ai* (the letter *au*), this Vidyā, O Great Goddess, is remembered as the purifier of the hands. (106)

The nine mantras to be extracted here each consist of three seed-syllables (*bīja*). Among them, the first set of seeds has the fixed designation "Vāgbhava. The second set is called "Kāmarāja," as such usage is observed in the Purāṇas and Tantras. In that regard, as follows:
In the fourth skandha of the Devībhāgavata:
"He in whose mind reside the Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and the Māyā-bīja as the third— no one is able to oppress him," and so forth.
Also, in the second chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"By means of the Vāgbhava [syllable], which possesses the splendor of the moon, she bestows the state of Lord of Speech;
by means of the Kāmarāja seed-syllable, which has the shimmering luster of a *śakragopa* insect..."
"O virtuous one, she who deludes the three worlds [is known] by means of the seed-syllable of Śakti," and so forth.

Regarding the third [group], however, names such as "Māyā" and "Śakti" are indefinite. In that context, he says "Vāgbhava" in order to establish two fixed names by way of referring to the first seed-syllable.
The procedure for the nomenclature of Vāgbhava. Likewise hereafter.
(p. 65) It is called *vāgbhava* because speech (*vāk*) arises from it; that in which desire (*kāma*) shines is *kāmarāja*.
These two names for the third seed-syllable become manifest during the stage of extracting the root-vidyā.
He will perform [the rite]. Alternatively, there is the rule for the first letter of the Mātṛkā with reference to Vāgbhava;
and the rule for the second letter of the Mātṛkā with reference to Kāmarāja. And those two letters, according to tradition, are accompanied by the bindu, even in the case of the pure Mātṛkā.

Due to the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*), the nasal bindu is not explicitly mentioned [in certain contexts] precisely because the intention is to establish that very [state] through its presence as *sabinduka*.

Since it is established solely by the oral tradition that in one's own scripture (*svaśāstra*) only the *mātṛkā* with the bindu constitutes the pure *mātṛkā*, and since this is not stated explicitly (*kaṇṭharaveṇa*), [the omission] is intended for that purpose in various places.

And there is the mention of the *bindu*. Therefore, one should not be mistaken into thinking that in such a case there is the utterance of two *bindus*, as in the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* with *bindus* in that particular instance. Having supplied the word "power" (*śakti*) by ellipsis, he extracts the third seed-syllable for the purpose of that [power] with the words "ending with *śānta*. This refers to the end of the letter *śa*.

The letter *ṣa*, followed by the syllable ending in it which is *sa*, followed by the letter *ai*, followed by the letter *o* at the end of that, followed by the letter *au* at the end of that, and joined with that; then, if joined with the *visarga* preceding the letter *ka* from among the *ka*-series, it becomes *sauḥ*.
This is the sequence of the three according to the order of recitation. Thus: *aṃ āṃ sauḥ*.

The three-syllabled Vidyā, presiding over the first wheel of the goddess Tripurā, becomes applicable for the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi) when employed according to the *Tāpanīya* [Upaniṣad], with the words: "Having performed the purification of the hands by means of this...
The seed-syllable situated between *e*, *o*, and *m* is intended solely for the manifestation of speech.
In the Rudrayāmala Tantra, however, the supreme syllable is specified.
The Mādana [letter], joined with Śakra [the letter *sa*] and combined with the fourth vowel, enriched above by the half-moon and the bindu—this is the extraction of Kāmarāja. (108)

Joined with the end of "śānta" (the letter *ha*) and the group beginning with *ka* (*kṣa*), and conjoined with the end of that which ends in *ai* (*au*), this is the Great Vidyā, the great source of prosperity for the Yoginīs. (109)
O Great Goddess, this is the family lore that accomplishes all purposes and goals;
O Gaurī, by means of this lore, one should effect protection for oneself. (110)

The seed-syllable consisting of twelve forms, recited between the vowels *e* and *o*, namely *aiṃ* with the *bindu*, is the Vāgbhava [seed-mantra]. Just as in the Māheśvara Sūtra (*e-oṅ*), there is here also the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). This very [mantra], even when devoid of the *bindu*, is the essence of speech, Sarasvatī.

The sense is: it serves for the composition and attainment of poetic skill, how much more so when accompanied by the nasal bindu. And thus it is said in the third book, ninth chapter of the Devībhāgavata (p. 66):
"Even a name that is indistinct, if uttered even incidentally..."
It bestows all desired objects, even those that are altogether difficult to obtain.
If one who is afflicted by fear, upon seeing a tiger or other such creature in the forest, utters "Ai Ai!
even without the nasal drop (bindu), it indeed bestows whatever is desired.
There was a twice-born man named Satyavrata, who was illiterate and a great fool;
having heard a syllable from the mouth of a boar, he then began to recite it himself.
By chance, he was born devoid of the nasal dot (bindu), yet that best of the wise became satisfied merely by the utterance of the vowel 'ai'. At that time, the Blessed Lady was pleased.
The Supreme Goddess, moistened with compassion, made him a king of poets;
and the twice-born Satyavrata became a poet renowned throughout the three worlds.
"Without propitiating Mahākālī, the Great Goddess, through both dry and moist [offerings]," and so forth.

Alternatively, [the practice may be] performed with the seed-syllable alone, unaccompanied by other seeds. For this very reason, the *Rudrayāmala Tantra* itself prescribes the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so on for the Vāgbīja alone.
O Supreme Goddess, I have previously explained in the Rudrayāmala Tantra the ritual procedure for each of the vidyās, beginning with Karaśuddhi.

This is because it will be explained in the fourth chapter. *Mādana* refers to that which pertains to *madana*; it is the letter *ka*. According to the lexicon: "The letter *ka* is *madana*, Brahmā, Krodhīśa, and Kulapālinī.
It is conjoined with *śakra*, which is the letter *la*. The fourth vowel is *ī*. Thus, this is [the syllable *kī*].
The seed-syllable *klīm* is known as Kāmarāja. By the term "Kāmarāja," the bestowing of sovereignty is indicated.
This is also stated in that very [text], in the seventeenth chapter:
"At one time, Vidalla arrived there."
"O eunuch! the son of the sage called out to him from nearby.
Having heard that, Sudarśana clearly grasped the single syllable accompanied by the *anusvāra*,
and he recited it again and again.
Then the boy, having mentally grasped that seed-syllable known as Kāmarāja,
recited it repeatedly, holding it in his heart with great reverence.
"Devoid of seers and meters, and lacking the ritual placements (nyāsa), meditations (dhyāna), and so forth...
(p. 67). "Ending with Śāntā," and so on, as before. By this, the Bālā-mantra in the form *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ* is established. *Kulavidyā* is another name for this very mantra. And thus:
"One shall employ [it]; then one should perform protection by means of the previously mentioned family-vidyā. Thus it is said.
He prescribes its application with the words "by this," [referring to] in oneself.

"Protection" (rakṣā) means guarding one's own sphere; for it is stated in scripture that "this Vidyā is the bringer of protection. As for the procedure to be described later, it is intended for the purpose of prescribing the sequence [of practice]; thus, neither part is redundant. || 107 ||
When the seed-syllable of this very Vidyā, containing Śiva, Māyā, Agni, and Bindu, is joined to the first word, then it takes the form of the seat of the Self (Ātmāsana).
When, in place of the first seed-syllable of this very family lore (kulavidyā), the syllable *hrīṃ*— composed of *śiva* as the letter *ha*, *māyā* as the letter *ī*, *agni* as the letter *ra*,
and the *bindu* as the *anusvāra*— is joined as the "Hṛllekhā" seed-syllable, while the other two seed-syllables remain unchanged, then [the mantra becomes] *harīṃ klīṃ*.

*Sauḥ*. This is the Vidyā; it constitutes the nature of the Goddess’s own seat (*ātmāsana*). Here, there is a transposition of *māyā* (the vowel *ī*) and *agni* (the letter *ra*). This is because the immediate precedence of the *bindu* (the nasal *m*) over the vowels is established by another [rule]. *Haḥ* is Śiva, the sky, *haṃsa*; thus, *ī*.
And the lexicon states: "Trimūrti" and "Mahāmāyā. || 111 ||
Furthermore, above this [first] Vidyā, there is an interval endowed with Śiva;
that is the Trailokyamohinī Vidyā, seated upon the Cakrāsana.

Furthermore, by the word "punarvidyā" (the repeated knowledge), only the third vidyā is meant, because it is the second vidyā itself that is being uttered again, according to the maxim that "that which has undergone a partial modification is not different [from the original]. Therefore, of the *punarvidyā*— that is, the *ātmāsana-vidyā*— that which was previously recited at the beginning...

That very [seed-syllable] consisting of the ignorance of the child (bālāvidyā), which is the self-seat mantra (ātmāsana) of this [deity], is to be recited later on above. The meaning is that the second vidyā becomes the fourth vidyā with a slight difference in its characteristics. As for the internal difference, however, it consists solely in the conjunction with the letter *ha*, which is conjoined with Śiva.

Thus, this Cakrāsana-vidyā is accomplished. As for the conjunction with the letter *ha*, since there is no specific rule determining its placement, it should be applied to each seed-syllable (*bīja*).

Furthermore, because a conjunction with a consonant is impossible at the end of a vowel, and because the separation of consonants that have already been established in their sequence [is not permitted], [the *ha* must be joined accordingly].

Due to the absence of authoritative evidence, it follows that the letter *ha* should be joined at the beginning of each seed-syllable (*bīja*). Thus, the mantra becomes *haiṃ hklīṃ hsauḥ*. However, some maintain that the first seed-syllable of the Bālā-vidyā is the first [of this sequence], while the second seed-syllable is above it; the interval between these two is what is referred to by the term "outer vidyā" (*vidyā-bahis*).
And it must be considered how she was obtained while still a child. Others,
however, read "the end of the beginning of Vidyā and so forth is endowed with Śiva," and [explain that] "of the beginning of Vidyā" refers to that which constitutes the beginning of the Mūlavidyā.

One should place the letter *sa*, which is the end of the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], above it. This reference is made here with the intention that the letter *sa* is the final [letter] in the *haṃsa* mantra. Others have explained that one should make the third seed-syllable, which is the end, conjoined with *śiva*; however, that is difficult and contradicts all the tantras. Alternatively:
Or rather, that too should be disregarded. || 112 ||
Furthermore, having first performed the Great Vidyā conjoined with Śiva and Candra,
this Vidyā which bestows all desires is established upon the seat of all mantras.
One should again recite that very same great lore (mahāvidyā) called Bālā, which was indicated by the first word in the preceding verse; this should be done even above this fourth [syllable].
There is the recurrence of the two words "above" (ūrdhva) from this [verse], and the verb must be supplied. That which is the interval between these two—

Regarding this, he says "Śivacandra": Śiva is the letter *ha* and Candra is the letter *sa*; the meaning is that one should make each seed-syllable (*bīja*) endowed with its first part by means of those two. Thus, the fifth mantra is established as *hsaiṃ*, *hsklīṃ*, *hsauḥ*.
Thus, this *haṃsa* is the innate Viṣṇu, the Lord of Bhṛgu, known as the Moon; so says the *Nandanakośa*.
According to the tradition, there is no insertion of the letter *sa* within the final seed-syllable (*bīja*).
However, in the two other views, it must be considered how the first word alone refers to the *Bālā* [Mantra]. This very [mantra]...
It becomes the vidyā for the seat of all mantras. || 113 ||
One should again recite that very same great knowledge (mahāvidyā) called Bālā, which was indicated by the first word in the preceding verse, even above this fourth [syllable].
There is an ellipsis of the two words "above this" (asya ūrdhvam), and the verb must be supplied. That which is between these two—

Regarding that, he says "Śivacandra": Śiva is the letter *ha* and Candra is the letter *sa*; the meaning is that one should make each seed-syllable (*bīja*) endowed with its first part by means of those two. Thus, the fifth mantra is established as *hsaiṃ*, *hsklīṃ*, *hsauḥ*.
Thus, this *haṃsa* is the innate Viṣṇu, the Lord of Bhṛgu, known as the Moon; so says the *Nandanakośa*.
According to the tradition, there is no insertion of the letter *sa* within the final seed-syllable (*bīja*).
