However, in the other two views, it must be considered how the initial word alone can refer to [the *haṃsa*]. This very [seed-syllable]...
It becomes the vidyā for the seat of all mantras. || 113 ||
Of the previously mentioned Vidyā of the Goddess’s own seat,
one should [place] the drops of water, Indra, and Śakti in their respective positions at the end, in due order.
O Supreme Goddess, having joined [the syllables] together with the half-moon and the resonance (nāda),
she stands upon the seat of the goal and its accomplishment through the differentiation of the pure syllables alone.

Regarding the *ātmasanavidyā* associated with the Goddess, which was previously described in the third position: following the sequence of the first and second seed-syllables without transgression, "water"—the letter *va*—is in the final region, in the place of the third seed-syllable; [and] Śakra [is likewise].

One should recite by joining the letter *la*, the energy (*śakti*), the letter *e*, and the *bindu* with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the resonance (*nāda*), and the seven [powers] beginning with *rodhinī*, in their proper sequence according to the established order. This is the sixth Vidyā, which differs from the third Vidyā solely through the difference in its individual syllables.

Being divided, it comes to rest upon the seat of the accomplishment of the goal (*sādhyasiddhāsana*). The sense is that this division is not merely a distinction made by independent phonemes, as in the case of the second, fourth, and fifth Vidyās. Here, by the word *toya* (water), the water-seed (*jalabīja*) located in the position of the teeth and lips is meant, and not—
The third letter of the *pavarga* [pa-pha-ba-bha-ma] is as in *vaśinī*. Regarding the section on the letter *va*, [it is stated]:
"Khaḍgīśa, Jvālinī, the wheel (*cakra*), and the jar (*kalaśa*) are synonyms for water," according to the lexicon (*kośa*).
"The letter *e* is the source of speech (*vāgbhava*), the power (*śakti*), the lord of the *jhiṇṭī* flower, the lips, the womb, and the wind.
Thus [it is said]. Therefore, the mantra is *harīṃ klīṃ bleṃ*.
It is accomplished. || 114 || 115 ||

Since the seventh vidyā will be explained in the Uttaratantra, he extracts only the eighth: "The first vidyā, mounted upon the seed-syllable *haṃsa* and seated upon the fire-throne, is the accomplisher of all aims for the rite of invoking the goddesses. (116)
*Haṃsa* is the letter *ha*. *Bījasama* means the seed (*bīja*) of all (*samasya sarvasya*), being equal to the seed;

the inversion of the word order follows the rule for *rājadantādi* compounds, as it belongs to that class of irregular groups (*akṛtigaṇa*). This refers, in effect, to the seed of the universe (*jagadbīja*), which is indeed the letter *sa*. Under the heading of the letter *sa*:

"I am Bhṛgu, the seed of the universe, named Śakti, possessing the speed of Haṃsa"—thus it is stated in the *Nandana*. However, the earlier authorities (prāñcaḥ) maintain that the meaning of the word *haṃsa* consists merely of the two consonants forming the *haṃsa-mantra*; they say that by this, both the letter *ha* and the letter *sa* are established. As for those who...

Some explain that *haṃsa* is its very own form and not a seed-name (*bīja-nāma*); according to their view, just as in the Śruti passage "The cave, *hasa*, Mātariśvan, the cloud, Indra," there would likewise be no mention of the *bindu* in the present context.
In reality, however, this word *haṃsa* has multiple meanings; and thus the lexicon states: *haḥ śivaḥ*.

"Sky is *haṃsa*"; and "that *haṃsa* is Viṣṇu, who is innate (*sahaja*). However, in this alternative view, regarding the sequence of the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) contained within a single word, the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) alone is the refuge. [One should contemplate] that primordial [goddess] in whom the letters *ha* and *sa* are mounted upon each seed-syllable.
Having placed each seed-syllable upon the seat consisting of the letter *ra*, which has the form of the fire of the ignorance of the ignorant, one should recite.
This is the intended meaning: before the consonants that are recited prior to the three vowels which constitute the limbs of the mantra, one should place the letters *ha* and *sa*.
"One should place the *repha* after them" means that the previously established consonants are to be inserted between the letter *ha* and the letter *sa*, specifically before the *repha*. Thus,
in the *vāgbhava* [mantra]...

Because the previously established *vyañjana* (consonant) is indeed absent, there is no intervention between the letters *ha*, *sa*, and *ra*. In the *Kāmarāja* [bīja], however, the sequence is as follows: after *ha* and *sa*, there are *ka* and *la*, and after those, the letter *ra*.
In the third *bīja*, the sequence is: after *ha* and *sa*, there is the previously established *sa*, followed by *ra*.

It is accomplished. However, those who are upright, considering such a sequence to be unstated in the root text, take refuge in the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) for that purpose. By that means, *hsraiṃ hsklrīṃ hssrauḥ*—this is established as the eighth mantra. This is the Vidyā.
This Vidyā shall be employed in the rite known as the invocation of the principal goddess, for according to the Śruti, it is superior to all others in the act of summoning. (116)
Having thus concluded the preceding section, he promises to extract the primary mantra: "O Goddess, in this way these great vidyās grant the accomplishment of all goals;
O Beloved, hear now the root-vidyā of Mahātripurasundarī. (117)
The meaning is clear. || 117 ||
Below that is Mādana; below that is Śakti; below that is Bindumālinī.
Aindra is situated within the seed-syllable of space (Ā), and below it is the letter of fire (Ra).
Joined with Māyā, Bindu, and Īśvara, and placed above all [the other syllables], this, O Goddess, is the Vāgbhava [bīja], which brings about mastery over speech. || 119 ||

Although various primary sciences (*pradhānavidyā*) are found in other tantras and in the *śrutis*— distinguished by divisions such as those of Manu, Candra, and others— and although among them there is no mutual relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) due to a lack of evidence, for this very reason there is neither superiority nor inferiority.

Furthermore, since [the distinction between the two] would entail a real difference [between them], and since such a difference is absent in the case of the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), that [distinction] is untenable. In this regard, first of all, there is no difference based on a difference in words, because the verbal root *vid* is one and the same.
Nor is there a difference based on repetition (*abhyāsa*), for even though the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is repeated nine times, it remains the same knowledge of Brahman.

Because it is a single entity; because the repeated mention is for the purpose of enjoining another quality in the form of being worshipped by Manu and others, and thus has a different purport; and because, although the statement "he brings forward the water" is heard six times for the sake of distinguishing the various explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), there is no difference in the act of bringing forward itself; nor [is there a difference] by way of number.

Regarding the statement "the twelve Mahāvidyās," which indicates a numerical count, it is logical that this number refers specifically to the number residing in the worshipper, since the mention of the number there is justified through its relation to the status of being worshipped by its own substratum; for there is no evidence for the existence of an actual, objective number [of deities].

There is no contradiction of their actual non-difference by the enumeration "the three are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara," because this number merely conveys that they possess the quality of number through the very number of their functions, such as creation and so forth; nor is there any contradiction by names such as Manu, Candra, and others.

This is because only those who have reached the culmination of the stage of lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) appear there; furthermore, since we observe that in some tantras the fifteen-syllable *Hādi-vidyā* is designated as "Lopāmudrā," while in other tantras that title is given to the seventeen-syllable *Kādi-vidyā*, these designations are not fixed.
Furthermore, [the definition] is fallacious because a single individual is seen to possess two names, such as Agastya and Lopāmudrā.

Nor can it be based on qualities (guṇa), for qualities that do not mutually cohere are not observed [to exist]. As for those who claim that there are distinctions of limbs (aṅga) due to the distinction of tantras...

p. 71) These are not causes of difference. For even though a disparity in auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) is observed among the various recensions (*śākhā*) regarding the Agnihotra and other rites, their non-difference is established in the section concerning different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*). As they say: "The single [sacrifice] is recognized across all recensions."

Regarding the word "karma": even in the Uttaramīmāṃsā, in the section beginning with *sarvavedāntapratyayaṃ codanādyaviśeṣāt*, it is indeed established that the Dahara-vidyā and other meditations taught in different Upaniṣads are non-different, despite differences in their ancillaries (*aṅga*). For this very reason...
The mutual combination of qualities is appropriate; however,

while those meditations consisting of mental acts might— by the principle of the "substratum" (tadadhikaraṇanyāya)— be considered of a single class, this does not apply here to the meditations which consist of the substance of the mantra as their constituent parts.

It should not be argued that difference [between mantras] is unavoidable due to the distinctness of their constituent syllables; for since all vidyās originate from Meru, there is no difference even in their constituent parts.
[The sequence is: Earth, Moon, Śiva, Māyā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇa, Adhva, and Mādana.
The half-moon and the bindu constitute the nine-syllabled Meru.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Jñānārṇava*, since none [of these] are composed of parts exceeding the nine [standard] components; and because there is no evidence for a difference in substance merely due to a slight difference in the number of parts, even when the dimensions differ—as in the case of "I who [was] in childhood... [and so forth].

This is because it has been established as such in accordance with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and other evidence, such as: "I experienced my two fathers, and now, in my old age, I experience my grandsons.
Furthermore, even though there is a difference in the substances consisting of the bodies of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others, their non-difference is observed. [The verse continues: *yuñjanti*...
Furthermore, regarding the verse beginning with "harī iṣirasya," although there is a difference in the recitation of the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda,

we have established its identity in our *Vṛttacandrodaya* in accordance with the *Nidānasūtra* and other authorities. For this very reason, even the coexistence of contradictory attributes is not incompatible with ultimate non-difference.
This is because [the relationship] is established just as in the case of Indra and Arjuna, by taking recourse to a conventional distinction (*vyāvahārika-bheda*).

By this, the view that there is a hierarchy [of fruits] based on the observation that other threefold knowledges (*trividyā*) are employed as subsidiary worship (*aṅga-pūjā*) within the meditation on a single knowledge is also refuted; for it is one and the same knowledge.

Even though there is a difference in the visualization of the worship according to the difference in location, the non-difference [of the deity] cannot be denied. For this very reason, the *Kalpasūtra* states that the goddess of the sixteen Yoginīs of the Wheel of Yoginīs—namely, the fourth among the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and the ninth situated in the Bindu-cakra—is one and the same; there is no difference in the mantra or the deity therein.
It must be understood that the special worship of that Great Goddess (Mahādevī) alone is to be performed in the four locations;

therefore, statements asserting the superiority of the *hādi-vidyā*—such as "the *hādi-vidyā* is *niṣkīlā* while the *kādi-vidyā* is *sakīlā*"—are merely expressions of partiality. [This is because] the mantra for the removal of the *kīla*...

Even though the *Hādī-vidyā* is mentioned in the textual recitation (*pāṭha*), its status as a constituent part of all [mantras] is not lost, according to the principle of the "combination of qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhāra-nyāya*). However, regarding the statement that "among mantras, the *Śrīvidyā* alone is supreme, and among those beginning with *ka*, the *Kādividyā* is likewise," and so forth—

Because it is supplementary to the ritual for reciting the thousand secret names (*rahasyanāmasāhasrotkīrtanavidhi*), its sole purport is the excellence of reciting the names; it does not possess a purport regarding its own literal meaning [as an independent statement]. "Indra is superior to the universe. (p. 72)

Because there is no establishment of Indra’s supremacy from such mantras as "ityādi," which have other intended meanings; and because statements such as "the *ka*-series alone is supreme, not the *ha*-series," even though they exist within their respective contexts, serve merely to praise what is being enjoined according to the maxim of "indirect censure" (*na hi nindā nyāya*).

Because superiority cannot be established. By this [it is meant that], based on statements from the *Jñānārṇava* and other texts such as "O auspicious one, these two sciences are difficult to obtain in the three worlds," the two fifteen-fold systems beginning with *ka* and *ha* are indeed the best. Furthermore, between those two, because it is worshipped by Kāmarāja, the fifteen-fold system beginning with *ka* is the best of the best; such are the declarations.

These [terms] are to be understood as being caused by the intensity of devotion (*bhaktipāravaśya*). Nevertheless, because the *Kādividyā* alone was first extracted as the source (*prakṛti*) of other vidyās in the *Tripuropaniṣad* and similar texts, even in the *Paramahopaniṣad*, which treats both vidyās as one, it says: "Desire is the womb (*kāmo yoniḥ*)."

Because she alone is extracted first by the Śruti beginning with "Kamalā," and because [the syllable] "īṃ" is also extracted from "kādi" in the Ṛk verse "catvāra īṃ bibhrati kṣemayantaḥ," this is done for the sake of conforming to such numerous scriptural authorities.
And because that very [Vidyā] was introduced in the verse beginning with "tām īkārākṣaroddhārām," he further elucidates that same Vidyā with the words "mādanaṃ" and so forth:
Kāma, Yoni, Kamalā, Vajrapāṇi, and Guhā.
The wind laughed, Indra [took] the cloud;
again, by means of Māyā, this all-pervading, many-syllabled Mother of the Universe, the primordial knowledge (Adi-vidyā), entered the entire cave.
Thus says the Śruti of the Śaunaka school in the Atharvaveda.
Therein, he explains the four terms beginning with *kāma* by means of the terms beginning with *mādana* in their respective order:
the seed-syllable (*bīja*) associated with *madana* (intoxication) is *mādana*, which is the letter *ka*; and that is indeed qualified by the vowel *ā*.

In the *Uktaśruti*, because there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of "all the *has* [consonants]" as being qualified by the letter *a*, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that establishes the necessity of the conjunction with the letter *a* for those *hasakalas* not contained within the *hṛllekhā*. In this very tantra, in the *Ṣaṭśatī*:
In the extraction of the Vidyā of the Fifth [Tithi] of the Five Peaks:
O Pārvatī, [the syllables] Kāma joined with Viṣṇu, Śakti, Māyā, and Śakra;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should apply the seed-syllable of Mahāmāyā at the end.
This is because, in the verse concerning the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*, Kāma is qualified by being "joined with Viṣṇu";

and because of this very indicative mark, as well as the statement in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara* that "in all the *kūṭas* of Śrīvidyā, the phonemes are to be recited together with their vowels," and that among them, there are two *hasau*s for each.

The phrase "three arts, three [times] three" refers to the combination of ten with the letter *s* (sva). And so, he will state in the section on the meaning of the tradition (*saṃpradāyārtha-prakaraṇa*):
"In the same way, the group of ten Śrīkaṇṭhas is indeed the designator of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). (p. 73)
*Śakti* is the eleventh vowel (*au*). *Bindumālinī* is the fourth vowel (*ī*). Regarding the section on the letter *ī*, the lexicon states:
"The supreme Śiva is *Śivā*; the fourth is *Tuṣṭi*, [and] *Bindumālinī*"; thus, *Kamalā* is simply another name for that very same [deity]. However, in the *Rasasārasaṃgraha*:
It has been stated [in the scriptures] that "mādana" is the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while "vikāsa" is said to be Śiva.
Also, in the *Haṃsapārameśvara*:
"Mā is declared to be Śakti, while dana is Śiva, who performs the act of acceptance."

By stating that "that very [power] is Mādana," it is said: "The letter *ha* is designated as Śiva," and so forth. In the *Ṛjuvirmārśinī* it is also stated: "It intoxicates (*mādayati*) and gladdens (*harṣayati*), thus it is Mādana; the letter *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
When the vital breath functions in another mode as the downward breath (*apāna*), the vital breath becomes speech-essence (*vāgrasa*), and the downward breath is Madana."
And because of the scriptural authority [of the *Śruti*]: below that letter *ha* is the power (*śakti*), which is the seed-syllable *sa* to be pronounced first.
It has been explained that by the term "Bindumālinī," the letter *ka* alone is intended according to the tradition (*saṃpradāya*).
All of that is beyond the path of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and is like a royal decree [without basis].

This is sufficient only to bind the disciples and does not lead to the satisfaction of those who know the logic and are authoritative; therefore, it should be disregarded. Furthermore, since the three *mādanas* will be taught separately from the three *vyoma*-seeds in the section on the Kaulika meaning, this [position] contradicts that. Therefore, it is *mādana*.

It is indeed the letter *ka*. For this very reason, in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*, while writing down the very words beginning with "In the case of the *Lopāmudrā* school, however... regarding the clear meaning of this text from the perspective of the *Kāmarāja* school, it is implied that the alternative perspective has an unclear meaning. And it is not [stated] in the *Uttaratantra*...
It should not be argued that, because the sixfold meaning to be described here conforms to the *Hādividyā*, it is appropriate to interpret this verse— which primarily concerns the *Kādividyā*—
in a different manner; for in that [sixfold meaning], the natural elegance (*svārasya*) of the first two meanings resides precisely in their conformity with the *Kādividyā*.
Because it will be explained later;

and because it is established by logic that the description of the meaning in a sentence read in the conclusion must follow the opening statement whose meaning is free from doubt. Therefore, even this statement of the Great Ones—

It should be understood that [this] is indeed non-authoritative, like a Smṛti rooted in greed, because it is based on partiality toward the particular Vidyā one worships oneself. The letter *va* (vajra) is the form of Indra;
it resides upon the head of the letter *ha*, which is the seed-syllable of Ākāśa. Below—that is, beneath the letter *ha*—...
The syllable of the blazing fire is *repha* (the letter *r*). *Māyā* is the vowel *ī*. The *bindu* is the *anusvāra*.

*Īśvara* is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). [The mantra] is joined with these; by the term "above all," the group of seven beginning with *rodhinī* is meant, because it is recited as being above them all. Having thoroughly conjoined [the seed-syllable] with these as well, one should extract it.

This very [syllable] becomes *vāgbhava*. In the Veda, the words *guhā* and *māyā* refer to the seed-syllable of *lajjā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*). If there is insistence that this text must also be interpreted as referring to the *hādī-vidyā*, then let it be stated thus: *mādana* is indeed the letter *ka*; below that, that very same [letter].

That which has *mādana* (the letter *ma*) below it is such an *akṣara* (syllable), namely the *śakti*, which is the letter *sa*. This is because the lexicon states that "the seed of the world" is a synonym for *śakti*, referring to the letter *sa*. Furthermore, in the compound *tadadhaḥśabda*, there is again a *bahuvrīhi* as before. *Bindumālinī* means "possessing a garland of dots" (*bindu*).
The meaning is "one who loves the pair of *bindus*"; that is to say, the letter *ha*. Accordingly, there is a lexicon (*kośa*) under the section on the letter *ha*:
"The Goddess is the lover of the pair of *bindus*, and the Lord is Meghaśyāmeśvara."

Consequently, the *ka-sa-hā* should be recited in reverse order; this is the resultant meaning. Regarding this point, it will be stated that the phrase "in the manner of the previous extraction" (*prāguddhārakrameṇa*), located in the third peak (*kūṭa*), serves as an indicator of the intended sense (*tātparyagrāhaka*). However, [this will be discussed] in the eighth chapter.

In the context of explaining the contemplation of the state of deep sleep as an ancillary of *japa*, the fact that the third *kūṭa* was previously extracted in reverse order— by the phrase "of the preceding syllables in reverse"—
would be contradicted if it were restated here as a unique qualification [of that *kūṭa*].
Furthermore, if the first peak-syllable were also extracted in reverse order, it would result in the loss of the unique character of the truth (satya).
Having thus extracted the first peak-syllable (kūṭa), he extracts the second peak-syllable:

"Having divided the seed-syllable of Śiva threefold according to the sequence of emission, maintenance, and dissolution, [the second syllable] consists of two [parts] devoid of the first [part], with the syllable of Madana below the first. (120)
Furthermore, O Maheśvarī, one should apply the seed-syllable of Indra (L) beneath Sthiti-Śiva,
and likewise the letter of fire (R) beneath Laya-Śiva.
Joined with the fourth vowel, and endowed with the bindu, the half-moon, and the crescent—
thus is this great seed-syllable, the Kāmarāja, which brings about great prosperity.

One should deposit the seed-syllable of Śiva, the letter *ha*, in three locations, one below the other. For these, the designations "creation," "maintenance," and "dissolution" have been established in their respective order for the sake of conventional usage and for other purposes hereafter. By the first...
The two words "rahita" (devoid of) are connected twice;
that is to say, one should make the first [of those] *ha* sounds devoid of the first [consonant], and both the second and third *ha* sounds devoid of the first *ha*.
Thus, the two *ha* sounds are split by the first *ha*, [and likewise] both the second and third by the first *ha*.

The meaning is that one should make it devoid of the letter *sa*. By this prohibition of the association with *sa*— which was not even applicable to the second and third *ha*s— it follows that the association with *sa* for the first *ha*, which is other than those, is necessary.
It is established [by this]: "He chooses one, he chooses two, he chooses three; he does not choose four, nor does he choose more than five.
For here, by the prohibition of choosing four, six, or more *ārṣeya*s, the possibility of choosing five *ārṣeya*s is observed. But this does not apply to bronze (*kāṃsya*).

This is because, in the *Śaṅkhasmṛti*, the term "heating" (*tāpana*) is explained by Aparārka as implying the heating of anything other than bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), precisely due to such a prohibition; furthermore,
that association with the letter *sa* does not occur for the first *ha* even when delimited by the preceding portion.

But [the phrase] "only after that" (paratraiva) means that for him, [the sequence] is obtained through the force of the designation "creation," because there is no other function prior to creation; whereas after dissolution (laya), there exist concealment (tirodhāna) and grace (anugraha). By this, the objection regarding the lack of naturalness in placing the letters *ja*, *la*, *na*, *ra*, and *ṇa* after Śiva, who is associated with dissolution, is refuted. For this very reason...

The purpose of the designations "creation" and so forth is merely for conventional usage, as these can be established even by terms such as "first," "second," and so on. The second *hakāra* is Sthiti-Śiva;
below that is the seed-syllable of Indra, the letter *la*. The third *hakāra* is Laya-Śiva; below that is the syllable of fire (*ra*).

One should apply it joined with the letter *ra*, the vowel *ī*, the bindu, the half-moon, and so forth; that which is thus [joined] becomes the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of Kāmarāja. || 120 || 121 || 122 ||
He extracts the third peak-syllable:
"O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of Māyā, joined with Mādana and Śakra;
having applied the seed-syllable of the Moon alone, O Varānanā. (123)

O Goddess, having set aside the sequence of emanation, one should first extract the seed-syllable of Śakti according to the sequence of extraction, by means of the application of the sequence of reabsorption.
In this regard, one position is that there is an injunction for the designation of one [seed-syllable] by means of the mention of either the *māyābīja* or the *śaktibīja*.

According to this position, the term "Maheśānī" is not a vocative; rather, being a qualifier of the seed-syllable, it is neuter and refers to the *Hṛllekhā*. Alternatively, [it may refer to] the *māyābīja*.

Hṛllekhā. According to the cited scripture, this is one syllable. "Mādana" (the letter *ma*) joined with "Śakra" (the letter *sa*), and the letter *ka* joined with *la*, making *kala*; this is the second [syllable]. The seed-syllable of the Moon (*candrabīja*) is the letter *sa*;
it is not joined with any other syllable, remaining as it is like "mādana. This...

Third: as for those who explain *ye tu śakrasaṃyutam* as a qualification of the seed-syllable of Māyā (*m*), for them, since the connection with another consonant after the anusvāra is not even applicable, the phrase "the prior connection" (*pūrvaṃ yoga*) would indeed be well-supported; nevertheless, there is a loss of the natural elegance of the qualification applied solely to the Moon-seed-syllable (*candrabīja*).

In our view, however, since the qualifying term read between the *mādana* and *candra* seed-syllables could logically be construed with both sides of the context, its exclusion is established by the qualifying term "only" (*kevalam*), which implies that it must be construed with the preceding [syllable] alone. Furthermore, [...]
A remote connection (*dūrānvaya*) of a qualifier separated by the word *mādana* is contrary to linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Nor should it be argued that,
according to your position, the application of the suffix *śakra* would occur even before *mādana*, because [the order is determined] by the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

Because such a refutation is possible; for in the extraction of the *kulavidyā*, even all [commentators] have taken refuge in the very order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) regarding the passage "the *mādana* joined with *śakra*. Alternatively, "joined with *śakra*" is an adjective qualifying both *māyā* and *mādana*. Therefore, *śakra* is to be written between those two.

"Likewise, since the accomplishment of that union occurs in both cases only when [the conditions] are present," he says "having abandoned" (*tyaktvā*), meaning that one should recite this triad in reverse order. He refers to the sequence of directness (*ānulomya*) that was adopted during the extraction of the preceding, immediately prior *kāmarāja-kūṭa*.

The meaning is that one should extract this by means of yoga in the form of the reverse order of the process of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*), having abandoned the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). In the case of the *Hādividyā*, the phrase "by the application of the process of dissolution" is a qualification of the sequence for extracting the first *kūṭa* according to the traditional method.
Easy to speak with. || 123 || 124 ||
Thus, O Great Goddess, this Mahāvidyā Mahātripurasundarī brings the three worlds under her control merely by being remembered. 125.

The mention of Śrīvidyā as non-different from the deity Mahātripurasundarī is intended either to express the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, or with the view that the mantra is the subtle form of the deity. This very Vidyā, when merely recollected...

When recited, it brings the three worlds under one's control. Since the subjugation of the three worlds is the singular attribute of Paraśiva, this recitation of the Vidyā results in the attainment of the state of Paraśiva; such is the meaning. And so it is heard in the *Sundarītāpinī*: "The fifteen-syllabled [mantra] of Tripura..."
"He who studies this obtains all desires; he obtains all enjoyments; he creates all worlds; he causes all speech to expand; he attains the state of Rudra;
having pierced through the realm of Viṣṇu, he pervades the Supreme Brahman—he who knows thus. And so it is said.

Just as in the injunction "one [should perform] the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices for the sake of all desires," where the mention of both the instrument and the result implies a *bhāvanā* (productive activity), so too here, by implication, the meaning is: "One should effect the state of Paraśiva and so forth by means of the recitation (*japa*) of Śrīvidyā. Consequently, because of its connection with a fruit, the recitation [is an action].

Once its primacy is established, by the principle that "that which bears fruit is superior to that which does not," it is proven that the *Vaśinī* and other mantras are ancillaries (*aṅga*) to the *Śrīvidyā*. And by that [primacy], those [mantras] recited in proximity to it, when worshipped,
quickly bring a person under control.

By the principle of the *arthavāda* regarding the *āmana-homa*, sentences that indicate results such as "the world" and so forth result in conveying mere praise (*prāśastya*), and do not constitute injunctions of results (*phala-vidhi*). Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*).
"Listen, O Goddess, first to Mahānityā, [who is] Tripurasundarī;
by her being known, O Gaurī, the agitation of the world is produced"—thus begins [the text].
"You alone, the enchantress of the universe, sport in their forms"—thus ends the Tantra.
Because of the concluding summary:
"The Great Tripurasundarī is established here in this great wheel."
Because of the repeated references to this tantra in the middle [of the work] through such passages as "p.

77)," it is understood that its primary purport lies precisely in the prescription for the worship of Tripurasundarī. And that worship consists of a specific type of mental activity. [The opponent argues: "It is not so, because of the indicative marks (liṅga) of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa)."

This is because such an interpretation is seen in the *Brahma-sūtras* and other texts, which state: "Because of the threefold nature of the meditation on the qualities (*cenna-upāsā*), and because of their being dependent [on the object], they are connected with it here. Some maintain that devotion (*anurāga*) directed toward a deity is itself worship (*upāsanā*). That is not correct;
for in injunctions such as "one possessed of devotion should worship," devotion is mentioned as distinct from worship.

Because such an explanation would be untenable, since it is *anurāga* (attachment) alone that is denoted by the term *bhakti*. This is evident from the *Śāṇḍilya-sūtra*: "Now, therefore, the desire to know devotion; it is supreme attachment to the Lord. Therefore, *upāsanā* (meditation) is simply an action distinct from attachment. And that [action] is of two kinds.

It consists of the form of reciting its mantra and the form of worshipping its yantra; for, according to the traditional grammatical lexicon (*dhātupāṭha*) which states "to recite (*japa*) [is] mental," it is understood that recitation is a mental activity. Since worship—whether in the form of meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth—is likewise of that nature, even that which consists of the offering of ritual services (*upacāra*) is not [external].

Because it is of the singular nature of a mental resolve (*mānasa-saṃkalpa*) characterized by the form "mine" (*mama*); and since the description of the mass of fruits resulting from the worship of the Tripurasundarī-yantra has already been set forth in seventeen verses, how can the maxim of "the fruitless being subordinate to the fruitful" (*phalavad-aphala-nyāya*) apply here in the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraheṇa*)?
This is a refutation. And this being so, it does not follow that recitation (japa) becomes a subordinate member (aṅga) of worship.
For it is said: "A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this.
Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa."
Because it is stated in the *Itimasmṛti* and other texts that japa alone is the independent means for achieving success (*siddhi*),

and because [the Lord] says, "Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of japa" (*yajñānāṃ japayajño 'smi*) and so forth, one becomes weary from japa in such practices as the worship of the King of Mandalas (*cakrarāja*), the recitation of the Vidyā, and the chanting of the Names.

Furthermore, because of the reading in passages such as "one who is weary from meditation should recite again," and because of the predominance [of the term] *pradhāna*, the primacy of *japa* is established— just as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice. Therefore, in the statement of the later Tantra,
"Having performed the worship of the wheel, one should thus perform *japa* with a concentrated mind," it refers solely to the time [of the ritual].

It is a conjunction, because both [mantra and ritual] have fulfilled their purpose, just like the New Moon and Soma sacrifices. However, the traditionalists maintain that even when recitation (*japa*) is performed independently elsewhere during worship, it is indeed a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that worship, just like shaving the hair and so forth. An indicator for this very point will become clear in the subsequent chapter.
Having thus taught, up to the extraction of the mantra for the arrangement of the wheels (*cakroddhāra*), by means of one hundred and twenty-five verses,
[the author] now proceeds with seventy-nine [verses] until the conclusion of the first chapter.

He teaches the worship of the *cakra* through these verses, beginning with "With this [mantra], the practitioner should begin the worship of this *cakra*" and ending with "one should dismiss it with the words 'forgive me. (p.
78) With this [mantra], the practitioner should begin the worship of this *cakra*.
By means of this *kādividyā* or *hādividyā*, [one worships] this previously extracted *cakra*;

for according to the statement "the *Śrīcakra* is the body of Śiva and Śivā," the meaning is that of Tripurasundarī, who is non-different from the *cakra*. Consequently, its application (*viniyoga*) is solely in the worship of the Great Goddess, and not in the worship of any other deity.
This is the meaning.
Now, at the commencement of worship, he prescribes the various necessary qualifications for the practitioner:
"But [the practitioner] whose body is reddened with saffron, and who is endowed with red garments and so forth... (126).
With his mouth filled with betel, he did not bow to us;
rather, he was arrogant, his limbs smeared with camphor powder and adorned with red ornaments. || 127 ||
The yogi is covered with red flowers, anointed with red perfumes and unguents;
seated upon a red carpet, he dwells in a house as crimson as lac.

The practitioner, whose mind is steady, may be adorned with all the ornaments of amorous attire, his body fashioned into three cities, or he may be impassioned by the mental resolve [of the deity]. (129)
By the word "clothing and so forth" (*vastrādi*), the inclusion of red flowers or female attire is intended;
as for the qualification "covered with red flowers" that appears later, it refers to those born from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* [wombs] mentioned previously.

There is no redundancy because of the explanations provided by the traditional authorities (*sāṃpradāyika*). Here, the fourth quarter [of the verse] conveys the path of self-worship (*ātmapūjā*), and that quarter consists of scrambled syllables (*vyākulākṣara*).
We shall reveal the key to its recitation in the *Uttaratantra*.

*Kṣoda* means powder. He is one by whom the body (*vigraha*) has been reduced to the state of the three cities (*tripurīkṛta*) through ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other such means. In the event that such a physical object cannot be obtained, he says: "colored by the mental resolve" (*manaḥ-saṃkalpa-rakta*). The meaning is that one should perform the mere visualization (*bhāvanā*) of the previously mentioned attributes. And therefore—

In the *Kalpasūtra*, the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "one who has prepared the *kavya* offerings, or one who is capable through mere resolve" refers to an optional alternative based on specific circumstances (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). Regarding the term "steadfast-minded," the word "may he be" (*bhūyāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Furthermore, the repetition of the word "sādhaka" (practitioner) is for the purpose of providing the subject (*uddeśya*) for the subsequent prescriptive qualifications. || 126 || 127 || 128 ||
On a level and pure plot of ground, smeared with cow dung, strewn with heaps of flowers, and fragrant with the scent of incense; || 130 ||
O Goddess, one should first draw the circle with vermilion powder or alternatively with saffron, making it beautiful and with perfectly straight lines. (131)
It has an equilateral triangle at its tip, possesses equal sides, and is exceedingly beautiful. (p.
79) "Equal" means made even. The method for performing that [leveling] should be consulted in works such as the *Kuṇḍodyota*.
Here, by the word "equal," it is understood that the leveling of the ground itself is intended.

It is also stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "On a level and pure plot of ground, one should draw the *cakra* on the earth using either vermilion powder or saffron powder. Regarding this, the moderns (*navya*) maintain that there is a word-break (*padaccheda*) as *asame* (on an uneven [ground]). That will be refuted later in the *Uttaratantra*. [The word] *śuddhe* (pure).
The ground becomes pure when it is free from the movement of impurities such as ants and the like,
and devoid of charcoal, chaff, hair, bones, and insects.
Purification of the earth occurs through sweeping, burning, the passage of time, or even by the treading of cows.
This is because of statements such as those by Yājñavalkya in the *Prayogasāra*: "with cow-dung, but not with that of a buffalo.

A "heap of flowers" (*puṣpaprakara*) refers to a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). "Mixed with that" means joined with it; that is to say, having offered a handful of flowers with the mantra prescribed in the *Kalpasūtra*. The *Uttaratantro* will later describe the mixing of yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*) and other substances.
In the absence of those, there is no requirement for vermilion or saffron.
This is prior to the placement of the vessels;
therefore, he will say later:
"One should establish the arghya vessel in the center of both the Śrīcakra and oneself," so it is said;

or rather, "prior to the ritual placement (nyāsa)," according to the Kalpasūtra. This is because the precedence of the preparation of the vessels (pātrāsādana) is already established by the very order of the text.
That [mandala] in which the tips of the three triangles, the four fire[-triangles], and the five moon[-shaped] powers are equal, straight, and do not deviate from the Brahma-thread;
that in which the weapons are equal— neither fewer nor more— and number forty-three.
It is exceedingly beautiful, characterized by the junctions and vital points (saṃdhi-marma) as they have been described. || 130 || 131 ||
One should place the arghya water, mixed with water, in a vessel made of gold or other materials that has a stand.
O Supreme Goddess, one should impregnate [the substance] consisting of rocanā, candana, saffron, and light musk with the elements of fire, sun, and moon. 133.
One should recite [the mantra] ten times and thereby satisfy the Yoginīs.

Regarding the general *arghya* offering, the text says "gold and so forth" (*hemādi*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), silver and other materials are included. These are described in the *Kulārṇava*:
[The vessels] are made of gold, silver, stone, tortoise shell, human skull, gourd, or clay;
or they originate from coconut, conch, pearl-oyster, mother-of-pearl, or glass.
A wise person should fashion a beautiful vessel made from a sacred tree;
one should avoid that which is too thin, too thick, cracked, or perforated.
"One should not have a vessel made of metals such as copper, bell-metal, and the like.
Here, "kapāla" refers to the *mahāśaṅkha*.
The *mahāśaṅkha* specifically bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, because of the syntactic unity of the compound;
by the term "muktā-śukti" (pearl-oyster), there is the exclusion of those oysters that do not produce pearl-pearls;
and by the term "puṇya-vṛkṣa" (auspicious tree), [there is the exclusion] of all trees other than a few such as the *aśvattha* and *palāśa*.
This excludes the *snuhī*, *vibhītaka*, and similar materials. By the term "extremely subtle," it is meant that [the vessel] is less than four finger-breadths in height and as much in width;
however, a wise person should not have a vessel made that is deficient by eight finger-breadths.

This is because a prohibition is seen in another tantra; for it has been explained by the traditionalists that the height and width are each four finger-breadths, thus making eight finger-breadths in total. [The wheel] is that extent by which the movement of the hand is obstructed for the purpose of offering libations and worship within the circle.

That [explanation] is too coarse. However, its form—beyond that which is specifically prescribed—is optional (*aicchika*). Regarding the specific form, it is observed in the *Bhūtabhairavatantra* that it has the shape of a vulva (*bhaga*).
Even though it is said: "Vessels of gold and silver grant all accomplishments."
For rites of pacification, a stone bowl is used; for rites of immobilization, one made of clay.
A coconut shell is for subjugation and the like; one made from tortoise shell is for malevolent rites (abhicāra);
a conch shell bestows knowledge; and a pearl oyster shell grants learning.
Skull-cups and vessels made of gourd bring about the perfection of yoga;
while rosary beads made from sacred trees remove all sins.
By these statements, it is understood that all twelve types of vessels serve a desirable purpose (*kāmya*);
nevertheless, because there is no distinction in their separate connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), it must be stated that they serve both purposes, just like the *khādira* wood.
And thus it is recorded in tradition: "O Goddess of Gods, among those mentioned here, one should prepare a single vessel."
O Goddess, they say the support (ādhāra) for the vessel should have three feet, or six feet, or four feet;
alternatively, one should make it circular in shape and beautiful to the mind.

[This refers to] that which is accompanied by a support (ādhāra) characterized by the definitions thus stated. Here, in the three positions beginning with the triangle, the states of being a triangle, a hexagon, and a square are respectively necessary. According to the tradition (saṃpradāya), in the circular position there is an absence of [these] feet.
Even in the circular position...
(81) They also say that there is an option regarding [the pedestal] having three, four, or six parts.

And according to the *Jñānārṇava*, that base may be made of gold, silver, copper, or other materials. As for its measurement, it is entirely optional up until the specific [proportions] are observed; it is simply the measurement of the vessel itself.

Some also maintain that it is measured by water, and not by any other cause, because it is perceived as having water alone as its independent instrument. As for the mixing with the first drop that is recorded in another Tantra,
that is merely for the sake of refinement (*saṃskāra*), like the rule "he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk," and so forth.
Therefore, there is no violation of independence.
By this, the statement from the *Saṃhitā*—“Having placed there a conch filled with water along with its cause”—is explained. *Rocanā* means *gorocana*. *Candra* [means]...

Camphor, saffron from Kashmir (kesara), labhu (a type of incense), and aguru; the meaning is that one should grind the five substances beginning with *rocanā* and mix them with water. From fire, sun, and moon, the elements arise—meaning their rays; the ten fire-kalās, beginning with *dhūmrārcis*, reside in the *ādhāra*.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the twelve solar digits (kalās), beginning with Tapinī, within the vessel, and the sixteen lunar digits, beginning with Amṛtā, within the water. In the *Manoramā*, however, it is stated that the base, the vessel,
and the water are to be contemplated as fire, sun, and moon respectively, while the five substances beginning with Rocanā [are to be contemplated as the lunar digits].

It has been explained that one should meditate [on the deity] as being composed of the five elements, beginning with earth. This alone is appropriate because it accords with the yellow color of Rocanā and so forth. The indeclinable *tat* refers back to the root-vidyā. Having touched water, one should [recite it] ten times.

The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra]. According to the *Manoramā*, however, the word "that" (*tat*) refers specifically to the third section of the Vidyā. The *yoginīs* are the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of Tripurasundarī.
Therefore, the refinement of that [water] is that one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with that same water of general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) upon those very [deities].
Having filled [the vessel] with pure water, one should worship it according to the prescribed cause;
there, O Dear One, one should worship the six limbs—this is the general *arghya*.
Thus, from the *Jñānārṇava*.

Alternatively, "the state of the Yoginīs" (*yoginīpada*) refers to the deities of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), such as the Ḍākinīs and others, because it will be explained in that very way in the *Uttaratantra*. However, according to the *Manoramā*, it refers to all the powers (*śakti*) that constitute the retinue of the Goddess.

Thus, when the general *arghya* has been accomplished, its application will be described in the eighth chapter, beginning with: "O Goddess of the gods, one should worship Mārtaṇḍa with the general *arghya*," and so forth. As for that which is stated in that very same place: "The *arghya* is indeed between the Śrīcakra and oneself..."

By the passage beginning with "one should install" (*pratiṣṭhayed*), the preparation of the *arghya* offering is described; specifically, that of the *viśeṣārghya*, because it is produced by means of a single substance. For this very reason, in that context, the statement "one should worship the sixteen lunar digits (*indukalā*) once the substance has been held" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the holding of the substance as an established fact.

This is consistent. Furthermore, as for that statement at the end—"the best of practitioners should likewise especially prepare the *arghya*"—that refers to the procedure for either the vessel of the self (*ātmapātra*) or the vessel of the guru (*gurupātra*). One should prepare this exactly as one does the ordinary *arghya*. However, the word "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*) signifies a distinction (*viśeṣa*).

Because of that meaning; for this very reason, the prescription for self-worship following immediately after that—beginning with "having worshipped the line of the Guru's feet" and so forth—is consistent. And for this same reason, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "Having thoroughly worshipped oneself, one should cause the spirits to tremble."

They say that by the very injunction for the worship of oneself (*ātmapūjā*) through speech, the preparation of one's own vessel (*ātmapātrāsādana*) is implied; otherwise, if one were to perform the self-worship using only the special *arghya* substance, there would arise the fault of making oneself impure (*ucchiṣṭakaraṇa*) before offering it to the principal goddess.

[This refers to] Śaṅkarānandanātha and others. By this [statement], that which was explained by Amṛtānanda in the passage beginning with "of the Śrīcakra and of the Self" and so forth, as being the rule for the *sāmānyārghya* (general offering water) alone— from the words "but when the substance has been held" up to "in the same way, the *arghya* specifically"— is [refuted].

The claim that this is the procedure for the *viśeṣārghya* (special water-offering) is unacceptable; for if it were the procedure for the *sāmānyārghya* (general water-offering), it would result in the omission of the latter portion following the worship of the solar digit (*sūryakalā*), which would necessitate looking toward another source [for authority]. Furthermore, between the two water-offerings, [the rule applies] to the former.

Furthermore, the description that the first part alone constitutes the latter [part], and the latter part alone constitutes the former, such that both combined constitute the complete ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*), contradicts the context of the text;
for even you accept the unity of the two four-hundred-verse sections (*catuḥśatī*) as a single treatise.

Furthermore, because it would result in the redundancy of prescribing the general *arghya* twice within a single tantra due to its being [already] established by consensus, this [objection] is of no consequence. Thus,
[the same applies] to the word *ambu* in the present *Catuḥśatī* and the word *dravya* in the subsequent *Catuḥśatī*.
This work has been composed by relying on its inherent natural sense (*svārasya*). However, if it is considered in this way:

since in the *Saṃhitārṇava*, the *Kalpasūtra*, and other texts, the conch alone is prescribed for the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), the option for gold and other materials applies only to the special water offering (*viśeṣārghya*) and so forth.

Because a specific injunction is observed, and because in the present verse the phrase "thereby one should satiate the Yoginīs" indicates that [this substance] serves as the means for the satiation of the Supreme Deity, this passage also refers specifically to the *viśeṣārghya* (special offering water). Therefore, in the expression "then with water," the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). This is according to the eighth chapter of the text.

The distinction is that the procedure for the special *arghya* (viśeṣārghya) involves the substance itself, whereas in this very text, the procedure for mixing water [with it] is given. Regarding its measurement, the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* states: "One should pour a mere portion of water into three parts of the special [substance]. As for the placement of the general *arghya* (*sāmānyārghya*), however—

It should be understood that because it is prescribed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the worship of Mārtaṇḍa, [the use of water] is implied. However, the intention of the *Manoramā* is that water alone serves as the instrument. The author of the *Lalitārcanacandrikā*, on the other hand, maintains that this is an injunction for a substitute (*pratinidhi*) in the event that the primary substance is unavailable. || 132 || 133 ||
O Goddess, having meditated upon the three cities endowed with the three seed-syllables.
O Goddess, one should perform the purification of the hands with the *sarvādya-vidyā*.

The ancient commentators maintain that the meaning is: "One should meditate upon the Śrīcakra, which consists of the three cities (*puratraya*)—namely the triad of Sun, Moon, and Fire—and is joined with the three seed-syllables (*vidyābīja*) of the Vidyā. However, it is also easy to explain that "the three cities" means "Tripura," and that "the three seed-syllables" is to be construed with the *karaśuddhi-nyāsa* (the ritual placement for purifying the hands).
In fact, in the *Tantrarāja*, following the two previously cited verses, a verse with a meaning nearly identical to this half-verse is recited:
"One should contemplate the three sections of Vidyā in the foundation, the heart, and the aperture."
"It is red because of the intensity of its radiance, and its own body is also red. Thus [it is said].

Its meaning has been stated in the *Manoramā*: "The radiance of the solar light of the second peak (kūṭa), located in the heart and intermingled with the fiery luster of the fire of the first peak situated at the base, is joined with that [first peak]."

While performing *prāṇāyāma*, one should contemplate the threefold light— both internal and external— which consists of the radiance of the third lunar segment (*khaṇḍacandra*) located at the *brahmarandhra*, and which has taken on a form merged with the aspect of the non-differentiated object of thought (*cetya*). By the term "first ignorance" (*ādyavidyā*), it is specifically the "childish ignorance" (*bālāvidyā*) that is previously intended.
Lest that [previous] application (*parāmarśa*) should inadvertently apply here as well, he says "beginning with *sarvā*.

One should cause the purification of the hands to be performed—that is, one should perform it—by means of the mantra called *Karaśuddhikarī*, which stands at the beginning of all the previously mentioned eightfold mantras. By this [mantra], [one consecrates] the *niṣādasthapati*.

The mention of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) here, as in the expression "one should cause [him] to sacrifice," is intended to indicate the role of the preceptor (*ācārya*). The procedure for this is stated in the *Kalpasūtra*: "Having performed the purification of the hands from Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, the third [Tattva], Mairdhya, down to the first Tala. One should repeat the three seed-syllables twice according to the logic of the "repeated staff" (*daṇḍakalita-nyāya*).

The meaning is that one should perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) by reciting "Salutation to the two middle fingers" (*madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ*) and so forth for the three [remaining] classes, then reciting the pair beginning with the thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*), and thereafter joining the six "sprouts" (*pallava*)—namely "Salutation to the palms" (*karatalābhyām*) and "Salutation to the backs of the hands" (*karapṛṣṭhābhyām*)—in sequence at the end of the six seed-syllables (*bīja*). This is the procedure. So it is.

This is called the Karaśuddhi-nyāsa (the ritual placement for purifying the hands). As for the fact that the authors of the *paddhatis* record a ritual placement using these very same seed-syllables (*bījas*) starting from the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and ending with the weapon (*astra*), they alone know the source for that. The sequence and the timing for the Karaśuddhi and other such ritual placements will be explained in the *Uttara-tantra*.
Then, O Īśvarī, one should offer the seat of the Self (Ātmāsana) and then the seat of the wheel (Cakrāsana).
"O Goddess, there is the seat of all mantras (*sarvamantrāsana*) and likewise the seat of the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished (*sādhyasiddhāsana*).

The terms 'seat of the self' (*ātmāsana*) and so forth are the names of the vidyās from the third to the sixth. Their application (*viniyoga*), however, is observed to be twofold. Regarding that, it is first stated in the *Kalpasūtra*:"

Having uttered the *māyā*, *kāma*, and *śakti* [syllables] and offered one’s own seat with "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Goddess," then having uttered the *śiva-yuga-bālā* [mantra], say "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Śrīcakra";
then having uttered the *śiva-bhṛgu-yuga-bālā* [mantra], say "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of all mantras," followed by *bhuvana-madana*.

Having uttered *KLEM* and performed the seat for the wheel-mantra deity with the mantra "Salutation to the seat of the Siddha-sādhya" (*sādhyasiddhāsanāya namaḥ*) upon the wheel using these three mantras;
for it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "Having performed the ritual of hand-purification, [one should worship] the deities of the four seats."
"One should place [the mantras] on the two feet, the two calves, the two knees, and at the mūlādhāra; thus it has been said."

In the *Jñānārṇava*, the combination of these two methods is observed; for while the root text prescribes the seat of the Self (*ātmasana*) by means of the verb "to give" (*dadāti*), it prescribes the remaining three seats by means of the verb "to perform" (*karoti*) in the subsequent verse, stating that one should then effect their protection.
Only when there is syntactic unity with the *Kalpasūtra* is the inherent intention [of the text] inferred. || 135 ||
Then one should perform the protection ritual with the family mantra previously mentioned. || 136 ||
By means of the application of the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) together with prostrations and other such acts.
Then, after the placement of the four seats (*caturāsananyāsa*), by means of the previously mentioned *kulavidyā*,

the *bālāvidyā*, and the three-syllabled mantra, one performs the application of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*)— namely, the heart, head, crest, armor, the three eyes, and the weapon— through the method of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

In the state of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), whatever yoga [is prescribed], by that [method] one should employ the words "heart" (*hṛdaya*) and so forth in the dative case at the end of the seed-syllables; that is to say, at the end of those [syllables], there is a salutation. By means of the words *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *vauṣaṭ*—which have the word *namaḥ* as their initial—[the deities] are to be addressed by way of their generic names (*jāti*).

The meaning is that one should perform protection by means of those well-known [mantras] according to that method. By the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) itself, the double repetition of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) is implied. And thus: *aiṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *klīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *sauḥ* to the tuft (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *aiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *klīṃ*...

The realized meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs with the respective mudrās using these six mantras: *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* and *sauḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Accordingly, at the conclusion of the placement of the four seats (*caturāsananyāsa*), the Kalpasūtra states:
"By repeating [the mantra] twice starting from Bālā..."
"The six limbs are fashioned by the placement of fingers numbering three, two, one, ten, three, and two.
Also, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"One should place [the mudrā] on the heart with three fingers, excluding the little finger and the thumb."
The knower of mantras should place [the mudrā] on the head with the middle and ring fingers.
Having placed the *śikhā* with the thumb, one should place the armor (*kavaca*) with the ten [fingers];
O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the placement of the eyes (*netra*) with those [mantras] prescribed for the heart.
"Then, O Dear One, one should place the Astra-mantra with the index and middle fingers;
the wise practitioner, having recited the mantra that provides self-protection twice, should perform the placement.
By this [it is understood that] the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of the Virgin Goddess Tripureśānī are also to be performed as before.

Thus, in the *Jñānārṇava*, although it is possible to refer to both types of six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*)— namely, the placement on the hands and the placement beginning with the heart— by means of the preceding term, [this occurs] in the section concerning the *Bālā* mantra (p. 85).

Because both types are traditionally taught: at the end of the placement of the five groups— having performed these, O Goddess of Gods, the placement of the hands follows next, by repeating the root-vidyā twice upon the surfaces of all the fingers.
This is because it is stated [in the scripture] as "the yoga of the sequence of the six limbs. Likewise, at the end of the installation of the nine yonis (*navayoninyāsa*), it is said:
"O Goddess, daughter of the Mountain, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in sequence with a double repetition, according to the numbers three, two, one, ten, three, and two."

And because of the statement "of the fingers," nevertheless, for the sake of agreement with other tantras, only the six limbs beginning with the heart (hṛdaya) are referred to. For this very reason, even in the present tantra, the term "six limbs" refers specifically to the heart and the others; this is also evident from the natural force of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "namaskāra etc. (namaskārādi).
Some, however, reading the root text as *namaskāraniyuktayā*, explain that the word *namaḥ* should be employed at the end of the vocative address of the deity for each individual mantra. Others,
on the other hand, read it simply as *namaskārādi*.
Omniscience, contentment, primordial awakening, sovereignty, eternal unimpaired power,
and infinite power— those who know the ritual rules declare these to be the six limbs of the all-pervading Maheśvara.

Based on this statement, they say that other phrases such as "to the abode of the power of omniscience" (*sarvajñatā-śakti-dhāmne*) should also be applied. Others, however, maintain that after reciting the complete *bālā* mantra,
one should recite only the single mantra "O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, protect me, protect me," joined with the [appropriate] caste-suffix (*jāti-yuktam*).

They apply [the mantras] to the heart and other [limbs]. These three points are indeed worthy of conviction through corroboration with other tantras; otherwise, they should be understood as invalidated by their mutual contradictions. As for that which is stated in the *Kalpasūtra* at the end of the *Karaśuddhi-nyāsa*: "Having uttered the word 'Kumārī'..."
"Protect me, protect me in the state of Mahātripurasundarī"—having thus placed his joined palms at the heart;

for there is not even a mention of the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) therein, so it is the previously mentioned *nyāsa* alone that is intended here. Regarding this, the moderns [hold]: since in the *Jñānārṇava Tantra* all the limbs are taught specifically for Bālā, she alone [is the subject].
The *prakṛti* (archetype) is [the Bālā-vidyā]. Those [mantras] recited immediately after it, beginning with Tripurabhairavī and ending with Śrīvidyā, are its *vikṛtis* (variants).

Consequently, by means of the *codaka* (general rule of extension), the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*)—along with all other ancillaries such as the morning rites—is obtained from that very source. And although in the *prakṛti* there is a double repetition of the *bālā*-seed syllables, [the same applies here].

In the modified rite (*vikṛti*), the repetition of the *kūṭa* twice is indeed proper by means of the principles that necessitate modification (*ūha*). As for the view held by the ancients—that the statement, "The six limbs of the maiden Tripureśānī are as before," is intended to sublate the modification obtained through logical principle (*nyāya*)—that is not correct; because [the rule] originates from the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Although the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is obtained by virtue of being situated within the section on the primary placement (*prākṛtanyāsakāṇḍa*) on page 86, [it is performed] after the four-seat placement (*caturāsananyāsa*), which occurs within the secondary placement (*vaikṛtanyāsa*) that follows the primary placement.

They argue that since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its attainment, and since the scriptural statement can be explained as being intent upon that [the six auxiliary sciences] alone, it is unreasonable to assume that its function extends even to the modification (*ūha*) and sublation (*bādha*).
This is incorrect; for the desired conclusion of yours is established even by the portion of the text stating, "And the six auxiliaries are as before."

This is because, according to the intention of the ancients, the phrase "by the maiden Tripureśānī" would otherwise lack purpose unless there were a modification (*ūha*) that overrides [the standard rule]; furthermore, the contradiction with the *Saṃhitāsūtra* and other texts is evident. || 136 ||
He describes the placement of the Vaśinī and others:
"In the locations of the head, forehead, between the eyebrows, throat, heart, and navel. (137)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) eight times, beginning from the base up to the arrangement (vyūhaka).
Here, by the word *gocara*, the wheel of *svādhiṣṭhāna* is meant;

it is treated as a singular compound because it is a part of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*). Regarding the phrase "as far as the *ādhāra*," the traditionalists explain that *ādhāra* refers to the *mūlādhāra*, and "up to" means extending from that base to the tips of the feet.
This means by the eight mantras of the goddesses of speech, beginning with Vaśinī; for,

since the ritual injunction following the six-limbed protection (*rakṣā-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) in the Sūtra prescribes only the placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight [goddesses] beginning with Vaśinī, and because their locations— starting from the head and so forth— are seen to be identical, it is that very same [placement] which is intended in the present verse as well.
It is determined as follows: in the *Uttaratantra*, however, after prescribing the fourfold nyāsa beginning with *karaśuddhi* to be performed twice, it is taught that during the second performance,
the *śrīkaṇṭhādi-nyāsa* is to be placed between the *rakṣā-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* and the *vāgdevatā-nyāsa*.
This is the distinction. However, the moderns (navyāḥ), considering that the claim by the ancients— that the word *gocara* signifies the *liṅga*—
is refuted by a lack of evidence, state that one should place the seventh *vāgdevatā* on the *mūlādhāra*, and the eighth from the base of the feet up to the tips of the toes.
That is not so; for the word *gocara* can refer to the place where one moves through water, and thus its application to the *upastha* (the perineum) is possible.
Furthermore, it is improper to abandon the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, which is situated immediately after the *maṇipūra*.
This is because [this sequence] is read with unanimous agreement in the *Saṃhitārṇava*, the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, and other such texts.

Since it is possible for the term *gocarapada* to be meaningful by virtue of its expansion through the *Kalpasūtra* as referring to the *liṅga*, and because it would otherwise be redundant, so too is the Sūtra: "Having uttered the fourfold *yādi* and the *vyūha*, [one says] 'Salutation to the Goddess of Speech, the Sovereign of All'—this is the *liṅga*. Thus ends the *vyūhaka*.

The word "up to" (*yāvat*) does not refer to another location, but rather refers precisely to the collection of locations mentioned, beginning with the head and ending with the forehead; that is, from the head down to the forehead,
and from the forehead up to the middle of the eyebrows.

It is also well-explained that [the sequence] from the middle of the eyebrows up to the throat, and so forth, is intended to indicate that each subsequent limb serves as the limit for the preceding one, starting from the base (ādhāra) up to the tips of the toes. However, this is not seen in the Sūtra. And this ritual placement (nyāsa) pertains to the mental worship of Vaśinī and the other goddesses.

The moderns [hold] that this is done "having accomplished the task. In the *Jñānārṇava*, within the section on ritual placement (*nyāsa*), in the verses concerning the extraction of the mantras of Vaśinī and the others:
"O Goddess of excellent vows, one should worship Vaśinī, the deity of speech."

The intention behind [the objection] "because of such recollections as... is as follows: that is incorrect, because those statements have the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*) as their primary purport; to assume they also have the ritual procedure of worship (*pūjāvidhi*) as their purport would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), since the mantras themselves constitute the instrument of worship.
This is because [the phrase] "one should worship" and so forth is appropriate as a mere restatement of what was already stated in the ritual procedure for the worship of the seventh enclosure:
"O Maheśvarī, at the end of the *ṭa*-group [of consonants], there is the seed-syllable of Vāyu situated upon the Earth."
Enriched by the moon-bindu upon the left ear, she is Vimalā, the sovereign lady of speech.
Thus, because worship is not mentioned by name in the verse concerning the extraction of the Vimalā-mantra, worship would not follow from it;

furthermore, because in other tantras worship is nowhere mentioned during the stage of ritual placement (nyāsa); and because, regarding the mental aspect of worship, no practitioner is introduced—therefore, this [objection] amounts to nothing. || 137 ||

Since the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) and other necessary rites will be explained later in the second half [of this work], he sets those aside and describes the meditation on the qualified form (*saguṇadhyāna*), which is not yet mentioned there,
with twenty-two verses beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*). Regarding that, in the Śruti [text], immediately after the phrase "consisting of all *lakṣmī*s,"...
He first explains the qualification "endowed with all the marks" as follows:
"Then [he saw] the Goddess, resembling a lotus, reddish like the rays of the rising sun. (138)
Resembling the hibiscus flower, comparable to the pomegranate blossom, resembling a ruby, and like water infused with saffron. (139)
Adorned with a network of tiny bells from the rubies of her shimmering crown,
she was surrounded by curling locks of hair resembling a swarm of black bees.
Her lotus-like facial orb resembles the fresh hue of the rising sun;
her soft forehead-ribbon is slightly curved like the crescent moon. (141)
The Supreme Goddess, whose creeper-like eyebrows have the form of the Pināka bow, whose eyes are playfully swaying with waves of joy and bliss; 142.
She whose golden earrings gleam with a mass of shimmering rays, and who,
with the full expanse of her beautiful cheeks, has surpassed the orb of the nectar-filled moon.
Her nose was clearly defined by the lines of creation fashioned by Viśvakarman and others;
her lips were red like copper, coral, or a bimba fruit, resembling nectar.
(88) She who has surpassed the ocean of the essence of sweetness with the sweetness of her smile, and who is adorned by a row of teeth as beautiful as pomegranate seeds and diamonds; 145.
She whose tongue illuminates the world with the seeds of jewels and speaks with pure speech, and who is adorned by a chin-region endowed with incomparable qualities. (146)
The great goddess Kambugrīvā, with arms as graceful as lotus stalks and delicate lotus-hands shaped like the petals of red lotuses.
The expanse of the sky was overspread by the moonlight of the nails upon her lotus-like hands, and her lofty breasts were adorned with strings of pearl necklaces. 148.
Her waist was beautifully adorned with three folds,
and she was graced by a navel that resembled an eddy in the river of loveliness.
She possessed hips adorned with a girdle fashioned from priceless jewels;
her rounded buttocks were like two elephants, and the line of hair upon them was like a supreme goad.
The Goddess has thighs as delicate as the graceful trunk of a plantain tree,
and she is resplendent with two knees that have the appearance of ruby crowns.
She was adorned with a pair of shanks resembling plantain trees in their beauty, with hidden ankles and a pair of feet whose foreparts surpassed the tortoise in grace. (152)
It was adorned with slender, long fingers and shining moon-like nails,
and it laughed with a continuous stream of splendor resembling a hundred moons.
She possesses the hue of the Japā flower, red as the Sindūra of the Lauhitya river;
she is clothed in red garments and holds a noose and a goad raised in her hands. || 154 ||
Seated upon a red lotus, adorned with red ornaments, she has four arms and three eyes, and she holds five arrows and a bow. (155)
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor,
and she held a betel-roll offered by Indra, the lord of the Karandavas.
Her body is crimson with the intense saffron of great musk;
she is enriched with every erotic adornment and decorated with all ornaments. (157)
(89) Her lotus feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels on the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
she is the one who generates joy for the world and brings delight to the universe. || 158 ||
The Goddess who attracts the world, whose form is the cause of the world, who consists of all mantras, and who is beautiful with every auspiciousness. (159)

She consists of all prosperity, is eternal, and is gladdened by supreme bliss; she resembles a lotus and possesses two forms characterized by contraction and expansion. This is understood through five similes, beginning with the rays of the rising sun: 1. Like the rising sun, she is the source of light for the world. 2. Like a lotus, she expands and contracts according to the needs of her devotees. 3. Like the moon, she bestows cooling peace upon those scorched by the heat of worldly existence. 4. Like a lightning flash, she appears suddenly to those whose minds are purified. 5. Like a wish-fulfilling gem, she grants all desires to those who seek refuge in her.

[She is] the Goddess, whose nature is a smooth, abundant, and lustrous radiance, inseparable from the light [of consciousness], characterized by a unique redness. She is filled with—meaning pervaded by—curly locks of hair that are dark as the black bees, with tips slightly curled. "Freshly rosy" refers to the rising sun; it is not the "slightly crescent moon" of the eighth day.

But she stands in the second [house] and so forth. She possesses a nose that is as straight as the thread used by Viśvakarman at the time of the primordial creation—referring to the Śaiva bow named Pināka—since it is observed that in the construction of houses and other structures, the straight Brahma-thread is laid down first. Or else:
She whose nose is such that the Vedas—the threads and indicative statements for the initial creation of His entire work—are clearly manifest in the form of her breath;
for according to the Vedic revelation, "The Vedas are His very breath. Having first created the Vedas...

Furthermore, this is established by the doctrinal tenet that creation was produced by those very [beings]. The copper is from the land of Nepal, for it alone is of the highest quality. [Her lips] are like nectar, delimited by the edges of her lips; they are the foremost in the splendor of a gentle smile through the sweetness of that smile. If a pomegranate seed were indeed a diamond known as *vajra*...

Then the teeth would be like that gem; or rather, "vajra" means a thunderbolt, used here as a metaphor for firmness, since we see its usage in medical texts such as: "Even if the teeth are loose, they grow back resembling a vajra. She was characterized by her arms; the third case ending is used here in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).

A cloth known as a *vitāna* (canopy) or *ulloca* (overhead awning) has been spread out over him. She is beautifully adorned by that middle region—the part of the waist—which is endowed with the very strength of the three folds (*trivalī*). By this, the slenderness of the waist and the fact that the three folds take the form of golden bands are suggested.
An *āvarta* is the swirling motion of waters. Her hips were like a *bimba*—a circular orb—due to their fullness;
she was one whose excellent goad was the line of hair (*romarājī*) upon that [hip], like an elephant’s.
A crown made of rubies is a *ṭopikā*. She was completely conquered by the forepart of her foot—that is, by the tip of her toe.
She who holds a tortoise and a turtle;
she whose left and right hands, positioned upwards, shine with a noose and a goad; and she who, with her lower left and right hands, bears five arrows and a bow—she is thus described.
As it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "The five arrows, beautiful and possessing the form of lotuses,
and the sugarcane bow, endowed with the qualities of bees."
The noose is fashioned from coral creepers and endowed with threads of fine linen;
clear like the crescent moon, the goad is capable of drawing [the elephant] toward itself.
"In the lower right hand [he holds] arrows, while in the lower left is a bow;
in the upper left is a reddish noose, and in the upper right is a supreme goad. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, regarding the five arrows in the *Kādimata*:
"O Īśvarī, the five flowers are said to be the lotus (*kamala*), the white water-lily (*kairava*), the red water-lily (*rakta*), the *kahlāra*, and the *indīvare*, as well as the *sahakāra*.
Therefore, in the compound of the *Saṃhitā* passage, "the lotuses themselves are the vowels (*akāra*)," the analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows. But as for the goad (*aṅkuśa*)...

"Made of gold" (sauvarṇa) is the oral tradition from the mouth of the Guru; the rest is clear. The connection with what follows is: "having remembered such a Nityā, the Great Nityā, named Tripurasundarī. (138–139)
Having recollected the Great Tripura-mudrā in the form of invocation, || 160 ||
The supreme practitioner, having invoked Mahātripurasundarī with the previously mentioned vidyā accompanied by obeisances and other rites, O fortunate one, [should proceed]. (161)
Having visualized [the deity] within the center of the wheel, one should then commence the worship;
that is, having formed the Mahātripura-mudrā, known as the Trikhaṇḍā-mudrā—this is the remainder [of the instruction].
With the previously mentioned invocation-vidyā, at its conclusion, [one should add] "namas" and so forth, or "nama iha āgaccha āgaccha" (obeisance, come here, come here).

Having performed the syntactical connection of the sentence, some explain according to what they have heard that one should invoke the Goddess into the point (bindu) in the center of the wheel, and having meditated upon her again as residing in that point, one should begin the worship.
