Others, however, [say] regarding the Great Tripura-mudrā...
Having meditated upon the nine mudrās, beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Yonimudrā, within the nine locations starting from the Mūlādhāra and ending at the Brahmarandhra,
one should invoke the Goddess by appending the five-syllable mantra "Subhage Namaḥ" to the end of the invocation-vidyā.

They say the meaning is "one should worship. However, the moderns [hold that] by the phrase "in the center of the wheel" (*cakramadhye*) in the *Jñānārṇava*—namely, in the passage: "Having invoked [the deity] in the center of the wheel with the three-part mantra (*trikhaṇḍā-vidyā*)... (p. 91)—...
The middle section of the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, formed by joining the palms with a cluster of flowers,

is said to be the triangular wheel (*tri-kona-cakra*) at its center. By means of that, having summoned [the deity] into the flowers and projected the form there, one should contemplate it as seated upon the pedestal through the offering of the handful of flowers.

They say that one should worship [the deity]. And this is appropriate, because invocation consists in the observation of a specific delimitation, and thus requires a delimiting form; and because the conceptualization of a form has the vidyā of the form as its instrument.

Since the recitation of the *mūrti-vidyā* (the ritual sequence for the form) would otherwise be inexplicable, it is necessary that the very act of invoking— consisting of projecting the light of consciousness residing within the heart outward by means of the mantra,
thereby confining the form within limits and seating it upon the pedestal— is the actual meaning of the term "invocation" (*āvāhana*).

For it is observed that even a complex entity consisting of many parts— beginning with the offering of the *avadāna* and ending with the final gift— is regarded as a single object. Therefore, having meditated upon the form by means of the *mūrtividya* (the knowledge of the form) to be described— which was taught by the ancient teachers (*pūrva-guru*)— within the center of the wheel, specifically within the triangle situated in the middle of the *añjali*.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "Having visualized [the deity] and having invoked [her] into the *bindu* by means of the invocation-vidyā, one should worship her.

This is to be explained because the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is set aside by the order of meaning (*arthakrama*). By this, consistency with the *Kalpasūtra* is also achieved. In reality, however—[even though she is] all-pervading...

Since even the grasping of only a single portion [of the Supreme Śiva’s radiance] according to the capacity of one's own intellect takes the form of producing limitation, it is possible for this to be denoted by the term *āvāhana* (invocation); therefore, the conceptualization of a physical form (*mūrti*) is not a constituent part of the meaning of the word *āvāhana*. Consequently, and so forth...

The unburdened meaning is as follows: having brought the internal radiance from the *trikhaṇḍā* [mantra] by means of the invocation-vidyā ending with *namaḥ*, and having cast it into the *bindu* via a flower, one should meditate upon the form described in the verse of meditation and perform worship; however, this is not the case for the *mūrti-vidyā* according to the method of this Tantra.

It is a constituent part of the *saṃcintanā*. For this very reason, its non-extraction prior [to that] is consistent. Its extraction in the *Uttaratantra*, however, is for the purpose of its application (*viniyoga*) in ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Nor is it the case that, having extracted it in the *Uttaratantra*, the *mūrtividyā* is mentioned as the seventh: "And that goddess is proclaimed as the seventh *mūrtividyā*."

It must be stated that the assignment of this name has as its sole purpose the communication of its application in the conceptualization of the form (mūrti). This is because the name is established as serving another purpose— namely, practical usage— in passages such as "One should place the form upon the support" (ādhāre vinyasen mūrtim), where the name proves effective for conventional discourse.
Therefore, the reading "namaskāreṇa yuktyā" as stated by the author of the *Artharatnāvalī* should indeed be accepted.
Here, by the word "pūjā" (worship), the offerings (*upacāra*)—whether five, ten, sixteen, or sixty-four—are intended collectively. Thus, according to the distinction of capacity...
The classification is established;

for although the number [of deities] takes many forms— such as sixteen and so on— due to the differences in the tantras based on whether certain categories of entities, such as those brought forth by meditation (*dhyānāvāhana*), are included or excluded.

(p. 92) By the very fact that meditation (*dhyāna*) and invocation (*āvāhana*) are specified separately from the act of worship (*pūjā*) through the two terms "having reflected" (*saṃcintya*) and "having invoked" (*āvāhya*), it is indicated that the sequence of the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and so forth, as enumerated in the *Tantrarāja* and other scriptures, is precisely what should be observed here. Furthermore, another indicator for this is found at the end of the chapter.
We shall explain [this]. 160 || 161 ||
O Goddess, they are the drops of Śiva and Agni, the drops of the sun and fire. || 162 ||
O Maheśvarī, the pair of seed-syllables that has arisen, joined with Māyā and the digit of the crescent moon, should be applied both simultaneously and in successive order. (163)
Therefore, as long as the Mothers consist of the splendor of Māyā, they are to be worshipped.
Śiva is the letter *ha*; Agni and Vahni are the letter *ra*. By the word "Dinakṛt" (the Sun-maker), the letter *śa* is meant.
Regarding the section on the letter *śa*:
"The Teacher is Dinakṛt-śayana, Subhagā, and Visphuliṅginī."

Thus, according to the *Kośa*: *Māyā* is the fourth vowel (*turyasvara*). That [vowel] is to be placed after *Śiva* (the letter *ha*) and *agni* (the letter *ra*), as well as after the sun (*dinakṛt*, the letter *sa*) and fire (*vahni*, the letter *ra*). Following that are the *bindu*, the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and the digit (*kalā*). From this sequence, the pair of seed-syllables (*bījayugma*) known as *Māyā* and *Lakṣmī*—namely *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*—is produced; by means of these, all the Mothers [are invoked].

"Venerable ones" (*pūjyāḥ*). The indeclinable *yāvat* here has the sense of totality. Furthermore, these two seed-syllables are conventionally referred to by the Tantrikas as the "two *tāra*s. Since this *dvitārī* is employed solely for the worship of the Śakti, it is not to be used for the worship of the male deity (*puṃdevatā*) or for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of female deities (*strīdevatā*), and so forth.

Even in the worship of the Śaktis, where there is a specific injunction for other mantras— as in the worship of Vaśinī and the others, or Kāmeśvarī and the others— there is no application of the two Tāras,
precisely because they are not required and because the general rule is set aside by that which is specifically prescribed. For this very reason:

Regarding the *Kāmākarṣiṇī* and others, when a conflict arises between two *tāra*s (oṃs) due to the rule concerning vowels, the restatement [of the mantra] is justified for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*); this is the meaning established by logic (*nyāya*).
However, in other systems (*tantra*), the authors of the ritual manuals (*paddhati*) employ two *tāra*s everywhere. But in the *Kalpasūtra*, however—

It has been stated that at the beginning of all mantras there is a conjunction with the *tritārī*, and that the *tritārī* consists of Vāc, Māyā, and Kamalā. Furthermore, its recitation occurs only after entering the sacrificial hall;
therefore, it should be understood that its application is not mandatory in the mantras for preliminary rites (*kṛtya*) prior to that point. || 162 ||
He states the remaining mantras for the deities who are to be worshipped:
Tripurā, Tripureśī, Sundarī, and Puravāsinī. (164)
Śrī, Mālinī, Siddhāmbā, and Mahātripurasundarī—these are the manifest, as well as the secret, the more secret, and the supreme [mantras]. (165)
(p. 93) One should worship the nine Cakrayoginīs by their names.

The nine words beginning with *Tripura* are the designations for the Mistress of the Wheels (*cakreśvarī*) starting with Trailokyamohanā. In the term *Tripureśī*, *Tripurā* is a separate word; this applies likewise to [the subsequent terms] such as *Īśī*.

That which is construed as a qualifier with respect to the seven words is compounded; by this, the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) and the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) apply. However, when compounded with the word *śrī*, there is no masculine form, because its inclusion in the *priyā* group is accepted. Regarding the word *puravāsinī*:

Even though it is construed as a qualifier, it is not compounded; for its meaning is "she whose former part [purā] consists of the word 'three' (tri)," thus the name *Tripuravāsinī* is established. By this, the following meanings are accomplished: 1. Tripurā, 2. Tripureśī, 3. Tripurasundarī.

Tripuravāsinī (4), Tripurāśrī (5), Tripuramālinī (6), Tripurasiddhā (7), Tripurāmbā (8), and Mahātripurasundarī— these are the names of the nine Mistress of the Wheels (cakreśvarīs). The names beginning with "Prakaṭā" (Manifest) and so forth, however,
are the names of the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇa-devatās) residing in those respective wheels, namely the Yoginīs such as Aṇimā, Siddhi, and the rest.

The term "collective form" (*samaṣṭirūpa*) refers to the inclusion of the six names— *Kulakaula*, *Nigarbha*, *Rahasya*, *Atirahasya*, and *Parāpararahasya*— by means of the word "Supreme" (*parā*). In another tantra, the deities of the eighth and ninth enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) are called *Parāpararahasyāḥ*.
Two names are recorded as *parāparātirahasyā*. Therefore, there is an option [regarding the name]. In the phrase *cakrayoginyaḥ*, this is implied by the word *cakra*, which denotes a collection:
the word *yoginī* is employed only after words such as *prakaṭā* that denote the aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) of yoginīs.
"Not after words such as *aṇimā* which denote individual entities" means [the following]:
those *Cakreśvarīs* and *Cakrayoginīs*. "By names" means by the names *Tripurā* and so forth, by the names *Prakaṭā* and so forth, and by the names *Aṇimā* and so forth; thus, first...
The method for formulating the mantra is as follows: two *tāra*s (oṃ), then the respective name, and at the end, the seven-syllable mantra (*saptākṣarī*).

Following the word *tripurā* and others, the word *cakreśvarī* [is added]; following the word *prakaṭa* and others, the word *yoginī*; following the word *aṇimā* and others, the word *siddhi*; and following the word *kāmākarṣiṇī* and others, [the same].

Furthermore, that "the *kalāpada* should be employed" and so forth is established by tradition (*saṃpradāya*) and established by indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*), as will become clear in various places. || 164 || 165 ||

Now, in order to specify the names of the Yoginīs beginning with Prakaṭā for the purpose of constructing the mantras, and because it is conducive to the contemplation of one's own self as the sole remainder through the summary of all [the deities], [the author describes] first the Cakra.

In accordance with the first and subsequent words found in such scriptural passages as "it becomes the deluder of the three worlds," and while suggesting that the worship of the lower [levels] is primary according to the order of dissolution (saṃhārakrama), he says:
Aṇimā at the western gate, and Laghimā also at the northern.
At the eastern gate, however, [one should place] Mahimā; at the southern, that called Īśitva; at the northwest, that called Vaśitva; and in the northeast, Prākāmya. (167)
Likewise, the accomplishment of enjoyment is in the southeast, while the accomplishment of will-power is in the southwest;
the accomplishment of attainment is below, and likewise, all desires are fulfilled above.
Thus, O Goddess, these great goddesses grant the accomplishment of all aims.
Upon the first square line, the ten *siddhis*, beginning with *aṇimā*, are to be worshipped.
Among them, the first four, beginning with *aṇimā*, are in the directions starting from the west and ending with the south.
The final tetrad, beginning with *vaśitva*, is located in the intermediate directions starting from the northwest (*nirṛti*) and ending with the wind (*vāyu*);

the remaining two are in the downward and upward directions—this is the distinction. Here, since the rule that "the east is the direction between the worshiper and the object of worship" is established for the worship of other deities, it applies here as well.

Some respect this; others, however, relying on the ancient tradition established by Śaṅkara, say: "When the worshipper faces west, then what is behind the Goddess is the west, and what is in front of her is the east;
but when he faces east, then what is in front of the Goddess is the west."

Regarding that, the oral tradition of the Guru states that the orientation of the directions is determined as follows: first, on the side facing the opposite direction from the one previously mentioned, the directions are established exactly as they are when worshipping while facing east. Consequently, in the case of worship performed while facing west, the *aṇimā* siddhi is located behind the Goddess, and [the *laghimā* siddhi] is on the Goddess’s left side.
"Laghimā-siddhi," and so forth. Between those two, [one performs worship] with "vaśitva.
According to the sequence beginning with "pākāmya" between *laghimā* and *mahimā*, [the worship is performed];
however, in the case of worship facing the other directions, *aṇimā* is placed in front of the Goddess.
The worship is performed in the sequence beginning with *laghimā* on the right side, *vaśitva* between those two, and so forth.
That both [of these views] are merely the attribution of one's own fault— arising from not having seen other tantras—
to the feet of the venerable Teacher (*deśika*) is recorded thus in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Goddess, when one raises the wheel facing the northern direction,
then that northern direction, O Goddess, is declared to be the eastern direction itself.
O Queen of the Gods, when the practitioner facing west raises the wheel, then the northeast becomes the southeast; of this there is no doubt.
Then the western direction should be known as the eastern direction, without a doubt;
likewise, the northwest becomes the southeast, and the northeast becomes the southwest.
"When the practitioner facing south raises the wheel, then the east is the right [side], while the southwest is the direction of fire.
Also, in the *Kulārṇava*: "When the practitioner, facing whatever direction, worships Tripurā..."

"Then the Goddess was behind, while Tripurā was in front, facing east and west. Thus, [the worshipper may face] either the east with the dual form— both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*)— or face another direction as prompted by a specific desire, as will be explained in the second chapter.
In every performance of the worship of Tripurasundarī,

the rule is established that the direction between the object of worship and the worshipper is the west (pratīcī). Consequently, the power of atomization (aṇimā-siddhi) is situated in front of the Goddess, and the power of levity (laghimā) is on her right side.
Between these two, in the intermediate corner, the rule should be understood as being of a single form, beginning with "vaśitva" (mastery) and so forth.
Below, between Nirṛti and Varuṇa; above, between Īśāna and Pūrva. As it is stated in the *Tattvavimarśinī*:
"The place of the upper [direction] is proclaimed to be between the directions of Indra and Īśāna;
the place of the other is proclaimed to be between Nirṛti and Ambupa.
And thus, one should place *prāptisiddhi* between the west and Nirṛti.

It results in the conclusion that, having performed worship [of the goddesses], one should worship the accomplishment of all desires (*sarvakāmasiddhi*) between Indra and Īśāna. As for those authors of ritual manuals (*paddhati*) who desire a transposition of the locations for these two accomplishments,

their statement regarding the procedure for the placement of the mudrās (*mudrānyāsa*) during the placement of the Root Goddess and the others— [The text here would continue with the specific ritual description.]
The root of delusion.

In front, on the right, on the bamboo-pole, on the left, and in the intermediate space, as well as above and below—these are the ten mudrās. Thus, according to the ritual procedure, the upward direction comes first.

Because of the mention [of the directions]—namely, that one should place the ten mudrās in the four intermediate spaces between the east, south, west, and north, as well as above and below—it follows from the meaning of that [text]. One should not, however, be deluded into thinking that this constitutes an option;
for by the force of the scriptural statement, even if such a sequence is accepted for the placement of the mudrās (*mudrā-nyāsa*), it applies to the worship (*pūjā*) as well.

Because there is no authoritative evidence for adopting that [position], and because a fixed option between the sequential and reverse orders of the upper and lower directions is observed in the *Prapañcasāra* and other texts;
therefore, in this tantra, on the third line of the earth-pavilion (*bhūgṛha*), by explicit statement (*kaṇṭharaveṇa*)...
Even though it is not explicitly mentioned by name, when that worship is indicated by the *nyāsa*, the sequence already established for the *siddhis* is appropriate.

Alternatively, since the sequence of the two directions is established by the very means of cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*), the sequence of *nyāsa* alone applies even to the worship of the *mudrās*. This is the case for the worship of the *siddhis* as well.
The attainment of perfection occurs specifically in the downward direction. Here, the three words beginning with *aṇimā* end in the feminine suffix *ḍāp*, not in *neman*.
Even when compounded with the word *siddhi*, there is no change to the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to established tradition. The same applies to the words *īśitva* and *avaśitva*.

Some also maintain that *prākāmya* and *īśitva* end in *-ghaṭṭa*. From the indicative evidence of such statements as "likewise in the south-eastern [direction] for the accomplishment of enjoyment" (*bhuktisiddhiṃ tathā'gneyyām*), and from the *Kalpasūtra*, it is established that the word *siddhi* is indeed a constituent part of the mantra. || 166 || 167 || 168 ||
(p. 96) He indicates the eight Mothers who are to be worshipped on the second square line:
Brahmāṇī at the western gate and Māheśī also at the northern [gate]. || 169 ||
One should place Kaumārī at the eastern gate, Vaiṣṇavī at the southern,
Vārāhī at the north-western, and likewise Aindrī in the northeast region.
O Great Goddess, one should also worship Cāmuṇḍā in the southeast and Mahālakṣmī in the southwest, as well as the eight Mothers who grant all desires. (171)
As before, two sets of four [deities] are to be worshipped according to their respective directions; however, the deities of the zenith and nadir do not exist here.

Accordingly, he will state in the section on the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Root Goddess and others: "Furthermore, excluding those of the zenith and nadir, the group of eight beginning with Brahmāṇī is [placed] on the right shank, and they are as described previously."
In this context, "worship" (pūjana) refers, according to tradition, to the offering of flowers and other substances as well as the pouring of drops (bindu).
Regarding that, the offering of flowers and so forth is performed once, while each libation (tarpaṇa) consists of three drops;

thus, the dual usage of the plural form and the word "threefold" (tridhā) in the *Jñānārṇava*—in the phrases "one should sacrifice in many ways" and "one should worship threefold"—is intended to convey this.
The statement from the *Svatantra-tantra*— “One should offer libations (tarpaṇas) into the mouth of the Goddess three times with the root-vidyā”— also serves as supporting evidence. Thus,
this dual pouring (ubhayaprakṣepa), consisting of both worship (*pūjana*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*), is contained within that mantra.

There is mention of both [the deities]. The mantras become such as: *hrīṃ śrīṃ brahmāṇīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi tarpayāmi* (I worship and satisfy the sandals of Brahmāṇī), and so forth. This is because, in the Tantric system, it is logical for a word expressing a case-factor (*karmakāraka*) to be construed with two verbs through *tantra* (elliptical repetition). For this very reason, in the case of Smārta rituals...

The learned (śiṣṭas) formulate mantras such as: "I invoke Gaurī, I establish her, I worship her, obeisance," and so forth. However, the moderns (navyas) state that the practice should be: "I worship the sandals of Brahmāṇī;
I satiate the sandals of Brahmāṇī. According to that view:

It must be considered whether these two are two separate mantras, or whether this entire sequence constitutes a single mantra. In the first case, there is a lack of evidence. In the second case, it would follow that each [hand] is to be employed individually;
for instance, at the very moment the right hand is occupied elsewhere, the left hand [would have to be used].

Since the distinction between the times for worship (*pūjā*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) is established here by the difference in the mantras employed, the [use of the] right hand is not obtained even for the libation. Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of using the left hand because the *tattvamudrā* alone is prescribed as the instrument for the libation.
One should offer libations as before three times with the *tattvamudrā*;
this *tattvamudrā* is said to be formed by the thumb and the ring finger.
Since that [objection] does not arise due to the observation of such statements in other tantras,
nor because its conclusion is provided by the statement from the *Svatantra-tantra*: "O Pārvatī, one should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand."

It should be stated that since the simultaneous performance of worship and libation is established by logic, the mention of the left hand is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and cannot serve as a restrictive injunction (*upasaṃhāraka*). For this very reason, the *Sūtra* of the Chāndogas states: "They cast away the blades of grass with their left hands."
Since the right hands are already occupied during the outward procession for the *bahispavamāna* chant and the taking hold of the Adhvaryu and others, the left hands are obtained by default;
thus, the mention of "with the left" (*savyaiḥ*) is merely a restatement. Consequently, even the *pravṛtta-homa* performed at that time is to be done with the left hand alone.

The established doctrine of the Sāmavedins is consistent with this. Furthermore, the insertion of a word ending in the accusative case— which is postulated solely due to the requirement of the expression "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi)— must necessarily take the form "Brahmāṇīm," and cannot contain the word "pādukā."

Because there is no evidence [for it]. Since the *Saṃhitā* statement, "One should utter 'I worship the sandals' (*pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*)," establishes that only the ritual action itself is to be performed with the *tarpaṇa* mantra, there is no evidence for its repetition; for in the latter case, the single utterance itself fulfills the requirement of both [the mantra and the action], and thus there is no basis for its recurrence.

In reality, however, because of the mention of *homa* (fire-oblation) in the aforementioned *saṃhitā* passage, the insertion of the word "tarpayāmi" (I satisfy) occurs specifically in the *tarpaṇa* (libation) that is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *puraścaraṇa*. This libation, moreover, is designated by the term "worship" (*pūjayati*) itself.

Because it has already arisen, there is no further requirement for words expressive of that [action]. For this very reason, injunctive statements are seen as "one should worship" (*pūjayet*) alone, and not as "one should satisfy with libations" (*tarpayet*). As for the statement of the Navyas, "O Goddess, one should offer a flower with the mudrā known as Jñāna," by means of this [statement], the worship with flowers—

They say that because of the concluding statement, "In that way, there should be libation and worship," one obtains the accompaniment of libation (tarpaṇa) in the worship with flowers; however, this must be examined, for since both the flower-libation and the worship are merely enjoined as having the root-vidyā as their instrument, how can there be such an application?
Granted that the attainment of *sāhitya* (conjunction) occurs through tradition alone, nevertheless,
since *sāhitya* consists in being simultaneous, that sentence serves to convey the status of being a constituent part existing at the same time.

Because the word *pūjayāmi* (I worship) alone indicates the primary act of flower-worship as the culmination [of the rite], it is that term which is employed, and not *tarpayāmi* (I satisfy). For this very reason, the moderns have stated regarding the act of libation (*tarpaṇa*) alone: "Even though flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) are present, [the libation] is subordinate to the worship."

Because its sole purpose is libation (*tarpaṇa*), it lacks the status of an independent worship (*svatantrapūjā*); therefore, when using the expression "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*), there is no requirement for the inclusion of the word "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*). Furthermore, according to the rules of libation, this [rite] cannot be designated by the verb "to worship" (*pūjayati*) because it is merely a constituent part of worship. Thus, the *Kalpasūtra* states:

One should perform the worship of all the deities of the wheels by casting unbroken rice grains and flowers from the right hand, which fall together with the first drop from the *śrīpātra* held between the thumb and ring finger of the left hand. And not of this...

Because it is recited in the section (*prakaraṇa*) concerning Śyāmā, it does not refer to Lalitā; for later on, since several ancillaries of the worship of Lalitā—such as "the practitioner of the *japa* of Lalitā shall not eat sugarcane," and so forth—are to be enjoined, the section concerning Lalitā continues even further on. Nor...

Even so, it must be said that this [subordinate context] is set aside by the [subordinate] section (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). For it is possible for even that [section] to be set aside by a sentence (*vākya*) supported by the scriptural text (*śruti*) of all the words in their unrestricted sense. Furthermore, in that case...

In the statement "tarpaṇa-pūjanam" (libation and worship), since libation itself is proclaimed to be of the nature of worship, the attainment of both [libation and worship] is implied by the very use of the word "pūjayāmi" (I worship). Otherwise, according to your own view, the usage would have to result in "I worship with flowers" and "I satisfy with drops."
Since the word *tarpaṇa* (satisfying) can possibly refer to the *bindu* (the drop) for the purpose of bringing about satisfaction,

and because the injunctions regarding consecrations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth must be established as having equal application (*sāmānavidhya*) to both the primary substance and its substitute, the term *tarpaṇa* is employed instead of terms such as *kāraṇa* (causing).

Because it is easy to pronounce; for this very reason, the formulation "I worship with libations" (*tarpaṇaiḥ pūjayāmi*) would be more appropriate—thus, that [other suggestion] is trivial. Therefore, in order to favor the Vedic terminology, one should say only "I worship the sandals of Brahmāṇī" (*brahmāṇīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*), and then offer a flower and a drop (*bindu*).
It is logical that one should insert [the mantra] according to tradition. Furthermore, if one considers it thus:

since the text "svāhā homa" occurs in the context of "having understood this very secret place, one should worship the wheel," it follows that even the *homa* which is an ancillary part of the worship belongs within the *naivedya*.

Because of this injunction, even its occurrence in that [specific] context serves only to introduce libation (*tarpaṇa*) as an ancillary part of worship; therefore, even then, it pertains either specifically to the injunction for libation where the verbal root *tarpayati* itself is used— as in "where one should satisfy [them] with that, together with the Yoginīs," and so forth— or else it refers to the independent rite of worship known as libation.

The application of the rule [of *samprasāraṇa*] does not extend here as it does elsewhere due to traditional usage; for the root *pūj* has been established as having a different meaning— namely, that it signifies the simultaneous offering of the *bindu*— by way of refuting the claim that it merely denotes the scattering of flowers.

For there is no evidence to justify assuming that the tradition functions to indicate the insertion of other words within the mantras of those [limbs]; for this very reason, in the *Kalpasūtra*, only this much of the mantra is extracted in the context of the primary Mahāgaṇapati-enclosure (*āvaraṇa*). As it says:

In all cases regarding the names of the deities, one should utter the name preceded by "Śrī" and followed by "pādukām," and then append the eight-syllable formula "pūjayāmi. When the eight-syllable sentence is thus produced by joining "pūjayāmi" after "Śrī" and "pādukā," that [formula] applies to the names of the deities.
The meaning is that one should join [the mantras]. By this—ending with the word "having uttered"—the injunction for the four-syllabled mantra is established;

thus, the doubt that the eight-syllabled mantra, which is enjoined again thereafter, would necessarily result in being accompanied by the word *tarpayāmi*, is refuted. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Raśmimālākhaṇḍa* of the *Kalpasūtra*:

The extraction of the mantra for the *lalitāṅga-pādukā* is established as the eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣarī*) from the name of one's own guru. This is because, according to the perspective defined here, the eight-syllabled phrase takes the form "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) and "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*). [This applies] to the *pādukā* mantra.
For [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence that one could not grasp the meaning of the phrase "I worship the Śrīpādukā.

Therefore, even the conjecture that the word "in the names" (nāmasu) is to be construed with the word "having uttered" (uccārya) is refuted precisely because it contradicts the Pādukā-mantra; so, enough with this elaboration. However, furthermore—
The insertion of the word *mātṛ* after the words *brahmāṇī* and so forth should be determined according to one's own tradition (*yathā-sampradāyam*). Thus ends the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*).
(p. 99) Although in another Tantra the worship of the *mudrās* is mentioned right here, in this present Tantra, regarding that [matter]...

Since the threefold conceptualization will be explained in the eighth chapter, it is easily understood that the enclosure is completed by those two [powers] and the group of Mothers of Accomplishment (*siddhi-mātṛ-gaṇa*) alone. By this, it is meant that in the scripture,
having first introduced the wheel, there arises the group of eight beginning with *aṇimā*, together with the group of eight measures (*mātrā*).

"It becomes manifest, it becomes manifest"—thus, the mention of two groups alone is appropriate. [Objection: But surely this is consistent only with the view that the *bhūpura* consists of two lines. However, in the view of a single line, since the groups of *siddhis*, *mātṛkās*, and *mudrās* would have no other recourse but that single line, [the repetition]...

Furthermore, worship [of the three lines] is indeed appropriate. In the view that there are three lines and three *gaṇas*, a determination based on the principle of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyanyāya*) is logical; however, in your position—where there are three lines and two *gaṇas*—it would follow that there is no possibility of determining the locations for the worship of the two *gaṇas*.

Because there is no rule governing the correspondence of numbers (*yathāsaṃkhyanyāya*), there is a lack of determining evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether, upon grasping any two lines, one should take the first and middle, the middle and last, or the first and last—
since [the matter] has been settled in the case of the *cakranyāsa* by taking the first and middle.
If it is argued that because there is no distinction in their being present [before one], the group of mudrās would also necessarily be worshipped on the third line, we say:

no. For there is no fault in worshipping the two groups of Siddhis (or Mātṛs) within the two central paths between the three lines, in accordance with the principle of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Therefore, it has been said:
In the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*, within the section on the Full Consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*),
it is stated that [the deities] are located in the ten sites of the Siddhas situated within the two corridors between the three square lines,
as well as in the eight sites of Brāhmī and the others, and so forth. And this being the case...

It should not be argued that because the sixteen or eight intervening spaces between the petals of the sixteen- and eight-petaled lotuses are likewise sixteen or eight in number without distinction, there would arise a doubt regarding the locations for the worship of the deities to be described hereafter; for this very reason:
This is because of the inferential evidence (*jñāpaka*) that one must not leave any empty space between the two petals;

by this, the prohibition stated in the *Bhūtabhairava-tantra*—beginning with "O Maheśānī, whoever should fashion filaments within this yantra"—is also logically justified. Furthermore, if [the filaments were present] in the root [of the lotus], among the group of Siddhis...

Since the two groups of Mothers are mentioned in pairs at each of the two gates, it is stated that the author of the present Tantra intends for the *bhūpura* (enclosure) to have only two lines, as is the consensus of the *Tantrarāja*. Therefore, according to the method taught in the *Tantrarāja*, one should worship the two groups within the two lines; and in the middle of those two...
It should be noted that we shall also explain later how, according to the method of this Tantra, each individual group (gaṇa) constitutes a separate enclosure (āvaraṇa). || 169 || 170 || 171 ||
Now, he indicates the deities to be worshipped on the sixteen petals:
the one whose form is the attraction of desire, the one whose form is the attraction of intellect, the one who attracts the ego, and the one whose form is the attraction of sound. || 172 ||
She whose form is the attraction of touch, and she whose form is the attraction of form;
she whose form is the attraction of taste, and she whose form is the attraction of smell. || 173 ||
She whose form is the attraction of the mind, and she whose form is the attraction of fortitude;
she whose form is the attraction of mindfulness, and she whose form is the attraction of names. || 174 ||
And likewise the supreme goddess who attracts seeds, as well as the one who attracts the self, the goddess who attracts nectar, and likewise the one who attracts the body. || 175 ||
O Great Goddess, one should worship [the deities] in the sixteen-spoked [cakra] by moving counter-clockwise;
this is indeed the group of sixteen digits (kalās) consisting of the digits of Māyā and Lakṣmī.
In this context, words such as *rūpā* and *rūpiṇī* are intended either to complete the verse or to indicate that the name is devoid of meaning; they are not, however, constituent parts of the name.
The name consists of only so much as *kāmākarṣiṇī*. [The term] *vāmāvartena*...

The meaning is "not in a clockwise direction. However, the interpretation that it begins from the petal in front of the Goddess is established in another tantra. Furthermore, what will be stated later in the section on the fourteen spokes—that it begins from the western [petal]—also serves as an indicator for this point. For this very reason, it says "beginning from the eastern petal."

The explanation [provided by others] is also incorrect, because it contradicts the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) and other authorities. There is a reading in some places as *vāmamārgeṇa* ("by the left-hand path");

even in that case, the meaning remains the same. However, those who composed the *Artharatnāvalī* maintain that, based on such various citations here and there, the worship of Sundarī is recommended specifically through the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*).

They say it is not by the southern path; such [claims] are to be disregarded due to a lack of authority. Furthermore, this contradicts the *Lalitāsahasranāma*, which states that she is to be propitiated via both the left and right paths, as well as the southern and non-southern paths. Indeed, one who is being born...

Furthermore, because the Vedic scripture states, "A Brāhmaṇa is born with three debts," and so forth, the constant discharge of these debts is censured for its absence in the Left-hand Path (vāmamārga), and because of the resulting delay in liberation, the learned cannot engage in that path with unshakable conviction. Moreover, even that worship which is performed using the substances of a hero (vīradravya) is merely [the Left-hand Path].
To claim that this is the "path" (mārga) is merely a manifestation of delusion produced by not having examined the Tantras;

for even in the worship of the Dakṣiṇāmārga, it is only the *kāraṇa* and so forth that function as the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is because there is no injunction for alternative substances—as there is, for example, between rice and barley—and because substances such as molasses and the like serve only as substitutes (*pratinidhi*).

Because the qualification for that [practice] exists only when the primary [method] is unavailable; for, by the force of the prohibition—"one who is capable of the primary rule (prathamakalpa) should not practice the secondary alternative (anukalpa)"—it is impossible for the primary qualified person to perform the other.
If one asks, "What then is the Vāma path?", we have already determined that very point in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara*.

"Take [it]! By means of the digits (kalā) of Māyā and Lakṣmī. Here, "Māyā and Lakṣmī" refers to the two preceding *tāra*s (the two *oṃ*s). Their repetition is for the purpose of [expressing] "do not obstruct by means of the digits," and also for the sake of obtaining the pronunciation immediately prior to the word *kalā*. In this context, the word *kalā*...

The elders [maintain] that [the vowel] is followed by the sixteen vowels. Regarding the phrase "the group of sixteen digits" (*kalāṣoḍaśaka*): *kalā* is the name of these goddesses. And according to tradition, that [name] is preceded by the word *nityā*.
By the principle of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyanyāya*), the term "sixteen" applies to each one individually.

This is for the purpose of indicating that one should join each syllable [of the mantra] with the Goddess in sequence. Accordingly, the mantras take such forms as: *hrīṃ śrīm aṃ kāmākarṣiṇīnityākalāpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth. Some, however, [place it] after the word *kalāpa*.

They also apply the word *devī* [to her]. In that context, it is equally well-stated that the word *devī* found in the root text [referring to] "the goddess who draws forth nectar" (*amṛtākarṣiṇī*) serves as the indicator. || 172 || 173 || 174 || 175 || 176 ||
Now he teaches the deities to be worshipped on the eight petals:
Anaṅgakusumā in the east, Anaṅgamekhalā in the south, Anaṅgamadanā in the west, and Madanāturā in the north. (177)
[One should worship] Anaṅgarekhā in the southeast, Anaṅgaveginī in the southwest, Anaṅgāṅkuśā in the northwest, and Anaṅgamālinī in the northeast. || 178 ||
One should indeed worship [the deity] within an eight-petaled great lotus that is encircled.

Within the enclosure of the great lotus (*mahāpadma*), inside a sixteen-petaled lotus, upon an eight-petaled lotus: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Anaṅgakusumā," and so forth are the mantras. Thus ends the third enclosure. || 177 || 178 ||
Then, he speaks of the deities to be worshipped on the fourteen-spoked wheel:
"The power Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, and likewise Sarvavidrāviṇī. (179)
She possesses the power of universal attraction and the power that causes universal delight; she possesses the power of universal delusion and the power that causes universal paralysis.
She possesses the power to bewilder all, as well as the power to bring all under control;
she possesses the power to delight all and takes the form of that which intoxicates all. || 181 ||
The power that accomplishes all aims, that fulfills all prosperity, the power consisting of all mantras, and that which brings about the destruction of all dualities. || 182 ||
Following the counter-clockwise sequence, starting from the west and proceeding to the south,
one should take hold of these goddesses, the sovereigns of the three worlds, and worship them.

Starting from the foremost goddess in the west—using the ablative case in the sense of "beginning from"—one takes [the thread] to the south; the resulting meaning is that one proceeds by way of one's own southeast and so forth, which amounts to a counter-clockwise direction. As for those who [perform this] during a west-facing worship:
Beginning from the back of the Goddess and taking [the vessel] to her right, one should perform the worship.
Regarding worship while facing east, they explain that one should begin in front of the Goddess and take [the vessel] to her right to perform the worship; this is a great error on their part. Here...
Since it was previously stated as a rule that the direction between the worshiper and the object of worship is the west (*pratīcī*), this uniformity applies everywhere.

Now, he teaches the deities to be worshipped in the outer ten-spoked wheel: "The goddess who bestows all accomplishments, likewise the one who bestows all prosperity, she who makes everything dear, and she who brings about all auspiciousness. (184)
The Goddess who bestows all desires, the giver of all good fortune, the pacifier of all death, and the remover of all obstacles. || 185 ||
The goddess, beautiful in all her limbs and the liberator from all suffering,
is likewise, O Queen of the God of Gods, [revealed] once again through this primordial knowledge.
O Goddess, one should worship the ten goddesses in the second enclosure.

Here, having enumerated them by means of words ending in the nominative case, such as "bestower of all accomplishments" (*sarvasiddhipradā*) and so forth, the syntactical connection is that one should worship that group of ten goddesses which has such a form. In the same manner...

It is by means of a counter-clockwise rotation alone. The meaning is that [the mantra] is to be inserted into the initial portion by means of the first *vidyā* as a constituent part of another mantra—that is, by the second *tārā*, and not by the *bālā* which effects the purification of the hands; one must not be deluded by this [latter interpretation], because that context has been interrupted and thus is not present here. Furthermore, of this...

The mention [of the mantra] is for the purpose that the *dvitārī* (the two-syllabled mantra) should not be obstructed by the mantras in the form of letters such as *ṇa*, which are taught in other tantras during the occasion of the *vāsanā*. Therefore, by this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it applies everywhere.
It is implied that the *mātṛkā*-yoga mentioned in another tantra is essential. Regarding the phrase "in the second enclosure":

in the previously cited verse, "Thus, O Goddess of Gods, the entire beautiful wheel is accomplished," the term "entire wheel" (*sarvacakra*) refers precisely to the collection of wheels beginning with the *manvastra* and ending with the *bindu*.

Because it has been grasped there, according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), the outer ten-spoked wheel itself is designated as the second; by this, the designation that will be made of the inner ten-spoked wheel of the upper circle as the third is also explained. Now, if one asks: "In this manner..."

If it is argued that although the outer and inner ten-spoked [mandalas] can logically be established as the second and third wheels (*cakra*), they cannot logically be established as the second and third enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), on this point the ancients explain [the matter] in a manner equivalent to silence. We, however, say: "This worship consists of nine enclosures."

In the Tantras, there is the proclamation regarding the bells: "And those veils (*āvaraṇas*) are the forms of the deities residing in the wheels (*cakras*) beginning with the city and ending with the drop (*bindu*)," so say many. That is untenable;
for since the deity of the *bindu* is the principal [deity], it is impossible for it to be its own veil. Nor, this being the case, is it logical...

One might wonder how she possesses the state of being the ninth Yoginī and how the *bindu* constitutes the ninth wheel (*cakra*). However, this is to be doubted, because there is no evidence for the necessary concomitance (*samaniyatatva*) between being a Yoginī, being a deity of a protective enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*), and being the presiding deity of a wheel (*cakrādhiṣṭhātṛtva*). For this very reason, [the deities] are simply the youthful goddesses (*yuvatidevatā*) of the six limbs.

The moderns, who follow the *Jñānārṇava*, maintain that there is a first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*). However, in this Tantra, the number of nine enclosures is established by counting the two pairs of deities on the two lines of the *bhūpura* separately, without including them within the *binducakra*. Regarding the three circles (*vṛttatraya*):
In the Kerala tradition, because the separate worship of certain deities is observed, some maintain that there are nine enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) according to that intention;
or rather, it is easily established by considering the weapons-deities (*āyudhadevatās*) as distinct enclosures.
This is because we observe such usage in the introductory statement of the *Ṛjuvimarśinī*, which introduces the worship of the weapons and the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*): "By this method as well,
for the purpose of indicating that there is no fixed rule regarding being 'first' among the enclosures, [the worship] of the mind-born [weapon] alone is placed first."
The statement "in the second enclosure" (*dvitīyāvaraṇe*) is made with the intention that the second wheel and so forth are logically established as being subsequent [to the first].

Alternatively, this statement is made with reference to the fact that at the end of the fourth chapter, the method of abbreviated worship (*saṃkṣepārcana*)— which includes the alternative of worshipping from the mantra-wheel (*manvasra*) up to the point of the bindu— is also described.
Therefore, in the mantra for offering the worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇa-pūjā):
"O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the attainment of my desired goal;
with devotion, I offer to You the worship of the [specific] enclosure, O Amuka."
In this context, since the term representing the number of each respective enclosure (āvaraṇa)—

in the form of "first," "second," and so on— must be inserted in place of the word "amuka," and because even the fourth enclosure (manvasra) is considered the "first" in the abbreviated worship (saṃkṣepārcana) when counting from the outer square (bhūpura), the words "first" and so forth [are used].
It should be understood that these [points] are indicated by implication through the necessity of being inferred. || 184 || 185 || 186 ||
Then the deity of the Antardaśā spoke: "She is all-knowing, all-powerful, and likewise the bestower of all sovereignty. (187)
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases, her very nature is the support of all, and likewise she is the remover of all sins. || 188 ||
The Goddess consists entirely of bliss and is the very embodiment of all protection;
O Great Mistress, she once again bestows the fruits of all desires. (189)
These ten deities are renowned for arising in accordance with their own names;
thus, O Goddess, these great goddesses grant the accomplishment of all aims. (190)
One should worship in the third enclosure according to the previously mentioned procedure.

"Svanāmasadṛśodayāḥ" means those whose emergence or exertion (*udaya-udyoga*) corresponds to their own respective names. This [rule] applies to all the deities of the preceding and subsequent enclosures as well.

It follows according to what is appropriate; that is to say, they possess the exertion directed toward such objects as correspond to the signification of the name. By the previously mentioned method, consisting of the arrangement of the two *tārās* in counter-clockwise order and so forth, [this applies] to the third enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).

In the detailed worship beginning with *aṇimā* and so forth, even in the seventh [stage], and in the abbreviated worship consisting of three [stages] beginning with the fourteen-spoked [wheel], [the procedure is as follows]. || 187 || 188 || 189 || 190 ||
Now he describes the worship of the deities of the eight-spoked [cakra]:
"O Great Goddess, listen to the worship in the middle cakra according to its sequence. (191)
[She who is] Vaśinī, Kāmeśī, Modinī, and Vimalā; [she who is] Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśī, and Kaulinī as well. || 192 ||
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship each name of the deities, accompanied by the previously mentioned seed-syllable, starting from below and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction.
O Maheśvarī, as far as the southern path, with red flowers;

for at the time of the extraction of the wheel (*cakroddhāra*), having pierced power (*śakti*) with power, and having again encapsulated them with the city of fire (*vahnipura*), one first extracts the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*) by means of this [mantra].
Other wheels have been extracted around that [central wheel] and around those [others];
therefore, because it resides in the very center of all, the eight-cornered [wheel] alone is designated here as the "central wheel" (*madhyacakra*).
The syntactical connection is: "one should worship the powers (*śakti*) such as Vaśinī and the rest therein"—listen to that worship.

Furthermore, this is another proposition intended to make one attentive so that one may remember the extraction of those respective mantras, which is interspersed within many other texts. The meaning is that it is endowed with those seed-syllables (*bīja*) which were previously stated in the preceding text. Each one...
Some join the phrase "endowed with their respective seed-syllables" here itself, below each deity's name; others,
however, joining it only later, should worship starting from the front of the Goddess and proceeding counter-clockwise (vāmāvarta) until the end on the right.

Regarding this, some commentators explain that the sense is that there is no conceptualization of directions such as "east" and so forth here. However, the intention of the ancients is that the phrase "with red flowers" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). It is more reasonable, however, to hold that this statement is made to indicate the necessity of using red flowers in the worship of the Goddess of Speech (*Vāgdevatā*). (Verses 191, 192, 193)
Now, he teaches the worship of the weapons in the four directions within the central path of the eight-sided and three-sided [mandalas]:
"In the sequence of the western, northern, eastern, and southern directions... (194).
O Great Goddess, one should worship in sequence within the fourfold center of the wheel the arrows of Kāma, his bow, and likewise his noose. (195)
(Page ṇo. 105–112 missing; p.

113) In the statement "The Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed] for the sake of all desires," it is established as a tenet that the term "all desires" does not denote results such as omniscience or traveling through the sky. However, this much is the difference:

The distinction here is that in the former case, the proximity to the fruits of all sacrifices is established by the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), whereas in this case, it is established by the very text itself. Furthermore, this rite is essentially of the nature of a preparatory practice (*puraścaraṇa*). As it has been stated in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara* regarding the rites to be described following this:

Because it is a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmyaprayoga*), and because the accomplishment of knowledge (*vidyāsiddhi*) required for such a rite is rooted in preparatory practice (*puraścaraṇa*), [the author] has not mentioned the *puraścaraṇa* without first addressing it.

Because it is inappropriate to discuss optional ritual applications (*kāmyaprayoga*) here, because the classification of the rosary (*akṣamālā*) must be explained specifically within the section on preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*),
and because of the mention of an abundance of obstacles, [it follows that] regarding such obstacles...

Since these [obstacles] are undesirable precisely at the time of *puraścaraṇa* because they obstruct success (*siddhi*), whereas in rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*) those aforementioned obstacles are themselves declared to be the fruit, it follows that being established in the vow (*vratastha*) and having a composed mind (*svasthamānasa*)—
that is, the stability of one's observances (*niyama*)— are absolutely essential only during the time of *puraścaraṇa*.

Regarding the propriety of the discourse, and so forth: even in the *Sundarīmahodaya*, by the phrase "one established in the vow" (*vratastha*), it is indicated that this refers to the recitation (*japa*) for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). Furthermore, since there is no mention of the regional fire-offerings (*deśahoma*) and other such elements which constitute its ancillaries, the subsequent description of optional rites (*kāmyaprayoga*) [is intended as a distinct procedure].
This was stated for the purpose of indicating that these [rites] must be performed immediately after the *puraścaraṇa*.

Consequently, because this ritual constitutes a *puraścaraṇa*, it possesses the inherent capacity to confer the fitness required for its application to rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*).

The phrase "one should bring everything under control through the pacification of the desire for fruits" ultimately results in the meaning that one becomes capable of performing all rites undertaken with specific desires. Consequently,
the meaning of the initial injunction is that one should cultivate such a capacity through the sequential worship.

Thus, since it is established that the *kramapūjā* alone is the primary subject matter (*prakaraṇin*) by virtue of its connection with the fruit— just like the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice— it follows that among those [mantras] recited within that context:
"One who is always pure should resort to [this] and recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times."
"Women certainly cause his mind to melt"—

since no specific fruit is heard mentioned in such injunctions as these, the principle that "that which lacks a stated fruit is subordinate to that which possesses one" applies, just as in the case of the *amanahomas*.

The recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras] constitutes the auxiliary practice (*aṅga*). Thus, performing the recitation with a certain number daily preceded by the worship of the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*), one should carry out the performance of worship continuously and with uniformity for as many days as are required to complete the three hundred thousand.

It is established that this is expressed by the term "cakra-sādhana. Following this, after describing various rites of worship for specific desires (*kāmya-pūjana*), and at the end of those, up until the conclusion of the chapter,
having described the worship performed with specific flowers consisting of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), in the fifteenth [chapter]...

Having explained the specific fruits resulting from the particular worship with jewel-made flowers in the [fifteenth] chapter, and having explained the practice of the three seed-syllables (*tribījasādhana*) and the rites for desired goals (*kāmyakarma*) to be accomplished thereby as they followed in sequence in the sixteenth chapter,
the practice of mantra (*mantrasādhana*) is taught in the seventeenth chapter; its essential nature consists of the constituent parts of worship (*arcana*).
The recitation of the mantra shall consist of one million repetitions.
O Goddess, one who is firm in his vows should worship the entire wheel;
he may worship the wheel situated both externally and internally, or he may worship only the central wheel.
Having propitiated [the deity] with ritual services, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra a thousand times;
standing before it, the master of mantras shall thereby obtain infinite fruit.
Alternatively, having meditated upon the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja) while endowed with mental worship, the wise one should begin the recitation; this shall become the destroyer of great sins.
Having thus begun and stated the differences in results for various types of recitation— such as mental (*mānasa*) or whispered (*upāṃśu*)—
and having prescribed a recitation of nine hundred thousand times:
"One should indeed recite the mantra of Tripurasundarī to the measure of nine hundred thousand."
The form of Rudra himself is the creator and the destroyer; this is manifest, there is no doubt.
He shall be worthy of universal reverence, always well-disposed, and possessed of all good fortune.

Having stated this, because [the text] mentions the regional fire-oblation (*deśahoma*) and so forth, it is clearly understood here that worship (*arcana*) is merely an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the commencement of the recitation (*japa*), just as in the statement of the *Kalpasūtra*: "Having worshipped Gaṇapati, one should begin the practice of Lalitā. For this very reason, a small undertaking brings security (*kṣemakara*).

The statement that "one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times according to the rule" is consistent with the option of performing either the external worship or the mental worship of all nine wheels, or specifically of the *saṃhāracakra* alone, or the *sthiticakra* alone. Consequently, on the very first day, one should first perform the preliminary rites such as the appropriation of the sacred site (*kṣetraparigraha*).

Having completed the preliminary rites (*pūrvāṅga*), and having performed the worship of the wheel (*cakrārcana*) according to any one of the methods mentioned later as time permits, and having recited the mantra (*vidyā*) one thousand times,
one should [perform it] from the second day onwards until midday, in a fixed number such as three, four, or more.

Until the completion of one million recitations, on those days when the count is reached, one should perform the *homa* and other rites after having performed the recitation (*japa*) even without worship. This constitutes the mantra-accomplishment within the context of the constituent parts of worship (*arcanāṅga*).
However, in the case of the accomplishment of the wheel (*cakrasādhana*), this is because recitation lacks primacy.
Because there is an absence of subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*) and so forth, it is consistent that such [rites] are not mentioned in that context.

Since worship is prescribed at the very commencement of the recitation (*japa*) in the practice of mantras, by this indicative mark (*liṅga*), the daily nature of worship is obtained in the practice of the *cakra*, which is the opposite of that. By means of this procedure...

By the phrase "he who," there is a reference specifically to the daily worship (*nityārcana*) along with its prescribed procedure (*setikartavyatā*); and since daily worship occurs every day, that [daily nature] is obtained. Alternatively, let it be granted that even in the context of mantra-accomplishment (*mantrasādhana*), the worship is daily; however—

The state of being conceptualized occurs through the differentiation of the central wheel (*madhyacakra*) and so forth. However, in the practice of the wheel (*cakrasādhana*), the specific distinction is that the worship of the entire wheel (*sakalacakrapūjā*) must be performed, and not the abbreviated form. For this very reason, the root text mentions only the worship of the entire wheel as a single point, without enumerating its subdivisions.
The description of the practice of the *cakra* is consistent with the exposition of the various types of worship at the end of the fourth chapter;
therefore, there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate between the practice of the *cakra* and the practice of mantras, as well as between worship and recitation.

The distinctiveness [of this system] is established by the natural flow of the *Jñānārṇava* through its reversal [of conventional norms] and the presence or absence of fire-offerings (*homa*) and so forth (p.
115). It will become clear that the present Tantra also has its natural inclination toward this very same point. At most, however—

If it is considered that in other tantras such as the *Saṃhitās*, there is also a prescription for oblations (*homa*) and so forth as a subsidiary part of the three-hundred-thousand recitations (*japa*), then let the status of the oblation as a subsidiary part be accepted on the basis of scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). Even though, in the practice of mantra-siddhi, the oblation is directly a primary subsidiary (*sākṣāt-pradhānāṅga*).

In the practice of the *cakra*, its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) will arise by the force of the scriptural statement, just like the *prayāja* offerings which are subsidiaries of the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice. This is because, in the *Saṃhitā*,
the injunction for the recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras] is found outside the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *cakra*-practice, thus constituting a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*).
Thus it is established that, by logical reasoning, it can easily be asserted that this is a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*). However, the ancients think as follows:

there is no such thing as a ritual action called "Cakra-sādhana" (Wheel-attainment); rather, the designation "puraścaraṇa" (preliminary practice) refers, by process of elimination, exclusively to the attainment of the mantra (*mantra-sādhana*). As for what is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:

Regarding the promise to explain the practice of the *cakra*, the term "practice of the *cakra*" (*cakrasādhana*) refers specifically to the optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*) to be described later following three hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).
However, the recitation (*japa*) being described immediately after the promise refers only to the practice of the mantra (*mantrasādhana*). And that—
Although it would have been appropriate to explain [this] in the seventeenth chapter, it has been taught here precisely because of its independence. For this very reason,
in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*, having extracted the recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras] from the section on the practice of the *cakra*,
its placement within the section explaining the recitation of nine hundred thousand has been made as an alternative option regarding the number.

However, Sundarīmahodaya, unable to tolerate its excellence, maintains that while three hundred thousand recitations are accepted as the means for mantra-siddhi, this specific mention here is intended solely to establish eligibility for the optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*). Nevertheless, according to that view, even the alternative recitation of nine hundred thousand would likewise apply here.

To the objection, "Why is this not mentioned [in the *Kulārṇava*]?", the reply is that it was not mentioned in order to suggest that one has the qualification for optional (*kāmya*) worship even with only this much [of the initiation]. This [interpretation of yours],
however, is a fabrication that contradicts the inherent meaning of the *Jñānārṇava* and the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*.

This is quite clear. But if this were so, there would be a contradiction with the internal consistency (*svarasa*) of the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* according to your own position. For in its twenty-ninth chapter, having made the formal promise: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the practice of the Śrīvidyā mantra," [the text proceeds as follows].

Having briefly stated, "O Dear One, one should perform worship with jewel-flowers, [or] with campaka flowers inlaid with jewels made of gold," and so forth; and having described the location for the practice of mantra-sādhana and the rosaries, as well as the recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras] and the fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part thereof, he then says: "Alternatively..."

Having explained in detail, up until the conclusion of the chapter, the procedure for reciting the vidyā nine hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind, as well as the fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth of that amount and so forth, [the author] states in the subsequent chapter:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the practice for the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja);
likewise, hear the sequence of application for this perfected vidyā.

Having thus made the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) and explained the optional rites of worship (*kāmyapūjā*), and having concluded that very section by briefly stating the practice of the three seed-syllables (*tribījasādhana*), the chapter is brought to a close. And here, the status of mantra-practice (*mantrasādhana*) belongs specifically to the recitation of three hundred thousand repetitions (*lakṣatrayajapa*) within those very optional rites of worship.

If it is argued that the status of the *cakra* as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is clearly understood [from this], that is true. However, the appropriate resolution here is simply that the author of the tantra, being independent in his will, is beyond reproach;
otherwise, how could there be a mention of the *ratnapūjā* within the section on the practice of mantras (*mantrasādhana*)?

In a context where ritual worship for specific desires (*kāmyapūjā*) predominates, since it is necessary to establish a distinction between those who are capable and those who are incapable— given that the choice between reciting nine hundred thousand or three hundred thousand mantras cannot be arbitrary— the recitation of nine hundred thousand is prescribed first.

Although it would have been appropriate to state [the number of recitations] as three hundred thousand after [the other details], the fact that it is stated in reverse order must be accepted as ensuring the purity of the context (*saṃdarbhaśuddhi*). Furthermore, by relying on this single tantra, it would be improper to alter two [passages] that otherwise possess contextual consistency.
It has already been stated that the recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras] is a separate ritual act from that which consists of the *cakrasādhana*.

As for the verse containing the promise (*pratijñā*) regarding the *cakrājasādhana*, the latter half of its first part—the method of explaining it—is missing; however, because [the author] is omniscient, it was likely supplied by his mind alone. Therefore...
Thus, in the latter half [of the chapter], there is the very sign of the conclusion of the explanation of the *cakra*-sādhana:

"Listen to the sequence of the application (*viniyoga*) of the perfected *cakra*. Although one should have said "of the perfected *cakra*," the statement "of the *vidyā*" is made with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the *vidyā*, the *cakra*, and the goddesses; this is seen frequently.

It is not at all contradictory when viewed from the perspective of common worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). Alternatively, it should be explained so as not to contradict other tantras, by taking the three previously mentioned characteristics and referring to them here via the word "thus" (*evam*). Or rather, let there be no [separate] *saṃhitā-tantra* of this kind.

Commentary: Indeed, it is not easy for anyone to establish a single coherent interpretation for all the Tantras without contradiction. However, the meaning previously described for the *Jñānārṇava* and the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* is indeed consistent with reason. Now, [one might ask]: if the recitation of three hundred thousand [mantras] is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) for the practice of the *cakra*, [what is its purpose]?

If it is asked, "Why is the prescription for optional recitations (*kāmyajapa*) not seen in the Tantras after the accomplishment of the mantra through nine hundred thousand recitations (*navalakṣajapa*), as is the case with the optional worship (*kāmyārcana*) performed subsequent to that?"— it is indeed seen so, according to the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*.

The form consisting of forty-five lakhs of recitations is for the sake of attaining desired results (*kāmya*). However, in our own tradition, in the seventeenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, following the description of the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*), it is stated: "Having first performed the obligatory oblation (*nityahoma*), one should then perform the optional oblation (*kāmyahoma*)," and so forth.

Since it is observed that offerings consisting of substances and instruments are prescribed for the sake of various high and low fruits, there is no evidence for the insistence that, in the case of optional rites performed after being accomplished by means of mantras, only the recitation (japa) form of the optional rite is required.

After performing the procedure for one hundred thousand recitations and having established those aforementioned locations, one should again remember [the deity] and, remaining there, recite one hundred thousand times while embodying the very form of the Goddess;
thereafter, this Vidyā becomes the subduer of the three worlds.

Or rather, it is easy to say that this [verse] is intended solely as an injunction for the recitation (japa) performed for specific desires; as for what was stated by the author of the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*—
that the word "lakṣa" here serves as a reminder of the three hundred thousand [recitations] mentioned in the section on the practice of the *cakra*— [that is incorrect].
[The opponent argues: "Because it is in syntactic agreement with the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*," (p.

117). This is not so; for it is an act of extreme audacity to claim that [the text] recalls something extremely remote, while abandoning its function as a reminder of the nine signs mentioned immediately prior.

Because there is no specific indication of a number, the change from the singular form remains the same in both positions. Even though, according to that view, the preceding text does not refer to nine hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), but rather to forty-five hundred thousand recitations performed for the sake of desire (*kāmya*), and that—
It cannot be touched upon here, because there is no purpose in reminding [the reader] again.
However, the purpose of reminding one who is distant [from the context] is the attainment of a connection with the *homa* (fire-oblation) and other rites that will be explained immediately following;
thus, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*. Nevertheless...
In the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*, it is stated that "by reciting this one hundred thousand times, one becomes the destroyer of all sins," and so forth;
thus, you yourselves have declared that the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists precisely of one hundred thousand recitations.

Since it was previously stated and because it forms a single syntactical unit with that [preceding statement], it can easily be explained—according to your own view—that here the recitation of one hundred thousand (*ekalakṣa*) alone is taught as the *puraścaryā* without breaking the singular number; therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.
However, according to the *Sundarīmahodaya*, the preceding text refers exclusively to the recitation of nine hundred thousand (*navalakṣa*).
However, that recitation does not have the attainment of the *vidyā* as its fruit; rather, it has the attainment of identity with Śiva (*śivasārūpya*) as its fruit.
It is this very recitation of three hundred thousand times mentioned in the fourteenth chapter that is stated here again by way of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*) principle.
Its fruit is the attainment of the *vidyā*. This pertains specifically to the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of one hundred thousand recitations for a woman.

By the passage beginning with "they indeed cause his mind, though well-stabilized, to melt," it is ordained that in the event of an obstacle, the practice should extend from the second hundred thousand up to the third hundred thousand;
therefore, the use of the singular form "lakṣam" (a hundred thousand) is not untenable. Furthermore, later on, there is the offering with *kiṃśuka* flowers.

The fire-oblations (homas) prescribed by the passage beginning with "one should perform [them] with a tenth part, O fair-faced one," etc., should be understood as constituting both types of *puraścaraṇa*: those performed without desire (*niṣkāma*) and those performed with desire (*sakāma*).
Thus, having performed the *puraścaraṇa* consisting of three hundred thousand recitations for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra (*vidyāsiddhi*), immediately thereafter—

It is established that the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) should be performed nine hundred thousand times; thus, two types of *puraścaraṇa* are obtained. Furthermore, in this way, consistency with the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* is also achieved, and for the sake of consistency with the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*, it is precisely the recitation of one hundred thousand times [that is intended].

This is indeed improper because it contradicts the established injunctions. As for the claim that when an obstacle arises during the performance of one hundred thousand [recitations], there is an injunction to extend it until one million, that is not correct;
for if that were the case, then in the absence of an obstacle, the *puraścaraṇa* would result in being either exactly one hundred thousand or exactly two hundred thousand recitations. And thus...
The breakdown of the unity of your desired statement remains as it was.
Furthermore, the option between nine hundred thousand and three hundred thousand is indeed intended by Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
yet you have spoken of their conjunction—consider well what kind of unity of statement this is!
However, there is no fault whatsoever in explaining the injunction for one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*) as being subordinate to the recitation of optional prayers (*kāmyajapa*).

Nor should it be argued that, under this view, there would be the undesirable consequence of this [injunction] being stated only after the description of the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other ancillaries for nine hundred thousand recitations; for if that were the case, [the present injunction would be necessary] in order to obtain the fire-oblation consisting of a tenth part of those [nine hundred thousand].

There would be the undesirable consequence of accepting that there are one million modifications (*vikṛti*). If this were accepted as desired, however, then the attainment of the optional qualities (*guṇakāma*) based on the *homa* would not occur according to the rule of the eighth [chapter]. Therefore, for the sake of obtaining an identical injunction (*samānavidhi*) for the two recitations (*japa*), it must be right here.
Because it is necessary to explain that [point], and so forth, it should be inferred by those learned in Nyāya; enough with this elaboration.
And prior to the extraction of the *cakra* in the first chapter—

Since the worship of that [Cakra] has already been described and because it was presented immediately prior, the author— desiring first to explain certain optional (kāmyā) rites pertaining specifically to the Cakra-worship— instructs on the preliminary practice (cakrasādhana) for the sake of establishing the requisite qualification (adhikāra), by means of seven verses: [The seven verses follow.]
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the yoga of mantra according to the rule,
by which it is worshipped by the practitioner through this procedure.
In that country, city, or village, agitation arises. This statement is made with the intention of the non-difference between mantra and *cakra*; [it refers to] the armor of the *mantracakra*. Yoga.
According to Amara, [the term refers to] "preparation, means, meditation, conjunction, and reasoning. This amounts to the *cakrasādhana* (the practice of the wheel).

By this aforementioned method (*vidhāna*), by the practitioner desiring the accomplishment of the wheel (*cakrasiddhi*), wherever it is worshipped (*prapūjyate*), there agitation (*kṣobha*) or an obstacle (*vighna*) arises. It is worshipped.

By this, it is shown that non-worship itself is the essential nature of the practice of the *cakra*. Furthermore, according to the ancient position, since this is indeed the practice of mantra (*mantrasādhana*), the term "mantra-yoga" remains as it stands.
In this view, the meaning of "is worshipped" (*prapūjyate*) must be described as "is recited" (*prajapyate*). [This is so] because [the result is attained] by the mere commencement of worship.

Due to the agitation of the minds of village women caused by the casting of their side-glances and so forth, the practitioner’s mind becomes deluded, resulting in a failure of the causal means. Therefore, by remaining steadfast and disregarding them, one overcomes the obstacles posed by city women; even when they treat him with contempt, he remains undisturbed.

The meaning is that an obstacle arises when those residing in that same locality, or those staying at a distance, come near him. However, the ancient authorities suggest that by the mention of "locality" and so forth, it is implied that one may stay anywhere at will for the sake of *puraścaraṇa*; and by that, [the practice] of what is stated in the *Paśu-śāstra*...
Some explain that there is a prohibition against the necessity [of visiting] mountain peaks, riverbanks, sacred fords (*tīrtha*), shrines (*āyatana*), and so forth;
but that is not correct. For it is stated in this very tantra, as well as elsewhere, "In whatever place a *liṅga* faces west," and so on.
Because the prescription of rules regarding place is frequently observed. || 1 ||
He describes the very manner of their agitation:
"Their minds were scorched by the intense heat of the blazing fire of desire. (2)
Women approach from afar according to the maxim of the ant’s bone;
