their hearts are deluded by spells, and the circles of their hips quiver. (3)
p. 119) O Great Goddess, by beholding that, all women are produced.

For the constituents known as skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow exist within one another, each preceding one residing inside the next. Thus, although situated in extreme secrecy, [the Self] resides within the dead body.
The marrow-element is indeed consumed by ants after they have crawled inside the bones;

this is the "ant-and-bone maxim" (*pipīlikāsthi-nyāya*). The meaning is that in this manner, even though the practitioner remains within a mountain cave, he is assailed, deluded, and consumed by women. The rest is clear. || 2 || 3 ||
But when even a single hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the women of the earth tremble.
If the mind of the practitioner is not disturbed even slightly in this way,
then all the Naga maidens in the underworld become agitated.

For the worship previously described must be performed daily; one should perform it together with heroes who are well-joined to the Kaula conduct, because of the statement in the *Uttaratantra* that "it is daily. And thus, whether this worship called the "accomplishment of the cakra" (*cakrasādhana*) is non-different from that [daily worship], or is another ritual act in the form of a modification thereof—

From that very [practice], the daily nature [of the rite] and the recitation (japa) of its constituent parts are obtained. Consequently, if the worship is performed according to the aforementioned method without obstacles for a duration sufficient to complete one hundred thousand recitations of the Vidyā, then all women dwelling upon the earth-sphere are agitated [by desire].

Regarding the expression "lakṣaikamātra," even though it is a *pūrvakālaika* compound, the absence of the prior placement [of the word *eka*] is due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). Alternatively, the word *lakṣa* is compounded with the word *ekamātra* itself.
Nevertheless, if the practitioner remains even slightly unperturbed, [he attains success].

The ellipsis is that one should worship until the completion of the second hundred thousand [recitations]. At that time, daughters of the *nāgas* come to the earth and create obstacles. Here, the term "having been recited" (*japta*) is used as a statement of established fact (*siddhavat-nirdeśa*) precisely to indicate that the recitation is obtained as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the worship. This refers to the second hundred thousand recitations.

Even though it is not explicitly stated with a loud voice, there is an ellipsis (adhyāhāra) of the words "second" and "third" lakṣas and so forth, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the concluding statement: "having thus recited three lakṣas.
This is also clear in the *Jñānārṇava*: "Then the best of practitioners should recite a second lakṣa."
"When the third hundred thousand has been reached, the celestial maidens cause [the drum] to resound," and so forth.

By this [statement], because of the natural force of the word *mātra* in the phrase "only one hundred thousand," and because the second and third hundred-thousands are not mentioned, this ritual action consists of exactly one hundred thousand [recitations]. In that very [action], obstacles created by the women of the three worlds occur in succession.

Thus, the interpretation that "three hundred thousand" constitutes a separate ritual act (karmāntara) is not to be accepted; for, as in cases such as "one initiation," "three initiations," "he chooses one," or "he chooses two," when a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatva) is possible, a split in the sentence (vākyabheda) is improper.

Furthermore, because there is internal inconsistency therein, even that interpretation which claims these three *karmas* consist of one, two, or three hundred thousand [verses] (*lakṣa*) should not be respected for this very reason. This being so,
as for what was stated by the author of the *Saubhāgyaratnākara* regarding the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* consisting of one hundred thousand [verses]:

Regarding the statement, "They say that *puraścaraṇa* is called 'eating' (*atti*)," if this is according to the intended meaning of that [previous] commentary, then that too must certainly be considered. However, if it is according to the reasoning to be stated in the fifth chapter, then it is indeed appropriate. || 4 || 5 ||
When he does not undergo even the slightest agitation on their account,
then the celestial women dwelling in heaven flee away.
O Goddess of the gods, having thus recited it three hundred thousand times while established in the vow, the supreme practitioner agitates the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
"By them" refers even to the Naga maidens; the genitive case is used in the sense of a general relationship (*saṃbandhasāmānya*).

Others hold that "by sight" (*darśanena*) is the ellipsis. "Then" means after the commencement of the third hundred-thousand recitations. Having thus recited three hundred thousand times according to the stated method, and having performed the sequential worship (*kramapūjā*) until the completion of the three hundred-thousand recitations.

Established in his vow, his celibacy remains unshaken even amidst a multitude of exceedingly powerful obstacles; for this very reason, he is the best of practitioners (*sādhaka*) and the foremost among those skilled in the rites of *cakra*-accomplishment. In the *Manoramā*, however:
The phrase "capable of agitating the three worlds" has been explained as "those who cause renown throughout the entire universe. || 6 || 7 ||

Thus, from the words "having written" (*likhitvā*) until the end of the chapter, he describes forty-three ritual applications (*prayoga*) consisting of the optional worship (*kāmyārcana*) and so forth of the *Siddhacakra*. In that regard, because there are six kinds of desirable fruits, there are [six] means for their accomplishment.

Ritual actions (*karma*) are also sixfold, distinguished by pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), immobilization (*stambhana*), causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*). Among these, pacification is the cessation of calamities; subjugation is the bringing under one's own control of kings and others.

*Stambhana* (paralysis) is the obstruction of activity; *vidveṣaṇa* (enmity) is the breaking of affection; *uccāṭana* (expulsion) is the causing of relocation to another place; the others are well known. Others, however, state that there are six types based on the distinctions of protection (*rakṣā*), pacification (*śānti*), victory (*jaya*), acquisition (*lābha*), suppression (*nigraha*), and destruction (*nidhana*).

*Prasajjyamānopadravaprāgabhāvaparipālanaṃ* (the preservation of the prior absence of impending calamities) is *rakṣā* (protection). *Prasaktopadravadhvaṃsaḥ* (the destruction of occurring calamities) is *śānti* (pacification). Victory in battle, gambling, and so forth is *jaya* (victory).
The attainment of desired objects through trade and other means is *lābha* (gain). The infliction of disease is *nigraha* (suppression). The remainder...

This is well known. In this context, they maintain that *stambhana* (paralysis) is included within *rakṣā* (protection), while *vaśya* (subjugation) and *ākarṣaṇa* (attraction) are included within *jaya* (victory); and *vidveṣa* (enmity) and *uccāṭana* (eradication) are included within *nigraha* (suppression).
Although the number exceeds six due to the infinity of desires and the resulting infinity of their means, [the classification remains as follows].

Although there is a loss [of specific details] somewhere, as in the case of logicians, nevertheless, because the specific subsidiary parts (aṅga-viśeṣa) are prescribed therein for each of the six types of rites, the result is the attainment of those respective subsidiaries through their inclusion within those particular rites.
And those constituent parts are to be seen in the twenty-third wave of the *Subhagāratnākara*.
Therein, he describes the ritual for subjugation (*vaśya*) in two verses:
"When, having drawn a large wheel, one places an image in its center..."
Then one should write [the mantra] joined with the name and contemplate it as blazing.
Even she who may be situated a hundred yojanas away and remains unseen,
being utterly freed from fear and shame, comes here completely deluded.
In the location of the *bindu*, for the purpose of drawing the effigy (*pratikṛti*) intended for the rite of subjugation (*vaśakarma*),
one should draw a large *śrīcakra* devoid of the *bindu*. Regarding the materials required for that drawing, in the case of subjugation, one should use vermilion or other red substances.

Either by the general rule, "it should be written," or by the extension of the rule prescribed in the archetype— "O Goddess, with vermilion powder or else with saffron"— one should, having prepared it with vermilion powder, contemplate the wheel there; thus it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* regarding this very ritual.

Since the ritual action is one and the same, the application of vermilion (sindūra) and other substances is possible through the principle of "taking up qualities" (guṇopasaṃhāra) from other recensions (śākhāntara), which is why they are not mentioned in the root text with that intention. As for the statement, "One should draw the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) with substances such as gorocanā,"...
In the *Jñānārṇava*, within the section on this very ritual action, there is a statement which,

although it is consistent only with the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*) because of the yellow substance used, nevertheless— due to its being expressly prescribed— is also an optional writing material. For this very reason:

Furthermore, it is equally well-argued that because they are restricted by the specific sixfold rites (ṣaṭkarma) as indicated [in the scripture], the ancillary elements (aṅga) mentioned in other Tantras within different contexts do not apply here. By this,
[the same logic applies] to the specific forms of worship of the Kāmya-cakra which constitute the six rites.

The separate treatment of the *cakrasādhanāntarādhikāra* and the various optional (*kāmya*) worship of the wheels (*cakrārcanā*) in the twenty-third and thirty-second chapters respectively is consistent with the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*. The phrase "endowed with a name" (*nāmnā saṃyuktām*) is an epithet of the image (*pratimā*). And as for the name...

The interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) with the *kāmarāja* seed-syllable is necessary, according to another tantra which states: "Blazing, accompanied by the name, and interlaced with the great seed-syllable. Śrī Vidyānandanātha explained that by the term "great seed-syllable," the *kāmarāja* seed-syllable is meant.

Regarding the *vidarbha* method, the *Śāradātilaka* states: "One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) situated between two [syllables] of the mantra; this is to be known as *vidarbha*. For example, in the case of the six-syllable *kūṭa*, one writes "Lakṣmī" between the second and third syllables.

The first syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) should be written between the fourth and fifth syllables, and the second syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished should be written there as well. However, if the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished are excessive, one should follow the principle that "the rule applies to each principal element."

Having repeated the mantra again and again, one should interlace (*vidarbha*) all the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is because the interlacing of the mantra takes the form of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the name.
However, the authors of the *Artharatnāvalī* [state that] having written the root-vidyā in the heart-region of the image, of that—
They explain that one should write the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in the genitive case in the middle of the letter *ha* of the *Hṛllekhā* [mantra], and below that,
between the letters *ra* and *ha*, one should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) in the accusative case, along with the verb "attract" (*ākarṣaya*).
Only they themselves know the source for this.
Because one obtains more syllables to be written than those prescribed by the general rule for mantras,

it has been said: "The individual soul (jīva), the vital breath (prāṇa), the mantra of the living soul (jīvamantra), the mantra of the self (ātmamantra), power (śakti), the two eyes, the pair of ears, and the tongue."
The object to be accomplished, the agent, the action, and its specific performance— these constitute two *gāyatrīs* due to the distinction between mantra and yantra.

The casting of the vital breath (*prāṇakṣepa*), the seed-syllable of the Sun located in the heart of the machine, the protective syllable, and the syllables that are the elements of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*);
thus, twenty limbs are to be inscribed.
"In each and every yantra, according to the tradition.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning of these two verses has been described by us in detail in the *Tṛcabhāskara*.
Since this too is a yantra, if the drawing of twenty [deities] is desired, then even in the daily worship (*nityārcana*) of the Cakrarāja—
Is the fault of writing that [name] difficult to extricate? Even if one accepts that [fault], the tradition alone is the refuge;
such is the direction [of the argument]. One should visualize her as blazing, being consumed by the fire of desire;
some say she is "deluded by the crest-flame of the mantra-fire. And that crest-flame has arisen from within the space between her two yonis.
Some say it should be "contemplated" (*cintya*); all of that must be relied upon as being in agreement with other tantras.
Regarding the phrase "a hundred *yojanas*," the word *śata* signifies "many," for according to another tantra, it is "a thousand *yojanas*.
The rest is clear. Furthermore, in this practice, it is not merely contemplation alone due to the force of the injunction "one should contemplate."
It should not be argued that worship is not the primary act because its connection with the fruit is not explicitly heard;

for that worship is obtained precisely through the mention of the drawing of the *cakra*. This is just as, for instance, the word *nirvapati* ("he offers") is heard in the sentences concerning the *saurya* sacrifice and others, while the word *ālabhati* ("he slaughters") is heard in the sentences concerning the *vāyavya* sacrifice and others.

The term *yajati* (sacrifices) is an indicator (*lakṣaka*) [of the specific rite], and the fact that it has the *darśa* and *dīkṣā* as its archetype (*prakṛti*) serves as a mark (*liṅga*); likewise here, by the mere word *cakra*, there is obtained the fact that this worship has the *nityārcana* (daily worship) as its archetype, according to the tradition (*saṃpradāya*). The same applies to what follows. And all these ritual applications (*prayoga*) last for a period of seven days.

Some [say] that there is only a single performance, or else repetition until the fruit arises—this is indeed logical. If it is argued that it is stated in some ritual application that one becomes a servant like a slave within seven days, [we reply: what of that? It is likewise stated that [the goal is attained] through six months of meditative yoga. || 8 || 9 ||
(p. 123) He describes another practice in two verses:
"Or else, having placed himself in their midst, when the mantra-practitioner contemplates everything as red and the person to be acted upon (sādhya) also rendered red. (10)
From that, O Goddess, he is born beautiful with all auspiciousness, beloved by all the world, and a practitioner of success, O Supreme Sovereign. (11)
The word *atha* indicates the commencement of another ritual application (*prayoga*); *vā* denotes an alternative. "Situated in the midst of that" means standing in the center of the wheel.

"Aruṇa" means equal to a thousand rising suns. "The object to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) refers to one who has become the subject of a rite for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). "Rendered crimson" means by the pervasion of his own splendor.
This is the meaning obtainable from the suffix *cvi*.

Also in another tantra: "O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon oneself as having the luster of a thousand rising suns, with an orange glow, and likewise the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) as having become orange."

The authors of the *Artharatnāvalī*, however, state: having brought one's own *kuṇḍalinī* out through the *vahā* channel and caused it to enter through the nostril of the victim, having unified it with the victim’s *kuṇḍalinī*,
and having rendered the victim’s life-force (*jīva*) swallowed by that [unified energy], one leads it to non-difference from one’s own seat (*āsana*).

They describe that one should draw forth a stream of nectar, slightly reddish in color, from the lunar disc at one's own *brahmarandhra*, and with it, flood the entire self along with the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
This is not seen in those two *Arṇava-saṃhitās*. Regarding the subjugation of the person to be accomplished, by means of the previous practice—
This is his conceptual construction; beauty and so forth are also its fruit. 10 || 11 ||
One should worship with all the red offerings accompanied by the mudrā;
joined with the very name of whomever [one worships], that person shall become submissive like a servant.

Although the word *mudrā* has many meanings, in this context it must be understood as that which is known solely from the mouth of the Guru— the practice called the "binding of the *yonimudrā*" which is performed by those following the tradition for the purpose of removing defects in the mantra.

"His body is armored with mudrās," because in another tantra there is the indication of the procedure for donning armor upon one's own body by means of mudrās. And it has been explained in that very same way in the *Ṛjuvimarśinī*:
"In whatever manner [the mantra] is joined with its name and interwoven (*vidarbhitam*), such is the method. And the manner of that is as follows:

This has been stated previously. For that [mantra] whose name is "vidarbhitam," this very commentary from the *Jñānārṇava* and other sources is appropriate. As for those who explain that both the names of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the practitioner (*sādhaka*), as well as the verbal action "make submissive" (*vaśī kuru*), must be written [into the mantra], their source remains to be sought. || 12 ||
He states another application with three [verses] (p. 124):
"Having joined the name of one who has not been seen [before] with that which resides in the center of the wheel, and having formed the *yonimudrā*, he attracts her in an instant. (13)
Whether she be a Yakṣiṇī, or a Gandharvī, or a Kinnarī, or a Mistress of the Gods;
whether she be the daughter of a Siddha, the daughter of a Nāga, the daughter of a Yakṣa, or a sky-walker (Khecarī). || 14 ||
A Vidyādharī, an Apsaras, or an Ṛṣi’s daughter such as Urvaśī, with the orb of her hips quivering from the agitation born of passion. (15)
Having joined the name of whichever form among the invisible yakṣiṇīs and others is suitable for conventional usage— placing it in such a way that it resides in the center of the wheel—
and having written only the nominal base (prātipadika) denoting her in the middle of the wheel, but not together with the mantra;

In this context, the conjunction consists of the *vidarbha* method; for it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "Having written the names of the invisible women and their letters in the center of the wheel. This alone is the distinction of this [practice] from the previous application.
However, regarding the formation of the *yonimudrā*, no specific instruction is heard in other tantras. As for those who...
Regarding the removal of defects in mantra, some maintain that the binding of the *yonimudrā* has also been taught as being included within the group of ten [mudrās] beginning with *saṃkṣobhiṇī*;
however, Śrī Harṣadīkṣita stated that they are not followers of the tradition (*asāṃpradāyika*). Therefore, here, according to the tradition...

Thus, until the perception of the specific distinction, this remains the refuge. A *yakṣiṇī* is indeed a distinct genus from a *yakṣa*; therefore, there is no tautology with the term "daughter of a *yakṣa*" (*yakṣakanyā*). Although [the category] is already established by the word "apsaras" alone, the mention of *Urvaśī* follows the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). And this—

The collection of words found in the two verses beginning with "yakṣiṇīm" (the yakṣī) serves as an adjective for the singular term "tām" (her). However, some, considering these to be adjectives for the phrase "sarvayoṣitaḥ" (all women) occurring in the ritual application to be described hereafter, maintain that this particular application pertains exclusively to human women.
They consider this to be in contradiction with other tantras. 13 || 14 || 15 ||
With just half a verse, he states another application:
"By meditating on the Great Kāmakalā, one may agitate all women.
That very meditation on the Kāmakalā which was previously prescribed as being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) is precisely what is intended here.

That which is performed with desire as its objective is also "kāmya" (desirable). Consequently, by the principle of the distinctness of conjunctions (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), this meditation serves both purposes. All women are the damsels residing in the three worlds.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, through the yoga of meditation on the Great Kāmakalā,
one may agitate the women of the heavenly realm, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld.

Thus, from the *Jñānārṇava*. Here, however, by the force of the word "tu" (but/however), the distinctness of this [practice] from the first one is indicated; thereby, the delusion that there is only a single practice consisting of four and a half verses within the present tantra is cast off.
(p. 125) Now, he begins to describe several ritual applications even without [the performance of] worship:
"Alternatively, one may use rocanā and saffron, or sandalwood in seven parts. (16)
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, the wise man should apply the *tilaka*.
Then, whomever he looks upon, speaks to, touches, or thinks of— [he becomes subject to his will]. (17)
And by means of wealth and his very body, he falls under [the other's] control like a slave.

Regarding *rocanā* (yellow pigment), *gorocana* (cow-gallstone pigment), *kuṅkuma* (saffron), and *kesara* (filaments): there should be an equality of parts between these two, according to the maxim that "when nothing is heard [to the contrary], they should be equal. As for *candana* (sandalwood), however—

From these two combined, take equal parts. One part of *rocanā* (bezoar) and one part of *kuṅkuma* (saffron), and then two parts of *candana* (sandalwood), O Goddess; one should grind them together evenly.
Thus, from another tantra.

As for those who explain that one should employ two parts of *rocanā* and *kuṅkuma* and only one part of *candana*, they are to be disregarded because they lack a foundation. The third case ending in the word *arthena* is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*).
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, [offer] flowers, fruit, fragrance, drink, and clothing. || 18 ||
Having recited it one hundred and eight times, whichever woman is sent forth with this mantra,
she— her heart being utterly deluded— is instantly drawn to him.

O auspicious lady, this forceful extraction (*haṭhākṛṣṭi*) is never obstructed anywhere. "Flower" is a metaphor for leaves and the like; "fruit" refers to food, betel, and so forth; "fragrance" refers to camphor and the like; "drink" refers to curd, milk, and the like; "garment" refers to ornaments and the like—of her [these are taken].
In this context, the gender is not intended to be significant. Likewise, in the previous application, in the phrase "he who beholds," [the gender is irrelevant].

Regarding "forcible extraction": if rituals for paralyzing the mantras of others are performed by means of a sādhya, then due to the superior power of that accomplishment, there will certainly be a counteraction of the practitioner's own ritual.
The meaning is that this application is not thwarted even by one who is powerful. "Bhadra" is either a vocative or a locative case. || 18 || 19 ||
Then, with eleven and a half verses, he teaches a single application: "One should draw an image on the surface of the ground in a secluded place using yellow pigment (rocanā). (20)
She was beautiful, adorned with charming ornaments and attire,
and joined to his forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the region of his birth.

Having written the syllables of *madana* (the god of love), interwoven within the "hook" (*aṅkuśa*) of the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) of one's birth-name, and embedded within all the joints of the limbs; 22.
Facing in that direction and having made his body threefold,
he should bind the Kṣobhiṇī mudrā and recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times.
Having directed [the disciple] to the fire-chamber, which is the abode of the digits of the moon and sun,
one should smear the ground in that secluded place with cow dung; there, with yellow orpiment,
one should fashion an image of the woman to be accomplished, endowed with attire and ornaments suited to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).

Having drawn [the diagram] correctly, one should write the Śrīvidyā mantra, beginning from her forehead and ending at the region of the yoni, incorporating her birth name and interlacing it with the *kroṃ* seed-syllable of the goad (*aṅkuśa*). The goad-seed syllable, the first letter of the birth name, and two letters of the Vidyā [are to be combined].
Furthermore, one should write the "hook" (aṅkuśa) and the second syllable of the name of birth, followed by the third and fourth syllables,

and so forth, in this manner. Then, having repeatedly inscribed that very second *kūṭa* in as many locations as there are joints in the body of that image, one should [place] that seed-syllable (*bīja*).

Having visualized [the seed-syllable] as having the luster of a pomegranate flower, dissolved within those respective joints, and facing the direction in which the woman to be acted upon resides, one should perform the nyāsas that induce the state of the deity; then,
having bound the *kṣobhiṇī* mudrā characterized by what will be described hereafter, [one recites] that seed-syllable.
The collective meaning is as follows: having placed [the deity] in the fire-chamber, which is the abode of the digits of the moon and sun, one should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times.
Regarding this, the application of cow-dung plaster is mentioned in the Saṃhitā:
"Then, on ground smeared with cow-dung, one should draw [the design] with yellow pigment (rocanā)."

The term *janmamaṇḍala* refers to the womb (*yoni*). However, some say that the word *bhāla* indicates the *ājñācakra*, while the word *janmamaṇḍala* refers to the *mūlādhāra*; thus, they maintain that one should write the *vidyā* within the six *cakras*.

That is not according to the syllables. As for those who explain that after the *aṅkuśa*, there are two syllables of the mantra, followed by the syllable of the name of birth—they must consider the basis for their abandonment of the established order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).
Furthermore, the fact that [the deity] has the radiance of a *dāḍima* flower is stated in the *Arṇava*: "The *līna*..."

"One should contemplate [the syllable] with the luster of a pomegranate flower within the joints of the body. This interpretation of the word *madanākṣara* as being synonymous with the seed-syllable *klīṃ* is unacceptable.
One should inscribe the *kāmakūṭa* merged into all the joints of the limbs.
This is because it contradicts the *Saṃhitā*.
Likewise: "One should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times with the seed-syllable and mudrā of Kṣobhiṇī;
one should unite her in the abode of desire, which is enveloped by the digits of the moon and the sun."
Because of this statement, the word *dahanāgāra* (fire-house), occurring in the root text, refers to the temple of Madana (the god of love).
Its application there, however, is due to the power of its inherent suitability (*yogyatā*) for the *mudrā*. Some, however, [interpret] by means of the word *dahanāgāra*...

It is said that the *mūlādhāra* of the practitioner is [the locus], and therein they speak of the union with the object of attainment (*sādhya*). Others, however, say that the *śrīcakra* itself is the circle of fire joined with the digits (*kalā*) of the moon and the sun. Both of these views are contrary to the *Saṃhitā*. (20, 21, 22, 23)
Then he describes the woman being drawn [toward him]: "Then she, her outer corners of the eyes trembling, was tormented by the arrows of the Bodiless One (Kāma). (2)
She had cast away the goad of fear, shame, and modesty regarding her own conduct;
her heart was drawn away, her fortitude destroyed, and she had abandoned her very life.
It was well-protected by earthen ramparts, palaces, iron chains, moats, and mechanical devices;
its broad hips were shimmering with the surging waves of rutting ichor.
[He beheld her] swallowed by the whirling power of the moving energy of the wheel of powers, her lotus-heart trembling from the application of fresh passion. (27)
Her garment was snatched away by the wind of the great mantra of the mind;
she appeared as if bewildered, agitated, exhausted, and fleeing. (28)
She was as if painted, as if unconscious, as if crushed;
she was as if dissolved, as if bewildered, and as if struck with terror. || 29 ||
She appeared as if bewildered, as if crowded, as if her mind were agitated;
she seemed as if hidden away, as if motionless, or as if she had entered into another state.
One may bring back even from hundreds of yojanas a woman who is whirling in the sky like a mechanical device set in motion by a great wind.
She whose ends of the eyes—the outer corners—were trembling; she whose own people were her own;

whose conduct was her proper behavior; whose policy was her moral conduct; she by whom the five goads beginning with "one's own people" and ending with "policy" had been cast far away; and she whose life-force and bodily luster had flown away.

A *vapra* is a rampart; a *prāsāda* is the palace of kings; a *nigaḍa* is an iron chain or staff used to block gates; and a *nadīyantra* is a moat containing an internal river. Even though [the city] was well-protected by these, it was assailed by surging waves of intoxication—great billows.
Her hips were quivering;

she was one who had been swallowed up by the pervasion and movement of a particular power within the wheel of powers that issues forth from the circle of powers— the retinue of the Goddess worshipped by the practitioner.

Some say it is the wheel of power (*śakticakra*) belonging to her, which is her *mūlādhāra*, [the state] of the Kuṇḍalinī energy as it rises from that; [a state] with a speed even greater than that of the mind.
She whose garment (*aṃśuka*) had been snatched away and drawn off by the wind of the mantra;
the fourteen occurrences of the word "iva" (as if) beginning with "vimūḍhām iva" (as if bewildered) serve fourteen times as indicators of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
[Such fancy is expressed] by means of words such as *manye* (I think), *śaṅke* (I suspect), *dhruvam* (certainly), *prāyaḥ* (mostly), and *nūnam* (surely).
Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is manifested by words, and the word "iva" (as if) is also of that nature.

Thus, according to the statement of the *Ālaṃkārikas*, this [passage] functions as a suggestor of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). "Filled with demons" means possessed by spirits; "distressed" means agitated. Amara states: "The words *vihasta* and *vyākula* are synonyms.
"As if having gone elsewhere" means as if appearing different. The rest is clear. || 24 || 25 || 26 || 27 || 28 ||
Now he states two applications for protection:
"Alternatively, having written the entire Mātṛkā on the outside of the wheel, whoever wears it at the root of the arm shall be invulnerable to all living beings. (32)
Having drawn the wheel on birch bark or similar material, encircled it with the *mātṛkā* letters, and worshipped it,
whoever wears it becomes invulnerable to tigers and other predatory beasts. And it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Dear One, one should write all the *mātṛkās* outside the wheel on birch bark,
a gold leaf, a silver leaf, or a copper leaf.
"He is invulnerable to all living beings, especially to tigers and the like. Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Saṃhitā*: "Alternatively, the knower of mantras, having encircled the *mātṛkās* outside the wheel, should worship that wheel correctly," and so forth. (32)
Now, according to the method of the *nikāyin* (grouped) sequence, he states several successive applications of preceding transformations:
"In that very way, O Great Goddess, through the application of the sequence of its own designations, one attains agelessness and immortality by means of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor. (33)

"In the same way" means exactly as in the previous application. The specific distinction, however, is that the writing of one's own name is done with sandalwood paste and other such substances. In the *Saṃhitā*, moreover, the mixing of musk and saffron is also mentioned.
Herein lies the detailed procedure for the writing of the name and so forth.
The purpose of this extensive treatise is to be seen in the *Artharatnāvalī*. || 33 ||
Furthermore, he speaks of the very applications for subjugation (*vaśya*):
(p. 129) "O Goddess, thus, by this procedure, [the mantra] written with *rocanā*, *aguru*, and *kuṅkuma* according to the arrangement of the wheel (*cakrayoga*), wherever it may be situated... (34).
Having pierced the name of the one to be accomplished with his own name within the center of the wheel, he quickly brings all the worlds under the control of his feet. || 35 ||

Having drawn the wheel encircled by the *mātṛkās* according to the previously mentioned method using yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and other materials, and having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in its center interlaced with one's own name, one should worship it. All people will come into one's presence; this is through the application of the wheel (*cakrayoga*), that is, by means of the method of drawing it.

He states that the restriction of supports such as birch bark and the like, as well as whether concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is performed or not within the body, is expressed by the words "In which... (*yasmin*).
O Dear One, having placed the seed-syllable— which is the nature of the Great Kāmakalā— in the middle, one should seize each individual syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished.
One should also encircle it on the outside with all the letters of the Mātṛkā;
having placed it within gold, one should wear it on the left arm.
Whether one wears it on the crest-lock, on a garment, or wherever else, it indeed makes the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, become its servants. (38)
It deludes the king, the horse, and the wicked elephant;
it [deludes] the thief, the lion, every foreign army, and the great planet. 39.
When worn in the form of a discus, it [protects] against enemies, thunderbolts, weapons, vetālas, and likewise rākṣasas, as well as bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.

The seed-syllable consisting of the Great Kāmakalā is the fourth vowel; with that placed in the center and written within a triangle, one should enclose each individual syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished, enveloping it on both sides.

In the *Vimarśinī*, it is explained that one should surround [the diagram] with the *mātṛkā* letters outside the nine-source wheel (*navayonicakra*), which itself is outside the half-wheel (*cakrārdha*). However, the author of the *Ratnāvalī* states that one should [place] the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) using the seed-syllable of the Kāmarāja-peak (*kūṭa*), which is situated in the middle of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).

Having knotted [the letters] and written them within a triangle, he explained that one should surround [the mantra] with the Mātṛkās in the very middle of the triangle outside the Kāmakūṭa, according to the method of knotting the syllables of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*).
However, in reality— even though the word "of the wheel" (*cakrasya*) is absent in the root text— by the principle of *nikāyin* (belonging to a class), [it is understood].

Because it has the preceding sacrifice as its archetype (*prakṛti*) and because of the concluding statement, "she who is maintained in the form of the wheel" (*cakrarūpiṇī*), the term "of the wheel" (*cakrasya*) is brought to mind;
thus, the meaning is simply "the center of that [wheel]" and "outside of that. As for the statement in the *Saṃhitā*:
"O Goddess, having joined the syllables individually with the *kāmakūṭa*,

one should encircle the names of those to be accomplished within a triangle, outside the *mātṛkā*s. In this case as well, because the phrase "having drawn the wheel" is understood from the preceding verse, it must be done in a manner that does not contradict that.

It should be explained as "outside the wheel" (*cakrādbahis*) alone; by this, the sublation of what is obtained from the original source (*prakṛti*) is not effected. It is logical that the support of the fourth vowel and the support of the *mātṛkā* are not to be adopted, due to the absence of authoritative evidence and because they contradict the *saṃhitā*. Here, at the beginning—

The sequence of the arrangement is as follows: first the *kāmakūṭa*, then the first syllable of Devadatta, again a *kūṭa* which is the letter *va*, again a *kūṭa* which is the letter *da*, and a *kūṭa* which is the letter *tta*.
Regarding the use of the plural number in the term "names of those to be accomplished" (*sādhyanāmni*) in the *Saṃhitā*, it is for the purpose of referring to multiple individuals to be accomplished.

It is implied that this application occurs only once; accordingly, in the present context, the analysis of the compound is simply "the syllable named after the object to be accomplished" (*sādhyanāman*). As for the statement in the *Vimarśinī* that in the phrase "consisting of the moving and the unmoving" (*sacarācaram*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the "wheel" (*cakram*), that is incorrect.
Having arranged them in that sequence, O beautiful one, one should place the Purāṇas at a crossroads in the center and also in the four directions.
Then, O Goddess, a great clamor arises there among the people,
and especially among women, even those who are hostile.

In the very same ritual application mentioned previously, the specific distinction is that in place of the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one substitutes the syllables of the names of cities such as Srughna, Pāṭaliputra, and so forth. Now, one might object: "If this is the case, since it is the city itself that is being accomplished, this is already established by the previous [method]. To this, he says: "And in the middle."

The sense is that the six wheels must be constructed for the purpose of burying them at the center of the city, at the crossroads, and in the four directions starting from the east; thus, because this is a specific instruction, it is not redundant. In this context, since the *Saṃhitā* states "in the directions starting from the east in sequence," [the same applies] here.

And because of the hearing of the word "ca" (and), there is indeed a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the six [powers], not an option (*vikalpa*). The intended meaning is that the entire city remains under one's own control. || 41 || 42 ||
O Dear One, one should meditate upon the earth, situated in the midst of this [universe], together with its mountains, forests, and groves, extending to the four oceans, and blazing with light. (43)
Through the practice of meditation for six months, another form of Madana is born;
merely by being seen, he attracts the worlds, and merely by being seen, he brings them under his control.
By her glance she agitates a woman; by merely looking, she removes poison.
By her glance she makes one a master of speech; by her glance she deludes everyone. (45)
By means of the gaze one effects possession, and by means of the gaze one may liberate everyone;
by means of the gaze one may destroy quartan fevers and other irregular fevers. (46)

One should contemplate the entire earth situated in the center of this wheel for six months; the accusative case here denotes an uninterrupted duration. The term "fever" (*jvara*) is an indicative mark for all incurable diseases. (43, 44, 45, 46)
This wheel, worshipped at night and colored with vermilion, effects a great attraction of women even from a great distance. (47)

"Colored with vermilion" means it is drawn with vermilion. "One should worship at night what is drawn with vermilion with a one-pointed mind"—this is because of its syntactic unity with the *Saṃhitā*. Therefore, the interpretation that one should first draw [the design] with turmeric or other substances and then fill it with vermilion is unacceptable. The word "great" (*mahat*) is an adjective qualifying the wheel.
Or, it is "maha" because it bestows a great festival (*maha*), or it is "maha" because it is a great attraction (*ākarṣa*) for the great ones; thus, it is both that and an attraction. || 47 ||
O Goddess, when she is thus worshipped always in the cardinal and intermediate directions according to the sequence of the quarters, then the entire world comes under one's control.

Facing whichever direction one wishes to bring under control, one should always worship [the deity] there uninterruptedly. In this manner, one gradually brings the entire world under control. Regarding this, they say that the name of the direction itself is the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). || 48 ||
Having written this on a fresh birch-bark leaf with a smooth interior,
one should inscribe the city in its center using yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (aguru), and saffron (kāśmīra).
If one should cause a vast region, a province, or likewise a district to be inscribed with one's own name and buried in the earth; || 50 ||
One should wear it on the hand, or on the neck, or at the base of the arm;
or on the crest-lock, or on the garment, or wherever else it may be situated.
O highly fortunate lady, this is the supreme wheel for agitating a city.
Having drawn the wheel on fresh, flawless birch bark, one should inscribe one's own name in its center and then write the name of whichever specific town, district, or region it concerns.
The meaning is that, having performed worship, one should carry out any one of the following: burying, wearing [as an amulet], or other such methods. || 49 || 50 || 51 ||
Milk of the *arka* plant, saffron, and likewise the juice of the *dhattūra* plant.
Having combined yellow pigment, lac-dye, the juice of lac, and an abundance of musk, this wheel is drawn with the name of whomever [it is intended for]. (53)
For him, there shall be no fear arising from thieves, robbers, disease, enemies, lions, snakes, or horses;
nor any arising from yakṣas, rākṣasas, vetālas, bhūtas, pretas, or piśācas. (54)
For him, there is no fear arising from spiders, scorpions, or insects, nor from jaundice or chronic fever, nor from the malevolent spells and sorcery of others. (55)
O Goddess, because of constant retention, Kāla, Mṛtyu, Yama,
and the others are not at all able to harm even a single hair properly in any way whatsoever.
Having mixed the seven substances beginning with *arkakṣīra* (milk of the *arka* plant) and having drawn a *cakra* with that [mixture],

for whomever one writes the name in the center, there is the cessation of all calamities for that person. The meaning is that if it is worn by him constantly, then as long as there is contact with his body, even death does not afflict him for that duration of time.

Here, by the word *alaktaka*, the juice produced from the application of substances such as the bark of the *barbūra* tree is meant, because the juice of lac (*lākṣārasa*) is mentioned separately. However, their coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [as synonyms] should not be accepted. [As it is said:
"The juice of the *unmatta*, lac, the milky sap of the *arka*, saffron, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*)."
Having combined musk and lac together, one should draw [the design].
Thus, because it contradicts the *saṃhitā* [of the Veda].

*Kāmalā* is the wife of fever (*jvara*). *Śītikā* is a cold-fever (*śītajvara*). By the elision of the vowel *a* (i.e., reading *ka-a-śīti*), the number eighty is obtained through the letter *ka*, which denotes "wind" (*vāyu*) according to the lexicon: "Ka refers to Brahmā, the Self, wind, and the sun."
Or diseases born of wind (vāta) are seized. 52 || 53 || 54 || 55 || 56 ||
Alternatively, one should place the goddess in the center, likewise situated within both triangles,
joined with the name below, and marked with yellow pigment and saffron.
And one should cause it to be buried; after seven days, [the person] will become a servant like a slave.

Regarding this, they explain that one should write the Vidyā four times—in the three corners of a triangle and in its center—and beneath that, in the four locations, one should repeatedly write the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (sādhya).

Some maintain that one should write the *kāmakūṭa* four times; however, in both cases, it must be considered whether the root syllables are actually inscribed. Regarding the reading "located within the belly of the triangle" (*trikoṇodaragāmi*), this is found only in certain manuscripts. In that version, the compound is easily explained as "the three corners and the belly."
However, the reading "going to both triangles" (trikoṇobhayagām) is indeed in agreement with other tantras. || 57 ||
One who desires to uplift others should constantly wear this [image] which has been marked and inscribed. (58)
Even one who is omniscient by name becomes mute at that very moment.

As for those who wish to uproot [the opponent] along with themselves, who desire to seize the initiative, or who wish to dispute in either scriptural or worldly affairs— the wheel, together with their names, [is employed].

Having written [the mantra] on birch bark or similar material with yellow substances, one should worship it with yellow flowers while facing the east and then wear it; the mouth of the opponent will become paralyzed. As it is said in the Jñānārṇava: "Having written it with yellow substances, one should worship it with yellow flowers."
Facing the eastern direction, one should paralyze all disputants.
"O Goddess, he who has a thousand faces becomes mute at that very moment;
indeed, by [reciting] his name, even a man as eloquent as a scholar becomes like a stone.
In some versions, the original reading is "indradiṅmukha" (one whose face is turned toward the direction of Indra). || 58 ||
He states the procedure for killing:
"Having also mixed it with the juice of mahānīlī, as before... (59).
Facing south, having burnt [the effigy] in the fire, one kills [the target] in an instant.

Having drawn a wheel with indigo juice and having joined the name of a Brahmin-defiler, an unrighteous person, or a hateful enemy according to the previously mentioned method, one should worship [it] while facing south.
In the fire, the enemy is burned; he perishes. || 59 ||
One should draw it marked with buffalo dung, horse dung, and cow urine.
Having written the name [of the person] situated between *ara* and *nāla*, being hated by all living beings,
one should mix the essence of buffalo dung and horse dung with cow urine; having drawn a wheel (*cakra*) with that,
and having inscribed therein "May Devadatta and Yajñadatta hate each other," and so forth, one should worship it.

One should place that wheel in the midst of *sauvīra* (antimony), or else in sour gruel (*kāñjika*). According to Amara, *āravālaka*, *sauvīra*, and so forth [refer to antimony]. The grammatical connection is as follows: he whose name is marked upon it becomes hated among all living beings. As for the phrase "the buffalo and the white [goat]," it refers to their mutual enmity.

Others maintain that [the mention of] cows and tigers is an elliptical expression for other animals as well; furthermore, some hold that the two types of dung alone are the substances for drawing, while cow’s urine is used merely for sprinkling the wheel. However, both of these views contradict the *Saṃhitās* and other authoritative texts. || 60 ||
Having applied yellow pigment (rocanā), one should draw [the figure] with a crow's wing-feather. || 61 ||
One should properly wrap a blue cloth with a blue thread;
when it is suspended in the air, it becomes a supreme means of eradication.

(134) Having drawn a wheel on a blue cloth with the substance of *gorocanā* using a pen made from a crow’s wing-feather, and having inscribed the name of the person to be targeted (*sādhya*) therein, one should worship it. Then, having wrapped that cloth with a blue thread and tied it to a staff, one should suspend it in the air. This results in expulsion (*uccāṭana*). || 61 || 62 ||
Having written [the mantra] with milk, lac, yellow pigment (rocanā), and the juice of mahānīlī, one should wear the wheel; thus the four castes will come under one's control.

Due to the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) of substances such as milk and so forth, and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), the writing materials are mixed together into a single substance. This is stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
"With [pigments] produced from the juice of great indigo, combined with yellow orpiment and mixed with milk..."
"One should draw a wheel with lac-dye and bring the four castes under one's control.
Herein, it is prescribed that the fifth substance, which has been omitted, should be added:
namely, *mahānīlī* and *rocanā*.

In the phrase "with milk, lac juice, and so forth," it is observed that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), this very same substance is intended even in the *Jñānārṇava*. In accordance with that, the particle "ca" (and) in the root text should also be explained as serving the purpose of including that [substance] in conjunction [with the others]. This is stated in the work titled *Śabdapradīpa* composed by Sureśvara.

"From the *Bhiṣakkośa*: 'It may be produced from *audbhida* salt, or it may be found in *kṣārikā* and *kaḍāhalavaṇa*. By this, the statement of Vimarśinīkāra—that four substances correspond respectively to the subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) of the four castes—is refuted."

The observation of a fixed distribution of white, red, yellow, and blue colors among clay and other materials according to the distinction of Brahmins and others within the context of recollection (smṛti) and so forth is rooted in delusion; however, that [delusion] is to be set aside by the perception of specific details in another Tantra. || 63 ||
By this very procedure, one should cast it into the midst of water;
through bathing, drinking, and so forth, he shall attain incomparable good fortune.

"By this very [means]," meaning by means of the five substances such as milk and so forth, in the form of drawing lines and the like; by the word "etcetera," the washing of the mouth is included, while the point that "those who drink these various [substances] come under one's control" is a matter established in other Tantras. As for what was stated in the *Vimarśinī* at the time of initiation and consecration:

The golden-plate wheel should be placed in the jar; furthermore, after the consecration, that wheel is to be given to the guru—this meaning is obtained from this [text], yet it is not seen in other tantras. 64.
By meditating upon her as blazing, one will truly cause agitation within seven days for the goddess situated in this center, whether she be a woman of the Nagas or a celestial maiden. 65.
The queen is the king’s consort; the city-dweller is any woman residing in the city.
One should meditate upon her as blazing within the center of the wheel; such is the meaning already stated previously. || 65 ||
If one whose soul is burdened by great sins should worship the Goddess with leaves of *śamī*, *dūrvā*, *aśvattha*, or even those born from the *arka* tree, [he shall be purified]. (66)
Within a month, a person destroys the impurity accumulated over seven lifetimes.
In the ritual of worship, the four sprouts of the *śamī* tree and others must be used together as a single unit.
This is because their conjunction, understood through the dual compound (*dvaṃdva*), is intended to function as a qualifying attribute of the object to be employed. For this very reason:

In the course of commenting on the verse from the *Jñānārṇava*, "With *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *kunda*, and *śatapatraka*," Śaṅkarānanda stated that these flowers, such as the *mallikā* and others, possess the status of being means for worship when combined together (*sahā*).
According to Amara, *kumārī* means "the sun" (*taraṇi*). They say that the term *arkaja* (born of the sun) is also an elliptical designation for its flower.
Now, with seven and a half verses, he describes thirteen applications:
"When one has drawn this wheel in yellow pigment and worships it... (67).
Facing the eastern direction, one should paralyze all disputants;
having drawn [the diagram] with vermilion, one should worship it while facing the north.
At that time, the world becomes entirely subject to his control.
Having then drawn [the image] with red ochre, he should worship it while facing the west.
He too shall become one who attracts all women and causes them to be subject to his will and agitation; facing the south, he should worship Kṛṣṇa with a discus.
O Supreme Goddess, for whomever [the mantra] is recited by name, a constant loss of the mantra occurs;
yet it is worshipped within the intermediate directions of those [points], O Parameśvarī.
O Goddess, when written with gorocanā and placed in the midst of milk, it causes paralysis, enmity, disease, and the eradication of enemies, while also bringing about subjugation.
Thrown into the midst of cow urine, it causes the eradication of enemies;
placed in the midst of oil, this wheel is supremely effective for creating dissension. (73)
Placed within buttermilk, it shall cause enmity;
situated in the midst of a blazing fire, it destroys all enemies. (74)

Here, worship is performed with yellow flowers alone; according to the statement in the *Arṇava*, "worshiped in the intermediate directions—the corners of Agni, Rākṣasa, Vāyu, and Śambhu"—and because this is established in common worldly usage, the fruits such as *stambhana* (paralysis) and others should be applied according to this very sequence. Therefore:
Since the sequence of east,
north, west, and south has already been established, the hypothesis that the sequence runs from Īśāna to Āgneya is refuted; rather, the sequence is from Īśāna to Vāyavya.

However, the author of the *Ratnāvalī* has committed a great error because his position is devoid of logical justification. By the phrase "in that manner" (*tadvat*), it is stated that yellow substances and the like should be used as the medium for writing in accordance with rites such as immobilization (*stambhana*).
If no specific substance is determined, then substances such as *rocanā* (yellow pigment) obtained by their very nature should be understood as the standard. || 67 || 68 || 69 || 70 ||
Alternatively, O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should draw a wheel of great luster with vermilion near a crossroads that is situated in a secluded place. (75)
O Maheśvarī, beginning from the very outside up to the center,
one should place there the Mātṛkā, starting with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.
O Maheśānī, that practitioner who worships at the time of night according to the sequence of the Kula conduct shall, at that very moment, become a Khecarī.
In a secluded place near a crossroads, free from common folk, one should draw a wheel with vermilion powder;
having inscribed the *mātṛkās* there, starting from the exterior and proceeding to the center,
one should perform worship at night according to the *kulācāra* tradition, accompanied by the *ma-pañcaka*.

The accomplishment of the state of a sky-walker (*khecaratva-siddhi*) occurs. As for the drawing of the *mātṛkā*: having formed a triangle with its apex facing oneself in the place of *aṇimā*, one should visualize two lines—one to the left and one to the right—facing the northeast (*īśāna*) and southeast (*āgneya*), so that a horizontal line falls above the central point.

Likewise, having visualized the eastern line, some say that one should write sixteen *mātṛkā* letters starting with 'a' and ending with 'tha' in their respective places, and write 'ha', 'la', and 'kṣa' in the three corners; or else,
in the place of the seat for all the deities beginning with Aṇimā, [one should write them] individually in the form of a snare (*vāgurā*).

Others maintain that all the *mātṛkās* should be written again and again; however, in reality, the [mandala] established by the Kerala tradition is proven by authorities such as the *Jñānārṇava*, which state: "For the sake of attaining success, [the mandala] is square, adorned with the letters of the *mātṛkā*, circular, and endowed with the *mātṛkā*s," and so forth.

There is a method for drawing the *mātṛkā* [vowels and consonants] within the *śrīcakra*, and this is its procedure; thus it is appropriate. That method is to be seen in the *Sundarīmahodaya*. (75) (76) (77)
O Maheśānī, by worshipping in that same manner on either of those two mountains, one truly attains freedom from old age and death; there is no doubt about this.

On such a mountain where there is but a single tree, by worshipping it according to the method previously described, one attains freedom from old age and death. Accepting the reading *ekatara* and explaining it as "without companion" contradicts other Tantras such as the *Arṇava*. || 78 ||

(p. 137) Now, he describes a single practice that accomplishes all siddhis: "Or else, O Mistress of the Gods, if the practitioner, with a steady mind, should worship at night in a cremation ground on a day corresponding to one of the great elements, as before. (79)
Wooden sandals, a sword, a vetāla, perfected substances, red arsenic, collyrium, a subterranean opening, a female servant, a yakṣī, and likewise the power of traveling to distant places. (80)
Whatever lineage of accomplishments exists within the three worlds,
the best of practitioners shall accomplish all of it instantly.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Śrī Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava.

The day of the great elements is the fourteenth; some say that it must be the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), while others maintain that it must also be joined with Tuesday. One whose mind is steady is fearless. [This applies] to one who has ascended the sandals (pādukā).
Walking even upon water; striking a sword with one's own hand and then regaining control over it;
subjugating a *vetāla*; dwelling together with the *siddhas*; the creation of priceless objects by mere thought; the restraint of the mind; [the power to walk on] stone.

The acquisition of a wish-fulfilling gem; an ointment that grants the power of seeing through obstructions; a subterranean passage for entering into the depths of the earth, caves, or mountains; the bringing under one's own control of two specific deities, namely a female servant and a yakṣa;
traveling to distant lands in an instant; and other such things as well.

Whatever lineage of accomplishments (siddhi-santāna), such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, exists in the three worlds in infinite varieties—all that one should accomplish by this very practice alone. For this reason, he is the best among practitioners.
In this very *Saṃhitā*, however, the repetition of this practice for a period of six months is prescribed.

In other tantras, various forms of worship consisting of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) are taught, which have as their fruit the destruction of sins committed over many lifetimes; with the intention that these too are to be accomplished by this very same procedure, the author said "whatever [is prescribed]. This means "all that has not been mentioned."
Because we see that the phrase "whatever [is] prior to the Agniṣomīya" (*yatkiṃcitprācīnamagnīṣomīyāt*) is described in that same manner, all is auspicious. 79, 80, 81.
Thus ends the second rest in the commentary called Setubandha on the ocean of the Nityāṣoḍaśikā, composed by the illustrious Bhāskara. || 2 ||

Now begins the third rest. Thus, having described the accomplishment of the *cakra* and its forty-three applications to be accomplished by means of the second chapter consisting of eighty-one verses, [the author now treats] the *mudrās* as well.

Desiring to indicate that the fruit [of the practice] is indeed accomplishment immediately following the practice of the wheel (cakrasādhana), and wishing to show the manner of their arrangement right here, Paramaśiva introduces a question through the aspect of reflective awareness (vimarśa):
The Goddess said: "O Blessed One, the mudrās of Tripura have been indicated but not fully revealed.
O Śaṅkara, tell me how their formation is performed."
They were indicated in the first chapter as being prescribed for performance during worship. || 1 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the mudrās which bestow the accomplishment of all aims;
by performing these, Tripurā becomes present before one's face.
By the rule "saṃmukhāt svāṅgāccopasarjanāt," the suffix *ṭāp* is optionally applied.

Since the invocation is the first stage of the worship, he first describes the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā*, which is useful for it and consists of the collective form of the nine mudrās to be described hereafter:
Having turned the hands over, one should make the two thumbs touch and be even;
having placed the two index fingers in a curved shape within the ring fingers.
O Maheśvarī, one should place the little fingers in their own positions;
this is the Great Mudrā of the Three Segments for the rite of summoning Tripurā.

Having placed the hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced within one another, one should grasp the tip of the left ring finger with the right index finger, and the tip of the right ring finger with the left index finger. Then, [join] the pair of little fingers, the pair of middle fingers, and the pair of thumbs.
And one should make them straight while facing each other.
This [mudrā], consisting of three segments joined in pairs, is employed for the invocation of Tripurā.
Here, the term "turning" (*parivartana*) refers specifically to the mutual insertion of the fingers. [The hands] are touched.

The two thumbs joined together, even and extended straight; the two ring fingers placed inside, and the two index fingers made curved in shape with their tips bent; having thus formed them, one should employ the two little fingers by joining them to one another. Here, the term "its own place" (*nijasthāna*) is used figuratively.
The meaning is that one should also apply the two middle fingers to the position above the middle joint.
This is obtained either through the etymological derivation (*yaugikatayā*) of the term *trikhaṇḍāpada* or by its conventional usage. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Great Goddess, by means of the rotation within both hands... (p. 139).
Having joined them, O Dear One, one should hold the ring fingers with the two index fingers.

One should join the two middle fingers at their centers, and then place the two little fingers below them; likewise, having joined the two thumbs, one should arrange them in three pairs according to the sequence.
This mudrā, named Trikhaṇḍā, is for the rite of summoning Tripurā. Thus [it is said].

Nor should it be argued that the name "Trikhaṇḍā" (Three-sectioned) should be applied because the yoga of the Middle [channel] is not explicitly mentioned according to the system of this particular Tantra, whereas it will be stated later that the Dvikhaṇḍā alone possesses the nature of the triad of digits beginning with Vāmā; for [the application of names] varies according to the difference between Tantras.

It should not be argued that this is because we see many differences regarding mantras, yantras, mudrās, and so forth; for when no contradiction is possible, it is improper to assume a contradiction between two options. For this very reason, in the phrase "located within the ring fingers" (*anāmāntargate*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is intended. Some, however, also interpret it as "located by means of the two ring fingers" (*anāmābhyām antargate*). || 3 || 4 ||
Having placed the middle fingers together and restrained them by the thumbs,
one should form the index fingers like a staff, with the ring fingers positioned above the middle fingers.
This, however, is the first mudrā, which causes universal agitation:
having joined the tip-joints of the little fingers and thumbs facing one another, one should also join the tip-joint of the middle fingers in the middle portion of those two joints.
This means that one should join the three tips of the little fingers, middle fingers, and thumbs so that they are mutually connected. Having joined the two hands in such a manner,
one places the right ring finger upon the middle joint of the left middle finger, and the left ring finger [upon the middle joint of the right middle finger].

One should insert [the two index fingers] over the middle joint of the right middle finger; the two index fingers, however, should be kept straight, with their tips directed toward the void (or the ground), and thus positioned. This is obtained from the inherent force of the word "above the middle finger" (*madhyamopari*). This is that mudrā.

She is known as Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī. By the phrase "this, however, is the first," it is implied that wherever the display of the mudrās is prescribed, one should begin the display from this very [mudrā] and not from the Trikhaṇḍā. And this...
The formation of the mudrā is said to be obtained through the natural force of the syllables.
The Jñānārṇava is also favorable to this same point:
"Having turned the two hands away from each other, place the two middle fingers together."
Then, having pressed [the tips] straight with both the thumbs and the little fingers.
"One should form the two index fingers like a staff while the ring fingers rest upon the middle fingers;
this is the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā, which causes the agitation of the three worlds.
However, it is stated otherwise in the *Tantrarāja*:
Having joined the nails of the little, ring, and middle fingers together,
one should place the two thumbs upon the joints of the little fingers and extend the two index fingers straight.

"The *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā causes the agitation of the three worlds. Regarding this, the earlier authorities maintain that one should perform it only when the middle fingers are in their central position and not moved to another location; the meaning is that they should remain in their own place. [The other fingers] are blocked by the little finger and the thumb.
Thus ends the qualification of the ring fingers. Some explain that one should place the two index fingers above the middle fingers like a staff;
however, in this view, there is clearly a distant syntactical connection (*dūrānvaya*), the redundancy of several words, and a contradiction with other tantras. || 5 ||
If, in this very mudrā, the two middle fingers are straight; || 6 ||
O Maheśānī, if it is performed in this way, then she becomes the bestower of all knowledge and wealth;
the meaning is that if even the two middle fingers of this *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā are straight like the index finger, and not that only the middle fingers are straight.
When the middle finger is joined with the index finger and the others are straight, that is the Sarvavidrāviṇī mudrā; it causes all things, moving and unmoving, to be dissolved.
Thus, from another tantra.
The middle and index fingers [are extended], while the little finger and ring finger are level [with each other]. || 7 ||
O Supreme Goddess, when the two middle fingers have the form of hooks,
this is the Ākarṣiṇī mudrā, which effects the attraction of the three worlds.
When the tips of both the index fingers and the middle fingers are bent in the *sarvavidrāviṇī* [mudrā] itself, it becomes the *sarvākarṣiṇī* mudrā.
As it has been said: "O fair-eyed one, one should make the pair of middle and index fingers curved."
"Then this very mudrā is the attractor.

Here, in the phrase "by the middle and index fingers," the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that the mudrā is characterized by those two [fingers] being bent. As for the little finger and the navel...

"Same" means equal to her own two [hands] which were previously in the position of the *mudrā*. However, "in the middle" (*madhyama*) is an epithet of the Supreme Goddess (*parameśvarī*); the meaning is that she exists in the midst of these *mudrās* in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as the nature of the powers beginning with Vāmā. Others, however, [interpret it as] of this very *mudrā*...

Having followed this [rule], they apply it as follows: "The little finger and the ring finger are to be placed in the middle of the *mudrā*, and the middle finger and the index finger are to be joined together" (p.
141). In this case, their similarity is to be established solely on the grounds of being objects of cognition (*prameyatva*) and so forth, rather than by way of curvature.

But if they were equal, the meaning of the injunction would be that one should also contract the little and ring fingers; and in that case, there would be a contradiction with other tantras, as well as a contradiction regarding the continuity [of the practice] and the futility [of the rule]. || 7 || 8 ||
Having formed the hands in the shape of a casket, with the two index fingers curved like hooks,
one should turn them in sequence so that the two middle fingers are positioned below them.
Gradually, O Goddess, having joined the little finger and the ring finger in that same manner, all [the fingers] should be made firm at the tips of the thumbs.
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is known as the one that effects all forms of possession (*āveśa*).
The description of the two hands being in the shape of a hollowed cup (*puṭākāra*) is for the purpose of establishing their mutual orientation away from each other;
otherwise, it would result in the fault of having no visible purpose. Therefore, the state of being turned away is obtained solely through the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*).
Thus, what was stated [by others] is refuted. In this manner, one should turn them face-to-face and cause the fingers to enter into one another.
Then, the two index fingers should have their tips bent toward each other; below those, the two middle fingers [should be positioned].

Below those, one should join the ring fingers, and below those, the little fingers, in that same sequence and in the manner of forming a hook; having made the fingers firm, dense, and without gaps, one should place both thumbs, turned downward, at the very top.

Regarding the phrase "the little finger and the ring finger," the word *kaniṣṭhā* is placed first according to the rule *alpāctaram*. This very mudrā is also called "that which causes universal possession" (*sarvāveśakarī*) and "that which brings all under control" (*sarvavaśaṃkarī*). || 9 || 10 ||
Having placed the two hands facing each other, with the little fingers positioned between the middle fingers.

The two ring fingers (anāmikā) are straight, with the two index fingers (tarjanī) outside them; then the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭha), shaped like staffs, are placed upon the region of the nails of the middle fingers.
This mudrā is named Unmādinī; it causes all women to become moistened.
One should firmly grasp the right little finger with the left middle finger, and the left little finger with the right middle finger. That grasping is of two kinds.
It is possible by placing the two ring fingers face upward and the two little fingers above them, while not placing them below; therein,
it is said "having brought the two hands face-to-face" to indicate approval of the second alternative,
[by] means of the two ring fingers being directed toward one another.

Because of its connection and because it is protected on this very side, there is a Vedic sandhi (euphonic combination) in the phrase *madhyage 'nuje*. "Anuje" means "in the little finger" (*kaniṣṭhikā*). Alternatively, the word *anuja* may be in the locative singular with the suffix *satī*. From that [ring finger], two straight lines extend outward; from those [two lines], two further lines extend at a distance on both sides.

Straight (p. 142); when the two middle fingers have their tips bent and the thumbs, shaped like staffs, are placed face down upon the nails [of the middle fingers], this is the mudrā named Sarvonmādinī. || 11 ||
Having placed her pair of ring fingers below in the shape of a hook (aṅkuśa), || 13 ||
One should also apply the two index fingers in that same sequence;
this is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes all purposes and goals.
Having formed the pair of ring fingers of this Unmādinī-mudrā in the shape of a hook (aṅkuśa), one should join the two index fingers in that same sequential manner in the form of a hook;
this is the mudrā known as Mahāṅkuśā. || 13 || 14 ||
Now, with nine [verses], he describes the khecarīmudrā: "O Maheśānī, having crossed the left arm over the right hand and the right arm over the left hand, and having turned both hands around... (15)
O Goddess, having joined the little fingers and the ring fingers in that same sequence,
both middle fingers should be placed above all, pressed down by the two index fingers.
O Maheśānī, one should also make the two thumbs straight;
this, O beloved, is the mudrā named Khecarī, the most excellent of all.

Placing the left arm over the right shoulder and bringing the right hand over the left in the manner of encircling, one should interlace the fingers of the two hands and grasp the left ring and middle fingers with the right index finger, and the right ring and middle fingers with the left index finger.
In the middle [position], however, one should place both [hands] straight above all. This is the mudrā known as Khecarī.
As it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"The left arm on the right arm, and the right [arm] from the region of the left."
Having established it, one should subsequently join it, indeed by reversing it in due order.
One should not obstruct [the fingers] with the pair of the little and ring fingers and the two index fingers;
then, having made the middle fingers straight, they should likewise be straight like a *yoni*.
"The two thumbs joined at the place of the earth constitute the khecarīmudrā.
However, in the Tantrarāja it is said: "Then, one should properly cross the left and right hands, [placing] the elbows [in that manner]."
One should bind the two wrists with the palms joined at their centers;
having bent the two index fingers, one should place the two thumbs below them.
"One should place the little finger and the ring finger crossed over on the back of the hand;
this is that Khecarī mudrā, which causes delight to Lalitā. Thus [it is said].
[One should place] the left arm beneath the right arm.

The commentary *Artharatnāvalī*, which states that one should join [the fingers] in this manner, is to be disregarded because it contradicts the *Arṇava*. As for the claim that one should place both index fingers over the middle fingers at the very top,
while making the two thumbs straight and touching the middle fingers like a staff— that too is incorrect.
This is indeed contrary to the Ocean of Knowledge. 15 || 16 || 17 ||
He describes the majesty of the mudrā:
"O Great Goddess, this [mudrā] has been fashioned as the snatcher of all splendor.
O Goddess, by merely binding this, the supreme practitioner is seen. (18)
He resembled a blazing fire, surrounded by all the hosts of Yoginīs,
including the multitudes of Ḍākinīs and Rākiṇīs, and the groups of Lākinīs and Kākinīs.
O Supreme Goddess, this [mantra] is to be meditated upon with the *sākinīs* and *hākinīs*.
O Goddess, by knowing this, one becomes dear to the *yoginīs*. (20)
Since this is proclaimed as the *samaya-mudrā* of all [goddesses],

and since this binding of the *khecarī-mudrā* constitutes the *samaya-bandha* of all the *śaktis*, therefore, by means of its formation, there occurs the offering of all splendors (*tejas*) and so forth; and by means of this knowledge—

The meaning is that one also becomes beloved by the deities and so forth. "Samaya" means a convention (saṅketa). The intended sense is the pervasion (vyāpti): whoever knows a particular convention is included within its secret code (kūṭa). || 18 || 19 || 20 ||
Now, relying on this very point, he describes the connection between the qualities and their results:
"Whether self-controlled or uncontrolled, in a pure place or even an impure one. (21)
Whether standing or sitting, walking or even motionless,
whether impure or having become pure, while eating or engaged in sexual intercourse— [one should not speak].
Having rotated the two middle fingers of the mudrā in sequence and joined them at the earthly station, one shall immediately attain the state of moving through the sky.

Having discarded the straightness of the two middle fingers of this very mudrā and having rotated them, one should join them at the position of the Earth (pārthiva). By that alone, the accomplishment of the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva-siddhi) is attained.
Herein, the qualification consists in the singular concentration [of the mind] and so forth.

The meaning is that, as in other ritual applications (*prayoga*), factors such as purity (*śucitva*) which delimit the locus (*adhikaraṇatāvacchedaka*), as well as temporal restrictions and so forth, are not necessarily required as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). However, according to the *Jñānārṇava*, the conjunction with the earthly station (*pārthivasthānayoga*) is obligatory because it constitutes a part of the body of the Sky-farer (*khecarī*); whereas, according to the *Vāmakeśvara*, [it is not].

The distinction is that it is "optional" (*kāmya*). They say that the "position of the earthly" (*pārthivasthāna*) is the location of the great bindu situated at the crown of the head. As for the threefold nature of *khecarī* described here in the commentaries of the ancients, the verse beginning with "of the mudrā" (*mudrāyāḥ*) is also [to be understood] according to those [respective traditions].

That [definition] is not stated by us because it is irrelevant to the present context.
