Since the word *khecarī* has multiple meanings, and since among those meanings there is no single essence of being *khecarī*—just as there is no single essence of being "saindhava" (salt)—and furthermore, because the specific restraint of the mind (*manonirodha*) and so forth lack the status of being the defining properties (*vibhājaka-dharma*) that differentiate that [essence], [it is not applicable]. || 21 || 22 || 23 ||
O beloved, having turned the two hands over so that they touch in the shape of a half-moon,
one should then simultaneously form a pair of the index fingers and thumbs.
One should place the middle finger, pressed down from below by the little finger;
likewise, the ring fingers should be joined at the very bottom in a curved manner.
This seed-mudrā brings about all accomplishments without delay.
First, one should perform a rotation in which the fingers of the two hands, having been mutually touched, are inserted into one another.
Then one should form the pair of the index finger and the thumb into the shape of a half-moon; that is to say, as if seizing by the neck.
By the word "simultaneously," it is understood that both pairs [of fingers] should be arranged in that manner.
Then, having pressed down on one's lower part with the two little fingers, [one places] the middle fingers...

One should join [the thumbs] at their tips according to the sense. Having inserted the two tips of the little fingers into the two joints of the middle and ring fingers respectively, one should cause the tips of the nails of the two middle fingers to touch each other; this is what is meant. Then:
Having placed the two ring fingers at the very bottom of the mouth, they should be joined in such a way that comfort arises;

this is the mudrā known as Bījā. In this very same [mudrā], it is stated in the *Tantrarāja* that the two index fingers take the form of a hook (*aṅkuśa*) and the tips of the nails of the two thumbs are joined.
The middle fingers are at the center, the sides, and the bottom; the little fingers are at the tips in reverse order;
the ring fingers are below, crossed; and the two index fingers are in the shape of a hook.
"Others say that this seed-mudrā is described as being at the very tips of those [other] nails.

However, some, stating that "one should place the two middle fingers below while they are held by the two little fingers," believe that the little fingers are to be inserted into the joint of the index and middle fingers.

Others, however, explaining that "the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhike) are held by the middle fingers," and regarding the term *kaniṣṭhāvaṣṭabdha* as a bahuvrīhi compound, maintained that one should enclose the pair of little fingers within the pair of middle fingers without bending them. Both of these [interpretations]...

It should be disregarded because it contradicts other tantras; for it is improper to abandon a possible point of agreement. However, in the *Jñānārṇava*, because there is a greater degree of contradiction, the method is indeed different.
Having formed a reverential añjali as it is turned, O Goddess, one should then place the two middle fingers at the tips of the little fingers, and thereafter hold the two little fingers.
O Dear One, the pair of index fingers and middle fingers should be firmly joined by the two ring fingers,
and the two thumbs should be brought together in the shape of a half-moon.
"O Śivā, this is declared to be the Seed-mudrā, which brings about all bliss. Thus [ends verses 24 and 25].
He describes the final *yoni-mudrā*: "The two middle fingers are curved in shape and positioned upon the tips of the two index fingers. (26)
Likewise, the ring fingers and the little fingers should be placed together;
all [the fingers] should be joined as one and pressed by the thumbs. (27)
This, however, is the first mudrā known as the *yonimudrā*.

Having formed the two index fingers in a curved shape like hooks, one should place the two middle fingers, turned upward, upon the tips of those index fingers. Then, [one places] the two little fingers...
Having crossed [the hands], one should grasp [the vessel] with the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*).
In this manner, having joined the four fingers—the two ring fingers and the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhā*)—one should restrain them with the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*).
That is to say, one should place the two thumbs face-down upon the nails of the two ring fingers.
Although such a meaning alone is obtained from the natural sense of the words, it could also be easily argued that there is no fault in the difference in mudrās due to the difference in tantras;

nevertheless, for the sake of consistency with other tantras, the interpretation as a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "those two [fingers] which have the ring finger in the middle"—is more appropriate. Consequently, the two ring fingers are crossed.
Having formed the index fingers in the shape of a hook, one should insert them between the two upturned middle fingers.
Below those two, one should place the two little fingers crossed and joined to the backs of the ring fingers.
The pressing with the thumbs is accomplished upon the middle joints of the middle fingers. Thus it is said:
In the *Tantrarāja*:

"Through the joining of the little finger and the thumb, the great *yoni* becomes the *trikhaṇḍikā*. This is the *yonimudrā*. Its mention here as the first among these nine [mudrās] is for the sake of [establishing its] priority.

Anticipating the question "How so?", they provide various explanations: some say that among them, the first is to be mentioned first because it is the most excellent; others, however, maintain that in the external sacrifice the *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā comes first, whereas in the internal sacrifice it is the *yonimudrā* alone.

They say it is for the purpose of demonstrating the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*). In that regard, one must investigate why the reverse order does not occur due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraheṇa*). Alternatively, because the *bindu* arises first in the construction of the wheel (*cakra*), and because it is to be demonstrated in the *bindu-cakra*, this [the *bindu*] holds primacy.
Alternatively: "This single Mahāmudrā has attained the state of Yonimudrā;
by her, one's own self is divided according to the various distinctions such as *saṃkṣobha* and so forth."
By this statement of the learned, they also say that its primacy is due to its being the producer of all other mudrās.

Alternatively, by the word "first" (prathama), the Goddess herself is meant, according to the Śruti: "I am the first-born of the Cosmic Order (ṛta)," and the Smṛti: "The first-born is Tripurāmbikā. In that regard, concerning the aspect of birth—

Because it is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatvāt*), there is no dispute that the very first word, which signifies all causes, is the designator of that [first cause]; therefore, the meaning is that this mudrā is indeed the first one, having the very nature of the Goddess.
Alternatively, among the ten mudrās previously mentioned, it is specifically the *trikhaṇḍā* [that is meant].

Because it is mentioned first, the word "first" refers to the *trikhaṇḍā*. Therefore, the meaning is that this *yonimudrā* is indeed the *trikhaṇḍā*, yet slightly different from it; for it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "The great *yoni* is the *trikhaṇḍikā*. This explanation applies to the compound *anāmikāmadhyagate*, which is a *bahuvrīhi*.

It is that which reveals the intended meaning (*tātparya*); therefore, the principle of the "lighter compound" (*tatpuruṣa-laghīyastva*) has no application here. Alternatively, just as there is a process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) for the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*), the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) is indeed established in other tantras as well.
For even when worshipping according to the order of emanation, the mudrās are not necessarily performed in the sequence beginning with *saṃkṣobhiṇī*.

It is appropriate to restrict [the display] to "those to be shown," because the nine mudrās are restricted to the nine wheels. For this very reason, in the case of the abbreviated practice consisting of worship of the central wheel alone, the display of mudrās does not follow the sequence beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī; rather—
[This occurs] precisely through the sequence beginning with the *vaśya-mudrā*. Thus, the mention of priority is intended according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*).
And by that, the implication is that worship is performed according to the order of emanation; this is the essential truth. || 26 || 27 ||
He concludes the description of the mudrās:
"O Great Goddess, these mudrās of Tripurā have been declared by me. (28)
These are to be employed at the time of worship according to their sequential order.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*.
By the phrase "according to their sequential order," it refers to the sequence of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*), beginning with *saṃkṣobhiṇī* and the others.

In the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), by means of the sequence beginning with the womb (*yoni*) and so forth, [the mantras] might—by way of abbreviation—serve merely for the purpose of the individual soul (*puruṣārtha*); it is for this reason [they are taught].
Thus, by the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*), their dual purpose is established. In that regard:

The application for the sake of attaining specific fruits, however, pertains only to the Siddhacakra and not to any other, because this [application] is taught following the accomplishment of the cakra (p.
147). Nor is the scriptural mention of the fruit of the mudrās a mere *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), as is the case with the hearing of the fruits of the *samidh* and other such offerings.
This must be considered, because of the discrepancy resulting from their being recited both within the context of the *Prakaraṇa* and outside of it;
furthermore, because the mudrās are mentioned independently in the third Upaniṣad of the *Sundarītāpinī*. May there be auspiciousness! || 28 ||
Thus ends the third rest in the commentary called Setubandha on the ocean of the Nityāṣoḍaśikā, composed by the illustrious Bhāskara.

Now begins the fourth rest (viśrāma). May the sandals of the venerable Guru be ever victorious! Having thus described the nature of the mudrās in the third chapter, which consists of twenty-eight and a half verses, [the author proceeds] to the practice of the *cakra*.
The [treatise], along with its ancillaries, being completed, the author now intends to explain the practice of mantra-sādhana, which has reached its proper occasion.

Desiring to state the individual sādhana for each of the *kūṭas* (syllabic clusters) that were previously presented as qualifiers by way of knowledge, he speaks regarding their method of accomplishment.
In order to define its essential nature, she introduces a question regarding other subjects as well with two verses;
the venerable Goddess said: "O Blessed One, the supreme knowledge of the mudrās has been fully explained."
Now, speak the practice for each individual syllable of the Great Goddess.
O Supreme Lord, [you manifest] great knowledge, power, pervasiveness, location, existence, and dissolution within the body through the distinction between the gross and the subtle.
The term *jñāna* is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). It refers to the Great Goddess, Śrī Mahāvidyā.

The "means" (*sādhana*) for each individual syllable or *kūṭa* is the method for attaining each respective accomplishment (*siddhi*). That knowledge is great; thus, it is "Great Knowledge" (*mahājñāna*).

This was stated with the intention of expressing the non-difference between knowledge and the object of knowledge; or else, it means "one who possesses great knowledge. Furthermore, the greatness of that knowledge consists in the fact that after its own establishment, there remains no portion of the knowable to be known, according to the Vedic scripture: "When this is known, all this becomes known. [And he possesses] power...

The greatness of knowledge; its pervasion as the soul of the universe; its transformation; its state as the support of the world; "bhava" (existence) meaning birth; and "laya" (dissolution) meaning withdrawal.
The terms "bhava" and "sthāna" are stated in reverse order for the sake of metrical constraint. The word "śarīre" (in the body) is in the dual number.
Thus, these are the eleven questions. The word "ca" (and) is intended to include those not explicitly mentioned; therefore, the meaning is:

"Tell [me] the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and so forth for the *vidyās* such as Karaśuddhi, as well as their weapon-mantras (*āyudhamantra*) and so forth. Here, this should be understood: *dhauta* is extremely white and most subtle.

The supreme Śiva (paraśiva) is like a highly precious, great cloth that is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). When that very [Śiva] is rendered solid by being smeared on all sides with an extremely white substance—the essence of food—he is said to be "fashioned. One who is similar to him is said to be "endowed with power" (*śaktiyukta*).

In that very context, by being marked with a subtle form in accordance with the design about to be executed, it becomes "marked" (*lāñchita*). The Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*), who is similar to that and distinguished by a subtle creation, is called the "Thread-Self" (*sūtrātman*). Then, through union with various colors, the cloth becomes "colored" (*rañjita*); this is the Virāṭ Puruṣa.
It exists. Here, the Supreme Brahman known as Paraśiva is, by its very nature, possessed of infinite powers (*anantaśaktika*).

As it is stated in the *Jñānavāsiṣṭha*: "The Supreme Brahman is all-powerful, eternal, perfectly full, and imperishable," and so forth. It is precisely the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the multitude of powers residing within that [Brahman].

Tripurasundarī. Because of such Vedic passages as "The power of the Divine Self, hidden by its own qualities," and because of the non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), there is no contradiction of Brahman’s qualitylessness (*nirdharmakatva*).
This has been stated by the venerable Padmapādācārya: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and eternity—these [qualities] exist..."

The dharmas, although not distinct from consciousness, appear as if they were separate; for this very reason, the established doctrine of the Tantras is that the Supreme Brahman is indeed characterized by such powers (śakti). Consequently, power (śakti) is also included within the very category of Brahman. This is also stated in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*:
"The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) of the Supreme Lord is said to be nothing other than pure consciousness (*caitanya*).
Consequently, just as on a clean cloth there can be no stains or the like, [the impurity] that causes densification— standing in the place of food-essence (*annarasa*)— is impossible."

Only Śakti possesses the capacity to produce creation. As for the fact that Paraśiva is the cause merely by virtue of His proximity, this is simply a synonym for the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatā*). Consequently, it is Śakti residing in Śiva alone that undergoes transformation into the form of creation. And as in this view:
The objections raised by the proponents of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) would be irrelevant;

this has been explained in detail in the *Varivasyārahasya* and other works. Here, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists of the connection of the essence of food with the cloth in its entirety, as well as its transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the nature of the two forthcoming creations. This is the mark (*lāñchana*).

The subtle body is *sūkṣma*; the colored [gross] body is *sthūla*. The connection between these two bodies at the first moment is *bhava* (becoming). Their continued existence for some time is *sthiti* (abiding).
Alternatively, the subtle body itself is *utpatti* (origination), while the gross body itself is *sthiti* (abiding). This is the case with a painting.
Furthermore, by means of washing, the cloth remains characterized solely by the smell and taste of the food; this is *laya*.

In this manner, the experience of reality (*tattva*) is *mahājñāna* (great knowledge). Liberation (*mokṣa*), which takes the form of its fruit, is *prabhāva* (power); such is the distinction. However, some maintain that *mahājñāna* is *prakāśa* (illumination), while *prabhāva* is...
Reflection (*vimarśa*) is their pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is their state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*). *Parā-vāk* is the locus (*sthāna*);
*paśyantī* is existence (*bhava*); *madhyamā* is dissolution (*laya*); and the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*) is *vaikharī*—so they explain. The source for this must be sought. (1–2)
The illustrious Bhairava said: Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme and great knowledge, the highest of all knowledges,
by the mere practice of which one does not sink into the ocean of worldly existence.

p. 149) Among all transformations, the supreme transformation is the great knowledge (*mahājñāna*) concerning the subject that undergoes transformation. Listen now to that which concerns the supreme reality (*paratattva*).
By means of such knowledge—merely by its being practiced, merely by its arising—[of that knowledge...]
The meaning is: because there is no dependence on any other auxiliary cause. || 3 ||
O Dear One, Tripurā is the supreme primordial power, the source of knowledge and the rest;
through her differentiation into the gross and the subtle, she is the Mother of the origin of the three worlds.
Indeed, until the limit of the time of dissolution of the entire world, the actions of deceased beings remain within the one, non-dual Brahman, swallowed up in a subtle form;
it is solely by virtue of the diversity of their ripening that the power of Brahman takes the form of the desire to create and so forth.

Although she previously existed in an unmanifest state, she then becomes manifest. This very one is the supreme power (parā śakti) named Tripurā; that is to say, she is the primordial, the first, and the causal source of creation.
Even though there exists the Supreme Brahman which is more primordial than even that, nevertheless—

Although this power existed from the first moment of that dissolution until its final moment, it was not capable of creation; however, with the intention that this power— in the form of the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) and so forth—
having become manifest by itself, brought about the successive stages of creation, [the author] says of it:

Thus, the designation "today" has been made. This power, although consisting of will (*icchā*), is also of the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) because it arises from that which is objectless; therefore, it is also of the nature of that [consciousness].
Indeed, this alone is capable of conceiving the triad (*tripuṭī*) of the knowable, the knower, and so forth; hence it is said, "from knowledge and the rest."

The meaning is "from beyond the triad consisting of knowledge, the knower, and the object of knowledge. For this very reason, the term *tripurā* is used as the designation for the substantive (*viśeṣya*) in order to suggest its etymological derivation from the three cities (*tribhyaḥ purebhyaḥ*). The word *jñāna* is a separate term acting as an attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) of Tripurā; its meaning is "having the nature of knowledge" (*jñānarūpā*). From the beginning...
Some maintain that the meaning is "from Brahman, who is the primordial source of all";

others hold that it means "the primordial form of the triad of powers consisting of knowledge, will, and action, which is of the nature of the tranquil state (*śāntā*) as their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*). This is that very power.

Regarding the production of both the subtle triple-world (*trailokya*) that is about to be created and the gross triple-world, *mātṛkā* is the mother, meaning she is their progenitor. Some, however, maintain that the "triple-world" refers to the three peaks (*kūṭa*) of *vidyā*, and that the *mātṛkā* which produces them is twofold, distinguished as gross and subtle, or by the divisions of *vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, and so forth.
They say that the meaning is that she was born from Śiva, who is of the nature of the letter *ha*, starting with knowledge (*jñāna*). || 4 ||
Now, it might be argued that the production of the three worlds is impossible since they are not perceived at the time of dissolution;
or, even if such production were possible, it would follow that even things like a hare's horn could likewise be produced, as there is no difference in their status.
To this, he says:
She whose essential nature consists of the entire aggregate of principles swallowed [by her];
at the time of dissolution, the entire aggregate of principles— the collection of thirty-six categories— is swallowed and devoured by her.

By which she possesses such a nature. Consequently, at the time of creation, she manifests the universe—which already exists within her own interior—in its subtle form, and nothing else. As it was said by the venerable Vasiṣṭha:
Just as the entire earth exists within the water inside an egg, so too does this [universe],
complete with fruits, leaves, creepers, flowers, branches, boughs, and roots, exist within the Self.
"Just as a tree exists within the seed of a tree, so too does this [world] abide in Brahman.

And thus, by the force of the resulting fruit, there is no possibility of the production of things such as a hare's horn—even in the form of a latent impression (saṃskāra)—due to their conceptualization as non-existent; this is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: since even Śakti, who devours the entire universe, must ultimately be admitted to have Paraśiva as her cause—because she herself is dissolved in him in a subtle form—it is sufficient that he alone, as the cause of the world together with Śakti, is postulated;
what is the use of this superfluous postulation of Śakti? Let it be the cause of that [Śakti] itself.
To the objection—"How can it be the cause of that [liberation] if it is contrary to the principle 'by what means'?"—he says:
"But when that [nature] has reached its final transformation, no other [cause] is admitted. (5)
The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and indicates necessity.

The meaning is that since the postulation of the transformation of power (*śakti-pariṇāma*) is necessary, the matter is accounted for by that alone; on the contrary, the postulation of a Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*) is not accepted because it would be purposeless. This is the underlying idea:

The position of the followers of the Upaniṣads (Aupanishadas), however, is as follows: the power called *māyā* belongs to the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*). And that [power] is indeed insentient (*jaḍa*). It alone is the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) of the world, whereas the Supreme Brahman is the illusory material cause (*vivarta-upādāna*). Therefore, because the world is also of the nature of *māyā*, it possesses insentience.

And there is falsity (*mithyātva*). However, the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*) are intended to show that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*), there is only one individual manifestation.
As for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in "All is Brahman," it is according to the principle of sublation (*bādhāyām*), and so forth.
But the position of the Tantrikas is that the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) residing in supreme consciousness belongs even to the followers of the Upaniṣads.

That very [power] is called *māyā* because it possesses infinite forms; for the scripture declares: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold," and "It becomes both *māyā* and *avidyā* by itself," and so forth. The phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is precisely its transformation. For this very reason, it is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Thus, this phenomenal world is a play of consciousness (*cidvilāsa*).

From the *Jñānavāsiṣṭha*: for this very reason, it is also real. This is because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "All is Brahman" finds its natural expression only in absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*).
Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptures on non-duality (*advaita-śruti*), since that which would cause contradiction—namely, a single, positive difference—is precisely what is absent.

This is because [the opponent] accepts that [the world] is substantial (pithya), and so forth. Furthermore, it is perfectly clear that the natural intent (*svarasa*) of the aphorisms of Vyāsa— such as "And [Brahman is] the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples," "Because of its being made by itself [and] because of transformation," and "Its non-difference [from Brahman], on account of words such as 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*)," etc.— also lies precisely in this same sense.
And thus, since power (*śakti*) is necessary as the cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in both positions,

*paraśiva* itself need not be postulated by the followers of the Upaniṣads as something superfluous; for [the latter] is merely an illusory appearance (*vivarta-rūpa*) compared to the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmin-mṛttikā*) required for a jar.

We perceive some other underlying cause; for this very reason, having asserted that "by the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all," the presentation of examples in the Śrutis, such as "just as, my dear, by one clod of clay being known [all that is made of clay is known]," becomes logically consistent. || 5 ||

Now, one might object: since we observe that powers such as the capacity to burn reside in fire and other substances, and since a power in the form of an attribute cannot exist without a substratum (dharmin), the substratum—Parashiva—must indeed be postulated for the sake of accounting for the nature of power; to this, he says:
For one who is devoid of power is indeed unable to do anything;
but when he is joined with power, O Supreme Goddess, he becomes capable.
The intended meaning is this: we do not postulate [an omniscient creator] out of a mere passion for [the existence of] power;

rather, because the manifold world consisting of earth and so forth is an effect, it would be impossible for it to exist without a cause. Even the logicians infer that earth and the rest possess an agent precisely on the grounds of their being effects.
This very meaning is also accepted by the followers of the Upaniṣads,
as the venerable Vidyāraṇya stated in his *Viveka of the Five Elements*:
"His power, Māyā, which is devoid of constituent principles (tattva) and is to be inferred from its effects, is like the power of fire."
"For no one perceives power anywhere prior to its effect. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, if the Supreme Śiva, who is postulated through the necessity of otherwise inexplicability (*anyathānupapatti*) regarding the nature of effects,

were devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), then because that inexplicability would remain unresolved, one must necessarily postulate even a single power (*śakti*) therein to resolve it. And it is said in the *Devībhāgavata*:
Śakti creates the universe; she indeed protects it in its entirety;
by her will, she destroys this world of the moving and the unmoving.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Hara, nor Śakra, nor Brahmā, nor Pāvaka, nor Sūrya,
nor Varuṇa are capable in any way whatsoever of accomplishing their respective tasks.
"For joined with her, those gods perform their respective duties;

she alone is perceived as the direct cause in all effects," and so forth. Furthermore, there is the *Śaktisūtra*: "Consciousness (*citi*), being autonomous, is the cause of the manifestation of the universe. It is not thus [that the world is produced by something other than consciousness].
For us, who maintain that power (*śakti*) is the cause, there is no deficiency in the non-conceptualization of Paraśiva,

because it would otherwise be impossible for him to be an effect. Furthermore, the impossibility of [Paraśiva] being a property (*dharma*) can be easily resolved by conceiving a single reality as having the dual nature of both property and substratum (*dharmī*).

This is because even the followers of the Upaniṣads accept the non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*). If the Supreme [Lord] were devoid of power, He would not be capable of performing any action; for [the capacity to act] consists precisely in possessing immediate desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and volition (*kṛti*) directed toward the material cause (*upādāna*).

Because its nature as an agent consists in being composed of the triad of powers—will, knowledge, and action—it becomes capable of producing effects only when accompanied by such powers. However, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) regarding Śiva’s accompaniment by these powers is not possible; therefore, it is not [the case that Śiva alone is the cause].
The meaning is that another [authority] is necessary. || 6 ||

Now, even if the status of being the creator of the world can be accounted for otherwise, it must still be postulated that Paraśiva exists for the sake of bestowing the fruits of action upon those devoted to ritual works (karmaṭhas), for the sake of liberation upon the knowers (jñānins), and for the sake of providing an object of meditation for the practitioners of devotion (upāsakas).

Anticipating the objection that—since actions, being insentient, lack the capacity to bestow fruit; since only the Nirguṇa (devoid of attributes) is to be approached by the liberated; and since there can be no worship without an object of worship—one refutes it as follows:
"In Śiva, who is subtle, no name or abode exists without Śakti."
O Great Goddess, even by means of knowledge, no action whatsoever brings about well-being.

However, at the time of relying upon meditative absorption (dhyāna), there is neither delight nor mental stability; for worship (*upāsanā*)— in the form of name-recitation (*nāmakīrtana*) and so forth— is not compatible with that which is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*),

because the delimiters of capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) and the delimiters of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) are themselves of the nature of attributes, and [such worship] would thus pertain to that which lacks them.

Because names do not function [independently]: since the state of being denotable (*bodhyatva*) in an object is also a specific type of power (*śakti*), just like the power of denotation (*bodhakatva*) in a word, its establishment is achieved simply by accepting that [power];
and because of parsimony (*lāghava*), since it is established by power alone in the manner described, what is the use of a "Supreme Śiva" (*paraśiva*)? [It is accomplished] by power alone.

By means of a property (*dharma*) such as the delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) means difficult to know because it is devoid of a basis for linguistic application (*pravṛttinimitta*); "name" (*nāma*) refers to the collection of words that denote or indicate; "abode" (*dhāma*) means illumination, which is the cognition produced by words; "does not exist" (*na vidyate*) means that it is not possible.

By this, the secret is intimated that the bindu which is written in the center of the Cakrarāja is the very form of Kāmeśvara. The placement of the Goddess within His lap is to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru; apart from that, there is no separate worship of Kāmeśvara alone.

Because Kāmeśvara, due to his subtlety, lacks both name and abode; because, according to the scripture "not this, not this," he is to be known only as the remainder after the negation of everything, and thus lacks all qualities (saguṇatva);
for this very reason, since there is no other alternative for the weapons of Kāmeśvara, they [are described] together with the weapons of the Goddess.
The worship will be described in the eighth chapter.
The womb (yoni) is triangular in form; with the bindu, it becomes the state of the Bindu (baindava).
That is the essential nature of Kāmeśvara and the essential nature of the support of the universe.

The statements from other tantras beginning with these words establish this very same point; that is another matter. Now, one might object: "Surely the application of words through association with imagined properties (kalpita-dharma), as well as their being the objects of the cognition produced by them, is indeed possible regarding those properties."
(153) Since it is not necessary for [the property] to have the same ontological status as the subject (*dharmisamānasattākatva*), he says:

"even by that which is known. The word "by another" (*pareṇa*) is to be supplied. Even if the knowledge of Paraśiva is established in some manner or other, regarding such knowledge, there is the production of liberation and the utility of ritual action (*karma*).
Nor is there any logical connection [between such knowledge and action], because such knowledge is exceedingly easy to obtain due to its being eternal;

the sense is that this is according to the Śruti: "Everything shines only after Him who shines. Likewise, the meaning is that when the Supreme is known, neither happiness (*śarma*), nor liberation (*mokṣa*), nor any action whatsoever exists [as a separate entity].
Therefore it is said: "Even Śiva becomes a corpse when deprived of Kuṇḍalinī;
for whoever is devoid of power is considered by the wise to be powerless."

Thus it is established in the *Devībhāgavata*. Now, one might object: even if Brahman appears in cognitions such as "I know the pot," we do not claim that determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) is a means to the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*); rather—
Because [the object] is a non-conceptual cognition whose single object is empty of all phenomena, he says "meditation" (*dhyāna*).

Since there is no possibility of the mind finding delight in that which is devoid of pure and impure phenomena due to its lack of beauty, meditation cannot occur; even if the mind were to engage with it through force, [it would not be meditation].

It would exist for only a few moments rather than for a long duration; therefore, the stability of meditation—which consists of firm support and is synonymous with non-conceptual samādhi—would not be achieved. The implication is that in the absence of that [stability], the goal of human life cannot be accomplished. As for *śakti*, however...

By virtue of its being the nature of both the attribute (dharma) and the substratum (dharmī), it follows—by implication—that name, abode, bliss, action, delight, and stability are all logically established. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*:
"Thus, that all-pervading power is discerned as Brahman."
It is declared by the wise to be of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa).
She who possesses attributes is to be served by those with passion, while she who is without attributes is to be served by those free from passion;
she is the untroubled mistress of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
"Or, when worshipped according to the prescribed rites, she grants all desired objects. Thus [ends verse 7].

Thus, having refuted the opponent who maintains that there is no Supreme Śakti apart from Paraśiva by means of a discursive debate (jalpa-kathā), he now addresses the questions regarding pervasion (vyāpti) and the two types of bodies (bhava-śarīra) by following the formal debate (vāda-kathā):
Having entered into the interior of the supreme path, she exists in the form of a subtle nature.
She remains as one who has swallowed every last seed and sprout.

The two words *vāmā* and *śivā*, which appear in the subsequent verse, are to be construed here as well. The "Supreme Path" (*para-mārga*) is none other than Paraśiva himself, because he is the substratum through his own pervasion; or alternatively, it is the path of the Supreme (*parasya mārgaḥ*), that is, of Paraśiva.
Having entered within the entirety of whatever constitutes the path and the locus of pervasion,
and having made even the moon of Paraśiva— which is of the nature of emptiness— appear as if pierced by causing it to swell, she,
being endowed with her two subtle forms and natures, [consumes] those things that have been swallowed whole.

This Śivā, abiding as the nature of those seeds which are the subtle bodies of all thirty-six principles without exception, and as the sprouts which are their respective gross bodies, is called Vāmā; she is the one who brings forth the universe.

The etymological derivation is "from vomiting" (*vamanāt*). Here, "form" (*ākāra*) refers to the configuration of parts, such as a tree's possession of leaves, flowers, fruits, branches, and so forth; its "essential nature" (*svarūpa*) is "treeness"—this is the distinction between the two.
The essence of food, existing within a cloth in the form of fragrance, pervades the entire cloth by means of its density.
The sense is that it is as if it has subsequently transformed into the state of various emerging specks and, after that, into the form of a mark. || 8 ||
Having thus explained the pervasion (*vyāpti*) within existence and in the subtle and gross bodies, he answers the questions regarding its location (*sthāna*) and dissolution (*laya*):
"Vāmā, Śivā, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā have attained the form of a triangle (*śṛṅgāṭaka*). (9)
But Raudrī, O Supreme Goddess, has the form of devouring the universe.

That form which consists of the parts beginning with the sprout and ending with the fruit, culminating in transformation among the six modifications of existence— this very transformation of its own nature is "stasis" (sthiti). And this form is called "stasis" either because it is predominant, or because, like a mountain peak, it is the final state of the sprout which consists of two leaf-like parts.

Alternatively, she is designated by the term *śṛṅga* (horn) due to her similarity to a horn; thus, the Goddess is called *Śṛṅgāṭā* because she moves (*aṭati*) within such a form. As for the designation of a triangle by the term *śṛṅgāṭa*, the etymology is the same: it is so called because a horizontal line moves between two lines shaped like horns.

In the case of the confluence of four paths, although there is a specific result arising from the water, it is nonetheless a case of conventional (nirūḍha) indication precisely because of its possessing such a form; this is another matter. The Goddess possesses such a state as the basis for her manifestation.

She is called "Jyeṣṭhā. Thus, the meaning is that at the conclusion of the period of the world's manifestation, she who effects its withdrawal by devouring the universe is designated by the term "Raudrī" because her activity is characterized by such [a nature]; indeed, she is Tripurā herself.
However, the Dīpakācāryas state:
The two lines, Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā, extend from the eastern tip to the northeast and southeast corners;
the transverse line to the east of the point is Raudrī. They explain that the synthesis of these three attains the form of a triangle, the shape of a *śṛṅgāṭaka*. || 9 ||

Now, one might object: "Since this [state] precedes the triple-city (tripura) even before the emergence of phenomenal expansion (prapañca), it is appropriate that she be called Tripurā at that time, but not during the stage of manifestation (sphiti) and so forth.

Anticipating this doubt, he states in two verses that the status of the Great Goddess as Tripurā is never to be set aside: [The two verses follow: "O Goddess, you are Tripurā because you are beyond the three cities; you are Tripurā because you are the supreme power of the three cities. You are Tripurā because you are the cause of the three cities; you are Tripurā because you are the dissolution of the three cities. "You are Tripurā because you are the three cities themselves; you are Tripurā because you are the mistress of the three cities. You are Tripurā because you are the essence of the three cities; you are Tripurā because you are the light of the three cities."
This is that supreme power, the one and only Supreme Goddess. (10)
O Goddess, Tripurā is threefold, having the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
O Dear One, [the power] consists of the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the power of will.
She creates the three worlds; thus she is celebrated as Tripurā.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, when presided over by the male form, become Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
their corresponding powers—Bhāratī, Pṛthivī, and Rudrāṇī—are called Knowledge, Will, and Action. These three alone are the constituent factors of the body of agency.
As it has been said: "That supreme power of Brahman, the creator of the universe, which is described as his will, becomes the Goddess when he desires to emit [the world]."
"It is to be known as exactly thus, and not otherwise"—
making this known with absolute certainty, she is called the power of internal knowledge (*antajñāna-śakti*) that acts instantaneously.
When the knower intends, "May this object become thus," and subsequently brings that very object into being, that process is here called action (kriyā).

Thus it is stated in the *Mālinīvijayatantra*. There is also the scriptural statement: "The powers of knowledge, strength, and action are innate (*svābhāvikī*). Regarding this, its commentators explain that "strength" refers to the power of will (*icchā*). The meaning is that these three are indeed the very nature (*svabhāva*) of Brahman and are not distinct from it. Consequently, at the time of creation...

The sense is that her status as Tripurā is not contradicted, because she consists of the triad of Jñāna and the others [Jñāna, Icchā, Kriyā] even at other times, and because she consists of the triad of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, or Brahmā and the others [Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra].
The word *pura* means "body. The analysis of the compound is: "she who has three bodies (*purāṇi*). || 10 || 11 ||
To demonstrate that even at the time of dissolution she is indeed Tripura, he describes her mode of being with four and a half verses, beginning:
"When she, whose form is curved, flashes forth from the seat of the Śṛṅgāṭa... (12).
Having pierced the solar orb of Śiva and melting the lunar orb, she is gladdened by the supreme bliss of the flowing nectar arising therefrom. (13)
That woman of noble family, having abandoned her own family, goes to another man who is devoid of auspicious marks, lacking in virtues, and destitute of lineage and beauty.
Then, wandering through the world again in whatever form she desired,
she became satisfied by that conduct and remained once more all alone.
She sports by herself, unmanifest, having attained the name Tripurā;
she is designated as the three principles and consists of the three powers of the phonemes. (16)

When the limit of the duration of persistence is reached, then the Goddess Śivā, emerging from the *śṛṅgāṭapīṭha*— which consists of the manifestation of the phenomenal world of earth and so forth in its gross form— becomes curved in shape by turning back; and because she faces inward (*pratyaṅmukhatvāt*), she possesses a crooked form.
Having pierced even the solar orb in the form of Śiva— which is known as the expanded *bindu* and the *kāmākhya*—

and having abandoned that form, one then dissolves even the lunar orb, which is the previously existing *bindu* of the nature of emptiness due to its consisting of nectar; [the one] who exists therein...

Resembling a flow of nectar, supreme bliss gladdens her, and she attains a state of identity with that [bliss]. This much is the manner of the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). For the *bindu*, which transforms into the face within the essential nature of the *kāmakalā*, is of the nature of the sun.

Furthermore, the secret convention (*samaya*) of the Tantrikas is that the subtle fourth bindu (*turīyabindu*) is of the nature of the moon. Having observed this very point, the author describes it again by means of an ornament (*alaṃkāra*), reminding us of the story of the wanton woman (*svairiṇī*): "The woman of the *kula*" (*kulayoṣit*). *Kula* refers to a group of those belonging to the same lineage.

And their homogeneity consists in being objects of a single cognition within the threefold structure (tripuṭī). She is related to that [structure], meaning she has transformed herself into the nature of the gross phenomenal world (sthūla-prapañca). In the alternative sense, she is a woman of noble birth; having abandoned the "family" (kula), which here means the phenomenal world—or, in the other sense, disregarding her own virtuous lineage—she becomes supreme.

The Supreme Śiva as the Puruṣa; in the alternative sense, the lover (*jāra*). "Without characteristics" (*nirlakṣaṇa*) means devoid of uncommon attributes; in the alternative sense, devoid of the auspicious marks described in the *Sāmudrika* [treatises]. "Without qualities" (*nirguṇa*) means transcending the three qualities such as *sattva*; in the alternative sense, devoid of qualities such as cleverness. "Lineage" (*kula*) refers to mother, object of knowledge, and so forth, as well as the form conditioned by them.
"Free from the state of being poisonous" means, in effect, having the nature of non-objective consciousness (*nirviṣaya-cid-rūpa*).

In the secondary sense (*pakṣe*), it means born of a wicked lineage and being unattractive. "Attains" (*eti*) means attains through non-differentiation; in the secondary sense, it means she sports with him. He describes the repeated recurrence of creation and dissolution with the word "then" (*tataḥ*): "Then..."

Following the dissolution (*pralaya*), which is the sole abode of bliss consisting of the state of the essential identity (*samarasa*) of Śiva and Śakti, [the Goddess] once again—being of a spontaneous nature and characterized by independent activity—manifests the universe within her own mirror by Her own will, according to the *Śaktisūtra*. Here, the word "own" (*sva*) refers to the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). Consciousness (*cit*).
Because she alone was introduced in the preceding sūtra as "the independent cause of the manifestation of the universe," [she is described as follows:

having caused the world to wander and transformed herself manifoldly into the form of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), she is again satisfied by that very conduct—the conduct of a wanton woman—and remains alone by herself, having abandoned her many forms. (In the alternative sense: The independent cause of the accomplishment of the universe, because she was the subject of discussion in the previous sūtra; having caused the world to wander and transformed herself manifoldly through the nature of phenomenal expansion, she is again satisfied by that conduct—the conduct of a wanton woman—and remains alone by herself, having abandoned her many forms. (In the alternative sense:)

She has abandoned people such as servants and the like; she is unmanifest (*avyaktā*), inaccessible to speech and mind, and in another sense, being unseen by people, she delights—that is, she performs the play of creation and so forth. She clarifies this very state of being unmanifest with the words "tattva" and so on: the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) are manifest; these...
One causes [the universe] to dissolve by means of the three principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
As it has been said: "The principle of Ātman extends up to Māyā; the principle of Vidyā should extend up to Sadāśiva."

"Śakti and Śiva are the Śiva-tattva; the Turīya-tattva is the aggregate of these. Thus, he dissolves the creation of sound, consisting of the fifty-one forms of the Mātṛkā, into the three Kūṭas of the Vidyā which are non-different from himself. Of the Kūṭas...

Because it sequentially takes the form of the letters *a*, *ka*, *tha*, *i*, *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa*; likewise, it dissolves the emanation of the *cakras*—which consist of the multitude of powers (*śakti*)—into the triad of subtle powers consisting of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).
Thus, even in the state where manifestness is avoided, she has attained the renown of being "Tripurā" because she possesses these threefold forms.
In this treatise, Kulakuṇḍalinī, residing in the triangle at the seat of the Mūlādhāra,
enters within the path of the Suṣumṇā in a subtle form; having pierced the sun situated in the Anāhata-maṇḍala and dissolved the lunar maṇḍala in the Sahasrāra by means of Akulakuṇḍalinī—

The meaning—that she, having been nourished by the streams of nectar arising from that [union], returns and comes to her own place—is also stated through double entendre (śleṣa) as will be explained in the *Uttara-tantra*. || 12 ||
He teaches the non-difference of the present Vidyā with such a Tripurā:
Vāgīśvarī, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), is the form of liberation in the *vāgbhava* [syllable];
in the *kāmarāja* [syllable], she is Kāmakalā, whose form is desire and whose nature is action (kriyā). || 17 ||
Within the seed-syllable of Śakti, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) is indeed Will (Icchā) in the form of Śiva;
thus the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī consists of three syllables. 18.

Within the three seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti, Vāgīśvarī—who is of the nature of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti)—stands in order as the bestower of liberation; Kāmakalā—who is of the nature of the power of action (kriyā-śakti)—as the bestower of desires; and the Supreme Power (parā śakti), who is of the nature of the power of will (icchā-śakti), as the bestower of dharma.
She is of the nature of Śiva and the bestower of dharma; the meaning is that in this manner, Śrī Mahātripurasundarī herself is the form of Śrīvidyā. || 17 || 18 ||
Now he answers the two questions concerning the power of great knowledge:
"Known through tradition, it releases one from the bonds of existence;
remembered, it removes sins; and recited, it destroys death. (19)
When worshipped, she destroys suffering, misfortune, disease, and poverty;
when offered oblations, she pacifies the flood of obstacles; and when meditated upon, she accomplishes all goals.

If such great knowledge concerning the reality of the Goddess is obtained through the sequence of uninterrupted traditional instruction descending from Paramaśiva down to one's own guru, it alone liberates one from the bondage of worldly existence; however, if it is obtained by other means, such as the study of books, it does not.
But it does not bear fruit; on the contrary, it leads only to misfortune. (p.
158) For those who are devoid of the lineage and are arrogant merely because of their knowledge, the Marīcīs manifest through their violation of the samaya.

This is because it will be stated in the *Uttaratantra*. By the expression "through the lineage," it is implied that the instruction of the *vidyā* must be received from the mouth of the guru, preceded by one of the seven types of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Having thus understood [it] from the mouth of the guru, it is then remembered once again.
Furthermore, when contemplated, she removes sin;
the meaning is that through recitation (japa), worship (pūjā), fire-oblation (homa), and meditation (dhyāna), she bestows fruits such as the destruction of death.
It is also stated in the Jñānārṇava:
O lady of excellent limbs, this knowledge has come down through the lineage of succession;
when remembered, it destroys the bondage of existence and removes all sins.
O Īśānī, when recited, she is the conqueror of death; when meditated upon, she is the accomplisher of all aims;
and when worshipped, she becomes the destroyer of suffering, misfortune, poverty, and fear.
"By means of oblation (*havana*), there is no doubt that she pacifies the flood of great obstacles.

Here, the recitations (*japa*), oblations (*homa*), and so forth being prescribed are independent (*svatantra*), because each is connected with its own specific fruit. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the preparatory rites (*puraścaryā*), oblations, and so forth are ancillaries (*aṅga*) to the recitation. In that case as well—

It is also easy to maintain that, by accepting their equal primacy, they are merely auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) through mutual association, as in the case of the Rājasūya and other such rites. Regarding this,
the ancient commentators have provided an exceedingly extensive commentary on twenty verses.

Describing [the matter] according to their own independent whims, they have written at great length regarding the lineages found here— such as the Lopāmudrā-santāna, the Kāmarāja-santāna, the Divya-ogha, the Siddha-ogha, the Mānava-ogha, and their various subdivisions— claiming that such a tradition has been handed down through these successions, though the meaning is merely their own fabrication.

They say this; yet all of that, although authoritative, has been set aside by us because it does not conform to the literal sense of the words, because it is not useful for the root text, and for fear of making the work too voluminous. || 19 || 20 ||
Having thus resolved these eight questions, and desiring to resolve the remaining three questions, he says— in order to focus the disciple’s attention:
"O Goddess of gods, hear now the means for accomplishing this triad of seed-syllables."
The meaning is clear.
Therein, first he describes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the practice of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable: "Clad in white garments, situated in the midst of a white dwelling... (21).
A man devoted to celibacy should worship with white flowers and with white food offerings such as curd,
milk, rice, and so forth.
Or, O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped her with white flowers of pure resolve, one should meditate upon the supreme Bāgīśvarī, who bestows the fruits according to one's desires. (23)

A "white residence" (*dhavalāvāsa*) refers to a mansion made of white plaster; this is an elliptical expression that includes [the wearing of] white garments and so forth. For this very reason, it is stated in another tantra: "Clad in white garments and anointed with perfumes and musk..."
"Adorned with a necklace shimmering with pearls, wearing white garlands. Thus, he is "devoted to celibacy," meaning one who has abandoned the eightfold sexual intercourse.
By the phrase "with milk-rice and so forth," the inclusion of ghee-balls, coconuts, and other such items is intended.
But for one who is unable to gather white objects, he says: "by visualization" (*saṃkalpa*).

The meaning is that one should contemplate even whatever objects happen to be at hand as being white. "One should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) means that while meditating, one should recite [the mantra]. Regarding this, the ancients [state]: "She has two arms and is white in color..."

They say she should be meditated upon as having the form of a young girl, holding a book and a rosary; however, this is a fabrication of their own imagination resulting from not consulting other tantras, and thus it should be disregarded. Accordingly, it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
The wise man, while recollecting Vāgīśī, should mutter the vidyā known as Vāgbhava,
[visualizing her] white as camphor and adorned with bright flowers and ornaments.
She is clad in exceedingly pure white garments, adorned with ornaments of diamonds and pearls,
and her hands are radiant with a rosary made of pure pearls and stainless gems.
"O Maheśānī, one should meditate [on her] thus—holding a book and a boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā), and bestowing fearlessness; by doing so, one shall become a sovereign of all vidyās.
As for the number of recitations (japa), since no specific number is seen, it follows the principle of one hundred thousand (lakṣa) per syllable, and thus consists of one lakh.
It is to be determined by the observation of distinctions as far as they extend. 21 || 22 || 23 ||
Thus, he describes the application for desired results (*kāmyaprayoga*) for one who has mastered the mantra:

"Then, [visualizing] her in the form of a seed-syllable (*bīja*), shining forth as far as the seat of Anaṅga, having pierced through the *brahmagranthi*, [one should contemplate her] on the tip of the tongue in the form of a lamp. (24)

Then, following the attainment of mantra-siddhi, one pierces the knot of Brahmā— the knot situated above the *mūlādhāra-cakra*— which is the Goddess of Speech (*vāgīśvarī*) in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, inseparable from the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable; [one thus reaches] the station of the bodiless Anaṅga, the Supreme Śiva whose essence is Kāmeśvara.

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: one should contemplate [the goddess] who shines forth from that *brahmarandhra*, ascending upwards, and having then caused nectar to flow, remaining on the tip of the tongue in the form of light.
Although it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"One should meditate on her as showering a rain of nectar from the base [of the spine] up to the aperture of Brahmā;
therefore, one should contemplate her, consisting of light and bearing nectar, upon the tip of the tongue."
"A fool may be equal to a stone, or even equal to a living being"—
even though Kuṇḍalinī is not mentioned here in this present Tantra, nevertheless,
by the sign of the piercing of the Brahma-knot in the root [text], and by the statement regarding the flow of nectar in another Tantra, [her existence is established].
That [number] is inferred. Some, however, maintain that the term "brahmagranthi" refers to the *brahmarandhra*.

But the ancients, due to a failure to perceive the lack of connection between the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) and the optional ritual application (*kāmyaprayoga*), explain all of this as a single ritual procedure; this should be disregarded because it does not take other tantras into account. 24.

Now, with nine verses, he describes the fruit of this practice: "One who has lost his heart, a rustic, a fool, a great sinner, or even a rogue who is unable to speak a single clear syllable—[even such a one may attain success]. (25)
One who is dull-witted, mute, extremely slow-minded, devoid of wisdom, and ruined intellect—even he becomes eloquent, like another Vācaspati. (26)

One whose heart and mind are ruined and defiled; others say this means one who has abandoned fortitude. A rustic person is one devoid of urban sophistication. An extreme transgressor is one hindered by the commission of mortal sins.
A dullard is one who is lazy. One of extremely poor intellect is one for whom retention is difficult to achieve. One whose wisdom has departed is one who has lost his discernment.
Though devoid of a physical form, with his intellect destroyed and his mind deluded, he nevertheless becomes eloquent like another Vācaspati. || 25 || 26 ||
He was a conqueror of the haughty assemblies of true scholars, possessed of unimpeded brilliance,
and a connoisseur of the essence of sound reasoning, the meaning of words and sentences, and the ornaments of speech.
One should compose [the work] like a garland of ocean waves struck by the wind, preceded by extremely delicate, expansive meters and poetic ornaments. 28.
O Goddess, by means of his poetic compositions, he becomes a creator of great epics (mahākāvya);
he is the conqueror— that is, the destroyer— of the arrogance and pride of the assembly, that is, the multitude, of true scholars who are the preeminent elephants of the quarters.

He is one whose splendor—whether as innate brilliance, eloquence, or the beauty of his countenance—is itself unobstructed, unimpeded, and unfading. Scripture is fourfold: the science of words (*pada-śāstra*), the science of word-meanings (*padārtha-śāstra*), the science of sentences (*vākya-śāstra*), and the science of sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha-śāstra*).

(161) As for the inclusion of other treatises within this very [system], we have already examined that in works such as the *Vṛttacandrodaya*. Here, they are subsumed under the term "word-meaning and sentence-meaning" (*padavākyārtha*). Their qualification is "possessing sound reasoning" (*sattarka*); the meaning of this is that they contain arguments that are not contradicted by the Vedas and are logically unassailable.

Alternatively, their reference is by means of the very compound *padavākyapada*. The word *artha* is to be construed with what follows, [referring to] *arthālaṃkāra* and *śabdālaṃkāra*. He is "one who knows" (*vid*) the essence—that is, the extracted core—of these. Some construe the word *sat* with the group of six beginning with logic (*tarka*). In that view:
To the question, "What kind of word exists apart from words and sentences? the answer should be given as: "It is of the nature of sound consisting of melody. Regarding the term *vāta*:
one should present [the subject] through sounds comparable to a mass of ocean waves tossed about by a violent wind.
Having discussed the composition of treatises (*śāstra*), he also speaks of the composition of poetry (*kāvyā*) in the verse beginning with *sukumāra*.

*Sukumārya* (delicacy) is a specific quality pertaining to words; *vṛtta* (meter) is a specific sequence of heavy and light syllables; and *asaṃskāra* (absence of ornamentation) refers to the lack of figures such as alliteration (*yamaka*) and simile (*upamā*). Of words...

By "compositions" (gumphaiḥ), it is meant specific types of literary arrangements. The term "Mahākāvya" (Great Poem) is an indicative mark that includes the ten types of dramas (rūpaka), the eighteen types of minor dramatic forms (uparūpaka), as well as mixed compositions and others. || 27 || 28 ||
He had reached the further shore of knowledge regarding the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the established doctrines of the Vedānta.
He was a knower of the statements of the Mīmāṃsā and Smṛti, as well as astronomy, history, and so forth;
he was a knower of many mantras from the Purāṇas, the Rasas, the Vādins, and the Gāruḍa.

He was a knower of the true meaning of the Pātālaśāstra, the Vijñānabhūta-tantra, and other treatises; he was highly skilled in various and diverse arts, beginning with painting and sculpture. || 31 ||
His every voice is refined by the noble sounds of the great prophecy;
he possesses knowledge of all languages and dialects, and he performs all forms of writing.
O Goddess, one becomes world-renowned as a knower of the study and meaning of various scriptures, a master of all literature, and an omniscient being.

The Vedas are the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, consisting of the ritual sections (*karmakāṇḍa*). The Vedāṅgas are three: prosody (*chandas*), ritual arrangement (*kalpa*), and etymology (*nirukta*), because the others are mentioned separately. The Vedāntas are the Upaniṣads. The Siddhānta is the scripture consisting of the five traditional lineages (*pañcāmnāya*). The science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*)...

The eighteen Siddhāntas beginning with those of Garga; the Itihāsas such as the Mahābhārata and others—by "and so forth" (ādi), works such as the Rāmāyaṇa and Vāsiṣṭha are included; the three Mīmāṃsās, distinguished by the divisions of Pūrva, Uttara, and Bhakti; the Smṛtis composed by Manu and others; and the Vākya, whether composed by Vararuci or of a worldly nature.
The Purāṇas are thirty-six in number. "Alchemy" (rasavāda) concerns mercury and similar substances; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), Caraka, Suśruta, and others are included.
The Gāruḍa [treatise] concerns magic (aindrajāla). The Pātālaśāstra concerns entering the openings of subterranean caves.

"Citrakarma" refers to painting; by the word "etcetera," the treatises on universal craftsmanship (*viśvakarma-śāstra*) concerning the construction of houses and so forth are included. In the compound *śilpāneka*, the qualifier has been placed last by virtue of the rule of optional suffixation (*bāhulaka*).
"Mahāvyākaraṇa" refers to the *Mahābhāṣya* and similar works. "All languages" refers to Mahārāṣṭrī and the other regional dialects.

The Māgadhī and other [Prākṛt] dialects; the cries and languages of beasts and birds; all scripts, including the eighteen such as the Yavanānī and others; various treatises, such as those of the Jains, Buddhists, Cārvākas, and so forth; and for the sake of these, the science of phonetics (śikṣā) and the like, as well as the processes of teaching and memorization.
Or [it refers to] the grammatical treatises (*śikṣā*) of Pāṇini and others, as well as the *Prātiśākhyas* and so forth. All branches of literature, beginning with the Vedas;
the Omniscient One, who knows the three periods of time. || 29 || 30 || 31 || 32 || 33 ||
Having concluded the practice of Vāgbhava, he promises the practice of Kāmarāja:
"O Great Goddess, such is this practice of Vāgbhava."
Next, listen as I shall describe the sādhana of Kāmarāja.
This is clear. || 34 ||
Likewise, O Beloved, she whose form is the essence of desire (kāmakalā) within the sphere of the sprout of passion has a body that blazes brightly, resembling the orb of the rising sun.
[She is] in the form of a flickering lamp-flame, raining down a stream of *bindus*.
Here, the ancients describe one ritual application (*prayoga*) in seven and a half verses;
others, however, [apply it] by means of the single word "likewise" (*tathā*), thereby extending the rules for the practice of the Vāgbhava-mantra.
Speaking thus, they consider the means for accomplishing desires (*kāmarājasādhana*) to be essentially concluded by that much alone,

and consequently interpret everything else as being directed toward the performance of a single specific desire. In reality, however, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is presented first in one and a half verses, followed by two ritual applications (*kāmyaprayoga*) in six verses.

It is logical that they are described [in this way], because it achieves consistency with the *Jñānārṇava*. As follows: "Now, O Supreme Goddess, the practitioner intent on the *Kāmakalā* should be beautiful with red ornaments and anointed with red perfumes and unguents."
Properly clothed in red garments, with his inner self as the essence of the Kāmakalā,
he should worship with various red flowers, saffron, and other such substances.
[Visualize her] from the base [of the spine] up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), having the nature of a shimmering lamp,
adorned with ornaments possessing the luster of the Bandhūka flower.
"Her hands perform the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), and hold a sugarcane bow and a flower-arrow.
(p. 163) Thus is described the method of *puraścaryā* as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*. That very same [method] is here taught.

"Madanāṅkuragocara" refers to the seed-syllable of Kāma (*kāma-bīja*), wherein the sprout of passion (*madanāṅkura*) is its sphere of operation (*gocara*). Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]

The sprout of passion (*madanāṅkura*) is the seed of desire (*kāmabīja*), because a seed takes the form of a sprout. Regarding that object, the art of desire (*kāmakalā*) should also be cultivated in the same manner as Vāgīśvarī.
Just as she is accomplished through garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and so forth, corresponding to her own color.
Likewise, this [practice] must also be accomplished by means of things consistent with one's own caste; such is the meaning.

The explanation offered by the ancients—that *madanāṅkura* refers to a specific kind of flesh found within the temple of passion (*madanamaṇḍira*)—is to be disregarded due to its lack of foundation. In the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), it is performed at the root-center (*mūlādhāra*) of a woman.

Furthermore, because the visualization of raining down streams of blood is not relevant to the present context, and because that is not mentioned even in the application of optional rites concerning the seed-syllable under discussion in other tantras; and in response to the inquiry as to what the color of the deity under discussion is, he says: "rising sun... Here, *bimba* refers to the ripe *tuṇḍī* fruit.
She is similar to those two; however, the similarity consists solely in their redness, due to the co-occurrence with the word *bimba*.

Therefore, for those ancients who consider "the orb of the rising sun" to be the sole standard of comparison, there is a mutual equality between the sun and the lamp-flame despite their being mutually contradictory.
Having raised the question "How so?", the postulation of a formal arrangement (*vyavasthā*) and so forth was rejected for the sake of its resolution.

This means that her form is like that of a lamp-flame which, while flickering, pervades from the base up to the *brahmarandhra*; in other words, it is like a thread of light being visualized within the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
In this manner, it should be understood that what is taught in another tantra has been indicated right here by the statement: "it rains down a stream of the nectar of the Bindu. || 35 ||
Thus, he states the application for one who has mastered the mantra in rites for specific desires: "She who has swallowed up the life-force of the entire expanse of the worlds. (36)
The ground of egoity is established by the pervasion of its own great majesty;
yet, from that state, it gradually shines forth as far as the limit of the bodiless (anaṅga).
Extending from the body to its very extremities, this single [reality] is thus of a dual nature.

Its "pervasion" (*ābhoga*)—that is, its expansion (*vistāra*) throughout all worlds in the three realms—is its state of being filled with the intensity of its own red luster; such is what is meant by "meditation" (*dhyāna*). By means of that, [all things] are swallowed up (*kavalīkṛta*).

She by whom the lives of all living beings are brought under her own control—regarding that, he states the reason for it with the word "mahā-": through the greatness of her own majesty (*svamahimākrāntyā*), that is, by the pervasion of her own grandeur;
or through the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*) which is situated in herself, remaining in its proper place and unwavering—that is, the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*).

The "ground" (bhūmikā) is the support. The intended meaning is this: during the stage of *puraścaraṇa*, one should meditate upon the thread of red light with its constituent parts, extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the aperture of *brahmarandhra*; and by means of its splendor, one should contemplate the entire universe as rendered crimson.

By that, the three worlds come under one's control. Why? Because, through the pervasion of one’s own sovereign power everywhere, everything is regarded as one’s own body; thus, by the arising of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃtā*) toward everything, all bodies are treated like one’s own body.

Because of the necessity of being subject to one's own mastery (*svavaśavada*). In the reading *dhvastāhaṃkṛti*, the word *ahaṃkṛti* refers to the individual egos (*ahaṃkāra*) of various living beings, not to the supreme *Ahaṃtā*. [The meaning is: "I am independent, not dependent on another."
The meaning is: because such conceit has not been cast off. This is one practice whose fruit is the subjugation of the three worlds.
And so it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The three worlds are filled with the sindūra of her splendor."
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate [upon this]; it shall delude the three worlds in an instant.
Kings, serpents, rākṣasas, and gods come under her control, O Queen of the Gods;
like Kandarpa, she is the one who steals away the pride of women.
"Whosoever contemplates her with the mind, she shall become submissive like a maidservant.
In this context, the word *tadīya* (her) means "belonging to the Goddess who is the thread of light previously introduced. As for the word *rājānaḥ* (kings):

The serpents and *rākṣasas* represent the world of the earth (*bhūrloka*); the gods represent the netherworld (*pātāla*); and this is an illustration of the heaven (*svarga*), thus providing an exposition of the three worlds. From the words "Kandarpa" up to "one should contemplate," another ritual application is described.
Its fruit is stated in the passage beginning with "the woman. Although the object to be contemplated therein is not explicitly mentioned, [it is understood].
In the present tantra, it says "in sequence" (*krameṇa*). The word *tu* serves to exclude the previously mentioned application.
Therefore, starting from the *mūlādhāra* up to the end of the *anaṅga*, and further up to the bodiless Kāmeśvara-Śiva—

It should be meditated upon as rising up gradually through the sequence of the cakras beginning with Svādhiṣṭhāna, ascending further and further, and then returning from the *brahmarandhra* to the end of the body’s limbs. [One should contemplate it] within the body of the desired woman, from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*.

Therefore, one should contemplate the Goddess Kāmakalā as repeatedly performing this coming and going, even unto the very root; that is to say, here, by the term "bodyless body" (*śarīrānaṅga*), either the body of Madana (the God of Love) or Madana himself as possessing a body is indicated. And that—
By the force of the statement "it is indeed the vulva-maṇḍala," it is understood that this contemplation refers specifically to the female body.
In this manner, the Goddess is one and the same, yet she is of two kinds—possessing both natures—according to the difference in ritual application (*prayoga*);
the word "should be contemplated" is to be supplied. As for the ancients, however, they [distinguish] between the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) and the two ritual applications.
Not discerning these verses, others explain them in a different manner;

that has not been presented here for fear of prolixity and because it is of no use. Nevertheless, the meaning stated by us should be accepted, even if it appears difficult, because it accords with other Tantras. || 36 || 37 ||
Then he states the fruit of the second application:
"Thereafter, O Goddess of the Gods, it belongs to those who pride themselves on every kind of erotic charm. (38)
O Goddess, for those possessed by passion, he is a subduer who surpasses even Madana;
any woman who comes within the range of his sight—whether she be a goddess or an asura—[is likewise overcome]. (39)
Is she a Vidyādharī, a Kiṃnarī, a Yakṣī, or a Nāga maiden? Or perhaps the daughter of a most formidable king, or a Siddha maiden? (40)
Her mind scorched by the fire of the blazing passion that is difficult to behold,
she was drenched with tears, her outer corners of the eyes trembled, and she was bewildered and overwhelmed by intoxication.
O Goddess, she who has surrendered her entire self becomes subject to his will.

The practitioner of the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) becomes the subduer of those possessed by passion and those who pride themselves on their beauty and such qualities; for he is even more powerful than Madana himself.
Distinguished by qualities such as beauty and the like, for this very reason, all the daughters of the gods, asuras, and others—
having their minds scorched by the unbearable fire of the passion ignited by the practitioner’s meditation—
became drenched by their stumbling, their hearts bewildered, and overwhelmed by intoxication.
The meaning is that, having surrendered their entire possessions and even their very selves to the practitioner, they remain under his control, having become his servants. || 38 || 39 || 40 || 41 ||
He states another application:
"Resembling the moon in rippling water, reddened by the rays of the rising sun. (42)
When visualized within the womb of the woman, she causes agitation at that very moment.
The meaning is that this very goddess is to be meditated upon within the womb of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), like the reflection of the red lunar disc in agitated water. || 42 ||
He states another application:
"That very [goddess], possessing the luster of the color of vermilion, when meditated upon in the heart," (43).
It is taught that she attracts the minds of women who are possessed by delusion and madness; this [phrase] "of women" is understood from the context, and it is connected with the word "in the heart.
Having rendered their minds thus possessed by delusion and madness—so it is said.
The meaning is that it is the attractor of that. || 43 ||
He states another application:
"Or else, she is stationed upon the head, raining down drops of blood. (44)
Showering drops of blood upon the heads of women, she stands as if meditated upon, acting as an attractor even when merely thought of. || 44 ||
(166) By means of the application of *dhāraṇā*, one brings the world under control.

There is also another application: that the subjugation of the universe occurs merely through the firm practice of meditation on the Goddess whose form has been described above. However, the ancients [interpret] these two half-verses as a single [application].

Those explaining the ritual application (prayoga) say that one should meditate firmly upon [the goddess] standing right on one's own head, raining down drops of blood; however, this should be disregarded because it contradicts the *Jñānārṇava*, which states: "One should remember the seed-syllable (bīja) on her head."
Now he promises to explain an even more secret application:
"Next, listen; I shall describe another application that is difficult to find on earth. (45)
By the mere knowledge of which the practitioner becomes intoxicated;
what need is there to mention [the result] when it is known and put into practice? This is the meaning. || 45 ||
In the third Upaniṣad of the Sundarītāpinī, he teaches the Wheel of the Kāmakalā as follows: "Situated in desire, situated in the midst of desire, and enclosed within the womb of desire. (46)
One should desire desire with desire; one should cast desire into desires.
Having accomplished the desired through desire, one will certainly cause that which abides in desire to tremble.

In the mantra of Pañcakāmeśvarī, there are five seed-syllables (bījas): Hṛllekhā, Kāmabīja, Vāgbhava, Caturthabāṇa, and Strībīja. Their sequential designations are stated in the Jñānārṇava, in the section on the Bālā-nyāsa, as Kāma, Manmatha, and Kandarpa.

[He is known] as Makaradhvaja and Mīnaketu. However, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā, "Mīnaketu" is merely another name for Makaradhvaja himself. As for the seed-syllable of the female (strībīja), its name is Mahākāma;
in another tantra, its name is Mohana. This being the case:
In the section on the practice of the seed-syllable Kāmarāja, it is stated:
"One should place the syllable *kāma* within the center of *manmatha*, leading it into the abode of *kaṃdarpa*.
Within that enclosure is the fish-bannered god (*mīnaketu*), who is entirely contained within the Great Desire (*mahākāma*)."
This is the meaning of the verse from the *Saṃhitā*: one should envelop each preceding seed-syllable with each succeeding seed-syllable. And this very point has been clearly stated in another Tantra:
One should make Kāma the vital breath (prāṇa) and cause Manmatha to form the body;
having made Kandarpa the abode, O Pārvatī, it becomes divided into two.
