"O Goddess, O lady of good vows, one should place the Makaradhvaja [mantra] in its six locations; having placed it within the Mohana [cakra], one should envelop it with his Māyā. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: first, having written the seed-syllable *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ), one should write the god of love (*manmatha*), the syllable *klīṃ*, all around it. When that is done, because Kāma is situated within, he stands in the place of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), whereas Manmatha—
Because it stands on the outside, it serves as the locus for the body;

one should write the syllable *aiṃ*, which is the form of Kaṃdarpa, doubled around that. Since the syllable *aiṃ* has the shape of a triangle, its doubling results in a hexagon. Then, having placed Manmatha within the interior [of that hexagon]—

It is established that one should draw a hexagon. This [hexagon] serves as the abode for living beings. Then, one should write the seed-syllable *brūṃ* (or *blūṃ*), the banner of the sea-monster (*makaradhvaja*), six times within its six corners.
Furthermore, according to another statement, it should be written precisely in the interior of the corners and not on their outer part. This is as follows:
One should place everything within the seed-syllable *strīm*.

Since it must be written specifically between the two lines of the letter *ī* within the *strī*-seed, it is said that "one should encircle it with *māyā*. However, some [teachers] say that one should encircle this with *māyā* eight times on the outside.
They explain [the instruction] as "one should envelop. However, the authority for this must be sought.

The authors of the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*, however, state: "In this context, when writing the letters of the fifth peak-syllable (*pañcamakūṭākṣara*), one should act in such a way that the entire yantra comes to reside within the fire-position of those syllables."
They say that the secret of the tradition is that it must be drawn after learning it from the mouth of the Guru;

therefore, according to their view, the entire yantra up to the end of Makaradhvaja is to be written precisely within the space between the letter *ta* and the letter *ra*. However, there is a specific distinction in the Jñānārṇava.

Having introduced the *kāmarājakūṭasādhana*, [it is said]: "O fair-faced one, from this meditation on the *kāmakalā*, the five desires delude the entire world; hear now the ritual application (*prayoga*), O Pārvatī."
O Goddess of the Gods, the previously mentioned desires should be understood as having five designations;
having pierced [the heart] with the first desire, place it within Manmatha.
Then, O fair-faced one, having formed the *kaṃdarpasaṃpuṭa* (the Kandarpa-seal), the syllable known as Makaradhvaja is placed within the interior of the corners; all of this [is thus accomplished].
"One should place it within the fish-bannered [god]; he shall delude this world.
This is proclaimed as the ritual application (prayoga) named 'Deluder of the Three Worlds'.
Herein, the *vidarbha* mentioned by means of the first seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*)—if that *vidarbha* [is performed]...

Although it has been stated in the second chapter that "the one between two" is characterized by such a definition, nevertheless, according to the tradition, in the present context, the sentence "make such-and-such a person subject to my will" alone is to be written within the womb of Bhuvaneśvarī;
this is what is implied in the *Ratnākara*. Regarding its writing, although there are four [methods]...

Although these positions were elaborated by the venerable Paramaguru in the *Puraścaraṇakaustubha*, we have demonstrated in the *Tṛcabhāskara* that they ultimately resolve into only two positions (pp.
168). And thus, it is precisely as being devoted to this yantra, which is approved by many tantras, that the [text] situated in the root [verse]—

The textual connection should be applied as follows: a practitioner characterized by desire—that is, by longing—should make that object of desire, such as Devadatta or another, whom he desires to bring under his control, subservient to his own will (*kāmastha*). This is done within the context of the five types of desire.
One should write [the syllable] containing the *hṛllekhā* (the letter *hrīṃ*) placed before it, according to one of the methods already mentioned.

Then, one should place that *hṛllekhā* syllable in the middle of the second *kāma*, the seed-syllable of Manmatha. Next, one should place that *manmatha* syllable between the two *kāmas*, the two Kandarpas.
One should enclose [the syllable] within the interior—the womb—of the two [triangles] that have attained the state of a hexagon.

Then, one should place the fourth Kāma, Makaradhvaja, within the six wombs (yoni) of Kaṃdarpa, which are the abodes of desire. Thereafter, that hexagon [is to be associated] with Kāma, whose banner is the fish.

One should surround [the mantra] with the fifth seed-syllable (*kāmitam*). For indeed, the state of being situated within the womb of desire (*kāmanā*)—such as that of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth—is precisely what constitutes being an object of will (*icchā-viṣayatva*); therefore, it is appropriate that the word *kāmita* means "surrounded. Having done this, the practitioner [should place the mantra] residing in *kāma*.
One should cause even that which is written within the first *ekāma*, the *sādhya*— which is fixed and immovable—

to tremble and bring it under control. Here, although there exist specific alternative names for all five *kāmas*, that which is difficult to understand by means of the general name alone [is intended].

Furthermore, the "transaction" (*vyavahāra*) of this machine consists in the elucidation of its meaning by making manifest the fact that it is accessible through the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), namely: "Who gave this to whom? This is the question:
"Who [gave] this object, which is intended as the goal (*sādhya*), to whom? [The answer is: "Desire" (*kāma*).

For the sake of desire (*kāma*): the first *kāma* [seed] takes from the second *kāma* [seed], as stated above. This means that the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) resides within the *hrīṃ* seed, and likewise resides within the *klīṃ* seed. *Kāma* is the giver;
this *kāma* himself has given it to him. *Kāma* is the receiver; this is what was given by him.

The third desire, taking the form of a triangle, having itself become adverse to itself, has grasped [the object]. Adversity consists precisely in the eastern-pointedness of that which has a western point. Even the single syllable *Aiṃ* becomes twofold, and by resorting to adverseness, it becomes a hexagon within its own interior.
"He established everything," so much is meant. "Enter the ocean at will":

because it has many corners, the ocean is indeed the third desire; the statement beginning with the address to be spoken later regarding the fourth desire is, "Enter within that [ocean] by means of desire. By desire, you...
"I accept this, O Kāma. O Kāma, O syllable *blūṃ*, this is your task:
that having entered the ocean, you yourself were born as the manifold ocean itself.
For there is another Vedic text stating, "Indeed, there is no end to desire, nor to the ocean. Therefore, within the ocean—that is, within its boundary—...
Out of necessity, I bind you with desire by means of the female seed-syllable (*strībīja*).
O Kāma, this is your sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); O desirous practitioner (*sādhaka*), this—whether it be a woman or a female form accomplished through this yantra—is your sacrificial fee.

p. 169) This is because of the meaning of the scriptural statement, "Let there be a shore. However, some [teachers] maintain that one should first visualize *kāma* as the goal, situated in the *mūlādhāra*; then, visualize it as situated within *kāma*, located in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*;
and subsequently, contemplate it as encased within the interior of *kāma* and the interior of *maṇipūra*. Thereafter...
One should desire and contemplate [the deity] enveloped by unimpeded desire (*kāma*). Then,

one should visualize the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as being placed at will, in sequence, within the desires— at the throat, the mouth, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)— thus in these nine locations.
The manifestation of the object to be accomplished (*sādhyavibhāvana*) is one application (*prayoga*). He states another application: "having desired what is desired by desire" (*kāmena kāmitam*).

They say that the meaning is: having mentally desired—that is, contemplated—any one of the nine [states] mentioned according to one's own will (*svēcchayā*), one should cause agitation in the object of one's own will residing in *kāma*. Others, however, [interpret] *kāma*...

One should contemplate the syllable *Hsīṃ* at the *mūlādhāra* and the *brahmarandhra*, imagining the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) being burned by the flames from below and simultaneously drenched by streams of nectar from above. In this very same manner, [one should contemplate] each of the two, Manmatha and Kandarpa.
One should contemplate [the target] as being consumed by fire and flooded with water;

this is the meaning of the three phrases beginning with "kāmastham. One should desire the object of desire through desire; one should subjugate the person to be accomplished by means of the three previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*) according to the method described above. [One should place] desire among desires.
One should scatter [the seed-syllables]. Having cast the Makaradhvaja (the Fish-bannered One) even into the six supports (*ṣaḍādhāra*), one should perform the burning and flooding.

They say that the meaning is: having encircled the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) with the Mīnaketu (Fish-bannered One) in the Unstruck (*anāhata*) [cakra] itself, one should agitate the objective of desire. However, both of those [interpretations] are merely a deception of disciples.

Let the wise alone understand this. Others, however, say that because of the reading in the section on the practice of the *kāmarāja* syllable-cluster (*kūṭa*), and by virtue of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the second cluster of the present Vidyā itself must be understood wherever the word "desire" (*kāma*) occurs elsewhere.
It is not to be accepted because it contradicts the statements in the *Jñānārṇava*, which were previously cited as being even more explicit.
There is also a contradiction with the Śruti, as follows: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the wheel of the digits of desire (*kāmakalācakra*):
*hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ blūṃ strīṃ*; these five desires exist pervading the entire wheel."

Having enclosed the middle *kāma* at the end of all [syllables] and pervaded the six-wheeled *saṃpuṭa* with the syllable *blūṃ*, one binds the target situated in the middle with the two initial [syllables];
he who knows that wheel and worships it upon birch bark draws in the entire world.

Combined with indigo, it paralyzes all poisons; combined with lac, it kills enemies, paralyzes movement, and brings the entire world under one's control. Therefore, the phrase "one should agitate at the root" should be explained as an illustration for results such as attraction and so forth. || 46 || 47 ||
Having concluded the practice of the seed-syllable of Kāmarāja, he announces the practice of the seed-syllable of Śakti:
"O Goddess of the gods, this indeed is the practice of Kāmarāja."
I shall explain, in brief, the means of accomplishment for the seed-syllable of Śakti.
This is clear. || 48 ||

(p. 170) Just as in the practice of Vāgbhava and the others, since there is no distinction made by form and so forth in the practice of Śakti, the method for her practice is intended to be the very same general method as the practice of mantras; thus, regarding the goddess to be meditated upon during the *puraścaraṇa*, she is the Power of Will (*icchā-śakti*).
He states the mere extraction of her essential nature: "But when,
O Tripurasundarī, having created and protected the entire universe, she who is the very essence of the seed-syllable of power is intent upon withdrawal."

The meaning is that when such a desire to withdraw [the universe] arises, that very [power], taking that desire as its causal motive (*pravṛttinimitta*), attains the status of being denoted by the term "seed of power" (*śaktibīja*).
Regarding this, the meditation for the time of *puraścaraṇa* is described in the *Jñānārṇava*:
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess within the body from the beginning of creation until its dissolution,
raining down streams of flowing nectar that destroy all poison.

Shining with a golden luster, possessing the brilliant radiance of a mass of lightning, she holds a jar filled with shimmering crescent moons, displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
"And bearing the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā), she is the manifest embodiment of nectar.
In this tantra, the fact that no meditation is mentioned even for the three peak-syllables (kūṭatraya) implies that the practice is accomplished through the aforementioned meditation alone.
Having thus described the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa), he states the ritual application for desired results (kāmyaprayoga) for one whose mantra has been perfected:
"One should contemplate [the deity] within one's own body from the beginning of creation until its dissolution. (49)
The movement from the *kulapadma* (the lotus of the *kula*) to the *akulapadma* (the lotus of the *akula*) is the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) of Kuṇḍalinī;
the reversal from the *akulapadma* to the *kulapadma* is the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). One should contemplate the limits of these two within one's own body. (49)
He states the fruit of this in three verses:
"Thereupon, O Mistress of the Gods, he becomes like another Vainateya;
by the mere sight of serpents, he effects their paralysis. (50)
He is like a steady rain-cloud for embodied beings, pouring down a shower of nectar;
he is the destroyer of the artificial poisons of doubt and the like, as well as of innate venom. || 51 ||
Surrounded by hosts of malignant diseases, seizing spirits, armies, and *ḍākinīs* in various forms, as well as *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and others, he appears like the Three-Eyed One. (52)
He states that [the poison] destroys even stationary poisons and the like, as if they were mobile poisons: "Stationary," etc.
"Stationary" refers to [poisons from] the *kākolā* and similar sources;
"artificial" refers to that which arises from the combination of substances; and "suspicion" means the thought, "I have consumed this."

It is delusion; because it also causes affliction, it possesses the nature of poison. Poisons such as those of serpents and the like are "great poisons" (mahāviṣa), while those originating from internal worms are "minor poisons" (upaviṣa). The phrase "like the three-eyed one" contains within it the intention of his association with the fire at the time of universal dissolution, by means of the poetic figure known as *parikarāṅkura*.
This indicates the state of having seven parts (*aṃśaka*). The rest is easy to understand. || 50 || 51 || 52 ||
Now he describes the ritual application (prayoga) to be accomplished by means of the three peaks (kūṭatraya):
"Alternatively, by whomsoever this Vidyā is meditated upon as complete, residing in the center of the birth-mandala, the heart-lotus, and the face-mandala. (53)
O Great Goddess, she alone possesses a luster equal to a ruby;
her eightfold sovereignty will soon manifest.

The previously mentioned applications, which are performed after the individual means for each of the three *kūṭas*, are accomplished by means of each *kūṭa* alone. This application, however, occurs through the conjunction of the three *kūṭas*. For this very reason, according to the stated method, for each individual *kūṭa*...

The qualification for this [practice] belongs only to one who has already performed three *puraścaraṇas*; however, one should not fall into the error of thinking that the qualification exists only after the completion of the entire *vidyā-puraścaraṇa*.
For if that were the case, it would follow that such a *puraścaraṇa* ought to have been described in the subsequent chapter itself. Therefore...

Thus, the expressions "or" (*athavā*) and "only" (*kevala*) here are appropriately used. It should be understood that the statement "the Vidyā is complete" (*paripūrṇā vidyā*) is intended to mean that it becomes complete only when there is a conjunction of the three *kūṭas*. For this very reason, in the *Arṇava*, regarding the phrase "then the *Trikūṭā* is complete":

The qualification "Trikūṭā" (the three-peaked one), which illuminates the meaning already stated, is thus rendered meaningful. By this, the objection—that although it was fit to be taught in the fifth chapter, it was instead spoken here by Paraśiva due to the context or his independence—is refuted. Alternatively: by one who has established each of the three *kūṭas* individually...

The meaning is that the *kūṭas* (syllabic clusters) may be employed individually according to the aforementioned method for the sake of attaining specific desires, or they may be employed collectively in the manner that will be described hereafter. "Complete" means consisting of the three *kūṭas* joined together with one another. "Janmamaṇḍala" refers to the lotus of the *mūlādhāra*.
The heart-lotus is the unstruck lotus (*anāhata-padma*). The center of the orb of the face is the command-lotus (*ājñā-padma*).

It goes to these three places; thus it is said. The meaning is that one should meditate upon the three peaks (*kūṭas*) as having the luster of rubies, sequentially at these three locations. However, furthermore:

Immediately after the practice of the previous peak (*pūrvakūṭa*), one should clearly contemplate [the visualization] up to the *svasthāna* (one's own station); the third, however, extends up to the *brahmarandhra*.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
Immediately after the accomplishment of each individual peak (kūṭa) one after another, it is remembered: "Then the complete Mahātripurasundarī, consisting of three peaks,
when meditated upon by the practitioner, swiftly brings the three worlds under her control."
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, through meditation, she who abides in the circles of the navel, heart, and face becomes red-radiant and as clear as a ruby.

"His sovereignty and good fortune arise with eightfold power. Now, the statement regarding the contemplation of the *vāgbhava* [syllable] in the navel region is not contradicted by the aforementioned method of contemplating the *mūlādhāra*. And this—

This was stated in accordance with the *Ṛjuvimarśinī*. However, in the *Artharatnāvalī*, the reading "even at the navel-maṇḍala" (*nābhimaṇḍale*) is accepted even for the root text. The phrase "by [the mantra] alone" means without the previously mentioned preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the complete Vidyā, which will be described later. The eightfold qualities consist of those beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with *vaśitva*. As for those who...

Regarding the visualization of the three peaks (kūṭatraya), they describe a difference in form; however, even though this does not contradict other tantras, it should be disregarded because there is no authoritative evidence for such a distinction in the present application. || 53 || 54 ||
Now, with five [verses], he speaks of certain fruits that are very easily accomplished for those who have mastered the seed-syllables of the three peaks (*trikūṭābīja*), each one individually:
"If a practitioner even merely remembers her name in his mind..."
At that very moment, O beloved, he becomes known within the wheel of the Mātṛkās.
At the very moment one recites the mantra of Mahātripurasundarī,
the command of the circle of Mothers (mātṛcakra) immediately transfers into his body.
O Supreme Goddess, by meditation alone, the practitioner shall become dear to all yoginīs of every form, like a son. (57)
But when, O Supreme Goddess, one worships her in her full form,
she bestows upon him at that very moment the supreme accomplishment of the Khecarī.
O Goddess praised by heroes, since sixty-four crores of yoginīs of great splendor abide here, having taken refuge in this wheel. (59)

By the mere mental recollection of her name, he is known—that is, possessed of knowledge—regarding the totality of the Sarasvatī within the *mātṛkācakra*; or rather, the meaning is that he is renowned within the circle (*maṇḍala*) of the Mothers. Of her... [p. 173]
By mere recitation (*japa*), the command (*ājñā*) of the Mothers is transferred to the practitioner. Some say this "command" is the *kalā*;

others say it is the perfection of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*). Still others maintain that just as the command of the Mothers is unimpeded throughout the worlds, so too is his. In reality, however, [it is stated] in the *Jñānārṇava*, in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*):
One should gaze at him with the gaze, and then close the eyes;
one should effect the transmission of the command until immobility arises.

The meaning is that the Mother herself performs that duty of the Guru known as the "transmission of command" (ājñā-saṃkramaṇa) which has been described here. By means of the power of yoga, the venerable Guru, perceiving through his own vision within the sight of the disciple, [projects] his own consciousness from his own body through the gateway of his eyes.

Having drawn it out through the eyes of the disciple, he himself, in the form of that consciousness, should pierce the mind of the disciple. This is the transmission of the command (*ājñā-saṃkramaṇa*), a secret to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru.
By the mere meditation upon this, all the Yoginīs develop parental affection for him as a son.

By the mere worship of her wheel, one attains the *khecarī-siddhi* (the power of moving through the air) over all forms of beings dwelling in the earth, water, sky, the subterranean realms (*pātāla*), and so forth. To ensure that the worship does not mistakenly apply to a physical image of her, he says: "One should worship her in her complete form."
"Sixty-four"—the word "each one" is to be understood as the remainder.

This is because the meaning—that within each of the nine wheels, beginning with the Trailokyamohana and ending with the Sarvānandamaya, there are sixty-four *koṭis* of *yoginīs*—is explicit in the *Tantrarāja*. (55) (56) (57) (58) (59)
He states another application of this very [mantra]:

"First, having meditated upon the related word in the center, the eight seed-syllables on the outside, and the *kalā* on the stage of the woman, one becomes as beloved as the bodiless god of love. (60)

In this regard, although it appears from the phrasing that something is being prescribed according to a systematic arrangement at the beginning, middle, and end, nevertheless, the elders have explained it otherwise: first,
when the related term has been established initially, it refers to the "wheel," meaning the wheel of nine triangles (*navayonicakra*).

Because it is first accomplished at the very outset during the occasion of drawing the Śrīcakra; [one should contemplate] the *kalā*, the Kāmakalā, in the center at the place of the *bindu*; and the eight seed-syllables—the eight seeds of Vaśinī and the others—in the eight external triangles (*yonis*).
Having thus contemplated this within the theater of the woman, that is, in the middle of the *yoni*—

The meaning is that he himself becomes as dear to her as the God of Love (Anaṅga). However, in the *Jñānārṇava*, the fourth quarter of this very verse is read as "like another Kāmarāja," which is the only difference; in this case, there is no contemplation of the *bindu*, because it has been set aside by the digit of passion (*kāmakalā*). || 60 ||
Having thus resolved the eleven questions explicitly stated in words, he now resolves other questions encompassed by the word "and" (ca):
"O Supreme Goddess, for each one of the vidyās beginning with Karaśuddhi..."
In the Rudrayāmala Tantra, however, the ritual procedure was previously proclaimed by me. (61)

Although the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*) for the mantras such as *karaśuddhi* and others were previously extracted from this very tantra, they need not be discussed here; for this tantra was composed solely for the sake of its principal mantra, and [the others] are merely extracted.

Their necessity here [in this context] arises from their being enjoined as ancillaries (*aṅga*). However, since the Rudrayāmala Tantra concerns many deities, I have already previously explained the practice of the means (*sādhana*) and so forth for each of these Vidyās therein; therefore, those who worship only that much [should follow] that very Tantra.
The sense is that they are to be seen. Each individual word has its own distinct meaning.

As for the method of their practice (*sādhanaprakāra*) as stated in the *Rudrayāmala*, it has not been presented here by us either, because it is of no use for the worship of Sundarī and because it is overly extensive.
Now, desiring to set forth the weapons and seed-syllables of Śiva and Śakti, he describes their power:
"Having become Madana through intoxicating [syllables], one should agitate the women of the heavens, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld with nooses, goads, bows, and arrows. (62)
In the same way, O Queen of the Gods, one whose body has been made into the triple-city by means of the Śaktis may accomplish even the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Devas, and Vidyādharas.

Madana is Śiva, the Lord of Kāma; by means of the *mādana* [practices] related to him, and by means of the *śākta* [practices] related to Śakti, Tripurasundarī, women become submissive through the accomplishment of the mantras of the weapons of Śiva.
The meaning is that men [attain this state] through the practice of mantras and weapons belonging to Śakti. || 62 || 63 ||
In that regard, the Śākta [syllables] are those produced in the Mahāvajraprastāra;
they are the Mādana-syllables, placed after the first [group] and joined at the very bottom of all. (64)

This is a specific tantra named the *Mahāvajraprastāra*. In that tantra, at the very end of the extraction of all mantras, following the first [syllable], the power-seeds (*śākta*) and the intoxicants (*mādana*), which are the arrows, are produced. Having first extracted the seed-syllables of the power-arrows (*śaktibāṇa*):
The ancient commentators explain that the meaning is: "later, the seed-syllables of Śiva’s arrows will be extracted.

However, in reality, the meaning is: "In the *Catuḥśatī* which follows the initial *Catuḥśatī* within this very Tantra, the Śākta arrows are extracted at the very end. [This is because] they will be extracted at the conclusion of the *Uttara-tantra*.

Up to this point—(p. 175)—it is appropriate to explain that the *mādana* [mantras] have been extracted from another tantra and should be sought therein, because at the end of the *Uttaratantra*, the extraction of the seed-syllables of the *śakti*-arrows is observed. In another tantra...
The extraction of that [seed-syllable] is as follows:
having written two "tha" letters situated in fire (the letter ra) in sequence,
they are adorned above by a mouth-circle (the letter u), an eye (the letter i), and a bindu.
O fair-faced one, this pair of arrows is said to be the Mādana [mantra] situated on the earth;
it is enriched with the fourth vowel and the bindu, having the form of sound (nāda). The letter ending in *pha* (pha) is joined with Indra (*i*) and adorned with the left ear (*u*).
O Dear One, the Moon, accompanied by Bindu and Nāda and possessing the vowel of creation (a), is joined with these five arrows; know them, O Pārvatī, and hear their names.

"O Goddess, [the mantras] are named Kṣobhaṇa (the agitator), Drāvaṇa (the liquefier), and likewise that known as Ākarṣaṇa (the attractor); Vaśya (subjugation) and Unmāda (inspiration) follow in sequence—these are the names, O Supreme Goddess.
The meaning of this is: the letter *tha* ends with *da*; those two [letters, *tha* and *da*], situated in fire (*ra*).

Having mounted the letter *ra* upon those two, one should join the first with the letter *a*, which is the "mouth-vowel," and the second with the "eye-vowel," the long *ī* (the left eye), and then add the bindu (*m*) to both. Thus, the two seed-syllables *drāṃ* and *drīṃ* are established. The letter *ka* is the "deluder" (*mādana*) situated on the earth.

The syllable *klīm* is mounted on the letter *la* and joined with the fourth vowel (*ī*), the *bindu*, and the *nāda*. The letter *ba* is the end of *pha* (*phānta*). Joined with the letter *la* (Indra), the left ear (*va*), the sixth vowel (*ū*), the *bindu*, and the *nāda*, it becomes *blūm*. The moon is the letter *sa*, possessed of emission (*sargavān*), meaning accompanied by the *visarga*: *saḥ*. Thus.
There are five seeds. || 64 ||
He extracts the seed-syllables of the fetters of Śiva and Śakti:
"The great fetter residing at the beginning and end is proclaimed as belonging to the individual (puruṣa).
The power of Rudra, known as Kuṇḍalinī, is called Māyā, the fetter of woman. (65)

The first of the *mātṛkā* is the letter *a*; its end is the letter *ā*, which is "pauruṣeya," meaning related to the Puruṣa, and is the great noose (*mahāpāśa*). As for the attainment of union with the *bindu*, it has already been explained previously and should not be forgotten. Some say that Rudra is Śiva himself, and that the letter *ha* is his power (*śakti*), that is, his capacity.
It is logical that the letter *ha* is the designator of Rudra, because the power (*śakti*) of which belongs to Rudra.

[The term] *kuṇḍala* means "possessing an earring"; the suffix *ac* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). Thus, the meaning is that the serpent (*kuṇḍalī*) is the lord of serpents (*bhujaṅgeśa*), and the letter *ra* is that which has such a name.

For in the *Śrīkaṇṭhādinyāsa*, Bhujaṅgeśa is placed in the position of the letter *ra*; therefore, by the word "Kuṇḍala," the letter *ra* is understood. *Māyā* is the vowel *ī*. Thus, it is indeed the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśvarī.

The ancients maintain that the meaning is "the noose of woman" (*strīpāśa*). However, in reality, since the complete seed-syllable (*saṃpūrṇabīja*) can be obtained by the word *māyā* alone, this forced interpretation is not appropriate;
furthermore, there would be the grammatical inconsistency of the feminine gender in the term *kuṇḍalā*. Therefore, it is simply another power (*aparā śakti*) of Rudra himself.

She is called Kuṇḍalinī. The phrase "non-different from that" is a praise of Māyā. Alternatively, *kuṇḍala* means removal; that is to say, withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). She has been cast like a coil of poison. This is because of the usage: "Then the Creator [performs] the coiling even of the Moon. By this, she is established in Śiva.
The meaning is that it is the power known as *saṃhāra* (withdrawal), because the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* is produced from the very verbal root *hṛ*, meaning "to take away" (*haraṇa*). || 65 ||
He extracts the bow and the goad:
"O Pārvatī, in the group of vowels, the fourth and also the second [are the letters];
the pair of bows belongs to the male and female [deities], while Kāma and Agni are the pervasive goad. (66)

In the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī, there is the vowel *a* (aruṇa) and the consonant-group *tavarga*. Among these, the fourth letter is *dhaṃ*, which is the bow of Śiva; the second is *thaṃ*, which is the bow of Śakti; *kāma* is the letter *ka*; *agni* is the letter *ra*; and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is the thirteenth vowel (*o*), with the bindu added according to tradition—this is the meaning.
The [commentators] say "prāñcaḥ" (the ancients). Here, a lexicon (*kośa*) must be sought that supports the meaning of the word *vyāpaka* as denoting the thirteen vowels.

In reality, however, it is the *praṇava* itself that is intended here, as seen in the *Nandanīya-mātṛkā-kośa* under the section on the *praṇava*, which states: "and [it is] the producer of all seed-syllables."

Because it gives rise to everything, it is referred to by the term "the all-pervasive" (*vyāpaka*). Therefore, even the oral tradition regarding the meaning of the *bindu* need not be sought after. The authoritative teachers maintain that this single seed-syllable *Aṅkuśa* belongs to both women and men alike, as no distinction is made between them. By that [means]...
One should investigate what the basis is for Vidyānandanātha’s statement that there is likewise a twofold division here, based on the distinction between the sixth vowel and the thirteenth vowel. 66.
Now, anticipating the objection— "Just as there are seed-mantras for the weapons, why have the seed-mantras for the mudrās not been extracted?"—
he says: "O Goddess, the mudrās belonging to Tripurā are endowed with the eight supernatural powers (siddhis)."
One should display those very same [mudrās] in all the cakras at the time of worship. || 67 ||

The mudrās associated with Tripurā bestow the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) by their very nature, and not through dependence on the practice of mantras and so forth. Therefore, at the time of worship, one should display those very mudrās for each cakra. By the use of the word "only" (*eva*), [it is implied that no other means are required].
The meaning is that, by implying the non-necessity of mantras, one should demonstrate [the rite] as being entirely without mantras.
Some, however, explaining this as merely the procedure for displaying mudrās, consider this verse to be indifferent to both the presence and absence of mantras. Others, on the other hand...
The "tenfold [siddhis]" refers to the group beginning with *aṇimā*. The "octad" refers to the group beginning with the *brāhmī* powers.
By the phrase "endowed with these," the period subsequent to their worship is indicated. However, the reading should indeed be "prapūjayet" (he should worship).
Therefore, some say that this is simply the procedure for the worship of the mudrās as qualified by time; however,

one must consider what the resolution is for the lack of coherence between the procedures for displaying the mudrās and performing worship within the context of the exposition on mantra-sādhana in the present chapter.

By the phrase "endowed with the eight supernatural powers" (siddhyaṣṭakānvitā), the indication of time is both obscure and redundant; for the display of mudrās was already mentioned at the end of the first chapter, and their worship at the end of the eighth chapter. || 67 ||
Now, one might ask: why is the method of practice for the vidyās, such as Karaśuddhi and others, not described here as it is in other tantras? To this, he says:
"Therefore, the Supreme Goddess Tripurā is the primary injunction."
O Goddess of the Gods, there exists no knowledge whatsoever that is equal to this.

The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Among these sciences extracted in this system, this Tripurā is the principal science; the others are its constituent limbs (*aṅga-bhūta*).
Therefore—

The intention is that these [subsidiary meditations] are not described here because it would result in an inconsistency to discuss the meditation on subsidiary sciences within a section concerning the meditation on the primary science. Furthermore, he states "not only this" to show that this [meditation] is not only primary in these [sciences] alone, but in all mantras as well. || 68 ||

For this very reason, he states that the majesty of Hari and Smara—consisting of their assuming the form of Mohinī and so forth, which was brought about solely by the worship of this [Goddess]—is recorded respectively in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa and the Kālikā Purāṇa: He says: [the following].
In former times, having propitiated this very science that deludes the three worlds, the Blessed Lord Hari assumed a form that deludes the three worlds. (69)
O Goddess of the gods, even Kāmadeva, having propitiated Mahātripurasundarī,
became the most beautiful and fortunate man in the world.

The verse from the *Saundaryalaharī* beginning with "Haris tvām ārādhya... was spoken by the venerable Bhagavatpāda specifically for the purpose of explaining these two verses. And it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Goddess of the gods, by propitiating her, Kāma became beautiful with good fortune;
and O Supreme Sovereign, O Beloved, by the worship of Tripura,
Hari became the deluder of the three worlds and has always remained the sustainer of the universe.
By propitiating this [deity], Brahmā became the creator of the universe.
"O lady of excellent limbs, the moon and the sun are the agents of creation and destruction. Thus [ends verses 69 and 70].

(p. 178) Because this knowledge (*vidyā*) is supremely excellent, he says that even he, being supremely excellent, is its worshiper: "O lady of excellent vows, even now this is performed by me as well while remaining established in this vow."
This should be recited at the three junctions of the day for the sake of attaining this state.

At the three junctions of the day— that is, at the times of the three rites known as the *saṃdhyāvandana*— this recitation is performed by me, even though I am already liberated from the bonds of karma, because I abide by this vow and am engaged in the observances such as bathing that are directly visible; it is done for the sake of gathering the world, and not for any other reason.

Bound by the noose of karma, the world must perform rituals such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), distinguished by the recitation of mantras (*japa*), preceded by the undertaking of such vows for as long as life lasts;
this is for the sake of attaining that state which is of the nature of Brahman, that station non-different from me.

For the sake of attainment. In this Tantra, this alone is the procedure for rituals such as bathing and the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā). However, it was stated previously that the specific details of those procedures are to be taken from the Kalpasūtra. || 71 ||
Now he describes the different modes of worship of the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) along with their respective fruits:
"O Goddess, by worshipping [the wheel] in the center, a man becomes a lord of speech;
likewise, by worshipping it externally, internally, and at the end, he becomes another Kandarpa. (72)
O Pārvatī, by means of this [practice] entirely, at all times, and joined with all the goddesses,
one should accomplish the siddhi of Khecarī, which is endowed with the qualities of aṇimā and the rest.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Śrī Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava.
Indeed, in the Tantrarāja, five types of worship are stated:
"O Goddess, listen to the specific varieties of worship proclaimed in the sequence of the daily rite."
But for those who are incapable of expansion, as well as in times of adversity, this [concise method] is recommended.
Otherwise, O Īśvarī, the worship with contraction would be meaningless;
the first [set] is by means of the weapons, while the second is within the nine yonis.
The fourth [mandala] is described as having fourteen spokes from center to edge according to the stated form;
the fifth destroys all suffering and affliction and grants one's desires. O Goddess of Gods, listen now to its procedure for the worship of Kurukullā.
"Thus, the fivefold worship has been described as bestowing the accomplishment of all goals.

(p. 179) Worship is of four kinds: [1] beginning with the weapons and ending with the *bindu*; [2] beginning with the *vaśinī* goddesses and ending with the *bindu*; [3] beginning with the fourteen-spoked wheel and ending with the *bindu*; and [4] beginning with the square enclosure (*bhūgṛha*) and ending with the *bindu*.
The fifth worship, however, will be explained in the *Kurukullā* chapter.

It consists of the worship of the subterranean chamber (*bhūgṛha*), the eight petals, and the nine *yonis*. Among these, one is complete, while the other four are abbreviated. For one capable of performing the extensive worship, there is no fault in performing the abbreviated worship.

On the contrary, the result is actually detrimental; such is the collective meaning. This being the case, when the root [text] is being prescribed, since there is a threefold division—namely, worship of the middle wheel (*madhyacakrārcana*), worship of the outer-middle (*bāhyamadhyārcana*), and worship of all (*sarvārcana*)—the term "worship of the middle" (*madhyārcana*) refers either to the worship of the weapons (*āyudhārcana*) or the worship of the nine wombs (*navayonyarcana*).

It is proper to explain it thus. Therefore, that which was stated in the *Rjuvimarśinī*—namely, that the worship of only the four deities residing in the triangle and the point (*bindu*) is what is expressed by the term "middle" (*madhya*)—is not to be accepted due to a lack of authority. In fact, in the sixth chapter [it says]:
This great wheel, consisting of nine wombs, is a mass of consciousness and bliss;
this ninefold wheel possesses mantras divided into nine parts.

By this statement, since it will be explained that the nine-yoni wheel alone constitutes the entire series of wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Sarvānandamaya, the term "central" (*madhya*) used here refers specifically to the wheel consisting of the nine yonis.

[This is] what is to be grasped. Thus, by the term "outer worship" (*bāhyamadhyārcana*), the worship beginning with the mantra-weapon (*mantra-astra*) and ending with the *bindu* is intended. This is because it is appropriate to designate the *saṃhāracakra* in the form of the nine *yoni*s by the term "middle," and the *sthiticakra* situated outside that by the term "outer."
The bindu is conjoined with the triangle; the eight-petaled lotus is within the eight-spoked [wheel];
the sixteen-spoked [wheel] is within the two ten-spoked [wheels]; and the earth-abode is within the world-spoked [wheel].
This is because, in accordance with such statements, this very [center] has been previously designated as the "all-wheels" (*sarvacakra*);

therefore, as for what was stated by the author of the *Sundarīmahodaya*— that the term "located between the outer and middle" refers merely to the wheel of maintenance (*sthiticakra*)— and likewise what was stated in the *Ratnāvalī*:
The claim that the wheel (cakra) defined as consisting of sixteen spokes down to ten inner spokes is denoted by the term "middle" (*madhya*),

whereas that which is excluded from being merely a lotus of sixteen or eight petals is denoted by the term "outer-middle" (*bāhyamadhyagata*)— both of these [positions] have been refuted in the sixth chapter.

This is stated in such a manner precisely because of ignorance regarding the threefold nature of the wheel that is about to be described; for if that term were conventionally established in that limited sense alone, he himself would not have written of other authorities,
and furthermore, in the first alternative, the worship of the principal deity would not be established.

In the phrase *madhyānta*, the word *anta* (end) has the sense of a limit (*avadhi*). The meaning is "up to the middle from the outside. It is "joined with all the goddesses," that is, joined with the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth.
The rest is clear. In the *Jñānārṇava* as well, only this threefold nature is taught:
"O Goddess, one who is firm in his vows should worship the entire *cakra*, whether it be situated externally and internally, or he may worship only the central *cakra*. (p.
180) Here, first there are nine enclosures (*āvaraṇas*); in their absence, there are six enclosures beginning with the eight-syllable mantra (*manvasra*).
The meaning is that when those [two] are not applicable, one should worship the three obstructions (*āvaraṇas*).
Furthermore, although these two types of abbreviated worship (*saṃkṣiptārcana*) are logically connected precisely at the end of the first chapter, they were not mentioned there;

for if they had been mentioned there, since they would have to be discussed subsequently even in the context of the practice of the *cakras* (*cakrasādhana*) and so forth, the worship— [the argument continues].
A conceptualization regarding the obscuration is encountered; therefore, so that the primary method alone may prevail in the practice of the *cakra* and other rites,

there is an occasion for explaining the secondary mode of worship when only that much is mentioned therein, specifically in the context of general ritual actions that depend upon the primary form of worship.
With this intention, the division of worship has been made right here; may all be auspicious. 72–73.
Thus ends the fourth rest in the commentary called Setubandha on the ocean of the Nityāṣoḍaśikā, composed by the illustrious Bhāskara. || 4 ||
I am a bee at the lotus feet of the venerable Guru. Śrī.
Now begins the fifth rest (viśrāma).

Thus, having expounded the collection of secrets beginning with the practice of the seed-syllables (*bījasādhana*) by means of seventy-three verses in the fourth chapter, that which has reached its opportune moment [is now presented].

Desiring to explain the practice of mantra-sādhana and so forth, [the author] introduces the question concerning what is to be discussed by first stating what has already been told: Śrī Devī said: "All this supreme knowledge of Tripurā has been proclaimed by you."
The knowledge of the ritual procedure for the reality of desire culminates in the state of the reality of liberation.
Now, O Śaṅkara, tell me the procedure for recitation and burnt offerings (japa-homa),
by the mere performance of which even one of dull fortune attains success.

*Kāma* is Paraśiva; his *tattva* is his actual nature (*vāstavasvarūpa*), and his *vidhi* is the method [for attaining it], meaning that which is accompanied by logical proof (*sopapattika*). The *tattva* consisting of liberation is the state (*bhāva*), namely the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*). That itself is the *pada*, the ultimate goal. Alternatively, *kāma*...
The characterization of the three aims of life (*trivarga*) has been provided; the knowledge of the means for accomplishing the four aims of human existence (*caturvidhapuruṣārtha*) has been stated.

Now, please explain the method for recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth, by which even one devoid of divine grace may achieve mastery over the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*), let alone others. (1–2)
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the practice of the Tripurā mantra, as well as the rules for recitation and fire-offerings, which bestow the desired fruits. (3)

In the practice of mantra-sādhana, there are indeed two methods: lifelong, regular recitation (japa) in the form of *puraścaraṇa*, and [the method] for rites intended for worldly results (*aihika-kāmya-prayoga*). However, for the latter, there is no qualification without *puraścaraṇa*. For the sake of results pertaining only to the hereafter (*āmuṣmika*), however, it may be practiced even without *puraścaraṇa*.
The established rule is that one's livelihood is sustained by the mere practice of constant recitation. || 3 ||
Regarding that, he states the first [option]:

"O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped the entire wheel according to the rule, O Goddess, [one may worship] either the center alone, or that which is situated between the exterior and the interior. (4)
If the practitioner of mantra, established at its peak and observing the vow, should recite it a thousand times, O Supreme Goddess, then there shall be infinite fruit. || 5 ||

The meaning is that, having performed one of the three types of wheel-worship mentioned previously according to one's capacity, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day while observing the specific rules. This interpretation has been provided here because of the natural force of the expression "yadi vā" (or else) in this verse; however, if [one follows] the word "vratasthaḥ" (situated in the vow) in the subsequent verse...

If one observes the natural sense of the word "should begin" (*ārabheta*), then, for the sake of consistency with the *Jñānārṇava*, one must accept what is stated in the second chapter: that it refers merely to the commencement of the *puraścaraṇa* recitation. However, some [hold that] the recitation performed after having bound the *yonimudrā*...

They say that because it serves to eliminate defects in the mantra, the number one thousand is prescribed in the Tantras for a single recitation; therefore, they maintain that this very same amount is here enjoined as the *puraścaraṇa*. However, that view is disapproved by many, as it lacks authoritative support. || 4 || 5 ||
For one who is unable even to perform the worship of the middle wheel alone, he says:

"Or, having meditated upon the wheel situated in the heart, and having contemplated the Supreme Goddess residing therein by means of the previously described method of meditation, one should begin the recitation. (6)
This was previously stated in the first chapter, and subsequently explained by the passage beginning with "padmanibhām" (resembling a lotus) and so forth.
He describes the different types of recitation according to the variation of voice:
"O lady of excellent vows, [one may perform it] by means of loud recitation (nigada), or in a whisper (upāṃśu), or even mentally (mānasa);
joined with the previously mentioned nyāsas, and with one's body armored with mudrās. (7)
It is called *nigada* because it is recited intensely (*nitarām gadyate*).

"With loud recitation" (*uccair-nigadena*) means by means of the mode of utterance prescribed by the Śruti. "In a whisper" (*upāṃśu*) means within the range of one's own ears; "mentally" (*mānasena*) means by means of syllables uttered by the mind alone. As it has been said:
In the *Jñānārṇava* (p.
182): "O Supreme Goddess, *nigada* is spoken with clear speech;
however, that which is unmanifest, with the mouth quivering, is proclaimed as *upāṃśu*."
"But the mental [recitation], O lady of excellent hips, possesses a form existing within the mind.
Among these three, each subsequent one yields greater fruit. And it is said:
"Recitation as a sacrifice is ten times superior to a sacrifice performed according to ritual injunctions."
"Whispered [recitation] is a hundredfold [more effective], and mental recitation is remembered as a thousandfold.
Thus, because it accords with the meaning of the verbal root *jap* (to mutter), it should be understood that the last [mental recitation] is primary, while the other two are secondary.
The previously mentioned *nyāsas* are those beginning with *avaśinī*. The *mudrā* is the *yonimudrā*.
To be known solely through the mouth of the Guru.
He describes the rosary useful for recitation (japa):
"One made of pearls, pure gems, large beryl, or produced from *putrajīvaka*, lotus seeds, or *rudrākṣa* beads. (8)
It was fashioned from red sandalwood, such as coral and ruby-colored varieties,
and was perfumed with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and musk.
Having gathered the rosary, his body is formed into three cities (*tripurī*).
By the phrase "ruby and so forth" (*padmarāgādi*), the inclusion of rubies, emeralds, and other gems is intended.
The visualization with saffron and other substances is an indication of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the rosary. [The rosary...]

and in a nine-triangular pit, the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva) is produced.

A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is said to be that which is endowed with the proper characteristics of the excavation, the navel, the arms, the corner, the girdle, the womb, and so forth. It is of eight kinds, due to the distinctions such as the womb-shaped pit (*yonikuṇḍa*) and others.
The distinction between these two is that the *yonikuṇḍa* is shaped like the vulva (*bhaga*) or like an *aśvattha* leaf, while it is triangular (*trikoṇa*).

In the term "eight-petaled" (*aṣṭapatraka*), the word "corner" (*koṇa*) is used as a partial designation; thus, by this, the phrase refers to two types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*): the eight-petaled and the eight-cornered. This is because later on, the rules for their respective fruits are shown separately for the two.

that refers to the prescription for the time following the oblation included within the *naivedya* offering, and not otherwise.

"A wise person should perform the *homa* with whatever materials have been gathered according to his capacity.

Thus, it should be understood that the mention of only two substances— mallikā and mālatī— along with the phrase "the Lord of Speech (*vacaspati*) smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*)" in the *Saṃhitā*, is intended on account of the unavailability [of other materials].
In the same way, this should be inferred for what follows as well. || 27 ||
O Pārvatī, karavīra and japā flowers combined with clarified butter [should be offered]. (28)
Having offered oblations, the practitioner of mantra attracts the women of heaven, earth, and the netherworld.
O Goddess, having offered oblations of moon-misture mixed with musk and saffron, [he achieves his purpose].
Thereupon, one becomes endowed with the power of the exuberant beauty of Kandarpa.

Here too, by the force of the dvandva compound, there is a combined instrumental function for both the hibiscus (*japā*) and the oleander (*karavīra*), according to the principle already stated. As it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: "With hibiscus flowers mixed with clarified butter..."

In the phrase "with such karavīras," although there is no *dvandva* compound, there is an intention to express conjunction (*sāhitya*) because of the concluding statement from the relevant tantra. Here, the indicator is the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) in the statement: "O fair-faced one, having offered milk, honey, curd, and ghee separately. In that case as well—

Since distinctness is already established by the very absence of pairing (*dvaṃdvābhāva*), the fact that the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) is stated again indicates that its purpose is to make known the inference of a mixture when distinctness is not explicitly mentioned in so many words. By this, the statement in the *Saṃhitā*, "In the three worlds [one should worship] with *karavīra* and *japā* flowers smeared with clarified butter," is justified. By this...
In the statement from the *Jñānārṇava* (p.

189), the claim that "in the absence of a pair [of deities], there is independent efficacy everywhere without distinction" is merely the delusion of Śaṅkarānandanātha; for it contradicts other tantras and so forth. [Regarding] Candra—

Camphor (*karpūra*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and *kesara*—these two alone are the substances for the desired goal (*kāmyadravya*). Musk (*kastūrikā*), however, is a purificatory substance (*saṃskārika*). The analysis of the compound is: "one who possesses those powers of excellence and splendor belonging to Kandarpa.
And it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Goddess, when camphor and saffron are mixed with musk and offered in the fire-oblation, O Goddess, Madana shall be conquered by the practitioner.
"O lady of virtuous vows, [endowed] with good fortune, grace, and even capability. (28) (29)
By offering campaka, pāṭala, and other such flowers, one shall indeed attain prosperity.

By the phrase "pāṭala and so forth," there is the inclusion of the *cāmpeya* flowers and the fruits of the *pāṭala* and other such plants mentioned in the *Saṃhitā*; for the *cāmpeya* is distinct from the *campaka*.
In the *Jñānārṇava*, however, the paralyzing of the world (*jagatī-stambhana*) is also stated as a fruit. In the *Sundarohodaya*, however—
That it was explained that "śrī" [is indicated] by *campaka* flowers and "stambha" by *pāṭala* flowers is not to be accepted, as it contradicts the Tantra.
O Goddess, by offering sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor together with incense,
one becomes a source of agitation for the wives of the immortals.
Guggulu comes first, and it serves as the refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the triad beginning with *śrīkhaṇḍa*.

However, in the *Jñānārṇava*, its status as a distinct substance is stated; these [substances] may serve as the means either individually or combined, according to the scriptural statement, "by various substances."
In every instance where multiple substances are enjoined by a single injunction for the sake of a single result, that [principle] applies; however,
the intention of the author of the *Sundarīmaho-daya* is that it serves merely as an exception to the sense of conjunction (*sāhitya*) understood from a copulative compound (*dvaṃdva*).
This is because [the author] has not consulted other tantras and has failed to perceive the natural significance of the distinct words contained within his own tantra;
so it has been stated. || 31 ||
Even a slave immediately attains [freedom] through a hundred-thousand-fold oblation of lotuses;
one who is unfortunate becomes fortunate through a hundred-thousand-fold oblation of white water-lilies.

The distinction is that *ambhoruha* (lotus) has a thorny stalk, whereas *kahlāra* has a stalk free of thorns. By this number of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), the number representing the tenth part—whether less or more—is superseded. || 32 ||

O Goddess, having offered a piece of meat smeared with the three sweets, and having performed the ritual and meditated upon Maheśvarī while going to a crossroads at night, one becomes a sky-walker (khecara).

The syntactical connection is as follows: having gone to a crossroads at night, having prepared a *pala* of goat meat smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) according to the rules of another tantra, and having offered it while recollecting Maheśvarī with the mantra, one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*). || 33 ||
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, by offering lājās mixed with curd, honey, and milk, one is not afflicted by diseases, nor by untimely death, Yama, and other such powers.

In this context, parched grain (*lāja*) is the substance for the fire-oblation (*homa*). The triad beginning with curd (*dadhi*) is the refinement of the substance. By this, there is the sublation of the optional clarified butter (*ājya*) and sugar. However, in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is stated:
"O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the oblation is performed with curd, honey, milk, and parched grain."
It is undoubtedly the destroyer of disease, the destroyer of time, and the destroyer of death.
Because it has been stated thus, it is said in the *Sundarīmahodaya* that all four possess the status of substances (*dravyatva*).

In reality, however, even there, the compound "curds, honey, milk, and parched grain" (*dadhimadhukṣīrairlājā*) is a genitive-tatpuruṣa (third-case tatpuruṣa) alone, and not a four-membered dvandva. This is because the compound is formed by the rule "mixing with food" (*bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam*).

This is because it is appropriate to explain it in that very way so as not to contradict the primary tantra. By this, the compound in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*—which states that "one becomes free from disease through oblations of honey, ghee, curd, milk, and parched grain"—is also explained. In this view, however, the only distinction is that there is no sublation of the ghee (*ghṛta*).

In the phrase "by Yama and others," the word "others" includes *parakṛtyā* (the magical rites performed by enemies) and so forth. Regarding the older commentators' explanation that it refers to "seizing by disease," the distinction between *roga*, *vyādhi*, and *ābhiṣaṅga* is to be considered. Furthermore, Time (*kāla*), Death (*mṛtyu*), and Yama are indeed distinct, as they exist in the form of specific deities. || 34 ||

Thus, considering that an extensive treatment of optional rites (kāmyakarman) is inappropriate in a work intended for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), he here briefly summarizes the ritual applications (prayoga) described in other tantras, which are even more limitless than these.

O Goddess, the ritual applications described through meditation, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth, as taught in all the manuals of mantras, will certainly succeed; of this there is no doubt. (35)

Those ritual applications for desired results (*kāmyaprayoga*)— whether accomplished solely through meditation, solely through fire-offerings (*homa*), solely through recitation (*japa*), or, by the force of the word "etcetera," through worship and so forth— which have been taught in those *kalpas* and *tantras* of all the mantras numbering seventy million and more; these [are what is meant].
The meaning is that all [mantras] are accomplished by this; however, one must state here what is specific to each individual case, and in this regard, no doubt should be entertained. || 35 ||
Anticipating the doubt as to how ritual applications (prayoga) performed with other mantras might be accomplished by means of this vidyā, he says:
"One should, however, place this vidyā in the position of the syllables of those respective mantras."
For when this [syllable] is accomplished, the Mātṛkā becomes accomplished. || 36 ||

p. 191) In the ritual applications described in other tantras that employ different mantras, wherever another mantra is enjoined, one should everywhere install this very fifteen-syllable vidyā. One should extract that [other] mantra and employ this mantra in its place. Or else:

Let those ritual applications be performed with other mantras alone; this mantra should not be deposited in their place by means of their expulsion. Nor should it be argued: "Since other mantras lack the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*), how can a practitioner of this [mantra] have the qualification for their optional ritual applications?"

Since all mantras have Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī as their primordial source (*prakṛti*), the accomplishment of the transformations (*vikṛti*) necessarily depends upon the accomplishment of all the letters that constitute that source.
Furthermore, because Śrīvidyā is non-different from Mātṛkā, once this [Mātṛkā] is accomplished, she too is accomplished.

He says "in this [Vidyā]" because it is already established. And thus, since all mantras are established by the establishment of this very one, all ritual applications (*prayoga*) for the worshippers of the Vidyā are indeed fruit-bearing; therefore, the specific mention of each individual [mantra] is simply redundant—this is the intended meaning. || 36 ||
If you insist that these ritual applications must be accomplished by this very vidyā alone,
then he says that this vidyā should not be placed merely alone in the positions of other mantras, but rather it should be employed as encapsulated within the mātṛkā.
One should install the Mātṛkāntaritā according to the path taught by the Guru;
O Supreme Goddess, this must be performed as it bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). 37.

The encapsulation by means of the *mātṛkās*—whether in direct order (*ānulomyena*) alone, or in both direct and reverse order (*anulomapratilomatayā*)—should be understood from the mouth of one’s own guru; having done so, everything should be performed by his command, for the meaning is that accomplishment (*siddhi*) will certainly occur. || 37 ||

But surely, since meditation (*dhyāna*), recitation (*japa*), and fire-oblation (*homa*) are established as distinct from one another according to the difference in their respective deities, there would arise great confusion if one were to accomplish the goal of another by means of a single practice; for this would result in a total intermixture (*sāṃkarya*) of all rites, thereby rendering the scriptures that establish these distinctions purposeless.

Anticipating this objection— that [the practice] may be performed by those proficient in coarse meditation, recitation, and fire-offerings, even without the framework of the coarse perspective, because everything is of a single nature when viewed with subtle vision— the author, desiring to provide a resolution while maintaining a hidden intention, states: "The subtle..."
He speaks of meditation and the rest:
Meditation is not the conceptualization of the gestures (mudrās), facial expressions, and other artistic forms;
rather, meditation is the state of supreme aesthetic integration (sāmarasya) arising from immersion in Śakti. (38)

The conceptualization of parts such as the face and so forth, the *mudrās* such as the boon-granting and fear-dispelling gestures, and the colors such as red and so forth, is not meditation; it is not ultimate reality, or rather, it should be stated that it is not intended [to be meditation], precisely because it is artificial due to being mentally constructed.

This is the state of being. And this [statement] is for the purpose of praising the reality by means of the maxim of "not-censure" (*nahanindānyāya*). That which is the nature of Brahman, namely pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*), is [bound] by the bond of ignorance consisting of the three impurities known as *āṇava*, *kārmika*, and *māyīya*.

It is logical that [the Self] is called the *jīva*. Therefore, all the powers (*śakti*) existing in Brahman are indeed present in the *jīva* as well; however, they are merely concealed (*tirohita*). And the means for removing this concealment are described in the *Śivasūtra* as being threefold, distinguished as *āṇava*, *śāmbhava*, and *śākta*.
When all one's own powers (*śakti*) have been awakened by any one of these means, one becomes Brahman itself. This universe is the accumulation of one's own powers;
through the contemplation of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), there is the dissolution of the universe.
Through the continuous immersion in the Great Lake (*mahāhrada*), one experiences the potency of the mantra (*mantravīrya*) and becomes equal to Śiva.

Furthermore, this has been explained in detail by Kṣemarāja and others in such sūtras as "The meeting [of the two] occurs once more" (*bhūyaḥ syāt proktam milanam*). This very point he states with the words "meditation" (*dhyānam*): [it arises] from the penetration of power (*śakti-samāveśāt*).

From the unfolding of the wheel of one's own power (*svaśakticakra*), there arises the state of *sāmarasya*—the oneness or unification—with the Great Brahman, who is most vast and most exalted. The suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of "unknown" (i.e., it is beyond conceptualization).
The meaning is that this alone is meditation (*dhyāna*) in its natural, uncontrived state. || 38 ||
Now he describes subtle recitation (sūkṣmajapa): "One should utter the internal sound while restraining the movement of the senses;
this alone is declared to be true recitation, for external recitation is not recitation. (39)

Being self-restrained, one should utter the unstruck sound (*anāhata-nāda*) as it expands within the intervals, by means of that action in which the movement— the activity directed toward their respective objects— of the sense organs, both the organs of knowledge and the organs of action, has been restrained and suppressed; this [is the practice].

Thus, *japa* [is truly such] because, through the practice of *nāda*, which is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all phonemes (*varṇa*), it produces the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of all mantras simultaneously; whereas external *japa*, consisting of the utterance of specific sequences of phonemes in the form of *vaikharī* speech, is not true *japa*.
It does not bestow the accomplishment of all mantras; the sense is that it produces accomplishment only for those specific [mantras] according to their respective sequences. || 39 ||

Now he describes the subtle oblation (sūkṣmahoma): One should not offer [oblations] into the external fire according to the various injunctions of the respective Tantras until one has offered the full oblation of the mind into the great fire of the Self. (40)

Since it is established in detail in works such as the *Jñānavāsiṣṭha* that the mind itself—consisting of volition and conceptualization—is the creator of the entire universe, the mind alone is the oblation (*havis*) whose form is the world.
The Self alone is the fire, because it consumes everything. For this very reason, the *Śaktisūtra* states:
The fire of consciousness, though concealed within the stage of descent (avarohapada), dries up the fuel of the object of knowledge by means of pure consciousness alone.

Therefore, as long as the "full oblation" (pūrṇāhuti) of the universe has not been offered into the fire of the Self, whatever is prescribed in various Tantras as being to be offered into the fire does not truly become an offering.

Because the oblation is not consumed [by external means]. The meaning is that when the offering is made within the mind into the Self, even an external oblation becomes a true *homa*. As it has been said:
"Within, incessantly and without fuel, blazing... (p. 193)
"In the fire of consciousness, which is the adversary to the darkness of sacrificial offerings,
and which is the ground for the blossoming of some wondrous radiance,
I offer the entire universe— beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva. Thus [it is said].

By the term "final oblation" (pūrṇāhuti), the dissolution of all mental fluctuations (manovikalpa) regarding the entire range of objects— however many such fluctuations exist in the form of mental states— is expressed. The oblation (homa) is considered to be the setting [of these] within the Self (ātman).
Thus it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*. Another method for the internal fire-sacrifice (*āntarahoma*) is also to be found in the *Jñānārṇava*. || 40 ||

Now, one might ask: "If it is logical that for those who worship such a Self there should be a commingling of all ritual applications, what then follows for those who worship Tripurā? To this, he says:
"The Goddess Tripurā is one's own consciousness; her redness (lauhitya) is the reflective awareness (vimarśana) of that."
His noose and goad, moreover, are known to consist of passion and hatred.
Sound, touch, and the other [objects of the senses] were his arrows; his mind became his bow; and the powers that sequentially produce the perception of the universe were his shafts. (42)

Thus, the Goddess Tripurā is one's own self-consciousness (*svasaṃvit*), because she precedes the triad [of subject, object, and means] and because she is self-luminous. The reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of that self is a synthetic contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) that has that [self] as its sole object, while not having anything else as its object. And that...
The redness is said to be precisely the form of passion (anurāga) within one's own self. And it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"One's own self alone is declared to be the deity, Lalitā, whose body is the universe;
that redness is its reflective awareness (vimarśa), and this is the contemplation (bhāvanā) known as worship."

Among the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), the principle consisting of passion (*rāga*) is the subtle form of the *pāśa* (bond), because there is no difference in its nature as a binder. The form of the *aṅkuśa* (goad) consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), namely hatred and anger, because it acts through the medium of that which is hated. As for what was stated in the subsequent chapter regarding the *aṅkuśa*...
Its nature as knowledge will be explained, and its contradiction therein will be refuted in that very place.

By the phrase "sound, touch, and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes form, taste, and smell. These five objects, consisting of the [five] elements, are the arrows composed of the flower-bow. Regarding their being beautiful in appearance at first, but in the end...

Because he is the Puruṣa. His own bow is the principle of the mind (*manastattva*), because it impels the senses—which have as their ultimate nature the objects of the senses—toward their respective objects.
As it is said in the *Rahasyanāmasāhasra*:
"Possessing the noose of the nature of passion (*rāga*), radiant with the goad in the form of anger (*krodha*),
having the mind as its sugarcane bow, and possessing the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) as its arrows"— thus [it is said].
Those very mental fluctuations (*manovṛtti*) which produce the manifestation of all objects are, in sequence, [the noose, the goad, the bow, and the arrows].
The powers existing in the sequence beginning from the square and ending with the circle of points (bindu-cakra) are to be known.
As it is said in the Vāsanā-paṭala:
"But there are other powers that move throughout the circles on all sides."
"Those [powers] are declared to be the causes of all conceptual constructions.

Thus, the five *abjas*, seven *arbudas*, and sixty million powers bearing secret names are established as existing within the nine wheels (*cakras*) in the chapter on the majesty of mantras (*mantravaibhavapaṭala*).
The meaning is that these are indeed of the nature of mental modifications (*manovṛtti*).
"O Dear One, in each of the nine *lalitā*-cakras, there are sixty-four crores of powers; when combined, they are those previously mentioned. Thus [it is said].
One should not, however, fall into the error of thinking that these functions are merely powers that serve as veils for [the attainment of] *aṇimā* and the other [siddhis]. || 41 || 42 ||
The eastern and western gates are known to consist of prāṇa and apāna;
time, the abodes, and the elements are the nine wheels in successive order.
Although four doors are mentioned in the context of the "Extraction of the Wheel" (*cakroddhāra*) regarding the subterranean chamber (*bhūgṛha*),

this is an explanatory elaboration (*vāsanā*) based on the intention of the view that there are only two doors, because in the section on worship, the doors in the eastern and western directions alone are reiterated in the passage beginning with "Aṇimā at the western door. [The subject here is] the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*).
The downward-moving breath (*apānavāyu*) is the eastern gate, and [the upward-moving breath] is the western gate. Time is one;

together with the three abodes known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and the five elements, there are nine wheels (*cakras*) in sequence. Alternatively, there are four abodes, including the state of the fourth (*turya*).

By the word "time" (*kāla*), the ninety-six powers and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) beginning with *aṇimā* are indicated. Of the time consisting of day and night—which is the collective totality of breaths numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred—there are ninety-six temporal segments (*kālakhaṇḍa*), each consisting of two hundred and twenty-five breaths (with a quarter). These...

The secret— that [the wheels] are sequentially of the nature of the powers (śaktis) beginning with *aṇimā*— is clearly stated in the twenty-seventh chapter of the *Manoramā*. Although the *Tantrarāja* does not explicitly state that the wheels consist of the nine principles beginning with *kāla*, the commentators have [described] the diagrams (*yantras*) in the thirty-fifth chapter.

In the commentary on the verse beginning with *mantrāḥ sarvatra*, having explained this very *vāsanā* of the nine wheels, the author wrote only the half-verse beginning with *kālo dhāmāni bhūtāni* from the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*, stating that it was taught therein for the sake of corroboration (*tatsaṃmati*). This being the case:

Since all the ancient commentators on the Vimarsinī and other works unanimously consider the fifth chapter of the root text to conclude with only thirty-four verses, [they do not recognize] the ten [verses] recited subsequently.
Those who omit verses found in manuscripts— even when they are coherent and required— should themselves be asked what their intention was. Furthermore,
regarding this [work] consisting of five chapters (pañcapaṭalī) composed of four hundred and thirty-five verses:
This bold assertion is for the purpose of justifying the designation "the previous four hundred.
It refers to the three and a half [verses] at the end of the first extraction of the *vakra*,
the seventeen forms belonging here to the second extraction of the *cakra*, and the ten [verses] of this [section].
The intention might be that there is an omission of verses; even so, this is still incorrect.

For, based on the evidence of certain verses written as belonging to this tantra by the very ancient author of the *Manoramā*, and because they are found in manuscripts, it is clear that some of them are not interpolations.

Since the matter is thus determined, it is appropriate to explain the etymological designation (*samākhyā*) itself as being figurative (*gauṇa*), without intending to express a state of deficiency or excess by even a single unit; for in the first verse of the *Śāradātilaka*,
the phrase "with fifty letters" refers to fifty-one due to its proximity to that number.
This is because it is seen that Śrī Harṣadīkṣita has provided an explanation [of this];
[namely] the word "dvātriṃśat" (thirty-two) found in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"She exists as one-fold, two-fold, and likewise sixteen-fold."
Or that which is divided into thirty-two forms—I bow to her who is higher than the highest.
This is because of the explanation here that [the preceding term] is followed by thirty-five consonants,
and because the nature of being a *gāthā* or *śloka* consisting of six, eight, or four lines (or feet) is also possible in some instances; therefore,
this very principle is adopted in order to maintain the restriction that there are exactly one hundred *ślokas* per chapter (*paṭala*).
And because it is already contained within the *Manoramā*, we have disregarded its detailed exposition here, as it would be purposeless. || 43 ||
Now, he states the underlying intention (vāsanā) for the worship of the Goddess:

"One should worship the Goddess, whose nature is pure consciousness, residing in the wheel of the organs of action, with the flowers of universal egoity for the sake of attaining all perfections. (44)
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*.

The "Wheel of Powers" (*śakticakra*) is the very collection (*cakra*) or assembly of the internal instruments, the senses, which are divided into the categories of knowledge and action; it is so called through the application of double entendre (*śleṣa*).

One should worship the Goddess Tripurasundarī, who resides in their midst, whose nature is pure consciousness, and whose sole form is non-objective knowledge, for the sake of all accomplishments (*siddhi*), for the attainment of the state of being the Self of all, and through that, for the success of all worldly applications taught in the Tantras.
The phrase "with flowers" is an illustration that serves as a mere metaphor for ritual offerings (*upacāra*). These offerings consist of the universal ego-sense (*viśvāhaṃkṛti*).

This means that within the entire universe composed of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), there is everywhere the sense of "I," which is the constant, supreme contemplation of the Great Ego (*parāhaṃtā*) in the form: "Brahman alone am I."
As it is said in the *Tantrarāja* (p. 196):
"Even when there is movement, the ritual services consist of non-negligence regarding identification with That.
This applies even during states such as dreaming, at which time the absence of reflective awareness (*ananusaṃdhāna*) is inevitable.
