The meaning is this: regarding the object of the contemplation of being composed of Brahman (*brahmamayatva*), the absence of negligence alone is sufficient; all other [preparations] are merely figurative, how much more so in the waking state? Something else has also been stated in that very same place:
"The knower is one's own self, knowledge is the precious offering, and the object of knowledge is situated externally."
"The worship of the Śrīcakra is said to be the unification of those [elements].
Here,
there is only the subtle body (vāsanā-rūpa-karaṇa-indriya-mātra) consisting of a few portions of the Nityās, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī.

By the force of the explanatory restatement (*yutyānuvāda*), it is implied that the "impregnations" (*vāsanā*) are those described in the *Tantrarāja* by twenty-one verses beginning with "The Guru and the primordial Śakti shall be... and ending with "...these are the impregnations. The manner of that [explanation] should be seen in that very [text], as it is not included here for fear of prolixity.
We shall elaborate upon this. Thus, by means of forty-four verses, the external and internal methods for the accomplishment of mantra (*mantrasādhana*) have been briefly stated.
From here on, the textual context will for the most part concern the internal [practice] alone; thus all is [established].
May there be auspiciousness. || 44 ||
Thus ends the fifth rest in the commentary titled Setubandha on the ocean of the Nityāṣoḍaśikā, composed by the illustrious Bhāskara. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth rest (viśrāma).

Having thus elaborated upon the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*) with four hundred and thirty-five verses, Paraśiva, desiring to instruct by means of an exposition on the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), [offers] a [verse] concerning that subject.
She introduces the Goddess’s question: The Śrī Devī said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who consist of the manifestation of perfect plenitude!"
In this Vāmakeśvaratantra, there are numerous points whose meaning remains unknown.
O Bhairava, you ought to explain those various matters in their entirety.

The term "Devah" (the God) means that which shines, which is to say, whose sole nature is light. And since this reality (*tattva*) is undifferentiated among all living beings, He is called "Devah" even with respect to them, because He is woven through them as their underlying continuity.

The meaning is "while playing. This is because of such scriptural passages as, "The one God is hidden in all beings. For this very reason, Mahādeva is of the nature of great light; for the *Nirukta* states, "The Great Self alone is the deity," and [the rule] *āt-mahataḥ* provides the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel.

Precisely because it is the Great Light, it consists of a perfectly full manifestation; that is, its nature is that very manifestation—its expansion and cognition—which is pervasive and complete on all sides through the delimitation of every object. This is because the suffix *mayaṭ* is used even when there is non-difference, as in such expressions as "the world consists of Brahman" (*brahmamayaṃ jagat*).

Since being the object of all things is pervaded by being the object of the collection of secrets— given that [the Lord] has knowledge as His sole body— it follows that you alone are authorized to teach not only manifest matters but also secret matters, just as in the case of the *Prakaṭārtha*.

The *parikara* ornament consists of three qualifying adjectives [describing] the "suggested meaning" (*dhvanir arthaḥ*). "Vāmāḥ" means beautiful; those very [meanings] when unknown are "vāmakāḥ. Regarding them, "īśvaram" refers to that which is capable of making them known; "tantram" refers to the system consisting of the two sets of four hundred verses, the former and the latter. The suffix *kap* is used in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāte*).
By the word "in this" (asmin), it is suggested that the subsequent four hundred verses (*uttara-catuḥśatī*) also belong within the *Vāmakeśvara*,

thereby indicating the unity of the preceding and succeeding sections as a single treatise (*eka-śāstrya*). Consequently, although there is a difference in intermediate subject matter consisting of manifest and secret meanings, [the work remains one].
The sense is that there is no difference between the scriptures because the subject matter is identical, as both take the form of the worship of Tripurasundarī. For this very reason,

even though the Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās expound the meanings of the Karma-kāṇḍa and Brahma-kāṇḍa respectively, they constitute a single scripture (*eka-śāstrya*) because they are indistinguishable in their focus on the meaning of the Veda.

This was suggested by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda in the *Ātmādhikaraṇa* (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya 3.3.54): "Because of the existence [of the self] within the body. Although beautiful meanings exist in two forms—distinguished as external sacrifice (*bahir-yāga*) and internal sacrifice (*antar-yāga*)—they remain entirely unknown; yet, among them, even one kind...
The word "tu" (but/however) implies that although they have been informed in this manner many times, there are still matters that remain unknown;

furthermore, by the suffix "-śas" in the word "anekaśaḥ" (many times), it is also stated that the secret meaning is appropriately manifold. This is according to the rule: *bahvalpārthāc chas kārakāt*.

For the author of the Vārttika has restricted the suffix *śas* precisely for the sake of propriety (*aucitya*). Furthermore, the fact that only a few secret meanings (*rahasyārtha*) were stated at the end of the previous chapter is indicated by the very phrase "even though [they are] many.
Thus, even now, as for whichever...
To that extent, you are capable of explaining those various unknown matters in their entirety.

Unknown matters are of three kinds, distinguished by the conventions of the *cakra*, the conventions of mantra, and the conventions of worship. Each of these, moreover, is further divided by internal subject matter and by the great variety of optional alternatives.
It is manifold. In that regard, by means of the distributive repetition "those various," it is stated that even the three types of meanings must be expressed.

By the word "without remainder" (*aśeṣeṇa*), the completeness of each sub-topic is indicated. Thus, the meaning is that all conventional meanings (*sāṃketika-artha*) must be explained in their entirety, one by one. — Bhairava.
He is filled with all powers. Thus it is said in the *Śivasūtra*: "Bhairava is the upward surge (*udyama*). The *Vārttika* also states:
"The upward surge is the internal vibration known as the full sense of 'I' (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāvanā*);
it alone [arises] from the complete integration of all powers."

"Because he completely swallows up the manifold conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) by virtue of being all-pervasive, he is Bhairava, [a name] whose meaning is thus literal. Alternatively, Bhairava is called the terrifying one, the controller of all; "from fear of him the wind blows... [and so forth].

This is because of the scriptural statement, "It blows. Furthermore, in the *Kampna-adhikaraṇa*, it is described that the quality of being terrifying—as conveyed in such scriptural passages as "A great fear, a raised thunderbolt"—is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the Supreme Brahman.
Precisely because of this terrifying nature, [the text] employs the imperative suffix *loṭ* (in the form *vadet*) rather than [other forms] intended for injunctions and the like.

It was simply said, "You ought to speak. By the statement, "The teacher should tell even the secret to a devoted disciple," it is implied that because instruction by qualified gurus to a qualified disciple is mandatory, [the author] says, "Speak. || 1 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme and great secret, the Heart of the Yoginīs.
Out of affection for you, I shall today speak of that which is especially to be guarded:

the secret within the cave, the identity of the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). "Drinking the truth in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest, most excellent [abode]—he who knows it hidden there..."

Based on such scriptural passages as "In the cave, in the highest heaven," even the meditation (*upāsana*) that results in that [realization] is secret. Furthermore, although that [meditation] is of two kinds—distinguished as external and internal—it is indeed a mystery (*rahasya*).
Because it is an extreme mystery even among those two, it is the "Great Mystery" (*mahāguhya*). For this very reason, it is superior to the *Catuḥśatī*.

This shall be explained later. For only one whose mind has been purified through the successive performance of external sacrifices has the qualification for this [internal practice]. Therefore, even in the Veda, the Upaniṣads are designated as the "Vedānta," the section concerning meditative worship (*upāsanā*).

And it is called *Uttaramīmāṃsā* because it is the scripture that establishes that meaning. It is named *Yoginīhṛdaya* because it reaches—that is, it attains—the heart, the mind, of the Yoginī Tripurasundarī;
in other words, it is what has entered the mind of the Goddess. This is because it cannot be known without the instruction of the Goddess.

This is a sound. Because it is an extreme secret, it has not been told to anyone until now. But this very day, out of affection for you, under the influence of my love for you, or because your command—in the form of my own will-power—is not to be transgressed; [I speak].

"Thus have I been commanded by you, O Lord, in the form of my own will"—as this is stated at the end of the Tantra. "I shall speak; listen, do not let your mind be distracted by other objects. For such [beings]...
The suggestion (*dhvani*) is that it is difficult to fathom. He states another reason for speaking of this even though it is not to be told:

"It is to be concealed" (*gopitavyam*). It is to be kept secret from specific individuals; the meaning is that it is not fit to be spoken to everyone without distinction, but is suitable to be told only to a few. To you...

The sense is that, because you are a true disciple, [this] must not be hidden from you; for there is the saying: "A teacher may reveal even a secret to a devoted disciple. However, the earlier commentators [hold that] since I am telling this secret, therefore you too—
They explain that it must be kept especially secret by reversing the relationship between cause and effect. || 2 ||
Now he commands this tantra to be propagated among those who are worthy: "Having been transmitted from ear to ear, it has reached the surface of the earth. (3)

This tantra has reached the surface of the earth (*avanītala*) from ear to ear; the ellipsis implies "you must practice it correctly. Alternatively, the connection with the preceding clause is that you must conceal it so that it remains properly obtained. *Avanītala* is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of *avanī* (the earth) and *tala* (the surface). *Avanī*...

The middle world (*madhyabhuvana*) is the *tala* world, which is the subterranean realm. This statement is made while remaining in the upper world (*ūrdhvabhuvana*). For this very reason, the *Svacchandatantra* employs the method of introducing the tantra through a series of questions and answers.

Because the meaning of the term "descent" (*avatāra*) is precisely the reaching of a lower location starting from an upper location; therefore, the sense is: "cause this [teaching] to circulate even throughout the three worlds. In the word *karṇāt*, the ablative case is used due to the elision of the suffix *-lyap*.
[The meaning is: having reached your ear, that which has issued from your mouth [shall reach] the ear of your disciple.

"Let him attain it. The same applies hereafter. By this, it is implied that there is a prohibition against grasping [the meaning] through other means such as books and the like. To provide an explanation—claiming that [the goal] was already attained previously without even the need to supply the word "do"—is contrary to the natural meaning of the words *adya* (now) and *iti*. || 3 ||
To distinguish those specific individuals from whom [the teaching] should not be given and those to whom it should be given by means of their uncommon qualities, he says:
"It should not be given to the disciples of others, nor to atheists, nor to women."
Nor for those who are indolent in service, nor for those who bring about misfortune. || 4 ||
In this context, the phrase "should be given" (*deyam*) is connected individually with each of the three subsequent quarters.
This is because the negative particle (*nañ*) is seen to be employed four times. Consequently, these constitute four prohibitions;
namely, the four [qualities] known as being a student of another, being an atheist, being unwilling to serve, and being one who bestows what is useless.

It is established that each of the *dharmas* possesses its own specific delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for being taught. Otherwise, even if one were deficient by one or two of the four *dharmas*, one would still be entitled to receive the instruction of that [text].
By this [it is meant]: "Knowledge indeed came to the Brāhmaṇa; protect me."

"I am your treasure. In the *Yāskalikhitasmṛti*, it is further explained that the word "na" (not) should be construed with each term in the passage: "Do not speak to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is unrestrained; thus may I be powerful. Here, "Vidyā" refers to the Śrīvidyā, and "Brāhmaṇa" refers to one who studies the Veda (*brahma*).
A Brāhmaṇa who knows the Brahman came to him. Having arrived, he said:
[The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word "Brahman" in the sense of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that.
(p. 200) The term "learned" (*vidvat*) is not employed for one who is merely endowed with knowledge of crafts and the like.
And Śrīvidyā is the sole cause of liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus, according to the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, by the term "Vidyā," this very Vidyā under discussion is primarily intended;
because it establishes these [other sciences], the Vidyās such as the Vedas and others are called secondary. To the question, "What did that Vidyā say?
it is replied: "Gopa..."—"Protect me; I am your treasure. By the mere act of protecting me..."

The meaning is: "I shall grant you all the goals of human endeavor. He explains what this "concealment" (gopana) consists of with the word "asūya": "And he who, though protected by the scripture, is envious"—the suffix *ṭhak* [is used] in the sense of "one whose mind [considers] 'it exists' or 'it does not exist,' [or] 'it is fate'"—he is "crooked," meaning deceitful in his desire to hear [the teaching]; "unrestrained," meaning one whose group of six internal enemies (*ariṣaḍvarga*) is not controlled.
"In short, [it means] being subject to anger, greed, and so forth. Do not speak to me in such a manner.

To the question, "What would happen if one did not speak to them? he says: "Vīrya... The meaning is: "If that were the case, I would be possessed of *vīrya*—that is, capable of bestowing the aforementioned fruit; in its absence, I would not be so."
This is further elaborated in the *Ātmapurāṇa*: "The knowledge of Brahman, having become utterly exhausted, went to a Brāhmaṇa most devoted to Brahman [and said]:
'Do not indeed treat me, who am served by all, as if I were a courtesan!'"
Protect me along with yourself, as you would a woman born of noble family;
for I am an inexhaustible treasure for you, both in this world and in the next.
Beginning thus: "Likewise, the disparagement of the virtuous, a constant lack of straightforwardness,
perpetual subjection to the senses, attachment to women, and lack of discipline."
The abandonment of devotion toward the guru through action, mind, or speech—
always avoid me from those in whom such faults as these exist.
"For by acting thus constantly, I shall be like a wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) to you;
otherwise, I shall become barren, like a creeper devoid of fruit"—thus [it is said].
And so, even for a teacher, there is the futility of knowledge merely through association with atheists and the like.

However, it has been stated that for atheists and the like, there is an absolute absence of fruit even upon the attainment of knowledge. Consequently, the very lack of fruit in teaching an atheist and so forth is the root cause of their being considered a fault; this is the sense. For this reason alone, the conventional designation of them as "unqualified" (anadhikārin) is logically consistent.

This is because the status denoted by the term "eligible" (*adhikāra*) consists precisely in being the enjoyer of the fruit. Furthermore, in the *Kādima-tantra*, after stating that "a disciple should be of such a nature as defined by the characteristics of a good disciple; otherwise, he causes suffering to the Guru," it is explained that the root cause of his harmfulness lies in his being a source of suffering for the Guru.
In the Kulārṇava as well, after describing the disciples who must be rejected with the words "one born of a wicked lineage is wicked," and so forth, it concludes:
"Therefore, one should by no means accept such a disciple."
"If one accepts [the disciple] out of delusion, that teacher is pervaded by sins.
By this, the seed of the defect—the acquisition of the disciple's sins—is stated.
This being the case, even one who is the disciple of another, if he is endowed with devotion toward another true Guru and [serves him] with service...
Since he has resided [there] for more than a year and is distinguished by qualities such as being an *āstika*, what is the underlying reason for his exclusion upon departure,
or how could he be disqualified?
Nor should it be argued that this is due solely to the force of the aforementioned *śruti* and *smṛti* texts.

Because of his freedom from malice, his eagerness to learn, and his sinlessness. Furthermore: "Just as a bee, greedy for honey, moves from flower to flower, so a disciple, greedy for knowledge, should resort to teacher after teacher."

This contradicts the aforementioned statement; for if being a disciple of another were itself the defining condition for lack of qualification, then the injunction to resort to another guru would be impossible. Nor does this apply even in your own system, as it is said: "Having properly obtained a family guru, one should not resort to another guru."

It should not be said that this contradicts the aforementioned statement; for that statement can also be reasonably explained as intending to mean that once one has attained the Kaula dharma, one should not rely upon teachers of Vaiṣṇava or other such dharmas. Alternatively, [one may interpret it thus:]...

The meaning is that because the Kaula doctrines are exceedingly profound, even though it is possible to obtain all of them from a single guru, one should not practice by serving many gurus in such a way that one receives only some portion from one and some other portion from another. [All of them] should be obtained from a single guru.

If, however, one does not find [a teacher] in every respect, knowledge must indeed be acquired even from another guru, according to the statement, "Like one greedy for honey. For this very reason, it is said in the *Śaktirahasya*: "In the Kaula tradition, gurus are infinite.
Furthermore, the *Kalpasūtra*'s rule regarding "worship of a single guru" also refers specifically to the attainment of a guru who is full of knowledge. Nor...

It should not be said that a disciple of a preceptor who is proficient in other systems of thought, such as Vaiṣṇavism, is referred to by the term "disciple of another" (paraśiṣya). On the contrary, because devotion to another deity actually fosters devotion to Sundarī, it is appropriate to accept him once devotion to Sundarī has arisen. In reality, however:

Regarding the consideration of eligibility for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) of one who has received initiation from Sundarī and is proficient in external sacrifice (*bahir-yāga*), how could a devotee of another deity be fit to be accepted under the category of a "disciple of another" (*paraśiṣya*)? Moreover, in the *Kulārṇava*, it is stated:
"A disciple of another, a heretic, a rogue, one who considers himself a scholar," and so forth.

It must be said that the abandonment [of the teacher] occurs precisely because of the prescription of punishment for the counter-position— that a curse from the deity would fall upon that teacher along with his disciples— since it would be improper even to speak of a curse when the seed of its faultiness is absent. As for the phrase "greedy for honey":

And because it has already been stated that there would be no room for such a statement—if this is argued, it is not so. For here, by the term "disciple of another," one is meant who possesses more intense devotion toward another teacher (*guru*) than toward himself. Nor does he lack qualification solely due to an absence of devotion to that [other] teacher, since devotion exists toward his previous teacher.
Because of the absence of the general state of devotion to the guru; or else,

because of the firmness of another guru’s pride, if there should be agitation of mind in the former guru upon the disciple’s resorting to another guru, such a disciple is here included under the term "disciple of another."
"When Hara is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one.

According to this saying, when there is an obstacle consisting of the Guru's anger, it is easy to say that even through the knowledge under discussion, the result will not arise. Therefore, if there is the permission of the previous Guru, then—
It must indeed be told even to such a disciple of another who possesses spiritual qualities. For this very reason, it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"One should report to one's own Lord any Mantras, Āgamas, or other teachings heard elsewhere;
with the Guru’s permission, one may accept them, but one should avoid what is undesirable."

Thus the statement is consistent. Nor should it be asked: "What is the fate of such a disciple when his former guru is of little knowledge and absolutely does not permit the disciple’s service to another guru? For in that case, once the relative degree of knowledge of the two gurus has been ascertained, [the disciple may proceed].
For when one's former teacher has set out upon a wrong path, it is proper to abandon him, just as one would abandon a harmful mantra;
for even a teacher who is conceited and ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done [must be abandoned].
"Abandonment is prescribed for one who has set out upon a wrong path"—so says the scriptural statement.

If one is personally incapable of determining the relative gradations [of spiritual progress], then, having ascertained that "I have no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) from knowledge in this life," one should remain devoted to one's former teacher alone. Thus, this...

The summarized meaning is as follows: if another disciple, endowed with all virtues, attends upon one's own self, then while that [other] teacher is still living, one should accept him without hesitation. However, if he has fallen onto a wrong path while that teacher is alive, one may accept him even without his permission.

But if [the recipient] has not set out on a wrong path, one should take [the property] only with his consent. And this rule—that it is for the disciples of others—is indicated by the dative case (*saṃpradāna-caturthī*) in the root text itself, whereas elsewhere the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used. The dative occurs precisely when the production of another's ownership is intended; in its absence, the genitive is used, as in "for the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya*).

In the two usages, "he gives a garment" and "he gives a garment to the washerman," because [the act] is established, and because ownership is defined by relation to ownership, and ownership consists in being the enjoyer of the fruit produced thereby, the presence or absence of the status of *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is itself the nature of entitlement or non-entitlement. (p. 203)
Because of the final conclusion [of the scripture],

and because it is indicated by the two case-endings that while other disciples possess the status of enjoyers of the fruit produced by the knowledge being imparted by you, others do not, the prohibition "it should not be given" applies here.
It is established that one who is intent upon a particular disciple of another [teacher] without the permission of his own guru is intent upon everyone else;
whereas the ancients hold that those who have, through the lineage, attained the entirety of the secrets and the ultimate truth in other sciences [are exempt].
And they say that those intended here as "disciples of others" are those who have already received the complete initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*).

In that regard, by the phrase "other *vidyās*," do the various divisions of *vidyās* such as Kāmarāja and Lopāmudrā and so forth mean to be expressed, or rather *vidyās* such as Bagalā and Śyāmalā? It is not the first [option], because there is no difference between them.

The latter [alternative] is not tenable, because since the ultimate secret of that [tradition] has been established at the very moment of extracting the vidyā, there is no difference [between them], and thus, upon its realization, there is no object to be abandoned; consequently, there is simply no need to look toward another guru.

Since the worship of powers such as Bagalā constitutes a preliminary stage (*pūrvabhūmikā*) to the worship of Sundarī, once devotion to Sundarī has arisen through that worship, even [the former] becomes worthy of being grasped (*grāhya*). Within this very *vidyā*, however, the distinction is determined by the presence or absence of the *pūrṇābhiṣeka* (full consecration).

It is refuted by the absence of authoritative evidence. As for the statement that "the sandals belong only to that guru who performs the full initiation," this serves as a restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) when multiple gurus might otherwise be considered options (*vikalpa*) in the procedure for joining the name of the guru at the end of the *pādukā* mantra.

This is sufficient for establishing what you intend. Furthermore, as for the citation from the *Gītā* regarding the principle that "nothing should be given to atheists," namely, "one should not cause a disturbance of intellect in the ignorant who are attached to action," that too must be considered; for there is an absolute difference between an atheist and one who performs ritual actions.

Service to the guru (*guru-śuśrūṣā*)—meaning the desire to hear—is here expressed through *nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā* (conventional metaphorical indication) as "service to the guru," because such service generally consists primarily of the desire to hear the words of the guru’s command. For those who are indolent or averse toward that [service], there is "misfortune" (*anartha*), which refers to enemies who bestow what is undesirable. Precisely for this reason, Indra said:

A doubt has been raised regarding the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman to Pratardana; for it is stated in the *Ātmapurāṇa*: "Even if these qualities exist in him, nevertheless he is indeed an enemy. Alternatively, *artha* means wealth;
those who give what is other than that are the givers of *anartha* (misfortune). Knowledge [is attained] through service to the Guru.
Because of the statement, "or by abundant wealth. || 4 ||
It should be given to one who has been tested and has resided [there] for more than a year;
knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, one shall immediately attain the power of moving through the sky.

"Beyond a year" (*vatsarordhva*) is an indication of the time suitable for examination; this is in accordance with another scriptural statement: "Character (*śīla*) is to be known by those who live together, and that [is known] over a long period of time. By this, the mention of a three-year examination in other tantras is explained. This is the triad of conventions (*saṃketa*) to be described hereafter. In the void (*khe*).
She who moves in the supreme void (*parame vyomani*) is the Goddess Khecarī (p. 204); her state is *khecaratā*. The masculine form is applied according to the rule *tvatalorguṇavacanasya*.
Thus, the Śiva-sūtra states: "Upon the spontaneous arising of Vidyā, [there is] the Khecarī-mudrā."

Regarding the phrase "the state of Śiva": this has been explained by the authors of the Vārttika as follows: "When there arises, by the will of Śaṅkara, the natural emergence and the innate manifestation of that Vidya whose form was previously described."
That state which is non-different from Śiva, the inner abider,
is precisely that vibration consisting of the surging forth of one's own full-blown bliss.
"Because she bestows joy (*mudaṃ rāti*), she is *mudrā*; she is *khecarī* because she moves in the sky of consciousness (*cinnabhaḥ*).
She is manifested for this practitioner whose essential nature transcends the universe.
And there is the Śruti: "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave, in the highest heaven. And therefore, he who...
The meaning is that he who knows that great secret becomes that very great secret; for the Vedic scripture declares, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed. || 5 ||
He begins the latter half of the scripture:
"O Supreme Goddess, the convention of the wheel, as well as the conventions of mantra and worship—such is the threefold convention of the goddess Tripurā. (6)
As long as one does not know these three supreme conventions, so long shall one not become a bearer of the supreme command within the wheel of Tripurā.

"Cakra" refers to a collection of powers (*śakti*); its "convention" (*saṃketa*) is its secret form. The meaning is that there are two conventions regarding mantra and worship: the convention of mantra and the convention of worship. The word heard at the end of the copulative compound (*dvaṃdva*) is connected with each [member]. In the three [cases]...

The suffix *kap* has the sense of "unknown. Having stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—that one becomes Brahman upon knowing the three conventions—he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "as long as" (*yāvat*). Within the *tripurācakra*, that is, in the midst of the assembly of the powers of Tripura, she is both supreme (*paramā*) and ignorant (*ajñā*), hence "supreme ignorance" (*paramājñā*).

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that what is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, which consist of injunctions and prohibitions contained within the Vedas, is "verbal *bhāvanā*. Indeed, it has been established by us in the *Mīmāṃsāvādakautūhala* that this [verbal *bhāvanā*] is precisely of the nature of the command of the beautiful lady of Tripura. And it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
Regarding the Himavat, the Blessed Lady said:
"My own supreme power, known as the Veda, ancient and primordial,
proceeds at the beginning of creation in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas."

p. 205) Her *dhara* (support) is the *āśraya* (substratum), which is the Goddess herself. The meaning is that without knowledge of this, one would not attain the essential nature of the Goddess. This is stated in the *Śaktisūtra*: "The attainment of lordship over the circle of deities of one's own consciousness.
The same meaning is also found in the *Śivasūtra*: "The perfection of lordship over the circle [of deities] arises from the emergence of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*)."
It has been established. || 6 || 7 ||
Therein, first, in order to explain the *cakravāsanā*, he reiterates the wheel previously described and makes a formal promise (*pratijñā*) so that the disciple may pay close attention:
"That pentad of powers [is explained] by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and the four fires by way of dissolution (*laya*)."
From the union of the five powers and the four fires, the arising of the cakras occurs.
O sinless one, I shall now describe this descent of the wheel (cakrāvatāra) to you:
by the union of five triangular *śaktis* and four triangular fires, the central wheel alone is produced from those nine *yonis*.

From the sense of conjunction in the form of an enveloping [gesture], by means of the two lotuses and the abode of the earth, there arises that which consists of nine parts—the full wheel. This is the descent of the wheel (*cakrāvatāra*), the essential and fundamental form of the wheel in the form of lines; this is Your [true nature].

The meaning is "I am speaking. The meanings of the words *śakti*, *sṛṣṭi*, *laya*, and *vahni* have already been stated previously. However, earlier commentators explain the word *saṃyoga* as referring primarily to the mutual union of *śakti* and *vahni*. According to that view:

Since the conclusion would merely be that the arising pertains only to the middle wheel (*madhyacakra*), there would arise a contradiction with the context, because the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the outer wheel (*bāhyacakra*) are also to be described subsequently.
Nor, even so, [is this the case] for the impressions of the *bindu*.

It should not be argued that there is a contradiction in the context because the possibility of its arising was not mentioned here, since it is intended to be described later; for, as previously stated, the *bindu*— which is non-different from Kāmeśvara— is of the nature of the supreme Śiva devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), and thus lacks any process of origination.

Or rather, it is because it was not mentioned [in the previous verse], either with the intention of establishing the bindu in the middle while drawing the circle with a compass during the stage of extracting the wheel, or simply due to that omission. || 8 ||
Now he speaks generally of that which arises from the totality of the cakras, beginning with Bindu and ending with the Earth-cakra:
"When that supreme Śakti, by her own will, [assumes] the form of the universe... (9).
When one perceives the throbbing vibration of the Self, then the arising of the wheel occurs.

For in the Pūrvatantre, the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama) is taught. Therein, by the statement "O Dear One, Tripurā is the supreme primordial power [arising] from knowledge and the rest," even that state which is the form of the vanishing phase of the prior non-existence of emanation— occurring prior to knowledge, will, and action— is [indicated].

A certain supreme power named Tripurā has indeed already been mentioned; in order to remind one of her, she is here referred to as "that supreme power" (*paramā śakti*), treating her as an established fact. That Goddess, by her own will, [establishes] her own state...

When one perceives that state of vibration (*sphurattā*), then the emergence—that is, the birth—of the wheel (*cakra*) which is non-different from the universe, namely the wheel beginning with the triangle, occurs; this is the meaning.
The underlying idea is as follows: according to the authority of mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), histories (*itihāsa*), and purāṇas, the creation and dissolution of the world take place.

Thus, there is no dispute [on this point]. Furthermore, that the mutual succession of these two occurs through the differentiation of individual instances—recurring again and again like the pots on a water-wheel (*ghaṭī-yantra*)—is established as beginningless; this too is certainly beyond dispute. And from that, [regarding] creation...

While describing any [particular] dissolution (*pralaya*), one must begin the description from that very dissolution itself. In this context, "dissolution" refers to the abiding for a certain period in the mere essential nature of Brahman—who possesses infinite power—just as the individual soul (*jīva*) abides in the state of deep sleep; it is that which existed during the prior state of creation...

Until the dawn of that knowledge, those multitudes of individual souls have not attained liberation; and those various unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*), as well as the five great elements in both their gross and subtle forms, remain within the Brahman at the time of dissolution in a subtle state, like cloth within a cotton seed. This is just as [the world remains] in the water within the cosmic egg.

This is because of the previously cited statement beginning with "barhī mahī. For this very reason, the commentary on the *Śaktisūtra* states: "Even when concealed at the stage of descent (*avaroha*), the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*) dries up the fuel of the object (*meyendhana*) by means of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). The intended meaning of the word "mātra" here is that [the fire], although it devours [the object], does not do so by way of its total identity (*sārvātmyena*).

It seizes [the soul] by a portion and establishes it as its own constituent (saṃskāra). Consequently, when the individual soul (jīva) awakens by itself after sleep, its very karma serves as the cause;
for at the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved and [the soul] is overwhelmed by darkness (tamas), it attains the nature of bliss.
And again, through the connection with the karma of another birth, that very same living being sleeps and then awakens.
Thus, as established by such scriptural passages,

there is the emergence of the initial mental modification (*vṛtti*) within Brahman— which is endowed with power— solely by virtue of the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings from the time of the previous creation; therefore, no other cause need be sought therein.

Nor should it be argued that if the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) alone were the cause for the first occurrence [of a body], then that same consequence would apply during the periods of dissolution, creation, and the intermediate state; for this objection applies equally even to the state of deep sleep. Furthermore, it is observed that striking and other such actions produce sensation at a later time.

This is because it is established through perception and precisely by the diversity of causes. Furthermore, that mental state (*vṛtti*) consists of desire; it is the manifestation residing within itself, having perception as its object, according to the fundamental natural tendency [of consciousness]: "By one's own will, one should perceive the manifestation of the Self. If, however, [one asks] regarding the manifestation of the Self: "I..."

If it is argued that because the knowledge of manifestation (*sphurattājñāna*) is the cause of the desire characterized by the form "may I see," knowledge must necessarily exist prior to desire, and therefore desire does not have primacy— then, since the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*), [one must acknowledge] the manifestation of the Self.

The phrase "having seen [it], [He] desired" (*dṛṣṭvecchati*) should be explained by reversing the word order; this is just as the phrase "he sleeps, he is awake" (*svapiti prabuddhaḥ*) in the cited scripture is explained as "having slept, he awakens" (*suptaḥ prabudhyate*). In reality, however, in the scriptural passage "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) [is followed by] "may I be many."

Because it demonstrates the form "May I be," the primary function consists of both desire and knowledge; this is also because it forms a single syntactical unit with other passages such as "He desired: May I become many. What more need be said?
By reflecting on other scriptural passages such as "That [Being] thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" it follows that she (Māyā) is indeed of the nature of action (*kṛti*) as well;

for there is no contradiction in accepting the commingling (*sāṃkarya*) of the properties of desire, knowledge, and action on the strength of scripture, or else, due to the fear of such commingling, these [properties] are not treated as universal classes (*jāti*), which would otherwise necessitate their mutual exclusion.

Or rather, this is another matter, because [the nature of Brahman] is not contradicted by its genus (*jāti*). By this, the scriptural passage, "His knowledge, power, and action are innate" (*svābhāvikī jñānabalakriyā*), is also explained. In that context, the word "power" (*bala*) is interpreted by the ancients as referring to "will" (*icchā*); for will, knowledge, and action are non-different from their substratum (*dharmin*).

In this context, it is established by logic that even the mental state (*vṛtti*) as it arises possesses these three characteristics. Furthermore, because the use of the singular number implies a *karmadhāraya* compound, the non-difference between them is established. In the phrase "by her own will" (*svecchayā*), the instrumental case denotes non-difference; the meaning is "possessing vision that is non-different from will. He demonstrates the object within that mental state:
"Of the radiance within the Self" means the radiance residing in the Self. And that is indeed creation itself.
For such is the very nature of Light: its own manifestation occurs precisely through the pervasion of objects.
It is like the light of a lamp, the sun, or moonlight, which exists even in the open sky, just as it does in relation to a house, a courtyard, and so forth.

For there is no manifestation [of light] without its pervading grass, leaves, wings, and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned rule is contradicted by the observation of a lamp manifesting even without contact with an object; for the lamp, like a gem which is the substrate for a mass of radiance, is distinct from its illumination.

Nor does it follow that, if it were distinct from those [elements], it could not be included within fire; for its inclusion is accepted just as in the case of a gem. Nor should it be argued that, while a gem is seen to possess gravity and density—indicating its earthiness—a lamp lacks these two, and thus its earthiness is untenable.
In the case of a column of smoke, because it is not perceived by those two [the eyes], there is an absence of the property of being pervaded by earth-ness (*pārthivatva*) in them;

for even though the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) is uniform everywhere, the conventional designation of "earthy" is sustained solely by the predominance of the earth-element, as is seen in the observation of a specific density in a lamp.
Furthermore, it is appropriate to accept that there is a predominance of the earthy element in relation to its radiance;
and the conventional designation of it as "fiery" (taijasa) is justified by its being a substratum for illumination, just as in the case of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and similar objects.
By this, the moon and the sun are also explained. And thus, of mere illumination...
Since manifestation depends upon the object, and since even the object manifests only through its connection with light,

and since the knowledge of manifestation is also of the nature of light, the very essence of that relationship between it and the objects— known as the subject-object relation— is itself the definition of manifestation.

And this state of possessing that [nature] occurs through any one of the relations of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*), sub-correlativity (*anuyogitva*), or identity (*tādātmya*). By this, the threefold empirical usage—"knowledge shines," "the jar shines," and "the relation between the two shines"—is all accounted for. It is the same for Brahman as well.
Since, by virtue of its nature as pure luminosity, the radiance (*sphurattā*) residing therein— through the relation of being the subject (*viṣayitā*)—

is essentially identical with the object-nature consisting of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), it is indeed appropriate that the word *sphurattā* has the meaning "emanation" (*sṛṣṭi*). This applies to both [the object] and that which resides in the relation between the object and its connection.

The word "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*) is used to exclude [the notion of] vibration belonging to those two [the body and the senses]. This very emission, which consists of the nature of vibration, is indeed action (*kriyā*).

For the words *kṛti*, *kriyā*, *yatna*, and *sṛṣṭi* do not differ in meaning; or rather, it is because of the metaphorical identification of the effort with its object. For this very reason, even though the *Purāṇas* and other texts were composed by Vyāsa...

The conventional usage is that "it is the work of Vyāsa. By the three words beginning with "tena" (by him), through the manifestation of his will (*icchā*), it is stated that there is an observation of the nature of the Goddess Śāntā, who consists of the union of will, action, and knowledge; for by these three words, the unity of will, action, and knowledge is intimated. Thus, this is [the meaning].

The conclusion is as follows: when the initial state named Śāntā—which consists of will, knowledge, and action, and takes the form "I shall expand the creation"—arises, at that very moment the manifestation of the *cakra* occurs;
for it is said that the Lord's creation is merely his will.
Because there is no delay, and because even the *vṛtti* (mental modification), being included within the creation, is not contradictory to its being contemporaneous with it; thus,
he now demonstrates that such a peaceful (*śānta*) primary *vṛtti* is indeed the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the *bindu-cakra*:
From the consciousness of the vibration of the bindu, which begins with the form of emptiness and ends with the visarga. || 10 ||
Because its ultimate reality is light, and endowed with the waves of its own vibration,
it has issued forth as the locus of the waves of the universe, consisting of the triad of subjects.
The supreme Brahman, implied by the five qualifiers beginning with "having the form of emptiness," is the substantive. From that Brahman, distinguished by those five such qualifiers,
proceeds the wheel consisting of the bindu.

The connection [of the word "bindu"] is established by drawing in two words from the subsequent verse: "it becomes. The ancients, however, say that "baindava" means that which is born from the *bindu*; since it is born therein, the suffix *-aṇ* is applied.
Thus, the meaning is "the triangle-wheel produced from the *bindu*. According to this view, although one ought to have said "the triangle-wheel," [the term "baindava" is used].

It should be stated that the expression "the bindu" (baindava) is used in some contexts for the purpose of indicating the non-difference between the bindu and the triangle, as the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states: "The bindu is conjoined with the triangle. And its purpose will be made manifest in the eight-petaled lotus (*manvasra*).

It will come to be. He describes the essential nature of the *cakra*: "consisting of the three Mothers. The Mothers (*mātaraḥ*) are the mothers of the universe, the goddesses named Will (*icchā*), Knowledge (*jñāna*), and Action (*kriyā*);
that whose self or essential nature (*ātmā svarūpam*) is the very aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) of that triad is [the *cakra*]. Of that which has been described...
This is because the primary function consists of the triad beginning with will (*icchā*).

The use of the term "Mother" (*mātṛ*) for the reference to will and the rest is intended to suggest, through wordplay (*śleṣa*), both its nature as the aggregate of the triad beginning with Vāmā and its nature as the aggregate of the triad of *mātṛkās* beginning with Paśyantī.

Precisely because she is the Mother (mātṛ), she is the locus of the waves of the universe; the universe, consisting of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), is indeed the "waves" (laharīs)—that is, the ripples—and she is their locus or support.
By describing the universe as being of the nature of waves, its similarity to the ocean is established through such a state of being.

This is implied [by the text]. Since all creations arise sequentially immediately after the emergence of such a state (*vṛtti*), the meaning is that it is the progenitor of the universe. Regarding the view that the term *baindava* refers to the triangle (*trikoṇa*), the prescription of the triangle’s *baindava* nature is because the Supreme Brahman itself is its cause.

The phrase "the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the *bindu*" is intended to be suggestive (*dhvanīyat*). Therefore, according to the established view of the ancients, the *bindu* is indeed the Supreme Brahman itself, and its function consisting of the act of gazing is the triangle. However, in reality, this [interpretation] is [preferable] because it is the first thing that presents itself, due to the natural force of the word *baindava*, and because it accords with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
It is appropriate that this section of the text is solely devoted to establishing the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the *bindu-cakra*.
Nor does this result in a contradiction with the context, since the subsequent section does not separately describe the *trikoṇa-vāsanā*;
rather, by merging the *trikoṇa* and the eight-cornered figure (*aṣṭakoṇa*), it describes the single *vāsanā* of the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*).

Because of the absence of that [lower state]: since the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the mere triangle is extremely extensive, it must be contemplated as a single unity after the realization of the identity between the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and the individual egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*) has been accomplished;
thus, by means of such [instructions] as "one should perceive the manifestation of the Self through supreme qualification," [the teacher speaks].

And because it will be explained separately later on. Therefore, the very act of *īkṣaṇa* (contemplative vision), consisting of the triad of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*), is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the *bindu-cakra*. That which is to be worshipped within that is the Supreme Brahman itself. Thus say the followers of the Śaunaka branch of the Atharva Veda:
They declare: "The city of Ayodhyā of the gods has eight wheels and nine gates.

Within it is a golden treasury, the heavenly world enveloped in light. In that golden treasury, upon a three-spoked base supported in three ways, there is that which is unmanifest and endowed with self; that indeed is Brahman."
In the Taittirīya recension, however, the specific distinction is that it ends in the nominative case.
It is joined with the eight wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Sarvasiddhiprada, composed of nine triangles, unattainable by others, and serving as the dwelling place of the deity.

Within that city of the Śrīcakra, there is a supreme treasury consisting of light, equal to heaven, known as the Triangle; in that triangle is established the Bindu-cakra, which is the nature of the triple aggregate. Within that Bindu-cakra, as if within one’s own self—

The ignorant perceive the latent impression that if the Yakṣa, who is a great being worthy of worship, is indeed Brahman; for the collective meaning is that it was Brahman alone who entered the city named Aparājita, which is distinguished by such attributes as "shining" and so forth. [This is] for those who meditate upon Brahman.
Furthermore, there exists a certain city named Aparājita, which is to be reached and from which there is no return;
within it are two lakes consisting of nectar, named Amara and Aṇya, as described by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda at the conclusion of his commentary on the Sūtras.

This Śrīcakra is non-different from that city. Here, the term "tri-pratiṣṭhita" (established in three) is not an adjective qualifying the triangle; for if it were so, the two words [referring to] "in that" (*tasmin*) would become redundant. Therefore, it refers exclusively to the Bindu.
By this, it should be understood that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the Bindu-cakra being composed of the three [powers] is established.
He distinguishes the Supreme Brahman, the observer who is the root of the *bindu*-cakra,

with the words "having the form of the void" (*śūnyākāra*) and so forth. "Void" (*śūnya*) means that forms (*ākāra*)— that is, shapes (*ākṛti*) consisting of specific arrangements of parts— are non-existent (*avidyamāna*).

(210) That which has that [void] as its form; that is to say, from that which is formless (*nirākāra*). "The end of emission" (*visargānta*) means that in which the manifold creation—the diverse emanation or various kinds of creation—comes to an end, that is, dissolution;
therefore, it means from that which pertains to the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). *Spadi* means slight movement.

The word *spanda* denotes a slight movement of the root [dhātu]. That which is intensified is *praspanda*, meaning an extremely subtle movement. "The subtle movements of the *bindus*" (*bindūpraspandāḥ*) refers to such consciousnesses (*saṃvidaḥ*), whose nature is knowledge, that constitute the multitudes of individual souls (*jīvarāśayaḥ*).

From that [ocean], the individual souls (jīvas) are the portions of the ocean of consciousness (cid-ambhodhi), which are like its drops (bindu)—that is, they are distinct parts of it, arising from the vibration of the bindu. This is according to the scriptural statement: "In this world of living beings, my own eternal portion exists as the individual soul."

By stating that the distinction is exceedingly slight, it is implied that it is merely an appearance and does not exist in reality. Even if the reading were *prasyanda*—derived from the root *syandū* (to flow)—the meaning "living beings are drops of flowing [consciousness]" would not be contradictory. [This refers to] the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

"Bhāva" means ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*), that is to say, the absolute nature (*pāramārthika-rūpa*). "Because its ultimate reality is manifestation alone" (*prakāśa-paramārthatvāt*) means because its sole essential nature is manifestation (*prakāśa-eka-svarūpa*). "Sphurattās" refers to the very waves that are the emanations (*sṛṣṭi*).

Because it is stated that creation occupies the position of waves within that ocean of consciousness— which is joined with those waves and possessed of shimmering billows— it is indicated that there is absolute non-difference between them, and that the appearing difference is merely imagined.
For this very reason, one must take care not to fall into the error of regarding Brahman as possessing manifold forms.
It has been stated that [the Supreme Reality] has the single nature of light (*prakāśa*). By this, it is asserted that the other forms belong to the universe.
Within the fivefold division of aspects—existence, manifestation, belovedness, form, and name—[it is the first three].
The first three are of the nature of Brahman; thereafter, the two are of the nature of the world.
Thus, according to the statement of the learned. Now, the esoteric meaning is as follows:
the production of the object and the production of the word arise simultaneously, like a sprout and its shadow, being mutually intertwined; for every object whatsoever is dependent upon words.

As it is said by the learned, "Word and meaning are joined together like [the two halves of] a single entity. Therefore, it must be stated that just as there is the nature of "meaning" (arthatva) in Brahman—the cause of creation—which consists of Śiva and Śakti, so too there is the nature of "word" (śabdatva).
In this regard, the letter *A* is the form of Śiva, and the letter *Ha* is the form of Śakti. As it is stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*:
"The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme light, and Śiva;

the letter Ha is the final one, consisting of the *kalā* (aspect), and is celebrated as being called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). These two, the letters A and Ha, do not possess the extremely clear form of the *vaikharī* (articulated) speech; rather—
They possess the most subtle essential nature; for among the forms of speech— namely Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and Parā— which are respectively subtler, subtler still, and most subtle than even Vaikharī.

Because there exist three kinds of phonemes (varṇas), according to the Vedic revelation: "The cave [of the heart] contains the three [phonemes]; they do not stir; humans speak only the fourth of speech. Furthermore, another even more secret elaboration of this has been clarified by us in the *Varivasyārahasyavyākhyāna*. To illuminate this very point:

Regarding the phrase *māha-śūnyākārāt*: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both void (*śūnya*) and the letter *a*. The term *visargānta* refers to that which has the *visarga* as its final element—that is, its last constituent part or its binder (*bandhaka*). This is because the root *at* (as in *ati*, *adi*) is listed in the *dhātupāṭha* with the meaning "to bind"; thus, the word *anta* carries the sense of "binder."

The vowel *a* conjoined with the letter *ha* means that the substratum (*dharmin*) in the form of Śiva is conjoined with the attribute (*dharma*) in the form of Śakti. Alternatively, the sixteenth vowel is expressed by the very term "ending in the *visarga*"; it consists precisely of both the forms of *a* and *ha*. Its qualification is "from the form of emptiness" (*śūnyākārāt*).

The meaning is exactly as before: "from the formless" (*nirākārāt*). In the first position, since the word *śūnya* is connected only with the letter *ā*, there is no emptiness (*śūnyatva*) in the letter *ha*; however, in this [second] position, the nature of emptiness is obtained for both—this is the distinction. Furthermore, [the mantra] ends with the *visarga*.
For, through the perception of the indivisibility of even that which consists of both the letters *a* and *ha*,
such [a unity] is perceived as being of the nature of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahman*). However, in the first case,
there would be a perception of the variegated Brahman (*śabalabrahman*) due to its association with other distinct phonemes.
This is the distinction. Therefore, the preference for the first position held by the ancients is not to be respected.

By stating "from that which has the form of emptiness" (*śūnyākārāt*) instead of saying "from the formless" (*nirākārāt*), it is intimated that the *ākāra* has the form of a single dot (*bindu*), while the letter *ha*, in the form of the *visarga*, has the form of two dots. This is indicated by the word *visarga* itself.

Even upon the attainment of the sixteenth vowel, the "final state" (antapada) signifies illumination conjoined with reflective awareness (vimarśa); this is for the sake of attaining the true meaning. By this, the following sense is implied: just as in the world, during the state of equilibrium between a woman and a man, when the white drop (śuklabindu) situated at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra)— [The text continues: ...descends to the heart-center, then, by the union of the two, the supreme bliss arises. Just so, here too, when the supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, enters the heart, she bestows the supreme bliss. Therefore, the meaning of the verse is that one should contemplate the supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, within the heart. Thus, the contemplation of the supreme Śakti is established. Furthermore, the word "supreme" (para) is used to distinguish her from the lower Śaktis, such as the Will-Śakti (icchāśakti) and others. It is said: "The Will-Śakti and the rest are called 'lower' because they are dependent on another; the Supreme Śakti alone is called 'supreme' because she is independent. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Moreover, the word "heart" (hṛdaya) is used to indicate the location where she resides. It is said: "The heart is the seat of all beings; there, the Supreme Śakti dwells. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti in the heart is established. Furthermore, the word "contemplate" (cintayet) is used to indicate the act of meditation. It is said: "Meditation is the constant flow of the mind toward a single object; that is contemplation. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. And finally, the word "always" (sadā) is used to indicate the continuity of that practice. It is said: "Practice should be performed without interruption; otherwise, it will not bear fruit. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Thus, the entire meaning of the verse has been explained. Now, the commentary on the second half of the verse is as follows: "Just as in the world, when the white drop situated at the aperture of Brahma descends to the heart-center, then, by the union of the two, the supreme bliss arises; just so, here too, when the supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, enters the heart, she bestows the supreme bliss. This means that just as in the world, when the white drop situated at the aperture of Brahma descends to the heart-center, then, by the union of the two—the male and female principles—the supreme bliss arises; just so, here too, when the supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, enters the heart, she bestows the supreme bliss. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Thus, the entire meaning of the verse has been explained. Now, the commentary on the third half of the verse is as follows: "Therefore, one should contemplate the Supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, within the heart. This means that therefore—because of the aforementioned reason—one should contemplate the Supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, within the heart. Thus, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Furthermore, the word "Supreme Śakti" (parā śaktiḥ) is used to distinguish her from the lower Śaktis, such as the Will-Śakti and others. It is said: "The Will-Śakti and the rest are called 'lower' because they are dependent on another; the Supreme Śakti alone is called 'supreme' because she is independent. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Moreover, the word "heart" (hṛdaye) is used to indicate the location where she resides. It is said: "The heart is the seat of all beings; there, the Supreme Śakti dwells. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti in the heart is established. Furthermore, the word "contemplate" (cintayet) is used to indicate the act of meditation. It is said: "Meditation is the constant flow of the mind toward a single object; that is contemplation. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. And finally, the word "always" (sadā) is used to indicate the continuity of that practice. It is said: "Practice should be performed without interruption; otherwise, it will not bear fruit. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Thus, the entire meaning of the verse has been explained.
