It is said: "The heart is the seat of all beings; there, the Supreme Śakti dwells. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti in the heart is established. Furthermore, the word "contemplate" (cintayet) is used to indicate the act of meditation. It is said: "Meditation is the constant flow of the mind toward a single object; that is contemplation. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. And finally, the word "always" (sadā) is used to indicate the continuity of that practice. It is said: "Practice should be performed without interruption; otherwise, it will not bear fruit. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Thus, the entire meaning of the verse has been explained. Now, the commentary on the sixth half of the verse is as follows: "Just as in the world, when the white drop situated at the aperture of Brahma descends to the heart-center, then, by the union of the two, the supreme bliss arises; just so, here too, when the supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, enters the heart, she bestows the supreme bliss. This means that just as in the world, when the white drop situated at the aperture of Brahma descends to the heart-center, then, by the union of the two—the male and female principles—the supreme bliss arises; just so, here too, when the supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, enters the heart, she bestows the supreme bliss. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Thus, the entire meaning of the verse has been explained. Now, the commentary on the seventh half of the verse is as follows: "Therefore, one should contemplate the Supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, within the heart. This means that therefore—because of the aforementioned reason—one should contemplate the Supreme Śakti, who is the innate nature of consciousness, within the heart. Thus, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Furthermore, the word "Supreme Śakti" (parā śaktiḥ) is used to distinguish her from the lower Śaktis, such as the Will-Śakti and others. It is said: "The Will-Śakti and the rest are called 'lower' because they are dependent on another; the Supreme Śakti alone is called 'supreme' because she is independent. Therefore, the contemplation of the Supreme Śakti is established. Moreover, the word "heart" (hṛdaye) is used to indicate the location where she resides. It is said: "The heart is the seat of all beings; there, the Supreme

It is established by experience that when one has entered the temple of desire, one becomes one with Śoṇabindu; at that very moment, devoid of external and internal measurement, only Brahman remains as pure bliss and shines forth. The Śruti also says: "Just as one embraced by a beloved wife perceives nothing external..."
"One knows nothing whatsoever, not even the interval [between oneself and others]. In the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is a modification of ignorance (*ajñāna-vṛtti*);

however, in the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), even that does not remain. This being so, for one established in such equilibrium who consists of the nature of bliss (*ānanda-ātmaka*), the common characteristic consisting of the capacity to produce an embryo [is absent].

Since this is observed even in the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti prior to creation, the extraordinary process (*alaukika-prakriyā*) should be inferred by means of the worldly process itself. In that context,
the *bindu* situated in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) does not enter the abode of desire (*kāmālaya*) at all.

But [it exists] as a partial aspect (*aṃśa*); otherwise, the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) would not be attained. Consequently, the *bindu* situated in the opening of the ritual injunction (*vidhibila*) is the *turīyabindu*, which is nameless. Its partial aspect, however, is the *bindu* situated in the temple (*mandira*), known as Kāmākhya, who is meditated upon by practitioners as Kāmeśvara. For this very reason, there are names such as "Kāma-mandira" (the Temple of Kāma) and so forth.
They come into being; not prior to that. (p.
212) For it was stated previously: "In the subtle Śiva, there exists no name or abode without power. This is so when the *kāma-bindu* has mutually entered into union with the *śoṇa-bindu*.
When there is clarity, the two dots (*bindu*), the emission (*visarga*), and the letter *ha* are designated as "reflection" (*vimarśa*) and so forth;

for just as with Śiva alone, it is impossible for Śakti alone to be the generator of creation and the rest. Otherwise, the very acceptance of Paraśiva would result in futility. This was established previously.

It has been stated that the refutation of Paraśiva serves merely to silence the proponents of the refutation of Śakti through a disputational discourse (*jalpa-kathā*), and not through a formal debate (*vāda-kathā*). Furthermore, this very Śakti, whose form is the letter *ha*, is called *kalā*; for it is said that "the final letter *ha* is the form of *kalā*."

This is because of statements such as those found in the *Saṃketapaddhati* and other texts. This is the *kāmakalā*. It is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*), meaning "a digit (*kalā*) characterized by desire (*kāma*"), or it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both desire and a digit," even though Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*).

Because its non-differentiated power (*abhinna-śakti*) is accepted, by extracting the mere essential nature (*svarūpa-mātra*) inherent within that power, there is the state of being the *turyabindu* (the fourth drop) in its isolated form. When there is the intention to express that very [nature] by taking the mere relation to power (*śakti-sambandha*) as the delimiting factor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), it is denoted by the term *kāmabindu*. Of that very [nature]...
When the relationship is intended to be expressed as a state of non-dual equilibrium (*sāmarasya*),
it is denoted by terms such as *visarga*. When that very same equilibrium is intended to be expressed as being included within bliss (*ānanda*), it is denoted by the term *kalā*.
In this *kāmakaletā*, which is the form of such a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*), there resides the power (*śakti*) of the letter *ī*.

For this very reason, the letter *ī* is also given the name "Kāmakaletā. As for the instruction of the elders regarding the writing of the letter *ī*, which demonstrates it as consisting of the constituent parts of the letters *ka*, *ma*, *vi*, *sa*, and *rga*, that—
These are devised for the intellectual ascent of those with dull wisdom and are not ultimately real;
they are like the coaxing of children who are still learning.
As Bhartṛhari has said: "By standing upon the path of the unreal, one then strives for the real."

For this very reason, regarding the drawing of the *kāmakalā*, the traditional teachers (sāṃpradāyikāḥ) write that wherever there is an injunction for it in the *Kālavakra* and other such texts, first there is a single drop (*bindu*), below that two drops placed horizontally, and below that the "swan-foot" (*haṃsapada*). This is the [nature] of bliss.

Because it is impossible to write [the letter *ka*] and because it is the locus for the manifestation of its parts, the drawing in the shape of a swan’s foot (*haṃsapada*) is indicative of the abode of desire (*kāma*). And this very point was stated by the venerable teachers:
"Having made the face the *bindu*, and the pair of breasts below it, and below that..."
"O Consort of Hara, he who meditates upon half of Hara as the digit of Love (manmathakalā) [attains success]"—
thus it is stated here. In that context, the point of the mouth (mukhabindu) is the point of desire (kāmabindu), and the pair of breasts are the two points of discernment (vimarśabindu).
The meaning of "half of Hara" (*harasyārdha*)—who is the Lord of the Half-Woman form (*ardhanārīśvara*)—is that his upper half is the womb (*yoni*).

Likewise, in expressions such as "half of the letter *ha*" (*hakārārdha*), the meaning is that the half of the letter *ha* (which is reflective awareness, *vimarśa*) is the portion pertaining to Śakti. The same applies to the term "half of *sa*" (*saparārdha*).

The meaning is that the letter *ha* follows the letter *sa*; therefore, even the writing of the letter *ha* and its demonstration by the teachers is solely for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect. To illuminate all of this, it is said:
"the sun of light conjoined with reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)," because bondage consists of the aforementioned state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*).
He clarifies this very meaning, which was merely suggested by the final word of the verse, with the words "from the flowing of the drops" (*binduprasyandasaṃvidaḥ*).

The meaning is: from that [source] whose essence consists of the secret of consciousness (*saṃvidrahasya*), namely the flow—either the movement from its own place or the emission—of the two drops, the white and the red.

This means "because of the ripening of a process similar to the process found therein. In human bodies and the like, consciousness (*saṃvid*) alone is the secret essence (*sāra*), which constitutes the distinction from stones and other such objects.
Therefore, the term "consciousness" (*saṃvitpada*) is used figuratively for the secret essence. And thus:
The implied meaning is that because the triangle has arisen from the *bindu*, it is of the nature of the *kāmakalā*.
For this very reason, he will state in the conclusion:
"The *cakra* is of the nature of the *kāmakalā* in its ultimate sense of expansion."

He says "prakāśa... [to show] that although this [reality] consists of the vibration of the bindu, it should not be considered insentient by following external analogies; for even though its essential nature is solely light (*prakāśa*), creation possesses diverse natures.

To the question "From what has it arisen?", he says: "By means of throbbing. Just as the waves of the ocean are of the single nature of water, so too the universe is of the single nature of Light alone.
"O friend, how can this phenomenal world, which is a play of Consciousness, cause you suffering?"

"O Rāma, has the indravāruṇī been made bitter by sugar?"—thus from the *Vāsiṣṭha*. The grammatical construction is: "How can the indravāruṇī, once made with sugar, be bitter? And thus the sense is that everything appearing as distinct from the nature of pure luminosity (*prakāśa*) is merely an illusion (*bhrama*).

Thus, this matter, which is of an extremely secret nature, has been written here out of a desire to favor the disciples and by the inspiration of the Goddess; as for the method of extracting the essential nature of the *kāmakalā* that is written by the authors of the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*, *Cidvallī*, and others,
that too ultimately culminates in this very same point.

There is a significant discrepancy regarding the derivation [of the letters]. However, it should be understood that this does not constitute a major fault, because it is stated that "the means for attaining the goal are not fixed. As for the earlier authorities:
from the letter *a* together with the *visarga* and the *śūnya*, the *kāmabindu* arises; from that, the *praspanda*.
Two *bindus* arise; from them, consciousness (*saṃvit*) arises as the half-moon (*hārdhakalā*).
Because its ultimate reality is light (*prakāśa*), and because through contact with light, a flow (*srāva*) is produced within reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
It is joined with the wave of vibration (*sphurattā-laharī*); vibration is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), and its "wave" is [its manifestation].

Emerging from the space between the two points is the half-moon digit (*ardhakalā*); from the syllable of *kāmakalā* conjoined with that, there arises the *baindava* [state], which consists of the three mothers in the forms of *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*.
They explain that the central triangle wheel has spread forth, having arisen from the fourth *bindu* known as Sadāśiva;
however, this is entirely meaningless.
It is corrupted by all the faults such as ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), displacement (*vyavāya*), modification (*vipariṇāma*), and restriction (*vyavadhāraṇa*);
it does not conform to the sequence of creation and contradicts established doctrine (*siddhānta*), and thus it should be disregarded. || 10 || 11 ||

Now, although the impregnation (*vāsanā*) of the triangle-cakra follows in the sequence, it is set aside because it will be explained later on for the purpose of indicating its suitability for those of the highest qualification; instead, [the following is discussed] as being useful only for those qualified for the present contemplation (*vibhāvanā*).

By means of the very union of the eight-petaled and the nine-cornered wheels, in order to indicate the necessity of meditating upon the triangle-wheel (*trikoṇacakra*), he states the underlying impression (*vāsanā*) of the nine-yoni wheel by merging both wheels:
"The wheel of the Bindu of this [triangle] shall again possess a threefold form."
Likewise, merit and demerit, as well as the selves, the object of knowledge, and the means of knowledge; (12)
This great wheel, consisting of nine wombs, is a mass of consciousness and bliss;
this ninefold wheel possesses a mantra divided into nine parts.

This very form of Ambikā, established upon the seat of the Vindava, is the seed-syllable of consciousness consisting of the fire of universal destruction; it resides within the eight-spoked [mandala] and is surrounded by the vowels.
The meaning is that this very *binducakra* of three forms possesses a triple form once again;

that is to say, each individual form itself becomes threefold, amounting to nine forms in total. Some, however, maintain that the single triangle itself, through the distinction between emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and dissolution (*laya*), assumes the state of the triangles of Śakti and Fire.

They say the meaning is that, having reached [the source], it became threefold. Lest there arise the misconception that the statement "the state of having three forms" refers to the emergence of the triangle from the *bindu*, he says: "Dharma...
*Dharma* and *adharma* refer to merit and demerit (*puṇya* and *pāpa*). The "selves" (*ātman*) are four: the Self (*ātman*), the Inner Self (*antarātman*), and so forth.

The distinction is that the *paramātman* is the "knowledge-self" (*jñānātman*). These [three] are well known as distinct deities in the *pīṭhanyāsa*. First, the definitions of these three are recited by the followers of the Atharvaveda in the *Ātma-upaniṣad*: "In the body, Brahmā is the self..."

The essential conclusion is that the inner self (*antarātman*), the enjoyer, the subtle individual soul (*jīva*), and the supreme self (*paramātman*) are one; however, it should be understood that the self consisting of knowledge (*jñānātman*) is indeed Brahman itself, non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*). Although it would have been more appropriate to explain it as "the individual souls" (*jīvātmānaḥ*), [this is so] because of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the ninefold wheel of origins (*navayonicakra*).
Since there is no rule that the state of having nine aspects (*navātmakatva*) is strictly necessary—
given the exceptions found in the subsequent explanations of the sixteen-petaled lotus, the eight-petaled lotus, and the enclosure of the earth (*bhūgṛha*)—
nevertheless, because the identity of number, when possible, produces a sense of wonder for those with a coarse vision, [it is mentioned].
The ancient commentators have explained [the term] precisely as such, according to the principle that it is improper to abandon [the practice] because it generates an excellence of devotion.

Furthermore, the qualifying attribute "consisting of nine" (*navātmaka*) serves as an indicator of this very meaning. The triad consists of the knower (*mātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*meya*), and the means of knowledge (*pramā*).

It was understood that even though the knowing living beings (*jīva*) are infinite, they are one in their nature as mothers; likewise so it is for the object of knowledge (*meyam*) and the means of knowledge (*pramā*). In the aforementioned primary state (*vṛtti*), merit and demerit (*dharmādharmau*) constitute the self (*ātman*) through their aspect of action (*kriyāṃśena*), while the knowers (*mātaraḥ*) constitute the object and the means of knowledge through their aspect of will (*icchāṃśena*).

The distinction is that [this occurs] by means of a portion of knowledge (*jñāna*). Thus, in the eight corners, Dharma and the others are placed according to the sequence beginning with Vaśinī; the distinction is that the central triangle is *pramā* (valid cognition). Alternatively, there are three deities in each corner;
or, by means of the two words "tathā" and "iti," there are six, one, and so on, such that the deities of the three corners are thus [arranged].
Nevertheless, since such an error might still occur, he points it out explicitly by name, saying:
"consisting of nine wombs. This wheel, consisting of nine wombs, is ninefold even in its latent impression (*vāsanā*), and possesses mantras divided into nine parts.
The eight mantras beginning with Vaśinī, together with the root-vidyā and the *ceti* mantra, constitute nine mantras.

Although there are three deities situated in the triangle, there is no loss of the number nine, because the single root-mantra itself is divided threefold and applied [to each deity]. This statement is made in order to indicate the specific origin of each respective mantra along with those various mantras.

The term *baindava* refers to the *bindu* itself; the suffix *-aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*). That very [bindu] is the seat (*āsana*), consisting of the function (*vṛtti*) whose nature is perception (*īkṣaṇa*).

When [the practitioner] has ascended upon that, there is the *saṃvartānala*, the fire of the time of dissolution which consumes the entire universe, namely Kālāgnirudra and Citkalā Tripurasundarī, within that *navayonicakra*.

Let it remain as it is. However, the ancient authorities maintain that the *baindava* [seat] consists of the fourth state (*turīya*) whose essence is Sadāśiva, having the form of the Bindu. As he will say in this very context: "O Goddess, the supreme seat of Sadāśiva consists of the Great Bindu," [referring to that which is] precisely above the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Sadāśiva.

They say this is because [the power] resides within Śiva and Śakti. In this view, it must be stated that this qualification is for the purpose of ensuring that when the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*) is grasped, it is grasped together with the *bindu*. Ambikā-śakti is the aggregate of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī.

This is an elliptical expression for the aggregate of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*), as well as for the aggregate of *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*— the latter being the state of peace (*śāntā*).
And that [aggregate] consists of the functional mode (*vṛtti*) whose nature is vision (*īkṣaṇa*).
Because it is produced from that, the wheel consisting of the nine *yoni*s also has the form of Ambikā, Śāntā, and Parā.

To the question "What are the nine *yoni*s?", he says: "Eight," etc. That which stands in the eight spokes—situated within the eight corners—is the central triangle surrounded by vowels. For that [triangle] consists of [the letters] beginning with 'a' and ending with the *bindu*.
The meaning is that these nine are the *yoni*s, marked with three lines formed by the fifteen vowels divided into three groups, and having their central portion occupied by the *visarga* vowel.
By stating "encircled by vowels" while omitting the word "triangle," it is implied that they are together with the triangular wheel (*trikoṇacakra*).

This is for the purpose of clarifying that the vowels arise [from it]. In reality, however, this eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭāra*) together with the triangle is indeed the form of Ambikā herself, produced from the *bindu*;
it is not the case that the triangle arises from the *bindu* and from that [triangle] the eight-spoked wheel arises in sequence. Thus, there is a distinctness of the triangle.

This treatise has the purpose of refuting [that view]. The earlier commentators, however, having explained the half-verse "the wheel consists of ninefold nature" as referring both to the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Sarvānandamaya,
and to the nine mantras of the Cakreśvarīs beginning with Karaśuddhi;
Some explain the verse beginning with "baindavāsana" as referring solely to the triangle (*trikoṇa*). (p.

216) That [explanation] is unacceptable because it is inconsistent with the context of the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*). Or, let it be that for the sake of consistency with the context, it refers specifically to the wheel consisting of the nine yonis.
The praise [of the Goddess] as consisting of the nine wheels, beginning with the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha), is thus justified:
"The Bindu is joined to the triangle; the eight-petaled lotus is in the eight-spoked wheel;
the sixteen-spoked wheel is in the two ten-spoked wheels; and the subterranean chamber is in the wheel of the worlds."
Thus, according to the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the *navacakrī* (the nine-cakra one) resides precisely within the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*), which consists of power (*śakti*) and fire (*anala*).
And since that [power] is characterized by the non-differentiation of the state of being the nine yonis, it exists even within the nine-yoni wheel; this is the meaning.
For this very reason, with respect to the *cakrī*, it is situated both externally and internally as a treasure (*nidhi*); or, in its absence, it is situated solely within.
It was stated previously that one should worship the *cakra*. 12 || 13 || 14 ||
Now, he states the underlying principle (*vāsanā*) of the secondary period (*antardaśā*):
The secondary period consists of the manifestation of light vibrating within nine triangles;
it brings about the vivid appearance of the nine syllables beginning with *Śakti* and ending with *Daśā*. (15)

"Navatrikoṇa" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there are nine triangles. In the case of a *dvigu* compound, the suffix *ṅīp* would have resulted [which is not desired here]. Therefore, the meaning is the *saṃhāracakra* (the wheel of withdrawal), consisting of the point (*bindu*), the triangle, and the eight-sided figure (*aṣṭakoṇa*). This refers to the inclusion of the wheel consisting of the nine *yoni*s.

Because it has been made known immediately following [the mention of] the *bindu-sāhitya*. Others, however, hold that by the word "nine" (*nava*) itself there are nine *yoni*s, and by the word "triangle" (*trikoṇa*) the *bindu* is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, there is a *dvandva* compound of these two words.
This [interpretation] is based on the fact that the word "triangle" used here refers to the *bindu*.
Furthermore, the interpretation of the previous term *baindava-pada* as referring to the triangle (*trikoṇa*) is unprecedented.
In reality, however, it is a *madhyama-pada-lopin* compound meaning "triangles consisting of nine parts.
Nor should it be argued that such an explanation of nine as having ten rays is unacceptable.
This is because it has been stated that numerical equality regarding the object of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is not a determining factor; or, even if it were a determining factor, then—

just as the author of the *Kāmakalāvilāsa* accepts thirty-seven [categories] in the *Hādividyā* according to the view of the ancients through the conceptualization of the totality and its individual parts among the thirty-six syllables— [the same would apply here].

Alternatively, it may be easily stated that in the present context, there are ten [triangles] by including the totality (*samaṣṭi*) along with the nine; and this is logical, because since the *bindu* is the sun, its shadow is impossible. Thus, the ten [triangles] are manifested as nine triangles and one totality.

The meaning is that the light (*prabhā*), which is of the nature of that [consciousness], becomes the first ten-spoked wheel (*daśāraka-cakra*) consisting of the ten vowels beginning with *Śa*, causing the manifestation of the ten phonemes starting with *Śa*. By its aspect of illumination (*prakāśāṃśa*), it is of the nature of that light; and by its aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśāṃśa*), it is of the nature of the consonants beginning with *Ma*.

The meaning is that one should contemplate [this]. The word "cakra" from the preceding verse follows very far as the substantive. "Śakti" refers to the letter *ma*. "The five Mothers and the nine Lords" refers to the sequence of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the feet and so forth.
Among the nine [deities] recited— consisting of the nine syllables *ha sa kṣa ma la va ra ya ūm*— which are the forms of Unmanī, Ākāśānandanātha, and the others,
[this refers to] Śaktyākāśānandanātha, who is recited in the fourth position.
Because it has the nature of the letter *ma*: those [letters] which have that as their beginning are the nine starting from *ma* and ending with *ha*;

the "end" is the single letter *kṣa*, the last of the *mātṛkā*. Thus, the meaning is that it is the manifester (*sphoraka*) of the ten syllables. [This occurs] through the letter *la* [merging] with the letter *la*.

This is because, with the intention of non-differentiation, we observe the rejection of many [other systems] such as the internal *mātṛkā*, the placement of other groups, and so forth; for it has been stated that the manifestation of the vowels occurs in the central triangle,
while the group of ten beginning with *ka* resides in the second decagon (*daśāra*), and the fourteen beginning with *ṭa* reside in the eight-petaled lotus (*manvasra*).

Furthermore, since the "throbbing" (*sphurti*) is about to be explained, it is appropriate to speak of the throbbing of the letters *a* and so forth—which arise subsequent to that—within this wheel (*cakra*). Moreover, in works such as the *Subhagārcāpārijāta*, the conjunction of the letter *ma* and others with deities such as Sarvajña is recorded. By this [it is shown that] in some tantras...

In the verse beginning "ramā-śakti-bīja-uddhāre," "candraḥ śaktirmahāśaktirbrahmāṇī kāmikādikam," the term *śakti* is seen to be applied to the letter *ra*; therefore, here the word *śakti* refers to *ra*. The first among these [nine letters] is *ya*, and the end of those nine is *kṣa*.

The explanation of the ancients, that [the word] "one" [refers to the letter *ya*], is refuted; for if the letter *ya* were already included by the word "beginning with *śakti*," there would be no need for another word such as "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*) which signifies a starting point.
Furthermore, there is the natural force of the separate mention of the nine beginning with *ya* and the tenth [letter] individually.

[Otherwise,] it would be contradictory, because it is appropriate to specify only the ten beginning with *ya*. However, in our own position, it should be understood that such a statement is indeed appropriate for the purpose of excluding the letter *la*. || 15 ||
Now he describes the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the outer ten-spoked wheel:

"Because it has as its objective support the manifestation of the ten elements (*bhūta*) and subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the form of the twelve-spoked [wheel]—consisting of the ten syllables beginning with Krodhīśa—is radiant. (16)

The pentad of elements beginning with space (the ether) and the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with sound—this group of ten is "illumination" (*prakāśa*); it is characterized by the property of being its manifestation and having that as its objective support, and is thus indicated as the means for achieving that. *Krodhīśa* is the letter *ka*, according to the *Śrīkaṇṭhādi* system of assignment.

Because the letters *kro* and *dhīśa* share the same place of articulation (*sthāna*), the meaning is that the second ten-spoked wheel (*daśāra*), joined with the ten letters beginning with that [letter], became manifest in a radiant form. Some, however,
say it is like the heat of the sun in a courtyard, while the light of that heat radiates within the house.

Following the natural sense of the term *dvidaśāra* (the two sets of ten spokes) located at the base, they consider that just as there are two shadows of the sun, so too there are two shadows of the *saṃhāracakra*, namely the two sets of ten spokes.
This is stated in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"In this group of ten, illuminated by the lamp of consciousness, consisting of the nine corners and the center,
these two shadows are seen as the nature of the two ten-spoked wheels.
Those who follow that [view] interpret the phrase "the elements and the subtle elements" (*bhūtatanmātrā*) as referring to the first ten-spoked wheel.

While correlating the ten objects of the senses— such as sound and so forth— with the words "vacana" and the rest in the second ten-spoked wheel by means of the term "sphūradrūpa," they raise the objection of redundancy with the sounds and other objects already present in the first ten-spoked wheel.

Relying on the twofold division of the five [objects] beginning with sound— namely, the subtle and the gross— they resolved the matter by taking the term "tanmātras" to refer to the subtle sounds and so forth within the inner ten-spoked [cakra], and by taking the gross sounds and so forth to be those grasped in the outer ten-spoked [cakra]. This, then, is...
Under the guise of explaining the first position, he indicates a total rejection [of that position], since they themselves have demonstrated the difficulty of patching over the root [text]. || 16 ||
Now he states the underlying principle (*vāsanā*) of the fourteen-spoked wheel:

"Through the transformation resulting from the union with the forms of the radiance of the four wheels, [it exists] in the form of the fourteen spokes, consisting of the instruments of consciousness. (17)
The four wheels (*catuścakrāṇi*) consist of four parts each, being composed of the manifestation of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the letters beginning with *khecarī* and ending with *jayā*.

This is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*), as in examples such as "accompanied by the three qualities" (*triguṇasaciva*) or "consisting of three syllables" (*tryakṣaramaya*). Therefore, it is not [a contradiction].
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule for *dvigu* compounds. These [circles] are those immediately following, beginning from the triangle and ending with the outer ten-spoked wheel.

The *bindu*, however, occupies the position of the sun; thus, it is not included [in this count], for the shadow of the sun does not fall like the branches, fruits, and leaves beneath a tree. Regarding these wheels:

Although there are twenty-nine triangles when taken together, because it has been made known that the triangle is intended to be non-different from the *bindu*, there are in fact only twenty-eight; for, in reality,
the *vāsanā* here treats the wheel of the triangle as distinct.

This is because the absence of any distinction from that [reality] was explicitly stated by the very words of the text as "this is indeed the form of Ambikā," and because the purpose of that statement is precisely to establish that [the universe] consists of the twenty-eight wombs (yoni).
In the context of the arising of the first ten-spoked [lotus], although the middle triangle is explicitly indicated by the phrase "nine triangles," it is not included therein in the present case.
Furthermore, the statement "four wheels" refers specifically to the point (bindu), the eight-spoked [lotus], and the two ten-spoked [lotuses]. As for the triangle...

Because it was not stated previously, and because it would contradict the natural significance of the terms of the four wheels (*cakra*) in this context, the aforementioned interpretation of the term *baindava* as referring to the triangle (*trikoṇa*) should not be accepted.
Consequently, the form consists of the splendors and shadows of the twenty-eight female energies (*yoni*).

That which is conjoined means mutually conjoined, which is to say its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). According to the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57), the optional suffix *bāhulaka* allows for the inversion of the order of the terms, so that the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is placed first. Thus, there is one [triangle] for each pair of triangular shadows.

"Conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) means: since conjunction resides in two [entities], the meeting of two things alone is what is naturally implied by the word "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*); for we frequently observe the meeting of shadows beneath trees. By that transformation (*pariṇāma*), which consists of such a nature, [is] the effect (*kārya*).

The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*). Alternatively, it means "by that which is the combined transformation of the forms of light. "Cognition" (*saṃvitti*) refers to knowledge; that is to say, it is the fruit of the instrument (*karaṇaphala*). By this, the fruits of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) are also included. Furthermore, those instruments which are the senses (*indriya*) for those fruits—those as well [are included].
The five organs of knowledge, the five organs of action, and the fourfold internal organ—

these constitute fourteen. The Wheel (cakra), characterized by that nature as its non-different essence in the form of fourteen spokes, is the ultimate manifestation of the fourteen phonemes beginning with Khecarī.

The meaning is that its expansion was composed of that [essence] and consisted of its transformations. According to the *Kośa*: "The syllable *ṭa* is *Ṭaṣṭa*, *Kapālī*, *Somavāh*, and *Khecarī*. This implies that this wheel (*cakra*) is indeed a transformation of the phonemes beginning with *ṭa*. Although, among the powers (*śakti*) of Śrīkaṇṭha and others, *Khecarī* occupies the place of the syllable *ṭa*...

Although it appears that fifteen syllables have been stated by means of the placement (*nyāsa*) of Jayā in the position of the letter *ma*, nevertheless, because the origin of the letter *ma* was mentioned previously, there would result an excess of fourteen spokes; therefore, [the placement occurs] at the end of Jayā.

Regarding the word *yeṣām*, one should understand it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom [there is this]. Alternatively, *jayāntaḥ* means that which has the letter *m* at its end (*anta*). Thus, there is a *dvandva* compound consisting of the thirteen [deities] beginning with Khecarī and the single one ending in *jaya*.
However, if one follows the explanation of the ancients (*prācām*) that the letter *bh* is denoted by the word *jaya* itself, then the source for that must be sought.
This is because it contradicts many authoritative sources, such as the *Kālabhadra*, *Jayā*, *Vedhā*, and *Itinanda*. However,

some maintain that these fourteen [triangles] are the shadows of the four wheels— beginning with the Bindu and ending with the inner ten-spoked wheel— and the ten triangles situated within the outer ten-spoked wheel.

The fundamental meaning is that the external ten-spoked [lotus] consists of triangles situated upon it, joined with four forms of light from the four wheels; "from their transformation" refers to this. Because they are situated at a distance, each wheel casts a single shadow upon the external ten-spoked [lotus].
They say that because of its proximity, it is logical that the shadow falls part by part. || 17 ||

Now, concluding the description of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the wheels (*cakra*) beginning with *bindu* as presented in their individual aspects, he states another collective latent impression that integrates them:
"Thus, [the wheel] consists of the radiance of Raudrī, flashing forth in the form of power (*śakti*) and fire. (18)

The wheel itself, manifesting in the form of five powers and four fires, though existing in such a manner as the various forms previously described, becomes another form of the power Raudrī through its collective aspect, consisting of the radiance of Raudrī. By the word "evam" (thus),...

Because another impression (*vāsanā*) is prescribed with reference to the specific nature of a prior impression, and because there is a rule that the delimiting condition of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) must be pervaded by the predicate (*vidheya*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) in the performance of both individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*) impressions.
It has been indicated. || 18 ||
(p. 220) Now, he states the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the remaining three wheels:
"The form of Jyeṣṭhā is the quadrangle; the form of Vāmā is the triple whorl.
Here, by the phrase "the triple whorl,"...
Two lotuses, one with eight petals and one with sixteen petals, are perceived as being enclosed within three circles.

That [pair of lotuses] is of the nature of the power Vāmā, while the earth-pavilion (bhūgṛha) is of the nature of Jyeṣṭhā. Since Jyeṣṭhā follows immediately after the power Raudrī, the purification (vāsanā) of the earth-pavilion itself was taught first in the root text.
One should not think that this very same sequence must be adopted during the stage of meditative cultivation (*vibhāvanā*) merely because of this.
Now, for one who is unable to perform such extensive cultivation, he states another concise method of mental impression (*vāsanā*):
The aspect of consciousness is the inner triangle, and Śāntyatītā is the eight-cornered [figure]. || 19 ||
The portion of Peace (Śāntyamśa) likewise consists of a sixteen-spoked [wheel] and a square enclosure;
it is surrounded by eight petals in the form of the radiance of the Vidyā-kalā.
It possesses a clearly manifest eight-petaled lotus by means of the form of *Pratiṣṭhā*,
and it shines with four corners resplendent with the form of *Nivṛtti*.

In the sequence beginning with "from space, air," there are specific powers residing in the five elements starting with space (gagana) and ending with herbs, which serve as the delimiters of the delimiters of the capacity to produce air and so forth; these are Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā, and Pratiṣṭhā.
The oral tradition from the Guru’s mouth, however, states that there are *kalās* (creative energies) bearing these names, including *nivṛtti*.

By the word "interior" (*antaḥ*), the *bindu* is expressed; and both that *bindu* and the triangle are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), because the non-difference between the *bindu* and the triangle has been established previously. [It is] situated within.

In the explanation of "that which is the triangle," however, since the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the *bindu* is not obtained, the continuity [of the previous term] should be respected. The governing scope (*adhikāra*) of the word "cakra" found in the thirteenth verse extends up to this point.
The rest is clear. || 19 || 20 || 21 ||
Since this very latent impression (*vāsanā*) is profound because its object is a wheel of uneven numbers— sometimes one, sometimes two, and sometimes three—
the author states another very easy-to-apply *vāsanā* for one who is unable [to practice the former].
O Goddess of the gods, in the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana,
there are Nāda, Bindu, Kalā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and likewise Vāmā.
Viṣaghnī, Dūtarī, and Sarvānandā are situated in sequence. (p.

221) Since worship was previously stated to begin specifically from the house of Bhṛgu, the *vāsanās* are taught here for the sake of immediate recollection in accordance with that [previous statement]. The word "nine" (*nava*) is a separate term; it refers to the nine beginning with *nāda*.

The grammatical construction is that "the specific deities are situated in the wheels in sequence. The ancient commentators maintain that *navacakra* is a single word, where the singular number is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). That is not correct;
for if the nominal stem were intended to refer to a single genus in order to connect with the singular number expressed by the case-ending (*sub*), [it would be inconsistent].
Because the number nine, which is conveyed by the qualifying attribute, cannot logically apply to the genus (jāti). || 22 ||
Now, for the sake of brevity, having restated the wheels by means of the very names of their presiding deities (vāsanā-devatās), he states another easy-to-remember (sulakṣa) vāsanā:
"The two partless [principles] are Nāda and Bindu; and Kalā is the very nature of Icchā. (23)

Jyeṣṭhā consists of knowledge (jñāna), while the remainder is action (kriyā); thus, she is composed of this triad. She is partless (niraṃśa), devoid of the intention to manifest divisions, and is of the nature of a totality (samaṣṭi). And here, she is of the nature of the previously mentioned "vision" (īkṣaṇa). Nāda and Bindu, which are her forms, are the earth-house (bhūgṛha) and the sixteen-petaled lotus (ṣoḍaśāra-padma) respectively.

These two are to be meditated upon: *Kalā*, which is the eight-petaled lotus and the form of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*); and *Jyeṣṭhā*, which is the fourteen-spoked wheel and the form of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). One should meditate on the remainder—from *Raudrī* up to *Sarvānandā*, and from the outer ten-spoked wheel up to the *bindu*-wheel—as the form of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Within these...

Among the four types of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), one should instruct the disciple in each one according to his specific qualification. He, in turn, should cultivate that very impression accordingly and must not cause a confusion of different impressions. Therefore, this is a settled alternative; otherwise, for no impression whatsoever—
Because, in the absence of firm practice, there would be the undesirable consequence that the fruit consisting of mastery over the mind would not arise;
for in works such as the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*, it is stated that firm practice of a single reality alone is the means to that end,
since meditative adorations (*upāsanā*) serve the human goal only by way of mastering the mind.

For the Upaniṣadic scholars have established the conclusion that even the meditations on the *udgītha* and other elements bound to the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice do not serve the purpose of the ritual itself;

this is because the authors of the *Kalpa-sūtras* did not enjoin them within the performance of the ritual like other subsidiary parts, and thus they are like the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood, which, though taught outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), does not serve the purpose of the ritual. For this very reason:
These meditations are recited outside the context of ritual sacrifices, both in the Atharvaveda and in the Vedaśiras section;
for if they were intended for the sake of the sacrifice, there would be an optional choice (vikalpa) between them, similar to the choice between rice and barley.
Therefore, according to their respective spheres of application—whichever [meditation]...

The established conclusion of those who know the section on worship (*upāsanākāṇḍa*) is that one should practice a single form of worship alone throughout one's entire life; and this entire principle is to be applied here as well.
This was not recorded by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* in the section on worship within the earlier *Catuḥśatī*.
This is because the absence of an injunction and the fact that they are recited at the beginning of those [sections] are equal. However, this much is the distinction:

the meditations performed by the Adhvaryu and others during the Prātaranuvāka and other times occur only within the context of the sacrifice (*kratu*), and are not for all times; whereas [meditations] such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and so forth...

(222) Those [meditations] that fall outside the ritual (*kratubahirbhūtāḥ*) are applicable at all times. However, the meditations found here occur both within and outside the worship (*pūjā*), as indicated by the sign (*liṅga*) that the worship is described twice due to the division of its sections (*kāṇḍabheda*). For that indeed...

This is for the purpose of establishing both the exclusion from and inclusion within the context. For this very reason, the ritual convention (*pūjā-saṃketa*) is placed at the very end here; for if it were placed at the beginning, it would follow that the other two conventions must be recited within that specific section, resulting in their application occurring in the midst of the sacrificial rite (*kratu*).

It would be established. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the worship to be described here constitutes a separate ritual act from the worship prescribed in the preceding *Catuḥśatī*—on the analogy of the *māsāgnihotra*—because the defining characteristic of a "separate context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) is absent due to the lack of association with non-subordinate qualities (*anupādeyaguṇa*). Moreover, [The text continues: ...Moreover, [the following applies]. If one were to say that this is a separate ritual act because of the difference in time, then it would follow that the *agnihotra* performed at dawn and at sunset would also be distinct acts. If one were to say that they are not distinct because of the identity of the name, then it would follow that the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices performed in the spring and autumn would also not be distinct acts. Therefore, since there is no other means of proof, it must be accepted that this is indeed a separate ritual act. To this we reply: It is not so. For even if the time is different, the *agnihotra* is not a separate act; rather, it is merely a repetition of the same act. And even if the name is identical, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are indeed distinct acts because of the difference in their constituent parts (*aṅga*). Thus, in this case as well, because of the presence of the subordinate quality of the month, this is a separate ritual act. This being so, the worship taught here is indeed a separate ritual act. But how can it be a separate ritual act when the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie view) has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. Just as in the case of the *māsāgnihotra*, where the monthly *agnihotra* is a separate act despite the identity of the name, so too here, because of the difference in the time of performance, it is a separate act. Or, it may be that the worship taught here is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the previously mentioned worship, just as the *prayāja* offerings are subsidiaries of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Why? Because of the proximity. Just as the *prayāja* offerings are understood to be subsidiaries of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* due to their proximity, so too this worship is understood to be a subsidiary because it occurs in close proximity to the previously mentioned worship. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* (the final conclusion) has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *āmanahomāḥ* (recitation-homas) are taught after the *samidhenī* verses; yet, because they are taught in proximity to the *iḍābhakṣaṇa* (eating of the *iḍā*), they are understood to be subsidiaries of that eating. Similarly, this worship is understood to be a subsidiary of the previously mentioned worship because of its proximity. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *rājasūya* sacrifice, the *abhiṣecanīya* rite is taught; yet, because it is taught in proximity to the *daśapeya*, it is understood to be a subsidiary of that drinking. Similarly, this worship is understood to be a subsidiary of the previously mentioned worship because of its proximity. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *vājina* offering is taught after the *pradhāna* (principal) offerings; yet, because it is taught in proximity to the *anuyāja* offerings, it is understood to be a subsidiary of those offerings. Similarly, this worship is understood to be a subsidiary of the previously mentioned worship because of its proximity. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are taught after the *pradhāna* offerings; yet, because they are taught in proximity to the *samiṣṭayajus*, they are understood to be subsidiaries of that *samiṣṭayajus*. Similarly, this worship is understood to be a subsidiary of the previously mentioned worship because of its proximity. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *anuyāja* offerings are taught after the *pradhāna* offerings; yet, because they are taught in proximity to the *samiṣṭayajus*, they are understood to be subsidiaries of that *samiṣṭayajus*. Similarly, this worship is understood to be a subsidiary of the previously mentioned worship because of its proximity. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *samiṣṭayajus* is taught after the *pradhāna* offerings; yet, because it is taught in proximity to the *anuyāja* offerings, it is understood to be a subsidiary of those offerings. Similarly, this worship is understood to be a subsidiary of the previously mentioned worship because of its proximity. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *anuyāja* offerings are taught after the *pradhāna* offerings; yet, because they are taught in proximity to the *samiṣṭayajus*, they are understood to be subsidiaries of that *samiṣṭayajus*. To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *anuyāja* offerings are taught after the *pradhāna* offerings; yet, because they are taught in proximity to the *samiṣṭayajus*, they are understood to be subsidiaries of that *samiṣṭayajus*. Similarly, this worship is understood to be a subsidiary of the previously mentioned worship because of its proximity. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *anuyāja* offerings are taught after the *pradhāna* offerings; yet, because they are taught in proximity to the *samiṣṭayajus*, they are understood to be subsidiaries of that *samiṣṭayajus*. Similarly, this worship is understood to be a subsidiary of the previously mentioned worship because of its proximity. But how can it be a subsidiary when the *siddhānta* has been stated? To this we reply: It is possible. For example, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, the *samiṣṭayajus* is taught after the *pradhā

For the relationship of original and modification (prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva) can only be postulated through the transfer of details (atideśa) and so forth when there is a difference in ritual action; however, that is not possible here,
because even the constituent parts (aṅga), such as the placing of the arghya water and other single items, are [performed] part by part.

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the statement that [the procedure] is divided between both; for while in one case all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) are taught, in the present case they are absent. And for this very reason, like the *grahamedhīya* sacrifice or the *soma* sacrifice, there is the originality (*apūrvatva*) of one or the other. By this—
The view that— by imagining that only those practices prescribed as the *cakrasaṃketa* and *mantrasaṃketa* constitute the subject matter of this context—

the worship prescribed later on should be considered a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of these is refuted; for it is precisely the worship previously prescribed, which is the primary element, that is intended here.

Because their identity is established through methods such as the analysis of constituent parts (*aṅga*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there arises no expectation for further subordinate elements (*bhāvyāntara-ākāṅkṣā*), and thus no possibility of imagining them to be subordinate to anything else; furthermore, since the meditations (*upāsti*) contained herein lack any mention of a fruit, they cannot function as the primary subject of a context (*prakaraṇin*). [One attains] immediate mastery of the sky (*sadyaḥ khecaratām*).

This is because the statement "one should go" is merely a declaration of the fruit (phala-śruti) made with reference to the three conventions; it does not establish that the worship performed here alone is the primary act. Therefore, the wheel-worship described by dividing it according to the distinction between the earlier and later sections is a single ritual action, which has two modes of performance:

One is devoid of worship, while the other is accompanied by it. Even in the Veda, specifically in the *Gopatha Brāhmaṇa* of the Atharvaveda, regarding the rites prescribed in the three Vedas (*trayī*), it is stated: "Now, therefore, concerning the places of sacrifice for the gods; the self is the place of sacrifice for the gods; faith..."

Although many latent impressions (vāsanās) regarding each individual limb of the rituals— beginning with the *devayajana* and extending from the laying of the fires (*adhāna*) up to the *Viśvasṛjāmayaṇa* sacrifice— are generally described by [the author] starting with the words "the sacrificial ground" (*devayajanam*),

because those [limbs] are not compiled together by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*, there exists for each single [limb] both the state of being devoid of them and the state of being accompanied by them.
For each action, there are two applications (prayoga), both of which are indeed entered into. These two are established according to the distinction of the qualified practitioner (adhikārin).

It was stated at the very beginning of the treatise that the qualification differs from one case to another, being conditioned by the varying degrees of purity of the mind. Of these two, the second application is impossible for the first [type of practitioner], whereas the first application belongs to the second [type].

Because it is easy to perform, this [rite] is optional; however, it is not prohibited for those in higher stages of life (āśrama) in the same way that the duties of a previous stage are prohibited. Consequently, if one who is qualified for the second [rite] desires to perform either the first or the second performance, then the completion of the ritual action is achieved here with only the few auxiliary elements (aṅga) mentioned in this context. Therefore...

Because this tantra possesses such a qualification [of the practitioner], there is no need for the elaborate worship involving the *pañcapañcika* and so forth with respect to him; therefore, it is not mentioned here.
This is in order to indicate that such [elaborate rites] are necessary only in the tantras intended for beginners (*prathamādhikārika*).

The explanation of that [is as follows]: the independence (*svatantratva*) of this tantra is also only with respect to such qualified persons (*adhikārin*), and not with respect to ordinary practitioners (*upāsaka*). The *Tantrarāja*, however, is independent only with respect to the first type of qualified person, but with respect to the second type of qualified person, it is dependent upon this very tantra.

Since even for those belonging to the second category of practitioners there are many varieties according to the gradations of their capacities, it is not inconsistent to describe the various types of conceptualizations regarding latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, whichever practitioner is qualified for a particular kind of worship, having learned that very method from the mouth of a teacher, they should practice it with great firmness from birth until death.
Siddham. It is the direction that those who know the logic of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā should further investigate this. 23.
Now, in order to complete the necessary portion regarding all four types of latent impressions (vāsanā) just mentioned, he says:
The wheel is, in its ultimate sense, the expansion of the form of Kāmakalā. || 24 ||

According to the method described, since the entire *cakra* has arisen from the *kāmakalā*, the whole *cakra* is indeed of the nature of the *kāmakalā*; for whatever is an emanation of something, that is its ultimate essential nature (*paramārthika-svarūpa*). Just as a jar is an emanation of clay, so is it [of the same nature].

The ultimate nature is indeed clay alone, according to the Vedic scripture: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth. And it has been demonstrated in the *Varivasyārahasya* that this very same meaning is stated even in the third peak (kūṭa).
Therefore, the meaning is that one should contemplate everything as being of the nature of Kāmakalā. || 24 ||
Having thus explained the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) pertaining to the external worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*),

[the author now speaks] for those of even higher qualification, who are characterized by the firm cultivation of the identity between the macrocosm (*brahmāṇḍa*) and the microcosm (*piṇḍāṇḍa*), regarding that very body.

He describes the threefold internal wheel-meditation: "In Akula, in that which is known as Viṣu, in Śākta, and likewise again in Vahni; [these are] not without meditation on the Nābhi, Śuddhi, the tip of the Lambikā, and between the eyebrows. (25)
In the Moon, in its half, in Rodhinī, in Nāda, and indeed in Nādānta;
then again in Śakti, in Vyāpikā, and within the sphere of Samanā and Unmanā.
Furthermore, within the Great Bindu, one should likewise contemplate the wheel in three ways.
Here, nineteen locations have been mentioned, beginning with Ākula and ending with Mahābindu.

Regarding the phrase "the domain of Samana and Unmanā," this means [the domain] of Samanā and the domain of Unmanā, because their distinct essential natures will be explained later in the root text itself. For, in the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra)...
Relying upon the *suṣumnā* channel, there are thirty-two lotuses (*padma*).
Among them, at the beginning and the end, two thousand-petaled lotuses exist with their faces turned upward and downward respectively.
Above the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the very bottom is an eight-petaled one, and above that is a six-petaled one.

The established position is that the wheels (cakras) begin with the Mūlādhāra. Among them, the Kulapadma is indeed six-petalled and situated below the Mūlādhāra; the Aṣṭadala and Sahasradala, situated below that, are called Akula because they are distinct from the Kulapadma. Thus, by the term "Akula," both [of these] are included.

In order to exclude the eight-petaled lotus [of the heart] which might otherwise be implied, the term *viṣu* is used as an epithet for *akula*. From the verbal root *viṣḷ*, meaning "to pervade," the sense is "the pervasive one. Pervasiveness, in this context, means being situated at the very bottom. Therefore, by the two words *akula* and *viṣu*, there is reference to one and the same thing: the lotus of a thousand petals located at the base.

The ancients say that this is called "the place" (sthāna); however, this is questionable, because in the very passage from the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha* cited by you, it is stated that the thousand-petaled lotus (*kulapadma*) is below the *sahasrāra*. [As it says: "Below and above the *suṣumnā*, it is joined with a thousand petals."
O Great Goddess, by its very nature it is of the form of power, auspiciously consisting of both Kula and Akula; O Mistress, these two lotuses abide eternally and imperishably.
Between those two, within the *suṣumnā*, are the lotuses that serve as the supports for the thirty [deities],
according to the statement:
"The lotus situated below consists of *kula*, while the one situated above consists of *akula*."

This is because the sequence of the subsequent [description] is clear. Furthermore, in that very same context, having introduced the lower lotus as "thousand-spoked and endowed with a pericarp and filaments," the statement, "O Goddess, the Kula-deity is situated in the center of the pericarp," also indicates that it is indeed the Kula-lotus.
As for the claim that the eight-petaled lotus is "non-kaula" (akula), that too is not correct. For it is stated in that very same [text]:

"Right there, above that lotus, in the middle of the Suṣumnā, one finger-breadth higher, having first described 'the lotus endowed with eight petals,' one should then meditate upon that which is accumulated by the Kaula Śakti in its center," and so forth.

Because of the statement, "The lotus of the *kula* has six petals and is one finger-breadth in height," even the six-petaled [lotus] possesses the nature of the *kula*. For this very reason, it is said:
"That woman of the *kula*, having abandoned the *kula*, goes to the Supreme Person."
It is devoid of characteristics, free from qualities, and bereft of lineage and form.

Thus, the interpretation of the former masters—that one leaves behind all the lotuses situated below and proceeds to the thousand-petaled lotus located at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)—is indeed appropriate. Therefore, it should be explained in this way: "Kula is distinct from Akula," and not otherwise.

It is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which no family (*kula*) exists. The sense is that, in comparison to which there is no other lotus of the family (*kulapadma*)—whether grosser or lower—and which is situated at the very bottom and is the most excellent of all. And such a lotus of the family is situated below.

It is indeed the thousand-spoked [lotus]. Because the others are situated directly above it and possess few petals, the term *viṣu*— which serves to distinguish it from the others by means of the word *ākula*—
is not an adjective for that [thousand-spoked lotus], as the word *viṣu* [already implies this distinction].
Furthermore, because it lacks the sense of being the support for all, and because the term *saṃjñā* (name/designation) would otherwise be inapplicable,

it is inferred that in another tantra the name *viṣu* might indeed belong to either the eight-petalled or the six-petalled lotus. [This is] distinct from the *mūlādhāra* and other centers situated above it.
Because of the explanation, there is the determination of the expressive power residing in the center of the thousand-spoked root-support (*mūlādhāra*);
for even the co-occurrence with well-known words serves to apprehend the expressive power (*śakti*).
However, the ascertainment of one or the other among these two must be performed by those who perceive the specific distinctions. By this, [the doubt] in a confused case...

The particle *ca* ("also") is likewise appropriate in the phrase "and in that which is known as *viṣu*. Furthermore, this being the case, there is no contingency of perceiving two dots (*dvirbindu*) in the phrase "in the moon of the *ājñācakra*," provided one adopts the position that there is only a single visualization of the location situated from *akula* up to the *mahābindu*.
Furthermore, even if that were the case, for us who maintain the distinction between meditative visualizations (*bhāvanā-bheda*),
it will be explained later that such a consequence does not follow. Moreover, in the section on recitation (*japa-prakaraṇa*) in the final chapter,
after stating the visualization of each *kūṭa* as non-different from the three respective wheels (*cakra*), [the text continues...]

You yourselves will explain that the non-differentiation and visualization of the three supreme *kalās*— which are parts of the final *kāmakalā* of the *kūṭa*— and the triad of *kuṇḍalinīs* situated in the *ādhāra*, the heart, and the *ājñā* [centers] is what is enjoined; this very point, in our view, refers to the triad of vowels at the end of the *kūṭa*.
And because the three *kuṇḍalinīs* are established in a single location, this is logically consistent. However, if there were identity between *Kula* and *Viṣṇu*,

then due to the inevitable descent of the final vowels of the three *kūṭas* upon the locations of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *viśuddhi*, and the middle of the *lalāṭa*, the fire and other elements situated in their respective lower cakras [would be affected].
Due to the lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) among the three *kuṇḍalīs*, the conceptualization of their non-difference would be inconsistent.

Furthermore, it will be stated that the sound (*nāda*) arising from the *mūlādhāra* constitutes the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the *mantraviṣuva* and so forth; and since that [contemplation] is completed precisely at the base (*ādhāra*) of the first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), the *nāda* belonging to that [first peak-syllable] arises from there.

Arising is possible; however, in the case of downward movement as far as the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, that is not consistent. In the *śākta* [state], it is at the four-petaled *mūlādhāra*, because that is the location of Kuṇḍalinī, who is of the nature of *śakti*. In the *vahnau* [state], it is at the six-petaled *svādhiṣṭhāna*, because fire (*vahni*) is present there.

As it was said by the venerable teacher, the Blessed One: "Earth in the *mūlādhāra*, an indescribable [fire] in the *maṇipūra*, fire situated in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, wind in the heart, and space above."

As for what the ancients [have said]: because the *Svacchandatantra* describes the form of fire (*vahni-bimba*) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the *mūlādhāra*, and because it describes the abiding of the power in the form of *hṛllekhā* in the pericarp of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, these two alone [are the first two stages] in sequence.

Regarding the phrase "denoted by the term *vahniśakti*": some say that, therefore, it should be read in reverse order as "*śākta* in the fire at the root. This is an extreme rashness, for the meaning can be established even without such a reversal.
[The centers are] *nābhi*, called *maṇipūra*, with ten petals; and *anāhata*, located in the heart, with twelve petals; and *śuddhi*.
In the throat, at the sixteen-petaled lotus named Viśuddhi,

on the tip of the *lambikā*— that which is known in the Veda as the "source of Indra" (*indrayoni*) because it hangs down between the two palates like a breast, and which corresponds to the location of the subtle tongue— is the eight-petaled lotus.

In the space between the eyebrows, situated in the middle of the two brows, is the two-petaled lotus known as the Ājñā-cakra. Regarding this, authoritative statements found throughout [the tradition] should be consulted in the commentaries of the ancients. "Indu" refers to the Bindu, and "tadardha" refers to the Ardhacandra. The locations and other details of the Bindu and the others will be explained immediately following this in the root text itself.
He will say [later]: "And these portions, beginning with *bindu* and ending with *unmanī*, are common to both the body and the mantra.

The ancients maintain that they are likewise common to the *cakra* as well, because of the prescription of the duration of measures (*mātrā*) and half-measures (*ardhamātrā*), and because of the prescription of the location above the *ājñā-cakra*."

Even if they are limbs of the mantra-body, what is the proof that they are limbs of the *cakras*? Furthermore, regarding the locations from *bindu* up to *unmanī*, are the *trailokyamohana* and other *cakras* to be meditated upon as being identical to those [limbs], or are they distinct from them? In the first case, since those very [limbs] have already been enumerated as six, how [could there be more]?

The commonality of the *cakras* [is as follows]: in the final [view], there is a contradiction regarding their being ninefold and consisting of nine mantras. Rather, it is a single *cakra* alone, whose constituent parts range from the *bindu* up to the *unmanī*.
Even a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is to be trusted only when it rests upon the firmness of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is conceived in relation to the *bindu*.

Furthermore, it is illogical for the half-moon and other [phonemes], which are distinct by position, to be included within the *bindu*; rather, the group of eight beginning with the half-moon constitutes a single-syllable component of the *nāda*.
This is because of the indicative statement beginning with, "by means of the letters numbering the lunar days (fifteen), produced from the three *hṛllekhās*," and so forth.
Furthermore, the possibility of there being eight syllables is detailed in the *Varivasyārahasyavyākhyā*.
However, the *mahābindu* resides only in the body and not in the mantra. Thus, among these nineteen [syllables]...

One should again contemplate the Śrīcakra in three ways in its various locations: one should contemplate the cakras already contemplated in the first group of nine locations within the second group of nine locations in that same sequence;
furthermore, one should contemplate those very same cakras in the nineteenth location, the Great Bindu—this is the meaning. || 25 || 26 ||
Now, he establishes the distinction of locations for the three types of visualization of the wheel (*cakravibhāvanā*) according to the difference in the qualified practitioners:
"Up to the *ājñā* [cakra], it is declared to be 'with parts' (*sakala*); beyond that, it is 'both with and without parts' (*sakalaniskala*). (27)
In the supreme state of *unmanī*, the partless (*niṣkala*) exists in three ways.
One should contemplate, in sequence, the nine wheels beginning with *Trailokyamohana* and ending with *Bindu*, situated within the nine locations from *Akula* to *Ājñā*. Therefore:

The forthcoming instruction, "at the location of the drop (bindu) between the eyebrows [in the deposition of the *grahanyāsa*, one should contemplate] the 'flow of nectar' (*sudhāsūti*)," becomes consistent [with this]. This very visualization is what is denoted by the term "sakala" (the manifest). For this very reason, the qualified practitioners here are the impure ones known as *sakala*. Therefore...

Immediately after the *ājñācakra*. This means beginning with the Moon (*indu*). The sequential visualization of the nine wheels, starting from the Moon and ending with the *bindu*, within the group of nine [wheels] culminating in *unmanī*—beginning with the *trailokyamohana* and ending with the *bindu*—is called "the differentiated and the undifferentiated" (*sakalaniṣkala*). In that regard, it is not merely...

Neither purely pure nor purely impure, such are the mixed *pralayākala* initiates (*adhikārin*) in the supreme station, the Great Bindu; therein, without mutual differentiation among the nine previously mentioned wheels—

The contemplation [of the deity] as remaining solely as the *kāmakalā*, which consists of pure consciousness devoid of objects, is called the "partless" (*niṣkala*). In that regard, the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) are the pure worshippers known as the *vijñānakevalas*. The characteristics and other details concerning these three types of worshippers are found in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara*.
We have already explained this in detail on the occasion of the commentary on the name *Paśupāśavimocanī*.
Furthermore, this systematic arrangement was indicated by the author of the root text through the very application of the designations "sakala" and so forth;
otherwise, those designations would fall into futility, since their utility is seen in subsequent usage.

Furthermore, through etymological derivations such as *sakala* (meaning "possessing parts"), which imply a gross impurity along with a measure of differentiation that establishes the relationship between part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*) by means of a "portion" (*kalā*), the status of being the presiding authority over the impure, mixed, and pure [levels] is also revealed through its derivative (*yaugika*) sense. Or rather, it is the words *sakala* and so forth themselves [that convey this].
One should understand that passages such as "possessing all authorities" (*sakalādhikārikam*) are intended to convey this meaning and are not merely technical designations.

The meaning is that the threefold nature previously mentioned, which exists in three ways, is established according to this method. And this is the meaning obtained from the oral tradition of the venerable [teacher].
It has been clarified by establishing it upon the root. However,
for those whose view holds that the designation "equinox" (*viṣu*) is a qualifier of *Akula*,
their followers [perform] the visualization of the entire *Sarvānandamaya-cakra* within the moon, and [the visualization] of the *Trailokyamohana-cakra*.

They say that the "mixed meditation" (*miśrabhāvanā*) constitutes a single stage for both [the Sakala and Niṣkala], otherwise there would be no room for their "partless meditation" (*niṣkalabhāvanā*). However, how can the contradiction with the root text—which states that "everything up to the Ājñā [level] is Sakala"—be resolved? This, however, can be easily explained by them as follows:

*Ājñānta* means "up to the end of the *ājñā*"—the moon (*indu*). There is a prefixing of the vowel *ā* before the word *ājñānta*; this has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). Thus, the final meaning is "including the moon. Furthermore, the word *tataḥ* does not signify mere immediate succession, but rather means "starting from the moon. This is because of the elision of the suffix *-lyap*.
The fifth [verse]: "Because that state is possible through the acceptance of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) culminating in the Command (*ājñā*).
However, the ancients [hold] that the portions of the wheels (*cakrabhāga*), beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Unmanī, are gross, subtle, and subtler.

One should contemplate [the deities] within the portions ranging from A-kula to Ā-unmanī— comprising the gross, subtle, and most subtle— as well as in the Great Bindu (mahābindu). Therein, beginning from the Viṣu of A-kula up to the Ājñā, the contemplation of the eight gross wheels (cakras) starting from the square and ending with the triangle is the "with-parts" (sakala) practice.
The contemplation (*vibhāvana*) of the increasingly subtle parts of the *bindu-cakra* within the stations beginning with *bindu* and ending with *unmanī* is called "with-part" (*sakala-niṣkala*).
They say that the contemplation of the consciousness of emptiness (*śūnya-saṃvit*) within the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) is "partless" (*niṣkala*). Of these...

The intention is that there is one contemplation (*vibhāvana*) consisting of eight auspicious positions (*aṣṭāśasthānaka*), while the three designations— *sakala* and so forth— apply specifically to its constituent parts. And regarding the phrase "again in the Great Bindu" (*punaścaivaṃ mahābindau*), the word "again" (*punaḥ*) refers to that which effects the designations *sakala* and so on.

And this is contrary to its own natural sense. The reason for proceeding to apply the designation "viṣu" as a qualifier to the *akula* state is rooted solely in this delusion; such is the secret of its underlying intention.
Now, [regarding] each of the states beginning with *bindu* and ending with *unmanī*:
He states the location, form, shape, and time:
"The shape of a lamp, measuring half a mora, is desired as circular on the forehead. (28)

That which has the form and the radiance of a lamp is "lamp-shaped" (*dīpākāra*). That which has half a *mātrā* is "half-measure" (*ardhamātra*). A *mātrā* is the duration of the pronunciation of a short vowel;
it consists of two hundred and fifty-six *lava*s. A *lava* is the smallest unit of time.
The time required for a fine needle to pierce through each individual leaf of a cluster of lotus petals is designated as a *lava*.
"Therefore, O descendant of Bhṛgu, a time more subtle than this cannot be perceived," according to this statement.

For this very reason, it is said in the *Vṛttacandrodaya*: "Two hundred and fifty-six *lava*s—those 'peas' of time—constitute one *mātrā*. Thus, [one *mātrā* consists of] one hundred and twenty-eight [breaths].
The duration of the anusvāra is that of a short vowel (lava); for it is stated that a consonant has a duration of half a mātrā.
On the forehead—that is, in the middle of the forehead—is the moon, circular in shape; "the moon" is the word to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. || 28 ||
It has the form of a half-moon, and above that, a portion measuring one foot;
likewise, it has the appearance of moonlight, consists of eight parts, is obstructive, and has the form of a blood-drop. (29)

Likewise, he whose luster and form are equal to his own name; that is to say, by his luster, his form, and even his name, he is "Ardhacandra" (the Half-Moon). Some, however, maintain that his form is like that of a lamp. A single *pāda* [of the mantra] is to be uttered in sixty-four *lavas* of time. Above that, over the *bindu*.
And this state [is reached] at the end of *unmanā*; here, the sounds follow according to the rule of transformation (*vikāra*).

She has the form of moonlight, the splendor of the moon; she possesses eight parts and thirty-two divisions of time. Her body, her physical form, is a triangle consisting of the power of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya-śakti*).

Just as the word *aśri* [is established], the word *asra* is also conventionally used for both blood and a corner, just as it is for tears. Therefore, even though there is no specific *nipātana* (irregular derivation) for the word *asra* in the *caturasra* section of the *suprātasuśvetyādi* sūtra, there is no fault. The etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) of the *rodhinīs* is found in another tantra:
Because she obstructs the attainment of the supreme state by Brahmā and the other supreme lords, she is called "Nirodhinī" (The Obstructress).

|| 29 || Between the two *bindus* is the staff (*daṇḍa*), which has the form of a phallus and the luster of a jewel; it consists of two parts of *kalā* and two parts of *nādānta*, blazing like lightning. || 30 ||

A line extending vertically upward and downward like a staff (*daṇḍa*), with two dots attached to its right and left sides; that staff is of the form of *śeva*. *Śeva* is a derivative of wheat flour, shaped like hair, well known as an ingredient for milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other dishes.

The meaning is that it is likewise subtle and soft. Others say that the vessel situated between the two testicles is called *śeva*. According to tradition (*saṃpradāya*), it has the luster of a ruby (*padmarāga-maṇi*).
However, in another tantra it is said: "It resembles the filaments of a lotus and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns."
