The "sixteenth part" (*kalāṃśa*) is a sixteenth part of a *mātrā*. Alternatively, the word *aṃśa* itself refers to a minute fraction (*lava*). Thus, the meaning is "the time of a sixteenth fraction"; the word "sound" (*nāda*) is to be supplied as the substantive.
By repeating the compound *kalāṃśa*, one may analyze it as *kalaś cāsau aṃśaś ca* ("that which is both a minute fraction and a part").
This is the attainment of the substantive [object]. Regarding *dhvani*, however, it is sweet and indistinct; some say that *kala* is defined by the *Amara-kośa*.

But the end of sound (*nādānta*) consists of double the parts; that is to say, it is to be articulated in a duration consisting of thirty-two parts, which is eight times the measure of a *kalā*. || 30 ||
The letter *ha*, however, shines forth joined with a bindu situated on its left;
likewise, the *śakti* [the letter *sa*] has the form of a rising head with a bindu situated on its left. (31)
And it is joined with the *bindu*. "Left" (*savya*) refers to the right and left [sides].
In the latter half of the verse, because of the usage of the word "left foot," the term "left" (*asavya*) here refers to the right.
The axle-rod extends upward and downward.
On the left side of its own forehead, the tip of the plow-like trunk is turned downward;

on the right side of its own forehead, in the middle region of the shaft of the pole, there is a drop (*bindu*) of such a form—this is the meaning understood from the mouth of the Lord as "the end of sound" (*nādānta*). Between the two drops...
The intention behind the statement of the ancients, "accompanied by a dot situated on the right side," is to be considered.
*Nādānta* means that wherein the end (*anta*) or dissolution (*laya*) of the *nāda* occurs.
This is according to other tantras such as: "That which is dissolved in the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*) within the channel (*nāḍī*), characterized by unmanifest sound (*avyaktadhvani*). etc.
The following [verse] follows: "O Goddess, the *bindu* consists of a circle (*vṛtta*), while emanation (*sarga*) consists of two *bindus*.

This half-verse is found in some manuscripts. Its meaning is as follows: all those individual *bindus* that constitute the body of the ninefold [group] beginning with the *bindu* are each spoken of individually.

One should understand the latent impression (*vāsanā*) to be as follows: all those forms consisting of two dots (*bindu*), which are said to range from the form of the *bindu* at the mouth and heart of Kāmākhyā, are in essence the white and red *visarga*. There are two *bindus*, one on the right and one on the left;
there, an upward line is placed upon the head of the left *bindu*. Such is the form of Śakti.
By the phrase "the drop situated on the left," there is an implied reference to the other drop situated on the right.
The analysis of the compound is: "she whose form is like that of a vein (śirā) rising—that is, ascending—from the drop situated on the left.
From this point onward, he will describe the metaphors (*rūpaka*) and so forth further below. || 31 ||
Pervasive, it has assumed the form of a triangle shining with the *bindu*;
furthermore, it consists of a straight line situated between two *bindus*. (32)

According to the tradition, by drawing a *bindu* in the corner of the triangle of power (*śaktitrikoṇa*) facing toward oneself, the form of the Pervasive Goddess (*vyāpikā*) arises; it consists of a line extending downward from above with two *bindus* attached to its upper and lower extremities— such is her form.

The word "samanā" is to be construed with the following verse. In the phrase "the straight line situated in the intermediate space," the form remains as the original base (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*. || 32 ||
The Samanā is the straight line shimmering with the Bindu;
likewise, the Unmanā is the body of Śakti and the others, radiant like the twelve suns.
An upward line should be drawn at the head of the *bindu*; this is the form of *Unmanā*.

When the *bindu* situated at the head of *Samanā* is removed, she becomes *Samanā*. For this very reason, because she is subtler than *Samanā*, her mind has transcended (*utkrāntamanaskā*). Even for yogins, [she is reached] by means of the mind.
The sense is that he goes by means of a narrow path. Words such as *samanā* and so forth are grammatically correct precisely because they belong to the *pṛṣodarādi* class.
The bodies of the four [energies] beginning with Śakti and ending with Unmanā possess a luster combined with the twelve suns. || 33 ||
Sixty-four [mātrās] above that, and then double, then double again;
such is the measure of the parts for Śakti and the others, and likewise for Manonmanī and Unmanī.
The time up to the end of *nāda* has been previously described. Beyond that—that is, above the end of *nāda*, among the sequence beginning with *śakti*—the meaning is "of the first.
The sixty-fourth part of a *mātrā*, consisting of four *lava*s, is the time of *śakti*.

This is the meaning. As for those [states] immediately following that, the phrase "twofold, twofold" by way of repetition means that the duration of the *mātrā* is twice as much as each preceding one. Consequently, in the *vyāpikā* there are two *lava*s; in the *samānā*, one *lava*; and the time of the *unmanā* consists of half a *lava*.
The opponent objects to this, saying "by Manonmanī. *Manonmanī* is simply another name for *Samanā*.
The meaning is that the time of *Unmanī* is exactly like the time of *Samanā*;
that is to say, time consists of a single *lava* (moment). Thus, her form, time, and portion (*kalā*) are derived from *Samanā*.
That [statement] is intended to mean that time, though existing, is difficult to perceive because it is subtle and conforms to the form [of the object];

for this very reason, in the root text, after stating "unconditioned by space and time," the subsequent phrase "that which is supreme and great" coherently expresses precisely this lack of temporal limitation.
The predecessors, however, maintain that "double, double" is not a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), but rather that it is doubled above *Śakti*;
then, after *Vyāpikā*, it is doubled again in *Samanā*, with each [level] being thus connected individually.
The two words [refer to] "of Manonmanī," which means "up to and including Samanā.
And that is a qualifier for "of Śakti and the others"; therefore, there is no temporal regulation here for Unmanā. Thus, Unmanī is exactly as she is now, without any previously mentioned qualifiers.
They say it extends as far as "formless" (*nirākārā*) and "inexpressible" (*niruccārā*).

However, this [interpretation] is tainted by the redundancy of the term *unmanī* following *manonmanī*, and by a forced and strained explanation; furthermore, it contradicts the natural sense of the subsequent verse, and thus it is disregarded. Moreover:

In the final chapter (*uttarapaṭala*), having established the fifteen vowels within the Vidyā and stated that she is divided into thirty-seven parts through the distinction between vowels and consonants, the state of being thirty-seven will be analyzed by including the three *nādas*.
By that indication, it is shown that the *nāda* is external to the fifteen vowels.

Since the status of being a *vyañjana* (consonant) is established, the statement that "a consonant consists of half a *mātrā*" indicates that it is composed of one hundred and twenty-eight *lavas*. Furthermore, if there were an absence of time for the *unmanā* state, which is a constituent part of the *nāda*, it would result in a deficiency of one *lava*.

Therefore, it should be understood that the interpretation "the time of *samāna* and *unmanā* is the same" is the correct one regarding their non-contradiction. Furthermore, it will be stated that the dissolution of the *nāda* in *unmanā* is the "equinox of time" (*kālaviṣuva*); if there were an absence of time in *unmanā*, this would contradict the internal consistency of that designation. Regarding that term...
Because it has the sense of being pervaded by time. || 34 ||
Beyond that is the supreme Great One, unconditioned by space or time;
it is naturally beautiful and reeling with supreme bliss.

"Beyond that" means, in effect, the station of the Great Bindu (mahābindu) characterized as being in the space above Unmanā. It is "unconditioned by space and time," meaning it is devoid of any limitation imposed by them. For this very reason, the statement "beyond that" is a description of its location.
This should be explained as having the sense of indicating the location (*deśa*). "Naturally beautiful" (*nisargasundara*) means lovely by its very nature.
"Whirled by supreme bliss" (*parānandena vighūrṇitam*) means pervaded by the bliss consisting of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti.
However, the earlier commentators [state]: "The location, essential nature, and so forth of the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) are not mentioned at all here in this Tantra; of that..."

Because it transcends all things (*viśvottīrṇatva*), it is beyond the reach of speech and mind. Therefore, "that state above" (*tadūrdhvaṃ padam*) means that which is above the collection of locations of the letters beginning with *ha* and ending with the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) situated within the *Hādividyā*.
This description refers to the state situated above even the levels of the three kinds of contemplation (*bhāvanā*).

They explain [it thus], but this contradicts the context; furthermore, it must be considered how speech and mind could function toward that which is even beyond the transcendent universe (*viśvottīrṇa*).
In this regard, [there is the mention of] the deities residing in the locations beginning with the Moon and ending with the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*), as well as their respective worlds.
And the detailed expansion of those respective kalās is to be understood from the commentaries of the ancients. || 35 ||

Now, in order to indicate that this is for one of the highest qualification (*uttamādhikārin*), who has achieved firmness in the contemplation of the identity of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and the individual egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*)— which was left unmentioned during the occasion of the initial extensive purification (*vistṛtavāsanā*)—
[the author speaks] immediately after the three contemplations beginning with *sakala*.
(p. 232) He teaches in detail, through twenty verses beginning with "ātmanaḥ sphuraṇam," the *vāsanā* (underlying intention) of the central triangle as it pertains to the [deities] in union:
"When one perceives the radiance (*sphuraṇa*) of the Self, that is the supreme *kalā*."
Having assumed the form of Ambikā, the supreme speech was uttered.

Previously, in the verse beginning with "That which is the Supreme Power," the function named Śāntā, whose nature is contemplation (īkṣaṇa), was described as the cause of the universe; for by that [function],
the two-fold creation of words and meanings is produced, and therein, from the creation of meaning, arise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

The causes are these very [entities], which, being incapable of producing an effect without power (*śakti*), are conceived as being distinguished by power and are called Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. Their powers, however,
well-known as Bhāratī, Pṛthivī, and Rudrāṇī, are called Will (*icchā*), Knowledge (*jñāna*), and Action (*kriyā*).

The causes of the creation of sound are Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī; and the cause even of these causes is the Power of Vision (Īkṣaṇa). Therefore, just as there is a collective totality (samaṣṭi) of the triad consisting of Will and the others, there is likewise a collective totality of the triad consisting of Vāmā and the others within that Power of Vision.
Furthermore, the state of being the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the triad beginning with Paśyantī must indeed be stated,
because there is no essential difference between being a cause and being a collective totality;
for the banyan seed is precisely the subtle-form collective totality of the leaves, flowers, fruits, branches, and so forth.

Consequently, just as the term *śāntā* is applied to a single cognitive function (*vṛtti*) by taking its capacity to produce the triad of desires as the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), so too that very same function, by virtue of producing the triad beginning with Vāmā, comes to be denoted by the term *ambikā*.
Taking the state of being the generator of the triad beginning with Paśyantī as the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*),

she is also designated by the term *Parā*. Furthermore, the Goddess who is the substratum of such a function is also expressed by terms such as *Śāntā* and so forth, because she is the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) with respect to that function, and because of the non-difference between the transformation and that which undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma-pariṇāminor-abheda*).
The meaning is that he was brought [to the teacher]. Here, some maintain that the word *parama* means "one who has attained peace" (*śāntāpara*). 36.

When Vāmā, in order to manifest the universe residing in the state of the seed-syllable (bīja), becomes intent upon its emission, she assumes the form of a goad (aṅkuśa) by virtue of vomiting forth the universe. (37)
Then this very power of will (icchā-śakti) exists in the form of Paśyantī;

the state of being a seed (bīja-bhāva) is its nature as a seed, which, being delimited by that attribute, remains contained within its own womb as the "concentration on the seed" (bījāvadhāna), according to the Śiva Sūtra, whose essence is radiant manifestation (sphurattā).

When the Supreme Power (parāśakti)— of whom the Commentator has said that she is the seed and the cause of the universe— becomes intent on manifesting the form of the universe, establishing it as delimited by the state of being an effect,
and emitting it outward, such that she has emitted the universe; at that time, she herself...
The power (*śakti*) is called *Vāmā* because she performs the act of vomiting the universe, or because her form is curved like a hook (*aṅkuśa*). Indeed, during the state of the act of vomiting,
she assumes the shape of a hook due to the conjunction of the agent and the object of that action.

233) It so happens. Consequently, the meaning is that the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is either the status of being the producer of the desired creation for the goddess Vāmāpada, or a specific curvature (*vakratva*) pervaded by such a creation.
In reality, however, the mention of the shape of a goad (*aṅkuśa*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the left line of the triangle.
And thus, the intended meaning is that one should contemplate the left line (*vāmarekhā*) as having the form of the goddesses beginning with Vāmā.

In this way, since there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) to determine whether the capacity to produce emission (*sṛṣṭijanakatva*) or emission itself—related through the relation of being its producer—is the delimiting factor (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for the denotation, it is established that both are such factors; [therefore, regarding] emission...

The term *icchā* (will), which is a synonym for *brahman*— also known as *vāmā*— is applied by taking its causal ground (*pravṛttinimitta*) to be [the power of] manifestation. However, the term *icchā*, which is a synonym for *pitāmahī-śakti* (the power of the Grandfather) and *bhāratī*, is applied by taking its causal ground to be the capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting of the nature of being a generator (*janakatva*).
The meaning is that this applies even to the state of *paśyantī*, because it too generates the creation of sound. || 37 ||
Likewise, Jyeṣṭhā is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and she is declared to be the intermediate speech (madhyamā-vāk). || 38 ||
"Consisting of straight lines, her form is renowned for the maintenance of the universe.

The locative case here is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), as in the expression "he kills the tiger for its skin. Taking the maintenance (*sthiti*) of the manifested universe as the causal occasion, [the term] *jyeṣṭhā* is used as a synonym for Viṣṇu.
Taking as its cause the verbal manifestation of the term *jñānaśakti*— which is a synonym for *tacchaktipṛthivī* (the earth of that power)—

the term *madhyamā* functions as before. For, just as in the case of the two wheels [of a cart] whose action consists in the outward projection of the effect from the cause, [this process] proceeds until the point of withdrawal.

Remaining for some time is straight; therefore, the middle lines of the triangle, which are the commands of the eldest [goddess], should be meditated upon as consisting of straight lines. When stability is the cause, these forms, having attained the state of being denoted by words such as "knowledge" (jñāna) and so forth, become manifest.
The meaning is: she whose bodies are delimited by various respective attributes (dharmas). || 38 ||
But at the time of its withdrawal, she assumes a form consisting of the bindu.
By the very sequence of return, this Raudrī, who is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), is intensely radiant with the form of a triangle; she is Vaikharī, whose body is the universe.

That very Śakti, having emerged from the form consisting of the Bindu in the nature of emission (sṛṣṭi), and having remained for some time in the nature of maintenance (sthiti), when she turns back again, intent on assuming the form of the Bindu, then,
taking the state of the universal withdrawal (saṃhāra) as the occasion, there occurs the Raudrī activity as before.

Words such as *vaikharī* function within that [speech]. One should contemplate the right line as having turned back toward the source of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), by virtue of being the goddess signified by such words.
Thus, although she is but a single goddess, she becomes differentiated through the qualification of various attributes.

The meaning is that [the Śrīcakra] shines within the form of the triangle (trikoṇa), whose body consists of three lines in the shape of a *śṛṅgāṭa*. For just as letters such as *ka* and others are remembered through the lines used as linguistic conventions (*lipi-saṃketa*),
and their respective meanings are remembered through those [letters], so too [is the reality remembered] by means of the lines of the triangle.

The ultimate meaning is that one should worship after practicing firmly so as to bring about the recollection of the ritual acts such as creation and of the goddesses who are their performers. || 39 || 40 ||
Thus, for the triangle, there are three lines— the left, the front, and the right— and one point;
these four correspond respectively to Will, Knowledge, Action, and Peace, and to Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā.

The four deities— Paśyantī, Madhyamā, Vaikhārī, and Parā— are thus described as being subsumed by way of a single thread (tantra) within the three-fold mental impressions (vāsanā). Now, in this very same sequence,
he states other mental impressions individually:
Due to the latent impression (vāsanā) of the one who possesses all forms, these four powers exist both within one's own nature and externally; they are, in order: Kā, Pū, Jā, and O. (41)
The *pīṭhas* are situated respectively in the root (*kanda*), the foot (*pada*), the form (*rūpa*), and that which transcends form (*rūpātīta*).
Just as the creation consisting of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is, so too is that which consists of one's own body;
for even the cosmic egg is the body of a specific living being known as Virāṭ.
Therefore, the process for our own bodies and for that [divine] body is one and the same;

the difference consists solely in their smallness or greatness. For this very reason, it is well known from the *bhuvana-nyāsa* included within the *mahāṣoḍhā* that even our own body possesses the nature of the fourteen worlds.

And thus, because the entire universe is manifested through these very four powers as the objects of the three cosmic functions beginning with emission (sṛṣṭi), these alone exist both in external creation and in the creation of one's own nature. Among those, in external creation, [there is] Kāmarūpa.

Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, and Oḍyāna—these sacred seats (pīṭhas) are forms of the Goddess, existing on the banks of the Lauhitya River and other locations, as described in the Kālikā Purāṇa and other texts;
they are indeed well-known. Regarding the body, however, he says: "the bulb" (kanda). The bulb is the root of the Suṣumṇā; by that...

The *mūlādhāra* is indicated; by the word "haṃsa" [the *mūlādhāra* is meant], therefore the heart; by "rūpa" [meaning *bindu*], therefore the space between the eyebrows; by "rūpātīta" [meaning the partless (*niṣkala*)], therefore the *brahmarandhra*. This has been stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"The *kanda* is the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti; the *pada* is proclaimed to be the Haṃsa;
the *rūpa* is known as the Bindu; and that which transcends form (*rūpātīta*) is the partless (*niṣkala*).
This means that in those respective locations, there are the four seats (*pīṭhas*), beginning with Kāmarūpa. Kā [refers to] Pūrṇagiri.

In the word *jāo*, each syllable is a partial name of each respective sacred seat (*pīṭha*); there is no euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) for the sake of making that [name] clearly known. Regarding the word *śaktayaḥ*, there is the elision of the medial vowel *ā*;
this is because of the technical rule (paribhāṣā) which states that when there is a conflict between prosody and grammar, prosody is more authoritative.

This has been described by us in the *Chandaḥkaustubha* as being indicated by Pāṇini in the sūtra "so'ci lope cet" and by Piṅgala in the sūtra "iyādipūraṇe" (p. 235). [In the case of the word *kṛti*], since it is formed with the suffix *ktic* in the sense of an agent (*kartari*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* should be applied according to the rule "kṛdikārād... (Pāṇini 4.1.45). || 41 ||
Suggesting that these very seats (pīṭhas) are, in sequence, the forms of the mandalas of earth, air, water, and fire, he says:
"The square, as well as the circle joined with six dots. (42)
Their forms are, respectively, a half-moon and a triangle;
their colors are proclaimed to be yellow, smoky-grey, white, and red. (43)
The element earth (bhūtatva) is square, yellow in color, capable of assuming forms at will (kāmarūpa), and identical with the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Kāmarūpa;

the element air (vāyutattva) is circular, marked on all sides by six dots, smoke-colored, and non-different from the sacred seat of Pūrṇagiri; the element water (jalatattva) is semicircular in shape and white.
It consists of the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara; the meaning is that it is the triangular fire-principle (agnitattva), red in color, and has the form of the sacred seat of Oḍyāna. || 42 || 43 ||

Now he describes the liṅgas situated on those various seats along with their specific attributes: "O fair-faced one, these liṅgas—the self-manifested (svayaṃbhu), the Bāṇaliṅga, and the other supreme one—are established upon these seats. (44)
Resembling gold, bandhūka flowers, and the autumnal moon,
it is Trikūṭa surrounded by its own radiance, a great self-manifested liṅga.
The Bāṇaliṅga is surrounded by the letters from *ka* to *da*, is triangular in shape,
has the form of a *kadamba* bud, and is surrounded by the letters from *tha* to *sa*.
It is of subtle form, encompassed by all the letters, the supreme liṅga;
it is the form of the bindu, the root of supreme bliss, arisen from the eternal state. || 47 ||

Here, by the term *liṅgāni*, according to the etymology "that which makes known a hidden meaning," the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and thought (*citta*) are denoted because they are the substrata for the manifestation of consciousness (*cit-sphuraṇa*).
These four *liṅgas* are located at the tip, the right corner, and the left corner of the triangle, as well as in its center.

The elders say that these [syllables] are to be meditated upon (*bhāvanīya*). "Golden-colored" means yellow; "bandhujīva-flower-colored" means red. "Enveloped by vowels" means endowed with the sixteen vowels. "Three-peaked" (*trikūṭa*) means possessing three summits;
others say it means having peaks consisting of the three *bindus*. The rest is clear. Thus...
Having described the nature of the three *liṅgas*, he states the nature of the supreme *liṅga*: "Subtle," etc.

It is of a subtle form, consisting of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the aforementioned three *liṅgas*; it is of the nature of the *bindu* (the point), consisting of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the *baindava-cakra*; it is the root of supreme bliss (*parānanda-kanda*), belonging to the supreme *mātṛkā*.

The ancients [state] that it is the essence, expressed by the word, ending with the word, and arisen from the mind of one seeking liberation (mumukṣu); however, in reality, even for the supreme *liṅga* which stands in the place of that which transcends form (*rūpātīta*),
in order to indicate its nature as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of Svayambhū and the others, [it is placed] upon the common substrates of those respective *liṅgas*.

It should be explained that the three qualifiers—*bindu-rūpa*, etc.—are intended to state that even within the *kanda*, *pada*, and *bindu*, there exists an arising that is otherwise unattainable. || 44 || 45 || 46 || 47 ||
Furthermore, for the entire mantra endowed with the three seed-syllables,
these forms of the expressed meaning consist of the Kula and Kaula principles.
These states known as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turya)—

these four are the forms of the "signs" (liṅgas) that constitute the objects denoted by the thirteen-syllable mantra of the Sakala type, which is joined with the three seed-syllables and the three peak-syllables (kūṭas). This applies either to the [thirteen-syllable] mantra or to the Turya-mantra.

The ancients maintain that because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, [the mantras] are non-distinct from them; however, in reality, it is more appropriate to state that by the word "sakala" (with all parts), the fifteen-syllable mantra itself is intended. This is because, in the *Pūrvatantra*, after describing the individual means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for each seed-syllable (*bīja*), the text proceeds to describe the means of accomplishment for the complete mantra.
Furthermore, because this very [text] is what is being grasped in the treatise; because the fourth vidyā has not been extracted and thus is not the subject under discussion;

and because of the natural force of the qualification "endowed with the triad of seed-syllables" (bījatritayayuktasya). Therefore, while there are three individual impressions (vāsanās) for each of the separate means, for the practitioner of the fifteenth [verse], they exist as the collective totality of the triad.

The fourth is the "vāsanā" (latent impression); this is what should be meditated upon. *Kula* means a collection of similar things; Amara states: "A *kula* or *yūtha* is a group consisting of similar members. Similarity (*sājātya*) here consists in being objects of a single cognition. Thus, the meaning is: the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*meyāni*). *Kaula* is their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*). Those things which consist of that are non-different from it.
Thus are the forms of the states such as waking and so forth. However, the definitions of these states are to be found in the Śivasūtras and other such works. || 48 ||
Having thus described the latent impression (vāsanā) of the complete wheel, he speaks of the latent impression of the Goddess presiding over it:
"But the supreme light of the past consists of the arising of one's own self-consciousness. (49)
The universal form, inlaid with the delineations of the universe according to its own will, is the nature of the Self—consciousness, beautiful with innate bliss. (50)

That *bindu* stands having transcended the past; it is the supreme splendor (*paraṃ tejaḥ*), the illuminator even of luminaries such as the sun and others ending with the mind, for the Śruti says, "the light of lights" (*jyotiṣāṃ jyotiḥ*). It is self-awareness, a cognition whose object is itself and nothing else.
It is of the nature of arising, having the single form of emergence, and is devoid of the six modifications of being (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*).

By its own will—meaning merely through the act of glancing, without depending on any other collection of causal factors—it is "inlaid" with a variegated painting consisting of the universe, that is, the world-nature. As it has been said by the learned:
"Obeisance to that wielder of the trident, who is praiseworthy for his artistic skill, who weaves the variegated picture of the world upon a wall-less surface without any material substrate. Thus,
the nature of the Self is consciousness, which possesses the universal form and is the essence of all.

In the *Śivasūtra*, it is well known that the nature of the Self is consciousness (*caitanya*). This is the bliss of spontaneity (*nisargānanda*), the innate bliss, and not that which arises from contact with sense objects. Therefore, it is beautiful and delightful.
With its radiance contracting through the expansions of the object, the subject, the means of knowledge,
and the act of knowing, it assumes the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭa), consisting of will, knowledge, and action.

Because it has been expended through its transformation into the fourfold nature of *māyā* and the rest, its light is slightly contracted. Thus says the Śruti: "One quarter of Him consists of all beings; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven. A *śṛṅgāṭa* is a triangle consisting of three lines.

And that is the assembly of deities. By this very [term], "will, knowledge, and action" (icchājñānakriyā), the *bindu*—which is their collective totality—is expressed, because it is attained through this alone. Thus, it is stated that all those four groups beginning with Vāmā which were previously mentioned are indeed the forms of this [Bindu] itself. || 51 ||
He rests upon Śiva, whose own form is the substratum for the manifestation of all forms;
he is exceedingly beautiful, seated upon the lap of Kāmeśvara as his couch.

That which has as its substratum Śiva— who is identical with that very form which delimits His state of transformation (pariṇāmitā), namely His own inherent transformative material cause (pariṇāmy-upādāna) which is the locus of the manifestation of the Universal Self— that [power] belongs specifically to the Power qualified by Śiva.

The sense is that because Śiva is the cause of the universe, he possesses the status of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of causality. That very Śiva, existing within the *kāmakalā*, is the *bindu* known as Kāma; by means of this illumination, there arises the discernment of the nature of Śakti as being dependent upon Him. Therefore, [the text] repeats that very point.

He states this with another word: "kāma" (desire). Even the description of the lap as a "paryaṅka" (couch) suggests, by way of indicating it as the support for the bed of bliss (*ānanda*), a particular kind of constraint (*yantraṇa*) of the god of love (*kāma*). For this very reason, it is said to be "extremely beautiful."
The secret. || 52 ||
He bears the noose consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti) and the goad in the form of knowledge (jñāna-rūpin),
while holding the radiant bow and arrow composed of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
Since desire alone, being synonymous with thirst, passion, and so forth, serves as the means for bondage, it possesses the nature of a fetter. As it has been said by the learned:
"Hope is a certain kind of wondrous chain for human beings."
"Bound by it, they run about; released, they stand still like the lame. (p.

238) Knowledge is a goad because it restrains the mind from its objects, and that restraint is not possible without detachment (*vairāgya*) from objects. And that [detachment] is indeed aversion (*dveṣa*). Detachment is aversion toward objects.
Because of this statement, that which was said at the end of the previous chapter— namely,
"His noose and goad are traditionally held to consist of passion and hatred;
sound, touch, and the other [objects] are his arrows, and the mind became his bow"— [is thus explained].

What has been stated is not contradictory; for there is no conflict between the latent impressions (vāsanā) mentioned previously and those mentioned subsequently, because the act of joining the arrow to the bow and the act consisting of the mental engagement with objects such as sound are of one and the same nature. || 53 ||
Possessing causes divided into eight types according to the distinction between substratum and that which rests upon it,
he is established upon an eight-spoked wheel and seated on a throne of nine wheels.

The support is Kāmeśvara; it is implied that his worship is not performed separately, but rather through the merging of his weapons with those of the Goddess. This is because Tripurasundarī alone is indicated by way of the specific attributes of Kāmeśvara’s weapons. It is she alone who...

Because it is described as having the nature of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic aesthetic), according to that principle, he is firmly established in the eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭāracakra*); however, by way of his form transcending the *binducakra*, he is seated upon the throne consisting of the nine wheels (*navacakrī*). || 54 ||
Thus, concluding the description of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the Goddess as the complete wheel, he teaches the latent impression of the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*):
"Such is the supreme radiance abiding in the form of the Śrīcakra."
It was completely enveloped by surging waves flashing from the mass of his powers.
In the manner thus described, supreme splendor itself became the body of the wheel (*cakra*).
Precisely because it vibrates through waves consisting of a multitude of its own powers (*śakti*)— the powers associated with the wheel, such as *aṇimā* and the rest— therefore...
"One should meditate on [the deity] surrounded by those who are non-different from Kāmeśvarī and Sarasvatī"— this is the ellipsis to be supplied. In this regard,

although various types of *vāsanās* (spiritual dispositions) are found in numerous texts such as the *Vāsanāsubhagodaya*, other Tantras like the *Tantrarāja*, and the Upaniṣads, even though all of them...

Although the explanation of the earlier commentators [is presented] in this manner, we have disregarded it because, according to the principle of the section on "the uniformity of all Vedānta teachings" (*sarvavedāntapratyayādhikaraṇanyāya*), there is no difference in the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*); thus, their exposition results solely in prolixity of the text. || 55 ||
Now, desiring to teach the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the ten mudrās to be worshipped according to their specific divisions within each enclosure (*pratyāvaraṇa*), he explains the term *mudrā*:
"When there is the illumination and the grasping of the universe upon the wall of consciousness... (p. 239)
She acts according to her own will, endowed with the desire to manifest her full creative power. || 56 ||
The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), however, arises from the gladdening and melting of the universe;

for when the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), desiring full transformations by its own will upon the previously mentioned wall— the substratum which is non-different from its own self— immediately after [the act of] gazing, [acts].
It effects the manifestation and awareness of the delineation of the universe. And so it is stated in the *Śaktisūtra*:
"By its own will, it unfolds the universe upon its own screen.
Here, the term "by its own will" (*svecchayā*) is explained in its commentary as referring to independence from material causes and the like.

This [power] culminates in that very act of mere glancing. At that time, having become that same power of action (*kriyāśakti*), it becomes known as *mudrā*, being characterized by the two attributes of gladdening and liquefying the universe;
this is the syntactic connection achieved by drawing down the two terms situated in the second half of the verse. This is the intended meaning:

For six modifications of existence (*bhāvavikāra*) have been enumerated for the universe by Yāska and others: "it exists, it is born, it grows, it transforms, it declines, it perishes. Among these, the first modification of existence, which consists of being (*sattā*), is eternal for the universe, because the universe exists even at the time of dissolution in the form of a seed.

Thereafter, five further transformations (vikāras) are intended [to be described]. Among them, the second transformation is the nature of *sattva* (purity), which is called "illumination" (*prakāśa*). Its definition is "the making manifest of that which was unmanifest. The third transformation is indeed "reflection" (*amarśana*), which consists in the state of becoming accessible to the heart by way of the notion "this."

Thus, since the definition stated by the elders results in a complete and part-by-part ascertainment of the specific property that delimits the object of a cognition in the form "this is such-and-such" regarding its causal factors, it is entirely consistent only when there is an increase in the family lineage. And so:

Following Tripurasundarī’s contemplation of the existence of the creation residing within her own self, there arises in her a desire concerning the second and subsequent modifications of the universe; this is precisely what is meant by *vicikīrṣā* (the desire to create). Nor does the application of the suffix *san* fail to occur because the desire for modification and the agent of that desire would have different subjects.

This is because the root *kṛ* (to do/make), when preceded by the prefix *sam*, has an internalized causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) relative to its original nature; or else, because the identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is also established in accordance with the doctrine that the transformation is that of [Śiva] himself as the Universal Self (*viśvātman*).
Therefore, he sequentially effects the origination and growth of the universe. These two are precisely manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*amarśana*).

Thereafter, it rejoices and causes the universe to dissolve. "Rejoicing" (anumodana) means favoring an action being performed by oneself or another; "dissolving" (drāvaṇa) means the expansion of a dense, contracted state through the loosening of its constituent parts. This is the process for the universe that has become one with the single essence.

It is appropriate that even the definition stated by the elders— that "melting" (*drāvaṇa*) consists of the unification (*aikarasya*) of those thirty-six constituent elements— should ultimately culminate in this very [state].
Thus:

Thus, it is Tripurasundarī herself—characterized by these two attributes consisting of the softening of the rice and being non-different from the aforementioned power of action—that is denoted by the term *mudrā*. || 56 ||
(p. 240) Now, regarding the mudrās, although the *Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* comes first because it is to be shown in the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*), nevertheless,
with the intention of [its] all-pervasiveness and so forth, it is the *Trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* itself that [is discussed] in the third chapter.
Desiring to teach the *vāsanā* (contemplative realization) according to the previously described sequence, he first states the *vāsanā* of the *Trikhaṇḍā*:
"When that consciousness called Mudrā consists of the three *kalās*, it is Ambikā. (57)
Then, having assumed a three-part form, she is proclaimed to be the presiding presence and the pervader of the entire King of Wheels (cakrarāja). || 58 ||

When Ambikā— the Mother who is consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the nature of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), non-different from such a power of action— becomes composed of three parts (*trikalāmayī*), meaning she becomes abundant with the three parts (*kalātrayapracurā*) or, in other words, becomes distinguished by the act of vision (*īkṣaṇa*),
then she assumes the form of the "Three Parts" (*trikhaṇḍā*). This is precisely the common attribute of being a *mudrā*.

The meaning is that, through the conjunction of even the act of gazing by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the Goddess, characterized by such attributes, is called Trikhaṇḍā. "Proximity" (*saṃnidhi*) refers to the presence of the deity’s splendor, precisely because she is the Great Goddess whose rays of power constitute all the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*). This is due to her being employed in the invocation.

She pervades all the wheels (*cakras*). Here, because the glance (*īkṣaṇa*) is the unified totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the triad beginning with *Vāmā*, those fingers on the right hand are the aspect of illumination (*prakāśāṃśa*).
Because [the glance] is the unified totality of the triad beginning with *Icchā*, those fingers on the left hand are the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśāṃśa*).

They say that the *vāsanā* is thus suggested: that by joining those [fingers] together in one place, the initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes the form of the unification of such a pair of triads. However, in reality, there is a distinction in the arrangement of the fingers according to the different tantras.
Because perception is frequent, because it is impossible for a perceived universal to pervade all things, and because even when it does occasionally occur,
it has not been mentioned by the author of the root text and is therefore irrelevant, the arrangement of fingers is merely a remote auxiliary cause.
While performing [the ritual], one should recollect the *vāsanā* (inner disposition) stated by the root-text; this is the essential truth.
It should be understood that other [details] are intended solely for the sake of inspiring confidence in those of dull intellect. || 57 || 58 ||
He states the latent impression (vāsanā) of the *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā:
"Furthermore, because of the abundance of the *yoni*, this very [mudrā] is the *sarvasaṃkṣobhikā*;
it is dominated by the power of Vāmā and resides in the wheel of the gateway. (59)

This very power of Ambikā, which is non-different from the power of action (kriyā-śakti), when perceived through the predominance of the womb (yoni) as possessing a multiplicity of limiting attributes (avacchedaka-dharma) that define causality with respect to effects delimited by various specific properties residing in abundant objects, then becomes the "Agitator of All" (sarvasaṃkṣobhikā).

This means "belonging to all people. For this very reason, when she is perceived as being primarily the power of *vāmā*, she becomes the "all-agitating" (*sarvasaṃkṣobhikā*), because *vāmā* possesses the conceit of creation.
[This occurs] in each individual thumb.
The meaning is that by joining the tips of the little finger, middle finger, and ring finger on each hand, there are three *yoni*s;
thus, one should remember that the abundance of causal factors consists of these six *yoni*s.
This is because the union of the two middle fingers, the two ring fingers, and the two little fingers constitutes precisely those three *yoni*s.
The statement of the Easterners (Prācāṃ) is to be disregarded because it contradicts the extraction of the mudrās as previously stated in the *Caturśakti*.

He states the meditative absorption (vāsana) for the mudrā that causes all things to dissolve: "She who brings stability to the agitated universe, who abides in the abundance of Jyeṣṭhā, whose form consists of gross sound and kalā, and who bestows grace upon all. (60)

In the [mandala] called Sarvāśāpūraka, she is this very one whose form is vibrating; she is the sustainer of the universe that has arisen from agitation. For this very reason, she abides in the abundance of Jyeṣṭhā, who possesses the conceit of maintenance (sthiti). This is because of the straightness of her four fingers.

Because the triangle is the state of the straight eastern line; the subtle form of sound is *nāda*, while its gross form is the syllable (*akṣara*). Therefore, within the gross *nāda*, there are the vowels beginning with *a*, which are sixteen in number, corresponding to the count of the *kalās*.

This means she consists of the sixteen syllables beginning with *a*. By the phrase "she is this very one" (*saiṣā*), it is stated that she possesses the general attributes that constitute the body of the Mudrā.
Through the conjunction of such particular and general attributes, she is said to be the bestower of grace upon all.
Grace, it is said, is the act of dispersing [the enemy]. || 60 ||
He states the seat of the mudrā that attracts all:
"By the equality of the Jyeṣṭhā and Vāmā [energies], she relies upon the primacy of emanation. (61)
This mudrā is the Attractress (Ākarṣiṇī), known as the All-Agitating (Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī).

Both properties included within the range of the delimitor of the denotability of the term "mudrā of agitation and causing flight" are also included within the range of the delimitor of the denotability of the term "all-attracting mudrā."

[This is] the inclusion. However, there is no equal primacy between the two, nor is there an absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*) regarding their relationship as qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*).
Rather, it is precisely "the state of possessing a left [hand] qualified by being the eldest" that must be included. Therefore, since creation (*sṛṣṭi*) functions as the qualified [subject],...
Because it is established as the mark of the vulva (*dvāma*), its curvature of four finger-breadths is appropriately displayed at the very top.
This well-known *mudrā*, known as Ākarṣiṇī, is traditionally held to reside in the wheel called Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, which is named for its power to agitate all things. (61)
He describes the seat of the mudrā that effects universal penetration:
"O Maheśvarī, she is in the form of the bindu situated in the space between the two voids. (62)
Through the intimate union of the self with Śiva and Śakti, she is remembered as the bestower of divine possession;
she resides in the fourteen-spoked wheel, her form being consciousness and bliss. (63)

As it is well-known in the Śruti: "As vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart," there exists the Mudrā, which consists of both Śiva and Śakti in a state of deep mutual embrace, manifesting in the form of a *bindu*. Therefore... [p. 242]

Thus, consciousness (saṃvit), whose very form is bliss, is said to be that which brings about divine possession (divyāveśa). However, the ancient teachers say that its meaning is that it has the form of the five voids (vyoma) situated within the six cakras, wherein there is one bindu between each pair of them. || 62 || 63 ||
He states the latent impression (vāsanā) of the seal that intoxicates all:
"Consisting of a crest of subtle form shimmering within the Bindu, and dominated by the power Jyeṣṭhā, she is the one who brings about universal intoxication. (64)
O you who are worshipped by heroes, she stands established upon the ten-spoked wheel;

shining in the midst of the aforementioned point, she is of subtle form. That flame in her center is well-known in the sacred scriptures as being "as slender as the awn of a grain of wild rice" (*nīvāra-śūka*); she is composed of that very essence.

Jyeṣṭhā is characterized by the predominance of Śakti; for this very reason, she is the Goddess herself, marked by the two straight fingers—the ring finger and the index finger—and resides in the outer ten-spoked wheel as the Sarvonmādana Mudrā. 64.
If this very [power] is dominated by the Vāmā-śakti and is characterized by curved fingers with the index fingers raised, she is called Mahāṅkuśā;
having intended that this is the distinction between these two, he says:
Furthermore, she who consists of the great goad is preeminent with the power of Vāmā.
In the same way, emitting the universe, she resides in the second decade,
intent on delighting and having assumed the form of a mudrā.
Consisting of a crest of subtle form shining within the cavity between the two Bindus,

the phrase "intent on delighting" here is a reiterative reference by way of exclusion (*avayuti-anuvāda*) to the general property that serves as the basis for the application of the term *mudrā*, [expressed] through its coordination with specific properties.
This is for the purpose of reminding one that [the object] enters into the scope of the delimitor of denotability (*vācyatāvacchedaka*). The rest is easy to understand.

Here, the half-verse beginning with "in the space between the points" (*bindvantarāle*) is not seen in some manuscripts. The ancient authorities, however, [state that the two points] are situated in the middle of the pericarp-lotuses located at the *mūlādhāra* and the *brahmarandhra*.
They say that there are two *bindus*, in the form of the *svayambhū-liṅga* and the *para-liṅga*.
Shining within them are the two crests (*śikhā*) in the form of Ambikā and Śāntā, which are indeed the *amṛtakuṇḍalinīs*;
the meaning is that they are identical with those. || 65 || 66 ||
He states the foundational state of Khecarīmudrā:
"Arisen from the friction of dharma and adharma, it has the form of consciousness. (67)
The supreme Khecarī destroys the defect consisting of the omission of actions arising from conceptual construction; she removes the diseases whose nature is conceptual construction. (68)
In the wheel known as Sarvarogahara, she resides as the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvit*).
Dharma and adharma are the actions that produce merit and demerit; the combination of these two is dharma-adharma, and their friction is *saṃghaṭṭa*.
It is the state of being a qualifier (prakāritā) as determined by a subjecthood (viśeṣyatā) delimited by a single property within a single cognition.

This means it arises from such a doubt as "Is this property dharma or adharma? It is "arisen" (utthitā), meaning it has come into existence following such a doubt, and is of the nature of consciousness (vitti-rūpiṇī).
It consists of a valid cognition (*pramā*) characterized by the perception of a specific feature,

taking the form "this possesses that which is prescribed as being pervaded by the property of *dharma-ness*," or it takes the form of a certainty (*niścaya*) in the form "this is indeed *dharma*. And that [cognition]...
It is produced by the study of the *Tantra* characterized by the compassion of the Guru. "Conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) is knowledge whose object is unreal;
for the *Yoga Sūtra* states: "Conceptual construction is that which follows mere words and is devoid of a real entity.
In the aforementioned doubt, this refers to the "unrighteous alternative" (*adharmakoṭi*). [This is because it arises from] meditation qualified as being unrighteous.

Because it is like a flower in the sky (*kha-puṣpa*). That which arises from it—that is, produced by it—is the omission of ritual action, consisting of performing it otherwise through lack of faith prompted by conceptual construction and through negligence.
By that [omission], those defects—which are evil unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) producing suffering in the next world—are manifested and generated; of these...

It is the destroyer of obstacles, the remover of mental and physical ailments (ādhi-vyādhi) that produce worldly suffering born of conceptual construction; it brings about the destruction of all those sins and diseases produced by even a fraction of a portion of unrighteousness within such doubt— [that wisdom] which consists in the perception of the particular.

The meaning is that valid cognition (*pramā*), which is non-different from that [consciousness], consisting of pure awareness (*saṃvinmayī*), and non-different from the power of action (*parākriyā-śakti*)—which is knowledge devoid of objects—is Tripurasundarī herself who, having become the Khecarīmudrā, abides in the wheel that removes all diseases.
As for the ancients: "Dharma is Śakti because it resides in Śiva; adharma..."

He is Śiva because he is devoid of all objective phenomena (*nirdharmaka*). Their union is *sāmarasya* (equilibrium). Conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is doubt; the actions arising from it take the form of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites. They say that [this practice] destroys the sin incurred by the omission of those rites. Therefore—

The meaning is that one should practice and display the *mudrā* in such a way that it— acting as a reminder of the aforementioned doubt through the union of Śiva and Śakti in the form of the movement and contact of the two arms, and aided by the joining of the fingers— reminds one of the stated matter in its entirety. || 67 || 68 ||
He speaks of the seed-syllable (bīja), the mudrā, and the latent impression (vāsanā):
"Furthermore, within the throbbing space [of consciousness] arising from the close embrace of Śiva and Śakti... (69).
Constantly manifesting the universe while remaining in a subtle form,
she is the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) in the form of the seed-syllable, abiding within that which consists of all accomplishments.
(p. 244) Even within the seed of a banyan tree, there is indeed some space, because of its all-pervasive nature (*vibhutva*).

It is the established principle that the entire tree exists in a subtle state within that most minute space. With the intention of conforming to that illustration, [the text speaks] of the seed of the world (*jagadbīja*).

It has been stated that [the universe] exists within the space (*vyoman*) flashing forth inside the pair of Śiva and Śakti, who possess a mutual, inseparable embrace. In reality, since even space is included within creation and its production is absent during the state of the seed (*bīja*), what is intended is precisely that it is "in the womb" (*garbha*) of Śiva and Śakti.

The meaning is that the Goddess herself is called the *bījamudrā* because of her specific identification with that primordial modification of existence (*bhāvavikāra*), which consists of the being (*sattā*) of the universe.
He now states the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the *yonimudrā*:
Furthermore, this Yonimudrā, which takes the form of a digit (kalā) and abides in the state of universal bliss, is the ground for attaining complete illumination.

This Yonimudrā is of that very nature which was shown as being denoted by the term *kalā* on the occasion of describing the essential form of the *Kāmakalā*. For this reason, it is the ground for attaining—that is, the cause of reaching—Paraśiva, who is the complete Light. And for this very reason, [it resides] within the *Sarvānandamayacakra*.
She remains established. || 71 ||
He states the reason for this very Yonidevatā being in the form of a mudrā:

"Because it consists of the consciousness of action (kriyā-caitanya), the wise man should always contemplate the supreme light (tejas) as being thus composed of the cakra and having the nature of will (icchā). (72)

The meaning is that the aforementioned power of action (*kriyāśakti*), characterized by exhilaration and liquefaction, is of the nature of consciousness; and when it exists as such, its very state of being a *kalā* is what is designated by the term "Yoni-mudrā. This refers to the general category of "mudrā-ness."

The sense is that [it is so] because all mudrās are established within the body. Here, this should be understood: what is called *vāsanā* (latent impression) is a subtle alternative form, such as aversion or knowledge in the case of a hook;
and the meaning is that its alternative form is precisely of such a nature.
Since worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not apply here, this must be accepted as being based solely on the authority of extraordinary scriptural words (*ārsa-vacana*).

However, when both such types of authoritative evidence are perceived, since there is no difference in the validity of either, both are indeed merely latent impressions (*vāsanā*). As for what has been stated by the elders in various places regarding the two types of gross-form latent impressions:
A common property is cited as a reason (*hetu*), such as the capacity of a goad to ward off an elephant made of mind when it is considered to be of the nature of knowledge.

That too is merely a poetic conceit of a reason (*hetūtprekṣāmātra*), devoid of any literal intent according to the logic of the locus of a reason (*hetvadhikaraṇanyāya*), and is not actually real. This being the case:
When he sips water three times, he thereby grasps the triad of "is," "shines," and "is dear";
when he wipes his face twice, he thereby abandons name and form.
In this manner, regarding all the daily rites (*āhnika-karma*) prescribed in the *Smṛtis*,
the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) being composed by poets through their own creative imagination in works such as the *Līlāviśvaṃbhara* and the *Bodhasāra*;
Just as other poetic figures, though they produce aesthetic charm by being mere metaphors of essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*),
are not useful for actual practice, so too in this context, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— though written down by the ancients— are neither seen in the original root text nor in other tantras.
One should not be deluded by a dullness of faith, thinking that [these states] were neglected by us for a long time.

Now, with the word "thus" (*evam*), he concludes the discourse on the *cakravāsanā* which began with the phrase "that supreme power" (*sā paramā śaktiḥ*). It is solely by the will of the Goddess, the supreme light, [that this occurs].

The meaning is that because this entire wheel has arisen [from her], the Goddess herself, distinguished by her will, is the form of all wheels; therefore, the wise one should always contemplate her as being neither asleep nor subject to death. || 72 ||

In the previous *Caturśatikā*, it was stated that the threefold wheel— consisting of the "entire" (*sakala*), the "external," and so forth— is to be worshipped in successive order for one who is unable to perform each preceding stage. This threefold division is intended to suggest that this [threefold nature] applies equally even to the worshipper, including their latent impressions (*savāsana*).
In connection with that, he also teaches its ninefold nature:

"Furthermore, the convention of the *cakras* is threefold and indeed ninefold," according to the manner of the statement found in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "The point (*bindu*) is joined within the triangle."
The entire wheel is included within the wheel of the mantra-source (manvasra) and so forth, which is designated by the term "situated between the outer and the middle.

Furthermore, because that which is situated between the outer and the middle is not distinct from the ninefold womb (*yoninavaka*) consisting of power (*śakti*) and fire (*anala*), it is a wheel whose nature is the ninefold womb.
This is the inclusion [of the others].
Keeping such a meaning in mind, in order to eliminate doubt, he describes the threefold nature twice, both concisely and in detail:
One [is formed] with one fire and two powers, and another supreme one again with two fires and two powers. || 73 ||
By means of those three fires, the triad of powers,
the two lotuses, and the triple enclosure of the earth, another [mandala] is formed.
"Five powers, four fires, two lotuses, and three earths—thus is the complete Great Wheel; its method is now demonstrated. (75)
Among those, the first should be known as the ninefold womb (navayoni), joined with the twelve;
one should know the supreme human womb (manuyoni) as the third immediately following that.
O Supreme Goddess, it has been described that the wheel possesses three types: endowed with eight, two, and eight petals, and provided with three squares. (77)

p. 246) Fire is one, and there are two powers; thus, it is one. Another, however, consists of nine by combining these three with another six. Yet another is formed by combining these nine with the two lotuses and the three earths. The explanation of this very [point] is "the five powers. By means of that which has nine wombs (yoni),...
It is joined with two [circles] having twelve spokes, and the second is the human birth (*manuyoni*). The rest is easy to understand.
As for the conjunction with the *bindu*, since it was not specifically mentioned, it applies to all three wheels without distinction. || 73 || 74 || 75 || 76 || 77 ||
In this wheel, having first worshipped the principal deity in the central *bindu*, there are two sequences regarding the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) who are to be worshipped.

Among these, the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) consists in the worship beginning from the nine triangles and ending with the earth-house (*bhūgṛha*). It is by this very sequence that emanation occurs.
Because it has been so described, the order of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama) is its reverse. To demonstrate that both types of worship are appropriate, he establishes the two-fold sequence:
"The emanation (sṛṣṭi) should proceed from the nine-yoni [triangle] up to the earth; the withdrawal (saṃhṛti), however, [proceeds in the opposite direction]."
"From Earth up to the nine sources (yoni)—this is the certainty of the scripture. (78)
This collective form is called the Tripurā-cakra;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes possessed of the wisdom of Tripurā. (79)
Now, having reached its turn in the sequence, he teaches the ninefold nature and the names of that [lotus]:
"O my beloved, I shall tell you of the ninefold state of the wheel:
the first consists of three earths, and the second has sixteen petals. (80)
Next, the eight-petalled [lotus] is proclaimed;
immediately after that, the fifth is the ten-cornered [figure], and the sixth is also the ten-spoked [wheel]. (81)
The seventh should be a lotus with seven petals, and the eighth a triangle in the center;
the ninth should have a triangle in its middle—now hear their names from me.
The wheel that deludes the three worlds, which fulfills all hopes, O Goddess, which causes universal agitation, and bestows all good fortune. || 83 ||
O Gaurī, this wheel accomplishes all aims, likewise provides all protection, removes all diseases, and is composed of all supernatural attainments. || 84 ||
And now hear, O beautiful one, of the ninth [cakra], which consists of all-bliss;
here the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī is to be worshipped. 85.
p. 247) The complete Great Wheel brings about freedom from old age and death.

Here, names such as Trailokyamohana and others are *yogarūḍha* (based on both etymological derivation and conventional usage); they are to be meditated upon as being qualified by such meanings, and it is for the purpose of making this clear [that they are mentioned].
These have been stated for the purpose of being utilized in the nyāsa (ritual placement) that will be described hereafter. This has been explained by the very words [of the text]. || 80 || 81 ||
He concludes the convention of the wheels:
"Thus, O Supreme Goddess, is this great convention of the wheels. (86)
Thus has been narrated by the Goddess Tripurā that which promotes liberation while living.
This is the sixth chapter of the venerable *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*.
Even though the meaning was narrated by herself, it is [considered] as having been told by her with the intention of non-difference between herself and the Goddess Tripurā.

It has been stated that "it was told. Or, [the word] "Tripurādevyāḥ" may be taken as a genitive. The fruit of knowing this convention is liberation while living (jīvanmukti). All is auspicious. || 86 ||
Thus, in the commentary titled Setubandha on the ocean of the Nityāṣoḍaśikā composed by the illustrious Bhāskara, the sixth rest-period (viśrāma) has been declared. 6.
Now begins the seventh rest.
Having thus taught the convention of the wheels (cakrasaṃketa) with eighty-six meaningful verses,
and desiring to teach the convention of the mantras (mantrasaṃketa) which follows in due order, [the author] makes a formal promise to ensure the student's attention:
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now I shall tell you the divine secret convention of the mantra,
by knowing which one becomes the Lord of the Circle of Heroes (vīracakreśvara), whose form is Tripurā.

The suffix *ka* in the word *saṃketaka* denotes something unknown; thus, I shall tell you your own secret mantra-convention (*mantra-saṃketa*), which until now has been unknown to anyone. The heroes (*vīra*) are the practitioners (*upāsaka*), and they are of three kinds, distinguished as the Sakala and so forth.

Among them, the pure ones are the most excellent; for this very reason, they are the lords of the host of heroes (*vīrasamūha*). Such a state arises through the knowledge of the secret conventions (*saṃketa*) of mantra. And for this very reason, he possesses the form of Tripurā and attains liberation that is non-different from the essence of Tripurā. This is an indicative illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes *sāyujya* and other forms of liberation as well. 1. p. 248)
The single mantra itself has become ninefold due to the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the forms of the Nine Goddesses of the Wheels (Navacakreśvarīs).
Those mantras were extracted in the very first chapter; he points them out here by name alone:
"The first is Karaśuddhikarī, and the second is Ātmarakṣikā."
Immediately after that, the third goddess is seated upon her own throne. || 2 ||
Then she is seated upon the wheel-throne, thereafter established upon the throne of all mantras;
the sixth is the one who dwells upon the thrones of the seeker and the perfected, the supreme embodiment of Māyā and Lakṣmī.
And that Mūrtividyā, O Goddess, is proclaimed as the seventh;
the eighth is the Āvāhanī Vidyā, and the ninth is the supreme Bhairavī.
The root-vidyā is likewise described as that which brings the three worlds under control.

Among these, the seventh vidyā, named Mūrti, has not been extracted there. We have already explained the reason for the non-extraction of this one alone in the section on invocation (āvāhana) in that very same work.
He extracts that [mantra] here: "Māyā," etc. Māyā is *hṛllekhā*. Lakṣmī is the seed-syllable of Śrī (*śrī-bīja*).

Parā is the third seed-syllable of Bālā. Thus, the Mūrti-vidyā consists of three syllables. Bhairavī means the consort of Bhairava, who is Paraśiva; that is to say, she is in the form of Tripurasundarī. || 2 || 3 || 4 ||
He states the application of these vidyās in the two nyāsas:
"Thus, in nine ways, they should be applied with effort at the time of worship. (5)
O Mistress of the Kula, these should be installed in sequence by the practitioner upon the tips of the feet, the shanks, the knees, the thighs, the anus, and the tip of the linga.
One should place the Mūrti-mantra upon the support (ādhāra), and within that, one should place the Āvāhanī-mantra;
O Supreme Goddess, the Vyāpaka-nyāsa should be performed with the Mūla-mantra.

Here, by the phrase "the time of worship," the time for recitation situated within the worship is indicated. For in the subsequent chapter, a fourfold installation (*nyāsa*) will be taught according to the divisions of time. Among those, at the time of recitation, the fourth [installation], consisting of fourteen parts beginning with the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), will be prescribed.
After the *parānyāsa*, the *cakreśvarīnyāsa* should be performed;

for, according to the maxim of Bādarāyaṇa, "at the end," when an unestablished sequence occurs within an established sequence, it should be inserted at the end—this is the meaning of that rule. Therefore...
Thus, even according to the alternative view that the procedure for all four types of *nyāsa* occurs only at the time of worship (*pūjākāla*),

their placement remains within the sequence beginning with *kara-śuddhi* and ending with *nyāsa*. This is provided one maintains the insistence that the term "time of worship" (*pūjākāla*) should be taken exactly as it is heard in the text, rather than being understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the time of recitation (*japa*).
It should be understood that the placement of these two occurs only after the installation of the *aṇimā* and other powers (*aṇimādi-nyāsa*).

Thus, having installed the six *vidyās* in sequence— at the tips of the feet, the calves, the knees, the thighs, the anus, and the tip of the *liṅga*— and having installed the seventh *vidyā* at the *mūlādhāra*, one installs the eighth above the seventh.
Having placed the Vidyā with the ninth [syllable], the meaning is that the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) should be performed over all the limbs using the root-vidyā. || 5 || 6 || 7 ||
He states another method of ritual placement (nyāsa):
"One should contemplate, within the previously mentioned locations beginning with Akula,
the nine wheels previously described, conjoined with the Mistress of the Wheels (Cakreśvarī)."

One should install [the deities] by sequentially reciting the respective Vidyās at the end of each, followed by the name of the respective Mistress of the Cakra (cakreśvarī) and the name of the respective Cakra, within the nine locations: Akula, Viṣurādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, Indrayoni, and Ājñā. [The seed-syllables are: *am*, *āṃ*, *sauḥ*.
Mantras such as "Obeisance to Tripurāsahita, the Wheel that Enchants the Three Worlds" (trailokyamohanacakrāya) are to be inferred [for the other wheels].
Regarding the external limbs, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consists of touching with the ring finger and thumb at the end of each respective mantra;
however, regarding the internal limbs, since physical contact is impossible, the intention is that it consists solely of mental visualization.
It has been stated that one should contemplate [thus]. And it is said in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra either with flowers, or with the fingers, or even mentally.
And here, during the stage of placement upon the body of the deity, it is performed with flowers; whereas for oneself, it is on the external body.

In the state of ritual placement (*nyāsadaśā*), it is "without name" (*anāmayā*); according to the tradition, the word *vā* signifies an alternative established by the mind within one's own internal body during the state of placement.
The joining of the thumb with the ring finger (*anāmā*) is established through the synthesis of other scriptural statements.

"Cakra consisting of nine parts" (*navāvayavaka*) is a *madhyamapadalopa* (middle-term-omission) compound; it means the *Śrīcakra*. By this, the use of the singular number is justified. Furthermore, the purpose of specifying the singular number is that the mantras of the Nine Cakreśvarīs are to be installed for a second time within the Bindu, Ardhacandra, and other [constituent parts].
"Lest it should lead to an over-extension.

Otherwise, since there is no difference in their being the locus for the visualization (*vibhāvana*) of the *cakras* such as the "Enchanter of the Three Worlds" (*trailokyamohana*), and since there is likewise no difference in their being included by the phrase "in Akula and so forth," there would result the necessity of further additional ritual placements (*nyāsa*). However, the ancients say:
The singular form "navacakram" is an archaic Vedic usage. || 8 ||
(p. 250) He states the names of those Cakreśvarīs in sequence:
"I shall declare their names according to the order of succession:
among them, the first is the goddess Tripurā, and the second is Tripureśvarī. (9)
The third goddess is likewise proclaimed as Tripurasundarī;
and the fourth great goddess, O Goddess, is Tripuravāsinī.
The fifth is Tripurāśrī, the sixth is Tripuramālinī,
the seventh is Tripurāsiddhi, and the eighth is Tripurāmbikā.
The ninth [syllable] is indeed the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī.
The qualification "Great" (mahat) is applied to the ninth [syllable] so that the delusion of its identity with the third [syllable] may not arise. (9–11)
He teaches the sequential worship of these Cakreśvarīs within the Śrīcakra:
"And one should worship these nine in sequence within the previously mentioned cakra. (12)

The word "nava" (nine) is a separate term. The meaning is that one should worship these nine Mistress of the Cakras (*cakreśvarī*)—beginning with Trailokyamohana—in the sequence of the *śrīcakra*, which was previously mentioned as being worthy of worship in the *Pūrvatantre*. By the phrase "previously mentioned," the group of nine beginning with Akula is referred to.

[The opponent says: "They are carried over [from the model sacrifice]. [The author replies: That is not so; for it would be redundant to provide an instruction again for a matter already obtained through extended application (*atideśa*).
Moreover, it would lead to undesirable consequences such as the loss of novelty (*apūrvatva*). || 12 ||
Thus, O Pārvatī, at the time of worship, the primordial power is of nine kinds;
yet that primordial power is indeed of a single form, bestowing freedom from old age and death.

The primordial Śakti of the primordial Śiva, though ninefold in form at the time of worship, is in reality of a single nature. When known thus, she bestows the state of being undecaying and immortal; the terms "undecaying" (ajara) and "immortal" (amara) are used here with the abstract state as the primary meaning. || 13 ||
The symbolic convention of that [goddess] is established in various forms;
it is obtained through the lineage of various mantra sequences. (14)
The symbolic convention of that primordial power (Ādi-śakti) takes various forms.
The conventional meaning of her vidyā is sixfold; however, her mantra is not singular either, such that a single mantra would possess six meanings. Rather, the mantra is of various kinds.

Due to the distinctions such as Lopāmudrā, Kāmarāja, and others, some meanings belong exclusively to the *Kādividyā*, some belong exclusively to the *Hādividyā*, and some are common to both. Taken together, there are six types of convention (*saṃketa*). Among these, which [is it]?
The meaning is that the determination of what constitutes the "meaning of the Vidyā" is obtained only through the traditional lineage (*pāramparya-krama*).

However, those of former times, believing that the six meanings belong exclusively to the *Hādi-vidyā*, explain the various mantra-words found here as being intended for the mantra of Cakreśvarī. That is incorrect.
Because there is no description of the meaning of the mantras of Cakreśvarī later on,

and because it will be demonstrated that the traditional meanings and so forth of the *hādi-vidyā* are not applicable [to them], and because only the *kādi-vidyā* has been extracted in the *Pūrvatantra*.

Furthermore, the conceit that the *ṣaḍartha* belongs exclusively to the *Hādividyā* must be abandoned, as it contradicts the opening statement and results in the opposite misconception; moreover, the difficulty involved in interpreting even the text of the *Pūrvatantra* as being subordinate to the *Hādividyā* has already been demonstrated in that very same place.
Therefore, it should be understood that the systematic arrangement we have set forth is indeed impartial. || 14 ||
Because the multitude of meanings to be explained is difficult to comprehend, he makes a renewed promise in order to ensure attentiveness:
"O Goddess, O sinless one, I shall explain that [system] to you in its sixfold form."
That is the meaning of the mantra.
He analyzes the meaning:
"The meaning of the ritual act (bhāvārtha), the meaning of the tradition (saṃpradāyārtha), the innermost meaning (nigarbhārtha), and the Kaula meaning. (15)
Likewise, it is the meaning of all secrets and the very meaning of the Great Reality.
Therein, desiring to clarify the meaning of the term *bhāva*, which was mentioned first, he provides its etymological definition:
"O Supreme Goddess, the meaning of *bhāva* is simply the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*). (15)

For the very nature of syllables is to convey meaning. Consequently, that meaning of the syllables which is not understood through mere phonetic recitation (*tāla*) and so forth, but is obtained solely through the function (*vṛtti*) of the syllables themselves—
being obtainable through the very nature of the syllables— is called the "meaning of the essence" (*bhāvārtha*).
This is the meaning. || 16 ||

Now he explains that very same point with nine verses: "O Dear One, the King of Mantras is always generated by the Yoginīs, as well as by the Vīras and the lords of Vīras, through the union of Śiva and Śakti. (17)
The Yoginīs consist of will, knowledge, and action, which are aspects of reflective awareness (vimarśa). These are the three:
Sarasvatī, Pṛthivī, and Rudrāṇī; for the plural number here refers to a triad according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya*. The Vīras are the practitioners.

There are three [categories] according to the distinction between the impure, the mixed, and the pure. The Vīrendras are the triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, who are non-different from Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, which constitute the aspect of manifestation (*prakāśāṃśa*). According to the *Śivasūtra*, "the Lord of Heroes (*vīreśa*) is the enjoyer of this triad."

Because the definition of the Vīreśa is stated as one whose contemplation of his own self (*svātmānusaṃdhāna*) does not waver even during the three states beginning with waking; and because, even when there is movement [of the mind], he is undistracted due to being absorbed in that [state]—this same meaning is also expressed in the *Tantrarāja* by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Therefore:
The lords of heroes (*vīrendra*) are those whose character is defined by the firmness of such latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
It is said that, due to the varying degrees of laxity in such latent impressions, they are called the three kinds of heroes (*vīra*) according to their respective gradations.
The union (*samāyoga*) and the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti constitute one [category]. Thus, there are ten.
This king of mantras has been generated by these [syllables]; the meaning is that it is composed of ten syllables which denote this [mantra].

This is the underlying sense: for in this vidyā there are fifteen syllables, among which the three syllables of *hṛllekhā* are well-known as denoting the Goddess, their meaning being already established.
This is because she is described in the *Triśatī-nāma* as "she who is denoted by the syllable Hrīṃ" and "she whose Vidyā is the syllable Hrīṃ.
Furthermore, the demonstration of her being devoted to that [Hrīṃ] is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"She is manifest through the void (*vyoman*) and she is the devouring [power] through fire (*agni*)."
"Their reflection is the vowel *ī*, and its friction [with the *bindu*] is the *bindu* itself.

Thus, one letter each from the second and third *kūṭas*—in the form of the letters *ha* and *sa*—will be explained later in the root text itself. Therefore, with the intention that only ten letters remain, [the text says...].
The composition of the mantra has been stated by means of exactly ten [principles]. And thus, for each and every *kūṭa*,
