whatever the number of syllables may be, the meanings of those [syllables]— such as the Yoginīs and so forth— as they have been stated respectively,
become non-different from the Goddess present in the *hṛllekhā* by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The meaning of each individual syllable is as follows: here, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in the absence of having contradictory case-endings, as in the example "curd and honey" (*dadhi-madhu*). Among those, the three *ka*-syllables refer to Brahmā and the others; the three *la*-syllables refer to the earth and the others.

The letters *ha*, *sa*, and *i* refer to the Heroes (*vīra*), because it is easily established by scholars—either through the *Ekākṣarakośa* or by metaphorical indication—that they signify those respective entities. The letter *e* refers to the Sāmāsya, because it is produced by the union of two *a*s that denote Śiva and Śakti. Alternatively, in this Vidyā...

It will be stated later that there are thirty-seven syllables; however, when these are counted while avoiding repetitions, only ten remain: the letter *a*, the letter *la*, the letter *sa*, the letter *ha*, the letter *ī*, the letter *e*, the letter *ra*, the letter *ka*, the *nāda*, and the *bindu*. What need is there for more? This applies to all types [of mantras].
In the Śrīvidyā as well, there are exactly this many syllables.
As it is stated in the Jñānārṇava: "The Earth, the Moon, Śiva, Māyā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇa, Adhva, and Mādana."
The half-moon and the bindu—these nine syllables are called Meru.

p. 253) "The mantras of Mahātripurasundarī originate from Meru. In these [mantras], the single letter *a* is not counted separately, with the intention that it lacks independence from the consonants. However, the letters beginning with *la* are indeed counted sequentially by means of the words for earth (*bhūmi*) and so forth. Therefore...

There is no contradiction with the number ten; therefore, these ten phonemes are to be explained as denoting the Yoginīs and so forth, respectively. Furthermore, the repetition of the phonemes is to be justified by the intention of referring to a plurality of individual instances. Among those, regarding the letter *e*:

By accepting that the final term [of the compound] functions as the qualifier (*viśeṣya*), the meaning of the sentence is that Brahman— which consists of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti— is non-different from the Yoginī and so forth. And of these two positions, the latter is supported by the entire preceding textual corpus consisting of the eight verses.

This is merely for the purpose of praising the Vidyā, like a partisan argument. In reality, however, because the work begins with "The meaning of the letters is indeed the meaning of the state" (*bhāvārtha*) and concludes at the end with "they consider it to be the meaning of the state," and because there is a reference to the second and third *kūṭas* in the middle, this textual composition [is understood] through these indicative marks (*liṅga*).

It is clearly perceived that every syllable is intent upon conveying its specific meaning, leaving no room for it to be merely a matter of praise; thus, this verse is devoted solely to conveying the meaning of the first *kūṭa* alone. Consequently, each individual [syllable]...

The phonemes beginning with *ka* are followed by "Vīrendra" and so forth. To indicate that the three [words] beginning with *ka* each end in the plural, there are the three words ending in the plural, namely "yoginīḥ" and so on. To indicate that the vowel *e* ends in the singular, the word "samāyogāt" is used in the singular.

Through the *hṛllekhā*, the specific object [of the description] is obtained. By that, it is stated that the meaning of the first *kūṭa* is: "Tripurasundarī, whose nature is that of the Yoginīs, whose nature is that of the Vīras, whose nature is that of the Vīrendras, and whose nature is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti. [The components are: *kā*, *e*, *ya*, and *lā*.

Following the *dvandva* compound, there is a *karmadhāraya* with the syllable *hrīṃ*. The elision of the case-ending (*su*) occurs according to the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). Even within the compound, the absence of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) is an archaic Vedic feature (*ārṣa*). Although the letters beginning with *ka* are accepted as separate words, the elision of the case-endings of the vowels *e* and *l* is likewise an archaic Vedic feature. || 17 ||
Establishing this very point, he explains the third peak:
"Consisting of that [consciousness], gladdened by supreme bliss, and having the nature of vibration."
Knowing the Goddess to be naturally beautiful, they attend upon her at their own will.

"Consisting of that" means non-different from the fourfold group beginning with the Yoginīs. To prevent the possibility of contact with suffering arising from the distinction between inferior and middling heroes (*vīra*), he says "supreme" (*paramā*). Supremacy is the state of being untouched by suffering; she is gladdened by such bliss.

"Joyful" (hṛṣṭāṃ) means "united" (yuktāṃ), that is to say, "undivided. "Vibration" (spandaḥ) refers to the universe consisting of the thirty-six principles (tattvas). "Having that as her form" (tadrūpiṇīm) means non-different from that. One might object that because of non-difference with even an unattractive object, she herself would become unattractive; therefore, he says: "naturally beautiful" (nisargasundarīm).
"Sweet by its very nature" (p.

254): this is the meaning obtainable from the third peak. This same meaning is stated later, beginning with "again" (*punar*) in the context of the third *piṇḍaka*, and ending with "she who possesses all forms" (*viśvarūpiṇī*).

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the *Vivaraṇa*. Having referred to the Goddess by means of the term *hṛllekhā*, the non-difference of everything (*sarva*) is enjoined by the word *sakala*.
The meaning is: "All this, indeed, is Brahman. The elision of the case-ending in the word *sakala* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
If one were to accept a compound (*samāsa*), there would be a violation of the principle of "single impulse" (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*). [This concerns] the subject and the predicate...
Or rather, there is no fault even in not accepting the existence of entities. He states the meaning obtainable from the *hṛllekhā* mantra: "the Goddess.
Having known such a Goddess through the mantra—that is, making her the object of verbal cognition—the practitioners worship Her in whatever manner they please, according to their own conduct.
They cultivate [this]. The suffix *ktvā* is used here for simultaneous action, as in the expression "having opened his mouth, he eats" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*). || 18 ||

He states the meaning of the "Middle Peak" (madhyamakūṭa): "In the eternal Brahman, whose nature is the union of Śiva and Śakti, and in that ground characterized by Indra, which is the locus of the embrace resulting from the expansion of its manifestation. (19)
Because it effects a form consisting of knowledge for the knower, she is of the nature of mantra.

That which is the union (saṃghaṭṭa) consisting of Śiva and Śakti—that state of equilibrium (sāmarasya)—is the object; within that Brahman, the "form consisting of knowledge" of the knower is his very nature as consciousness (cinmayatva).

Because of that cause, she is "of the nature of mantra," meaning she protects the one who recites (*mantṛ*)—this is the sense of "mantrarūpām"; the connection with the preceding word is "the Goddess" (*devīm*). By this, the *Śivasūtra* "The mind is mantra" is explained: consciousness itself, when descended into the state of the cognizer and contracting its objects of cognition (*caitya*), is the mind (*citta*).

And the Śaktisūtra is also consistent with this. The phrase "the manifestation of that" (*tatprathā*) and so forth is intended to suggest that the knowledge concerning Brahman is not conceptual (*savikalpaka*). The "manifestation," "extension," or "expansion" (*prasara*) of that Brahman is the universe (*viśva*); it is the ground of its embrace.
The meaning of that [statement] is as follows: even though the substratum of those [attributes] is indicated by such sovereignty belonging to Indra, it is not qualified by them.

Since the state of having as its object something qualified by attributes such as being the creator of the universe is excluded by the term "indicated" (*upalakṣita*), the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of knowledge—consisting in its having the mere substrate (*dharmin*) as its object—is established.

And "unbrokenness" (*akhaṇḍatva*) consists in possessing an objectivity that is distinct from conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-prajñā*). By stating this, the shadow-explanation of the middle peak (*madhyakūṭa*) has been indicated: the letter *ha* is Śiva;
the letter *sa* is Śakti.
The three *ka*s and the two *ha*s are proclaimed as the portion belonging to Śiva;
the remaining syllables belong to Śakti, while the syllable *hrīṃ* is of the nature of both.
According to the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*,
because the word "Self" (*ātman*) indicates that the state of *sāmarasya* consists of the non-duality of both, these two syllables form a *karmadhāraya* compound.

[The term] *dhvanitaḥ* [is explained as follows]: *haṃ* and *tat-saṃ* together form *hasaṃ*, which is the nature of Śiva and Śakti merged in mutual union. The word *brahmaṇī* is the meaning of the letter *ka*; for the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) states, "Ka is Brahman. By the particle *tu*, a *karmadhāraya* compound of *hasa* with *ka* is expressed.
*Hasaṃ* and *tatkaṃ* together form *hasakaṃ*, which is Brahman consisting of the Śiva-Śakti of equal flavor (*samarasa*).

By the statement beginning with "the manifestation of that" (*tatprathā*), it is stated that the word *hasaka* refers, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to the substratum alone and not to that which is qualified by the property-limiting factor (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) [of the primary denotation]. *Hasakahā* means "that which destroys *hasaka*."

He is one who possesses knowledge whose object is such Brahman. This is established because the root *han* signifies "going," and according to the grammatical rule that "those [roots] which signify going signify knowing," this interpretation is appropriate. This compound is stated with the locative case of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*) in the word *brahmaṇi*. The fact that *han* has the meaning of "knowing" is indicated by the word *jñātuḥ*.
It has been made known. *Hasakahalā* is so called because she takes—that is, she assumes and makes non-different from herself—the *hasakahana*.

This is indicated by the phrase "due to the formation of the aspect consisting of knowledge. When this [term] is compounded with *hṛllekhā*, the form is established through the application of the *puṃvadbhāva* rule. This very meaning has already been stated according to its constituent parts.
This is stated by the phrase "condensing her who has the form of mantra. And thus:
She whose nature is the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti, who consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara;
she who takes the forms of Vāṇī, Aparṇā, and Umā, and who is the essence of the three types of worshippers.
Taking for herself, by means of her own self, the non-conceptual knowledge of Brahman— which consists of both Śiva and Śakti merged in mutual equilibrium— she [attains it].
The Goddess Mahātripurasundarī is the essence of all reality; such is the meaning of the underlying intent.
Regarding this, he says:
"But their collective form is Mātṛkā, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti). (20)

The meaning is that when the individual qualifying attributes, described as having the sense of each respective peak (kūṭa), are unified and joined together in their collective form, the Supreme Power (parāśakti) becomes the Mother, who is the meaning of the mantra. || 20 ||
Now, by stating that the Goddess is non-different from the mantra and non-different from the universe,

[the author] establishes the non-difference between the mantra and the universe— which might otherwise be questioned— by means of their sharing a single material cause (*upādāna*), just as a jar and a bowl are non-different from the clay of which they are both produced.
To demonstrate this, he says:

"In the Supreme, which consists of the abiding within the emission at the center-point, there is a reflection of her [the Goddess] in the form of the Crooked One (Kuṭilā), which is a portion of the void. (21)
Furthermore, she abides in the space of vibration (*spanda*) which is the manifestation of the central vital breath (*madhyaprāṇa*);
and again, in the middle mantra-cluster (*mantrapiṇḍa*), and again in the third cluster. (22)
The non-dual radiance of the peak of Rāhu [shines forth].

For in the *kāmakalā*, first there is the fourth drop (*turīyabindu*); below that is the drop called Kāma; below that are the two drops called the emission (*visarga*); and below that is the state known as the "half-syllable" (*hārdhakalā*). In that regard:
Between the fourth state (*turya*) and the emission (*visarga*), there is the point (*bindu*) called *kāma*; that *bindu* and the *visarga*,
as well as that which is situated within them by way of the nature of consciousness— those two syllables consisting of these,
namely the letter *a* contained within *kāma* and the letter *ha* contained within the *visarga*, though both of them are indeed supreme.

However, even in the form of *vaikharī*, they are in the supreme form of *parā-mātṛkā*, that is to say, in the form of the Void (*śūnya*). Some say the meaning is "at the beginning and end of *mātṛkā*. These two are of the nature of the Crooked One (*kuṭilā*), of the nature of the Curved One (*vakra*), or of the nature of Vāmā—that is to say, the generators of emanation. Some say they are of the nature of *akula-kula-kuṇḍalinī*. Of her...
The two forms of the Supreme Brahman consist of form and sound; these are the counterparts of the Goddess.

Regarding this, some maintain that these two imperishables (*akṣara*) are the sound-forms of Śiva and Śakti, and are thus alternative forms of Kulakuṇḍalinī. However, this would be redundant with the term "having a curved form" (*tat-kuṭilārūpaka*).
Having designated the syllable by means of such numerous qualifiers, he also designates it by its name as "viyatkale.

*Viyat* is the letter *ha*; *kalā* is the light, which is the letter *a*. This is because of the lexicon stating under the section on the letter *a*: "Light is Supreme Śiva. Some maintain that by the word *viyat* the letter *a* is meant, while *kalā* is the half-measure (*ardhakalā*), which is the letter *ha*.
That is to be reflected upon. He demonstrates that such a supreme form consisting of two syllables exists within the mantra by saying "the middle vital breath" (*madhyaprāṇa*).

Within the second peak (*kūṭa*) of the middle mantra-cluster, that which is the middle among the three *ha*-syllables—the second *ha*—is precisely that which has the nature of the expansion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is contained within the emission (*visarga*) and is the supreme form (*parārūpa*), is the letter *ha*. Its manifestation (*prathā*), its expansion (*prathana*), or its grossness (*sthūlatā*)—that is, its nature as *vaikharī* speech—is the vibration-space (*spandavyoma*) which is the letter *ha*.
It is called "vibration" (*spanda*) because it vibrates, that is, it arises; it is "vibration-space" (*spandavyoma*) because it is the space from which that vibration arises.

This is because it will be stated later that "from the letter *ha*, space (*vyoma*) was produced. Alternatively, it may mean that space is that which consists of the vibration whose nature is manifestation. Within that [space], moreover, resides the supreme *mātṛkā* whose essence is the letter *ha*.
However, some, joining the word "middle" (*madhyama*) twice, [interpret it as follows]:

Those who explain that "therein" refers to the central *hakāra* within the *madhyamakuṭa*, interpret the term "central breath" (*madhyaprāṇapada*) as referring to consciousness situated in the center of the *visarga*. This has been explained in accordance with the oral tradition; otherwise, [one would have to follow] the principle of what is first encountered.

It is more appropriate to explain that [the letter *a*] resides in the very first *ha*. Now, one might object: this textual passage is naturally intended to refer to two things—the letter *a* situated within the middle *ha* of the second *kūṭa*, and the letter *ha* situated in the *hṛllekhā* of the third *kūṭa*; for at the beginning, the letter *a* [is mentioned].

Because the letter *ha* is taught later, it is appropriate to explain the concluding passage (*upasaṃhāra*) in accordance with that same sequence; furthermore, the locative case in "in the sky" (*vyomni*) is intended to have the meaning "after" (*para*).

If it is argued that this is likewise because the locative case in *rāhukūṭe* is easily understood as the seventh [case], and therefore how can the meaning be said to be obtained through the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*), [the answer is]: True. However, regarding the sequence of the letters *a* and *ha* presented at the beginning [of the text]...

Because of the separation [of the two parts] by the singular-numbered qualifier *pratirūpam*; because the expression *viyatkale* indicates the letter *a* following the letter *ha*, thereby establishing that the reversed order (*viparītakrama*) is the one in common usage; and because there is no obstacle to the subsequent specification of the individual letters (*vyakti*) according to that very same order. For this very reason, [it is said]: *saṃ te prāṇo...*

Since the verb "gacchatā" (going) ending in the singular is incompatible with its connection to "saṃ yajatrairaṅgāni" (may the limbs be united) which ends in the plural, there is a break [in the sentence].

Consequently, even though it is capable of being connected with "saṃ yajñapatirāśiṣā" (may the lord of the sacrifice be united with his blessing), there is no *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of the missing word). Rather, [the verb connects only with the preceding phrase].

It was established in the *Bhedalakṣaṇa* that another word must be supplied [to complete the sense]. However, according to the view of the ancients— who explain even the term *viyatkale* in accordance with the sequence introduced [in the *Bhedalakṣaṇa*]—
there exists another tradition for the sake of preserving the transmission, even regarding the portion already explained.

This is the general direction regarding that which is to be taken as refuge. However, the meaning established by tradition is indicated by the specific mention of the second and third *kūṭas*. Regarding the placement of the planets (*grahanyāsa*) within the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) as it is being heard, it will be stated in the section on the mouth: "The letters *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* constitute the *kūṭa* of Rāhu."

And [it is said]: "together with the four letters beginning with *śā* and *rāhu* itself. In that context, the two non-dual letters (*advayau*) are the *sa* and *ha*, which are distinct from the first pair; between those two as well, by virtue of suitability, it is the *sa* alone [that is intended], because in the third *kūṭa* there is no conjunction of the vowel *ā* with the letter *ha*. This applies in both cases.

The word "punaḥ" (again), being heard here, signifies a second time and confirms the nature of the supreme *mātṛkā* as distinct from *vaikharī*. Even in a single phoneme (*akṣara*), both the element of sound (*dhvani*) and the element of the letter (*varṇa*) indeed exist, just as in the case of gold according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*).

Like the mutually blended portions of earthy and fiery elements, for this very reason there is the experience of properties of sound—such as high pitch (*tāratva*) and so forth—in the phonemes (*varṇa*). That sound (*dhvani*) in the phoneme is indeed the *nāda* that generates all phonemes; for it is *nāda* alone that is initially of a subtle (*parā*) form.

According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), [the sound] arises from the *mūlādhāra*, reaches the *maṇipūra* and *anāhata* centers, and through its conjunction with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*), it transforms into the states of *paśyantī* and *madhyamā*; finally, at the throat, it assumes the form of *vaikharī*, consisting of articulated phonemes (*varṇa*). And within that resonance (*nāda*)...
In that which is the cause of all phonemes (*varṇa*), all phonemes indeed exist in a subtle form, just as fruits, flowers, and so forth exist within a seed. Just as within a single seed-enclosure,
though it is one, when divided into two parts— the anterior and the posterior— there exists everything consisting of various constituent parts.

Just as a tree exists within [the seed], so too, within the Nāda-Brahman—which is divided into two parts in the form of the letters *a* and *ha*—exists the entire phenomenal world consisting of phonemes, both worldly and Vedic. For this very reason, the recitation of all phonemes occurs precisely between the letters *a* and *ha*. As for the letter *la*:

Because of its non-difference from the letter *la*; because the letter *kṣa* is not distinct, being of the nature of a combination of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*; and because Brahman consists precisely of the union of the letters *a* and *ha*, it is in the Śrutis shown to have the form of "I" (*aham*). Thus: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, it is said: "At that time, he knew only himself as 'I'. In the *Aitareya Upaniṣad*, it says: "Therein, 'I, I'... and also: "'Who are you? 'I,' he replied," and so forth. Furthermore, in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"That light which is the self of the universe, capable of manifesting both itself and others..."
"He alone is called 'I'; such is his state of being 'I-ness' (ahaṃtā).
For it is precisely because Brahman has the nature of "I" that its worship is also taught in the form of "apprehension as I" (ahaṃgraha) and so forth—as in: "I alone [am Brahman]."

One should meditate upon Bhavānī as such; for, because the Cause is of the nature of the "I" (ahaṃ), its pervasion extends through the entire phenomenal world, just as clay pervades jars, bowls, and other objects. For this very reason, the word *asmad* (we/I) is classified as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). The *Tapanīya-śruti* also states: "All this is indeed one; therefore, it is 'I'."

Regarding the phrase "the designation of all": for this very reason, with the intention that such a meaning is extremely secret, it is stated in the *Tantrarāja* by means of a convention: "One should know the first and the last. The first is the letter *a*, the last is the letter *ha*; their combination is *ahaṃ* (I), which is its meaning.
Also in the *Mālinīśāstra*, the *Siddhāntatantra*, and others:
"Mantras devoid of their initial and final [syllables] are like autumn clouds;
the characteristic of a guru is this much: he should impart the initial and the final."
Regarding the realization of the wheel of the *mātṛkā*, Varadarāja has also stated in the *Śivasūtra*: "Therefore, by means of the letters 'a' and 'ha', [the Self] shines forth as the non-dual 'I',
having embraced the phenomenal world within Śiva and Śakti."
Furthermore, another essential secret regarding this matter has been revealed by us in our *Varivasyārahasyavyākhyāna*. And in this manner,
since everything consists of the state of aesthetic resonance (*sāmarasya*) between the letters 'A' and 'Ha', so too does the mantra.

There is no dispute that such a pair of phonemes exists within the mantra because of its true nature (*tathātva*). For just as in a *vaṭa* tree, although there is an infinity of seeds, a pair of parts of the sprouting generative seed exists somewhere that possesses a form identical to the generative seed itself; however, it is simply difficult to perceive.
Likewise, in the present case as well,

there are the two letters *a* and *ha*, which consist of the supreme *nāda* and are the progenitors of the *vidyā*; these two are non-different from Sarasvatī, who is the *mātṛkā* non-different from the entire expansion of words (*śabdaprapañca*), and are non-different from Śrī, whose nature is Brahman.

Because their location must necessarily exist somewhere yet is difficult for others to discern, they have been revealed by the Omniscient One alone— the World-Teacher, whose essence is compassion and who desires to favor His devotees— through many symbolic means. (21–22)
He also states the relevance of demonstrating that [point] within the present section describing the meaning of the state (*bhāvārtha*): "But for one who is not established in stillness... (p. 259).
Of dharma and adharma, which are to be expressed, and which consist of poison and nectar; || 23 ||
She who possesses the forms of the universe is said to be joined with the expressive syllables (*vācakākṣara*).

"Moving" (*cala*) means the state of movement, the state of flux, perishability—that is, impermanence (*anityatā*). This designation is primarily focused on the substratum (*dharmin*). "Unestablished" (*asaṃsthita*) means incomplete; [she is] eternal (*nitya*).

The established meaning is "of that which is both eternal and non-eternal"; that is to say, of that which is non-eternal in the form of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) and eternal in the form of Brahman.
For this very reason, Kṛṣṇadāsa stated in the *Śivasūtra*: "Even during its [the world's] activity, there is no exclusion [of the Self], because of the state of being its own cognizer."
And here, there are two states designated as "the state of being an effect" and "the state of being an agent.
Among these, the state of being an effect is perishable, whereas agency is imperishable.
"Only that effort which is directed toward an effect is here sublated," and so forth.

Dharma, because it is the nature of Brahman, is Śakti. Adharma is Paraśiva, who is devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka). Poison is saṃsāra; nectar is liberation (mokṣa). [This occurs] by means of the impermanent nature of saṃsāra.
The syllable *ha* is the signifier (*vācaka*) of the signified (*vācya*) power that has undergone transformation (*pariṇata-śakti*).
The syllable *a* is the signifier of the signified Supreme Śiva, whose nature is eternal liberation (*nitya-mokṣātman*).
Through the union of these two, the mantra takes the form of Śiva and Śakti. So too does the entire universe.

Because it is produced from Śiva and Śakti, it is of that very nature; and because they share a single material cause, there is non-difference between the Mantra and the universe—thus is stated the logical justification for the meaning expressed by the third Kūṭa. || 23 ||

Having thus described, with supporting arguments, the threefold meaning of the three *kūṭas* which consist of three subordinate sentences, he says the following while concluding with the previously stated meaning of the mantra as a single sentence in the form of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*):
One should contemplate Parāśakti as the sister (bhātṛkā) in her collective form.
Meditating upon the primordial Śakti, who consists of the three peaks (kūṭas) and whose nature is both collective and individual, they consider her to be the true meaning of existence.
By means of the synthesis of the meanings of those three subordinate sentences,

and through the mutual requirement [of each], they again conceive of them as a single unified sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*), while meditating upon the Supreme Power, Mātṛkā— the primordial power non-different from Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī.

The foremost of practitioners, making the object of the cognition produced by the mantra their own object of meditation, consider that which is to be meditated upon to be the "meaning of the essence" (bhāvārtha) of the mantra. The phrase "consisting of the three peaks" (kūṭatrayātmikām), however,
is intended to express the non-duality between the mantra and the deity.

In that regard, it is intended to indicate that for those who worship each individual peak (*kūṭa*) alone, only the meaning of the intermediate sentence (*avāntaravākyārtha*) should be meditated upon, whereas for those who worship all three peaks, the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*) should be meditated upon.

It has been stated that she possesses both collective (*samaṣṭi*) and individual (*vyaṣṭi*) forms. By this, it is also implied that the three *hṛllekhās* are necessary in order to obtain the substantive (*viśeṣya*) within the intermediate sentence-meanings (*avāntaravākyārtha*).
Thus, the meaning derived from the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) has been described in its threefold aspect. This very approach is the natural preference (*svarasa*) for the *Kādipakṣa*.
The letter *e* alone is the natural [meaning] of the term "the union of Śiva and Śakti" (*śivaśaktisamāyoga*). Even in the view that begins with *ha*,
one must somehow construe it such that either the letter *ha* or the letter *sa* is expressed by either of the terms "Yoginī" or "the union of Śiva and Śakti."

However, the Prāñcas, considering this entire text to be solely concerned with the *hādī-vidyā*, explain it in another manner. For instance: in the first *kūṭa*, there are seven syllables together with the letters *ha*, *ra*, and *ka* situated within the *hṛllekhā*; [and] the *yoginīs* are *Bhāratī* and the others, while the *vīras*...
"Brahmā and the others" refers to three pairs: the letter *ha* is Brahmā, *sa* is Bhāratī;
*ka* is Viṣṇu, *la* is Pṛthivī; *ha* is Rudra, and *ra* is Rudrāṇī. Thus, there are six syllables dedicated to these three pairs, whose collective form consists of Śāntā and Ambikā.

The couple is to be expressed by the single syllable *mīṃ*. The word *vīrendraiḥ*, located at the base (*mūla*), though ending in the plural and being exclusively masculine, denotes the couple as a collective whole (*samaṣṭi*).
Although the letter *ha* in the middle of the second *kūṭa* is to be recited at the beginning of the third *kūṭa*, it belongs to the third [kūṭa].

The second *kūṭa* alone was recited [in this context] out of a desire to indicate its nature as a *śakti-kūṭa*—that is, its being composed of the letters of *Śakti*—and out of a desire to suggest its status as a *sthitikūṭa*. Although this very same [second *kūṭa*] is recited here, it remains essentially the same as that [original one]; thus, all three *kūṭas* consist of seven syllables each.
They become identical in form; therefore, the meaning of the other two peaks (kūṭas) is exactly like that of the first peak. However, this is the distinction:
by the very resonance of the state of persistence (sthitirūpatā) of the second peak, [the nature] of the first and the final peaks [is indicated].
Because each individual *kūṭa* (syllabic peak) is indicated as having the nature of both emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*),

and because it is further divided into three sub-categories— emission and so forth— the triad of couples residing in the first *kūṭa* takes on the presiding identity of these three respectively: emission-of-emission (*sṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), emission-and-stasis (*sṛṣṭisthiti*), and emission-and-withdrawal (*sṛṣṭisaṃhṛti*).

The presiding over these three— maintenance-creation, maintenance-maintenance, and maintenance-destruction— is the function of the one situated on the second peak. However, for the one situated on the third peak,
it is destruction-creation, destruction-maintenance, and destruction-destruction.
This constitutes the state of identifying with these three; therefore, there is no tautology.
Since the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti-kūṭas correspond respectively to the Pūrva-āmnāya, Dakṣiṇa-āmnāya, and Paścima-āmnāya, there is such a ninefold union.
Furthermore, because it does not have the form of a redundant repetition (*anavakara*), there is no tautology.

And thus, by means of these four pairs (*mithuna*) denoted by the letters of the Vidyā, this King of Mantras, which takes the form of the Hādi-vidyā, is generated and contemplated as having brought about the union (*mithunīkṛtya*) of Śiva and Śakti; so it is stated in the root text.
This is the meaning of the first verse. Now, he states the meaning of the subsequent fourth peak (*kūṭa*), which consists of *māyā*: "tanmayīm" (composed of that).

This means [the goddess] whose denoted object is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) that denote the four pairs consisting of Bhāratī and the others, as well as Brahmā and the others.
The author provides an etymological explanation of the word *mantra*: "consisting of the essence of Śiva and Śakti.
The intention is that its status as a *mantra* is established because it performs the functions of reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*) within the fourth peak (*kūṭa*). Now, one might ask:
what are the characteristics of that fourth *mantra*? To this, he says: "Of these," referring to the three peaks.
The forms [of speech] are *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. This [present form], however, means that it is the form of the supreme *mātṛkā*.

Now, one might ask: "The Power (*śakti*) denoted by the fourth peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) consists of both the letters *a* and *ha*; where do these two reside within the mantra? To this he says: "In the middle, with the bindu. It is precisely because these two exist within the mantra [that they are present there].
He states that the Fourth Vidyā consists of the universe with the words "the moving one" (*calattā*).

Precisely because the Fourth is the self of the universe, yogis, perceiving it as the Supreme Mātṛkā and conceiving the three individual *kūṭas* as being of the nature of Paśyantī and the other [levels of speech], consider it to be the intended meaning (*bhāvārtha*).

This very exposition is proclaimed as the refutation of this [position] through the illustration of the maxim: "The description of its own nature is itself its refutation. Following this, two other positions have also been elaborated by us in the *Varivasyārahasya*. Thus, among these six positions, whichever—

Thus, for the wise worshippers, that very intention of the Supreme Śiva (paraśivāśaya) is the essential meaning (bhāvārtha) that reaches the heart; this is the general direction [of the teaching]. || 24 || 25 ||

Now, he defines the meaning of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*), which follows in sequence, in twenty-two and a half verses: "The oral tradition, whose nature is great awakening, resides in the mouth of the Guru."
And the greatness of the manifestation in all forms is that which rests upon Him. || 26 ||
O Supreme Goddess, O Beloved, listen attentively to how the entire universe is pervaded by the primordial Vidyā consisting of Śiva, Śakti, and the rest. (27)
The universe consists of the five elements, and that eternal [Prakṛti] is composed of them;
the Root-Vidyā is likewise composed of them, and I shall describe it to you.

For previously, it was stated that in the Goddess, the states of being composed of mantra and being composed of the universe are primary; however, since the properties of being mantra and being the universe are mutually exclusive (parasparābhāvavyāpyatva), their coexistence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the Goddess would not be possible.

Because it was stated that "one should unite," the non-difference between the mantra and the universe was established as a means to justify that [union]— specifically by virtue of both being produced from the syllables denoting Śiva and Śakti— and not as a primary point. Now, however, [it is shown that this applies] even to those things derived from a single *udumbara* seed.
Considering the aforementioned argument weak because one observes absolute difference between fruits, leaves, insects, wood,
and so forth, the Blessed One— who is the universal self (viśvātman) of the mantra—
maintains that there is non-difference between the mantra and the universe solely by way of the relationship of material cause and its effect, since the universe has evolved from the mantra.

It is intended as the primary subject. Alternatively, since previously the non-difference of the Goddess and the mantra was established by way of their functions of *manana* (contemplation) and *trāṇa* (protection), it is precisely this non-difference of the Goddess and the mantra that is intended here as the primary subject.
Furthermore, the universe consists of the thirty-six *tattvas*; consequently, in the phrase "consisting of the five elements," [the same principle applies].

The term *bhūtapada* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other principles (*tattva*), or it is intended with the view that even the thirty-six [principles] will be divided fivefold, as will be stated later. The established position is that this triad—Viśva, Sā, and the eternal Goddess Mūlavidyā—is composed of the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattvamaya*). In that regard:

It is well known throughout the world that even for the Goddess, her identity with that [Śiva] is beyond doubt, because she is the transformer of the universe; however, although there is no contradiction in the Root-Vidyā being produced from the letters *a* and *ha*, which denote Śiva and Śakti, just as the world is.
Since an absolute distinction must necessarily exist between the worm and the wood,

how could [the Self] have transformed itself into the form of the entire universe through that [distinction], such that there could be non-difference with it? Given its such intractability, the greatness of the mantra’s manifestation as the universal form remains doubtful.
The object of that great awakening— which is the basis for its being supreme and beyond doubt, and by means of which one must cultivate an awareness characterized by certainty—
is correctly and excellently indicated by the term "the meaning of the tradition" (*saṃpradāyārtha*).

O Supreme Goddess, my beloved, I shall tell you exactly what kind of gift it is— transcending all things, passed down through the lineage of gurus and supreme gurus, standing like wealth, and residing only within the mouth of the guru, obtainable solely through the grace of the guru; listen attentively.

The interpretation [is as follows]: The explanation offered by the ancients—that *mahābodha* (Great Awakening) is the awakening of a "great" light that is unconditioned by space and time—is unacceptable because it contradicts the sūtra *tvāt-mahataḥ*.
The phrase "by means of Śiva’s power and so forth" is a qualifying attribute containing a reason. || 26 || 27 || 28 ||
In the *Hādividyā*, beginning from the very first syllable that presents itself, he states the promised meaning:
"From the letter *ha* space (*vyoma*) is produced, and from the letter *ka* the wind (*prabhañjana*)."
From the letter *ra* arises fire, and from the letter *sa* comes the origin of the water element.
From the letter *la*, the earth was born; therefore, it consists of the universe.
From the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), which has transformed into the nature of the letter *ha*, space and the other elements were produced.
Nor should one be surprised by this description of the production of objects from words, as it is not unprecedented.

If it is argued that [the world] arises from sound, we say no; for even in the *Sūtra* of Vyāsa, it is stated that "from sound [arises] the origin of objects," as established by both scripture (*śruti*) and tradition (*smṛti*).
The demonstration of this should be seen in its commentary (*bhāṣya*). As for the phrase "but from the letter 'ka'," etc.:
The term *kāmakalā* refers to the vowel *ī*.

(p. 263) There is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) of the word *kakāra*—which denotes the first syllable of the compound *kāmakalā*—upon the vowel *ī*, which is what the word *kāmakalā* signifies.
For in the Sūtra, it is seen that by the word *makāra*— precisely through such an indication (*lakṣaṇā*)— the manifestation of that [state], the five *makāras*, the cause of the *mudrās*,
and purification and so forth are included; and in the *Tantrārambhastava*, which begins with "O Kāmapūrṇaja," the syllable *ja* refers to the *Jālandhara-pīṭha*.

And because of its inclusion: since the syllable *kāma-kāla* is extremely secret, it is improper to pronounce it aloud; therefore, an indirect, symbolic indication is what is appropriate there. As for the earlier commentators, they maintain that the wind is produced by the three *ka*-syllables contained within the mantra.

They explain it exactly as it was heard [in the source text]. That is incorrect, because it contradicts the subsequent passage beginning with "even by the three great māyās. For in that [passage], it is stated that only the four instances of the syllable *ī* signify the four types of contact (*sparśa*).

Furthermore, this is because it will be clearly stated later in the passage, "The seed-syllable of the possessor of qualities is also the denoter of the qualities," that the very phonemes which generate those respective elements serve as the indicators of those respective qualities;
and because the four *ka*-phonemes are absent from the Vidyā-mantra.

Furthermore, it is because it is impossible for [the letter *ka*] to characterize the fourfold contact (*sparśacatuṣṭaya*). Moreover, by the statement "of this [mantra] by the triad of Krodhīśas," it will be explained that the three *ka*-letters serve only to indicate the three types of practitioners.
Also, because the letter *ka* lacks the status of being a seed-syllable (*bīja*) of air (*vāyu*), and not because the letter *ya* alone is the seed-syllable of air.

It should not be argued that even in your own interpretation—where [the substitute] is regarded as having the nature of a *kāka-kalāpa* (a flock of crows)—that absence [of the original form] is equally present;
for [the substitute] is accepted as being similar to the original, just as *nīvāra* grain is similar to *vrīhi* rice.

Therefore, by way of similarity, there exists both the quality of being produced from the same place of articulation (*ekasthānotpannatva*) and the quality of being the substituendum (*sthānika*) for one another.
And the experience of hearing also accords with this. What more need be said?

It is well known that even the unity of phonetic symbols across different scripts is rooted solely in their mutual similarity, since even that serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in determining common worldly experience. Otherwise, how could this be so?
In the *Pikanema* dispute, let the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) be consistent with its basis in the usage of the Mlecchas.

Although all these reasons are equal regarding the similarity between the vowel *u* and the seed-syllable *va*, nevertheless, since the vowel *u* does not exist within the Veda (*vidyā*), while the syllable *va* does, [the former] cannot be accepted when a very similar [substitute] is available.

Since the letter *sa* resembles the letter *va*—which, like the *pūtaka* letters, belongs to the dental class—it is entirely logical to state that it generates the water element (*jalatattva*). Therefore, when this position arises, the author of the root text himself raises an objection regarding the contradiction with the rule: "The seed [of an element] must possess the qualities [of its corresponding element]."

It will be explained [later]. The word *tu* (but) is used for the very purpose of indicating such a distinction from the letter *ha* and others; likewise, the word *ca* (and) after *sakārāt* (from the letter *sa*) has that same meaning.
Therefore, because it generates the five elements, that Vidyā consists of the universe (*viśvamayī*) and is non-different from the universe (*viśvābhinnā*).
Now, if this is so, then for the sake of manifesting the *vidyā*, each individual consonant beginning with the letter *ha* would suffice; what is the use of their multiplicity? To this, he says:
"The qualities (*guṇa*) are declared to be fifteen; Śivā consists of those [elements]. (30)
Among the five elements in their un-pañcīkṛta state, each individual element is divided into two halves; one of these halves is further divided into four parts,
which are then mixed into the other four elements respectively, so that each [element] becomes unique.

Sound, touch, and so forth are perceived even in the other [elements]. There too, because the elements arise in the sequence "from the Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth," the qualities residing in the progenitor [are indeed present in the offspring].

The persistence [of qualities] occurs within the series of produced effects, not within the series of producers of those produced effects; for the principle is simply that "the qualities of the cause initiate the qualities of the effect.
And thus, regarding the quality of space...
Sound has fivefold variety because it persists from ether down to earth;

touch, as a quality of air, has fourfold variety because it persists in only four elements; likewise, color has threefold variety, taste has twofold variety, and smell has onefold variety—thus, taken together, these are the varieties of the elements.

There are fifteen qualities. Among those, the echo that is heard in caves and other such places as a resonance of sound is the quality of space (ākāśa). The sounds of air and so forth, as well as touch and the rest, are already well known. In this manner are the qualities of the elements.
Since the number fifteen is well-known, the Vidyā of Śiva is also composed of that [number],
meaning it consists of fifteen syllables beginning with the letter *ha*. According to the sequence already stated,
there are five *ha*s, four *ī*s, three *ra*s, two *sa*s, and one *la*.
The intended meaning is that they abide in a single knowledge (*vidyā*). If it is asked, "In that case, why are two *la*-letters recited as being in excess?
[the answer is: "Because she is Maheśvarī, who possesses a threefold nature due to her connection with the three worlds," according to that text.
Because the authors of the root text themselves will provide the resolution of this doubt;

for although in the first and second *kūṭas* there is indeed the letter *la*, known as *duḥspṛṣṭa*, since in some *tantras* their extraction is seen under the term "the syllable of delusion" (*mohārṇa*). For this very reason, in the commentary on the *Brahma-sūtra* regarding the Goddess...

It has been stated that the word *īla* is derived from the verbal root *īḍ*, meaning "to praise. Consequently, since there is only a single letter *la* in the third *kūṭa*, the aforementioned doubt does not arise; nevertheless, in this present Tantra, [the letters] *ḍa* and *la* are treated as identical.

It should be understood that since a doubt might arise because the extraction of the first syllable of *hṛllekhā* is seen even in the three *kūṭas* by means of the word "Indra-bīja" itself, [the author] will resolve it by another method. || 30 ||
Now, even if seventeen syllables are necessary according to the method stated above, one might object that additional syllables such as 'a', 'ka', and so forth are redundant; therefore, he says:
Whatever power is proclaimed to belong to whichever object, that is the Goddess who is the Sovereign of All, and that [object] is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) himself. (31)

For there is no entity whatsoever that exists without a seed and a purpose, according to the maxim that "even a fool does not act without aiming at a purpose"; how much more so in the case of the Lord, who is present everywhere—this is the meaning. And therefore, in respect to every entity...
Power (*śakti*) indeed exists in the form of the capacity to produce its respective specific effects.

That [power] is *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), and its substratum is *prakāśa* (light); such is the meaning. And it is said in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "The female gender is Gaurī; the male gender is Nīlalohita."

The meaning is this: the universe is not composed solely of fifteen qualities (*guṇas*), for it consists of thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) and even more categories of entities exist; and all of these are pervaded by Tripurasundarī, whose nature is Śiva and Śakti. And as for Vidyā...
If that were not all-pervasive, how could the non-difference between Vidyā and Īśvarī be established, since— unlike Śiva and Śakti—

they would lack pervasion of the entire universe? Therefore, for the purpose of manifesting and making known [the reality] as the self of the entire universe, the letters beginning with A, Ka, and so forth, are indispensable.

But the predecessors [object]: "Now, in the fifteen-syllable mantra, there are only five syllables—*ha*, *ka*, *ra*, *sa*, and *la*; what is the purpose of the other ten? To this he replies: "The qualities (*guṇāḥ*).
That [mantra] consists of them; it consists of fifteen syllables made up of vowels along with their consonantal adjuncts (*vyañjana*).

The meaning is that these are to be meditated upon as possessing fifteen qualities. Now, one might object that it is impossible to speak of the *vidyā* as having a nature consisting of fifteen aspects because such a thing is inconceivable; to this, he says: "Of whatever... Since the entire universe is pervaded by Śiva and Śakti, [it is possible].

They explain that the point is this: how could it be impossible for Śiva and Śakti, who constitute the universe, to pervade even a single part of the universe, since that is established by the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic? That is incorrect, because later on there is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that the consonants beginning with *ha* alone consist of the qualities of the elements (*bhūtaguṇa*).
Because that would contradict [the fact of] being currently opened;

and because it was not previously stated that vowels (*svara*) together with consonants (*vyañjana*) are the generators of space (*vyoman*) and so forth; furthermore, the vowel *a* heard in the word "hakārāt" is not the base (*prakṛti*) for the suffix *kāra*; for the vowel *a* is separated [from the consonant].

Regarding the term "of the consonants" (*vyañjanānām*): according to the *Taittirīya-Prātiśākhya-sūtra*, these [consonants] are prescribed merely as being pronounced between the base form (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). This is because the inclusion of the letter *a* in the sūtras beginning with *hayavaraḍ* is for the purpose of indicating that in the rule *varṇāt kāraḥ*, only those [consonants] qualified by the vowel *a* are to be understood.

For this very reason, it is said "rādiph" (beginning with *ra*) and not "e-pha" (beginning with *e*). Even though it is said: "O Rāvaṇa, names beginning with the letter *ra*—such as Rama—and even jewels, cause me great terror because of Rama."

In this context, just as the very collection of phonemes consisting of the letter *r* qualified by the letter *a* is the base (*prakṛti*) for the suffix *-kāra*, the derivation of that suffix from the collection is established by the indicative authority (*jñāpaka*) of the term *vaṣaṭkāra*.
For if only a single *r* were the base, it would contradict the exception (*apavāda*) stating "from *r* etc., [the suffix] *pha*."

Because [otherwise] the suffix *kāra* would not apply. Just as in that case, here in "hakārāt" and so forth, it is said that the letter *ha* qualified by the vowel *a* (*akāra-viśiṣṭa-hakāra*) alone is the base;
nevertheless, since there is no letter *ra* qualified by the vowel *a* in the mantra, [the rule] states "from *ra*, fire" (*rephād agniḥ*).

There is no risk of [the rule] becoming a mere restatement (anuvāda) due to the specific qualification of the vowel *a* at the root. Alternatively, the vowel *a* is not included within the category of the original base (*prakṛti*) for that much alone. If that is so, then by virtue of its being read in proximity to those [cases], let it be the same for the phoneme *bha* and others as well;
such is the direction [of the argument]. || 31 ||

But even so, does this not contradict the "ringing proclamation" heard in the Tantras and Purāṇas that there are fifteen syllables in the Vidyā? Therefore, the existence of additional syllables is not logical, since it is through them that the pervasion of the entire universe would be accomplished. Or, if they do exist—

There is a contradiction with the designation "consisting of fifteen syllables. Anticipating the objection that this is like a rope with snares at both ends, he resolves it by stating that both are appropriate due to a distinction in their application:
"That Vidyā, whose nature consists of the qualities of the elements, is pervaded by fifteen syllables."
And likewise with five, six, and even four syllables. || 32 ||
Through the division of vowels and consonants, she is divided into thirty-seven;
through the division into thirty-seven, she takes the form of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
And this Vidyā, whose nature transcends the [lower] principles (tattva), is always meditated upon;

for by the statement "later on, through the distinction of vowels and consonants," it is implied here that [it is meditated upon] through the unity of vowels and consonants. And this unity belongs to the whole (aṅgin) as distinguished by its parts (aṅga).
This is with the intention of [counting them as] a single unit. Consequently, the second and third [syllables], being mere vowels (*svarāḥ*), are indeed without limbs (*niraṅgakāḥ*).
The *l*-sounds, the *ā*-sounds, and the *ī*-sounds—both types—are each distinguished by a single limb (*ekaikāṅgaviśiṣṭāḥ*); there are six such [syllables].
Furthermore, according to the *Yājuṣaprātiśākhya*, this includes the consonant at the beginning of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) and the *anusvāra*.

Because the status of being a preceding limb (*pūrvāṅga*) has been prescribed; the other seven vowels are qualified by their own respective preceding limbs. It is another matter that, according to the method of the *Prātiśākhyas* such as the *Bahvṛca-prātiśākhya*, the status of being a succeeding limb (*uttarāṅga*) is also possible for the syllables beginning with *hṛllekhā*. However, regarding the triad of *nādas*, [the rule] in the *Prātiśākhyas* and other texts...
Even though their status as constituent parts (*aṅga*) is not described separately,
because they are taught in conjunction with the *bindu*, they possess the status of constituents just like the *bindu*. Thus,
the twenty-two consonants are constituents of the vowels, and of those [consonants]...

The designation [of the *sāmidhenī* verses] as fifteen is established because they have been so stated; this is demonstrated in the scriptural passage beginning with "He is indeed Prajāpati, the seventeenfold," specifically in the text "‘Āśrāvaya’ has four syllables," etc.,
according to the rule "the first syllable is elided after ‘catur’ and ‘śat’."
p. 267) For elsewhere in the *Smṛti* as well, the counting of syllables is well-known by this very method.

"Knowledge" (*vidyā*), "beings" (*bhūtāni*), and "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) form a *dvandva* compound. "Knowledge" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the other principles (*tattvas*). By that, it consists of thirty-six principles.

The meaning is "the root-vidyā. Alternatively, it means that which consists of the three qualities—sattva and the others—which have become reflections of consciousness (cicchāyā) and have attained the nature of vidyā. The resulting sense, however, is that it takes the form of the principles (tattvas) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
Or rather, its meaning is simply that vidyā is composed of consonants (vyañjana) denoting the qualities of the elements (bhūtaguṇa). Therefore, [the objection] here does not apply.

One should consider that the fifteen vowels are proclaimed by the ancients to consist of fifteen qualities (*guṇa*), because it will be stated later that only the consonants, beginning with *ha*, possess the nature of the qualities. Therefore, [the following applies] to the thirty-seven syllables in their respective order:

The interpretation of the predecessors— that the subsequent verse speaks of "the thirty-six principles and the one that transcends the principles" in this manner— is also not tenable; for [this] text [deals with] the meanings of the thirty-seven syllables which are to be analyzed later on.

Because it serves merely the purpose of providing a brief summary; for, given that the introduction states "the tradition is of the nature of Great Awakening" and the conclusion states "the meaning of the tradition has been declared," the intermediate portion of the text functions solely to convey the single subject matter designated as the "tradition."
Since the unity of all [the texts] is established,
there is no occasion for the two types of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) you have mentioned— which exceed the meaning of the traditional transmission—
because that would result in a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, in the case of the *Vaiśvānara* sacrifice, when a son is born...

Thus, since the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) is established by the opening statement "In whom [the Self] is born" and the concluding statement "In whom [the Self] is born," those sentences concerning the eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth— which are recited in the middle—
serve solely as supplements (*śeṣa*) to that [concluding statement] by way of establishing the result of the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*), and not otherwise.

In the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*, it was accepted that these two [passages] enjoin a separate oblation (*havirantara*). Likewise, since these two impressions (*vāsanā*) can be justified as being subordinate to the subject matter to be explained— serving merely as a concise introduction— it is not [the case that they are independent].

It should be understood that the postulation of independence is logical. He divides the fifteen syllables according to their distinct *kūṭa* forms in order to exclude any lesser or greater number—with the words "by five" and so forth. Regarding "vowels" (*svara*): vowels are those which shine by themselves; the consonants (*vyañjana*) are those manifested by them.

"Among those, because the vowels are independent, the consonant is that which is manifested by them," according to the statement in the *Tantrarāja*. Thus, by the very force of this etymological derivation, he refutes the capacity of the consonants to fulfill the required number of syllables.

"By way of division" means by imagining all [the syllables] as distinct words. And this being the case, there is no occurrence of *jaś*-substitution for the three *ka* sounds; for although the status of being a "word-final" (*padānta*) would apply to a single-syllable word by virtue of the principle of "designation as if possessing [its own properties]," that status is rendered non-obligatory (*anitya*) by the indicative marks (*jñāpaka*) such as *suppitau ṭakitau*, and thus it does not occur here.
It is so called because it possesses thirty-seven distinct divisions (*prabheda*) as its constituent parts (*avayava*).

Regarding the word *saptatriṃśatprabheda*, the suffix *in* (denoting possession) is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.115 (*matvarthīya*), while the suffix *ac* is applied according to 5.2.127 (*arśa-ādyac*). Consequently, in the expression *tena prabhedena*, there is no occurrence of the plural number.

This Vidyā, through a collection consisting of thirty-seven components, defines and makes known the thirty-six fundamental principles (tattvas). Furthermore, it is such that its own intended meaning—the object to be known—is beyond those principles; thus, it is meditated upon and contemplated by yogis throughout the three periods of time. This is the meaning.

In the word *sada*, there is also sometimes the reading *mayā*. There is one [syllable] consisting of the eleventh vowel (*au*), two from the seed-syllable of the Moon (*sa*), three each from the seed-syllables of Fire (*ra*), Earth (*la*), Krodhīśa (*ha*), Bindu, and Nāda; four from the Kāmakalās;
five from the seed-syllables of Space (*ha*); and ten from the Śrīkaṇṭhas—thus it is.
The principles (tattvas) and that which transcends them are expounded by thirty-seven syllables;

this is the meaning of the summary of the traditional doctrine (saṃpradāyārtha). In the Hādividyā, however, two elements are lacking: one Kāmakalā and one of the eleven vowels, while the Moon-seed (candrabīja) is present as one.

The seed-syllable of space (*vyoma*) is one, and there are two *Śrīkaṇṭhas*; thus, four [syllables] are added. Consequently, they amount to thirty-nine. Among those, regarding the letter *ha* in the middle of the second *kūṭa* and the first letter *ā* in the third *kūṭa*, [the explanation is given] in the section on the meaning of the underlying essence (*bhāvārtha*).
Because they are described as being the cause [of all], one should describe them as thirty-seven by setting aside those two [categories].
As it is said in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"Her form is manifested through the divisions of the vowels, consonants, and the three points taken together."
"Vidyā consists of the thirty-six principles and is also that which transcends the principles, being absolute. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, we do not know which tantra that calculation belongs to. Furthermore, those earlier authorities who, following that [calculation], apply it to this very tantra should be questioned as to what the basis is for abandoning the three *nādas* and adopting the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) here. Now, [one might object]: "But..."

In the *Pāṇinīya-śikṣā*, during the enumeration of phonemes (*varṇa*), it is stated that "sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes are recognized according to the view of Śambhu"; since *nāda* (the unmanifest sound) is not included in this count,

and because it consists merely of resonance (*dhvani*) and thus lacks the status of a phoneme (*varṇa*), it possesses neither the quality of being a vowel (*svara*) nor that of a consonant (*vyañjana*).

Since they are necessarily absent in the absence of that [phoneme] because they are pervaded by the property of being phonemes (varṇatva), and since thirty-seven are mentioned at the root specifically through the division of vowels and consonants, it is not appropriate to include the *nādas* among them;
consequently, it is established that [the phonemes] are indeed differentiated into thirty-six.

The attainment of the totality (*samaṣṭi*) occurs through the impossibility [of the thirty-seven categories] otherwise and by the statement that they demonstrate the reality beyond the principles (*tattvātīta*), because that [totality] consists of the fourth principle (*turīya-tattva*).
The *ātma-tattva* extends up to *māyā*, while the *vidyā-tattva* would extend up to *sadāśiva*.
Śakti and Śiva are the Śiva-tattva; this is the fourth principle (turīya-tattva), which is the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of these.

Thus, according to the words of the learned authorities. Nor should it be asked: "Since the collective reality (*samaṣṭitattva*) is that which is to be purified, being by nature eternally pure and transcending all categories (*tattvātīta*), how can it have that [impure] nature?
For the Fourth State (*turīya*), which consists of the body of the Great Cause (*mahākāraṇadeha*), possesses the forms of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies.
Even for one who has transcended the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), because [the self] takes the form of the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*), there is the mantra:

"May my sheaths of food (*annamaya*), vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and bliss (*ānandamaya*) be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil. (p. 269)

Because [the self] is enumerated only among those things to be purified (*śodhya*), for this very reason, with the intention that it does not possess the nature of Brahman, the *Anandamaya-Adhikaraṇa* is explained in a different manner, having set aside the view of Upavarṣa and others who consider it to be so.

If it is argued that this has been described by the venerable Ācāryapāda [Śaṅkara], it is not so; for in his *Bhāṣya* on the *Śaunaka-sūtra*, which asks whether an *anusvāra* is a consonant (*vyañjana*) or a vowel (*svara*), he states that the *bindu* consists of neither. Consequently, since the three *bindus* would likewise fall outside the category of both vowels and consonants, they ought not to be counted in the present context.
Furthermore, in the *Yājuṣa-Prātiśākhya*, by the rule "the remainder are consonants" (*śeṣo vyañjanāni*),

the definition of a consonant is stated as being a phoneme distinct from a vowel; thus, the inclusion of the *bindu* as a consonant is necessary, as indicated by the word "vā" (or) in Śaunaka’s sūtra.

It should not be argued that an explanation based on the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is itself improper; for since the distinction of *svarabhinnatva* (being differentiated by tone) is optionally attributed to the *nāda* (sound), its status as a consonant (*vyañjana*) is established. Nor should it be argued that because *nāda* consists of resonance (*dhvani*), it lacks the nature of a phoneme (*varṇa*); for just as the nature of clay (*mṛttva*) exists in a jar, so too does it exist in phonemes.
Since *dhvani*-ness is accepted [as a property], it is not pervaded by the absence of *varṇa*-ness (i.e., *dhvani* is not a *varṇa*). Nor should it be argued:

"If it were a *varṇa*, why is it not enumerated among the *varṇas* in the *Śikṣā* and other texts? For even though it is not enumerated there, we maintain that the long *ḷ*-sound (*dīrgha-ḷkāra*) is intended to be a *varṇa* according to our view.

Because their non-inclusion [in the list] is not a disqualifying factor. Now, one might argue that the long *ḷ* vowel possesses the status of a phoneme (*varṇatva*) because it is recited separately among the fifty-one *mātṛkā*s;
however, if that were the case, the simple *bindu* and the *upadhmānīya* would fail to attain the status of phonemes. Nor can it be argued that [this applies to the *nāda*].

If it were a *varṇa* (phoneme), it would necessarily be counted among the consonants (*vyañjana*), which would entail—by the rule that "a consonant is subordinate to a vowel"—its connection with a vowel. Furthermore, since *anusvāra* possesses the status of a vowel as well, its inclusion [as a vowel] would be acceptable.
Moreover, in the *Navārṇameru-mantra*, the letter *ka* is seen to be recited even after the vowel *ā*. As for *nāda*...
According to the view of the Easterners (*prācām*), because [consonants] lack the status of being phonemes (*vyañjana*) due to having a duration of less than half a *mātrā* by one *lava*,
they are not included even when counting a certain number of phonemes useful only for their own specific treatises; thus, they are not counted among those well-known elsewhere.

The reality, however, is simply that there is an exhaustive enumeration of "color-ness" (*varṇatva*) within the phonemes (*varṇa*). Now, if it is argued that in the very *Prakṛtatantra* itself, the usage of the term "sound" (*dhvani*) is observed for seeds (*bīja*), points (*bindu*), and resonances (*dhvani*) as being of the nature of the planets (*graha*) within the three peaks (*trikūṭa*); [we reply:]...

Furthermore, since there is even the conventional usage of the term "syllable" (akṣara) in such passages as "by the thirty-five syllables arising from the three *hṛllekhās*," what is the point [of that objection]? Moreover, because the nature of resonance (*dhvanitva*) is all-pervasive. Furthermore, if *nāda* were merely of the nature of sound (*dhvani*), the description of its meaning within the Tantras would be impossible.

Furthermore, there would be no separate description of the time for its eight constituent parts. Nor is it possible for it to function as a reminder of the ritual object in the same way as the sound of a chariot; for while it may serve as a reminder in that specific instance due to the injunction that it occurs at the same time as the commencement of the Māhendra-stotra, this does not apply to other instances of the sound of a chariot.

Because of its absence [in that case]. And in the present context, there is a disparity because the *nāda* is assigned a specific power (*śakti*) with respect to a particular meaning, whereas it does not possess such a status everywhere. Furthermore, regarding the absence of *bindu* from the class of consonants as stated in the sūtras of Śaunaka and others, even the author of the *Kāmakalāvilāsa* [states] that [it arises] from the consonants...
Even though the three *bindus* are not explicitly present in the root word due to their being counted separately as *anu*s, this is understood simply because, in the subsequent stage of exposition,
we see the description of their meaning as "Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva" by means of the three *bindus*.

Even against your will, you must explain that by the word "vyañjana" (consonant) here, the *bindus* are also intended because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). This is equally applicable to the triad of *nādas*, as the subsequent description of the meaning states: "Peace (*śānti*), Power (*śakti*), and Śambhu are the awakening of the triad of *nādas*."

Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the duration of half a *mātrā*, just as there is between different consonants; therefore, we do not perceive any reason whatsoever for abandoning the triad of *nādas*. Consequently, it is established that the *Kādividyā* consists of thirty-seven components by that very [reckoning].

Since there is no impossibility [of its being otherwise] in that case, even the apprehension of a collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) is entirely untenable; for one obtains a syllable (*akṣara*) that denotes something transcending the principles (*tattva*). In reality, there is no evidence that the term "transcending the principles" refers to the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*).

Even though it transcends the three bodies (*dehatraya*), because it is of the nature of the fourth principle (*turyatattva*), it is impossible for it to transcend the principles (*tattva*); therefore, since it must be declared as being solely the Supreme Brahman, there is no necessity for including a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*).
On the contrary, in the *hādividyā*, it is that which brings about the forty subdivisions of the collective totality.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the root text, which states that [the Vidya] has thirty-seven divisions through the distinction of vowels, consonants, and both, as well as by their non-distinction. Therefore, in the *Hādividyā*,
according to the requirements of the present Tantra, [the division occurs] through the abandonment and inclusion of the three *nādas* taken as a collective whole.
It should be understood that even for the teachers who protect speech (the Siddhas), a description divided into thirty-seven [categories] is difficult to accomplish.
By this, one should consider that the anxiety as to how the state of thirty-seven could exist in the Kādi-vidyā as it does in the Hādi-vidyā is,
on the contrary, merely a void regarding the Kādi-vidyā itself.

Wandering about with the desire to avoid that [objection], the various lineages of gurus, establishing the number thirty-seven, teach their disciples that the counting of the second [vowel] as a *saṃdhyakṣara* (diphthong) and the third as being long— thus consisting of two syllables each— is established by tradition (*saṃpradāya*).

Furthermore, the succession of texts beginning with the *Cidvallī* must be understood as refuted, for— being rooted in the delusive activity of Amṛtānandanātha— they follow the maxim of "the blind leading the blind."

Because even for the remaining three *kāmakalās*, there is no difference in their length, and they would result in an excess of syllables; therefore, it is appropriate to justify that there are exactly thirty-seven effect-syllables (*kāryākṣara*), while the description of the meaning of the sentence is as follows:
Since it is improper to describe the meaning of a sentence by omitting two words merely through the combination of the meanings of the constituent parts, enough of this prolixity. || 32 || 33 ||

By this much of the treatise, it has been stated in a general manner that the nature of *vidyā* consists of the entire collection of categories (padārtha) beginning with the real qualities (*bhūtaguṇa*) and ending with that which transcends reality (*tattvātīta*); now, that very same [nature] is [to be explained] preceded by the statement of their respective definitions.
He explains by making it clear: (p. 271) "Among the elements, beginning with earth, each subsequent one is all-pervasive. (34)
The lower element, however, is the pervaded; its qualities reside in the pervader.
O Goddess, they are situated within the pervaded things through the distinction of gross and subtle. (35)
In the phrase "earth and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes water, fire, air, and space.

Among these, each subsequent element is more pervasive (*vyāpaka*), generative (*janaka*), and instrumental (*prayojaka*). Since pervasion is observed in the case of clay with respect to the jar produced from it, the term "pervasive" refers to the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
Similarly, pervasion (*vyāpakatva*), defined as the state of not being the counter-positive (*apratiyogitva*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing therein, remains entirely intact.

However, the distinction is this: possession of that [property] is by way of the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*), whereas the absence has its counter-positiveness delimited by the relation of transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). Below...
Each preceding term is pervaded by and produced by each succeeding term;
and "produced" (prayojya) consists in not occurring in that which possesses a transformative absence (pariṇāmyabhāvavat),
while its occurrence in such an absence is restricted precisely by the two aforementioned relations.

Therefore, for that reason, the qualities (guṇas) which reside in the pervader (vyāpaka)— being inherent in both the producer (janaka) and the prompter (prayojaka)— also abide in the pervaded (vyāpya), namely in the produced (janya) and the prompted (prayojya). Those qualities situated in the cause are called "gross" (sthūla), while those same qualities situated in the effects are called "subtle" (sūkṣma).
This is the meaning. || 34 || 35 ||
Anticipating the objection, "What relevance does that have to the present subject?",
he demonstrates the syllables that denote the thirty-six principles:
"Therefore, sound, which is the quality of space, exists pervading air and the other elements."
One should perceive the fivefold sound by means of the seed-syllables of space situated within the Vidyā-mantra. || 36 ||
The supreme [reality], consisting of resonance, abides within them in the form of their cause.
It may be the seed of those possessed of virtues, and it is also the designator of virtues. || 37 ||
Because of the relationship of cause and effect, there is an intended expression of their identity;
since the qualities of the pervader reside within the pervaded, therefore sound—the quality of the all-pervading ether—resides pervading air and the other elements: air, fire, water, and earth.

Sound is fivefold. Therefore, by means of the five *ha*-syllables—the seeds of space (*vyoma*) residing in the Vidyā—the practitioner (the remainder of the sentence) should characterize the fivefold sound. According to the view of the ancients, "characterization" (*lakṣaṇā*) is the apprehension of the impossible through the possible.

The practitioner alone is the agent by virtue of being the locus of the mental presence [of the object]. This is because the function known as *lakṣaṇā* (indication), which consists in a relation with what is possible [to be denoted], is itself a mode of operation. Furthermore, even under the view that [the function] resides in the word, according to the established doctrine that "case-endings arise based on the speaker's intention," when there is an intention to express the word's status as an instrument (*karaṇa*), [it belongs to] the practitioner.

The agency of the instigator (*prayojakakartṛtva*). Now, an objection is raised: it was stated in the section on the meaning of verbal roots (bhāvārtha-prakaraṇa, p. 272) that the middle *ahaṃkāra* denotes reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). If that [middle *ahaṃkāra*] were also to indicate the word (*śabda*), there would be a contradiction of two simultaneous functions (*vṛttidvaya-virodha*). To this [objection]:

He said: "Of those. Among those five *ha*-letters, the syllable *ha* in the form of the *visarga*, which exists as the causal form—either as the cause of the universe consisting of the Śrīcakra or as a constituent of the body of Kāmakalā, the cause of the world—that indeed consists of resonance (*dhvanimaya*).

It consists solely of *nāda*. For this very reason, it is "supreme," meaning subtler even than the subtle, namely the body composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). While the letter *ha* in its gross form as *vaikharī* signifies the phoneme (*śabda*), the *ha* in its supreme form denotes the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*).

The intention is that there is no contradiction between the two functions (vṛtti), because it has been stated that a single word can convey two meanings through a difference in its grammatical forms (padavyakti).

However, in the system of the Hādī-vidyā, they apply this half-verse as being intended to describe the purpose of the sixth letter *ha*; thus, the sixth *ha*-syllable [is distinguished] from the five preceding *ha*-syllables.

The meaning is that the *nāda* which serves as the cause is that which makes [the reality] known. It is also easily explained that the sense is: "that which is beyond even the thirty-six *tattvas*—the *nāda*-Brahman—is the supreme [object], namely the letter *ha* in the middle of the *kāmarāja* [mantra]. This is in accordance with the meaning stated in the section on the essential import (*bhāvārtha-prakaraṇa*).

Because [otherwise] there would be no possibility of agreement; and because that meaning, not being connected with the meaning of that sentence, must necessarily be employed in this very context. Now, one might ask: how can there be a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the letter *ha*, which denotes space, in words such as "wind" (*vāyu*), given the absence of any possible relationship? To this, he says:

It would be as follows: according to the general rule that "whatever syllable denotes a thing possessing a certain quality indicates that very quality inherent in it," since the designation of the quality of sound (*śabda*) is established for the letter *ha* which denotes space (*vyoman*), [it follows] for that very sound...

Even when there is a connection with another reality, the previously established indication (lakṣaṇā) is not impaired; for there is no impairment whatsoever of the indication when those indicated by the word "staff"—namely, the staff-bearers—go to another place.
