Nor does that [indication] cease even when they go to another place.
It should not be argued that metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is appropriate because of the non-separation from the connection with a staff;

for even though sound resides in air and the other elements, since the persistence of the cause in the effect is necessary, the persistence of space exists in all four [air, fire, water, and earth] as well.

The sense is that this non-separation from space is equally applicable to the present case as well. For this very reason, he will state in the definition of the meaning of the word *tejaḥ* (light/heat): "Light is essentially form (*rūpa*), for it is produced by its seed.
This is because the property of being non-different from what is signified belongs to the indicative (*lakṣaka*) term just as it does to the denotative (*vācaka*) one.
To demonstrate its actual existence, he points to it as a secondary indicator using the term "denotative" (*vācakam*).

The intended meaning is that there is no difference between the denoted and the denoter, just as there is none between the indicated and the indicator. Alternatively, the syntactical connection is: the seed, which is the denotator of those possessing qualities (*guṇavat*), also becomes the denotator of the qualities themselves.

The meaning is that because the letter *ha* possesses expressive power (*śakti*) only with respect to sound (*śabda*), its power is not lost even when sound is the delimitor of the denotable object (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); thus, the letter *ha* is also the denoter (*vācaka*) of sound. Consequently, the word "should indicate" (*lakṣayet*), although appearing at the beginning [of the verse], means "one should know," since its agent is the practitioner (*upāsaka*).

Regarding the word "kārya" (effect): since air and space stand in a relationship of cause and effect, and with the intention of expressing the persistence of space within air and so forth, it is appropriate to employ *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for its quality, namely sound. Alternatively, [the term] "ākāśam" (space)...

According to the method stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*— "that which is born from the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) and has sound as its quality is *vidhi*"— or according to the Naiyāyika method— "sound [arises] from space"—
the non-difference between sound and space is intended here by virtue of their relationship as cause and effect.
The meaning is that, just as with the element ether (*ākāśa*), both *śakti* (primary denotative power) and *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indicative function) are applicable to the letter *ha*.

In reality, however, the meaning is that the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which denotes those possessing qualities (*guṇavatām*) also becomes the denoter of the qualities themselves; that is to say, it is the denoter of the qualified entity. [This applies] in the mantra.

Because no other syllables are specified for those denoting the elements; and because sound and the others are designated by the term "guṇa" alone, omitting the term "tanmātra," this same principle applies to sattva, rajas, and tamas as well—which will be discussed later—since there is no difference in their status as *guṇas*. This is what is implied.

Now, in a cognition produced by the letter *ha* and others which denote space (*vyoman*) and so forth, is sound (*śabda*) and the rest the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) or the qualifier (*prakāra*)? It cannot be the first [option], because that would entail the repetition of the letter *ha* and so forth in order to avoid contradicting the maxim regarding what is uttered only once (*sakṛduccarita-nyāya*).
Because it is impossible for multiple meanings and multiple modes of qualificands to be presented from a single word without repetition;

nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, because since the qualities have been reduced to being the delimiters of the denotability (*vācyatāvacchedaka*), it is impossible for the denoter to be non-different from them, and thus the intended meaning is not established. For indeed...
Since there exists a non-difference based on the genus (*jāti*) of words and so forth, even though there is no non-difference among the denotata of words, phonemes, syllables, and so on,

he says "kārya" (effect) etc. Even if the intended [conclusion] is not established because there is no causal relation between the denotatum and the delimitor of denotability (*vācyatāvacchedaka*), in the present case—

The sense is that even if one accepts the cognition of the delimitor of the denotable (vācyatāvacchedaka) as a qualifier by virtue of its being produced by the denoted (vācya), it is nonetheless logical that the letters are non-different from the denoter and are not repeated. || 36 || 37 ||
Having thus indicated the syllables of space, he explains the syllables of air as they follow in sequence: "By means of the triad of Mahāmāyās and also by the cause, the Bindu. (38)
O Goddess, one should meditate upon the fourfold tactile sensations of air, fire, water, and earth as they have arisen, according to their distinction as gross and subtle. (39)
The three *mahāmāyās* consist of the three *īkāras* forming the *hṛllekhā*; the *kāraṇabindu* is the *kāmakalā*.
Regarding [the statement] "the three forms of *ī* are *mahāmāyā*," the *Śivottama-kośa* states:
"Śiva is *tuṣṭi*, and the fourth is *bindumālinī*. This is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the *bindus* situated within the *śrīcakra*.

"By reason of" means that it has been stated previously that the *bindu* consisting of the *kāmakalā* is the cause of the *cakrabindu*. By this, there is the exclusion of the syllable (*akṣara*) to be described later in the context of the *kaulikārtha*, which is non-different from the *cakrabindu*. This refers to the letter *ī* without the *nirbindu* (dot) as the fourth.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the fourfold touch— consisting of one gross [touch] residing in air and three subtle [touches] residing in fire and so forth— as having arisen from the four *ī* vowels.

In the *hādi* system, however, the vowel *a* situated in the first syllable of the third *kūṭa* is to be understood by the term "causal *bindu*" (*kāraṇabindu*). The qualifier "causal" (*kāraṇa*) is employed to suggest that the status of being the cause of touch for that which is the cause of all is established by the logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*). [This is] the *bindu*.
The letter *a* is emptiness (*śūnya*). For this very reason, in the section concerning the letter *a*, [it is stated] that Kāmeśī and Vāsinī are "space" (*viyat*);
thus, the word "space" in the lexicon is used as a designation for the letter *a* in the form of a dot (*bindu*), in order to exclude other instances of the letter *a*.
This is because the letter *a*, which is the form of all causes, is itself the form of emptiness. However, the ancients [hold a different view].
Some explain [the term] as "by the *bindu* called Kāmākhya, which constitutes the body of the *kāmakalā*. That is not correct;

for such a form, distinct from the three *mahāmāyās*, is not seen in the *hādividyā*. Furthermore, it is improper to count again that which has already been counted once as a constituent part of the triad. This would result in an inconsistency.
Furthermore, since there is no decisive reason for choosing one over the others, it would follow that all three must be counted.

If you accept this consequence, there is an excess of thirty-seven [categories]. If you resolve this by discarding two of them, then why such hostility toward our own method? (Even though) such hostility is equal regarding the discarding of either pair, nevertheless—

Furthermore, according to your view, because the grasping of the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) is accepted and the three *nādas* are difficult to discard, the contradiction regarding the number remains as it was; moreover, no author of any philosophical system (*darśana*) agrees that the individual components of a single syllable can independently function as constituents of the meaning of a sentence. Therefore, [this is not the case].
This is a minor matter. || 38 || 39 ||
Now he explains the syllables of fire:
"The triad of forms is manifested by those three *repha*s;
for the primary form of fire is produced by that seed-syllable. (40)

The triad consists of those [qualities] residing in fire, water, and earth. Now, one might ask: since two of these reside in water and earth, how can they be characterized by the seed-syllable of fire? To this he says: "the primary" (pradhāna). This has already been explained. || 40 ||
Now he explains the syllables of water:
"By means of the moon-seeds situated in the Vidyā, the gross and the subtle are known as *rasa* (flavor);
their connection in the world is understood as that between *rasa* and nectar. (41)
(With the seed-syllables of the Moon, which are *sakāra*s;
*so haṃsaḥ*). According to the lexicon: "The innate (*sahaja*) is Viṣṇu, Bhṛgu, and Īśa, and is designated as the Moon.
(The gross is pervasive and resides in water; the subtle is all-pervading and resides in earth.)
Even by the two plural expressions "the seed-syllables of the Moon residing in the Vidyās," only the number two is expressed;
for the expressed rasa is described as being twofold— namely, gross (*sthūla*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*)— each occurring individually.

And because there is an absence of a third case-ending; for the Mahābhāṣya describes the grammatical correctness of the plural number even when there is duality, on the basis of usages such as "my eyes are beautiful" and "my feet are delicate. [This applies to] the phrase "in the belly, the Śava, and the wind-quarters," which occurs in the section concerning the ritual placement (*cakranyāsa*).

Furthermore, this meaning is also accepted by the ancient masters who explain that the phrase "by the lords of heroes" (*vīrendraiḥ*) found in the section on the meaning of the intended sense refers to the two corners,
and that the term "Śāntāmbikā" refers solely to both [corners]. In the present case as well, according to their view, it is only the second half [of the verse] that [is relevant].
Furthermore, because this plural number must necessarily convey the number two by way of being an explanation of the third *sakāra*, it follows from this that,
due to the presence of the plural number here, the entire text concerning the meaning of the tradition (*saṃpradāya*) refers exclusively to the *Hādividyā*.
The satisfaction of those who think thus and are partial to that view is rejected because it is merely pleasant at first sight.
With the intention that even a single word does not exceed what is required for recalling the absence of a further [quality], he says: "is remembered" (*smṛta*).
The meaning is that one should remember two flavors by means of two similar [words]. Now, [an objection]:

Since there is no difference in the luminosity of the moon, the sun, and fire, it would be more logical for the seed-syllable of the moon (*sakāra*)—just like the *repha* of the fire-seed-syllable—to indicate form rather than taste, as there is no possible connection [between the latter and taste]. To this, he says: "The connection," referring to that between taste and nectar.
The meaning is that the connection is indeed well-known. The word *amṛta* refers both to nectar (*sudhā*) and to water.
The underlying idea is this: the lunar orb is not of the nature of light, but rather of the nature of water;
for within the watery orb, due to the varying degrees of proximity and distance from the solar rays, [it reflects them] partially.

When there is a connection, those very solar rays, having been reflected therein and turned back from it, acquire a state of non-heat due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), like solar rays reflected within a mirror;
spreading upon the earth, they become designated by the term "moonlight" (*candrikā*). This is as follows:

This is clear to those who know the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). As for that water in the lunar orb, whether it is purely of the nature of nectar (*amṛta*) or otherwise is a separate matter.

Consequently, just as the seed-syllable *va* is the designator of water in general, so too the seed-syllable *sa* is the designator of a specific kind of water; this is the only distinction. It does not amount to more than this.

Regarding the letters *va* and *sa*, there is no doubt that they possess the same characteristic as being inherent in that [word], just as in the case of the two words in the sentences "a hamlet on the river" (*nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), where there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the bank.
Even though, in the absence of the letter *ya*, [the letter *la*] is like its very close counterpart, so too in the absence of the letter *va*...
Even by the principle of the sixth [chapter], which states that when something very similar is unavailable, one may take what is slightly similar,
this [interpretation] is well-supported; nevertheless,
since taking what is slightly similar is considered a resort of last resort (*agati*), the primary solution remains superior even to that.

It should be understood that this was stated by the authors of the root text (*mūlakāra*). However, in the case of the *hādi-vidyā* (the vidyā beginning with *ha*), one of the two [rasas] must be indicated by the two *sa*s. This is because, by the force of the statement, the plurality of the indicators (*lakṣaka*) and the duality of the indicated (*lakṣya*) are established in exactly that way. [This is done] for the purpose of indicating the single individual soul (*jīva*).

And because the ten *a*-sounds that are about to be mentioned (p. 276) have been observed [therein]. However, the earlier commentators say: "He says 'connection' (*saṃbandha*) to answer the question, 'For what purpose is the third *s*? Since the emergence from the ocean of nectar (*amṛta-samudra*) is well-known, for that reason as well..."

They explain that the meaning is that the third syllable, *sa*, indicates the "taste" (*rasa*) contained within [the ocean] because of its watery nature. In that case, one must endure the difficulty of applying the term "taste" (*rasa*) metaphorically to the ocean, and so forth. || 41 ||
Now he explains the letters of the Earth:
"Fragrance is the quality of the Earth; its script signifies fragrance. O Maheśvarī, it possesses a threefold nature because of its connection with the three worlds. (42)
The expressive seed-syllable (*bīja*) for that Earth, Gandhavatī, is the letter *la*.

According to the *Kośa*, "La is Śakra, Pūtanā, and the Earth. That [syllable] expresses fragrance because the capacity [to denote it] exists even in the delimiting factor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of fragrance. Of fragrance...

The mention of "guṇatva" (the state of being a quality) in relation to "gandha" (smell) is intended solely to indicate its status as a delimitor of possibility (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*). Although that smell, being devoid of distinctions such as gross or subtle, fulfills its purpose through a single syllable (*la*) alone, there are three *la*-syllables here with the intention of referring to the three types of smells belonging to the three worlds.

The three worlds consist of the upper, middle, and lower divisions. However, in reality, in accordance with the Vedic scripture stating that "from the earth come herbs, from herbs comes food, and from food comes the person," the three worlds intended here are those consisting of the earth, herbs, and food. For this very reason, it will be stated further on:

Purity of context is achieved in the description of the person (*puruṣa*). Alternatively, in the *pañcāgnividyā* within the dialogue between Śvetaketu and Pravāhaṇa, the scripture states: "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'person'. [This refers to] the milk and other sacrificial offerings being offered into the Gārhapatya and other fires.

Because specific transformations are prescribed for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) representing heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman, and because among these the earth alone is designated here by the term *vasuṃdharā* as the first, there are two further *la*-sounds to designate the remaining two [the man and the woman].

Although the Veda indicates the oblation as "water" (āpaḥ), the phrase "the three worlds" is used to suggest that it actually takes the form of food; "the three waters" is its intended meaning. Indeed, the earth alone, having assumed the forms of plants, food, and semen, becomes the person (puruṣa).

By this explanation, it is implied that for the organs of perception and the organs of action, which are produced from the five elements, the letters beginning with *ha* alone are their designators. || 42 ||

Now he explains the letters beginning with *ka*: "The supreme body of the subjects—whether impure, pure, or mixed—is revealed by this [letter *ka*] through the triad of Krodhīśas situated within the Vidyā. (43)

Even those initiates who have received Śaiva initiation are of three kinds according to the degree of their impurity (*mālinya*); they are practitioners (*upāsaka*) who have attained a new birth in the form of that initiation.
And for them, having attained that subsequent birth in the form of initiation...
That which is the supreme, most excellent body (*vapuḥ*) is expressed by the three *ka*-letters. The letter *ka* is Krodhīśa;
for according to the lexicon, "Who is Krodhīśa? Mahākālī; [and] Kāmadeva is the illuminator.
Here, this should be understood: the three fetters (*pāśas*) are the individual soul (*aṇu*), karma, and Māyā.

In this context, *aṇu* (the atomic) refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*), and it is of two kinds: the absence of the knowledge of the Self as the Self within the Self, whose nature is consciousness; and the knowledge of the non-Self, such as the body, as the Self. These two types, taken together, are called the *āṇava-mala* (atomic impurity).
Because it delimits the otherwise undelimited Self;
and because the *Saurasaṃhitā* states that "it is called *mala* because it is minute (*aṇu*) and due to its impurity (*mālinya*), being the cause of the atomization of the Self.
Furthermore, *adṛṣṭa* is karma capable of bestowing a body produced by enjoined or prohibited actions. That too—
Both types [of impurity], consisting of merit and demerit, together are called the *kārmaṇa* (karmic) impurity.

The multiplicity of the single Self is *māyā*. Although it is of many kinds, it is collectively called the *māyīya* (illusory) impurity. Among these three, each subsequent one is pervaded by each preceding one.

This very knowledge is bondage; it is clearly stated in the commentary on the *Śivasūtras* and also in the *Pratyabhijñā* that the group of wombs (*yonivarga*), the creative power (*kalā*), and the body constitute bondage. Bound by all three of these fetters (*pāśas*) is the impure *paśu* (bound soul); bound by *aṇu* and *karman* alone is the mixed one.

The pure one is bound by even an atom [of impurity]. Furthermore, in another Tantra, these very [states] are designated respectively as *sakala*, *pralayākala*, and *vijñānakevala*. However, setting aside these designations, the use of terms such as "impure" (*aśuddha*) and so forth is for the purpose of indicating their respective characteristics. In that regard:

Although purity (*śuddhatva*) is the absolute absence of any impurity whatsoever, since that [absolute purity] is impossible for those other than Brahman, purity in the case of individual souls (*jīva*) must be defined as the absence of all other impurities while possessing some degree of impurity. And that single specific impurity is the *āṇava* (atomic) impurity.
This is because, due to the mutual pervasion of the *kārmaṇa* and *māyīya* [sheaths], it is impossible for either one to exist independently of the other.

Likewise, impurity (*aśuddhatva*) consists in being possessed of all impurities; "mixedness" (*miśratva*) is the commingling of the characteristics of the pure and the impure, as there is no definitive criterion [to distinguish them].
This means that there is a conjunction (yoga) with the pure *āṇava* [kala] and the impure *kārmaṇa* [kala];
for the *māyīya* [kala], since it pervades the former two, its conjunction would result only in impurity. Therefore, [the text speaks of] the impure, the mixed, and the pure.

Even though the [expected] sequence is appropriate, it is not adopted; for it is from the knowledge of the mixed [state] through its conjunction with that [pure state] only after the knowledge of purity has arisen. By this, the doubt is dispelled as to how there can be a prior placement of the word "impure" (*aśuddha*), which is not more venerable and does not have fewer syllables. This is because the rule *ajādyadantam* (Pāṇini 2.2.33) is superseded by the subsequent rule *alpāctaram* (Pāṇini 2.2.34).
Because of sublation (*bādha*). Among these, the first two are each of two kinds, according to whether the impurity (*mala*) has been digested or not;

the last one, however, is of two kinds, according to whether the defilement (*kaluṣa*) has reached completion or not. Among them, the impure ones—those whose three impurities have been digested, such as the Krodhabhaṭṭārakas and others—are one hundred and eighteen *upāsakas*.

There are [such beings]. Furthermore, Śiva alone bestows grace upon others by assuming the form of a teacher (*ācārya*). However, for those whose three impurities (*mala*) are not yet ripened, he assigns them to various wombs (*yoni*) through worldly experience (*bhoga*) in order to ripen those impurities; even this is indeed a form of grace.
But when the impurities and so forth have not been ripened, there occurs only a general form of grace (*sāmānyānugraha*).
Out of a desire to show favor, he impels [beings] toward ripening within various wombs.
Because of this statement:
those who possess both impurities in a mature state are the presiding persons (ādhikārika-puruṣas), such as the world-protectors (lokapālas) and others;
whereas those who possess both impurities in an immature state are the mixed ones (miśras), who are born only in the highest wombs due to the power of their karma.
The *puruṣas* are pure, having completed their impurities; these are the nine *vidyeśvara* lords and so forth.

The seven crores of great mantras, however, are pure but have not yet completed their impurities. Nor should it be suspected that they are insentient (*jaḍa*), for although the body of sound is insentient, they possess sentience just as we do.

Because consciousness is established [in them], for this very reason, with the intention of referring to their state as individual souls (*jīva*) while still possessing unripened *āṇava* impurity, the mantras are designated by the term "atoms" (*aṇu*). And it is said in the *Mṛgendrasaṃhitā*,
on the occasion of describing the birth of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*):
"Then Śiva, free from beginningless impurity, the all-doer and all-seeing,
removes the net of bonds from the individual soul (aṇu) who was previously cast into transmigration.
Thus, having set aside birth as an authoritative office-holder (adhikārika), [it refers to] one who has attained birth as a mantra (mantrajanman).
This is the meaning of the transposed term. Furthermore, a more detailed exposition on this point should be sought in the Śaiva scriptures.
The meaning is that these three subjects (*pramātṛ*), who possess two forms each, are to be understood by the three *ka* syllables.
(43) Now, as for those impure individual souls (*jīva*) whose three impurities (*mala*) are still unripened, they too are of two kinds.

There are those who perform heroic deeds and those distinct from them. Among these, the first are indicated by the letter *ka*, because only those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*) are included therein. Furthermore, although all living beings are present according to the Vedic order immediately after the description of the earth, it is appropriate to describe those who are most venerable first.
But those that are not highly honored are placed last, and they are infinite; for this very reason, he indicates them by means of many *akāra*s:
"In the same way, the group of ten Śrīkaṇṭhas is the designator of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). Here, Śrīkaṇṭha is the syllable *akāra*.

"Aḥ is Śrīkaṇṭha, Sureśa, and Lalāṭa, having a single mother"—so says the lexicon (*kośa*). And these ten indeed reside within the Vidyā; therefore, he says "the group of ten. Although the first letter 'A' situated in the third *kūṭa* denotes *prakāśa* (light) in the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha-prakaraṇa*), [it is included here as well].
Since it has been determined [that the *nāda* is included], one should have simply said "the group of nine" (*navaka*) upon its exclusion;

nevertheless, the meaning stated there refers only to the form of the *parā* state, and not to the form of *vaikharī*. Therefore, by including that [the *nāda*] within it, it is called "the group of ten" (*daśaka*). These objections and their resolutions [will be addressed] at the occasion of defining the meaning of the letter *ha*.

This has been demonstrated right there by the original authors (*mūlakāra*) in order to resolve the contradiction regarding the simultaneous occurrence of two functions; therefore, it is not reiterated here again.
"In that same way" means "to some extent. Some say it means "like Paramaśiva. As for the letter *a*: [text follows].

Thus, it is the designator of Śiva as well as of the individual soul (jīva). These ten are the designators of the unmanifest (avyakta) and of all individual souls, both those who perform heroic deeds (vīrakarmaṭha) and others. This is according to the maxim: "Setting aside the specific object, the general object follows."

This is because the term *avyakta*, which denotes the generality of the individual soul (*jīva*), culminates in a specific [meaning]. And this has been stated in accordance with the opinion of the ancients; however, in reality, the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva constitute its characteristics and its syllables.

As the Blessed One proceeded to describe [the elements], having first described those five elements alone in accordance with the order of creation stated in the Śruti, he [then described] the qualities produced from them as being non-different from them,
as well as the organs of knowledge and action which are likewise produced from them.
By stating the identity of cause and effect, these [phonemes] have indeed been described in a general form;

for since all of them consist merely of transformations of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), there is no further portion to be described beyond that. Their being produced from and cognizable by the letter *ha* and so forth has already been stated. Thus...

When the twenty principles— namely the pentad beginning with earth, the pentad beginning with smell, the pentad beginning with the organs of action starting with the anus, and the pentad beginning with the vital breaths (prāṇa)— have been described, then, even though it follows in sequence, one must bypass the quartet consisting of mind, intellect, ego, and primordial nature (prakṛti) to reach the twenty-fifth principle as well.

Although the Puruṣa is described in the Śruti immediately after the Earth and is thus established as the twenty-first principle, there is no evidence for the exclusion of those four [principles] following the description of the Puruṣa; therefore, the term *Śrīkaṇṭha* is intended precisely to describe that [Puruṣa]. For this very reason...

In the previous [verse], because there is no distinction in being bound by the three impurities (*mala*), all *sakalas* are indeed referred to by the term "impure" (*aśuddha*), and not merely the *vīrakarmaṭhas*, as there is no evidence for the latter restriction. Consequently, since the definition of the individual soul (*jīva*) has already been completed, it is improper to state its definition again here. Furthermore, the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers only to *prakṛti*.
Regarding the *jīva*, as it has been stated by the teacher Pañcaśikha:
"The wise declare that the unmanifest *pradhāna* is without beginning or middle, beyond the Great Principle (*mahat*), and eternal."
Also in the *Sāṃkhyasaptati*:
"Subtle, without marks, insentient, without beginning or end, likewise characterized by productivity,
partless, indeed one, and common— such is this Unmanifest."

For this very reason, even the singular number [is used]. For if it referred to the individual soul (*jīva*), one would have said, "the designator of the unmanifests" (*avyaktānām hi vācakam*). And that *prakṛti* is the aggregate of the three qualities (*guṇatrayasamaṣṭi*), having the nature of a thread; for it has been determined thus in the *Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra*: "Sattva and the others are not properties of that [soul], because they are of its very nature. This, then, is the definition.

To make this understood, it is said "in that same way," meaning "possessing the three qualities" (*guṇatrayavat*). For in your own position, that [unmanifest] would result in being devoid of purpose. The compound is *guṇavat* (possessing qualities) and *tad-avyaktam* (that unmanifest). And such a statement would apply to those who possess qualities.

The phrase "the seed" is intended to remind one of the aforementioned principle. Consequently, the meaning is that the vowels, which denote the primary principle (*pradhāna*) as possessing qualities (*guṇa*), also denote the qualities themselves;
that is to say, they denote the three principles consisting of ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and mind (*manas*). Of these...

This is because it is established by our own philosophical tenets (*siddhānta*) that [the Self] sequentially possesses the nature of each individual quality (*guṇa*), namely *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*.

If you ask, "Since pronouns denote what has been previously mentioned, how can the word 'that' (*tat*) denote a quality not previously mentioned? [we reply: Where was *paraśiva* previously mentioned? He is "all" (*sarva*).

If it is argued that [the term] "Maheśvara" [is used here], then even more proximately, in the phrase "the seed of those possessing qualities," the qualities (*guṇa*) themselves are indeed included. If it is argued that Śiva is also included by the very word "Śrīkaṇṭha," that is equally true for us as well; for "Śrī" means poison, and "Kaṃ" means the water of the Gaṅgā.
*Ṭha* is the lunar disc;
*ṭha* is said to be in the great sound (*bṛhaddhvani*) as well as in the lunar disc—thus [says] the *Anekārthadhvanimañjarī*. These three [letters] are [placed] in reverse order.
This is an illustration of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Thus it was said by us in the *Śivastuti*:
"By you, who sequentially bear the moon, fire, and poison—white, red, and black—is not the state of relative intensity (*taratama-bhāva*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* revealed to us?"
In the present context as well, the quality of *rajas* is evident because of the observation of jealousy and other such emotions between Gaṅgā and Pārvatī.
Now, one might object: "But these three [qualities] emerge from the word *Śrīkaṇṭha*, which denotes the letter *a*, according to the conventional meaning of the word."
If it is argued that [the evidence] has not been presented, this is equally true for you as well:
"The Lord does not have a lotus-seat; the Gandharvas arise from the scraping of those peaks; the two wheels moved on the path before him; he was the one who cleared the way."
Salutations to that Lord, whose disciple Jīva became the sovereign of those who were enemies of his own master,
and who was himself intent upon the destruction of his foes.

In this regard, even though [the object] was not previously presented as being connected to the meaning of the sentence from the preceding word, we observe that it is referred to by subsequent pronouns appearing in later sentences merely through some kind of presentation; for example: "The bow is not of false material, nor is the bow the lotus-seated one."

*Gandharvas* are horses as well as a class of divine beings; *cakre* refers to chariot wheels and the Sudarśana discus; *patrī* means an arrow and a winged bird; *jīvā* denotes a bowstring and Bṛhaspati. Among these, the first meanings are connected with the sense of the preceding sentence, whereas the latter meanings are connected with the pronouns situated in the subsequent sentence.
The established position is that [these] are being referred to.
Therefore, the meaning is that by means of the ten *a*-sounds, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as qualified by mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is indicated.

Since it has been established in the section beginning with "tadavyaktamāha hi" that even the Supreme Brahman may be designated by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*), here, by means of the word "unmanifest" employed in the sense of *prakṛti*, there is the presentation of Paramaśiva, who transcends the [twenty-four] principles; therefore, the word that denotes Him here is the syllable *ekāra*.
He explains:
"O Goddess, the eleventh, which is supreme, stands as the very life-force, just like that. (44)
Indeed, that single Puruṣa is born in many ways;
he is the letter *e* (ekāra) in eleven [forms]. Regarding the section on the letter *e*:
according to the lexicon, "The conjunction (*saṃdhi*), Ekādaśa, Bhadrā, Padmanābha, and Kulācala."

This is because it is the eleventh in the sequence of the Mātṛkā, and because of the practical application [of the mantra] as "the eleventh support, the seed-syllable consisting of three corners. It is the vital breath (*prāṇabhūta*) of both the principles (*tattva*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and that which transcends the principles; just as the vital breath, residing within the body, causes the body to move.

The meaning is that he remains as such. Although Śakti alone is the generator of all things, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that even the inactive Śiva is the cause by mere proximity (*saṃnidhi*), it is the Supreme Brahman itself—transcending the [lower] principles—that is denoted here by the term "Prāṇa. For this very reason, in the *Prāṇādhikaraṇa*...

It has been determined that the word *prāṇa* refers to the Supreme Brahman. For this very reason, it was not stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is produced by the letter *e*, as is the case with other syllables, nor that the letter *e* is its designator; for both of these are impossible in the case of that which is eternal and devoid of attributes.
With the intention of asserting the non-difference between word and meaning, it was stated merely that the phoneme (*varṇa*) alone is the vital principle.

Alternatively, since the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) have been previously described, among those remaining, the eleventh is Śiva himself; for he too is included within the [totality of] principles.
The qualifier "para" (supreme) is used to indicate its transcendence. In this manner, the single word "sat" itself, when repeated, conveys both the term and its meaning.
The phrase "tadvat" (possessing that), as before, has the sense of "something more," signifying "possessing infinite power."
That is neuter, or else it is the supreme Brahman. He states its definition as "the One":

the True Person (*satpuruṣa*). This is because [He] is well-known in such scriptural passages as "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Person, dark and tawny; the Person is indeed Rudra," and so forth. Paraśiva alone is the One.

The meaning is that because [the universe] arises from Him—who possesses infinite power (*ananta-śakti*) in many ways—therefore He possesses the power whose nature is *prāṇa*. However, although there are twelve Śrīkaṇṭhas in the *Hādi-vidyā*, it was previously stated that among them, one corresponds to the touch residing in air (*vāyu*). Therefore...

It should be explained that of those eleven which remain, ten refer to [the principles] beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta), while the eleventh, the letter *a*, refers to that which transcends the categories (*tattvātīta*). However, the earlier commentators [state]: "Among the twelve, ten..."
The first eleven denote the individual soul (jīva). The eleventh denotes the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the support of the soul.

The final twelfth, however, is "Puruṣa," denoting Paramaśiva. Now, one might ask: since the intended goal is accomplished by these three alone, what is the purpose of the nine others? To this he says: "One," etc. Indra...

The sense is that the multiplicity of those [forms] is intended to illuminate the meaning established by such scriptural passages as, "He moves through many forms by means of his powers (māyās)," and "The single Self of beings indeed resides within every being. Furthermore,
this "Person" (puruṣa), who is counted as the twenty-fifth principle among the categories (tattvas) and is well-known from scripture as "Rudra is indeed the Person," is the individual soul (jīva).
This was stated by relying on that specific position; however, when the Virāṭ-puruṣa himself is counted as that [total], the individual soul (jīva) consists only of the ego (ahaṃkāra) and so forth.
For in this case, the internal senses of embodied beings are indeed distinct from their objects.
The mind is internal compared to these; therefore, the intellect is more internal still in this context.
The individual soul (jīva) is internal even to the intellect; its state is that it has attained the nature of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā).
Beyond this is always to be known that which is the unmanifest cause.

If this is considered on the basis of the statement from the *Ātmapurāṇa*, then, since the state of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtva*) actually resides within the internal cause, and since that [cause] is enumerated among the principles (*tattva*) as threefold— distinguished as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*)— those very [principles], such as the impure (*aśuddha*) and others, are the cognizers. Therefore...

Thus, the sequence of the impure, the pure, and the mixed is also logically established, because they consist of the qualities of *tamas*, *sattva*, and *rajas* respectively. Although the term "knower" (*pramātṛ*) refers specifically to individual souls (*jīvas*),
nevertheless, due to their non-difference from Brahman, their state as knowers is their supreme, extracted essence or body.

Since they consist of the very forms of mind and so forth, they alone are denoted by the three aspects. Having thus defined the unmanifest (avyakta) which follows in sequence, the Virāṭ Puruṣa himself is then described by the eleventh syllable. And he, being the collective totality of individual souls (jīva-samaṣṭi), is indeed the vital breath (prāṇabhūta). He is one.

The word "even" (sannā) is also appropriate there in that very context; for this being so, the well-established sequence of the principles (tattvas) is not violated. However, that which transcends the principles will be spoken of at the very end by the term "peace" (śānti). || 44 ||
Now he explains the seed-syllables of the *bindu* and the seed-syllables of the *nāda* which denote the remaining eleven principles:
"The deities Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and [Anāśrita-]Īśa have limited forms. (45)
By means of the three drops (bindu), they are said to be of immeasurable and infinite forms;
Śānti, Śakti, and Śambhu are awakened by the triad of sounds (nāda).

Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, Kalā, Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva—these are the eleven [categories]. Among them, Sadāśiva is he who perceives the universe through the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā). Īśvara is he who perceives that very same universe through the sense of "this" (idantā).
The cognition of non-difference between "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and "this-ness" (idaṃtā) is Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā). The cognition of difference between those very two is Māyā.
Consequently, there are five [powers] existing in the Supreme Brahman, known as omnificence, omniscience, eternal contentment, eternity, and independence.
The powers (*śaktayaḥ*), which exist as unrestrained deities, become restrained and contracted; thus, in due order, they assume the five designations beginning with *kalā*.
The individual soul (*puruṣa*) alone is said to be the substratum of such contracted power, as expressed by the letters *e* and *o*. This is as follows:

In the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*, it has been established by Amṛtānanda that just as Brahman transcends all categories (*sarvatattvātīta*) and is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, so too are Śiva and Śakti likewise unconditioned. This is also the case for the notions of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "this-ness" (*idaṃtā*) in their most subtle form.

Because they are characterized by differentiation, they possess a slight deficiency due to being undivided, and a slight excess due to being limited; thus, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā are of an intermediate nature, like a touch that is neither hot nor cold. As for Māyā and the others, however—

The established position is that [these categories] are indeed limited, because they are constituted solely by the distinctions among deities. Furthermore, within these thirty-six principles (tattvas), the sequence proceeds as follows: from the earth up to the ear, then up to primordial nature (prakṛti), then up to illusion (māyā), then up to Sadāśiva, and finally up to Śiva. Thus is the order.

This is the state of the five principles beginning with Earth; this very point is expressed by the statement that "this universe consists of the five elements. Likewise, from Earth up to Māyā, the manifest form is of the nature of *sat* (Being), while the aspects of consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*) are concealed. Precisely because they are of such a nature, these possess the character of the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*).

In the triad beginning with Śuddhavidyā, the aspects of *sat* (existence) and *cit* (consciousness) are unobscured, while the aspect of *ānanda* (bliss) is obscured; it is precisely because of this that they possess the nature of the *vidyā-tattva*. In the case of Śakti and Śiva, however, no aspect whatsoever is obscured, and therefore they possess the nature of the *śiva-tattva*. In all these cases, the fundamental [principles] are as follows:

The statements of the eastern commentators are to be seen in their commentaries (*ṭīkā*). This being the case, in the present context, the word *rudra* denotes "radiance" (*tejas*), based on the Vedic scripture: "This Agni is indeed Rudra.
By that [word], there is the presentation of the seven principles beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *māyā*, which are denoted by the term "the principle of radiance" (*tejastattva*).

Among those, because they are described as being male, the six deities are understood by the term *rudra*. *Īśvara* is well-known; *sadeśa* is *sadāśiva*. He states their definition with the word "limited" (*mita*); the meaning is that their natures are circumscribed. These three are represented by the three *bindus*.

However, since Śuddhavidyā is subordinate only with respect to Īśvara and Sadāśiva, it too is represented by the Bindu alone, according to the principle stated that "it becomes the seed for those who possess qualities.
As for the fact that even the ancients [interpret] the term *rudra-pada* as referring specifically to the seven principles beginning with Tejas:
They explain it thus, but that is incorrect, because it results in abandoning the well-established meaning; for according to your own view,
this *vāsanā* is indeed distinct from the two *vāsanās* consisting of fifteen qualities (*guṇa*) and thirty-seven principles (*tattva*).
(p. 284) Because in this [system], there is no necessity for an exhaustive enumeration of all principles (*tattva*);
for you have described only the pentad beginning with earth and the ten sense organs as being denotable.
Just as there is the exclusion of certain [elements] included within the *tattvas*, so too is there the exclusion of those not included among the *tattvas*.
Because there is no contradiction in its inclusion within the compendium (*saṃgraha*), and because you yourself have described *śānti* here as not being included among the principles (*tattva*).
Nor is that [state] something beyond the principles; for even that is not necessary, since it serves the purpose of the twelfth principle, Śrīkaṇṭha.

It should be understood that, in accordance with the requirement for the introductory injunction— which teaches the thirty-seven categories— to convey its intended meaning (*tātparya*), such a strained interpretation does not constitute a fault. He explains the word *nādān* as "immeasurable and immeasurable" (*amitāmita*).

By means of repetition (*vīpsā*), the state of being unconditioned from the very beginning is expressed; by this, the exclusion of Īśvara and Sadāśiva—who are slightly conditioned—is effected. Therein, Śakti and Śiva are denoted by the words *śakti* and *śambhu*, respectively. By the word *śānti*, it is Brahman itself that transcends the categories (*tattva*). Brahman.
This is because of the scriptural statement, "Peace. For by that peace, [the text says], "I bring peace for my two-footed and four-footed beings";

and because, through the qualification of peace as being the nature of all-pervading peace (*sarvaśānti*) in these mantras, its essential nature as transcending all categories (*tattvātīta-svarūpatā*) is made clear. Furthermore, it is not the case that Brahman is merely peace in this context...

It should be understood that the word *brahman* refers to the Veda; for its reference to the Veda is certain from its being mentioned in conjunction with "the Brāhmaṇa" and "peace" (*śānti*). Furthermore, the scriptural authority for this is the passage: "The Brahman is long-lived, as it is long-lived through the Brāhmaṇas," where Kṛṣṇa is both the Brahman and the source.

Furthermore, in the *Smṛti*, it has been stated by Dīkṣita and others that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "Brāhmaṇa" serves as such a determinative factor. As for the passages beginning with "The earth is peace," they are not contradictory, as they are intended to show that Brahman is the self of all. This applies to the beginning and end of the *Brahmavidyā*.

The recitation of the mantra "Peace! Peace! Peace! (*śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ*) is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the word "peace" (*śānti*) has Brahman as its referent; for at the beginning and end of the universe, Brahman alone remains. Although this being the case, it would have been more appropriate to say "Śakti, Śambhu, and Śānti," in accordance with the sequence previously introduced.

Nevertheless, since the knowledge of Śiva— which transcends reality— is dependent upon that [power], and because the knowledge of power is also a cause for the knowledge of Śiva by virtue of being characterized by such power,
[the author] first [mentions] power and Śiva in order to suggest this definition.
"Peace has been established by the Blessed One. However, the ancient teachers [state]: "The Sound (nāda) is the entire universe;
having pierced through from below by the downward power (adhaḥśakti), it reaches the limit of the upward power (ūrdhvaśakti).
Merged in the aperture of Brahma (brahmabila) via the channel, it is characterized by unmanifest resonance (avyaktadhvani)."

Thus they say, on account of such a statement. However, one must investigate what evidence has been presented by them for the designation "pacification" (*śānti*) of such a dissolved sound (*līnanāda*). || 45 || 46 ||
(p. 285) Now, describing how the supreme status of this mantra among all mantras—as obtained through the meaning of the oral tradition—is established, he concludes:
"In the ring at the root of the snare, the threads and other elements are swallowed up."
Likewise, all mantras are established here within this Vidyā. || 47 ||
The meaning of the tradition, received through the lineage of gurus, has been declared.

A *vāgurā* is a net for catching fish; its primary point is a single ring (*valaya*), through which threads are strung, and at the ends of those threads are knots. Just as that very ring is the support for all of them, so too is this *Śrīvidyā* the support for all mantras.

Since it has been previously described that these [powers] are included within the *buddhitattva* (the principle of intellect) by virtue of their nature as subjects who are internally pure yet turbid, the ancient authorities say: "This fourth [power], which consists of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of being composed of all mantras, is taught as entirely independent. The traditional meaning according to this method is as follows:

The meaning is that [this teaching] has been received by me solely through the lineage of gurus, and you too must instruct those who are worthy solely through the lineage of the succession of gurus. At the beginning, from the qualityless Brahman, speech arose in a subtle form as *dhvani* (resonance), which is of the nature of *unmanā*. That—

Svacchandabhairava, the disciple of the qualityless Brahman, having understood the tantras, composed them in an abbreviated form and spoke them to Anāśriteśvara. He, expanding upon them, told them to Śāntyatītādevī. She told them to Sadāśiva. He—

He composed [the scriptures] in countless, immeasurable, and vast quantities, extending beyond all limits, according to the distinctions of the five traditions (pañcāmnāya) and so forth. Thereafter, they became exceedingly renowned through the sequence beginning with the Lord (Īśvara), the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), and the Rudras such as Śrīkaṇṭha; such is this lineage of gurus.

It has been stated by the elders: "In all these cases, the original source statements (mūlavacanāni) are to be found in the commentaries of the ancients. Here, the cognition produced by the thirty-seven words has as its qualificandum that which transcends all categories (tattva), has all categories as its qualifiers, and has non-difference as its relation."

This [identity] is obtained through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). However, since the fact that [the identity] is produced by those respective phonemes is also mentioned in this context, its status as an object of verbal cognition is likewise necessary; for in its absence, the manifestation of non-difference between the knowledge (vidyā) and the universe (viśva) would be impossible.
Just as light possesses two powers— namely, the state of being the object of apprehension and the state of being the subject of apprehension—
in the same way, these two exist separately for all words.

By this statement, the meaning of the letter *ha* is as follows: the void (*vyoma*), its quality (sound), and its corresponding sense organ. Where there is a sublation of being produced from that specific syllable, there the mere non-difference from that syllable serves as a qualifier for its object; and thus, according to the circumstances, by virtue of being produced from those respective syllables—
And because they are non-different from those respective syllables, with reference to their respective denoted (vācya) and indicated (lakṣya) meanings,
the verbal meaning consists in the injunction of non-dual identity— which transcends all discourse— within them. Thus,
the subsequent mental realization of the non-difference between the Goddess and the Vidyā, due to their being the generators of the universe, is of the nature of mental cognition.
It should be observed. || 47 ||
(p. 286) Having thus ascertained the meaning of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*), he teaches the meaning of the innermost essence (*nigarbha*), which follows in due order:
"O Great Goddess, the meaning of the innermost essence pertains to Śiva, the Guru, and the Self. (48)

The term *nigarbha* means "the innermost core," like a fetus (*garbha*) within; it signifies that which is most secret. It refers to the meaning that is the object of such realization, wherein Śiva, the Guru, and the Self are perceived as non-different objects.
Thus ends [verse] 48.
Having thus described its essential nature, he promises the instruction upon it:
"O Mistress of the Gods, I shall describe its method to you by way of a mere indication."
Through the contemplation of the identity of Śiva, the Guru, and the Self, one becomes identical with that [reality]. || 49 ||

Through the contemplation of the mutual non-difference— the identity— of the triad consisting of Śiva, the Guru, and oneself, and through the verbal cognition produced by the firm and repeated practice of the knowledge of mantras which is of that nature (the identity), [one realizes] that which consists of that identity.
The meaning is: "I shall tell you in brief that specific mode which serves as the qualifier for a cognition whose qualificandum is Śiva and so forth. (49)
He says that very thing:
"Having realized the partless nature (niṣkalatva) in Śiva, and likewise the identity with that form in the Guru, and through the power of beholding Him, the self's own nature as Śiva. (50)
Bowing with devotion and untainted by the emergence of doubt, one should meditate upon Śiva,
the Supreme Śiva; having realized His partless nature (niṣkalatva) among those devoid of qualities,
and having made that the object of the awakening produced by the first-occurring Vāgbhava-kūṭa, [one should do so] even regarding one's own Guru.

Having realized that state of being— that formlessness which is established by the second peak (kūṭa) reached through the sequence and attained through the firmness of contemplation on non-difference from the partless—
and having likewise realized it for oneself through the power of being gazed upon by her compassionate side-long glance;
One should contemplate the state of being the essence of Niṣkala Śiva as established by the third *kūṭa*.

For in the *Hādividyā*, the word *hasa* refers to the short vowels; the elision of the letters *ra* and *va* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. The "parts" (*kalā*), such as the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, are short, having abandoned gross form and existing solely in the nature of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

That in which there is the *hasakala*— that is to say, the Supreme Śiva denoted by the *hṛllekhā*— this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. According to the method explained in the section on the meaning of the *bhāva*, the first three syllables situated in the second *kūṭa* refer exclusively to the partless (*niṣkala*) Brahman.

That which draws forth—that is, attracts—and connects [all things] through non-differentiation is this very Guru, *hasakahala*. He too is indeed expressible as *hṛllekhā*, for it is said: "Śiva himself, bound by human skin, is considered the Guru."

In the third peak (kūṭa), the term "sakala" (with parts) refers specifically to the practitioner (upāsaka), while [the term] "sat" refers to one's own Self; the construction is that even he is "niṣkala" (without parts), which is the meaning of *hṛllekhā*. Now, in response to the doubt as to how that which is indeed "sakala" can possess "niṣkalatva" (partlessness), he says:

Regarding the phrase "bowed by devotion" (bhaktinamra): the sense is that for one who possesses devotion to the Guru and the Deity, the stain of doubt is removed according to the principle that there is no contradiction between the presence and absence of qualities— just as in the case of a red crystal and its lack of redness— since qualities are adventitious while their absence is innate.
For that high-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the teacher as for the Divine, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth clearly.
Thus it is heard. || 50 ||
He teaches the Kaulika meaning in seventeen and a half verses:
"I shall explain the Kaulika [meaning], which pertains even to the wheel and the deity. (51)
The identity of the knowledge (vidyā), the guru, and the self (ātman), along with its method, is now demonstrated.
The Śrīcakra, the Śrīmātā, the Śrīvidyā, the Śrīguru, and the self—these five are said to constitute the "Kaulika meaning," which is their oneness. *Kula* refers to a collection of similar things.

According to Amara, *kula* means a group of those belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*). This commonality (*sājātya*) consists in being delimited by a single attribute, as well as in the state of being composed of the sixfold nature of Gaṇeśa and the others. That very [attribute] which was described as residing in the Goddess in the auspicious opening verse at the commencement of the treatise is what persists through the five [forms].

There is one single reality (*dharma*). I shall explain the non-duality of the five—the families (*kula*) possessing that [reality] and the kaulika matter connected to them, which is to be established by mantra.
That specific characteristic of those five, consisting in their being delimited by the single reality, is as follows:
The meaning is that it is demonstrated and established with excellence. || 51 ||
With the letter *la*, [one draws] squares, joined with three circles.
O Dear One, the pair of lotuses consists of the Śaktis and is of the nature of Agni and Soma.

By means of the three *la*-sounds, three squares are produced, whether as the expressed meanings (*vācya*) or as the expressive signs (*vācaka*). In either case, there is mutual non-difference between them, because of the identity of cause and effect, and of the signifier and the signified.
Because the letter *la*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of earth, possesses the capacity to generate or to signify the square mandala of earth;
for this very reason, the circle marked by two lotuses possesses the capacity to generate or to signify the mandala of water,
which consists of the specific waters that are the seed-syllables of the moon.

With the intention that it is appropriate for the three *sakāras*, he says: "vṛtta" (circular). The sixteen-petaled lotus is lunar in nature (*somātmaka*); the eight-petaled one, however, is fiery in nature (*agnyātmaka*). The three circles are indeed one; thus, they are produced by or denoted by the three *sakāras* belonging to Śakti. This refers to the water-mandala (*jalamaṇḍala*).

Although other tantras describe it as having the shape of a half-moon, the *Svacchandatantra* describes it as having the shape of a full moon, stating: "The water-reflection should be known as perfectly circular and marked with a lotus."
In the section on the letter *sa*, [the following are mentioned]: the seed of the world (*jagadbīja*), the one named Śakti, Haṃsa, Vegavatī, Bhṛgu—thus says Nandana. (52)
By means of the nine syllables produced from the three *hṛllekhās*.
O Dear One, that which arises from the three drops consists of nine wombs.
The wheel, however, is endowed with three mandalas and consists of power (śakti) and fire (anala). || 54 ||

In the *hṛllekhās*, there are three [syllables]; following those are the three syllables consisting of *vyoman* (ha), *agni* (ra), and *kāmakalā* (ī). Those which have arisen as a collective whole—namely, those nine syllables beginning with *bindu* and ending with *unmanī*—are the "three plus" (*trayottarāṇi*).

The term *saṃbhūtāni* is a compound formed by the elision of the middle word (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*). He explains the enumeration by dividing the *kāmakalā* into its constituent parts as "the three dots" (*bindutraya*) and so forth. Consequently, for each *hṛllekhā*, there is the letter *ha*, the letter *ra*, the dot called *kāma*, the two dots called *visarga*, the *anusvāra*, the *ardhacandra*, and the *rodhinī*.

Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpikā, Samanā, and Unmanā—these, together with the fourteen [others], constitute forty-two syllables. By means of these forty-two syllables, there is the wheel consisting of the nature of the Yoni, which is composed of five Śaktis and four Vahnis; thus, it consists of forty-two triangles and is of the nature of fire and power.

It has arisen. This very [mandala], endowed with three circles and consisting of Sun, Moon, and Fire, has its meaning made known by the verse "the third, however, is Hutāśana" in the *Pūrvacatuḥśatikā*; for it is precisely this wheel consisting of the nine wombs (*navayoni*) that possesses the nature of all wheels.
This is because it has been established in that very [work], and because the mention of the union with the three mandalas is justified by this much alone.

Alternatively, "the three points" (*bindu*) is also an elliptical expression for the three sounds (*nāda*). The phrase "endowed with those" is intended to indicate that, when combined with the *bindus* and *nādas*, only the single fourth vowel (*turyasvara*) is to be counted. And thus:
The meaning is that the ninefold *yonicakra* is produced by the three *hakāras*, the three *rephas*, and the three *ekāras*.
Now, one might object: "In the first interpretive position, since there are forty-three triangles, how can one of them be omitted here? And not [that]..."

If it is argued that one should state that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) will be explained later along with the *bindu* separately, and that this would contradict the statement [made earlier] that [the *mātṛkā*] consists of eight *yoni*s, we say: no. For at the time of the extraction of the *cakra*, there is an injunction for the non-difference of the second power from the first power.

Since the first Śakti and Īśāna constitute the eight-cornered [figure] in the southeast corner, even if that specific corner portion is separated out, the remainder does not lose its nature as a nine-yoni (nine-triangle) figure.
Having thus described the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha), the two lotuses, and the wheel of nine sources (navayonicakra),
he states the underlying doctrine (vāsanā) for the central triangle and the point (bindu) which follow in sequence:
"By means of the three seeds of space (vyomabīja) itself, it is endowed with the triad of subjects (pramātṛ)."
(289) It consists of will, knowledge, and action, and is joined with the flow of the downward breath (ādana). || 55 ||
O Goddess, the seat of Sadāśiva is supreme and consists of the Great Bindu;
thus, the wheel composed of mantra is the supreme body of the deity. (56)
The central triangle is denoted by the terms will, knowledge, and action,
because it has been previously stated that it is permeated by their latent impressions (*vāsanā*). It is conjoined with that form which is the triad of intoxication—
the three *ka* letters— and for this very reason, it is associated with the triad of subjects (*pramātṛ*).

It is endowed with the triad of practitioners, such as Sakala and others, as described in the section on the meaning of the tradition (*saṃpradāyārthaprakaraṇa*). Its seat is Sadāśiva himself; such is the wheel consisting of the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*), which is either produced by or denoted by the three *vyoma*-seeds, that is, the three letter *ha*s. [Likewise] by the three letter *ka*s.

The three corners [of the triangle] are formed by the three *ha*s, which is to say, the *bindu*. This wheel (*cakra*), which constitutes the interior of the deity’s body, is the universe; in this manner, it consists of mantra and is non-different from mantra.
According to the ancients, however, by means of the nine syllables residing in the *hṛllekhā*, it takes on both forms: the triangle and the eight-cornered [figure].

The wheel of the nine wombs has arisen; the wheel situated above it, which consists of the three powers and the three fires and takes the form of two ten-spoked wheels and one fourteen-spoked wheel, has arisen from the three *ha* syllables. The *bindu*, however, has arisen from the three *ka* syllables.

They explain that by the textual passage ending with "the supreme body" (*paraṃ vapuḥ*) in the manner described—"the state of the three mandalas is indeed the supreme triad of power and fire"—the non-duality of the wheels (*cakra*), mantras, and goddesses is stated.
That [explanation] is to be considered. For if the term "mandala" were to denote each individual pair of power and fire, [it would follow that there are six mandalas].

Because there is no evidence for it; and because, after the description of the two lotuses, there is no seed-syllable (*bīja*) for leaping up and running toward the eight-cornered [mandala]. Nor can it be resolved by claiming that its description occurs before the ten-spoked [wheel] and others, that is, prior to the emergence of the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*).

This is because the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), which is established for the drawing of the form beginning with the *bindu* and ending with the enclosure of the earth, is not followed here; and furthermore, because it contradicts that very order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) which is established for the worship and is indeed adopted here. However, this point must be noted here:

Among the five—*cakra*, deity, *vidyā*, guru, and practitioner—there are four non-dualities for each one, corresponding to its four respective counterparts; thus, there are twenty non-dualities in total. Among these, that which is the non-duality having the *cakra* as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and the deity as the correlate (*anuyogin*) is...

In this manner, since [the deity] is related to the deity (*devatā*) and related to the wheel (*cakra*), by removing these ten repetitions, exactly ten non-dualities (*abheda*) will remain. Now, there are four non-dualities of the wheel with the four [entities], beginning with the deity; and of the deity—
There are three [types] together with the triad of *vidyā* and so forth; two together with the *guru* and *śiṣya*;

and one together with the *śiṣya* of the *guru*. These ten non-dualities (*abheda*) have been described in the context of establishing the fivefold nature of the *cakra* and so forth as being essentially composed of the six deities beginning with Gaṇeśa.
They exist as such. Precisely because they are delimited by a single such property (*eka-dharma*), they possess homogeneity (*sājātya*);

for this very reason, this [text] also possesses the status of *kaulika* meaning. Furthermore, precisely because it conveys a single such object, this work also possesses syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). And that is the *kaulika*...

Because of the opening statement, "I shall speak," and the concluding statement, "Thus has the Kaulika meaning, honored by the heroes, been told," [the connection] is necessary. This is due to the same logic applied to the passage concerning the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*).
Consequently, there is non-difference between the *vidyā* and the *cakra*, because they share the same material cause (*upādāna*) as their substrate (*upādeya*).
However, because the Goddess and the Wheel are established as a single essence, there is non-duality, just as in the case of the array of bodies created by a yogin;

yet, if one were to describe the non-duality of the Goddess, the Vidyā, the Guru, and the Sādhaka on the grounds that they possess the sixfold nature beginning with Gaṇeśa— as will be explained later— then there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) due to the difference in the objects of cognition (prameya).
Furthermore, a deficiency would result from the failure to mention the two non-dualities of the wheel and the guru, and of the wheel and the practitioner;
yet neither of those [omissions] is appropriate. Therefore, the preceding textual passage is solely intended to explain that the wheel consists of the sixfold nature beginning with Gaṇeśa.
The subsequent [verse], however, which is devoted to explaining those four beginning with the Goddess, is quite clear.

This being the case, since all five are delimited by a single common property, it is stated that each one is eternally non-different from the other four; thus, there is neither deficiency nor syntactical split.

The description of the generation of the parts of the wheel by means of the syllables of the mantra, however, serves to illuminate the non-duality of the five [deities], since it culminates in the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) through the identity of the produced and the producer.

For without that, the meaning of the mantra for the Kaulika would be untenable. The manner of this is as follows: by these six words—the three *la*s and the three *sa*s—the Yoginīs beginning with Ḍākinī are each individually signified. They are presented separately in the manner of "Ḍākinī is one" and "Rākinī is one," and so forth.

However, when the six cognitions consisting of relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) have arisen from the two nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the mutual relation (*parasparasaṃsarga*)—consisting in being constituents of a single aggregate—is understood through the semantic force of the sentence. Thereafter, there arises the cognition in the form "the six yoginīs. And then...

Since the nature of consisting of the six Yoginīs exists even within the five wheels (*cakras*) and so forth, the understanding is that this pentad is mutually non-different from one another. Furthermore, because this [understanding] arises through the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of a sentence composed of six words, it is either verbal or purely mental; this is another matter. [The group consists of] the hexad beginning with Gaṇeśa.

And [the deities] are Gaṇeśas, planets, lunar mansions, Yoginīs, zodiac signs, and sacred seats (pīṭhas). Among these, because Gaṇeśas and sacred seats are of the same number, the other is rendered redundant by the mention of either one; with this intention, only their fivefold nature is described here. And in that regard, although [the deity] is indeed in the form of Gaṇeśa and so forth...
Since the sequence for the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) has been established,

it would be appropriate to describe the sequence for the wheel (*cakra*) as well according to that very same order; nevertheless, because the reason for abandoning the established sequence will be stated later, there is another sequence.

p. 291) In order to establish the fivefold nature [of the wheel] through the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama) arranged therein for the sake of conformity with the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*)—which is to be resorted to—he first teaches that the wheel consists of the *yoginīs* with the words "by the letters *la*" (*lakāraiḥ*). For its nature as consisting of the *yoginīs* is indeed...

The twofold nature of the sixfold group beginning with the *ḍākinīs* and the eightfold nature of the group beginning with *Vaśinī* will be explained. In the present context, by counting the three circles as one and dividing them into six— namely, three squares and two lotuses— the circle is defined by that [sixfold] division, resulting in eight [sections].
The intended meaning is that [the wheel] consists of the Yoginīs. He states its nature as the planets with the words "hṛllekhā" (the heart-line).

He states its nature as the zodiacal signs with the words "bindu" (the point). By counting the *bindu* and *nāda* together with the long vowels *ī*, the nine-spoked wheel (*navayonicakra*) consists of the nine planets. However, by treating the *bindu* and *nāda* as one and distinguishing them from the vowel *ī*...

By calculation, because the three circles situated outside the ninefold wheel of origins (*navayonicakra*) are produced from the triad of *bindu* and *nāda*, it takes the form of the twelve zodiac signs (*dvādaśarāśi*), with the intention that its twelve parts related to the wheels are produced by twelve syllables.

This is what he says with the words "the three mandalas. This means "the three circles. We have already demonstrated previously that the position of six circles is mentioned in the *Tantrarāja*. He states that the wheel (*cakra*) consists of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) by combining the aforementioned components, beginning with "space" (*vyoma*). Here, [there is] the point (*bindu*) and the sound (*nāda*).
The calculation is by way of individual separation. Thus,
there are three each of the letters *la*, *sa*, *ha*, *ka*, the bindu, and the nāda, making eighteen,
plus the nine syllables residing in the *hṛllekhā*.
The parts of the wheel produced by twenty-seven syllables consist of three squares,

two lotuses, six circles, a nine-yoni wheel, and for the central triangle, its three corners, three lines, and one point— thus making twenty-seven; the meaning is that this constitutes the form of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
By virtue of the separate mention of the triad of subjects— which consist of will, knowledge, and action— the lines and corners of the central triangle are counted individually.
To illuminate the pun that is about to be explained, he describes the nature of the Goddess as being the Wheel itself:
"Of the deity," [so it is said]. 55 || 56 ||
He states that the Wheel has the nature of Gaṇeśa:
furthermore, by virtue of having the nature of one hundred and eleven deities, the Great Goddess possesses the state of being Gaṇeśa.
[These consist of] the ten beginning with Aṇimā, the eight deities beginning with Brāhmī, and the ten mudrās.

In the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha), there are twenty-eight [deities]. In the six wheels, beginning with the sixteen-petaled lotus and ending with the eight-spoked wheel, there is one deity per spoke; thus, there are sixty-six in total. Then, adding the eighteen weapon-deities—eight in the [sixteen-petaled] circle, three in the triangle, and six young maidens of the six limbs in the bindu—there are seventeen [additional deities] combined.
There are one hundred and eleven deities. By calculating the division of these limbs, which are the forms of the places of worship, the nature of the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) as Gaṇeśa is established.

And [there is] the nature of being the *pīṭhas*. Although the Gaṇeśas and the *pīṭhas* each possess fifty-one individual forms, by virtue of the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "gaṇa," which indicates a large number in its general form, [they are understood as such].
By the intent that it follows the principle of the *aparimitādhikaraṇa*— insofar as it refers merely to another inclusive number beyond the previously specified higher number—
it is understood as referring simply to the number twenty-seven.

The nature of being Gaṇeśa has been stated. The word *mahādevī* refers to the *cakra*. This is precisely for the sake of suggesting this, as it was stated immediately following [this passage] that "it is the supreme body of the deity. As for what the ancients [said]: "The state of being a *rāśi* [is formed] by those excluding the last"—in the subsequent text, the state of being a *rāśi* should be applied to the *vidyā*.
Having explained that by the word "and" (*ca*), the status of Gaṇeśa and others should also be applied [to the letters], they demonstrate the method of that application according to their own will:
"The status of Gaṇeśa [is established] by the lines of the central triangle consisting of the *akatha* [vowels]."

The nature of the planets is represented by nine wheels; the nature of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) by three circles, an eight-spoked figure, and ten outer spokes; and the nature of the Yoginīs, such as Brāhmī and others, by eight triangles.

"The state of being a *rāśi* [zodiacal sign] consists of the five powers (*pañca-śakti*), the four fires (*catur-vahni*), the two lotuses (*padma-dvaya*), and the earth-house (*bhū-gṛha*). This [definition] is disregarded because it is not rooted in the original source and because it is refuted by the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*).
Thus, having explained the nature of Gaṇeśa and others within the *Cakrarāja*, [the author now discusses] the deity whose turn has arrived in sequence.

He expresses their identity with her through this very text using a pun: "Eleven. For these deities are indeed of the nature of the rays of Tripurasundarī; therefore, the Great Goddess, the Śrīmātṛ, possesses the state of Gaṇeśa.
It is precisely out of a desire for brevity in the composition that the sequence beginning with Gaṇeśa is placed within the Cakrarāja by means of such a pun.
[He] was abandoned.
Now, [the author] states that the state of being the planets (grahātmatva) belongs to the Goddess by right of succession: "Together with the Moon, Sun, and Fire" (verse 57).

Furthermore, through will, knowledge, and action, conjoined with the three qualities, that Goddess takes the form of the planets. As stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "Will is the region of the head, and Knowledge is situated below it."
For her action resides in the feet; she is peaceful, situated in the middle of half of the heart.

Because it has been stated thus, the various limbs are grasped by the words "desire" (icchā) and so forth; together with the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—and with the eyes accompanied by Soma and the others, they collectively constitute the form of the planet (graha). This is the meaning. || 57 ||
He states that the Goddess consists of the nature of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), even by means of the organs of knowledge and action: || 58 ||

Furthermore, O Goddess of the gods, by means of those very internal instruments for that purpose, as well as by primordial nature (prakṛti), the qualities (guṇas), and the self bound to masculinity; || 59 ||
The constellations have arisen as physical forms.

(p. 293) Among the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, there are twenty-five principles beyond Niyati; among these, that which is called the bondage of personhood is the principle of Puruṣa.
Nature (*prakṛti*) is the equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇatrayasāmya*); it is twofold, namely the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Among these, the unmanifest is denoted by the term "nature" (*prakṛti*) itself, while the manifest is denoted by the term "qualities" (*guṇa*), as established in the *Svacchandatantra*. The statements supporting this should be consulted in the commentaries of the predecessors. Therefore:

The principle of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva) should be divided and counted as twofold. The internal organs (āntarakaraṇa) are three: ego (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi), and mind (manas); for wealth (vitta) is not counted among them separately.
The ten organs of cognition and action (jñāna-karmendriya) are well known. Their objects (tadartha)—the spheres of those [organs]—are sound and so forth.
And there are speech and the rest. Among these, speech is fire (*tejas*); movement is earth (*bhū*); grasping is water (*vāri*); emission is air (*vāyu*);
and space is bliss (*ānanda*). Thus, there are twenty-six;

the twenty-seventh is the Self (*ātman*)—the meaning is that [the body] is thus born with the stars as its constituent parts. However, the ancient teachers [hold it to be] by means of the mind (*citta*).
Counting the means of destruction as fourfold, they explain the term "ātman" as a qualifier of the bondage of masculinity. || 58 || 59 ||
He describes the Goddess’s nature as that of the Yoginīs: "Now it is said [regarding] the Yoginīs:
she is also [associated] with Ḍākinī and the others, who are the mistresses of the bodily constituents such as the skin. (60)
