Accompanied by the Yoginīs established within the eight groups (vargas),
she who possesses a universal form shines forth, having assumed the form of a Yoginī.

The word *atha* is intended to express an alternative, since indeclinables possess multiple meanings; thus, it means "or else. "When she—the wicked one—has been slain and the lion has been struck down, you must return quickly, having bound and seized that Ambikā for our sake."

This is because such an explanation is seen in the commentary on the verse of the *Saptaśatī*, and because the usage "jonlāvathāmbudheḥ" is also found in the *Vṛttaratnākara*. [The elements] beginning with skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow...

The six are the Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, and Hākinī. Because she consists of these, the Goddess is composed of Yoginīs. Alternatively, the eight classes (vargas)—namely *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *ra*—and the eight [Śaktis] beginning with Vaśinī who reside within them: the meaning is that one should contemplate her as having the form of the Yoginīs by virtue of being composed of them.

For this very reason, the interpretation of the Kashmiris and of the author of the *Manoramā*— who take the word "yoginī" in the verse beginning with "having the form of the Gaṇeśas, planets, lunar mansions, yoginīs, and zodiac signs" as referring to Vaśinī and the others—
is justified. As for those who maintain that there are seven yoginīs, including Yākinī, who presides over Venus:

They explain that these very [vowels] are established in the eight groups because they are seen to abide within the seven cakras, from the *mūlādhāra* to the *sahasrāra*, accompanied by one letter per petal.

There is a contradiction [with the scripture] because, although the sevenfold nature was previously mentioned during the description of the *cakra*, it was not stated during the subsequent description of their manifestation as the forms of the Yoginīs within the *vidyā*. Furthermore, there is the logical impossibility of describing Yākinī separately from the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the six beginning with Ḍākinī.

Furthermore, even if the Ḍākinīs and others were associated with the Mātṛkās respectively, there would be a contradiction regarding the inherent force of the term "eight groups" (*varga-aṣṭaka*), as they lack the nature of being [phonetic] groups;
moreover, this would contradict the explanations of the ancient masters of Kashmir and elsewhere. This is also indicated by the use of the words *api* and *ca*.
Furthermore, there is the sublation of that [distinction] by the natural understanding of a conjunction between two things that are mutually distinct.

Nor should it be said that this contradicts the alternative (vikalpa) stated by you; for even though the Goddess possesses the nature of a conjunction of her two bodies—consisting of both meaning (artha) and sound (śabda)—there is still a distinction between the one or the other.
Because it is possible to conceive of the assistance rendered by the meditation through the three alone. || 60 || 61 ||
He describes the nature of the goddess as the aggregate (rāśi) [of vital breaths]:
"Prāṇa, apāna, and samāna, as well as udāna and vyāna;
furthermore, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. (62)
The individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—these constitute the nature of the aggregate.

The five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa and the five winds beginning with nāga are specific types of air residing within the body, well-known in the medical tradition (vaidyaka-tantra). The individual self is the bound soul (paśu).

She is described as having the form of the *sakala* (the manifest) and so forth; however, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all. Thus, because she consists of twelve aspects, she is composed of the zodiac signs (*rāśimayī*).
Now, as the occasion for the Vidyā has arrived, he describes its form as Gaṇeśa and others:
"Consisting of three rows beginning with A, Ka, and Tha, and following the sequence starting from the third [vowel]. (63)
Gaṇeśa became Mahāvidyā, the supreme speech consisting of the primordial Word.

The sixteen letters beginning with *a*, the sixteen beginning with *ka*, and the sixteen beginning with *tha* are indicative of the letters *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa*. Therefore, the third peak consists of the vowels beginning with *a* and the form of the letter *ha*; the second peak, however, is—
The first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) consists of the form beginning with *ka* and the form of *la*; the second peak-syllable consists of the form beginning with *tha* and the form of *kṣa*.
Thus, because the Vidyā consists of fifty-one units, it possesses the nature of Gaṇeśa. Although the word *paṅkti* is well-known to denote the number ten, in the present context—

"Sixteen more. Since it is well known from the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that there is one *pa* and six *ta*s, when these two numbers are written in sequence, they become sixteen. The ancients, however, maintain that the word *paṅkti* refers to a group. In the term *tripaṅktyātmā*, the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited by the rule *man-*, and the suffix *ḍāp* is optional.

By the phrase "parāvāg-ādi" (beginning with *parāvāk*), *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī* are included. Furthermore, the claim that [Gaṇeśa] possesses the status of Gaṇeśa because he consists of this fourfold speech is incorrect, as it contradicts the *Aparimitādhikaraṇa*. Therefore:
This is intended merely to state its essential nature; and that very nature has already been explained in the *Trikoṇavāsanā*. || 63 ||
He states that Vidyā has the nature of a planet (graha):
"And [Vidyā] consists of the planets within the three peaks (trikūṭa) of the seed-syllables (bīja), the points (bindu), and the resonance (dhvani). (64)

The seed-syllable ending in *ī*, one *bindu*, and one *dhvani*—these three constitute one *kūṭa*. Thus, the Vidyā, consisting of nine syllables across the three *kūṭas*, becomes the essence of the planets (*grahātmikā*).
In the phrase "of the *dhvanis*," the genitive case is used in the sense of a general relationship, functioning here as a third-case [instrumental] sense.
But the very statement that "it is Vedic" is itself Vedic.
He describes the form of the Vidyā as consisting of stars:
"By means of the syllables produced from the three *hṛllekhās*, which are equal in number to the lunar days (*tithi*)."
This [goddess], who has the form of the lunar mansions, consists of twelve other syllables.
The letters ha, ra, ka, bindu, and nāda— these five, each associated with a *hṛllekhā*,
together with fifteen others in the form of consonants, amounting to twelve, thus totaling twenty-seven.
This knowledge has the form of the lunar mansions. || 65 ||
He speaks of the nature of the Yoginīs and the nature of the Rāśis:
"The state of being a Yoginī belongs to the Vidyā through the six Śākta syllables beginning with Śakti which are included within the Vidyā;
and the state of being a Rāśi belongs to the Vidyā through those [syllables] excluding the last. (66)

The power (śakti) inherent within the Vidyā is the letter *ī* at the end of the *hṛllekhā*. Therefore, there is one *kūṭa* beginning with that [letter] and ending in *repha* (*r*). The power of Śakti is the single letter *ī*; thus, with two letters in each *kūṭa*, there is the state of being a Yoginī through these six syllables. Alternatively, it is the first [syllable] of the power *hṛllekhā*.

There are three *la*-letters and three *sa*-letters, making six. Although there is a distinction between the first position, where the entire *vidyā* constitutes the state of being a *yoginī*, and this position, where it is only a single part,
[the aforementioned *yoginīs* associated with the King of Wheels remain the same].

Since it is stated that [the mantra] arises from the three *la* sounds and the three *sa* sounds alone, and since it is improper to abandon the identity of cause and effect when it is possible, this very interpretation is correct. Therefore, one should disregard the group of six mentioned by the ancients— consisting of the three *hṛllekhās* and so forth— because the term "Śāktapada" was previously understood as referring to the *sa* sound.

Furthermore, since you yourself have already explained it here as being intended for the *hṛllekhā*, an interpretation [of it] as something else would be untenable due to contradicting that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). The final three seed-syllables of shame (*lajjābīja*) are excluded;
by counting the preceding syllables when they are joined with those [remaining ones], there are twelve syllables, which constitute the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*).

The status of being the fifteenth belongs to the *hṛllekhās* precisely by virtue of their distinctness. Consequently, the meaning of the term "exclusion" (*varjana*) here is simply the absence of those *hṛllekhās* as characterized by such distinctness.
And that [absence] is indeed caused by the absence of the qualifier. However, the ancients maintain that it is caused solely by the absence of the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
In that view, it should be understood that the status of being a "heap" (rāśi) belongs only to a single portion of knowledge, and not to the complete [knowledge] itself. || 66 ||
Thus,

concluding the non-difference of the deities of the wheels and the vidyās by virtue of their being delimited by a single reality (ekadharma), and having extended by analogy to the teacher and the disciple the method stated by the Goddess, he concludes the Kaulika meaning:

Thus, Maheśvarī, whose form is the expansion of the universe and who takes the shape of the wheel, is described as having a body identical to that of the Goddess; and her Guru’s body is likewise so described. (67)
And through His grace, even the disciple shines forth, being of that very same nature;
thus has the Kaulika meaning been declared, O Goddess worshipped by the heroes. (68)

The Vidyā, whose form is all-pervasive (viśvaprathākārā), the Cakra-form, and the manifest Maheśvarī as the deity—these three are non-different because they consist of fivefold nature according to the manner described above. This half-verse is not seen in some manuscripts. The rest is clear. || 67 || 68 ||
He explains the meaning of all secrets, which follows in sequence, with four verses:
"O sinless one, I shall likewise tell you the meaning of all secrets:
when [the energy] in the form of lightning at the *mūlādhāra* has assumed the form of the *vāgbhava* [syllable]," (69).
The Vidyā, whose form consists of fifty phonemes endowed with thirty-eight kalās,
is of the nature of Kuṇḍalinī and pierces the three maṇḍalas.
Resembling the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning, with a form like a lotus fiber,
it is attached to the lunar orb in the sky and has the nature of a stream of nectar.
The entire universe is eternally pervaded by her whose nature is eternal bliss; the realization that "she is one's own self" is the secret meaning, O Maheśvarī. (72)

In the lotus of the *mūlādhāra*, which resembles lightning, is the *vāgbhava* syllable, the letter *e*; its nature (*bhāva*) is that of the letter *a*, which has the form of a triangle (*trikoṇa*). "Having attained that state" means having reached that very triangular form.
"The letter E is Vāgbhava, Śakti, Jhiṇṭīśa, the lips, and the triangle"— so says the lexicon (*kośa*).
Thus, the indication according to the method of the Dravidian *prāṇāyāma* is for the purpose of illuminating that this *vāgbhava*-cluster is denoted by the letter E.

Established there in the form of Kuṇḍalinī and non-different from it is Vidyā, which is indeed Śrīvidyā. And she is indicated by the fourth vowel in the mantra. This is because, according to the lexicon under the section on the vowel *ī*, the word *jihmā* refers to Kuṇḍalinī, stating: "Vaiṣṇavī, Baindavī, [and] Jihmā. Alternatively, the vowel *ī* refers to the triangle (*trikoṇa*), while the vowel *e*—
"Devoted to Kuṇḍalinī": it is divided as *vāgbhavākāratāgatā* (having attained the form of the Vāgbhava) and *ī*. Regarding the section on the letter *e*, the lexicon states:

"The female consort, the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), moonlight, Kuṇḍalinī, and the womb (*bhaga*). That which comes into being through the powers of speech (*vāgbhiḥ*)—namely, Parā, Paśyantī, and so forth—is the Vāgbhava triangle. It is the manifestation of the Self.
The ancients, however, maintain that it is because it is stated as such [in the verse] "one should see" (*paśyet*). He qualifies Kuṇḍalinī with the word "eight" (*aṣṭa*):

there are ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire, possessing the ten letters beginning with *ya*; twelve digits of the Sun, possessing the twenty-four letters beginning with *ka*; and sixteen digits of the Moon.
[The vowels] possess sixteen sounds. Thus, there are thirty-eight *kalās*.
She whose body consists of the fifty letters conjoined with these [is the Goddess]. This meaning has been expressed by the word *hṛllekhā*;
for although the letter *ha*, according to the convention of the *Ekākṣaranighaṇṭu*, has the power to denote the moon alone, it is used here through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
It signifies the awakening of both the moon and the sun, due to the possible connection (*śakyasaṃbandha*) with the nature of moving through the sky.

Alternatively, the letter *la* itself, though denoting the eye, refers here to the sun; the letter *ra* refers to fire; and by the vowel *ī*, their digits (*kalā*) are indicated, according to the lexicon which states: "The fourth digit is Bheruṇḍā."

The letter *la* signifies the number three, and the letter *ha* signifies the number eight; it can also be easily stated that when these two are arranged in sequence, they become thirty-eight. This being the case, by the principle of remainder (*pariśeṣa-pramāṇa*), the letter *ka* is to be understood as denoting the *mūlādhāra*.

In the context of the Lopāmudrā-vidyā, the Sun and Fire are denoted by the letter *pra* (the first consonant), and the Moon by the letter *sa*. She in whom their digits reside is Hṛllekhā; the meaning is that she is Kuṇḍalinī. He explains the second *kūṭa* with the words beginning "maṇḍala," etc.: in the Mūlādhāra is the fire-maṇḍala, and in the Anāhata...

Having pierced through the three—the solar disc at the *ājñā-cakra* and the lunar disc—she is attached to that lunar disc which resides in the sky within consciousness, in the upper portion beyond the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*).
Her essential nature is the wave of the nectar-stream arising from attachment to that [disc]. *Haḥ* signifies the sun.

The fire that, together with the moon, strikes and pierces them is *hasakaha* (the piercing one, *ghnī*). She is both that [fire] and the wave (*laharī*), for in the *Durvāsas-vidyā*, the letters *ha* and *ra* are taught even when separated. The phrase "ten million lightning bolts" is merely a description of its essential nature. Here, there are several [instances of] grammatical rules required.
The apparent contradictions have been resolved by us in the *Varivasyārahasyavyākhyāna*.

Likewise: "Because the verbal root has many meanings, because of the inclusion of the term 'bahula' (diverse), because of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* class, because it is listed in the *ākṛtigaṇa*, and because of the formation of *uṇādi* suffixes according to one's own will."
(p. 298) "In Vedic usage, because all rules are optional, the grammarians' instruction is in agreement with this matter as stated by Manu.
Thus he explains the third *kūṭa* [with the word] *sadā*; the words "by which" (*yayā*) are to be supplied. By which, always...

The entire universe is pervaded by that which has the nature of Being (sadrūpa); this very Kuṇḍalinī is one's own Self, and the realization that she is non-different from oneself is called the "esoteric meaning" (rahasyārtha), which is the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) according to the method taught in the *Svatantra-tantra*— namely, "being manifested through the Void"— by means of the third *hṛllekhā*.

The pervasion of the world has been stated. By the word *sakala*, the practitioner (*upāsaka*) is denoted. And by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), non-difference is understood; such is the meaning. || 69 || 70 || 71 || 72 ||
He teaches the meaning of the Great Reality (mahātattvārtha) which follows in due order:
"O Goddess, I shall tell you that which is called the meaning of the Great Reality;
it exists in the partless, supreme, subtle, indefinable state, which is set in motion by consciousness. (73)

The unification of one's own self within the supreme reality that transcends the void, whose form is light and bliss, which is beyond the universe yet consists of the universe—this is the true application of the self. (74)

In the partless, which means without divisions or limbs; in the supreme, which is greater than the great; in the subtle, subtler than the atom; in the indefinable, beyond the reach of the senses; in that which exists as pure being, accessible only through contemplation; in that which transcends the ether, the progenitor even of space; in the Supreme Reality.

In that which is the ultimate reality, whose form is light and bliss, whose nature is consciousness-bliss, transcending the universe, beyond the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), yet consisting of the universe— a reality non-different from the thirty-six principles—
the unification of one's own individual soul (*jīvātman*), self, and mind through the non-duality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva.

"Mental visualization" (*manasā vibhāvanam*)—in accordance with the method stated in the *Śivasūtra*, "the union [of the individual soul and Śiva] occurs repeatedly"—means, in effect, the establishment of the identity (*aikya*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva. Since such an object is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*), the knowledge of it possesses a unique objective reference (*viṣayatā*) distinct from that of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); therefore, regarding that which produces such [knowledge]:
Even though the mantra, like "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and other such great statements (*mahāvākya*), is indeed a mahāvākya,

the knowledge arising from it through the differentiation of words and their meanings necessarily possesses parts (*sakhaṇḍatva*); nevertheless, there are the six means of proof (*pramāṇa-ṣaṭka*), beginning with the introductory context (*upakrama*).

Rather than postulating a comprehension of an indivisible meaning through the secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) of all words according to an already determined purport, it is more appropriate— by grasping the purport through the statement of Paraśiva— that the power (śakti) of the mantra itself resides in such an indivisible meaning.
Because it is logical to conceive [the mantra] in this way, its status as the meaning of the mantra is established.

Furthermore, by stating that the meaning consisting of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*), Paraśiva himself has implied that other meanings are not essential, since they are not grounded in the letters. And this being so—

It should not be suspected that the effort to determine whether the meanings of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) and so forth are grounded in the literal letters is futile; for since those meanings lack indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*), such an effort is necessary. This is because [the meaning] is qualified by many constituent word-meanings.
It is observed that a meaning which is composite is conveyed by words such as "pervasion" (vyāpti) or "limiting condition" (upādhi) even without a division into base and suffix;
by that same logic, it is easily stated that the power of a mantra resides in its indivisible essence within the innermost core of its meaning.

And the apprehension of power (*śakti*) arises solely from the word of Paraśiva; for logicians accept that the very will of the Lord (*īśvara*) constitutes power. Therefore, regarding the *Kāmarāja* and *Lopāmudrā* vidyās—and indeed, what need is there to say more?—each one of the fifty [mantras] distinguished by the various traditions such as those of Manu, Candra, and others, [is established].
The unity of purpose among the mantras and the absence of any deficiency in the auspicious means of worship for their respective practitioners are thus consistent. Nevertheless,
since it is improper to postulate an indivisible power when the literal meaning is possible, it has been stated accordingly.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the statement in the root text that "the meaning of the syllables (*akṣarārtha*) is precisely the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*"); for in the phrase "the meaning of the syllables is the meaning of the verbal root alone, [who is] the Supreme Goddess," the word "alone" (*kevala*) indicates that while the meaning of the verbal root is obtained solely through the function of the syllables, others [are not].

Because meanings— even those apprehended by the mind— manifest through *dhvani* (suggestion) via both verbal presumption (*śabdārthāpatti*) and objective presumption (*arthārthāpatti*), how else could it have been indicated by the authors of the root text themselves when they stated that [the power of mantras] "spreads forth from the root itself" by means of a sequence of various mantras? By this, that which...
The insistence that these six topics are exclusively devoted to the *Lopāmudrā-vidyā* of the ancients,
resulting in the repeated mention of that very vidyā in various contexts,
is based solely on partiality and is therefore not to be trusted; for therein is also a contradiction with the original source.
And because it has been demonstrated therein. || 73 || 74 ||
Now he establishes the non-difference of the Supreme Śiva from the universe:
"At that time, the state of being manifest belongs to both darknesses and lights;
therefore, the universe is everywhere of the nature of inseparable existence. (75)
The Great Reality shines forth, radiant with the essence of divine play;

for it is that which makes manifest the darkness of objects such as jars— which are insentient by nature— as well as lights that are inert illuminations, and even cognitions in the form of mental modifications.

It is the destruction of the veil residing in the consciousness (caitanya) delimited by the respective natures [of objects]. And that occurs precisely when there is the manifestation of Brahman—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. For in the cognition "I know the jar," both the jar and the individual self (jīvātman) are objects of the cognition in the form of a mental modification (vṛtti); yet that modification is illuminated solely by Brahman, which is Brahman itself.

However, the established position is that [consciousness] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), according to the Śruti: "Everything shines only after Him who shines" (*tameva bhāntamanubhāti sarvam*). For this very reason, the venerable Ācārya Bhagavatpāda stated: "In the cognition 'I know,' this entire world shines only after Him who shines. The logicians (*tārkika*), however, maintain that [the cognition] is simply "this is a jar."
The form of the cognition of a jar [is distinct]. However, it is accepted that the cognition of the cognition, which consists of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), is indeed distinct. (p.
300) But for the followers of the Upaniṣads, even in reflective awareness...

Considering that it is necessary for [the cognition] to have the object of the determinate judgment (vyavasāya) as its own object, and thinking, "What is the use of a determinate judgment that contradicts an internal experience?", they accept the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya) itself as standing in the place of the determinate judgment.
However, since the manifestation of knowledge belongs to Brahman alone,

it is maintained that there is no dependence on another subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), and thus it is not defiled by the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"That knowledge which is the knowledge of 'this,' that knowledge which is the knowledge of 'I,' and that knowledge which is the knowledge of both—know that knowledge to be my very body.
This being so, Brahman indeed shines forth in every act of cognition. And therefore, whenever...

The meaning is that, by the rule that "whenever there is the manifestation of Brahman, at that very time there is the manifestation of the universe," Brahman is non-different from the universe. Nor should it be argued that, on this basis, only a temporal concomitance (*kālikavyāpti*) between the knowledge of Brahman and the knowledge of the universe is established, and not the identity of their objects; for [Brahman is...]

This is established even by the inference: "The jar is non-different [from consciousness], because it is the object of the cognition of the jar"; the details of this are found elsewhere. *Avinābhāva* means non-separateness, that is to say, non-difference. Alternatively, it is called *śarvataḥ* because of its non-difference from Śarva (Śiva) in every respect; or rather, it is with Śiva.

The meaning is that the Great Reality (*mahātattva*), which is the non-dual form of the universe, shines forth even within the practitioner who is radiant with the essence of divine play (*divyakrīḍārasa*). By implication, this refers to one whose mind is pure and radiant with the essence of that divine play, which is the supreme worship. As for the earlier commentators, [they ask]: "What [is there to say] regarding that which is self-luminous?"
He says "it is manifested" in order to avoid the search for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). They say that "divine play" and so forth are vocatives addressed to the Goddess. (75)
Preceded by a state in which all conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations have been cast aside.
This secret meaning is greatly concealed and produces immediate conviction;
it has been seen in the great ocean of knowledge, O Pārvatī, and there is no doubt regarding it.
Established in the treatises on the seats of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), he bestows divine perfection.

"Volition" (*saṃkalpa*) refers to mental action—that is, a contrary determination. "Conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) refers to doubt, that which has an unreal object, or verbal cognition; having cast aside the entire persistence of these, [he remains].

Only afterwards does it produce immediate wonder. Such is this secret meaning; for that very reason, it has remained concealed until today. It is found in the *Mahājñānārṇava Tantra*, in the seats of learning (*vidyāpīṭha*) such as Kāśī and Kāśmīra, and in the commentaries (*nibandha*) such as the *Brahmasūtra* and other treatises.
The meaning is that since this has been seen by all the Noble Ones (Āryas), no doubt should be entertained here.

According to the ancients, however: "The great ocean of knowledge" refers to *samādhi*; "the seats of knowledge" (*vidyāpīṭhas*) refer to the *kūṭas* beginning with *vāgbhava*; and their "bindings" refer to the sequence beginning with the *bindu* and *ardhacandra*, ending with *unmanā*.
They say that beyond the state of *unmanī*, during the stage of *samādhi*, this matter has been seen by me alone; therefore, it is to be trusted by you—this is the meaning. || 76 || 77 ||
O Goddess, by those devoted to the Kaula conduct and intent upon the meditation on the sandals (pādukā), || 78 ||
By those intent on the gathering of yoginīs, who have received the divine consecration.
By those who are free from the stain of doubt and whose minds are always joyful. || 79 ||
O Goddess, O beautiful one of the Kula, it is obtained through tradition by those who are experts in the secret meaning known [to them]; not otherwise, I swear this to you.

The two types of conduct, namely *kaulācāra* and *pādukācāra*, are well known in the *Kulārṇava* and other texts, and have been compiled and written down by the author of the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*. These consist of the temple (*bhavana*), the wheel (*cakra*), the mantra, and the worship (*pūjā-vāsana*). [One should practice] with those devoted to this triad.

The gathering of yoginīs: a married woman (*suvāsinī*) between the ages of sixteen and thirty-two is called a yoginī. The worship of the Śrīcakra is performed by unifying three such women—or no fewer than three—with one who is a knower of the *Urdhvāmnāya*. This is the characteristic of the cakra.
Because it is described in that very manner in the Kulārṇava.
As it is said: "O Kuleśvarī, wherever there is a Kulācārya who knows the truth of the Āgamas, and likewise, O Dear One, three, four, or five Kaulika Śaktis,"
O Goddess, O Queen of the Gods, they may be worshipped either individually or in the form of couples,
well-adorned with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings.
And they dwell there joyfully, accompanied by the intense bliss of the ultimate state, with various kinds of food and meat provided with the six flavors.

"That is called the Śrīcakra, or it is also called the Vṛnda," as stated in the tenth chapter (Ullāsa). Those by whom the two types of divine consecrations— the initiation-consecration (dīkṣābhiṣeka) and the full-consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka)— have been obtained [are eligible for] the sacrificial offerings among the materials for worship.

The suspicion of unrighteousness due to the ritual consecration (*saṃskāra*) prescribed in the scriptures for sacrificial animals, and the very suspicion of being subject to the dualistic scriptures regarding the result of this [practice]— the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīvabrahmābheda*)— are the stains from which they are free.
The compound is formed as *apatāpa-ūḍha-mukta-patita-apatrasta-alpaśas*.
Nor should it be argued that there is no compound when joined with a prefix other than the prefix *apa*;

for since the word is recited three times as *apeta*, *apoḍha*, and *apatrasta*, it is understood that the absence of compounding applies only when joined with those specific instances and not with others. Furthermore, by the use of the term *alpaśaḥ* (rarely) in the sūtra, the rarity of such doubt is indicated.

The meaning is that [this state] is to be attained through the power of concentration; therefore, it may be suspected even by those who possess only a small amount [of merit], provided they are free from doubt. By those whose minds are always joyful—that is, at all times liberated from worldly anxieties—meaning, by those intent on constant contemplation. Of one who possesses eternal contentment...

Because the role of gatekeeper to the door of liberation is described in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*, [the text refers to] those experts and masters who have understood the secret meaning through the very lineage beginning from Paramaśiva down to their own guru. (p. 302)
This goal is attained only by practitioners distinguished by such specific qualifications;
otherwise, if even a single qualification pertaining to this matter were absent, it would not be attained. The meaning is: "In this regard, you yourself must swear an oath. || 78 || 79 || 80 ||

By stating that in the absence of the aforementioned qualification— namely, "by way of tradition" (pāramparyeṇa)— there is not only an absence of fruit but, on the contrary, a succession of misfortunes, he suggests that this qualification is absolutely more essential than the other qualifications.
Those who are devoid of the lineage and are arrogant merely on account of their knowledge—
for them, through the violation of their commitments, the Marīcis manifest as portents.
They "perform transformations" (vikurvanti), meaning they undergo changes, produce dangers such as disease, and cause the destruction of the next world. || 81 ||
But he who, rejoicing in the contemplation of the taste of divine flavors, [performs this] on a festival day for a deity, a guest, or a lunar mansion, or even on the day of the Sun; || 82 ||
He who always offers libations with honey and other substances to the rays of the sun attains,
in particular, perfect enlightenment.

"Divyarasa" (divine essence) refers to the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti; he is one whose mental activity (*manovṛtti*) consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) rejoicing through the tasting of and contemplation upon that [essence]. "Deities and guests" refers to the fourteenth lunar day and so forth. "Nakṣatra" (asterism)...

[This refers to] the birth-star of Puṣya, the birth-star of [the practitioner], and so forth. The boon of Vivasvat, the Sun—on these days, one certainly pleases the deities such as Marīci and Aṇimā by means of the rule; the meaning is that one performs the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjā). From here onwards, the verse-line contains scrambled syllables: "kāraṇānandapūrṇa" (filled with the bliss of the cause).
That is its meaning. The sequence for reciting it is as follows:
"He who knows not the sequence—Devatā, Ratha, Gomūka—is mute regarding the jumbled syllables, even though he may be Devatā, Ratha, or Go. Thus it is said.
Thus, one who is habitually engaged in constant and specific contemplation attains the realization of the perfect and indivisible [Reality]. || 82 || 83 ||
O Goddess of gods, such a state of being, consisting of great knowledge, is attained immediately by men through the grace of the supreme teacher, O Goddess. (84)

Such a state, consisting of great wisdom—even though it is a flow of mental fluctuations—is obtainable solely through the grace of the venerable Guru's feet, and not by mere knowledge of the scriptures alone. (84)

(p. 303) He concludes the secret convention of the mantras: "Thus, O Goddess, this supreme knowledge, which is the domain of the scriptures of the Vidyās, has been explained by me out of affection as a secret, consisting of six difficult parts. (85)
"By whose immediate awakening one becomes the Lord of the Circle of Heroes (vīracakreśvara).
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Śrī-nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*.
[The compound] *durgā-duravagāha-ṣaṭsaṃkhyāka-vidha* means that in which there are six kinds or modes (*prakāra*) that are difficult to penetrate.

The syllables of the *Vidyā*—that is, the fifteen and thirty-seven syllables of the *Śrīvidyā*—are themselves the *Āgamas*, because, being non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*), they communicate what is beneficial; thus, they are the Vedas. Their scope is their subject matter. It is not the Triple Veda (*trayī*).

The absence of the masculine gender [in the word *jñāna*] is as in the case of the term *śrutigocara*. Such a secret—that which stands as if within a cave (*guhā*)—is "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it is by means of this that the Supreme (*parama*), the most excellent, is known; for it is the cause of the object's own experience. It has been explained precisely through "the beloved," that is, solely through the love generated by the service and other acts performed for you.

By the immediate and supreme realization of this meaning, the Lord of the assembly (*cakra*)—that is, the Lord of Heroes (*vīreśa*), the enjoyer of the triad, whose definition is set forth in the *Śivasūtra* for the heroic practitioners (*vīra-upāsaka*)—comes to be; thus all is auspicious. 85.
Thus, in the commentary titled Setubandha on the ocean of the Nityāṣoḍaśikā composed by the illustrious Bhāskara, the seventh rest-period has come to an end.

Now begins the eighth rest (viśrāma). Having thus taught the secret convention of the mantras through eighty-five and a half verses, he makes a formal promise to ensure the disciple’s attention, in order to teach the secret convention of worship which follows in due order:
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O sinless one, I shall now tell you the secret convention of worship,
by the mere awakening to which one who is liberated while living rejoices.

The sense is that if one is liberated while living merely by knowing the conventional designation (*saṃketa*), then such a state is established even more easily—by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*)—through the worship of the *cakra* preceded by such contemplation (*vibhāvanā*). || 1 ||
He divides worship [as follows]:
"O Gaurī, your eternally manifest worship is established through three distinctions: the supreme (parā), the non-supreme (aparā), and the third, which is both supreme and non-supreme (parāparā). (2)
The meaning is that the eternal worship of yours described in the previous *Catuḥśatī* is of three kinds, and not of the occasional (*kāmyā*) or occasional (*naimittikī*) types. || 2 ||
He characterizes them in sequence:
"The first is the state of non-dual being, the sphere of all movement;
the second is the worship of the wheel, which is always performed by me. (3)
Thus, O Goddess, the third [state] consists of knowledge and is composed of one's own self-manifestation;
it is to be known as the supreme and highest. Now listen to the ritual procedure.
The *parā* [form of worship] occurs when there is a general absence of the appearance of duality; the *aparā* occurs when there is a general absence of the appearance of non-duality;
and the *parāparā* occurs during the stage of practicing the dissolution of duality—these are the characteristics of the threefold worship.
In that state where no duality exists, such a "bhāva" is a particular modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttiviśeṣa*).

It remains and becomes the subject (*viṣayin*). Because they move forth extensively and turn toward their objects, they are called the "active senses" (*pracarāṇīndriyāṇi*). Their range is the object (*viṣaya*). Among those objects that appear within the cognitions produced by all the senses, there is the manifestation of the pervasive aspect of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*).

But it does not apply to name and form when they have followed [the self]. This is that knowledge known as "truth-bearing" (*ṛtambharā*) in the *Yoga Sūtras*. That is the first worship, called the Supreme (*parā*).
Wherever the mind goes—whether externally or internally, O Beloved—there [it is to be offered].
In each of those instances, the consciousness of the Lord is manifested through the path of the senses.

This is well-known among the traditional authorities (*abhiyuktas*). That worship described in the *Pūrvatantre*—beginning with the "earth-house" (*bhūgṛha*) and ending with the "point" (*bindu*)—which is performed by me daily, is the second [type].

This was stated in this manner to indicate that even one who is qualified for the supreme worship (*parapūjā*) should perform this [lower worship] as well. In that which consists of knowledge (*jñānamaya*),...

In Brahman, whose sole nature is consciousness, the manifestation of one's own self as non-different [from it]— that is to say, the practice of the non-duality of both— is the third [state]. It is this [third state].
In the abode that is the singular forest of light, I cast all conceptual constructions, such as those of emanation and so forth,
through the act of worship, like offerings of clarified butter into a fire.
By such statements as these, [the practice] has been described by the learned authorities. Among these, the *parā* (supreme) is to be known as the best;
the *parāparā* (intermediate) is the middling; and the *aparā* (inferior) is the lowest—this is what is meant by implication. The meaning is:
"Now, listen in due order to the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) and the specific performance (*itikartavyatā*) of these. || 3 || 4 ||

Therein, he describes the supreme worship that presents itself first with three verses: [One should meditate on] the sandals of the Guru located within the Mahāpadma forest, which are the source of speech (vāgbhava), whose form nourishes the entire world, and who shower the highest nectar. (5)
Having reflected, he was reeling with the intoxication of the contemplation of supreme non-duality;
intent upon beholding the resonance spreading within the small space [of the heart].
Always turned inward and free from the internal chatter of conceptual forms,
he is exceedingly beautiful, his contraction shattered by the radiance of the consciousness-light.
In the central region between the pervasive seat (vyāpikāsana) and the throne (āsana), there is the thousand-petaled lotus itself;

because it is covered by many petals, it is the "Great Lotus Forest" (mahāpadmavana). Situated within that—that is, located in the middle of its pericarp—is the Vāgbhava [syllable], which is the letter *e* and the triangle. Therein...

The Guru’s sandals— the Akula Amṛtakuṇḍalinī who is the essence of one's own Lord, non-different from Paraśiva, and established by the mantra of the Guru’s sandals; she whose form nourishes the universe,
who nourishes all things moving and unmoving through the expansion of her own cooling rays, and who rains down the supreme nectar.

Having contemplated her as raining down a continuous and dense shower of the essence of consciousness, and having realized her as non-different from oneself, one should become equanimous, reeling with the intoxication and bliss of such supreme non-dual realization. This constitutes the acceptance of the Guru’s grace following the worship of the Guru.
As it has been said by the learned:
"The form of Śiva is one, self-luminous; the body of his self-reflection (vimarśa) is the other; of these two..."
The supreme *pādukā* is held to have the nature of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium), belonging to the Guru who is the very self of Supreme Śiva.
The Guru, who is Śiva himself, being of the nature of self-luminous consciousness,
is gracious toward the summit of all categories of existence;
that grace of his is here the purification of the principles (tattva-śodhana).
Having attained it, the fortunate one experiences joy. Thus [it is said].
Having accepted this favor, one should perform the internal recitation (*japa*); thus he says: "In the *dahara*," etc.
The *dahara* is the space of the heart; within it, in its center, is the *nāda* which moves along.

He is intent upon and devoted to the beholding and continuous contemplation of the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*), which is the primordial nature of all mantras. For this very reason, he is averse to and turned away from that *japa*— which consists of the utterance of either speech or mind, taking the form of discursive thought (*vikalpa*), possessing many millions of aspects, and being swallowed by duality (*dvaita*).
One should always be inward-turned, with the mind not projected outward. And it is said in the fifth chapter:
"One should utter the internal sound (nāda) while restraining the movement of the senses;
this alone is declared to be japa, for external japa is not true japa."

He whose contraction and limited manifestation have been shattered by the unfolding of the *citkalā*— which has hitherto appeared contracted— through its expansion into a state of all-pervasive, unlimited radiance; for this very reason, he is exceedingly beautiful.
The meaning is that he is the one who experiences the fruit consisting of the state of being a beautiful woman born from the parasūjā [parasūjānyasundarī].

|| 5 || 6 || 7 || Thinking that the worship of the Supreme (parā-pūjā) has the subordinate worships (aparā-pūjā and parāparā-pūjā) as its constituent parts, based on such scriptural statements as "One who is not a god should not worship a god" and "Having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva."

Without omitting the worship of others, he describes another worship and the supreme worship by means of a concise formula (tantra): "Having performed self-worship with substances that gratify the senses..."
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body, preceded by the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
One should perform the worship of the deity, whose nature is the Self, with substances such as fragrance that produce delight in the senses. As it is said in the *Āmnāyarahasya*:
"The deity of the Self is to be worshipped with fragrances and other objects perceivable through the doors of the senses."
"By its very nature, it is to be perfectly propitiated; this is that great sacrifice for the knower.
Following such self-worship, one should perform the forty-four *nyāsas*, which consist of establishing the assembly of deities within one's own body.

He said: "In the case of the *ātmapūjā* and the *nyāsajāla*, the sequence obtained through the textual order (*pāṭhakrama*) results only in a subsequent time in accordance with the Vedic sequence (*śrautakrama*) regarding certain items to be mentioned hereafter;
it does not, however, mean immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*). And this is in accordance with the view of the ancients."

This has been explained. In reality, however, following the opening statement "within the range of all common practice" and preceded by the conclusion "by means of the senses," there is an injunction for [the rite] to be a constituent part of worshiping others; therefore, it is worship with scents and so forth.
The body itself is the object of worship for another, not for oneself;
for that [self-worship] occurs subsequent to the placement of the vessels following the array (*nyāsa*).
And therefore, [one worships] the Guru situated at the head and the *nāda-avidyā* residing in the heart.
Simultaneously with the manifestation of non-duality between the Self and the Goddess whose form consists of all-pervading, all-encompassing *citkalās*,
while enjoying sense objects through all the senses,

[the yogi] possesses a single essence consisting solely of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) whose object is the mere stream of bliss produced by that [enjoyment], [thereby transcending] all else.

This composition of the text should be understood as having this much as its intended meaning: that "supreme worship" consists in remaining for some time without the loss of the object [of consciousness].
Therefore, it should be kept in mind that the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) must be performed without any interruption from such supreme worship. 8.
He defines the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa):
"The first deposition is with the Gaṇeśas; the second is considered to be with the planets (grahas);
the third shall be with the lunar mansions (nakṣatras); and the fourth with the Yoginīs. (9)
The fifth is to be known by means of the *rāśis* (zodiac signs), and the sixth is declared by means of the *pīṭhas* (sacred seats).
This sixfold installation (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) has been proclaimed as invincible everywhere.

The six [suffixes] such as *gaṇeśa* (in *gaṇeśam*, etc. possess intermediate apūrvas (unseen potencies) formed by the name-constituent (*nāmaghaṭita*) ritual acts; from these arises the supreme apūrva (*paramāpūrva*). [The verbal root *nam*] functions by taking the capacity to produce such a supreme apūrva as its delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).
The "sixfold deposition" (ṣoḍhānyāsa) is the name of the ritual act according to the principle of [naming after] its characteristic feature. || 9 || 10 ||
He reveals the greatness of the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa):
"He who has thus deposited [the mantras] upon his limbs is to be worshipped by all yogis;
for him, there is no one in the worlds—neither father nor mother nor anyone else—to be worshipped. (11)
He alone is worthy of worship by all; he is himself the Supreme Lord.
O Pārvatī, whoever bows down to one who is devoid of the sixfold nyāsa, [he incurs sin]. 12.
"He soon meets with death and falls into hell"—
regarding the phrase "him whom one should bow to," it is established in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara* that the meaning is "one should bow to him with anger. And this is appropriate.

One should bow down without any other refuge to the sky, the wind, fire, water, and earth; to the luminaries, living beings, the quarters, and trees; to the rivers and oceans—whatever exists is the body of Hari.
Thus, according to the method stated by Viṣṇu Bhāgavata, because one who has no other [deity] must necessarily cultivate the contemplation of the Goddess everywhere, everything is to be saluted;
on the contrary, there is no inferiority relative to oneself that could serve as a limiting factor for non-salutation.
Furthermore, because there would arise a contradiction with the practice of non-duality (*advaitopāsti*) through the repeated contemplation of that which is pervaded by difference;
for there would be no setting aside of heterogeneous cognitions (*vijātīyapratyaya*).
Nor [is it the case that] even excellence relative to oneself, which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for being an object of salutation— p. 308) [is sufficient].

It should not be argued that this defect is exactly the same because [the relationship] is pervaded by difference; for, according to such statements as "Brahmins who are equal to one another are mutually gurus," it is precisely the state of being distinguished from others through mutual injunctions that constitutes the delimitor of the status of being worthy of salutation. Nor is it the case that...

It might be suspected that the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable because "being distinct from oneself" must also be included as a qualification therein in order to exclude self-prostration; however, this is not so, because prostration to oneself is indeed accepted, both through the contemplation of one's own nature as Brahman and on the basis of the statements of authoritative teachers such as, "Salutations again and again to me. This is because [the Self] is non-different.

Since this meaning is also indicated by the word "iti" in the *Bhāgavata*, the sense is that even by a mere angry prostration performed by such a devotee, misfortune befalls the hater; how much more so, then, by means of curses, malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), and the like. Therefore—

The intent of this [passage] is to establish that he (the Lord) is worthy of all worship. In the same way, this should also be inferred in the statement that reveals the "bursting open" (*asphoṭana*) of the one who is to be saluted by those performing the deposition of powers (*śaktinyāsa*).
The rest is easy to understand. || 11 || 12 ||
And I shall describe the method of the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) to you, O sinless one.
Vighneśa, Vighnarāja, Vināyaka, Śivottama, Vighnakṛt, Vighnahartā, Vighnarāj, and Gaṇanāyaka. || 14 ||
He has one tusk and two tusks; he is elephant-faced and stainless;
he wears matted hair, has a long face, spike-like ears, and the bull as his emblem. 15.
Gaṇanātha, Gajendra, Śūrpakarṇa, Trilocana, Lambodara, Mahānāda, Caturmūrti, and Sadāśiva. || 16 ||
Āmoda, Durmada, Sumukha, Pramodana, Ekapāda, Dvijihva, Śūra, Vīra, and Ṣaṇmukha. || 17 ||
The Bestower of Boons, Vāmadeva, Vakratuṇḍa, Dvituṇḍaka, Senānī, Grāmaṇī, Matta, Vimatta, and Mattavāhana. || 18 ||
Jaṭī, Muṇḍī, Khaḍgī, Vareṇya, Vṛṣaketana, Bhakṣyapriya, Gaṇeśa, Meghanāda, and Gaṇeśvara. || 19 ||

Herein are fifty-one names, beginning with Vighneśa. Among these, due to differences in various tantras, occasional variations in the names and variations in parts of the names are observed; for example, "Agninetra" occurs in place of "Trilocana," and "Dīrghavaktra" occurs in place of "Dīrghamukha."
In place of "kapardabhṛt," [the forms] "kapardavān" and so forth [are used]. 13 || 14 || 15 || 16 || 17 || 18 || 19 ||
He describes the meditation upon these [deities]:
"Resembling the young morning sun, with elephant faces and three eyes, holding a noose, a goad, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and accompanied by their Śaktis. (20)
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should place these [deities] according to the positions of the Mātṛkās.

[The central deity is] like the midday sun, glowing with the hue of a fresh dawn. Starting from the upper left hand and ending with the lower left hand, the weapons are placed, accompanied by their Śaktis, together with Puṣṭi and the others.

Or [one may worship them] together with the powers (śaktis) described as having six characteristics according to the different tantras, such as hearing and so forth. This accompaniment does not consist merely of meditation; rather, there is also the application of their names within the mantra. In this regard, some write the separate usage: "Vighneśvarāya Śriyai Namaḥ" and so on.

Others, however, say that "vighneśvaraśrībhyāṃ namaḥ" is a *dvandva* compound. But the moderns [hold] that in many instances, such as "bhavānīśaṃkarābhyām" and "lakṣmīnārāyaṇābhyām," the name of the Śakti invariably comes first.
They say that because such usage is observed, the formulation "by Śrī and Vighneśvara" is indeed appropriate.

However, this must be addressed here: let the primacy of the name Śakti be granted; for in the *Jñānārṇava* it is stated: "Vighneśvara is joined with Śrī, and likewise Vighnarāja with Hrī," and so forth.
Because the order of recitation for Gaṇeśa and His Śakti is not intended to be significant, and because we observe even the reverse order in the statement "Śivottama joined with Śānti," however,
[the sequence] follows the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19).

Because their subordination is understood through the instrumental case endings following words denoting capacities (*śakti*), even in such expressions as "joined with tranquility" (*śāntyā yuktaḥ*), the predominance of Gaṇeśa alone is understood by way of the relationship between qualifier and qualified; thus, it is stated in the present Tantra as well: "The first installation (*nyāsa*) is with the Gaṇeśas."

Since it is stated that for the Gaṇeśas alone, the third case-ending (instrumental) expresses their status as independent instruments, and since both [the Śrutis and the Gaṇeśas] possess equal primacy, it is more appropriate for the nominative case-ending to follow words such as "Śruti" just as it does after words like "Vighneśvara"; therefore, the third case-endings [used after] words such as "yukta" and "sahita" [are incorrect].
Furthermore, the assumption that [the term] lacks an intended meaning would result in the absence of evidence for the dual compound (*dvandvasamāsa*),
which indicates equal primacy between the two;
however, if the placement (*nyāsa*) of the pair is prescribed by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application), then a dual compound signifying mutual association would be appropriate.
However, when even a pair [of deities] is installed in sequence, the ritual application (*prayoga*) is indeed distinct due to the specific qualification of mutual association.
For this very reason, in the *Rudrayāmala*, in the section on the propitiation of Mahāgaṇapati, it says:
"Thereafter, one should propitiate the pairs, such as Siddhi and Āmoda, according to one's desire."
Thus, having established the extraction of the mantra, it has been performed precisely with the words joined together:
first one should utter the *praṇava*, then one should pronounce *lakṣmī*,
then the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa, and thereafter [the syllable] accompanied by *siddhi*.

(310) "I satisfy Āmoda"—thus four times in the same manner; likewise, "I satisfy Siddhi together with Āmoda," four times in succession, and so forth. In the present case, however, for the pair [of deities], it is done either by the method of simultaneous recitation (*tantra*) or sequentially (*krama*).

It should be understood that because Gaṇeśa alone is not the presiding deity (devatā), but rather Gaṇeśa accompanied by Śrī who is the deity, the formulation "Obeisance to Vighneśa accompanied by Śrī" (*śrīsahitavighneśāya namaḥ*) and so forth is the appropriate one.
This is like the positions of the Mātṛkās; that is, each [deity] corresponds respectively to a single letter of the Mātṛkā and to its respective position.

This is a qualifier for the act of ritual placement (*nyāsakriyā*). Therefore, this suffix is *matup* (possessive), not *vati* (adverbial). Consequently, the practical application should be inferred as follows: having uttered "Aṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Obstacles endowed with Śrī," one should perform the placement on the head, and so forth. || 20 ||
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the planets:
"One should place the Sun, together with the vowels, below the heart. (21)
O Dear One, one should place the moon, the source of nectar, in the location of the *bindu* by means of the four letters beginning with *ya*;
and the son of the Earth (Mars) in the pair of eyes, as the lord of the *ka*-group.
O Dear One, one should place Budha, the lord of the ca-group, upon the heart;
and Bṛhaspati, the lord of the ṭa-group, in the region of the throat.
One should again place Śukra, the lord of the ta-varga, in the heart;
and Śanaiścara, the lord of the pa-varga, in the navel, O Goddess of the Gods.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should place Rāhu together with the four vowels beginning with *ā* in the mouth, and Ketu together with the letter *kṣa* in the anus.
By the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*. "Below the heart" means at the junction of the heart and the stomach;

according to another tantra, it is at the heart itself; [it is] in the location of the *bindu*. For the sake of consistency with the *Jñānārṇava*, its meaning is "between the eyebrows"; some say "in the middle of the forehead," but that is not correct.
In that regard, the support (*ādhāra*) and the location of the *bindu* have been proclaimed;

for, according to the statement in the *Svacchanda Tantra*, those very [authorities] have explained the term "location of the *bindu*" as referring to the space between the eyebrows. [The phrase] "the source of nectar" refers to the moon. By means of the four letters beginning with *ya*,...

It is accompanied by *yaralava*. The suffix *tayap* is used in the sense of a part of a number; the plural number is employed precisely with the intention of referring to its constituent parts. "The son of the Earth" refers to Maṅgala (Mars). The phrase "the lord of the *ka*-group," however, is intended to suggest his association with the *ka*-group. Likewise, [it is located] above the heart and below the pit of the throat (*kaṇṭhakūpa*).
In another tantra, however, it is said that "Budha" is below the heart. [The letters] are the four vargas beginning with *śa*, along with *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*.

Regarding the phrase "accompanied by the letter *kṣa*," this refers to the anus (*pāyu*) or the rectum (*guda*). In another tantra, however, a conjunction with the letters *la* and *kṣa* is taught. If...

Furthermore, for the sake of consistency with other tantras, the letter *kṣa* found in the present tantra is explained as being intended to indicate the letter *la* as well; thus, in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is stated that in the ritual placement of the constellations (*nakṣatra-nyāsa*), one uses the letter *kṣa*, and thereafter the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the visarga (*visarga*) for [the placement of] Revatī.

By the same logic, since it is necessary for the letter *kṣa* to function as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the letter *la* in order to conform with other tantras, the statement in the *Sundarīmahodaya* that the writing of the ritual manuals (*paddhati*)— namely, "laṃ kṣaṃ aṃ aḥ revatyai namaḥ"— is baseless is not to be respected.

In this regard, the ritual procedure for application should be inferred in the manner beginning with "aṃ śrāṃ0 sūryāya namaḥ" [and] "at the heart" (hṛdayādha), and so forth. || 21 || 22 || 23 || 24 || 25 ||

In the *Jñānārṇava*, the forms of the Sun and the other planets are described as objects of meditation (*dhyeya*). Among them, the Sun and Mars are red; the Moon and Venus are white; Mercury is dark blue; Jupiter is yellow; Saturn is black; and Rāhu and Ketu are smoke-colored. Thus...
Her left hand rests upon her left thigh, while her right hand bestows boons (*vara*). However, in another tantra,
she is said to be accompanied by the Śaktis Renukā, Amṛtā, Dhātrī, Śaṅkhinī, Śāṅkarī, Jñānā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇā, and Dhūmrā, all of whom display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
It is also seen in the Jñānārṇava, for example:
"One should meditate upon those beginning with the Sun as red, white, likewise red, dark-blue, yellow, pale-white, black, smoky, and smoke-grey. (26)
O Goddess, they assume forms at will, adorned with divine garments and ornaments;
they rest their left hands upon their beautiful thighs and grant boons with their right hands.
"Dhūmradhūmra" means exceedingly smoky; the rest is clear. || 26 || 27 ||

He describes the ritual placement of the constellations (nakṣatras): on the forehead, the right eye, the left [eye], then on the two ears, the two nostrils, the nose, the throat, and then on the two shoulders. || 28 ||
Then on the pair of elbows and likewise on the pair of wrists, on the hands, at the region of the navel, and thereafter on the waistband. (29)
Regarding the pair of thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, and the two feet— as well as the eyes—
the specific mention of "the right eye" and "the left" rather than simply "the eyes" is for the purpose of establishing a fixed order.
Consequently, for the pairs beginning with the two ears and ending with the two feet, the right is first and the left follows.

It should be understood that "behind" (paścāt) means "at the back. Regarding the term "waist-band" (kaṭibandha), the singular number is used with the intention that, just as one hand has only one single wrist-joint (maṇibandha) and not a twofold division into right and left, so too the waist-band is likewise one.
However, the proponents [of the opposing view] maintain that singularity is not intended to be expressed, and the meaning is simply "two waistbands";
otherwise, they argue, the number twenty-seven would be untenable. This is questionable;
on the contrary, if there were two types of waists, the number would result in twenty-eight. Nor is there a pair of elbows behind...

It should not be argued that there is no contradiction regarding the number [of joints] by accepting that the intended meaning here is "the two parts behind the elbow," because it is well known that the front part situated in the middle of the hand is denoted by the term *saṃdhi*, while the back part alone is denoted by the term *kūrpara*.

Because there is no possibility of excluding anything from the subsequent term, for this very reason, in the external placement of the *mātṛkās*, the convention is simply "in the joints of the arms" (*doḥ-saṃdhiṣu*). And in the placement of the sixteen-spoked wheel to be described later, the convention is simply "at the elbows" (*kūrpara*); there is no requirement for further qualification therein.
If it is argued that such a strained interpretation must be adopted in order to avoid contradiction with other tantras, let it be so.
Now, he provides a word-by-word analysis of the syllables here:
"A pair, one, three, the Vedas [four], one, one, two, and then [one]. (30)
One pair, a pair, a pair, a pair, and a pair in sequence;
one pair, three, one, three, one, one, and one.
A pair, one, a pair, three, a pair, joined with the bindu and visarga—
O Dear One, the determination of the letters for the constellations has thus been declared in their proper order.

Although the bindu and visarga are present at the end of the vowels according to the sequence of the *mātṛkā*, having extracted them from there and joined them to the end of the letter *kṣa*, their first pair, *aṃ* and *āṃ*, should be recited at the beginning of Aśvinī;
then one, *iṃ*, for Bharaṇī; and three, *īṃ*, *uṃ*, and *ūṃ*, for Kṛttikā.

The above should be applied accordingly. The meaning is that Revatī is joined with four [syllables]: *laṃ*, *kṣaṃ*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ*, consisting of the paired bindus and visargas. In eleven [syllables], there is the application of one syllable each;
in ten [syllables], there is the application of two syllables each; and in four [syllables], there is the application of three syllables each.

The distinction is that there are four [letters] for each of the two constellations. However, in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is stated that there are two letters for both Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā; this is the specific difference.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the mention of the letter *kṣa* in the case of Revatī is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the letter *l*. And this [is] with half [a verse].
In some manuscripts, these two verses are not seen. || 30 || 31 || 32 ||
Now he describes the meditation on the lunar mansions:
"Resembling the blazing fire of time, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, with hands in the gesture of salutation, beginning with Aśvinī, they are all adorned with every ornament. (33)
O Goddess, well-worshipped one, one should place these [mantras] in these locations;
by the phrase "with hands granting boons and protection," the state of having four arms is indicated. The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*;
thus the practical application is: *aṃ āṃ aśvinyai namaḥ*, and so forth. (33)
Now he describes the placement of the Yoginīs:
"In the Viśuddha, the heart, the navel, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and the Mūla. (34)

O Queen of the Gods, the lords of the elements should be placed within the command (ājñā) along with the deities beginning with *ḍa*; they should be properly meditated upon as being endowed with nectar and other [substances]. (35)

In the throat for purification; "mūlaka" is the combination of "mūla" and "ka"; because it is a part of a living being, it is treated as a singular compound. This means at the root-center (mūladhāra) and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
In the Ājñā [center] between the eyebrows; [this refers to] the elements.
They are the masters and mistresses of skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
The seven deities beginning with *Ḍā* are Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, Hākinī, and Yākinī.
By the phrase "beginning with Amṛtā" (*amṛtādīti*), the inclusion of Ākarṣiṇī and the others is intended. They should be installed together with these [deities].

The meaning is that one should place the principal deity, such as Ḍākinī and the others, upon the pericarp in the center, and then place Amṛtā and the rest upon its petals; they are to be meditated upon according to the method taught in another tantra—this is the implied sense. Although it was previously stated in the *Rudrayāmala Tantra*, which is the tantra under discussion, that "the ritual action has been explained."
Although it would be appropriate to follow the very same method found there even for this subject matter, nevertheless,

since agreement with the *Jñānārṇava* is observed in many instances such as the worship of the *kāmya*-cakras and the optional fire-oblations (*kāmyahoma*), there is no doubt regarding that [method] seen in the *Mahājñānārṇava*, starting from the passage beginning with "There, Pārvatī... and so forth.

The meaning is that because they are also indicated by his consent, one should place the Yoginīs according to the very method he taught; furthermore, even though [the deities] such as Amṛtā are not explicitly mentioned there, one should place them here because they have been specifically described in this context.
In that regard, the extraction of the mantra of Ḍākinī is as follows in the Jñānārṇava:
Having uttered the two seed-syllables of Ḍāṃḍī, O Dear One, [one says] "Ḍamalāvarayā," enriched with the left ear (va), the moon (u), and the nasal sound (nāda); then also: "Ḍākinyai namaḥ."
"Hrīṃ śrīṃ; at the end of the vowels, one should utter [the syllable] 'mā', followed by the two words 'rakṣa'.
O Dear One, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the region of the throat in the *viśuddhi* [cakra], for the skin-ātman.
The meaning of this is: "ḍa ma la va ra ya" is the *kūṭa*. The sixth vowel is the left ear.
The anusvāra follows the letter *i*. Having pronounced the sixteen vowels at the end of the vowels, one says *mā*, which is the dative singular of the word *asmad* (we).
At the end of that, one should utter the word *rakṣa* twice. By the force of the dative case in *tvagātmane*, [one adds] *namaḥ*.
The phrase *iti-padam* is drawn as common to all *nyāsa*s. Thus, the mantra is established as:
*ḍāṃ ḍīṃ ḍamalavarayūṃ ḍākinyai namo nhīṃ śrīṃ aṃ āṃ māṃ rakṣa rakṣa tvagātmane namaḥ*. By means of this mantra...

Having placed Ḍākinī in the pericarp of the sixteen-petaled lotus located in the throat, one should place the sixteen deities, beginning with Amṛtā, upon its petals— each conjoined with a single vowel— in accordance with the internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa. Her visualization is as follows, according to the *Sahasranāma*:
Residing in the Viśuddhi-cakra, she is red in color and has three eyes; she holds the khaṭvāṅga and other weapons, is endowed with a single face,
delights in milk-rice (pāyasa), dwells in the skin, and strikes fear into the world of bound souls (paśu).
The body of Ḍākinī is encompassed by the great powers beginning with Amṛtā:
Amṛtā, Ākarṣiṇī, Indrāṇī, Īśānī, Umā, Ūrdhvakeśī, Ṛddhidā,
Ṛkārā, Ḷkārā, ḹkārā, Ekapadā, Aiśvaryātmikā, Oṃkārī, and Auṣadhī.

Ambikā, Akṣarā—these are the [goddesses] beginning with Amṛtā. However, some, having recited the vowels as before, recite the mantra "tvagātmānaṃ māṃ rakṣa rakṣa namaḥ," asserting that the authority for this lies solely in the secret convention (*saṃketa*) of one's own guru. In this very context, the mantra consists of the three initial *ma* sounds.

In the case of Ḍākinī, there is a group of four *repha*s (the letter *ra*) in the place of the vowels; from *ka* to *ṭha* are the phonemes in the place of the word "skin," and if the word "blood" (*asṛk*) is used, it is the mantra of Rākiṇī. There is a group of four *la*s, from *ḍa* to *pha*, and if the word "flesh" (*māṃsa*) is used, it belongs to Lākīnī. A group of four *ka*s, from *ba* to *la*, is for "fat" (*medas*).
If the word *pada* (place) is followed by *kākinī* with the four [consonants] *va*, *ṣa*, *śa*, and *sa*, it is the place of bone (*asthipada*) for *sākini*.
These are to be placed in the Anāhata, Maṇipūra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, and Mūlādhāra [cakras].
If there is the group of four *ha*s and *hakṣa*, it is the place of marrow (*majjapada*) for *hākini*; this is located between the eyebrows.
The four *yakāra*s, the fifty letters, and the term "semen" (*śukrapada*) belong to *Yākini*.

This [group] is to be placed in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), because these lords of the elements (*dhātunātha*) reside precisely there. For this very reason, the sequence as "root" (*mūla*) and "radical" (*mūlaka*) is not intended in the root text.
The deities such as Kālarātri and others, as taught in the *Svacchanda-tantra* and other scriptures, should be understood from the commentaries of the ancients.

The meditations on Rākiṇī and the others, which are found in the *Sahasranāma*, have been described by us in their commentary (*bhāṣya*). As for the claim of the moderns that the deity Hākinī resides in the *brahmarandhra*:

It should not be placed between the eyebrows. There is no authoritative basis whatsoever for the placement of Yākinī as the deity of semen; therefore, they say that she is not mentioned in works such as the *Subhagārcāratna*. That view is to be reconsidered, because it would result in the term "in the Ājñā" being rendered meaningless in the present tantra. As for what [is said]:
In the *Jñānārṇava* (p. 315), it is said:
"O Great Goddess, one should sequentially place the *ḍākinī* residing in the phonemes *ha* and *kṣa* within that [cavity];
this is the placement (*nyāsa*) accompanied by the *yoginīs* in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)."

Thus, just as the formulation of the *hākinī* mantra [is obtained], the formulation of the locations (*sthāna*) is likewise obtained by the very phrase "in that same manner. Similarly, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the pentad of *ḍākinī* and the others upon the supporting wheels (*ādhāracakra*) consisting of the syllables of their respective mantras is exactly like that.
The meaning is that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) occurs on the two-petaled wheel (*dvidalacakra*) which serves as the support for the letters *ha* and *kṣa* that constitute the *hākinī* mantra;

for it is appropriate to conceive of it in this way in accordance with the phrase "in the *ājñā*" as recorded in another tantra. Nor [is there any contradiction] regarding the term "the aperture of Brahmā" (*brahmarandhra*).
It should not be argued that the explanation [of this passage] must be understood as referring to the *ājñācakra* on the authority of other tantras;

for since a general rule is restricted by a specific one, if a specific instance were to refer to another specific instance, there would be no deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), and the opposite interpretation would also result. Consequently, [the reference is] to the *brahmarandhra*.
Since the word *iti* would otherwise result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*), and because of the expectancy for that [word], one should—
by the recurrence of the three words "in that same manner," "place in sequence," and "one should"— place Yākinī,
who is joined with all the previously mentioned syllables in their proper order, likewise accompanied by the mantra, in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

The meaning "one should place" (*vinyaset*) is what must be explained here. Furthermore, in this context, the names of Lalitā beginning with "dwelling in the Viśuddhi-cakra on all sides" and ending with "having the nature of Yākinī Ambā" are precisely those that convey the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Now, one might ask: among these names, [what of] the seven Yoginīs, who possess syllables, locations, and coverings?

If it is asked, "Since there is no rule for *nyāsa* by means of mere verbal recitation, how can the rule for *nyāsa* be altered in accordance with that [recitation]?"— this same objection applies equally to you as well.
For in the *nyāsa* of the fifty-one *pīṭhas* which is about to be described, [the mantra] is "Prāṇeśvarī, giver of life."

[The term] "consisting of fifty seats" (*pañcāśatpīṭharūpiṇī*) is [so called] because one seat has been omitted due to the force of the reading in the names of Lalitā. [This is illustrated by] the injunctive statement: "The Āgneya [offering] is indeed the head of this sacrifice, the Upāṃśuyāja is the heart, and the Agnīṣomīya is the two feet."
Furthermore, since the primacy of the *upāṃśuyāja* is determined merely by its position in the sequence of the three principal offerings,

it is likewise appropriate to determine that *hākini* is to be placed between the eyebrows and *yākini* in the *brahmarandhra*, based on the force of their respective positions within the sequence of the *ḍākinī*s and others assigned to their respective cakras.
"Whatever is read in a particular context, that is understood as being of such a nature"—according to this maxim.

For this very reason, in the present Tantra, the letter *ka* in the word *mūlaka* should be explained as referring to the *brahmarandhra*, and not, as the ancients did, with the intention of the suffix *ka* having its own primary meaning (*svārthika*). Nor is this...

It should be understood that the commentary [on this term] is "afflicted" (kliṣṭa). This is because, in the subsequent section on the deposition of the constellations (*rāśinyāsa*), such an interpretation of the word *bāhumūlaka* is established as being accepted by all, and thus there is no contradiction. This applies to the deposition of the worlds (*bhuvananyāsa*) included within the Great Sixfold Deposition (*mahāṣoḍhānyāsa*).

(p. 316) Since the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seven [deities] beginning with the *ḍākinīs* has already been established, and since one must endure the difficulty that arises from the presence of all of them according to the phrase "the deities beginning with *ḍā*" in the present context; and furthermore, this being the case, in the section concerning the *kaulikārtha*...

It should not be argued that, because of the phrase "also by the Ḍākinīs and others who are the lords of the elements such as the skin," there would be the consequence of including all seven [deities] here as well; for although that may be the case there due to the indicative evidence of the passage beginning with "then by the six syllables of the Śaktis," in the present context it is exactly so in accordance with the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seven Yoginīs mentioned in another Tantra.

Because it is logical to explain it thus; by this, the unanimity of many authors of ritual manuals (*paddhati*) is established, and therefore, due to its contradiction with that, the statement in the *Subhagārcāratna* is not to be respected—this is the direction [of the argument]. (34-35) Now, he states the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the zodiac signs (*rāśi*).
On the feet, the genitals, the belly, the heart, and the base of the arms—beginning from the right foot and ending with the left foot. (36)
O Pārvatī, the zodiac signs beginning with Aries are to be placed along with their colors;

"the root of the arm and the head, and the combination of those two" means in the armpit and on the head. These same six locations, from the feet up to the head, may also be arranged in reverse order.
He says they are to be joined [as follows]: "the right," etc. By the word "Aries and so forth" (*meṣādi*), Taurus and the others are included.
"By colors" means characterized by specific forms; namely:
red, white, green, pale-yellow, variegated, black, tawny, brown, reddish-brown, speckled, and smoke-colored.
Some say that "having meditated in the sequence beginning with *mrani*," means "accompanied by the syllables. || 36 ||
Now, he states in sequence the letters of the Mātṛkā that are to be applied there:
"A group of four, a triad, three, a pair, a pair, and two. (37)
Five, five, five, five, and then five;
four are in Meru-bhīma, and for Kanyā, the five beginning with Śa. (38)
In Cancer and Leo, there are two letters each;
in Taurus and Gemini, three letters each; in Aries, four; and in the other seven zodiac signs, five each.
In those same [seven], for Virgo, however, there are two additional [letters]: the bindu and visarga, meaning the letters beginning with *śa*.

Meru is the letter *kṣa*. This is because of the lexicon stating that within the section on the letter *kṣa*, Meru is indeed the final phoneme. However, in the *Jñānārṇava*, there is a distinction: there are two syllables for Taurus (*vṛṣabha*), four for Gemini (*mithuna*), and the letter *la* does not exist for Virgo (*kanyā*). The practical application begins with: *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ meṣāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Aries), and so forth. This...

The one and a half verses concerning the constellations and the two and a half verses have been explained by us at the very occasion of commenting on the introductory verse of the treatise. || 37 || 38 ||
(p. 317) Now, with eight verses, he describes the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*): "O Goddess, O Beloved, one should place the seats in the locations of the *mātṛkās*.
Their names are being told; listen attentively, O Beloved. (39)
Kāmarūpa, Vārāṇasī, Nepāla, Pauṇḍravardhana, Purasthira, Kānyakubja, Pūrṇaśaila, and likewise Arbuda. || 40 ||
Āmrātakeśvara, Ekāmra, Trisrotas, Kāmakoṭaka, Kailāsa, Bhṛgunagara, Kedāra, and Candrapuṣkara; || 41 ||
The Śrīpīṭha, Oṃkārapīṭha, Jālandhra, and likewise Mālava;
Kulāntaka, Devikoṭa, Gokarṇa, and Māruteśvara.
