Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Rājageha, Mahāpatha, Kolāpura, Melāpura, Kāleśa, and Jayantikā. || 43 ||
Ujjayinī is Citrā, Kṣīraka is Hastināpura;
Uḍḍīśa is called Prayāga, and the sixth is Māyāpurī. || 44 ||
The lord of waters, Mount Malaya, Meru the best of mountains, as well as Mahendra, Vāmana, and Hiraṇyapura; || 45 ||
Mahālakṣmī’s garden and the parasol of shade beyond it—these are declared to be the sacred seats (pīṭhas) that exist in the form of the Mother-letters (mātṛkā). 46.
By beginning with the phrase "the locations of the Mātṛkās" and concluding with the phrase "those whose form is the Mātṛkās," the number of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) is indicated as fifty-one.

This is because there are exactly that many locations for the external *mātṛkā*-nyāsa. For this very reason, it is stated even more clearly in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, beginning with: "Then one should install fifty-one seats in their proper order," and so on, [specifying they are] "joined with the sequence of the letters" in the locations of the letters.

The section ends with the word "vinyaset" (one should place). The method for this is as follows: in the phrase "Āmrātakeśvara-ekāmram," because a collective *dvandva* compound is accepted, there are exactly two *pīṭhas*;
the same applies to the phrase "Mahālakṣmī-pura-udyānam. In the phrase "Malayaḥ śailo merurgirivaraḥ," [the same principle applies].

The two terms *śaila* and *girivara* are not qualifiers of Malaya and Meru; rather, they designate two distinct sacred seats (*pīṭha*). Among them, the seat named simply *Śaila* is well known as Śrīśaila in the southern region. The one named *Girivara*, however, is located in the west.
In the land of Saurāṣṭra, there is the place renowned as Girinātha. As for that which is mentioned in the *Jñānārṇava* (p.
318), beginning with "the collection of the fifty seats," regarding the arrangement of the fifty seats upon the locus of the Mātṛkā:
And regarding the statement in the conclusion, "one should perform the placement" (*nyaset*),

there the word "fifty" (*pañcāśat*) also refers to fifty-one, because a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on proximity is possible. This is stated in the verse concerning the visualization and placement of the external *mātṛkā*.

In the *Jñānārṇava*, it is stated, "rich with the forms of the fifty letters," as in the passage beginning "whose face and arms are divided by the fifty scripts," and likewise in the passage beginning "whose face and arms are fashioned by the distinctions of the fifty letters"; such is the definition [of the Goddess].

Because it is so observed. For this very reason, the commentator on the first verse of the *Śāradātilaka*— which reads "by the fifty letters flowing incessantly from the body of eternal bliss in succession"—
explains that the word "fifty" (*pañcāśat*) actually refers to fifty-one, due to its proximity in number.

They explain [it as follows]: Furthermore, in the statement from the *Jñānārṇava*, "Malaya, Mahāpīṭha, Śrīśaila, and Meruka-giri," since the word "Meru-parvata" is not mentioned and because the use of the term "giri" (mountain) conforms to the propriety of usage and involves the application of the suffix *ka*, it should be interpreted as being distinct [from the mountain Meru], namely as "Giri."

The same applies to the *Subhagārcā*, the *Ratnādipaddhati*, and other such works. Those moderns who propose the formulation "to the seat (pīṭha) of Mount Laṃbheru" should be understood as either acting with reckless audacity or being mistaken. However, some [hold] that Kāleśvara is the great seat (mahāpīṭha), while the *Jñānārṇava* [states it is] the syllable Om (praṇava) and Jayantikā.
Those who recite [the text] state that there are fifty-one [pīṭhas] by including the seat known as Praṇava. Others, however, omit the word "Praṇava" and utter the word "Mahāpīṭha" twice;
having thus determined that there are exactly fifty seats, they effect the omission of either the letter *kṣa* or the letter *la*.

Thus, even those who argue with one another [regarding this] should be understood as refuted. As for the moderns (*navya*), because it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava* that "one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the locus of the Mātṛkā," they maintain that the *grahanyāsa* and *kāmaratinyāsa* should be performed with the letters of the Mātṛkā, just as in the case of the statement: "One should place the Goddess with the letters of the Mātṛkā."

They state another position, claiming that because the combination of vowels (*arṇasāhitya*) is not mentioned, even the conjunction of consonants (*varṇayoga*) is lost as far as the scriptural evidence extends; yet, having themselves written down the statement from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*—"those [phonemes] joined in the order of writing" (*lipikramasamāyuktāni*)—how could they have forgotten it? This is a matter of wonder. Thus ends the direction [of the argument]. Aṃ.

The ritual application begins with "Salutation to Kāmarūpa," and so forth. Many authors write the names with the word *pīṭha* (seat) as their suffix, such as "to the seat of Kāmarūpa. Regarding this uniformity, one might ask: why do they not likewise write "to the asterism Aśvinī" or "to the zodiac sign Aries," and what is the reason for this discrepancy?
They should be questioned. (39–46)
Having first concluded the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), he prescribes the deposition of the wheel (*cakranyāsa*):
"Having thus first performed the sixfold [deposition], one should perform the deposition of the Śrīcakra.
It has been stated that the word *ṣoḍhā* is the name of the ritual act according to the principle of "designation by its description" (*tatprakhyanyāya*). For this very reason:

Because it lacks the sense of the sixfold [division], it does not possess the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*); consequently, there is no elision of the accusative singular ending in the form *ṣoḍhām*.
Alternatively, that [form] is archaic (*ārṣa*). Even though the sequence of preceding and following [words] is established by the very recitation [of the text],...
The use of the suffixes "-kṛtvā" and "-itvā" is for the purpose of ensuring that the placement (*nyāsa*) of Cakreśvarī and [the other deities] prescribed at the time of worship is not interrupted;
otherwise, since the placement of Aṇimā and the others would also be enjoined at the very same time of worship, [there would be a conflict].

Because there would be no determining factor for the sequence, it would follow that the two-fold placement of Cakreśvarī might also occur immediately after [the previous stage]. Furthermore, the term *cakranyāsa* denotes the entire collection of the nine intermediate placements (*avāntaranyāsa*) that will be described hereafter; and although that—

Although two types of placement (*nyāsa*)— consisting of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*)— will be described through the distinction between the placement of the root goddesses beginning with *Aṇimā* and the placement of the [other] goddesses beginning with *Ādi*,

nevertheless, because it is the placement of the wheels (*cakranyāsa*) that is promised as being "listen! in accordance with the sequence of worship, and since only those beginning with *Aṇimā* are explained, there is only one such *cakranyāsa*.
But another [form] is the non-repetition (*āvṛtti*) of this very ninefold intermediate arrangement (*avāntaranyāsa*), characterized by the quality of transposition (*vyutkrama*).
And this being so, there is no resulting distinction between the two rites on account of that quality;
for both are included within the procedure for the wheel-arrangement (*cakranyāsa*).

There is no distinction between the two actions because neither is prescribed as being produced by an original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) through a specific name. Nor is there a distinction based on a technical designation (*saṃjñā*),
because the terms *mūladevī* and so forth, as well as *kāṇimā* and so forth, are etymological (*yaugika*) like the term *dārḍhyāyaṇa*.
Nor is this fourfold deposition (nyāsa) to be performed as "worshipped by the heroes" (*vīravandita*),
for there is a distinction based on the number mentioned in the words to be spoken hereafter;
because that [number] lacks coreferentiality with the karma being produced, it is eleven.
This is because, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, there is no factor that creates a distinction [between the acts].

Furthermore, other means of establishing difference—such as a different word (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), or a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*)—are not even to be suspected here. For this very reason, it is said:
"One should again perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the Root Goddess (*mūladevī*) and ending with *aṇimā*."

The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is appropriate at the beginning of the second placement (*nyāsa*), because it naturally conveys the sense of repetition. Likewise, the placement of the wheel of stability (*sthiticakra-nyāsa*) prescribed in another tantra is not a separate ritual act. For this very reason, the *Kalpasūtra* states: "Having placed [the mantras] in the sixfold wheel, or having placed them again..."

The dual number is appropriate; for if it were a separate ritual act, the plural number would have resulted. Therefore, with the intention that there is only one *cakranyāsa* which is performed twice, the singular number is employed in the original injunction:
"Listen, O Dear One, to the *cakranyāsa* of Mahātripurasundarī. (47)

The vocative address "O Beloved" (priya) is intended to suggest: "I shall tell this to you, though it has not been told to anyone else, because of my affection for you"—this being the supreme means of purification that has not been explained to anyone, even though it remains untold to others.
This serves the purpose of the poetic figure known as *parikarāṅkura* (the sprout of embellishment). 47.
Therein, he states the three components of the Trailokyamohana-cakra-nyāsa in sequence:
"One should perform the placement starting from 'Oṃ Caturasrādyarephāyai namaḥ' and so forth. (48)
Then, [one places them] on the right shoulder, the back, the tips of the hands, the buttocks, and the toes of the feet;
then on the toes of the left foot, the buttocks, the tip of the hand, and the shoulder and back. (49)
O beautiful one, [these are] by virtue of their pervasiveness at the root of the crest-lock, the shoulders, and the back:
the shoulder, the back—that is, the posterior part—of the base of the arm, which is one location;
the tips of the fingers, which are the extremities of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); and the *sphikka*, which is the joint of the thigh. Of these...

The term *samāhāradvaṃdva* (collective copulative compound) refers to "the toes together with that" (*tat-sahitāḥ pādāṅgulyaḥ*), which is a *madhyamapadalopī* (elliptical) compound; this is then joined with the word *dakṣa* (right) to form a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. By this, these four are the positions on the right side. He now describes these same four positions on the left side in reverse order:

Regarding the word *vāme*: although it is part of a compound (*vāmapada*), it has an implied connection with the other [words] as well. *Cūlīmūla* means the root of the crest, that is, the place where the tuft of hair originates. *Pṛṣṭha* means the back part of the body. Some say this refers to the front and back parts of the head itself. In those [parts] together with those two...
The syntactical connection is that one should perform the placement with joined palms (añjali) in such a way that it becomes pervasive across the previously mentioned locations.
Thus, all the pervasive placements (vyāpakanyāsa) within the cakras and nyāsas to be described hereafter must likewise be performed so as to pervade those respective locations. || 48 || 49 ||
In these very ten locations, one should place the ten [siddhis] beginning with aṇimā. (50)
O beautiful one, those accomplishments reside within that [triangle] as its pervasive essence;
O beloved, one should also say: "Salutation to the central line of the square. (51)
Having thus assigned the [deities] beginning with Brahmāṇī to her eight locations— namely,
the two big toes, the two sides, the head, and the two flanks— 52.

"On the left and right knees, and likewise on the two shoulders"—here, the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). By the word "beginning with" (*ādi*) in the phrase "beginning with *aṇimā*," there is the inclusion of the nine powers beginning with *laghimā*, which were mentioned previously in the *Catuḥśatī*. Within that [is]:
Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the mantra of the central line over the regions slightly anterior to the right shoulder,

the back, and so forth, one should place the eight [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī in the eight excellent locations of that central line; therein, the two big toes together constitute one [location].

Regarding the locations: although "the two shoulders" suggests two locations, according to the tradition there are actually four, as this accords with the four cardinal and four intermediate directions. Starting from the two big toes, the right side, and the head, [the sequence continues] through the right knee, the right shoulder, and the left shoulder.
One should place [the mantras] in sequence ending with the Sun, according to another tantra. "On the other side" means on the left side.

The masculine gender in "jānvoh" (on the knees) is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). The word "outside" (*bahiḥ*) should be construed with both [locations] by way of the "crow's eye" maxim (*kākākṣinyāya*); they are to be placed there.

Thus there is an anticipation (*apakarṣa*) of the word from the subsequent verse. Regarding the phrase "of the central line of the square," we have demonstrated in the *Vṛttacandrodaya* that even with the addition of one extra syllable, there is no violation of the meter. || 50 || 51 || 52 ||
The four final lines should also be deposited with the mantra: "Obeisance to the final line. || 53 ||
One should install [the mantra] as all-pervasive within the body up to the end previously mentioned;
then, one should install the ten mudrās in its ten locations. (54)
Then, one should assign eight of those [vowels] to the eight locations beginning with Brahmā;
the remaining two should be assigned to the dvādaśānta and to the big toe of the foot.

In the body (*vigraha*), one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*) with the mantra upon the final line, by means of internal delimitation, starting from the two big toes and so forth as previously described. Then, there are ten mudrās at ten locations on that line.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*). Anticipating the question, "How is the placement of the ten [mantras] to be done in the eight locations of the eight *sūktas*?
he provides the resolution: "Brahmāṇī and so forth. One should place the eight [mantras] in the eight locations;
the remaining two should be placed at the *dvādaśānta* and on the two big toes of the feet.
The construction is with the four verbal forms of the action "one should place" (*nyaset*) within the four sentences.

It has been stated that the verb "they should be placed" (*nyastavyāḥ*) is to be supplied from the preceding context. However, the earlier authorities maintain that the word *brahmāṇyādyāḥ* found in the rule for the placement on the central line is in the accusative case.
Those who labor [under this view] establish a connection with the word *vinyasya* (having placed) found there,
and then interpret the word *atra tyanyastavyāḥ* (those to be placed here) as meaning "one should place" because it refers to deities suitable for placement and because they are pervasive;
that is not correct, because in the case of the placement of lines, the line itself— derived from the words of the mantra— is the deity.

Because that would result in a contradiction with the plural number [of the term]. The upper region of the forehead, which is one finger-breadth wide, is designated by the term *dvādaśānta* (the "end of twelve"), because there exists the solar orb consisting of twelve *kalās* there.
That which is known as the *ṣoḍaśānta* (the "end of sixteen") is the lunar mandala at the *sahasrāra*.
Below that location is the solar orb, possessing twelve powers.
The Dvādaśānta is known to be located above the Bindu, measuring one and a half finger-breadths.

Because of this statement, the term "the place of the big toe" (pādāṅguṣṭhapada) refers to both big toes, as there is no reason for selecting one over the other and because they are presented [in the mind] simultaneously. 53, 54, 55.
Having thus described the placement of the Trailokyamohana-cakra, he now describes the placement of the Sarvāśāparipūraka-cakra:
"Within that, [one should say] 'Salutation to the sixteen-petaled lotus'."
Having performed the placement [of the central deity], one should then place Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others upon its petals.
The petals [are assigned to] the back of the right ear, the shoulder, the elbow, the back of the hand, as well as the thigh, the knee, the ankle, and the sole of the foot. || 57 ||
p. 322) Likewise, this group of eight is considered to begin with the sole of the left foot.

Within the interior of that final square line, on its petals—that is, on the sixteen petals (the singular number is used for the class)—are [the goddesses] beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī and beginning with Anaṅgakusumā.

The deities to be described hereafter are those mentioned in the first chapter. The term "right side" follows the sequence from the back of the ear down to the tips of the soles of the feet across eight locations. By the phrase "from the left sole," etc., there is an inclusion, in reverse order, of the locations starting from the left ankle up to the back of the left ear. (56)
He states the placement of the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa-cakra: "And within that, [one should place] 'Salutation to the eight-petaled lotus'. (58)
Having placed [the mantras] upon these petals, on the right temple, and on the collarbone;
and on the left side, within the thighs, at the ankles, the thighs, the collarbones, and the temples.
One should then install the eight Śaktis, beginning with Anaṅgakusumā.
The *śaṅkha* is the bone of the forehead; the *jatru* is the joint at the base of the arm; the *gulpha* is the ankle-joint; the rest is easy to understand. (58–59)
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the wheel that bestows all prosperity: "Salutation to the fourteen-spoked wheel within that" (tadantaścaturdaśāracakrāya namaḥ). || 60 ||
Having performed the placement [of the central deity], one should place the fourteen Śaktis, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhikā, in its corners; I shall now describe its corners.
On the forehead, on the right side, between the right cheek and shoulder,
on the other side, between the thigh and calf, and starting from the left calf, O Pārvatī— (62)
On the left thigh, on the left side, on the left shoulder, on the left cheek, on the left part of the forehead, and likewise on the back—thus [it is said]. (63)

The forehead (*lalāṭa*) is the middle portion of the brow; this is the first location, as it is indicated as a separate term rather than being used in a compound. Following that is the right side, because that is the subject under discussion; this is the second location. Then there is the group of five: the right cheek, shoulder, side of the torso, thigh, and calf.

The five middle parts—these seven locations are indeed the left-side [channels]. In reverse order, there are five, making twelve. Including the left side of the forehead as one, there is the thirteenth location, because they are taught as a collective whole. From the back of the head upward from the depression [is the next].

The fourteenth [chapter]. This has been explained (p. 323) in accordance with the statements from another Tantra written in the *Kramottamapaddhati* composed by Nijānandanātha. Others, however, [place] the first of these on the right head and the last...

Some say that one should place [the mantra] on the left head; others, however, believe that among these [days], the seventh and eighth should be placed on the right and left [shoulders]. Still others, considering "the right part of the forehead" as a single location through grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), [interpret it] by means of the word "back" (*pṛṣṭha*).
They say that both the left and right pitcher-positions (kumbhasthala) should be grasped; however, that is incorrect.
[Verses 60, 61, 62] He now describes the placement (nyāsa) of the wheel that accomplishes all aims (sarvārthasādhakacakra):
"Then, O Pārvatī, [one should say] 'Salutation to the ten-spoked wheel' (daśāracakrāya namaḥ)."
Its corners are the roots of the right eye and nose in the [right] eye.
One should then place [the syllables] in the two sides of the belly, in the wind-corner, and in the two knees and the anus;
and again in the corners known as the belly (south) and fire (southeast).

O Dear One, there is a group of ten Śaktis beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā. Then, by means of the delimitation within the mantra-weapon (mantra-astra), the phrase "I shall describe the corners" is understood to carry over. According to some, the word "to be meditated upon" (*bhāvanīyāni*) is the ellipsis. The two locations are the right eye and the base of the nose.

*Anyanetrakaṃ* refers to the left eye. [It is located] at the corner of the belly in the region of the left arm’s root, because that which is situated immediately adjacent to the left eye is what is intended here. [It is located] at the corner of the belly in the region of the wind (northwest) in the root of the left thigh. Furthermore, the plural form in *akṣīṇi me darśanīyāni* is a Vedic usage.
Because they are parts of a living being, there is the potential for them to be treated as a singular compound. Here, the sequence is: first the left knee, then the anus, and then the right knee;

this is because the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), or because the strength of the object of knowledge (*prameyabala*) prevails over the strength of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇabala*). [The next part is] the lower right corner of the abdomen.
The root of the right thigh; the right side of the abdomen, which is the southeast corner; and the root of the right arm.

By virtue of the division of the intermediate directions (vidiś) located here, the division of the cardinal directions (diś) should also be inferred for the placement of the weapons and other rites to be described. || 64 || 65 ||
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the wheels that provide all protection: "And within that, one should also say: 'Salutation to the wheel with ten spokes, etc. (66)
Having performed the placement [of the seed-syllables], one should place the ten [deities] beginning with Sarvajña in its corners,
as well as on the right nostril, the corner of the mouth, the breast, and the scrotum.
The perineum, the left testicle, the breast, the corner of the mouth, the nose, and the tip of the nose—these are to be known as the ten corners (koṇas). || 68 ||
“Ending with that” means within the ten-spoked [wheel]. “Beginning with the ten-spoked” refers to that which has the word *daśāra* at its beginning;
this refers to the phrase *cakrāya*, meaning by the preceding mantra itself, namely *namaḥ daśāracakrāya*. This is because both [mantras] are denotable solely by the word *daśāra*.

The convention of designating [parts] as "outer" and "inner" was devised by the ancients for the sake of convenience and non-confusion; therefore, those two terms do not constitute constituent parts of the mantra itself. As stated in the *Pūrvatantre*: "The middle [triangle], likewise the eight-spoked, the two ten-spoked, and the fourteen-[spoked]," and so forth; however, the fifth...

The sixth [wheel] shall also have ten spokes, because it is so designated in the *Uttaratantra* and elsewhere; for even though the mantra is one, when there is the recollection of the mantra's meaning, its recollection will occur according to the specific arrangement of each [wheel]. Therefore, in the ritual manuals (*paddhati*s)...

Regarding the inscription of the two words "outside" (bahiḥ) and "inside" (antaḥ) as constituent parts of the mantra-body, one should place one's trust solely in the corroboration found in other tantras. By this [explanation], the word *tad* itself—being an indeclinable (*avyaya*)—conveys the sense of "in the middle of that.
Furthermore, regarding the interpretation of the phrase "and inside the ten-spoked [wheel]," etc., the mantra is indeed "inside the ten-spoked [wheel]," and so forth.
Here, the very mention of "internal" (*antaḥ*) serves as an indicator for the placement of the word "external" (*bahiḥ*) in the preceding [mantra];
thus, although it is easy to establish this within the system [of the *Tantra*], one must nevertheless pay heed to the [textual] agreement.
As for the ancients: having first written "to the ten-spoked wheel" (*daśāracakrāya*), they [insert] the mantra "to the internal ten-spoked wheel" (*antardaśāracakrāya*) here.

They write: *sṛkkiṇī*, meaning the corners of the mouth. Words such as *stana* (breast), *vṛṣaṇa*, and *muṣka*, though masculine by gender, are neuter when there is an intention to express the equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇatrayasāmya*), just as in the rule "in a *bandhu* [compound] within a *bahuvrīhi*.

As for the short vowel in the second instance of the word *sṛkkiṇi*, it is according to the rule: "The forms ending in *ṅī* and *āp* are optionally [shortened] in technical names and in the Veda" (*ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasorbahulam*).

It is a matter of general rule (*bāhulaka*). It is clearly stated in the *Vṛttacandrodaya* that the rules of grammar may be set aside by the more powerful rules of prosody (*chanda-lakṣaṇa*) in accordance with the requirements of the meter. [Regarding] the *sīvanī*, the vessel situated between the two testicles—he now describes the *kṛtanyāsa* which removes all diseases:
Having also placed [the mantra] "Obeisance to the wheel beginning with the eight-spoked one" within that,
one should assign the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī to its corners.
The chin, the throat, the heart, and the navel—these four right sides should be known; and the left sides, beginning with Maṇipūra, are likewise to be understood.
And this set of four sides, along with these eight corners,

is within the inner portion of that ten-spoked wheel. With the mantra beginning with the word "eight-cornered" (*aṣṭakoṇa*) followed by the word "wheel" (*cakra*), joined with the word "salutation" (*namaḥ*), one performs the pervasive ritual (*vyāpaka*).

One should place [the seed-syllables]. However, the Easterners (Prāñcaḥ), explaining the word "first" (*āditva*) as meaning that the eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭakoṇacakra*) arose prior to all other wheels—such as the triangle (*trikoṇa*) and so forth—considered it to be a constituent part of the mantra. That is incorrect; for the word "first" [applies] even to the inner ten-spoked wheel (*anta-daśāra*).
Because it would result in its becoming a constituent part of the mantra; because it too has arisen previously between two of its own kind;

and because it is recited in the root [text]. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the context of the sequence of cakras beginning with the sixteen-petaled one, as well as a discrepancy with other tantras.
Since there is the possibility of other [suitable] locations, the question "why must this one be accepted? is irrelevant.

In the phrase "of the throat, heart, and navel," although they are parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), the absence of the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). [The same applies to] Maṇipūra and so forth.
"Beginning with the navel," etc. The remainder is easy to understand. || 69 || 70 ||
He states the placement of the weapons and so forth:
"One should place [the weapons] externally in the four directions of the triangle situated at the heart. (71)
Having likewise placed the arrow and bow, the noose and goad, one should place them in the corners of that [triangle], namely in the front, right, and left corners. (72)
One should place the goddesses Kāmeśvarī and the others, as well as the central goddess,
within that which exists in the center of the heart— a hollow space in the shape of a downward-pointing triangle—
and on its outer part, in the four directions, at the time of describing the placement (*nyāsa*) of the outer ten-spoked wheel (*daśāra-cakra*).

In the [circles] whose portions have been indicated, one should place five arrows and two bows each, according to the division of Śiva and Śakti, as well as the nooses and the goads; the sequence of the directions is stated in the *Pūrvatant*ra itself as being in the order of west, north, east, and south.

Regarding the phrase "in the corners of the heart [diagram] belonging to Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu," the authority for this must be considered in the *Kramottama-paddhati*. The use of the word *śara* (arrow) and *pāśa* (noose) without case-endings is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

Alternatively, the dual-ending compound may be used because one intends to express the unity of the genus (*jāti*) with respect to each individual. This applies to the "upper installation" (*uttaranyāsa*).

From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the passage, "arrows for the eyes and two bows for the eyebrows," where two bows are mentioned, [the author] states the placement (*nyāsa*) of the wheel that bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhipradacakra*), beginning with the words "in the corners" (*koṇeṣu*). However, the reading of the authors of the ritual manuals (*paddhati*) is simply "to the triangular wheel" (*trikoṇacakrāya*). He then states the placement of the wheel consisting of universal bliss (*sarvānandamayacakra*), beginning with the word "in the center" (*madhye*).
The meaning is "in the Bindu. [One should worship] the Goddess Tripurasundarī.

Since the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) is taught only in contexts where there is a plurality of deities, it is absent here because of the unity of the deity. However, the traditionalists perform the pervasive placement with the mantra "Obeisance to the Bindu-cakra" (*binducakrāya namaḥ*). The evidence for this is as follows:

And it will be stated [later]: regarding the placement (nyāsa) of the powers such as *aṇimā* and others, the formulation of the mantra is exactly as described in the section on worship (*pūjā-prakaraṇa*) in the *Pūrvatanttra*; the specific difference therein is that the word *namaḥ* is employed in place of the seven-syllable mantra, and there is an absence of the conjunction of the two *tārās*.
It has been described by us. || 71 || 72 ||
He concludes the placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa):
"O Goddess, thus has this most secret sequence of placement been declared by me. (73)
This must indeed be kept strictly secret by you, O lady honored by heroes.
It should be given to one who abides by the commitments, and never to one who is not a disciple.
This, which is more secret than the secret, has been revealed to you today.

It refers to that [teaching] whose method (*prakāra*) is the most hidden sequence (*guhyatama-krama*). It is more secret because it should not be taught to anyone except for a specific purpose. Conventional disciples (*sāmayika*) are of two kinds, distinguished as disciples and sub-disciples.

The non-temporary [initiations] are likewise [restricted]. Among these four, only those disciples who abide by the *samaya* are qualified, not the other three; thus he says, "to one established in the *samaya*. The *samaya*—the Kaulika convention—is set forth in ten chapters of the *Rudrayāmala* and elsewhere. One who abides therein... [does not... (na).
The meaning is "he pierces. Here, by the injunctive portion [of the mantra], two are excluded, and by the prohibitive portion, one;

thus, three are eliminated. Regarding "your": the intention is that this is due to [the relationship] being conventional and because of [his] status as a disciple. || 73 || 74 Having thus taught the placement of the wheels (*cakranyāsa*) according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), that very...
He says that one should perform the rotation according to the order of emanation:
"One should again perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with the Root Goddess and ending with Aṇimā. (75)
One should perform the rite called *cakranyāsa* again;

for, according to the principle of "being known by that name" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), the term *nyāsa* is a name [for the rite], just as in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa passage, "He performs the *prayāja*s. Thus, one should perform the *nyāsa*.

The statement "one should install" is not redundant; for this very reason, regarding the statement in the *Gītā*, "But those who worship Me with devotion," the teacher Jaimini considers the word "devotion" (*bhakti*) to be a name for ritual action (*karman*).
Thus it is said in the *Śāṇḍilya-sūtra*: "By name, [it is so] according to Jaimini, because of its possibility."
The phrase "from the Root Goddess (mūladevī) up to the power of atomization (aṇimā)" serves as a qualifier for either the ritual action or the name. In this context,

the terms "Root Goddess" and "atomization" refer respectively to the placement of the wheel consisting of universal bliss (sarvānandamayacakranyāsa) and the placement of the wheel that fascinates the three worlds (trailokyamohanacakranyāsa).
This is because each individual placement of the intermediate wheels—from the *avadāna* to the end of the *pradāna*—constitutes a single constituent element (*padārtha*).

Therefore, there are nine wheel-arrangements (*cakranyāsa*) alone; it does not include the deity-arrangements (*devatānyāsa*) contained within each individual arrangement, nor those of the root goddess (*mūladevī*) and the *aṇimā* and other powers.

One should not be misled by the superficial appearance of the word "svārasyāt" (by its own inherent force). This is because there is an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the forthcoming instruction: "One should place Kāmeśvarī and the others [on the head], and Sarvasiddhi and the others on the throat," and so forth.
Furthermore, since sequence depends upon the constituent entities (*padārtha*), it does not apply to the parts of those entities. For this very reason:

In the section concerning the handfuls, the skull-cup, the ointment, the salve, the shaving, and the purification, it was established by the rule "by one" that the performance of each individual handful is rejected [as a collective act]. And this being so, regarding the three line-drawings which are constituent parts of the Trailokyamohana-cakra placement—

There is no fault of inversion. If it were said that the sequence is reversed part by part for the sake of establishing that [order], then there would be the consequence of an inversion even among the deities;
for although such an inversion does not apply in those specific cases—given the indicators such as "Kāmeśvarī and so forth" and so on—[the objection remains].

This must be stated because, otherwise, it would be unavoidable that [the rule] "one should install the eight deities of speech" and so forth—prescribed by the injunctions—would apply [to those lines as well].

However, if one were to avoid this by assuming that [the injunction] indicates [the application] only with respect to the general [category], then there would be no reversal of the line-installations. Thus, this is like a rope with snares on both ends.

For there is an exception provided by such statements as, "In that very same manner, having established [the sequence] according to logic, one should place the ten mudrās at the root-support (mūlādhāra)," which is analogous to the scriptural sentence: "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates the Brahman. Regarding those [other] statements, [this is the exception].

For it must be stated that the meaningfulness of the words "the ten mudrās" and so forth lies precisely in their function as prescriptive injunctions for the sequence [of the ritual]. Now, one might object: in those scriptural passages, the mudrās, the Mothers, and the Siddhis are mentioned as being to be installed (nyastavya) in the mūlādhāra, the right shank, and the left shank respectively. In those [passages]...

In the absence of the state of accomplishment of the *mudrās*, there would follow a reversal of their respective substrates due to the inversion of the sequence of categories (*padārtha*). Therefore, those injunctions— such as "the *mudrā* is indeed in the *mūlādhāra*"— are meaningful precisely for the purpose of regulating the substrates.
Nor can there be an annulment of the rule regarding sequential order by the rules governing the restriction of locations,

because the two have different scopes and because there is no contradiction between them. Following the placement of the Sarvāśāparipūraka-cakra upon one's own seat, [the sequence proceeds] from the left shank down to the end of the Mūlādhāra.

This is because it is possible to perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *siddhimātṛ-mudrās*. Nor should it be argued that, following the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, the presentation of the *mūlādhāra* alone will occur in accordance with the sequence of meaning; for such a sequence of meaning is inappropriate, as there exists no relationship of produced and producer between the *svādhiṣṭhāna* and the *mūlādhāra*. Of that...

Furthermore, sequence [based on position] is weaker than scriptural sequence (*śrautakrama*). For this very reason, even the sequence based on the order of recitation (*pāṭha*) is rejected for restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*), because it is weaker than that as well—if you argue thus, do not say so.
For scriptural sequence can be established even without conflict between the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) and the sequence of recitation.

In the Trailokyamohana-cakra-nyāsa, because the state of being the ninth position constitutes the form of the Śrī-krama, there is no loss of that [status] even if its components are arranged out of order. In reality, having accepted that the three line-installations (*rekhā-nyāsa*) are distinct entities, [the status of] the term *aṇimā*— [...is maintained].
However, if one accepts the priority of the placement of the first line (*prathamarekhā*), there is not even a trace of any fault.

Here, the evidence is the statement regarding the placement of each individual line as a pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) separately, just like the pervasive placement of each individual wheel (*cakra*). For this very reason, in the *Padma Purāṇa*...

In the *Pāṇḍuraṅgamāhātmya*, having established that the sacred field (*kṣetra*) has the form of the *Śrīcakra* and having stated the presence of Viṭṭhala at the central point (*bindu*), eleven enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) are described along with him.
Thus, by means of a reverse-order arrangement of the *cakranyāsa* composed of these eleven constituent elements—

The reversal of sequence applies only to the ritual objects (*padārtha*) themselves, not to the installations (*nyāsa*) of their constituent deities. This is because, in accordance with established practice, the aforementioned indicators (*jñāpaka*) are accepted as referring to the general category [of the object]. Therefore, the rope does not hang from both sides; such is the direction of the argument. || 75 ||
One should worship Mahātripurasundarī within the Great Bindu situated in the triangle;
then, one should assign Kāmeśvarī and the others to the triangle of the head, starting from the east. (76)
The depression seen on the head in childhood is what is understood here as the triangle (*trikoṇa*).

Having installed the Goddess in the Great Bindu situated in its center by means of the root mantra (*mūla*), one should install Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī in the eastern, southern, and northern corners of that triangle; this is the meaning.

By stating that "the placement of Mūladevī and so forth is implied by this very [phrase]," the ancient authorities intended to convey that the first half of this verse does not exist in their own manuscripts. || 76 ||

One should place the arrows on the eyes, the two bows on the eyebrows, the two nooses on the ears, and the two goads on the tip of the nose; thus one should perform the placement starting from the right.

Just as with the eyes and ears, a twofold division of the tip of the nose should be inferred based on the distinction between the right and left sides; this is indicated by the phrase "beginning from the right. Here, one should place the weapons of Kāmeśvara separately on the right and those of Kāmeśvarī separately on the left, and not otherwise.

They are as if united in the placement of the primary wheels (*prathamacakranyāsa*); the distinction is that although they share the same presiding deity, there is no single *tantra* because of the difference in location. || 77 ||
One should install the eight goddesses of speech according to the sequence of the garland of skulls;
O fair-faced one, the cakras beginning with the Bindu are also to be installed. 78.

One should place the eight [powers] beginning with Vaśinī in the eight directions starting from the east upon whichever parts of the head the rosary of Rudrākṣas and other beads touch while being placed on the shaven head; this is done by following the sequence of directions starting from the east and then the south.

The term "in a clockwise direction" (prādakṣiṇyena) is understood. Now, having mentioned the *binducakra*—the final limb of the previous arrangement of cakras—and the nine cakras of the subsequent arrangement of cakras, [the author] states right here, in this context, the pervasive arrangements (*vyāpakanyāsa*) for all of these: "beginning with the *baindava*" (*baindavādīni*). Here, the word *cakra* [refers to...]

It indicates, by means of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) according to the principle of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāya*), the wheels beginning with the *bindu* and ending with the sixteen-petaled lotus, as well as the lines that constitute the components of the earth-castle wheel (*bhūgṛhacakra*).
Therefore, starting from "Salutation to the *bindu*-wheel" (*binducakrāya namaḥ*) up to "Salutation to the first line of the square" (*caturasraprathamarekhāyai namaḥ*).

The meaning is that one should perform the pervasive placements (*vyāpakanyāsa*) at the beginning of each respective placement of the deities of the wheels (*cakrīyadevatānyāsa*) using these eleven mantras. Otherwise, since only the placement of the deities is mentioned for the second wheel, the number of pervasive placements would result in being incomplete. This very point...
Nor does [the text] prescribe or indicate the placement of the *bindu*-cakra within the first arrangement of the cakras.
As for what the ancients [say]—namely, why the placement of the enclosure of Vaśinī and the others is not mentioned—it is replied:
"The *bindu* and so forth. The nine cakras beginning with the *bindu* must indeed be placed, because they are gross.

They explain that the [levels] beginning with the half-moon and ending with *unmanī* are to be meditated upon; therefore, in the context of gross placement (*sthūlanyāsa*), the intention is that only the gross [levels] are to be placed. If this is their intended meaning:

Since the term *cakrapada* here refers to the deities situated within the *cakra*, and since the placement (*nyāsa*) of those deities has already been explained in detail and specifically, this general procedure would otherwise be redundant. Therefore, it serves two purposes: first, the attainment of the placement of the Speech-deities (*vāgdevatā*) not previously mentioned; and second, the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of other such mental visualizations (*vibhāvana*).
And so it is said. But then this is incorrect, because the word *cakra* does not refer to the deity located therein.
Likewise, the stated purpose is also untenable, because a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) cannot apply to something that was not previously suggested for inclusion.
Furthermore, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Goddess of Speech has already been explicitly stated [elsewhere]. Now, in that manuscript...
The half-verse beginning with "muṇḍamālī" would not exist; for this very reason, it is said that its commentary is also not seen there.

If one were to argue thus, there would be a contradiction with the subsequent portion of that same work. Since the names of the goddesses beginning with Sarvajñā are not mentioned in the text following this, how can it be determined that they alone are to be accepted?

Having raised this doubt, [the author] has already provided the resolution by specifically mentioning Vaśinī and the others first, and Sarvasiddhipradā and the others later; thus, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it follows that only Sarvajñā and the others are intended in the interval between them. || 78 ||
He describes the placement [of mantras] beginning with Sarvajña:
"At the root of the eye and at the outer corner, again at the front and upper part of the ear, at the crest and so forth, at the lower half, at the remaining half, and on the back of the ear. (79)
One should place [the mantras] at the ear, the outer corner of the eye, and its root.

The phrase "beginning from the right" is to be understood as carrying over. By this, it refers to the root of the right eye, the junction of the nose and the eye, the outer corner of the eye (apāṅga), and the front part of the ear.

There are two locations: the upper part and [the lower]. "Cūḍā" refers to the hair situated on the head. Its beginning is the depression located at the back of the neck; because it is precisely from there that the hair begins, it is designated as the "beginning of the cūḍā. This is stated in order to exclude the depressions at the front of the neck and other such areas.

Because of the qualification "beginning with the crest" (*cūḍādika*), there are two locations for such a depression: the southern part and the northern half for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is what he says:

"the remaining half. Therefore, the meaning is that one should place [the deities] beginning with Sarvajñā in the ten locations: the right ear, the back, the front part, and the root and outer corner of the second eye.
The predecessors, however, considering that the portion consisting of the hair on the head and so forth takes the form of the forehead, explain it thus:

"The tradition is that one should place the fourth deity behind the ear and place the fifth on the forehead; the sixth [should be placed] in the depression at the back. This begins from the root of the eye.

The first half of the circular arrangement has been described. He says "in the remaining half" (*śeṣārdhe*) to indicate that one should likewise perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in the remaining half as well. Lest it be thought that the placement should begin from the root of the eye even in the remaining half, he says "at the back of the ear" (*karṇapṛṣṭhake*) and so forth; this is as follows.
This should be disregarded as merely a means of binding the disciple, intended for the purpose of removing one's own delusion. || 79 ||
One should place [the mantras for] all accomplishments and so forth at the throat, proceeding in a clockwise direction. (80)
The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) located in the eight corners of the heart [mandala] are also [to be worshipped] as before.

The phrase "aprādakṣiṇyena" is not a compound; otherwise, one would simply have said "vāmāvartena. Therefore, the meaning of the word "pūrvavat" (as before) is likewise "prādakṣiṇyena" (in a clockwise direction).

[The goddesses] are identical in form to all the previously mentioned cakras. The nominative case [in "manukoṇasthāḥ" and "caturdaśārasthāḥ"] is used in the sense of the accusative, according to the rule "supāṃ supo bhavanti. Alternatively, the word "nyastavyāḥ" (they are to be installed) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 80 ||
At the navel is an eight-petalled lotus; there, on the left side, is the backbone.
One should place the first four [syllables] on the abdomen and the left side;
one should place the other four beginning from the space between the backbone and the left side.
Having visualized an eight-petaled lotus within the navel,

one should place the four [deities] beginning with Anaṅgakusumā in sequence upon the four petals located in the four directions starting from the west— namely, the back, the left side, the abdomen, and the right side.

One should place the four lines beginning with Anaṅgarekhā upon the four intermediate petals, starting from the northwest corner (vāyavyakoṇa) and extending to the southwest corner (nairṛtyakoṇa), in the space between the two bamboo stalks on the left side.

According to the lexicon *Kośa*, which states "the right (*savya*) refers to the south and the left (*vāma*)," this word [in the context] refers to the right; for if it were intended to mean the left, [it would be inconsistent].
The word division is *tva-savyā*. || 81 || 82 ||
One should place [the deities] in one's own *svādhiṣṭhāna* from the east to the south.

Having meditated upon a sixteen-petaled lotus in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, one should install the *nityās* beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī on its petals, starting from the eastern petal. Thus far has been explained.

He refutes the practice of circumambulation by stating "ending with the right" (*dakṣāvasānakam*). The meaning is that here they should be deposited in a counter-clockwise direction. However, the earlier authorities say that four *śaktis* should be deposited in each of the directions. That is not correct, because in all [types of] deposits...
Since the contemplation of each respective wheel is necessary,

it is appropriate that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*)— just like the worship— should be performed upon the petals already contemplated, according to the principle of corresponding enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhyanyāya*).
This is because the necessity of such contemplation is indicated by the mention of a specific location in the passage, "the eight-petaled [lotus] in the navel" (*nābhau tvaṣṭadalam*).
The best of practitioners should place the ten mudrās in the mūlādhāra. || 83 ||
In front, on the left, on the rear, on the left, and in the intermediate space, there are ten mudrās—above and below; furthermore, excluding those above and below.
The first group of six Brahmā-mantras is on the right calf, and they are arranged as before;
then, starting from the left calf, they are likewise arranged in the sequence beginning with the left. (85)
One should place the eight Siddhis upon them; two should be placed on the soles of the feet.

[The others are placed] in front in the eastern direction, on the right in the southern, on the lineage (vaṃśa) in the western, and on the left in the northern. In the intermediate spaces—that is, in the four corners starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast—[they are placed] upon the eight petals.
Since the commencement is observed starting from the very first intermediate direction (the northeast),
the suspicion regarding a sequential order beginning with Īśāna and ending with Vāyu is refuted, according to the maxim that "what is determined in one instance [applies] everywhere.
"Above and below" refers to the upper and lower regions of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) situated within the *mūlādhāra*.
In this manner, one should place the ten mudrās in the ten locations. Regarding the placement on the central line, he says:

"excluding the upper and lower [locations]. One should place the eight deities—four each—in the cardinal directions starting from the east and the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, proceeding clockwise.
The exclusion [of the ninth and tenth deities] was already established simply because of their non-existence;

this is merely restated by the phrase "excluding the upper and lower. However, the ancient authorities [hold that] the phrase "furthermore, excluding the upper and lower" is connected specifically with the statement regarding the third line. Before...

Regarding the phrase "and on the left," they explain it while mistakenly thinking that the reading is not "punaḥ" (again) but rather "repha" (the letter r); however, in response to the doubt—namely, why one should perform the placement by means of meditation on the ten mudrās at the *mūlādhāra*—he says "punaḥ" (again). By the word "again," [it is indicated] that [one should also do so] at the navel.
The locations previously described as the "eight petals" are now further stated to be those which are to be grasped here as well:
in the spine (the backbone), on the left (the left side);
by the word "and" (ca), the belly and the right side are included.
The connection between the two terms "vaṃśa" and "savyapada" is through transposition. "Vāme" refers to the intermediate space in the northwest (vāyavya) corner;

by the word "ca," the inclusion of the northeast (īśāna), southeast (āgneya), and southwest (nairṛta) corners is intended. The extension of the rule from the four intermediate directions starting with the northwest to those ending with the southwest serves as the indicator of the intended meaning regarding the four cardinal directions from west to north.
Now, one might ask: "Are 'above' and 'below' two distinct locations? To this he replies:

"described as above and below. This means that the location above is between Indra and Īśāna, while the location below is between Varuṇa and Nirṛti. However, this [interpretation] is extremely erroneous.
"The very description of its own nature is proclaimed as its negation"—this is the general direction.

He states the placement of the first line: "the left calf," and so forth. Beginning from the front part of the left calf, [he describes] in what order [the letters are placed] upon each respective limb of the right calf.

With the intention that when the placement of the eight deities (*devatāṣṭakanyāsa*) is likewise performed on the left calf, it results in the exact opposite [of the previous order], he says: "in the sequence beginning with the left" (*vāmādikramataḥ*).
This refers to the directions east, north, west, and south, as well as the intermediate directions starting from northeast (*īśāna*) and ending at southeast (*āgneya*).
The meaning is "gradually. Regarding "on the soles of the feet," that is, on both soles;

since they are present [there] even now, and because it has been stated that the sequence begins with the left, the order is first the left and then the right. However, the ancient authorities [hold that] by the phrase "as before on the right shank,"...
Having explained [the sequence] as being in the western direction and in the intermediate directions beginning with the northwest,
and having intended the recurrence of the word "as before" (*pūrvavat*) even here in the phrase "the left shank" (*vāmajaṅghām*),
and having explained it as "starting from the western part," [he explains] the phrase "in the order beginning with the left" (*vāmādikramataḥ*).

They have explained that, having accepted the meaning of the sequence beginning with the space between the left [shoulders], one should place the remaining two [syllables] upon a single foot; however, it is clear that all of this is merely due to negligence. || 83 ||
Having first performed the withdrawal of the placement of the wheels (*cakranyāsa*), he establishes its latent impression (*vāsanā*):
"The placement that has emanated from the Cause is like a lamp lit from another lamp. (86)
Having performed the placement in this manner, O Goddess of the Gods, one should contemplate [it] as non-different from one's own self.

That which is the cause—the Brahman that has attained the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti, the cause of the entire universe—from that this rite called the *cakranyāsa* has issued forth. Therefore...
He confirms that it is indeed of that very nature through the analogy of a lamp, according to the logic of the ultimate reality of expansion (*prasāraparamārthanyāya*).

Thus, having projected [the deities] upon one's own body in the manner described, one should contemplate the two causal placements (*kāraṇanyāsa*)—namely, "one's own" (*sva*) and "the self" (*ātman*)—in their respective order as non-different from each other. The word *sva*...

The word *jīva* refers to the individual soul (*jīvātman*), while the word *ātman* here refers to the body. According to Amara, "one's own (*sva*) [is used] for kinsmen and for the self (*ātman*)," and according to Viśva, "the self (*ātman*) [is used] for the body, for fortitude, and for the living being (*jīva*). The intended meaning is that one should contemplate oneself as non-different from Tripurasundarī, and one's own body as non-different from the assembly of deities who constitute her enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).
Then, being composed, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) beginning with the purification of the hands.

Following the *sṛṣṭicakranyāsa*, one should perform the fourfold nyāsa taught in the previous Tantra: the *karaśuddhinyāsa*, the *caturāsananyāsa*, the *rakṣāṣaḍaṅganyāsa*, and the *vāgdevatānyāsa*. || 87 ||
Now he describes the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the nine sources (navayoni):
one should place [the mantras] upon the two ears, the chin, the temples, the mouth, the two eyes, the nose, the two shoulders, the heart, the two elbows, and the two sides of the belly. || 88 ||

One should place the three seed-syllables, known as the nine yonis, upon the knees, the two hands, the feet, the private parts, the two sides, the heart, and the two breasts, together with the throat. (89)

Although these two verses were not cited in the commentaries of the ancients, they are explained here because they are found in manuscripts. Here, among the twenty-seven constituents (*avayava*), each triad of constituents constitutes a single source (*yoni*); furthermore, in their three corners—

The meaning is that one should again place the three seed-syllables (*bīja*). Regarding this, the author of the *Saubhāgyaratnākara* maintains that the term "three seed-syllables" refers to the three seed-syllables of Bālā; however, the *Subhagārcāratnākara* maintains that it refers to the three *kūṭas* of the Pañcadaśī (the fifteen-syllable mantra). As for the [mantra] marked with nine triangles by means of Bālā Tripureśānī—

Regarding the statement in the *Jñānārṇava* on page 333, "one should perform the placement" (*nyaset*), that which is obtained through extension from the *Bālā*— namely, that one should place [the mantra] marked by the nine-yoni— is restated; then, by the phrase "of Tripureśī," it refers to the *Pañcadaśī*.

This is intended to prescribe *bālā* as the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, the Navyas (modern scholars) maintain that because the term "of Tripureśānī" (*tripureśānyāḥ*) ends in the genitive case, the syntactical construction—namely, "one should perform the placement of the nine *yonis* associated with the fifteenth [syllable]"—prescribes *bālā* alone as the instrument. For this very reason, in the subsequent internal placement of the nine *yonis*, [the text] mentions *bālā* again.

They say that the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is appropriate here in the phrase "having recited" (*samuccārya*). That is not correct; for if that were the case, since [the action] would already be obtained from the original context (*prakṛti*), the injunction of it again would result in redundancy. Nor can it be argued that even though the placement (*nyāsa*) is obtained from the original context, its performance serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the sublation of the seeds by the three *kūṭas* that would otherwise occur.

It must be said that this [repetition] serves a purpose; for, since no injunction is seen prescribing the three *kūṭas* as the instrument, it is impossible for the *kūṭas* to sublate the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) will be meaningful as indicating the repetition of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the nine *yonis*. Or, let there be the rule for placement by the *bālā* mantra alone in that Tantra.

In the present context, however, it should also be understood that [the placement] is by means of the *kūṭas* alone. Here, regarding the placement of the triangles (*trikoṇanyāsa*), it may be according to the clockwise sequence starting from the front tip as written;
or, following the order of the textual reading "in the two ears and the chin," it may be first in the two ears and then in the chin. Even in that case—
Since it has been stated in various places that the right side and so forth apply to the ears, eyes, and other organs, it is the same here as well.

However, for the sake of consistency with conventional practice (*ācāra*), it is appropriate to perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the left ear first. This is because the phrase "from the left and so forth" (*vāmādikamataḥ*) is present nearby, making its recurrence possible. Furthermore, this nine-yoni placement (*navayoninyāsa*) is of two kinds.

[The practice] is divided into external and internal. The external has just been described. Regarding the internal, many [teachers] maintain that one should visualize nine yonis—square and circular, with their tips facing oneself—at the nine locations beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and ending at the *brahmarandhra*; and therein, the ritual action is to be performed. In that regard:
The authoritative source for this must be sought. As for the statement in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Having again uttered the *bālā* [mantra], one should contemplate the square;
through the application of placement (*nyāsa*), one should contemplate the *golaka* as the *śrīcakra*."
O Goddess, having mentally conceived nine locations— the six cakras, the forehead, the hairline, and the aperture of the head— one should thereafter perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should place Śrīvidyā at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), and behind her, the Gurus in their proper sequence;
then, O Goddess, the Tithinityās, conjoined with the vowels of the Mātṛkā.
"O Goddess, one should install the bestowers of good fortune upon the face as [one does] with the *mātṛkā*s;
thereafter, the knower of mantras should install the *Prakaṭā* and others in the *ādhāra* and other locations. This is the end [of the passage].
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: after the external installation of the nine *yoni*s, [the subsequent installations follow].

Furthermore, having recited the *Bālā* [mantra], one should contemplate the *Śrīcakra*—extending from the square (*caturasra*) up to the sphere (*golaka*)—as the means for ritual placement (*nyāsa*) within the nine locations beginning with the *mūlādhāra* and ending with the *brahmarandhra*, and then place [the deities] therein. By implication, this means the deities of the *Śrīcakra*. The word "square" (*caturasra*)...

"Bhūgṛha" (earth-cave) refers to the [central] dot (*bindu*). The word "golaka" refers to the *bindu*. By the use of the verb "one should install" (*nyaset*), it might follow that only one hundred and eleven deities are established; therefore, he says "Śrīvidyām.
One should install the Goddess in the *bindu*, the three currents (*oghatrika*) behind her, and the thirty Nityās in the triangle immediately following that.

The meaning is "distinction. Having thus performed the complete placement (*nyāsa*) of the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*), one should perform the placement of the mandala of the eternal goddesses (*nityāmaṇḍala*) upon the face. Then, one should perform the placement of the nine Yoginīs, beginning with Prakaṭā, upon the nine locations starting from the support (*ādhāra*). However, some [teachers] [perform this] with Bālā.

They say that the meaning is as follows: first, one should contemplate the fourfold flow and the two circles; then, the placement of the eternal maṇḍala; and then, one should place the Yoginīs, such as Prakaṭā and the rest, who are distinguished by the Trailokyamohana-cakra.
That is not correct, because [the phrase] "one should contemplate the Śrīcakra" is distantly separated from the statement regarding Prakaṭā and the others.

Because [the claim] that it follows from the sequence is illogical, and because the statement "Śrīvidyā in the *brahmarandhra*" would result in being disconnected from the context. However, the moderns [hold that] in the section on the worship of the Śrīcakra,
following the worship of the Root Goddess—
Since the worship of the *tithi-nityās* and the worship of the *guru-maṇḍala* have not been mentioned,

a placement (*nyāsa*) that contradicts such a sequence is not appropriate here. Furthermore, because the *nityā-maṇḍala* is to be placed specifically within the triangle, [it cannot be placed] in the mouth or in the locations of the vowels.
The description of that placement (nyāsa) is inconsistent; furthermore, the contemplation of the square and the circle following the placement of the nine sources (navayoni-nyāsa) is redundant.

Therefore, there is not even a mention here of the placement of the wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra-nyāsa). As for the half-verse beginning with "śrīvidyāṃ brahmarandhre tu," it has been interpolated by some deluded person from another tantra.

For this very reason, half of that is not seen in the *Tantrasāra*. Or, if it is not an interpolation, it should be explained as teaching the *Śrīvidyā-nyāsa* and the *Guru-nyāsa* independently. Therefore, the nine *yoni*s, which are surrounded by squares and have their tips facing oneself, [are to be placed] upon the *ādhāra* and so forth.

They explain that this entire section is intended solely for the purpose of prescribing the internal installation (*nyāsa*) of the nine *yoni*s by means of circumambulation starting from one's own heart and so forth;

however, they claim that the meaning of the phrase "by means of the yoga of the installation of the spheres" (*golaka-nyāsa-yogena*) must be reflected upon and understood from the mouth of the Guru. This is an extreme act of rashness.

Since there is no functional contradiction between the sequence of worship (*pūjākrama*) and the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsakrama*), it is proper to perform the practice exactly according to the scriptural injunctions; for this very reason, the placement (*nyāsa*) at the beginning of the daily rites (*nityā*) is also appropriate. Nevertheless, by the statement "then the Tithinityās," the rule for placement within the triangle (*trikoṇa*) is established.

Furthermore, there is no fault [in our position], because it has been explained that the injunction "one should perform the placement (nyāsa) as in the Mātṛkā" refers to a distinct placement performed at the conclusion of the Śrīcakra-nyāsa. Moreover, the claim that the visualization of the square and the circle— being enjoined by the verbal text— is redundant is truly astonishing, especially from your own perspective.
What is the answer to the claim that the *Śrīvidyā-guru-nyāsa* is redundant? To assert that it is an interpolation is sheer temerity;
for the mere fact that it is not seen in another manuscript is not a decisive reason [for its rejection].
This is especially so in the absence of any discussion regarding the *cakranyāsa* within the sentence: "one should meditate upon the Śrīcakra."

What is the recourse regarding the position [of the opponent]? To claim that there is acceptance [of the practice] even in the absence of even a scent of words expressive of the contemplation of the nine *yonis* and so forth, while there exists a multitude of words such as "Śrīcakra" and the like, yet no such practice occurs—this statement is either partiality or delusion. As for the statement that the meaning of the word *golaka* is to be known from the mouth of the *Nātha*, [it is likewise problematic].
This is merely for the sake of binding the disciple.

Therefore, when the authors of the *paddhatis* write down the internal placement of the nine *yonis*, they must seek the source in another tantra; such is the direction [of the argument]. || 88 || 89 ||
He describes the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Śrīvidyā: "O Goddess, [it is performed] on the head, the secret place, the heart, and the three eyes;
likewise on the pair of ears, the mouth, and the two arms. (90)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Vidyā on the back, the knees, and the navel;
[and] on the secret place and the *mūlādhāra*. The word "knees" (*jānunī*) is used in the singular to denote the plural;
thus, there are fifteen locations, upon which one should place the fifteen syllables in their respective order. However, the ancient authorities [state]:

Those who claim that the placement (nyāsa) of each individual syllable-peak (kūṭa) constitutes a fivefold repetition of the Vidyā know the authority for this themselves; on the contrary, it contradicts the Kalpasūtra, which states: "The root [is placed] at the head from the fifteen syllables of the root Vidyā," and so forth.
This is clear. || 90 ||
Furthermore, one should perform the purification of the hands, the seats, and the six-limbed yoga. || 91 ||

Furthermore, one should place Śrīkaṇṭha and the other [deities], as well as the goddesses of speech, in the foundation; then, in the heart, at the crest, and in the station of Bindu, one should install the fire-wheel and the others.

After the placement of the Vidyā-mantras, one should again perform the purification of the hands (kara-śuddhi), the four seats (caturāsana), the protection (rakṣā), and the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa);
having performed the placement of Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, one should then install the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā).

The meaning is that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the four deities, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, upon the four locations starting from the *mūlādhāra* using the four mantras beginning with the Fire-wheel (*agnicakra*). However, the earlier commentators introduce this passage by stating that it provides the names for the rites beginning with "Purification of the Hands" (*karaśuddhi*).

They maintained that there is no repetition of the fourfold nyāsa; however, that contradicts the word "tat" (that) [in the text], and furthermore, it renders the statement "one should perform the Karaśuddhi and other nyāsas with a concentrated mind" purposeless.
Even when two injunctions involve repetition, the meaning is established by the recitation through a single performance.
And there is no fault in the determination of the sequence [of deities].
(p. 336) The installation of Śrīkaṇṭha and the others is as described in the twenty-first chapter of the *Mantramahodadhi* by means of nineteen verses beginning with "The sage shall be Dakṣiṇāmūrti."

That [procedure] should be seen explained in that very same place. As for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*) and so forth, it has been written by us in the *Varivasyāprakāśa*. || 91 || 92 ||
The entire triad of principles, conjoined with the three seed-syllables of Vidyā,
extends from the feet up to the navel, then to the throat, and likewise to the head.
Having deposited [the mantra] as all-pervasive and having again made it one's own,
one should once more satisfy the Goddess with the gentle and fiery liquid nectars.
The triad of principles consists of the *ātmatattva*, the *vidyātattva*, and the *śivatattva*;

their collective totality is the fourth principle (*turīyatattva*), which is the whole. Their essential natures have already been described previously. [In the compound] "Vidyā, the fifteenth, and the three seed-syllables," there is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound.

One should perform the application of these four principles (*tattva*) together with this tetrad. In that regard, the sequence established in other tantras is as follows: the application of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) occurs in the first three principles, while the application of the fifth [seed-syllable] occurs in the fourth principle.
Accordingly, there arise the mantras such as "Oṃ, obeisance to the *ātmatattva*," and so forth. However, the ancients [hold a different view]:

Those who accept the *tatpuruṣa* as the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the Vidyā, however, apply the thirteen-syllabled Turīya-Vidyā to the fourth principle (*turīyatattva*). That is incorrect according to the syllables. He states the places of placement (*nyāsasthāna*) according to the sequence of the mantra, beginning with "from the feet," up to the throat.
From the navel up to the throat; from the throat up to the head. The word "tathā" (so) implies that the syllable *aṅ* is to be joined [to each]. This means it is pervasive throughout all the limbs.
Having again made the Supreme Brahman one's own self and contemplated it as non-different from oneself, he states the supreme nyāsa:
"One should satisfy" (saṃtarpayet): this [term] *saumya* refers to Soma; because the group beginning with *brāhmaṇa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied.
This [term] *āgneya* refers to Agni; the rule "the suffix *ḍhak* should be stated after *agni* and *kali*" applies everywhere.
One should satisfy the Goddess—who is non-different from one's own self—with the nectar-fluids of the Moon and the Fire.
In the lunar orb situated at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), there is the Amṛta-kuṇḍalinī in the form of a liṅga;

in the root-channel, there is the Agni-kuṇḍalinī in the form of a yoni. From the state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya) of these two, which extend downward and upward respectively, [the nectar] flows forth.
The intended meaning is that one should experience bliss through the showers of the stream of nectar from the positions designated as Saumya and Āgneya in succession. || 93 || 94 ||
He concludes the section on ritual placement (nyāsakāṇḍa):
"O Goddess worshipped by heroes, in this manner the fourfold placement should be performed;
likewise, O Beloved, the sixfold placement beginning with aṇimā and that beginning with the Root Goddess. (95)

For the sake of perfect accomplishment, the practitioner must perform the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) consisting of six parts, beginning with the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*). Furthermore, the [depositions] beginning with *aṇimā* and those beginning with the Root Goddess each consist of eleven parts.

(p. 337) [The ritual] consists of sixteen components beginning with the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*). Among these, the fourfold group consisting of the purification of the hands, the four seats (*caturāsana*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and the goddess of speech (*vāgdevatā*) is performed twice.

Then follow the deposition of the nine sources (*navayoni-vidyānyāsa*), the deposition of Śrīkaṇṭha and others, the deposition of the fire-circles (*agnicakra*), and the deposition of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*).

There are six [types], including the *parānyāsa*. This is because two others—the *cakreśvarīnyāsa* and the [*cakreśvaranyāsa*]—are mentioned at the beginning of the seventh chapter; thus, due to this distinction, if one follows the procedure for performing the *aṇimā* and other [siddhis] after these [two nyāsas], there are exactly fourteen components. Thus, by means of forty-four [components]...
The meaning is that four group-depositions (gaṇanyāsa) are formed by means of these ritual placements (nyāsa). || 95 ||
He states the arrangement of these four groups of nyāsas according to the distinction of time:
"Either at the time of morning [ritual], or at the time of worship, or during the rite of fire-oblation (homakarma). (96)
At the time of recitation, or otherwise, the practitioner (sādhaka) of preeminent rank may perform their application individually, or he may perform them all together at the time of worship.
At the time of dawn, following the rites beginning with the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) and ending with the ritual placement of the Mother-syllables (*mātṛkā-nyāsa*);

at the time of worship, prior to the setting out of the vessels (*pātra*); during the rite of fire-offering (*homa*), at the commencement of the *homa* performed at the time of the food offering (*naivedya*); and at the time of recitation (*japa*), after the offering of the Kula-lamp—according to this systematic rule.
Regarding the inability to perform [the entire rite], he says: "Or all at the time of worship. "All" refers to the fourfold [rite].

The sense is that the sequence has already been stated according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) and the scriptural order (*śrautakrama*). Thus, the refined meaning is this: after the supreme worship (*parapūjā*), there is the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), and then the eleven [powers] beginning with *animā*.
Then follow the two external and internal installations of the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*); then the eleven [deities] beginning with the Root Goddess;

then the fourfold set consisting of the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), the four seats (*caturāsana*), the protection (*rakṣā*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and the Goddesses of Speech (*vāgdevya*);
then the two installations of the Nine Yoginīs (*navayoni-vidyā*); and finally, again, the triad beginning with the purification of the hands.
Furthermore, there is first the single [placement] beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha; then the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) beginning with Vāgdevī, the fire-wheel (agnicakra), and so forth;

and the supreme placement (parānyāsa). Having combined these three, there are forty-four placements. Following that, one performs either the lower worship (aparapūjā) or the intermediate worship (parāparapūjā) as an ancillary part.
It is established that the sequence begins with the placing of the bowls (pātrāsādana) and so forth. || 96 || 97 ||
Having prepared the seat extending up to the thirty-six principles (tattvas),
one should then offer the bali-oblation with the mantra of the Guptā and other Yoginīs.
Having first visualized each subsequent element as being situated above each preceding one among the thirty-six principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva,
and having uttered them in order from Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and so forth, up to Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva;

One should visualize oneself seated upon that very seat, in the form of Brahman, by means of the mantra: "Obeisance to the Yoga-seat whose essence is Reality. Accordingly, the Kalpasūtra states: "Seated upon the seat with the seat-mantra. This is what is meant by the visualization surrounding such a seat.

A single category (*padārtha*) consists of the constituent parts beginning with the visualization of sitting upon the locus of reality (*tattvādhikaraṇa*) and ending with the ornamentation of the wheels (*cakrālaṅkāra*).
Since these constituent parts serve the purpose of stabilizing the seat, they constitute the procedural form (*itikartavyatārūpa*) belonging to the "seat" (*āsana*).
