Because of this, the meaning established is that after arranging the seat (*āsana*) and performing everything [as prescribed], one should perform the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsajāla*) following the ornamentation of the wheel (*cakrālaṃkāra*), due to its syntactic connection with what precedes it.
This is because if the word "arranging" (*parikalpya*) were connected with the word "should give" (*daded*), the word "then" (*atha*) would result in being redundant.
Since the connection must be stated with the very action mentioned in the preceding verse,

one should not suspect that this very scriptural statement (*śruti*) should also sublate the sequence obtained through the order of the text (*pāṭha*) regarding the worship of others (*parapūjā*) and the placement (*nyāsa*), because the suffix *-kta* in the phrase "but self-worship is enjoined" (*vihitastvātmapūjanam*) is also a scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Because, by both scriptural authority (*śruti*) and traditional recitation (*pāṭha*), it is only the *śruti* that must be restricted.

Now, he explains the very limbs of the act of sitting upon the seat with the words beginning with "guptā": the compound *guptādiḥ* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* meaning "the first [of the group] beginning with Guptā," which signifies one who is manifest (*prakaṭā*). And [the term] *guptādi*...

The term "Guptādayaḥ" (the Guptas and others) is formed by a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) that sets aside the *dvandva* (copulative) compound of the singular and plural forms; its meaning is "the nine [goddesses] beginning with Prakaṭā. By the mantra of those Yoginīs—that is, by the well-known collective mantra (*samaṣṭimantra*) in the form "Samasta-prakaṭā... and so forth—[they are worshipped].
One should offer, that is, one should give, the *bali* in the form of food, water, and so forth. The deities of the *bali* are indeed those indicated by the words of the mantra.
Now, the word "atha" (then) indicates the immediate succession following the first constituent part, which consists of the act of seating and the visualization (*vibhāvanā*).
By virtue of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) ending in "dadat" (giving), [the sense of self-benefit is implied].

Because the *ātmanepada* characterized by the low-pitched (*anudātta*) accent is not mandatory when derived from a different verbal root (*dhātu*), the form *dadet* occurs in the *parasmaipada*. This offering of the *bali* is also a subordinate part (*avāntara-prayoga*) because it serves to dispel obstacles that might arise until the completion of the *āsana-pūjā*.
And because it is performed [after] the seat (āsana), it is indeed an ancillary part of that very seat. However, the predecessors [hold that]: the word "seat" (āsana) refers to the Śrīcakra;

the phrase "beginning with the secret" (guptādi) is to be supplied as preceding the word "manifest" (prakaṭa); and the word "offering" (bali) refers to a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). By this, after the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa), one [regards] oneself as the Śrīcakra.
They have explained that the meaning is: "Having meditated [upon the deity], one should cast a handful of flowers upon one's own head with the collective mantra (samaṣṭimantra).

However, this has been disregarded because it contradicts the maxim "the meaning of another word is not intended in an injunction" (*vidhau paraśabdārtha*) and because it violates the sequence of the Kalpasūtras and other such texts. || 98 ||

O beautiful one, by breaking the knots of the syllables in the form of the *piṇḍa*, there is the destruction of obstacles through the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Vidyā upon the secret place, the heart, the mouth, and the head. 99.

According to the method stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*, "The body (*piṇḍa*) is the power Kuṇḍalinī," and so forth, the word "body" (*piṇḍa*) refers to the Mūlādhāra; by the word "word" (*pada*), due to proximity, the Maṇipūra is meant;
and by the word "form" (*rūpa*), the Ājñācakra is indicated. In these three, respectively—

The knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra exist. Thus, by the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the fourfold set—namely, the three peaks (*kūṭa*) beginning with Vāgbhava and the Root-Vidyā—upon the four locations beginning with the secret part (the secret part being indicated by the word "secret," and the forehead by the word "mouth"), the piercing of the three knots occurs. By that [means]...
The meaning is that the internal obstacles are thereby destroyed. However, some (p.

339) explain that by the word "knot" (granthi), the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is meant; therein, the placement (nyāsa) of the seed-syllable of the Fourth State (turīya) should be performed. || 99 ||
Having thus explained the removal of internal obstacles, he now states the means for removing the three types of external obstacles— classified as terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial—
the knower of mantras, having dispelled the obstacles present in the sacrificial hall:
May those beings depart who are situated upon the earth. || 100 ||
May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva;
may those on the earth be struck down by the blow of his heel, and those in the sky by the clap of his palms.
One should dispel divine obstacles with the weapon-mantra and with one's gaze;
then, one should contemplate a wall of fire in all directions, above, and below.

Reciting the mantra consisting of the verse beginning with "apasarpantu," one should strike the ground with the left heel; by this, terrestrial obstacles are dispelled. The meaning of the mantra is clear.
[Then,] with the middle and index fingers of the right hand, one should strike the palm of the left hand.

With the *tāla* gesture, one should destroy the obstacles situated in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Here too, the previous mantra alone serves as the ear-mantra (*karṇa*), because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra—namely, "those beings who are makers of obstacles"—illuminates the meaning inherent in the ritual application without distinction. For this very reason, regarding the phrase "having dispelled the obstacles" (*vighnānutsārya*), [the same mantra applies].

The two [factors] residing in the earth and the sky are indeed specific types of obstacles. The statement "one who knows the mantra" is intended to indicate that the mantra serves as the instrument precisely for their removal. However, according to the principle of repetition with each primary act (*pratipradhānanyāya*), the mantra should not be recited twice; for in the case of a second recitation—
Because the phrase "established on the ground" would otherwise result in revealing a meaning that is not syntactically connected [to the rest of the mantra], the conclusion is this:

one should utter the mantra only once while simultaneously performing the striking with the heel and the clapping of the hands, thereby effecting the removal of the two obstacles. By this very logic...
He sets aside this mantra—which is obtained as the instrument even for the removal of divine obstacles—with the word "astra.

This means: the mantra used in the *pañcadaśī* (fifteen-syllable) ritual for the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) beginning with the heart; others say it refers to [the mantra] by its generic class alone, namely "astrāya phaṭ"; some also say it refers to the word *phaṭ* alone. [This is done] by means of the gaze.
By gazing with a fierce look; then, one should visualize a wall all around the ten directions to ward off the fear of fire. 100, 101, 102.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship Mārtaṇḍa with the general offering (sāmānyārghya),
together with the power of light (prakāśaśakti), radiant and brilliant like the dawn.
And [the deity] with its retinue of planets and so forth, illuminating universal splendor.

(p. 340) Indeed, in the ritual procedure for arranging the vessels (*pātrāsādana*), the authors of the manuals state: "The jar (*kalaśa*), the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*), the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*), the self-vessel (*ātmapātra*), the guru-vessel (*gurupātra*), and the vessels for the Śakti, the *baṭuka*, the enjoyment (*bhoga*), and so forth."

They draw [the figures] according to their respective forms. Having placed that vessel among them according to the general procedure for the *arghya* offering, one should worship the Sun together with the power of manifestation (*prakāśa-śakti*) using the water therein. He is one whose ornaments and attire are red. The eight planets are Soma and the others; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), Māṭhara is included.
Piṅgala, Daṇḍa, and Caṇḍāṃśu are taken as the attendants; others hold that the six limbs are taken. 103.
O Goddess, with the Saumya, Āgneya, and Yuta [yantras], along with rocanā, aguru, and kuṅkuma; || 104 ||
Uttering the root mantra correctly, one should draw the king of wheels;
then, with the root mantra of the Yoginī, one should cast a handful of flowers.
One should ensure that [the vessel] is by all means not empty—using gems, pearls, or corals, or by reciting the root-mantra in reverse; for if it is empty, many obstacles arise.
The triad beginning with *gorocanā* (cow-gallstone), when ground with the fluids of the lunar and fiery [substances], is the means for drawing the wheel (*cakralekhana*).
Regarding the pen (*lekhanī*), it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava* that it consists of gold and silver.
The terms "lunar" (*saumya*) and "fiery" (*āgneya*) have been explained immediately below in the section on the supreme deposition (*parānyāsa*).
"Kuṇḍagola" refers to the fluid [of sexual union]. This is stated in the *Kumārīkalpa*, concerning the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*):
"One should draw this upon copper smeared with kuṇḍagola, joined with self-arisen flowers, and treated with saffron and agallochum."
Also in the *Svatantra*: "Having thus disposed the body, the wise man should draw the King of Wheels on gold, silver, copper, stone, or on the eight metals."
Svayaṃbhū flower, kuṇḍagola, rocanā, aguru,
kāśmīra, musk, liquor, and sandalwood from Malaya;
"This fragrance has been fully described as always dear to Caṇḍikā;
with this combination of fragrances, one should draw the yonicakra. As for the predecessors, they say: "Saumya is camphor; ghanasāra is known by the name candra."

From the *Kośa*: "The *āgneya* [is] from Kashmir; it is the flame of fire born in Kashmir," according to the *Kośa*. This pentad, being rubbed with the *kāraṇa*, is explained as the "cause" (*kāraṇa*).
Thus, in the section on the supreme deposition (*parānyāsa*), the author of the root-text has indicated the meaning of the terms *saumya* and *āgneya*.

(p. 341) Even though they have established this themselves, how is it that they forgot it here? As for what was stated in the *Pūrvatantṛa* regarding the independent causality of vermilion (*sindūra*) and other substances, that should be understood as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) in the event that such materials are unavailable. But the moderns (*navyāḥ*) [hold that] when [the offering is made] on the ground...

The *bhūprastāra* (earth-diagram) is written; they state that the rule is as follows: if it is a filling of the *meruprastāra*, it should be done with saffron powder (*kuṅkuma-rajas*); if it is on a copper plate or similar surface, it should be written with a paste of *rocanā* (yellow pigment) or the like.
The authority for this must be sought from you, as it is what you accept.
In the *Jñānārṇava Tantra*:
"On a level and pure patch of ground, one should draw the wheel upon the earth using either vermilion powder or saffron powder."

Thus, in this verse, on the contrary, by the word "equal" (*sama*), the *bhū-prastāra* is indicated as the intended one, because the *meru-prastāra* is not accepted in your own system (*bhavattantra*). As for the statement from the *Arṇava*: "O Goddess, there is no doubt that even the Śrīcakra is of the form of Meru," that refers to this [particular] cakra.

In another statement, "It is extracted by means of the syllables of the Śrīvidyā which have the form of Meru," the reading "merurūpam" [along with the *bindu*] is disregarded; instead, the term "śrīvidyārṇa" is accepted as a compound,
because the mantra named the nine-syllabled Meru is a constituent part of the entire Śrīvidyā mantra.

Furthermore, because it has been explained by you yourselves that the statement— "the letter *la* is the seed-syllable of the earth (*pṛthivī*), and by that the circle of the earth is expressed," and so forth— is intended to convey a similarity based merely on the possession of the attribute of being all-pervasive, there is a contradiction. As for what was also said:
Since it would result in the redundancy of the two words "bhūpradeśe" and "bhuvi," one might argue that the text should be divided as "asame" (on uneven ground), and thus explained to mean:
"One should draw [the mandala] on uneven ground on the earth itself, in accordance with Mount Meru.
But even that is not correct; for by pulling down the verb "likhet" (one should draw), the two [clauses] would become separate sentences.

Because there is no pointlessness to those two constituent words; and because even in this tantra, by means of a sentence with an identical phrasing—namely, "on a level and pure portion of ground"—the very *bhūprastāra* (ground-array) is implied, and thus it is appropriate to explain it in this very way for the sake of consistency with that [other text]. Or, let it be so.
Although the Meruprastāra is merely alluded to here as being accepted in the *Tantrarāja*, the *Gaurīyamala*, and other such works,

there is a distinction between the rule "with yellow pigment (*rocana*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*)" and the rule "with vermilion powder (*sindūrarajas*)," despite the lack of difference in the use of the instrumental case;
for in one instance it refers to filling with dry powder, while in the other it refers to [filling] with mud.

The two views—that "lekhanam" (writing) refers to the previously mentioned arrangement or that it is something else entirely—are both without authoritative basis; this is the general direction [of the argument].

As for the term "uccārayan" (pronouncing), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), or it intends the teacher’s status as an instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*), as in such examples as "one should cause the purification of the hands" or "one should cause a Niṣāda chieftain to perform a sacrifice. The earlier authorities, however, [hold a different view]...

They explain that by supplying the two phrases "one should recite" (*uccārayet*) and "one should write" (*likhet*), it means that one should either write it oneself or have it written by another's hand. According to this view, the person from whose hand the wheel is to be written must be a practitioner who has performed the preliminary recitation and other rites.

Thus, such a persistent insistence becomes devoid of any valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇaka*). Furthermore, the established custom of writing by the hands of lay artisans who have practiced the art of calligraphy would also be contradicted by the statement that "only one habituated to the practice of writing should write the yantras, and no other."
Then, one should cast [the offerings] into that wheel with the root-mantra of the Yoginī.

One should adorn it by making the wheel non-empty. Regarding the absence of flowers, he says "jewels" (maṇi). In this view, he sets aside the collective mantra (samaṣṭimantra) with the word "in reverse order" (viloma). And this reversal refers to the *kūṭa* syllables, but not...

It should be understood that there are fifteen syllables. Obstacles, such as those arising from the earth and so forth, [arise] through the interruption of the seat (*āsana*), which consists of sitting until the completion of the worship. By this, [the purpose of] such an ornamentation of the wheel is indicated.
By way of suggesting that its purpose is the removal of obstacles, it is indicated that this is the final component of the rite concerning the seat (*āsana*).

Thus, the sequence made explicit in the *Kalpasūtra*— namely, "having fashioned the seat, having drawn and adorned the *cakra*, one should perform the network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*)"— is thereby signaled.
As for the inversion of the parts of the seat that is observed in the Kalpasūtra, it should be understood as being based on another tantra. || 104 || 105 || 106 ||

In order to set aside the status of being a subordinate part of the ritual seat (āsana-padārtha), which was obtained through the intermediate context of the general *arghya* offering, he says: "One should establish the *arghya* between the Śrīcakra and oneself."
Because the *āgama* suffix is not mandatory in the case of a technical treatise (*śāstra*), there is no insertion of the augment *puṅ* in the word *pratiṣṭhayet*.

Although the word "middle" (*madhya*) here denotes a specific location rather than being used in its simple sense, it nevertheless refers to the determination of the central region of the wheel-self (*cakrātman*).
The meaning— that one should perform the placement of the *arghya* vessel only after the drawing of the *cakra*, because it is impossible before the drawing of the *cakra*—
is obtained from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*). Precisely because it is based on an indicative mark,
the sequence prescribed by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) for the placement of the seat (*āsana*) and the ritual deposit (*nyāsa*) is not sublated by this [contextual indication].

Therefore, having performed the sequence beginning with sitting on the seat and ending with the visualization of the fire-enclosure (*vahniprākāra*), having drawn the *cakra*, offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and performed the previously mentioned supreme worship (*parā pūjā*), one should arrange the ritual vessels (*pātrāsādana*); such is the established procedure. It is likewise stated in the *Kalpasūtra*, even though...

Since this sequence is established even by the subsequent statement in the text beginning with "situated within the square" (*caturasrāntarālastha*) regarding the procedure for the general *arghya* offering,
it is not [established] merely by the order of the recitation or by the presentation of the constituent parts of the rite of the seat (*āsana*).
The performance of the general *arghya* offering proceeds [first], nor does that of the worship of Mārtaṇḍa.
This is because, since the latter has the general *arghya* as its instrument, the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) overrides the order of textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).
Nevertheless, since the subsequent text has the specific *arghya* as its instrument, it also applies here.

This purpose is appropriate under the view that [the text] prescribes what is to be done. Here, the word *ātman* refers to one's own seat (*svāsana-sthāna*), while the word *śrīcakra* refers to the arising of the *bindu*; such is the established tradition.

From these two [measures], as in the case of the injunction "he measures half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi minoti*), a specific location is indicated. In the middle part of that [location], the placing of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*) is prescribed.
And that middle part belongs to the location thus indicated.

Since it is untenable without a threefold division, it implies such a division; and that division, by the maxim "it should be equal, as nothing is heard [to the contrary]," is indeed equal. Consequently, the extent of the space from the point of the *bindu* of the drawn or installed wheel to the location of its own seat—that entire space—[is divided].

It is established that one should divide [the area] equally into three parts, set aside one part each from the eastern and western sections, and place the vessels in the middle section. Furthermore, the fact that each of those individual parts measures twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) is a point obtained from another tantra. This is the placement of the vessels (pātrāsādana).
Proceeding [with the description]: between the object of accomplishment (sādhya) and the means of accomplishment (sādhaka), there should be thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgula);
twelve finger-breadths above, and likewise one finger-breadth in the lower part.
"A wise person should place it there, situated in the middle with twelve finger-breadths [of space]," according to this statement;
thus, "a finger" (aṅgula) means twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśāṅgula). By this, having left a space in front...
In the *Prapañcasārasaṃgraha*, regarding the drawing of the wheel,

it is stated that according to the tradition, one should leave a space of one *aratni* from one's own seat and draw it on a piece of ground measuring one cubit (*hasta*) beyond that, upon a supporting pedestal (*pīṭha*) raised to the height of a line level with one's navel.
By Śaṅkarānandanātha.
Now, he describes the general establishment of the *arghya* (offering water) with five verses:
"O Goddess of the Gods, within the interior of the square, in the six corners... (107).
Having worshipped the six seats, one should again worship the four thrones within the triangle, O Goddess, in sequence as *kā*, *pū*, *jā*, and *o*. (108)
Having worshipped the *arghya* and the feet [of the fire], one should worship the ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire;
having established the vessel there, one should worship the digits of the Sun therein.
One should worship the twelve digits of the Sun (sūryakalā) beginning with Ka and ending with Da in the vessel;
then, when the substance has been held [therein], one should worship the sixteen lunar digits (indukalā).
And one should meditate upon Amṛteśī in the center of that by means of the Navātman mantra;
then, O Gaurī, one should satisfy the deities of the bodily constituents with the Navātman mantra.
One should satisfy Ānandabhairava with the mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*.

Regarding this, there is the injunction for the sequence of offering the oblations beginning with Vaiśvānara, stating: "He who, having carried fire in a vessel (*mukhya*) for a year, should pile the fire-altar (*agni*)."
Just as in that sentence, by the very fact of its inclusion within the scope of the subject (*uddeśya*),

the status of being an injunction (*vidheya*) is accepted even for the alternative of not performing the retention (*dhāraṇā*) known as "the year"— which was not explicitly prescribed by another verbal statement— so too is it here.

Since several items, such as the drawing of the yantra and so forth, are included within the scope of the subject in a single sentence, the injunction must be inferred [from that context]. Therefore, this is the collective meaning:
one should [construct] a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and a square for the Goddess and for oneself.

One should perform [the rite] with perfumes and so forth on one's own left side, situated in the center. For in the *Jñānārṇava*, regarding the phrase "having fashioned a square mandala on the left side," the word "left" refers to the left of the Goddess;
this is because one's own left side presents itself more immediately to the mind. Thus, it is precisely on the left side of the Goddess that [the rite is performed].
Because of the ease of performance obtained when offering worship with the general *arghya* after constructing the mandala, the general *arghya* vessel is placed specifically on one's own right side.
For this very reason, in the ritual statement for the procedure of placing the jar, which has the sole purpose of satiating the retinue deities, it is said:

Regarding the statement "having placed the maṇḍala to the left," the modern scholars (*navya*) maintain that only one's own left side is intended. This, however, is questionable; for although there is no difference in the immediate appearance of one's own left side, it is improper to offer a divergent interpretation based merely on the convenience of ritual performance. Therefore:

One should worship the six seats, beginning with the Ocean of Nectar (Sudhārṇava), in the six corners by proceeding clockwise from the eastern corner, using the six mantras of the Mistress of the Wheels (Cakreśvarī) such as Tripurā, respectively. Then, in the center of the triangle, at the location of the Bindu, one should worship with the Root-Vidyā.
Having worshipped the seat of Kāmarūpa, one should worship the seats of Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, and Oḍḍiyāna with the three *kūṭas* in a clockwise direction starting from one's own front;
these should be worshipped within the corners by means of the word "antara" itself, which includes the four objects of worship.

Because the presence of the [five] locations is possible; therefore, having worshipped with the mantra "Oṃ aiṃ, obeisance to the support of the arghya vessel, which is the ten-kalā-souled fire-maṇḍala," and having established it upon the arghya-vessel base, [one worships] "Yaṃ, obeisance to Dhūmrārcis."

With these ten mantras beginning with "ityādi," one should worship the ten digits of fire (*vahnikalā*) in a circular form, proceeding clockwise from the front [of the fire]. Upon that base, one should place a vessel made of gold or the like, or a conch shell, [reciting]: *klīṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane arghyapātrāya*.

Having honored with "Namaḥ" and having established [the deity] therein, one should worship the twelve digits of the Sun (sūryakalā), beginning with Tapinī, in the form of a circle. One should worship those solar digits by means of mantras produced by joining the twelve letters beginning with *ka* and the twelve letters beginning with *bha*. Here, by the word "beginning with *bha*" (*bhādī*), [the sequence] is in reverse order (*prātilomyena*).

The letters beginning with *ba* and ending with *ḍa* are taken [as the basis], according to the tradition (*saṃpradāya*), and not the letters beginning with *ma*, even though they are possible. Therefore, the mantras become: *kaṃ bhaṃ tapinyai namaḥ*, *khaṃ baṃ tāpinyai namaḥ*, and so forth. In that context, *sauḥ* is for the lunar orb (*somamaṇḍala*).

Having filled [the vessel] with pure water using the mantra "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of sixteen digits, the nectar of the *arghya*," and having offered the substance in the form of a mere drop from the causal source, one should worship the sixteen digits of the Moon (*soma*) with the mantras beginning with "Aṃ, obeisance to Amṛtā. Then...
Having first visualized and worshipped Amṛteśī, the presiding deity of the cause, with the nine-syllable peak-mantra (kūṭamantra) in pure water,
one should again [worship] the group of six or seven, beginning with Ḍākinī, with another nine-syllable peak-mantra.

Or one should worship with [the mantra] ending in *namaḥ*. With that same [mantra], ending in *vaṣaṭ*, one should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) into the very midst of pure water for Ānandabhairava. The extraction of the two *kūṭas* consisting of nine syllables is as follows in the Jñānārṇava:
Śiva and Candra [are the first two syllables], ending with Mātṛkā; then Kāla, Śakra, Ambu, and Vahni; and Vāyu joined with the left ear (the letter *u*) and with Bindu and Nāda.
Having uttered this seed-syllable, as well as Ānandabhairava ending in the letter *ṅ*,
joined with the crest-mantra (*śikhā-mantra*), one should again write the seed-syllable.
"Leaving aside the first *candra*, one should place *karṇa*; one should join *vāmākṣi* [to it].
Then, for the goddess Sudhā, there is *vauṣaṭ*; this is Ānandabhairava.
Here, *śiva* is *ha*, *candra* is *sa*, the end of the *mātṛkā* is *kṣa*, *kāla* is *ma*, and *śakra* is *la*.

*Ambu* is *vaḥ*. *Vahni* is *raḥ*. *Vāyu* is *yaḥ*. *Vāmakarṇa* is the vowel *ū*, and it is joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*. At the end of this seed-syllable (*bīja*), "to Ānandabhairava, *vaṣaṭ*"—this is one mantra.
Again, in that very same [mantra], by the transposition of Śiva and the Moon, there is the place of the vowel *u*.
By joining with the vowel *ī*, one forms another seed-syllable (*kūṭa*); at the end of that, "to the Goddess Sudhā, *vauṣaṭ*" is another mantra.
Some maintain that these two, when combined, constitute a single mantra. Here, the second mantra belongs to Amṛteśī. At the end of the first mantra’s seed-syllable, [one adds] "obeisance to Ḍākinī."

The discernment is that, by means of such combinations, six or seven mantras should be employed. Since a great variety is observed among the mantras of the *kalās* and so forth mentioned here according to different tantras, and since not even one of them has been selected as the definitive intent (*ihaidamparyeṇa*), there is an option (*vikalpa*).
Having thus prescribed the procedure for the general *arghya* in detail, he teaches the special *arghya* by means of a half-verse, preceded by its extension [to the previous rules]:
"In the same way, the best of practitioners should prepare the special *arghya*. (112)

Just as the general *arghya* has been prepared, one should prepare another *arghya* in exactly the same manner. The distinction is this: that [general *arghya*] was made with ordinary water, whereas this [special *arghya*] is made with special water. For this very reason, the procedure for the general *arghya* using water is taught in the *Pūrvacatuḥśatikā* as being performed in a vessel of gold or other precious materials.

One should place the *arghya* water on the common support (*sādhāra*) with two verses. Regarding this, four alternative positions have been demonstrated by us previously. Among those, if the position is that it concerns the procedure for the general *arghya*, then there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the procedure prescribed here with the procedure prescribed there.
According to the view of the author of the *Manoramā*, however, there is a combination [of both types] in that very same place;

this is also the case according to the view that the rule for "special water" (*viśeṣārghya*) concerns the mixing of water. According to the view of the *Candrikā*, which holds that a substitute is used when the special substance is unavailable, the properties of the *soma* plant apply to the water as well, just as they do to the *pūtīka* plant.

[The preceding rules] pertain to specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*). In reality, however, regarding the position that [the text] prescribes a ritual injunction (*vidhi*), it is more appropriate to understand that passage as being intended for the general injunction regarding the *arghya* offering; for otherwise, the natural consistency (*svārasya*) of the detailed exposition of those specific properties would be violated. This is because of the natural sense of the word "water" (*ambu*), and because [the injunction] takes precedence over the case-ending of the subordinate term (*upapada-vibhakti*).

Furthermore, due to the greater force of the case-ending (kāraka-vibhakti), there is also an injunction for application (viniyoga-vidhi) stating: "One should worship Mārtaṇḍa with that [offering] which has been produced there as a general arghya, just as one satisfies the Yoginīs. The phrase "of the Śrīcakra and of the self" is the injunction regarding its place and time. By those [verses] following it...

The procedure for the special *arghya* offering consists of five and a half verses. Among these, the latter half constitutes the rite of origination (*utpattividhi*), while the preceding group of five verses constitutes the rite of performance (*itikartavyatāvidhi*); such is the distinction.
For there is no authoritative basis for the insistence that the description of the performance must necessarily follow immediately after the rite of origination.

Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the natural force (*svārasya*) of the statement "again, the substance" (*punar dravye*); for the word *dravya* is not used by the Tantrikas in its natural sense to refer to water. Furthermore, the sprinkling of drops is merely a consecration (*saṃskāra*), as in the case of [the rule] "he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk," and so forth.

Furthermore, such a designation is inappropriate because [the vessel] lacks the nature of containing substances within it as its substratum; for in the *Kalpasūtras*, the *Jñānārṇava*, and other texts, the worship of the *kalās* and the worship of Amṛteśī and others situated upon the foundational maṇḍala are both performed specifically with the *viśeṣārghya*.

Furthermore, by following such a procedure, many contradictions would arise; moreover, such extensive detail regarding the placement of the general *arghya* vessel is not observed in other tantras. Nor is it the case that vessels of gold and so forth are not seen in other tantras for the general *arghya*, for it is usually the conch (*śaṅkha*) that is prescribed.

Thus it should be recited. Even there, since the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "gold and so forth" (*hemādi*) could include the conch as well, there is no greater contradiction [with other authorities]. By this, the explanation of the ancients—that the general rule for the *arghya* offering is established by five verses—is refuted, as that very section [of the text] contains...

However, the claim that the rule for the specific *arghya* begins with the words "But when the substance has been separated" (*vidhṛte tu punardravye*) and so forth, while the phrase "in the same way the *arghya*" (*tathaivārghyam*) serves as an extension of the general *arghya* rules, is not to be accepted because it contradicts what precedes and follows. Nor should it be said that the rule for the specific *arghya* is contained in these five verses alone.

For the designation of "guest-offering" (*arghya*) does not apply to those two anywhere. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, the prescription in the subsequent text for the distribution of materials to the teachers and to oneself would be contradicted due to the absence of such materials; for even there, it is specifically the *viśeṣārghya* (special guest-offering) that serves as the instrument.

Therefore, the Kalpasūtra states: "Having prepared the special *arghya* water, one should worship the Guru’s sandals (*gurupādukā*) three times on the head with its drops, saying 'The wet [substance] blazes, svāhā!'; one should then offer those drops into the *kuṇḍalinī* within oneself—this is the purification of the *arghya*."

"Śivam" (p. 347). For even in the present tantra, since the worship of the Guru and others is taught immediately after the procedure for the special *arghya*, there is the cognition of the former [action] as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) by virtue of the subsequent sentence, just as in the case of the two sentences "There is clay" and "Make a vessel. As for what the moderns [say] when that is the case:

It was stated that because the Goddess’s [portion] would have been used first and their respective [portions] would have been used later, there would be the fault of *ucchiṣṭa* (remnants); therefore, those two vessels were set aside. That is not correct; for by using another vessel, one may take a small amount of water from them specifically for the worship of the Guru and others.

There is no possibility of the fault of being "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa), because only that much [of the substance] is enjoined; furthermore, it is only after the offering has been presented to Bhairava that it is then employed for oneself. Moreover, since the fault would only apply to eating what is obtained through worldly attachment (rāga), a prohibition does not apply to what is prescribed by Vedic injunction (vaidha). Otherwise, [the following would occur]:

Even in cases such as the consumption of the remnants of animal sacrifices (*pāśuka-havis*), there would arise great confusion due to the occurrence of the fault of transgressing the prohibition, "One should not eat meat. By this [it is shown that] the worship of oneself must be performed using only unconsecrated substances.

The audacity of some has been cast aside; therefore, according to this tantra, the placement of only two vessels is desired. As for the placement of a *kalaśa* written by the authors of the *paddhati*s, that too is not seen in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, the *Jñānārṇava*, the *Kalpasūtra*, and so forth. Hence...
The elders teach that this [mantra] is to be employed only in the case of a purely conventional (sāmayika) worship;
however, the moderns [hold that]:
"By worshipping the Moon with this, one becomes fit for all forms of worship."
Having thus worshipped the entire Śrīvidyā, one should worship her on all sides.

Having refuted the reading "sakala" (entire) everywhere in the verses of the *Jñānārṇava*, such as "O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped the entire wheel according to the rule," he [insists] that only the word "kalaśa" (the jar/vessel) [is intended].
Because it is authoritative, they laboriously justify the installation of the jar (*kalaśasthāpana*) as being the intention of the author of that particular tantra. || 112 ||
He says that one should worship the gurus with this very same special arghya water:
"Having worshipped the line of the guru's feet, one should offer it again to Bhairava;
impelled by his command, one should then present it to the row of gurus. (113)

Having taken the water contained in that vessel with another vessel, one should worship the lineage beginning from Paraśiva and ending with one's own guru— visualized upon one's own head— with the *pādukā-mantra* using the *arghya* water, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and other offerings drawn up by the other vessel; [then, one should offer it] to [the deity] residing in one's own heart.
The meaning is that, having offered that water to Kāmeśvara together with Kāmeśvarī and having received His command (*ājñā*),

one should again worship the three lineages of Gurus— known as the *divya*, *siddha*, and *mānava*— upon one's own head. As for the earlier commentators (*prāñcaḥ*), however— [the text continues with their specific interpretation].
p. 348) Having lifted the *arghya* vessel up to the forehead and, with that water,

having satiated the lineage beginning with Paraśiva and the triad of lineages (*oghatraya*) upon one's own head, and having again offered it to one's own Guru— who is of the nature of Bhairava— as if to Śiva, [one should then proceed] by the command of that Guru in the visible row of gurus.

Some explain that one should "offer" [the vessel]; however, this is incorrect, because it contradicts the prohibition stated in the *Tantrasāra*, which says that the arghya-vessel must not be moved until the completion of the worship. Furthermore, since the lineage of direct gurus is only occasional...
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the scriptural teaching that [the Guru] is eternal; and there is a lack of evidence for interpreting the term *bhairava* as referring to the Guru. || 113 ||
Taking the remainder of that [offering] and performing the homa in the fire of Śiva, which blazes on all sides,
one should carry out the rite while reciting the *pādukā* and the root-vidyā.
When the Great Light is intent upon the withdrawal and emission of the universe,
one should offer the movement of the rays into the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī by means of the mind.
The identity of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and "this-ness" (idaṃtā), conceived within the *sruc* ladle of Unmanī,
is the great oblation (*mahāhavis*) whose substance arises from the intensity of churning.
Having repeatedly offered oblations, the wise one, whose very form is innate bliss, should worship the Śrīcakra, which is the manifestation of the expansion of his own self-luminosity. 117.

Having taken the remnant of the oblation belonging to the Guru, while reciting the mantra of the Guru’s sandals and the root-vidyā, one should offer it into the Śiva-fire— which possesses universal radiance, whose splendor flows forth from every side, and which is non-different from one's own self. Even if the reading is "into the fire of desire" (kāmāgni), it refers to that which is the nature of one's own consciousness.

It should be explained that Agni is indeed Kāmeśvara. The meaning is that one should offer oblations after having contemplated oneself as fire and the universe as one's own rays. Here, by the use of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the word "japan" (reciting), it is appropriate that the two mantras are merely descriptive references (*anuvāda*) to the action being performed, as they indicate simultaneity with the oblation.

It is indicated that [the phrase] "suvāsā" functions as a mantra, just like "paravīrasī. By this, it is implied that one should offer the remains of the oblation again and again until the completion of the mantra, doing so without leaving any residue. For this very reason, the repetition (*vīpsā*) in the expression "having offered, having offered, he himself... is appropriate.

Therefore, according to the principle of each primary act (*pratipradhānanyāya*), there is no repetition of the two mantras— as occurs with the *āmana-homa* mantra— but rather, like the mantra for sprinkling the altar (*vediprokṣaṇa-mantra*), the two mantras are employed only once.
As for the number of oblations (*homa*), it is indeed indefinite, since it must continue until the remnants of the sacrificial offering (*haviḥśeṣa*) are completely disposed of.

In reality, however, there are three rites according to the three verses. Therefore, due to repetition, there is a distinction between the acts. Consequently, it should be understood that there are exactly three oblations performed simultaneously with the threefold recitation of the two combined mantras.
He describes the second oblation, preceded by the mental impression (*vāsanā*) regarding the vessels, the sacrificial offerings, and so forth:

"Great Light" (mahāprakāśa): Light is indeed fire, non-different from one's own self. Its greatness, however, arises from its all-pervasiveness, as well as from its blazing without fuel and its state of being unextinguished.
And thus, there is a sign of the mantra in another tantra:
Within the fire of consciousness— which blazes forth internally and incessantly without fuel, which stands as an adversary to the darkness of delusion,
and which is the ground for the unfolding of the rays of some wondrous light—
"I sacrifice the universe, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva.
Thus, withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is destruction (*nāśa*) and emission (*vamana*) is creation (*sṛṣti*).
Because those two functions are accomplished solely through His will, the Light [of Consciousness] is intent upon them; it is by its own will alone.
Based on the statement, "He swallows and also emits the entire world," one should visualize that fire within the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī;

having conceived the mind as the sacrificial vessel and visualized the mental modifications (vṛttis), which are of the nature of its rays, as the oblation, one should offer them. One should turn inward those modifications that were flowing outward through extroversion.
The intended meaning is that one should unite [the offering] within one's own self. And thus there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra:

"With the mind as the sacrificial ladle, I perpetually offer the flow of the senses as an oblation into the fire of the Self, which is kindled by the fuel of merit and demerit, along the path of the *suṣumṇā*."

The ancients maintain that the instrumental case in *manasā* expresses the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). According to that view, the purification must be performed by the mind as the instrument; this is justified by the statement of the elders: "by means of a pure mind" (*śuddhena manasā sārdham*). Alternatively, [the purification] is preceded by mental cultivation (*vāsanā*).

He speaks of the third *pūrṇāhuti*: "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) is grounded in the self; "this-ness" (*idaṃtā*) is grounded in the universe. Their unity is their occurrence in a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇavṛttitva*);
this is an adverbial modifier for the act of churning. Their co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is such that it is not artificially induced.

It is that very non-conceptual self-aware cognition (*ātma-nirvikalpa-vijñāna*) in which the true reality— the essential nature of things that has become perfectly condensed through the intense churning and refinement of mental activity— is manifested and made an object of experience.

One should offer the "great oblation" (mahāhavis), prepared and meditated upon in the ladle (sruvikalpita) characterized as previously described, into the fire of Śiva; by this elliptical connection, the meaning is that one should likewise cause even such knowledge to dissolve into one's own self. And it is heard in the *Brahmabindūpaniṣad*:
"Knowledge dwells within every being like clarified butter hidden in milk;
it must be constantly churned by the mind acting as the churning-stick.
Thus, the extraction of such a realization is stated in the *Sūtagītā*:
By means of the instructions of the scriptures and teachers, and through reasonings that follow the scriptures.
Having firmly ascertained the Self as the witness of all and being well-established,
one should regard everything that appears as other than one's own self as being without distinction.
Having realized it as being nothing but one's own self, and having further determined through one's own direct experience that this non-dual self is pure Brahman;
Having dissolved even that certainty into one's own non-dual, changeless pure consciousness,
and having realized that very dissolution as the nature of consciousness itself through its absolute state;
"This foremost sage, a knower of Brahman, should himself remain as the manifest [Brahman].

Such is this supreme state (niṣṭhā), which is both based on the Vedas (śrautī) and consists of one's own direct experience (svānubhavātmikā). As for the earlier authorities, however: "I-ness (ahaṃtā) is the means of knowledge (pramā); 'this-ness' (idaṃtā) is the object of knowledge (prameya); the identity of these two—"

[The opponent] explains that the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a reality consisting of the equilibrium of those three [aspects]. This is questionable because it does not conform to the literal meaning of the words. Thus, after the three oblations preceded by such contemplation, [the deity] is one whose body (*vigraha*)—that is, whose form—is innate (*sahaja*), unconditioned bliss (*ānanda*).

In this context, the wise one— whose nature has been described as beginning with the form of emptiness (*śūnyākāra*) and ending with the visarga (*visargānta*)— being possessed of a concentrated mind, should worship the Śrīcakra, which is described therein as the expansion of the manifestation of his own self-awareness (*svaprathāprasarākāra*), by way of the extension of the waves of his own creative radiance (*sphurattā*). By means of the qualifying phrase "the expansion of the manifestation of his own self-awareness," [it is indicated that]...

The characteristics of the higher and lower worship have been recalled. By this, it is implied that, in comparison with the exclusive lower worship mentioned previously in the Tantra, the middle worship alone is always appropriate to perform.
Because it is extremely inferior to worship accompanied by practice that has cast off even the scent of the drink of non-duality (advaita). || 114 || 115 || 116 || 117 ||
O Goddess, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Dūtī, as well as Kṣetreśa and Dūtikā,
at the outer gate, along with the goddesses beginning with Svastikā.
The male and female messengers (dūta and dūtī) of Gaṇeśa and Kṣetrapāla are their respective powers (śakti). Having worshipped this pair of couples on the two door-panels,
the goddesses such as Svastikā, Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Padmā, Kālī, and others are to be worshipped at the outer door.
Then, in the triangle beyond that as well, having invoked the lineage of gurus situated in three rows and the Great Goddess within them, one should worship again.

Within the triangle, in the region behind the central bindu, having worshipped according to the tradition the lineage of gurus consisting of the divine, the perfected, and the human streams (divya-siddha-mānava-ogha), seated in three rows and numbering [respectively] seven, four, and eight; p. 351).
Having invoked that well-known Great Goddess within the bindu-cakra therein, one should worship her again with ritual offerings. || 119 ||
Qualifying her further, he describes the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the ritual services (*upacāra*):
"The Goddess, who resides within the Mahāpadma forest, whose form is the bliss of the Cause (*kāraṇānanda*), who rests upon my lap, and who bestows the fruits of desire and will. (120)
One should worship you with offerings and other articles consisting solely of your own essence.

[One should worship] the Great Lotus Forest, the thousand-petaled lotus, and her who resides within it. That which is the causal bliss—the bliss of Brahman which is the root-source of the multitude of drops of sensory bliss—is the bliss of Brahman.

For there is a scriptural authority stating, "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss. Alternatively, the word *kāraṇa* means that which is born from the cause; the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born therein. She whose body (*vigraha*)—that is, whose essential nature (*svarūpa*)—is that very bliss, is she; [the phrase] refers to that Great Goddess. Or rather, [it means] for this great deity...

Form: According to the Śruti, "That which is honey," one should worship you—who rest upon my lap and reside on the couch of Paramaśiva—with offerings consisting of nothing but yourself, according to the mantra:
"The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman."
According to the words of the Blessed One:
"The wise one should offer the earth together with fragrance, the sky with flowers,
the wind with incense, fire with a lamp, and taste with food."
By such statements as these, [it is shown that] because the upacāras consist of the five elements, in the section concerning the meaning of the tradition:
"O sinless one, the universe consists of the five elements, and you are eternally composed of them."
The ancients maintain that because it has been stated thus, the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) consist of the Goddess herself.

"Object of desire" (*icchākāma*) means the object of one's will. Although the water for the feet (*pādya*) comes first among the offerings, the fact that the food offering (*naivedya*) is taken as the primary item is stated in the *Viśuddheśvara Tantra*:
Among these aforementioned offerings, whatever food, drink,
or other substances may be available, one should mentally imagine them upon the three root seed-syllables;
then, saying "I worship the Pādukā," one should cast flowers three times.

By this statement, it is intended to clarify the distinction that when the practice of offering physical oblations is impossible, the injunction for a mental offering applies to subjects other than the *naivedya* (food offering). For this very reason, Vyāḍi said:
"Even though [the offering] is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from the *Bālā* [tantra], [it is specified] by the words 'the *naivedya* endowed with six flavors,' and so forth."
Furthermore, the rule "one should offer [the oblation] to Tripurā, whether it has a form imagined by the mind" (p.

352) is intended to exclude the alternative prescribed in the *Paddhati*. Alternatively, there is no verbal distinction between the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and the *bahuvrīhi* when applied to words such as "naivedya" and so forth.

The single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) [compound] is based on similarity of form; however, in reality, the meaning is simply that one should worship with offerings ending in *naivedya*. This is because, in the sequence, that very [offering] is the first. Furthermore, when worshipping other deities, the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) is prescribed only after the worship ending with flowers.

In this context, such a statement is made for the purpose of refutation; thereby, its consistency with the Kalpasūtra is established. This is because, in that [text], only the sixty-four services ending with the food offering (naivedya) are prescribed prior to the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇārcana). Alternatively, one must accept that "naivedyamādayaḥ" is indeed a dvandva compound.
Furthermore, within the triangle, there are the forms of reflections of its own radiance. || 121 ||
The eternal goddesses, who consist of their respective lunar days, correspond to the specific rites performed for desired ends.

Here, the word "one should worship" (*arcayet*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. One should worship the Nityās, who are not distinct from their respective lunar days (*tithi*), within the central triangle of the triangle. However, the modern scholars (*navyāḥ*) state that in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said that one should visualize another great triangle within the circle of the central triangle and worship there; and furthermore, having visualized...

Since it is appropriate to explain that in the statement from the *Arṇava*, "the great triangle," there is merely a visualization of a single triangle as being large in order to accord with the *Kalpasūtra* of another tantra, it is not at all a novel assertion.

This is trustworthy. In the *Tantrarāja*, however, worship is said to be performed at the *bindu* alone; that the worship may also take place within the square enclosure will be explained at the end of the section on the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*). Their names, moreover, are stated in the root text itself at the beginning of the scripture. As for the extraction of their mantras, it is identical in both the *Kalpasūtra* and the *Tantrarāja*.

In the *Jñānārṇava* and other texts, however, [the visualization] is distinct: it is stated that one should meditate upon her—the Goddess who consists of the very vibration (*sphurattā*) of that [central] Goddess—as the form of the reflection of the Goddess's own delight, possessing an appearance identical to the Goddess through [the power of] knowledge (*jñāna*). And it is said in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
The meditation on the nine obscuring powers (navāvaraṇa-śakti) should be identical to that of the Goddess;
however, apart from the Kāmāṅka yantra, the ornaments, colors, weapons, and so forth [of these powers] differ.
"O Supreme Goddess, that is equal to all the locations of the wheels without exception. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Saṃhitā*:
"Alternatively, one should contemplate all the rays as being in the form of the Goddess."
By the two plural expressions "consisting of those respective lunar days" (*tattattithimayī*) and "those respective [deities]," this is what is meant:
first one should worship the specific lunar-day goddess (*tithinityā*), and afterwards one should worship all the lunar-day goddesses.
The method for that has been stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
At this time, O Goddess, one should worship the Tithinityā;
O Maheśvarī, these Nityās begin with Kāmeśvarī and end with Vicitrā.
One should worship the lunar days (tithis) in the form of the sequence from the first day to the full moon,
having visualized a great triangle in the order of the front, right, and left [corners].
Having thus described five [deities] on each of the three lines— with the *ṣoḍaśī* in the center—
beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), O Daughter of the Mountain;
One should worship each Nityā daily and shall attain great good fortune;
O Maheśānī, one should worship the circle of lunar days during the dark fortnight.
O Varārohā, from Vicitrā up to Kāmeśvarī,
they are to be worshipped in reverse order in other places, O Parameśvarī.
O Goddess of gods, he who [meditates upon] the sixteen digits of the moon in their proper sequence,
O Great Goddess, attains good fortune through the instruction of his Guru.
Having worshipped the eternal goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī in their proper sequence,
one should then worship the Tithinityā three times, O Goddess, for the sake of good fortune.
"Furthermore, one should worship the eternal Śrī Tripurā for the sake of attaining good fortune.

Herein, by the half-verse beginning with "at this time," an unprecedented injunction for the worship of the Tithinityā is established. The term "time" (*samaya*), however, is a restatement of the sequence as obtained from the textual reading. As for the singular number in "the Tithinityā," since it resides in the predicate (*upādeya-gatatvena*), [it does not restrict the object].

The meaning is that one should perform the worship of a single specific *tithinityā*, because she is intended [by the context] and because she is present [in mind]. Then, by means of the verse beginning with "Kāmeśvarī and the others," one should contemplate the worship of all fifteen *Nityās*; and by the words beginning with "vibhāvya ca" (and having contemplated), one should [perform] the procedure required for that.

And by the statement, "Having performed [the rite] and having made the emission, one should worship the Sixteenth," the worship of Tripurasundarī herself, the Mahānityā, is prescribed immediately after the preceding worship. Therefore, the subsequent text is for the purpose of explaining these three modes of worship. In that regard:

By the phrase "beginning from the first lunar day" (*pratipattithim ārabhya*), the rule for the sequential order of each individual daily worship (*nityāpūjā*) is established according to the distinction between the bright and dark fortnights. Since the sequence beginning with Kāmeśvarī has already been fixed in the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*), the daily installations (*nyāsa*), and so forth, it is as if Citrā [is placed] within such a sequence.

Lest it be feared that even if their sequence is inverted, the worship of Tripurasundarī might occur either before Citrā or not at all due to the lack of a fixed order, the mention of them again by the phrase "the sixteen Kalās" serves to reinforce the rule by ensuring her worship immediately after Kāmeśvarī.
The method of worship for the Tithinityās, which has been described in the textual passage ending with "thus, by the instruction of the Guru" (p. 354), is the constant [daily] rite.
It consists of the worship of the fifteen Nityās within the fifteen vowels situated upon the lines of the first triangle.
Regarding the *jyā* [bowstring] for the release (*visṛpyai-sarge*), one should worship the *ṣoḍaśī* with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) at the center;

however, the distinction in the *Kalpasūtra* is that there is neither the initial single daily worship (*nityāpūjā*) nor the reversal of order (*vyutkrama*) during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Then, by the passage beginning with "starting with Kāmeśvarī... [the sequence is established].

Following the threefold worship, one should again perform the worship of each individual Nityā twenty-one times—characterized by that number of three—as in the case of [the injunction] "one should recite the Anuvāka," and so forth; thus, a desired (kāmya) rite is enjoined.
However, that does not sublate the obligatory (nitya) rite, because of the word "again" (punar).

Because the conjunction [of the two] is explicitly stated by the term "and" (ca), which functions according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*) as being connected to both the preceding and the following [clauses]. And thus, the meaning is this:

if one desires Lakṣmī, having performed the three aforementioned modes of worship, one should worship Tripurasundarī after having thrice worshipped the respective *tithinityā*. To illuminate this very point, it is said:

"At the root, 'according to the desired rites' means that one should worship in accordance with the presence or absence of one's own specific desires. However, some say that even the threefold worship and so forth are indeed obligatory (*nitya*). It is with this latter view in mind [that the following is stated].
The Prāñcas explain that the section concerning optional rites (*kāmyakarma*) is in fact intended for the worship of the eternal cycle (*nityacakrārcana*),
because it is the object of desire for all practitioners due to its status as a source of manifold fruits.
Others, however, [hold that] after the third worship, one should worship the respective *tithinityā* only once.

One should worship. They consider that since she has been worshipped twice—in the first worship and in the second worship—the mention of her as being "threefold" is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Others, however, maintain that the passage beginning with "Kāmeśvarī and the others, [the Nityās] ending with Vicitrā," was spoken specifically with reference to the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*).

This is an illustration [of the principle] regarding the precedence of each respective *tithinityā* and the commencement of the ritual practice (*ācāra*) of the *tithinityā* immediately preceding it. Consequently, on the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) of the bright fortnight (*śukla*), the goddesses beginning with Bhagamālinī and ending with Kāmeśvarī are to be worshipped; on the third lunar day (*tṛtīyā*)...

The sequence begins with *Nityaklinna* and ends with *Bhagamālinī*, and so forth. Likewise, because [the list] beginning with *Vicitrā* in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is also illustrative, there are sequences such as those beginning with *Citrā* and ending with *Kāmeśvarī*,
those beginning with *Jvālāmālinī* and ending with *Citrā*, and those beginning with *Sarvamaṅgalā* and ending with *Jvālāmālinī*, and so on.
The moderns say that the sequence begins from the first day (pratipad) of the dark fortnight; they also accept this [other] view.
Both of them alone know the basis for such an interpretation. Since it is well-founded, one should understand that the arrangement follows the respective tradition. || 121 ||

Now, regarding the wheels beginning with the Trailokyamohana, he teaches the mental cultivation (*vāsanā*) of five categories— namely, the Yoginīs, the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*), the Siddhi, and the Mudrā for each wheel— according to the order of worship taught in the *Pūrvatanttra*.
There, in the wheel that deludes the three worlds, are the manifest Yoginīs.

Because they possess the gross form of the *mātṛkā* and because they pervade the skin and other [bodily constituents], the Yoginīs should be known as manifest within the self that is the expansion of the gross universe. (123)

There, among the nine enclosure goddesses, or in the direction to the north of the Nityā worship, the deities to be worshipped are called the *Prakaṭayoginīs*. These are the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) in the form of the powers such as Jyeṣṭhā and Nivṛtti belonging to the *Trailokyamohana-cakra*, which have been previously described.

In those [energies], the group of eight beginning with *aṇimā* becomes manifest; [therein is] the fourfold Mātṛkā consisting of Parā, Paśyantī, and so forth. The meaning is that it is because of having the form of that which is gross, named Vaikharī, which consists of the groups of letters *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*. And thus it has been stated at the very commencement of the scripture:
"In the *Dvādaśaślokī*, she is praised as 'the Mistress of the eight great siddhis arising from the eight groups [of letters].
He states that the group of eight beginning with Brāhmī has a manifest form in the words 'tvagādi' (beginning with skin).
In medical science, the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen."
These [seven] are well-known. However, in the Vedabhāṣya, it is stated that the eighth element is named *ojas*.

The presiding deities (*abhimāninī-devatā*) for these are the eight [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī, respectively. Their abodes within the body are located in places such as the space between the eyebrows, the hips, the navel, the heart, the throat, the mouth, the nose, and the forehead.

The term *chedana* (cutting) is well-known in the treatises of the ancients. Consequently, because the body composed of skin and other elements is gross in comparison to the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) and so forth, the deities associated with that [gross body] are also manifest.
Now, if this is the case, then regarding the attainment of powers (*prāptisiddhi*) and the fulfillment of all desires (*sarvakāmasiddhi*) mentioned in another Tantra:

Anticipating the question of how the ten mudrās, which have been described as objects of worship, can be manifest, he provides a definition that applies to all of them, beginning with the word "sthūla" (gross). The ellipsis "and because they abide [therein]" is to be supplied. In the wheel whose nature is the gross manifestation of the universe—consisting of the thirty-six principles—which takes the form of the earth element (*kṣiti*), [the mudrās reside].

The meaning is that even because of being situated in the subterranean chamber (*bhūgṛha*), there is manifestness (*prakaṭatva*). By this, it is implied that what is heard in the *Sundarītāpinī*— namely, "it becomes possessed of the eight [siddhis] beginning with *aṇimā*, it becomes possessed of the eight [powers] beginning with *samāna*, it becomes manifest"— should be explained as having the purpose of indicating the attainment of those [powers], such as the accomplishment of *siddhi*.
He describes the meditations on *aṇimā* and the other [powers] in ten verses:

"O Great Goddess, the eight *siddhis*, beginning with *aṇimā*, are established; they are exceedingly red in color and likewise hold the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*). (124)

"Those who hold the great jewel of contemplation and bestow the fruits of one's desires"—the word "eight" is used to indicate that the Śruti speaks of eight [forms] with the intention of distinguishing them according to the eightfold groupings. Regarding the phrase "vara-abhaya": [this refers to the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness].
"Holding a noose and a goad in her left and right [hands]," as stated in the *Mantramahodadhi*.
She bears upon her head the "Great Jewel of Thought," the gem known as the *cintāmaṇi*. || 124 ||
O Dear One, the deities beginning with Brāhmī should also be worshipped there in their proper sequence.
Brahmāṇī is yellow in color and adorned with four faces;
her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and she holds a water-pot and a rosary of beads. (126)
In that very place, on the second path or the second line, there is a *kuṇḍikā* (a water-pot) and an *akṣa* (a rosary). || 125 || 126 ||
Māheśvarī is white in color, three-eyed, and holds a trident; O Dear One, she bears a skull, a deer, and an axe in her hands.
This deer. || 127 ||
Kaumārī is yellow in color and holds a spear and a javelin; she grants boons and shows the gesture of fearlessness—thus she should be meditated upon, O Goddess of the Asuras. 128.
A *śakti* is a weapon well-known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as *saintī*; a *tomara* is indeed known as *loḍa*, found in the training ground (*khalūrikā*). || 128 ||
Vaiṣṇavī is dark-complexioned, holding a conch, a discus, a mace,
and a lotus in her lotus-like hands, and she is adorned with divine ornaments.

The discus is known as Sudarśana and has a thousand spokes. The mace (gadā) is well-known in common parlance as *gudā*. The lotus (*abjaka*) is the *padma*; for in lexicons such as "or in the masculine:
*padma*, *nalina*, etc.," the phrase "or in the masculine" applies up to the end of the list including "lotuses and water-born flowers," thereby establishing its masculine gender. || 129 ||
Vārāhī has a dark complexion and is radiant with the face of a boar;
she holds a plow, a mace, a sword, and a shield in her arms. (130)

*Potrī* means a boar (*varāha*). According to Amara: "Varāha, sūkara, ghṛṣṭi, kola, potrī, kiri, and kiṭi" are synonyms for a boar. *Hala* means a plow (*lāṅgala*). *Kheṭaka* means a shield (*carma*). || 130 ||
Aindrī, however, has a dark-blue complexion and holds a thunderbolt and a blue lotus in her hands;
Indrāṇī is the one whose luster is like that of a dark-blue sapphire.
Cāmuṇḍā is black in color, and she likewise holds a trident and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
She holds a sword and a vetālaka with her right arms,
and she holds a serpent, a shield, and a bell with the others, as well as a skull-cup.
A *vetāla* is a specific deity who is the lord of *bhūtas* and *piśācas*. A *nāga* is a serpent or other similar beings. 131–132.
Mahālakṣmī, O Supreme Goddess, is yellow in luster and holds a lotus, a mirror, and a citron fruit. (133)
Padma refers to two lotuses; mātuluṅga is the citron (bījapūra). || 133 ||
Having meditated thus, one should then worship these goddesses and Tripurā, the Mistress of the Wheel;
she is remembered as the purifier of the hands due to the stainlessness of the organs of action.
The accomplishment arising from the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi) is established here as *aṇimā*.

These [powers] range from *aṇimā* up to the Great Lakṣmī (*mahālakṣmī*). She who is named Tripurā, the sovereign of the Wheel that Enchants the Three Worlds (*trailokyamohana-cakreśvarī*), and her corresponding Vidyā, bear the name "Purifier of the Hands" (*karaśuddhikarī*).

He explains [this] with the words "of the organs of action" (*karmendriyāṇām*). Since the two hands are specific forms of the organs of action, the word "hand" (*kara*) is indicative of the organs of action in general.
Their "purity" (*vaimalya*) consists in the washing away of the evil produced by them, and their "agency" (*kartṛtva*) [is the capacity for that].

The meaning is that the word functions by taking its basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) as that [specific state]. He states that each individual *siddhi* must be worshipped after being meditated upon as non-different from the respective Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*), saying "born of Karaśuddhi" and so forth. Furthermore, the author of the root text himself will later state that in the ninth wheel, Yonimudrā is to be worshipped.

It will be stated [later]. By that indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), the meaning to be described here is that, because of the word "and" (*ca*), the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā is also to be worshipped. || 134 ||
Now he speaks of the latent impression (vāsanā) of the second enclosure:
"The digits (kalās) consist of the wonder of the mass of sixteen pulsations. (135)
And because they consist of the act of breathing, they belong to the sixteen vital breaths beginning with prāṇa;
and because they are perceived as being of the nature of the vowels which serve as seeds, they take the form of seeds. || 136 ||
O Dear One, because they are internal and preeminent in the process of emanation, the Guptayoginīs—beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇī and Rūpā—are considered to be so situated. 137.
In the wheel named Sarvāśāpūraka, one should worship with the left [hand];
these [deities] hold nooses and goads, are red in color, and are clothed in red garments. (138)
The perfection consisting of the purification of the vital breath is the power of lightness (*laghimā*) for the experiencing self;
she, as Tripureśī and Mistress of the Wheel, is to be worshipped with all ritual offerings. (139)
The sixteen movements (*spanda*) are those things characterized by vibration:

the five vital breaths, such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and the eleven sense organs—thus making sixteen. Among these, movement consists solely of the motion of the wind (*vāyu*). In the case of the sense organs, it consists solely of their orientation toward their respective objects.

Vibration (*spandana*). All these are "vibrations" (*spanda*) because they are denoted by the term "prāṇa," as in the Śruti passage: "When the primary *prāṇa* departs, all the *prāṇas* depart after it. (p. 358) [This refers to] the first occurrence of the word *prāṇa*.

This is because the venerable commentator Śaṅkarācārya has explained the second occurrence of the word "prāṇa" as referring to the fivefold functions beginning with breath (prāṇa), and [the other] as referring to the eleven sense organs. Sapta...
This is because the movement [of the breath] has been specifically qualified, as determined in the second section (adhikaraṇa) of the Uttara-mīmāṃsā; furthermore,
the "wonder" (*camatkṛti*) consists precisely in the "conglomeration," that is, the unification, of these sixteen vital breaths (*prāṇas*),
which— being by nature in constant vibration— are difficult to achieve through immobilization in a single place.

Because they produce wonder (*camatkāra*). According to the etymology "the perfect milking is fulfillment" (*prapūraṇa*), wonder is precisely the state of fullness consisting in one-pointed absorption in one's own Self; [the mantras] are those which produce that, are non-different from it, or are composed of it (*tanmayī*). He explains this very point with the words "of breath, etc. (*prāṇādi*).

The sixteen vital breaths (*prāṇas*) consist of that which animates and sustains life; for their wandering toward other objects, by abandoning the state of being solely intent upon their own Self, is itself the nature of death. And it is said in the *Kramodaya*:
"Stability itself is the wonder, even without contact with sense objects. Thus [it is said].

The commentators of the earlier period, however, explain the first half [of the verse] as follows: the sixteen principles (*tattva*) consisting of the five gross elements, the ten sense organs, and the mind constitute the "collection" (*saṃdoha*), meaning an aggregate;
and the others are the ten vital airs (*vāyu*), namely *prāṇa* and so forth, as well as *nāga*, *kūrma*, and the rest.
They explain the second half of the verse, "Thus there are sixteen vital breaths," as follows: the six bases of support are to be sought in another scripture;

likewise, [the letters] are accompanied by *anusvāras* because they have become seeds (*bīja*), for without such accompaniment, syllables lack the nature of seeds. This is through the realization of their identity with such vowels.

Because they go toward the state of being the seed of creation (*sṛṣṭibīja*) in the form of seeds, and because they abide in a latent state as being more internal than the elements such as the skin, the digits (*kalā*) beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī are considered "Secret Yoginīs" (*guptayoginī*); one should worship them in the wheel that fulfills all desires (*sarvāśāpurakacakra*). Thus [it is said].

In the term *yoginī*, there is no requirement for a second case ending when it functions as the object of the verbal root "to consume" (*āhāra*) such as sound and so forth; however, the ancients maintain that the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative. One should worship these [energies] by moving to the left—starting from one's own front and proceeding counter-clockwise—because they have become the seeds of emanation and are thus dominated by the power of Vāmā.
The interpretation that this refers to the "left-hand path" (*vāmamārga*) is merely a display of dogmatism. He describes the meditation on these [deities] with the word "māśa":

regarding the sixteen [aspects] of the experiencing self (*bhoktṛ*), which consists of the aggregate characterized by the Śruti statement, "The wise call the self joined with the body, senses, and mind the experiencer."
The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are non-different from that purity; *laghimā* is the Siddhi Tripureśī.
By the word "and" (*ca*), it is meant that the *Sarvavidrāviṇī-mudrā* is also to be worshipped.
[Verses 135–139] He states the purification (*vāsanā*) for the third enclosure:

Abiding in the form of the eightfold *prakṛti* and situated within the eight groups beginning with the *ka*-group, Anaṅgakusumā and the others reside in the [mandala] that causes universal agitation. (140)
And because they are most intimate, these [goddesses] are considered to be more secret;
one should worship them as red in color, holding nooses, goads, bows, and arrows in their hands. (141)

[She is] endowed with the quality of the beauty of resting in the stages of the body and so forth, belonging to the sovereign enjoyer who is the self of the intellect assuming various forms as objects of enjoyment. 142.

The Sovereign Lady of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), who is the Supreme Goddess in the form of the purity of intellect and the perfection of greatness, is to be worshipped with all ritual offerings. || 143 ||
For in the Sāṃkhya system, twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are enumerated:

primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the great one (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the five gross elements (*bhūta*), the ten sense organs (*indriya*), the mind (*manas*), and the person (*puruṣa*). Among these, primordial nature is the first of them all.

The first [tattva] is the modification (vikāra) of nothing else. The seven beginning with the second, however, are modifications of their respective preceding principles and are the material causes (prakṛti) for their respective succeeding principles. The sixteen beginning with the ninth, however, are only modifications of what precedes them; they are not the material causes of anything. But the twenty-fifth is neither the modification of anything nor the material cause of anything.
And such is the actual state of things. This very point has been stated by the noble Kṛṣṇa in the *Sāṃkhyasaptati*:
"Root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification; the seven beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) are both nature and modification;
the group of sixteen is modification only; and the Person (*puruṣa*) is neither nature nor modification."
Among these, the first eight principles (tattvas) are understood here by the term "the group of eight prakṛtis" because they are of the nature of prakṛti; the rest is clear.
He states the *vāsanā* (meditative identification) for the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*) named Tripurasundarī: "That-that," etc.

The enjoyer of that which is to be enjoyed— consisting of the cognitions of forms such as jars and cloths— is for this very reason the Great Lord (*mahīśitā*), like a sovereign king. Within his four locations known as the *mūlādhāra*, *anāhata*, *ājñā*, and *sahasrāra*, there exists [a power] in each one individually.
Rest (*viśrānti*) is the attainment of innate bliss preceded by the cessation of the fatigue born from wandering on the difficult path of *saṃsāra*.
That itself is the quality called beauty (*saundarya*); she is endowed with it and is the bestower of it. And as it has been said:

"O Six-faced One, those who are liberated in the aggregate (piṇḍa), liberated in the word (pada), liberated in form (rūpa), and those who are liberated in that which transcends form (rūpātīta)—they are truly liberated; of this there is no doubt. Such is the purity of intellect known as *ṛtambharā* (truth-bearing) therein.

The meaning is that Prajñā—characterized by the apprehension of truth as stated in the Yoga Sūtras—is the Supreme Goddess named Tripurasundarī, the Mistress of the Cakra; she alone is the Mahimā-siddhi, and by the word "and" (ca), the Sarvākarṣiṇī-mudrā is also to be worshipped. || 140 || 141 ||
(p. 360) He describes the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the fourth enclosure:
