"For one whose consciousness has blossomed through the piercing of the twelve knots, preceded by the experience of Śakti due to the immersion in the state that culminates in emission (*visarga*). (144)

By means of the four phonemes, which consist of the expansion of the power of unfolding (unmeṣa-śakti) dominated by the power of will (icchā-śakti), and which likewise take the form of the union with Akula; || 145 ||

Even when mixed with the vowels beginning with *sa* (the nature of the heat of the object of knowledge) and conditioned by the will (*icchā*), they are endowed with two syllables whose form consists of the penetration of the power of the Kula. || 146 ||
O Maheśvarī, because they have issued forth as the very essence of power,
they have come down through the lineage of the tradition into the wheel that bestows good fortune.

In the Grammar Tantra (*vyākaraṇatantra*), this fourteen-syllable [sequence] is the *aṇ* pratyāhāra by means of the letter *pa*. That very same [sequence] is called the Bhūtalipi mantra in the Mantra Tantra.
And so is its extraction: [The sequence follows: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au.

"The five short vowels are the junction-letters [saṃdhivarṇa]: space, wind, fire, water, and earth. The analysis of the compound is "water (kaṃ) and earth (dharā). And the tradition holds that these letters, although appearing in the form of *vaikharī* speech, exist only in the form of *madhyamā*.
The fourteen deities situated in the fourteen-spoked wheel have emerged from the multitude of powers (*śakti*) who take pride in the phonemes of the *bhūtalipi* script; these phonemes,
in turn, arise from the *akula-liṅga* through the differentiation of the six wheels of the *kulakuṇḍalinī* located at the *mūlādhāra*.

Indeed, almost all [phonemes] arise during that very state of experiencing the nectar (amṛta) upon emerging from yoga. Among them, the letter *a* arises from the *akula-liṅga*; the letter *i* from the power of will (*icchā-śakti*);
the letter *u* from the power of its unfolding (*unmeṣa-śakti*); and [the letter *m*] from the Kuṇḍalinī, which is a mixture of will and unfolding.
The letters *ṛ* and *ḷ*. From the union of Akula with such Kuṇḍalinī, the letters *e* and *o* arise. From the further union of Akula with those two, the letters *ai* and *au* arise.
In this manner, the other phonemes are produced.
This should be reflected upon as described in works such as the *Parāpañcāśikā*, the *Saubhāgyasudhodaya*, and others.
This very point is stated [in the verse] with the words "twelve": for each wheel (*cakra*), there are two knots (*granthi*)—one below and one above.
By piercing these, there occurs the emission (*visarga*) of the Kundalinī consciousness, which shines upward.
The state of immersion (*āveśa*) that occurs during the phase of the "end of the sixteen"— that is, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) at the end of the sixteen vowels—
from which arises the experience of the Śākta Kaulikas, preceded by that [immersion], so that it may come to pass accordingly.

Likewise, because these deities have issued forth as an extraction— the very essence of the Śakti characterized by the fourteen arisen phonemes, which is the Kuṇḍalinī in the form of the aggregate of all powers— they are called the "Yoginīs of the Tradition" (saṃpradāyayoginī). Of such a meaning...

The construction is: "because it has come down through the sequence of oral tradition" (p. 361). He states those phonemes with the two verses beginning with *unmeṣa*. Of these words ending in the third-person plural, [the number] is fourteen.
The substantive must be supplied [in the compound]. Alternatively, the substantive is "those consisting of the letters *vedya*, *uṣman*, *rūpa*, and *sādi*.

That is, by those [letters] which possess an expansion (*prasara*) from the power of unfolding (*unmeṣa-śakti*), namely the letter *u*; [the suffix] *ac* is applied after *aśan* (according to Pāṇini 5.2.127). By those [letters] which possess the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) as their primary support, namely the letter *i*.
The "non-family" (akula) refers to that which arises from the union of the previously mentioned [vowels] and the two yet to be mentioned; this is the nature of the four groups of phonemes.
By the phrase "by those having that nature," it is implied by context that these function as qualifiers specifically for the diphthongs (saṃdhyakṣara).

But the predecessors— having explained it as "union with Akula" and considering it to be an adjective qualifying the four phonemes— also extract the letter *Ā* independently by means of the word "Akula. That is untenable, because [the word] is construed as an adjective.

Because independence is untenable; for if that were the case, it would contradict the statement "by the four," since you yourself have explained that term as "by the four. Regarding the letter *ra*, which is the nature of heat—that is, the nature of the sensation of warmth—belonging to the fire-cuṇḍalinī whose form is consciousness (*saṃvit*); [it is taught] by Śrīkaṇṭha in the section on the letter *ra*.
"Ūṣmā hṛdayam" [is taken] from the Nāndana-kośa. Regarding that *ūṣman*, "sādi" is an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Since there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*) in the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is no mandatory prior placement [of the adjective]. The meaning is: "accompanied by its own *ādi* (beginning), namely the letter *ya*. [The compound means: "by those [letters] in which there are vowels (*arṇa*) beginning with *sa* that have the form of the *ūṣman* to be known."

That is to say, by those [consonants] which possess the *repha* (the letter *r*) accompanied by *yakāra*. Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "by those phonemes (*arṇaiḥ*) whose own nature (*svarūpa*) is the form of the heat of the object of knowledge (*vedya-ūṣman*), and which are accompanied by the first [letter]. According to Pañcānana, however, the *ūṣmans* are of the nature of volition (*saṃkalpa*) belonging to the object of knowledge, which consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).
Among the letters *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, that which has *sa* as its initial is the letter *ha*;

furthermore, those two—*ya* and *ra*—have that (*ha*) as their initial. Since these two follow the letter *ha* among the letters of the five elements beginning with space (*vyoma*), the meaning is: "by means of the three letters *ha*, *ya*, and *ra*."

They have explained that there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a second word "ādi" (beginning). That is weak; for it is impossible for the word "sādi" (having a beginning), which is heard [in the text] together with the supplied word "ādi," to form a compound.
Even if a compound were formed, since the action would be connected only with the *anyapadārtha*—namely, the *yakāra* and *repha*—[the intended meaning would not be established].
Furthermore, because the letter *ha*, as a constituent element of the compound word *samasyamāna* and so forth, cannot obtain connection with the action;
and because the letters *ṛ* and *ḷ* are conceived by the speaker’s intention as having a mixed form, they are treated as such [by those who follow that view].
The term *kula* is also an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *akula*. The word *samāveśa* ends in the suffix *ghañ* and denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇe*).

The Kula-śakti and the two types of immersion (samāveśa) reside within its own nature, which consists of two phonemes—the pair of phonemes in the form of *a* and *ha*, and the pair of phonemes in the form of *va* and *la*. From these two pairs, [emerges] Akula-kuṇḍalinī in the form of the letter *a*; that is the locus of her immersion.

At the thousand-spoked [lotus] is the lunar disc consisting of nectar, in the form of the syllable *va*; Kulakuṇḍalinī is in the form of the syllable *ha*, and her place of immersion is the Mūlādhāra, the earthly mandala,
in the form of the syllable *la*.

"Thus, endowed with four"—this is the meaning. However, earlier authorities, accepting a *tatpuruṣa* compound for "the two absorptions of *kula* and *śakti*," extract only the two letters *va* and *la*.
That is not correct, because it would result in a deficiency due to the failure to obtain the letters *a* and *ha*.
Because it has been stated that the two [possibilities of] extraction mentioned by you are impossible. || 144 || 145 || 146 || 147 ||

O Goddess, by virtue of the power of the auspiciousness of their form, which consists of uninterrupted expansion, these [powers] are named according to their meaning and are like the power of atomization (aṇimā). || 148 ||
Preceded by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, these [mudrās] bestow the purification of the body, senses, and so forth;
and the power of mastery (īśitva-siddhi) is also attained in the three previously mentioned cities.
Tripuravāsinī is established through the distinctions of yoga and the other afflictions (kleśas);
O Goddess, one should worship all of these with every type of offering. 150.

Uninterrupted manifestation is knowledge that does not have difference as its object; that very form is *saubhāgya* (fortune), that itself is *bala* (power), and the yoga directed toward that is the "etymological power" (*avayava-śakti*).
Because of the existence of that [power], they reside in the wheel called *Saubhāgyadāyaka*, which is designated by a term that is both etymologically and conventionally established (*yogarūḍha*).

The deities beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and the others are mentioned; their visualization is stated as "Aṇimā" etc. This means they hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and carry the cintāmaṇi jewel. However, according to the *Bṛhattantra*, they hold a mirror and a noose in their left hands, and a drinking vessel and a goad in their right hands. They [reside] in the body and the sense organs.

The purification of the elements (dhātus) such as the skin and so forth is of that very nature; the accomplishment of mastery (īśitva-siddhi) is likewise. By the word "and" (ca), one should worship these: the Mudrā who brings all under control, the one named Tripuravāsinī, and the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśvarī). He explains the term *Tripuravāsinī* with the words "as previously stated. That which was stated here and there [is as follows]:

The yoga—that is, the connection—has as its object that which is known as the "triplet" (*tripuṭī*), consisting of the three cities (*puratraya*) in the form of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). And that [yoga] is established through the differentiation of the knower and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the measure of difference (*bhedamāna*) is included. By that, there is affliction (*kleśa*), namely, the affliction of dualistic cognition (*bhedajñāna*).

For it is established by such scriptural passages as, "He who perceives even a slight difference in this [identity] becomes subject to fear; indeed, fear arises from duality," that there is a great disparity regarding the capacity to produce fear. Some maintain that yoga itself is the primary affliction and the first suffering. By means of its distinction—that is, its destruction—one attains the state known as *vyutpanna*.
Therefore, it has been stated that the word *vāsinī* has the meaning of "cutting," as distinguished from the word *vāsī*, which denotes the instrument for carving wood. || 148 || 149 || 150 ||
He speaks of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the fifth veil:

"Of the eternal sounds residing within the nine apertures of the self, [he perceives] by means of the form of the great universal [sound], which consists of the nature of differentiated resonance. (151)
(363) By means of the ten syllables in the form of shadows, which represent both unstable and stable objects of cognition, the Yoginīs of Kula and Kaula bestow all accomplishments. 152.
White, with hands bestowing boons and fearlessness, and adorned with white ornaments;
they possess their names according to their literal meaning, due to their application in protecting [beings] from the conceiving of their own expansion. || 153 ||
She is the foremost bestower of all accomplishments within the wheel that grants all aims;
she is the Mistress of the Wheel because she is the cause of the prosperity of the three worlds. (154)
O Great Goddess, Tripurāśrī, who arises from the purification of the mantra, is declared to be the power of subjugation (vaśitvasiddhi); one should worship all of these. 155.

Now, starting from below and extending upward within the *suṣumṇā*, there are ten joints; in their midst are nine spaces, which are designated by the term "apertures" (*randhra*). Pervading those ten locations, [the breath] arises for as long as the body lasts.

The *nāda* that is heard through proficiency in the practice of following the resonance (*nādānusaṃdhāna*) is called the *madhyamā-vāk*. Although that single *nāda* is one, it is designated by various names according to its delimitation by different locations: the unmodified (*avikṛta*), the void (*śūnya*), the contact (*sparśa*), and the resonance (*nāda*).

(madhyamā) that accompanies all things— [the text continues] ...by means of that which possesses the form of such sound, namely the Great Universal (mahāsāmānya) which pervades the ten divisions
The meaning is that they are characterized by *dharma*. That is to say, they are of the nature of the middle state (*madhyamā*).

The objects of knowledge (*vedya*) are the five elements (*bhūta*); these are of two kinds according to the distinction between effect (*kārya*) and cause (*kāraṇa*). Among them, the effects are unstable because of their falsity (*mithyātva*); the causes are stable because of their reality (*sattvatva*).

For the Śruti declares: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the reality. And those effects—the gross elements such as space and so forth—and their causes—the five subtle elements such as sound and so forth—exist by means of the shadow-forms of these [subtle elements].
They are characterized by ten syllables consisting of the *ka*-group and the *ca*-group, which are of the nature of light. This very point has been stated in the *Cakrasaṃketapaddhati*:

"Because it has as its objective support the manifestation of the ten elements (*bhūta*) and subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the twelve-spoked wheel has a throbbing form consisting of the ten syllables beginning with Krodhīśa.
By this, the following explanation of the ancients [is refuted]: "The objects of the organs of action are unstable cognizable things."
Speech and so forth, as well as sound and the rest which are the objects of the sense organs and are stable and perceptible—

when there is the conjunction of both the *iṣṭa* group and the *tavarga* group, which consist of the reflections of those [objects], all phonemes possess the nature of stability; the meaning is that in the absence of that [conjunction], they are absent.

This is because it is clear to those who know the threefold method of the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* (p. 364). "Kula" is the triad (*tripuṭī*), and the "Kaulika" is the self whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Yoga is precisely the non-duality (*abheda*) of these two; [the goddesses] possess that [yoga]. Alternatively, "kula" refers to the senses, "kaulikas" to the objects, and "yoga" to the relationship of cause and effect.
Thus say the ancients. He states the meditation upon these [energies] with the words "white" (*śvetā*) and so forth.

One's own manifestation (*prathā*) is the expansion as the self of all. The contemplation (*manana*) of that—that is, its reflection through logical reasoning—is itself protection (*trāṇa*), because it consists of the fulfillment of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

Because the etymological name [of the wheel] is based on its connection with the form of being a giver of that [attainment], and because the power of its constituent parts exists, the ten deities beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā reside in the Sarvārthadāyaka-cakra. She states that the term *Tripurāśrī* is also etymologically appropriate (*anvartha*), as it denotes the cause of prosperity for the three worlds: ... [She says: "The term *Tripurāśrī* is also etymologically appropriate (*anvartha*), because it expresses the cause of the flourishing of the three worlds."
Regarding the phrase "of the three worlds": others maintain that the word *lokatraya* (three worlds) also refers specifically to the *tripuṭī* (the triad).
Regarding the attainment of mastery (*vaśitva*), he states the purification of the mantra: "purified by the mantra.
This means it is produced by the purification consisting of the aforementioned reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*).
This is an indicative illustration of the Unmādinī-mudrā. 151 || 152 || 153 || 154 || 155 ||
He states the latent impression (vāsanā) of the sixth enclosure:
"O Goddess, [the worlds] are manifested by the Kundalinī, who faces both upward and downward;
through the will of Kula, they consist of the expansion of the letters beginning with 'Ka' due to their externalization. (156)

In the wheel that bestows all protection and causes all penetration, the supreme [energies] are to be expressed as the forms of the entry into one's own essential nature within the nigarbha-yoni. 157.

These [deities], beginning with Sarvajñā, are established, holding in their hands books and rosaries; they are the nourishers of the ancient cities of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the objects of knowledge. 158.
She is known as Tripurāmālinī, the Mistress of the Wheel who deludes all;
she is the purification of the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) and has attained the perfection called prākāmya.
One should worship these deities in sequence with all ritual offerings.

These goddesses, beginning with Sarvajñā, have arisen during the state [of consciousness] produced by the downward and upward movement of Kuṇḍalinī. For this very reason, they are designated by the term *nigarbha*, because they reside most intensely (*nitarām*) within the womb (*garbhe*).
To the question, "How is it that those [powers] which have arisen in such a secret place have become manifest? he says:
"by the will of the Kula. By the will of the Kula—that is, by the desire to create the Tripuṭī—those powers emerged outwardly.
For this very reason, they became composed of the phonemes beginning with *va* and *kha*, and so forth. Here, the word "beginning with *ka*" (*kādi*) is used according to its literal sense.

The ancients maintain that [the term] "following the ten letters in the form of the *ka*-group and *ca*-group" refers to the ten letters beginning with *ka*. However, in order to avoid contradicting the *Cakrasaṃketa*, it is more appropriate to explain it as "following the ten letters beginning with *ma*," though this is a strained interpretation.
According to the *Tantrarāja*, "Kādi" refers to Kālī, while "Śakti" refers to Tā; thus, there are two powers by virtue of being the agents of these two views.
Let the word *kādi* here be understood as referring to *śakti* through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the accepted agency, or as referring to *Kālī*.

As for the word *śakti*, it has already been explained in the verse beginning with "the nine starting with *pra*" as being intended to include everything up to *ma*. [In that context: *ma* is Kālī; *ka* is afflicted time (*kleśita-kāla*), Mahākāla, Yama, and Ravi.
In the *Kośa*, the word *Kālī* consists of the letter *ma* alone, or the letter *ka* alone as a portion of the word *Kālyādi*;

this is like the letter *ka* in the word *prabhañjana* [which is derived from] a portion of the word *kāmakalā*. Furthermore, the letters beginning with *ṭa* are not mentioned in the *Cakrasaṃketa* within the *Mantrasra*; however, in the *Pūjāsaṃketa*, there is the extraction (*udghāta*) of the vowels (*aṇ*).
It must be stated how the mutual contradiction—that fourteen castes (*varṇas*) have been mentioned—is not avoided;
for since a resolution is impossible in that case, an option (*vikalpa*) alone would be logical.
However, when non-contradiction is possible, an option tainted by the eight defects is improper. One's own (*svam*) means innate (*nijam*).
Form (*rūpa*) is Brahman; its "possession" (*āveśa*) is its manifestation as unobstructed.
Just as the manifestation in the form "I am [the] element" (*bhūta*) is conventionally designated as "possession by the element" (*bhūtāveśa*), so too is this [state].
For this very reason, it is called the wheel named "The Performer of All Protection" (*sarvarakṣākara*).

This is because the meaning of the term *rakṣā* (protection) is precisely the removal of the veil concerning the state of being the self of all. As for the description [of the goddesses] as "those who have a book and a rosary in their hands," this refers to the visualization (*dhyāna*) of Sarvajñā and the others.
In the compound, the word *hasta* (hand) is placed first according to the rule *saptamī-viśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 2.2.35).

Although the word *mālinī* is derived from the verbal root *mal*, meaning "to wear" (*dhāraṇa*)—as in the term *tripuramālinī*—the word *mālinī* here has the sense of "nourishing" (*poṣaṇa*). With the intention that roots have multiple meanings, he explains it as *mā-viti*. Regarding the long vowel in the term *tripurā*, when there is a conflict between metrics and grammar, metrics [prevails].

This is according to the maxim *balīyas* ("the stronger [prevails]"). The "attainment of knowledge" (*vidyāpti*) consists of the specific purification of power (*śakti*) through its fifteenth state, which bestows the capacity for the manifestation of its own fruit. That very nature is the *prākāmya-siddhi* (the power of irresistible will). And the term *prākāmya* has been explained by the ancients as follows:

"Fluid, solid, hard, gross, subtle, light, heavy, manifest, and even more unmanifest—your sovereign power (*prākāmya*) resides in these manifestations. With the word "and" (*ca*), one should also worship the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā. (156) (157) (158) (159)
He states the latent impression (vāsanā) of the seventh enclosure:
"From the root of the knots that vibrate due to the cessation of the impact of the vital winds (vāyu). (160)

By means of the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), which is empty of internal consciousness within the heart, and in accordance with the sequence of the classes of consonants touched by the seed-syllables, vowels, and *kalās*. (161)
O Goddess, worshipped by heroes, you reside in the wheel that destroys all diseases and is radiant with the destruction of worldly existence, together with the secret Yoginīs. 162.
The Siddhayoginīs, beginning with Vaśinī, are red in color, sealed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and hold a book and a rosary. 163.
O Maheśvarī, one should worship Śuddhavidyāviśuddhi, Bhuktisiddhi,
Īśvarī, and Tripurāsiddhi with offerings of drops (bindu) and libations (tarpaṇa).
Through the restraint of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, there occurs a collision of one with the other;

this is well known from the statement in the *Gītā*: "They offer the *prāṇa* into the *apāna*, and likewise the *apāna* into the supreme *prāṇa*. By that [restraint], the two knots (*granthi*)—which have been throbbing and swollen due to their orientation toward their respective functions—are [resolved].

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "arisen from such a mūlādhāra-cakra which possesses two knots situated above and below. That whose consciousness—meaning knowledge—is within the heart; it is to be known by the mind alone, and not otherwise.

That is to say, it is perceivable by the external senses such as the eyes and so forth; for this very reason, the meaning is that it is extremely subtle, as if empty. Such is the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city);
indeed, there are five organs of action, and likewise the others [the five organs of perception].
The organs of cognition, the four beginning with the mind,
the five vital breaths starting with prāṇa, the elements beginning with ether, as well as desire, action, and darkness— these eight again merge [into their source].

In this verse, [the letters] are characterized by their own nature as being of the same class as the gross "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) enumerated therein. They are in the form of seeds (*bīja*), distinguished by the *bindu*, and consist of the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*. And those classes of consonants are touched by them.

The [letters] designated as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*— thus, following the sequence of the eight groups [of consonants] together with their bindus— are uttered immediately thereafter. Because of their subtlety,
they are denoted by the term "Secret Yoginīs" (*rahasya-yoginī*), namely Vaśinī and the others, within the wheel that removes the diseases consisting of transmigratory existence.
They are established [therein]. She is the Sovereign (Īśvarī), the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), capable of removing disease.

Śuddhavidyā is the cognition of the identity between "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and "this-ness" (idaṃtā); its purification consists in its dissolution into pure consciousness (cinmātra). By means of that [purification], she brought about the perfection of enjoyment (bhuktisiddhi), and by the word "and" (ca), the Khecarīmudrā as well.
One should worship. "Vīravandita" (worshipped by heroes) is either the locative case or a vocative. The rest is clear. || 160 ||
He states the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the eighth enclosure:

"O Goddess, consisting of the three powers, they are the expansions of the abode of consciousness (*ciddhāma*), auspicious, having the form of the *kalā* of the fire of universal destruction (*saṃvartāgni*), and supremely secret. (165)
O Sovereign of the Gods, the cause of the perfection whose nature is entirely full resides in the wheel known as Sarvasiddhimaya, which is adorned with weapons.
The four deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha), beginning with Kāmeśvarī, are stationed there;
their weapons as well are red in luster, with their tips blazing with their respective weapons.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, they should be worshipped as bestowers of fruits upon the meditator;
both yours and mine, they bring about the subjugation of men and women. (168)
O Goddess of the Suras, skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—these, joined with the second vowel, are your arrows. (169)
Tripurāmbikā is the mother of the ancient [deities] such as Vāma and the rest; O Maheśvarī, because her nature is supreme sovereignty, she is the accomplishment of will.
O fair-faced one, one should worship these with every ritual offering.

During the occasion of the contemplation on the triangle, those three powers which were described—Kāmeśvarī and the others—are the three deities who are essentially composed of them; for they are supreme precisely because they are the expansion of the rays of consciousness.
These are supreme and of an extremely secret nature; they should be meditated upon as equal to the flames of the fire occurring at the time of *saṃvarta*, the dissolution (*pralaya*) of a *kalpa*.
By the repetition "full, full," extreme fullness is expressed. Such [is it].
Success (*siddhi*) is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); with respect to that, the three [powers] combined are the cause.

For this very reason, the *cakra* which is its support is designated as "the bestower of all success" (*sarvasiddhiprada*). Dispelling the suspicion that the weapons constitute a separate internal enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), he says: "The weapons," and "the seat" (*pīṭha*).
The meaning is that they are the presiding deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) such as Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, and Jālandhara.

To suggest that the mention of "eight wheels" in the Śruti passage, "having eight wheels and nine gates," intends the inclusion of the Bindu-cakra within the Trikoṇa-cakra itself, [the author] has stated that there are eight wheels.

It has been stated that there are four [consorts] together with the principal deity; however, the ancients maintain that their purpose is indeed threefold. Alternatively, the word "four" may be construed with the phrase "also the weapons.
Thus, the four weapon-śaktis also hold their respective weapons over their heads with both hands.

They are situated. From the word *āyudha* (weapon), by the rule "from words denoting an instrument [of action], the suffix *a* is added in the sense of habitual practice," the suffix *a* is applied; from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. However, the ancients maintain that this word *andhasaḥ* is masculine. In reality, however, it is also [found] in the eighth enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).

It is stated that "the four deities of the seats" (pīṭhadevatāḥ) are to be worshipped in order to indicate that the presiding principal deity of the Oḍḍiyāna seat must also be worshipped. Accordingly, the Kalpasūtra states: "In the triangle [are] Vāk, Kāmā, Śakti, and Samastapūrvā."

(368) Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Mahādevī reside in the *bindu*; the fourth [of these] is for the non-differentiation of these three with the Root Goddess (*mūladevī*). The worship of Kāmeśvarī and the others as the fourth [member] is the ninth [goddess] among the sixteen *Nityās*, the Yoginī-cakra goddesses, who resides in the *bindu*-cakra.

Thus, there is only one [deity], and there is no distinction of mantra-deities therein; rather, it is the special worship of that very Mahādevī which is repeated in four locations. Your [mantras] effect the subjugation of men, while my [mantras] effect the subjugation of women. It is precisely because the word "woman" (*strī*) was not used previously that [this distinction arises].

This is a suffix forming a compound. She extracts the seed-syllables of the Goddess and the Bāṇa [mantras] as follows—beginning with *tvak*. *Tvak* (skin) is the letter *ya*. This is because the lexicon states:
"Under the heading of *ya*, *tvak* is Vālī, the pervasive wind (*vyāpaka-vāyu*). *Asṛk* (blood) is the letter *ra*. This is because the lexicon states:
"*Ra* is blood; *ra* is the wrathful one. *Māṃsa* (flesh) is the letter *la*. Under that same heading, it says: "The wielder of the Pināka bow (*pinākī*)."
"Meat" is designated by the letter *m*, according to the lexicon (*kośa*). "Fat" is the letter *v*; for the lexicon states: "Fat is *va*, Varuṇa, and subtle.

Regarding bone and marrow, the final letter among the vowels is the fifth consonant *sa*, which has the color of semen; this is the meaning. Within the sections governing *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*, the boy named Saumya is the bone, and Suśrī is the heat (*ūṣman*).
According to the lexicons, "bull" (*vṛṣa*) refers to marrow, while Bhṛgu is the second vowel, *śukra* (semen).

In the mantra of Tripurācakreśvarī, it is the second syllable; in the sequence of the Mātṛkā, the remainder is that it is conjoined with the *bindu*. As for the extraction of the seed-syllables of the other weapons, that is treated in the fourth chapter itself.
The three cities were destroyed by you two, with Vāmā as the eldest and Raudrī [as the youngest]; that Ambikā is Cakreśvarī.
Absolute sovereignty is indeed the perfection of will. By the word "but" (tu), the seed-syllable and the mudrā are also included. || 165 || 166 ||
He speaks of the latent impression (vāsanā) of the ninth enclosure:
"O Goddess, in that which consists of universal bliss, which is the supreme Brahman, the ultimate. (171)
And Mahātripurasundarī, whose nature is consciousness, is to be worshipped according to one's own conduct; she is equal in both the "I-ness" and the "this-ness."

The Goddess, whose form is the great *kāmakalā*, who bestows the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), the vidyās, and so forth, consists of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*); she, whose nature is fifteenfold, is to be worshipped. (173)
The ninth [deity], Bhairavī, is the supreme eternal one (nityā) consisting of those respective lunar days;
however, the mudrās for each cakra are impelled by the *Cakrasaṃketa*.

The Bindu-cakra, named Sarvānandamaya, is indeed the very form of the Supreme Brahman. Within it, that Yoginī of the supreme and non-supreme secret is also of the nature of pure consciousness; however, she is not of the nature of knowledge consisting of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), but rather is that which pervades all mental modifications.

Intending to suggest that the witness (sākṣin) is the substrate for the occurrence of a mental modification (vṛtti), as well as for the prior non-existence and the destruction of that modification— and that it is experienced at the junction between two modifications—
he says, "I-ness" (ahantā). The modification whose object is the knower is "I-ness."
The state of "this-ness" (*idaṃtā*), however, pertains to the object of knowledge.
As stated by Paraśiva: "That which is the knowledge of 'I', that which is the knowledge of 'this', and even the knowledge of those two—know that [knowledge] to be my very body."

The meaning is: by means of one's own conduct (*svarācāra*), which is free from the restrictive constraints prescribed in the ritual manuals (*karmakāṇḍa*), and by means of the experience of the great sovereignty (*mahāsvātantrya*) established in Paraśiva. That there is "no counting of anyone" is according to the *Kalpasūtra*. Furthermore, its nature as the Great Kāmakalā has been explained previously.
The attainment of the *siddhis* of the *pīṭhas*, *vidyās*, and so forth is "attainment-siddhi" (*prāptisiddhi*),

because it consists in the acquisition of the nature of the presiding deities such as Kāmeśvarī, the *vidyās* such as Vāgbhava, and the mastery over sacred seats (*pīṭha*) such as Kāmarūpa. The great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is the *yonimudrā*.

In the *Kulārṇava*, within the section on the *Parā-prāsāda*, there is the statement: "The *vanamālā*, the *namomudrā*, and the *mahāmudrā* [are formed] in due order. Here, the term *mahāmudrā* refers to the gesture of the joined palms (*añjali*) with the thumbs drawn inward and pressed together.

For even in the commentaries by the traditionalists, it has been explained by the ancients as being the *yonimudrā*. It consists of fifteen parts, either consisting of fifteen syllables or taking the form of the *tithinityās* beginning with Kāmeśvarī. It is born and it grows.

Or, it consists of the five future periods (*daśā*) beginning with this one; its non-mention is due to the fact that the period of existence (*asti-daśā*) is inherent. It consists of the various lunar days (*tithi*), having the nature of the lunar days starting from the first (*pratipad*). It is eternal (*nityā*), consisting of the *kalās* known as *sādā*. By the division [of the word] as "anavamī," she is the most excellent of all; as "navamī," [she is the ninth].

Among the nine sovereigns of the wheels (*cakreśvarīs*), she is the last; Bhairavī is the most terrifying of all, according to the Vedic scripture: "From fear of her the wind blows," and so forth. She is *parā*, transcending the triad beginning with *paśyantī*. She is to be worshipped—this is the syntactical connection. Within the nine wheels...

The meaning is that the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of the goddesses of the *mudrās*, who have been described as worthy of worship, are explained precisely in the *Cakrasaṃketa*. || 171 || 172 || 173 || 174 ||
The wise practitioner should worship Nityaklinnā and the others within a square or a triangle, according to the requirements of the rites for desired results. 175.
The third lunar day (*tithi*) is the *Nityā* Nityaklinnā. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), Meruṇḍā and the others are included.

From the spokes of the wheel come Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Vajreśvarī, because they alone are specified in the section concerning worship within the triangle. And thus, that worship of the *Tithinityās* which was previously mentioned [is to be performed there].

The repetition here of that [term] is for the purpose of indicating that, just as there is an occasion following the initial worship of the principal deity, so too is the time following the second round of worship optional;
however, it is not repeated twice because, unlike in passages such as "again, and indeed the purification of the hands" (*karaśuddhiṃ punar caiva*), the word "again" (*punar*) and others are absent.

(p. 370) Since the worship of the eternal [mantras] is exhausted by the purpose of indicating the two-fold sequence through their respective double recitation, there is no division of the ritual action (*karmabheda*), because there is no repetition (*abhyāsa*) in the form of a further hearing that has no other purpose. However, the ancients [hold this view] regarding Kāmeśvarī and Bhagamālinī.

Some say that because [the first three] have already been worshipped, this is a separate worship specifically for the remaining thirteen Nityās. That is not correct; for since Vajreśvarī has also already been worshipped, it would follow that there is worship of only twelve [remaining deities]. This is so even though the triad beginning with Kāmeśvarī shares a single name.
Furthermore, because a difference in the deity necessarily follows from a difference in the mantra;

for even though the Mistress of the Third Wheel bears the name Tripurasundarī, the established doctrine (siddhānta) maintains that there is indeed a distinction between her and the Root Deity due to the dissimilarity of their mantras. For this very reason, it is stated in the Kalpasūtra:

It has been stated that the special worship (*viśeṣārcana*) of that Great Goddess (*Mahādevī*) is performed in four locations, and not in five. Nor should it be asked: "Even though a difference in mantras is observed for Kāmeśvarī and the others—who constitute the *tithinityās*—due to differences in the tantras, how is it that there is no [difference in their nature]?"

This is because the distinction between deities necessarily entails a distinction between the mantras; for those two mantras are subject to option (vikalpa) according to the principle of different Vedic branches (śākhāntara-nyāya). By this, even the difference in visualization (dhyāna-bheda) for the triad beginning with Kāmeśvarī—derived from the Tithinityās—is also logically consistent. As for the phrase "in accordance with the rites for specific desires" (kāmya-karma-anusārataḥ), that has already been explained previously.
This has been explained. As for the followers of the *Pañca*, they explain that passage as referring to obligatory rites (*nityakarman*);
however, they explain this present passage as being for the sake of desires such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth, through meditation on the flowers and other [substances]. In that regard:
Only they know the discrepancy:
that within the intermediate space of the square, in the path between the two lines of the square, there is a group of eight beginning with *sāṇi*, each measuring one *mātrā*.
This is stated in the first chapter (*paṭala*) regarding the performance of worship, and in the final chapter (*paṭala*) regarding the section on the underlying intention (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, since the position of two lines alone has been adopted, the absence of any other path renders the lack of a decisive criterion (vinigamanāviraha) impossible to suspect;
this applies equally to the positions of one line and three lines in the same context.
According to the established principle, since the determination of the intermediate space is possible in a sacrifice with a single *puroḍāśa* as well as in one with multiple *puroḍāśas*,
the ancient commentators explained the term "intermediate space" (*antarāla*) as referring to the area between the earth-chamber (*bhūgṛha*) and the sixteen-spoked wheel (*ṣoḍaśāra*).
That is weak, because the sixteen-spoked wheel has not been mentioned. In reality, however,
on the ground occupied for the purpose of drawing the wheel,
after having drawn everything from the *bindu* up to the three circles (*vṛtta*) on all sides—
A portion of ground measuring slightly less or more than eleven finger-breadths remains;

in the view that this consists of a single-lined square enclosure (*bhūpura*), that line should be drawn on the inner edge of the enclosed ground. Otherwise, there would result the futility of enclosing such an area.

Consequently, in the case of multiple lines, those lines are produced as being within those respective intervals and not outside them. For this very reason, the conventional usage of "first," "second," and so forth in the arrangement of a wheel (cakranyāsa) is consistent only with a sequence beginning from the boundary line and moving inward.
And thus, in the present context, by the term "interval" (antarāla)—

It should be understood that because the inner portion of the first line is apprehended due to its being the first to present itself, the interpretation of the ancient masters— intending the earth-house to consist of a single line— is indeed correct. || 175 ||
Having propitiated the deities with incense that destroys all obstacles, and having thus performed the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*), one should offer the family lamp (*kuladīpa*). (176)

O Dear One, having offered a handful of flowers that shines with its own self-luminous radiance both internally and externally, one should then perform the recitation (japa) with a concentrated mind. 177.

The first quarter of the seventy-sixth verse contains disordered syllables; there, *ali* is the first [syllable]. The rest is clear. Having taken the cause for purification, the meaning is that one should perform the libation (*tarpayet*) according to the method stated by us in the first chapter. [Regarding] the word "fragrance" (*gandha*) here—

Because it ends in a plural suffix, it refers to specific substances. And since that [substance] functions as the instrument in the metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), it is indicated with the instrumental case-ending. And because that very metaphorical usage of being the instrument is presented through a conventionalized indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), there is an injunction for the excellence of those [substances] and so forth. This being the case, however, [the following objection does not apply].
It should not be argued that the rule regarding the preliminary sequence of rites— stating that "one should worship with offerings such as *naivedya*"—

renders the term ending with *naivedya* redundant, because it would have been more appropriate simply to say "with [offerings] up to the palm-leaf fan (*tālavṛtta*)," for [the term is used] precisely to avoid such redundancy.

Because it is conceived that the offerings of incense and so forth are presented twice— once before and once after the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa)— according to the division into "self" and "other"; for this very reason, it is recorded in the *Jñānārṇava* as occurring prior to the enclosures:
"Having worshipped the Supreme Deity with the sixteen services (upacāras). Thus it is stated.
Furthermore, even after the description of the enclosures (āvaraṇa), it is remembered again:
"Having fully honored [the deity] with services such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata). Thus it is said.

The phrase "with incense" (*dhūpaiḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating, as before, the combined excellence of the offerings beginning with incense. Therefore, the meaning is that after the subsequent enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), one may again present either the offerings beginning with fragrance (*gandha*) or those beginning with incense (*dhūpa*). Accordingly, the *Kalpasūtra* states at the end of the enclosure:

Having offered incense, lamps, mudrās, libations, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth as before— here, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes items such as betel-leaf that are outside the sixty-four [standard offerings]—
he prescribes the subsequent limb of the rite, while implying that this much alone constitutes what is designated by the term "worship of the circle" (*cakrapūjā*):
Regarding "the wheel" (*cakra*): the *kuladīpa* (family-lamp) is a lamp whose essence consists of the ignited *kuladravya* (substance of the family).

This is because the independence [of the lamp]—understood from the compound as having *kuladravya* alone as its instrument—is well-established both in the Veda, as in the case of "the *rathantara*-sāman," and in common worldly usage, as in the expression "water-drinking. Its latent impression (*vāsanā*)...
He prescribes [the ritual] with the words "inside and outside. Thus, there is a mark in the mantra:
"O you of immeasurable splendor, having unified the inner light and the outer light, one should offer the lamp in three ways."

By the phrase "thus" (*ittham*), the completion of the section on the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*) is indicated; this implies that since recitation (*japa*) is not mentioned within that specific section, the connection expressed by the words "then, having made a handful of flowers" (*puṣpāñjaliṃ tataḥ kṛtvā*) is merely for the purpose of indicating time (*kālārtha*), and does not constitute a relationship of primary and subordinate member (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*). This is what is being suggested.
It is also indicated that *japa* (recitation) is the primary element. For this very reason, the connection with the fruit is also recorded in the Smṛti at the conclusion of the procedure for *japa*:
"O Pārvatī, for one who contemplates in this manner at the time of *japa*..."
"All accomplishments (siddhis) are swiftly attained through your grace.
As for the fact that immediately thereafter there is again a reference to the ancillaries of worship (*pūjāṅga*) but not to the recitation (*japa*),
its sole purpose is to indicate that [the recitation] also possesses the status of being an ancillary by virtue of falling within the "sandwich" (*saṃdaṃśa*) [of those references].

Therefore, the established meaning is that even though recitation (*japa*) is independent when there is no worship, it becomes a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of worship when worship is being performed. Consequently, by the logic stated in the *Śāṇḍilya-sūtra*— that "the external and internal [elements] both [apply], like the *Aveṣṭi* and the *Sava" [sacrifices]— [this applies] to the recitation.
It is established that the application is twofold. || 176 || 177 ||
The threefold nature of recitation (*japa*), distinguished by types such as the audible (*nigada*) and others, has been established in the fifth chapter.

Since it was demonstrated in that very place that among these, mental recitation (*mānasa*) alone is superior to the audible (*nigada*) and whispered (*upāṃśu*) forms, he now teaches its specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in detail:
O Great Goddess, in the three peaks and also in the triad of Kuṇḍalinīs, there is a conjunction of each preceding set of cakras in the form of sound (nāda). || 178 ||

Within them are the vital breath (prāṇa), fire (agni), the syllable of illusion (māyārṇa), the digit (kalā), the point (bindu), the half-moon (ardhacandra), the obstructress (rodhinī), the sound (nāda), the end of sound (nādānta), and the power (śakti) accompanied by the pervasive one (vyāpikā). 179.
O Dear One, *samanā* and *unmanā* are situated at the *dvādaśānta*;
then, once again, they reside in the central channel in the form of the *mūlakuṇḍalinī*.
O Maheśvarī, when the universe is oriented toward emanation and remains in a state of stability,
there is only the successive joining [of elements] in the form of sound (nāda).
O Goddess, in the third [center] which has a variegated form, there is the twelfth digit (kalā). Among the nine— namely,
the first thousand-spoked [lotus], the one called Viṣu, Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna,
Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, the tip of the uvula, and the space between the eyebrows— [this resides].

It has been established in the *Cakrasaṃketapaṭala*, during the exposition of the visualization of all [deities], that the nine wheels— beginning with the Trailokyamohana and ending with the Sarvānanda— reside sequentially in their respective locations. Among these, three wheels constitute each individual *kūṭa* (syllabic peak) in this manner.

Due to the non-difference between the nine wheels and the three peaks (kūṭas), each respective peak should be visualized in its corresponding location. Consequently, starting from the base of the wheel of Akula up to the top of the foundation (ādhāra), one should visualize the five letters beginning with *ka* in successive upward order.

One should visualize [the seat] as consisting of a square, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and an eight-petaled lotus, undivided according to their respective portions, and having the color of fire with a drop (bindu).
Indeed, one should contemplate the non-duality between the Vahnikuṇḍalinī who resides at its tip and the Kāmakalā that is the final part of the Hṛllekhā within the Vāgbhava syllable.
Because these two fall into a single location, one should contemplate this group of nine subtle syllables— consisting of the *bindu*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and so forth—

as non-different from the *nāda* that constitutes the body of the six syllables contained within the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa*, since they are of the nature of pure *nāda* alone. The syllables of the *Kāmarāja*.
Starting from the root of the Svādhiṣṭhāna and extending upward to the tip of the Anāhata,
there are fourteen spokes; these are divided according to their respective portions by outer ten-spoked and inner ten-spoked wheels,
and they consist of groups of letters equal to the sun, empowered by the sound (nāda) and the fiery syllables of the first peak (kūṭa).

These are to be meditated upon. For one should contemplate the non-difference between the solar *kuṇḍalinī* which resides at the tip of the heart and the *kāmakalā*—consisting of the *hrīṃ* syllable and the *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja—because these two are situated in the same location. As for its ninefold [emanation] beginning with the *bindu*:

As before, it should be contemplated as non-different from the *nāda* that constitutes the body of the subsequent peak (*kūṭa*). Then, the four syllables of the power-peak (*śaktikūṭa*) are of a color equal to the moon,
yet they are more intensely variegated by the two— the solar and fiery colors and the *nāda*— belonging to the preceding and further preceding peaks.

Beginning from the root of purity up to the end of the middle of the eyebrows, one should contemplate [the cakras] as undivided according to their respective portions by means of eight-cornered, three-cornered, and bindu-cakras positioned higher and higher. For at the tip of the Ājñā [cakra], the Soma-kuṇḍalinī resides.

And because that Śaktikūṭīya [syllable] and the Kāmakalā residing within the Hṛllekhā fall into a single location, one should contemplate their non-difference; however, the ninefold group beginning with the Bindu belonging to this [Kāmakalā] is to be considered separately.

The collective meaning is as follows: beginning from the region of the middle of the forehead, one should contemplate in a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*) across nine successive locations, according to the method described for the contemplation of the "entire" (*sakala*) and "partless" (*niṣkala*). This applies to the first and second *kūṭas*, which consist of the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and maintenance (*sthiti*).

In this regard, the secret is that the negation (*apahnava*) of the group of nine beginning with *bindu*—which consists of successive stages of withdrawal—is clearly manifested therein as the nature of withdrawal belonging to the third peak (*kūṭa*). As for the literal meaning: it refers to the three peaks (*kūṭa*), namely the three seed-syllables beginning with *vāgbhava*; or to the triad of *kuṇḍalīs*, specifically in their respective final vowels (*ekāra*).

Regarding the section on the vowel *ī*, [it is stated] that Vaiṣṇavī and Baindavī are "crooked" (*jihmā*), according to the lexicon; for here the word *jihmā* serves as an indicator for the synonym of Kuṇḍalinī.
However, others maintain that the term *kuṇḍalī* refers specifically to the half-digit (*kalā*) contained within each respective *ī*.

Of the wheels, beginning with the Trailokyamohana and so forth, [the reference is] to those preceding ones; the ellipsis is "of those whose names are creation, maintenance, and dissolution. Their conjunction in the form of sound (*nāda*) means their identity with the respective sounds of the *kūṭas*, as pertaining to the three wheels. This refers to the initial triad of wheels.
The meaning [of the passage] beginning with "that which is called the *sṛṣṭicakra* is non-different from the *nāda* connected to the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*" (p.

374) is as follows: the word *cakra* itself, through repetition (*āvṛtti*), denotes the *kuṇḍalinī* residing in the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, and the *ājñā*. By means of the *kapiñjala-nyāya* (the maxim of the partridge), the number three is obtained due to the plural form.
And that these Kuṇḍalinīs reside precisely in the Ādhāra and other locations is stated in the Svacchandatantra:
"In that regard, the Ādhāra, the heart, and the location of the Bindu are proclaimed.
Regarding this, the ancient masters themselves have explained that the term "location of the Bindu" refers to the space between the eyebrows.

This has been explained. Although it would have been more appropriate to explain it here in the same way—as referring to the middle of the forehead—since in the section on the deposition of the *grahas*, those very [authorities] explained the word "bindu-sthāna" in the verse beginning with "sudhā-saktim" as meaning the middle of the forehead; on the contrary, [the middle of the forehead...]
Thus, when the *somakuṇḍalinī* is accepted, because the final *parārdha-kalā* of the third *kūṭa* is also to be contemplated in that very place according to that system,
there is a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which is conducive to the contemplation of non-duality. Nevertheless...
In that system, because the final *kalā* of the first and second *kūṭas*,

which fall within the *svādhiṣṭhāna* and *viśuddhi* [cakras] respectively, necessarily possess a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) with the two *kuṇḍalīs* located at the *ādhāra* and the heart, [this occurs] in one respect.

Their intention is that even the attainment of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not the determining factor. Consequently, the syntactic connection is: "the joining of the wheels, which are the *kuṇḍalinīs*, within the triad of *kuṇḍalinīs*.
By the single word "in the triad of *kuṇḍalinīs*" (*kuṇḍalītritaye*), both the digits of the heart (*hārdhakalā*) and the *kuṇḍalinīs* are [referred to].

The ancients maintain that through *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness), one attains the realization of non-duality. Nor should it be argued that, according to the statement— "The form of the lamp (*dīpa*) is half a mora and is desired as a circle on the forehead"—
the forehead alone is the proper location for the *bindu*, for [this is not the case].

Because the space between the eyebrows is the location of the *binducakra* according to the method previously described—and because, for the Śākta school, a *bindu* is desired at the midpoint of the eyebrows both by the application of red sandalwood paste and by the rule for the *tilaka*—that [point] is also a location of the *bindu*.
Among the *kūṭas* within those [locations], the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the letter *ha*. In the section on the letter *ha*, it is said: "The thunderbolt (*kulīśa*) is night."

From the *Kośa*: "Prāṇa" refers to the letter *ra*. "The digit of the syllable of Māyā" refers to the letter *ī* residing in the syllable *hṛllekhā*. "The fourth digit, Bheruṇḍā," according to the *Kośa*, refers to the letter *ī* in the section on *ī*. By the very term "syllable of Māyā," the letter *ī* is meant; however, the ancients maintain that this [digit] itself is the "digit. [This applies] to the nine [deities] beginning with Bindu and ending with Unmanā.

Their essential natures have been explained in the *Cakrasaṃketa* itself. "And Unmanā" — the word "exist" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Among these, from Prāṇa up to Unmanā, they are described as being situated at the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), by virtue of their location in the upper portion above the center of the forehead. [This refers to] the group of nine beginning with Bindu.
...until, at the point when the universe was about to be created,

they were situated above the final vowel of the *vāgbhava* mantra— which is non-different from the *kuṇḍalinī* residing in the *mūlādhāra*— in the form of the *mūlakuṇḍalinī*, at the forefront of the three wheels consisting of the earth-wheel (*bhūgṛha*) and the others within the wheel of creation.

Furthermore, within the form of the stability of the universe (p. 375), in the middle [state] consisting of the wheel of stability (*sthiticakra*), at the end of the triad of wheels beginning with the wheel of emanation (*srṣṭicakra*),
and above the final vowel of the middle peak-syllable (*madhyamakūṭa*) which is non-different from the middle *sūryakuṇḍalinī*.

It is the sequential conjunction and non-differentiation of the previously heard [syllables] with the subsequent second and third *kūṭas*, without merely contemplating their respective forms and so forth;
this occurs in the third *kūṭa*, which is variegated in form through the blending of the colors of fire, sun, and moon, and whose nature is thus painted.
The group of nine ending with *unmanī* and *manonmanī*, along with *dvādaśīkalā*—this is the remainder [of the list].
Thus, the connection is with the word ending in the present participle (*śatṛpratyaya*) located in the following verse: "contemplating these three actions.
As for the earlier commentators, they split the term *dvādaśānta* as *dvādaśa-anta* (ending with twelve), meaning the twelve beginning with the letter *ha*.
Some explain that [the letters] stand at the end in reverse order; however, that is not correct.

Because, by the presence of other words denoting only the nine [letters] beginning with *bindu*, and because there results a successive conjunction of all twelve in the form of *nāda*, the conclusion is reached in the recitation (*japa*) of the *turīyakūṭa* alone.
It might be so; however, that is not even desired by you. 178 || 179 || 180 || 181 ||
O Queen of the Gods, there is again the group of six voids and the five states. || 182 ||
Meditating with the mind upon the seven forms of the equinox (*viṣuvat*), one should recite the mantra.
There are six voids (*śūnya*) obtained through the oral tradition: five voids resembling the eye-spots on a peacock’s tail feathers, and one formless void.

There are five states known as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turya), and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta). There are seven equinoxes (viṣuvant) whose characteristics will be described hereafter: breath, mantra, channel, the tranquil state, power, time, and principle. By the word "and" (ca), the nine wheels previously mentioned are included, along with the mind.
While meditating, one should recite [the mantra] simultaneously with that contemplation; the meaning is that one should mentally visualize the syllables according to the method described. || 182 ||
He explains the eighteen [principles] beginning with Śūnya in sequence:
"O fair-faced one, having set aside three by three within the twelve [locations] ending with Agni. (183)
O Dear One, one should understand that there are three voids, each separated by a single interval;
beyond the third void, in the supreme place, one should contemplate the Great Void (mahāśūnya).
Beginning with the letter *ha* situated in the third *hṛllekhā* and ending with *unmanī*, there are thirteen positions, including the *mahābindu*.
Among these, the six letters located in the six positions—namely *ha*, *ī*, *ardhacandra*, *śakti*, *mahābindu*, and that which is above it—are as follows: [the six letters].
"One should contemplate them as empty"— this is the collective meaning obtained from the natural force of the syllables. For instance,

having referred back to the previously mentioned locations beginning with the letter *ha* by means of the term "following," one proceeds through the odd positions starting from *ha* by means of the phrase "separated by one."
The procedure for the great void (*mahāśūnya*) position in the abandonment of the equal positions is as follows:

(p. 376) By this rule, even when that [void] is obtained in the seventh and other odd positions, there is an exception to it by means of the phrase "fire and so forth" (*agnyādi*). Fire is the letter *ra*. Counting from that, the twelfth [position]—

The Great Bindu (*mahābindu*). One should understand that among these locations, by setting aside three in each, one is void (*śūnya*). The meaning is that one should know there are three voids within the Half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the Power (*śakti*), and the Great Bindu.
Through the discernment of what is attained and what is not attained according to this rule, [the void] belongs to the Power alone (or the Great Bindu alone).

The conclusion is as follows: either the rule of alternating by one [syllable] itself results in the letters *ha* and *i*, or it results in the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*) which is formless, located beyond the three voids and even above the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*). In reality, however, in this view—

An objection arises: "Since it has been stated that [the channels] end at the eighth from Rodhinī and so on, why was it not said that one should know there to be two voids (*śūnya*)? Therefore, this must be explained otherwise. The three voids are as before; furthermore, the phrase "separated by one each" refers only to the spatial location starting from the positions of Fire and the others, and not otherwise.

Because there is no evidence for its persistence beyond that point. Precisely by virtue of the separate mention of the sixth, the Great Void (mahāśūnya), the injunction must refer only to the two voids.
However, if the reading "ekaikāntaritaṃ dvayam" (the two separated by one each) is encountered, then even that dispute does not arise. And therefore:

In the locations of the letter *ra*, the nasal bindu (*n*), the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the power (*śakti*), the great bindu (*mahābindu*), and that which stands above it, there are six voids (*śūnya*). Alternatively, as stated later in the passage beginning "fire, *māyā*, time, consciousness, and the downward moon," the place of time (*kāla*) is situated between the fourth vowel (*ī*) and the bindu.
It shall be counted separately; thus, the twelfth is indeed Unmanā. In this view, it is logically consistent that the Great Void (mahāśūnya) resides precisely within the Great Bindu (mahābindu).
Therefore, it is established that there are six voids (śūnya) in the [six stages of]: Repha, Kāla, Bindu, Nāda, Antamanā, and Mahābindu.

The predecessors, however, maintain: starting from the letter *ra* up to the *dvādaśānta*, one should understand the three [levels] as *repha*, *bindu*, and *rodhinī*; and again, after skipping three more—namely *na*, *da*, and *anta*—one should know the six [levels] as *vyāpikā* and *unmanā*. Thus, having set aside the three voids (*śūnya*), one should know the six voids (*śūnya-ṣaṭka*). And that [sixfold sequence] consists of two pairs, each separated by one [level] and each consisting of single units.
The meaning is that it stands between each pair [of letters]. By this, there is one *eph* between the letter *ha* and the vowel *i*;

in its place is one void (*śūnya*), and so on, such that there are six voids in the six positions beginning with the letter *ra* and the bindu. From the three voids, the final [void] is in the middle of the group of six voids.
In the station of *unmanā*, one should meditate upon the sixth [state], the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), which is of the nature of space.
By implication, this means that the others are equal to the moon. As it has been stated by the venerable masters of the *Vijñānabhairava*:
For one meditating on the fivefold emptiness within the mandalas of variegated forms like the feathers of a peacock,
the supreme emptiness becomes the very body of the ether beyond the inner space.

They explain [the word] as *iti*; however, this is extremely unsatisfactory. For, if the counting begins from fire (*agni*), there would be no twelfth state for the *unmanā*; furthermore, using the locative case (*saptamyā*) in the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyārthe*) is contrary to grammatical rule (*anuśāsanaviruddhatvāt*). Moreover, the repetition (*vīpsā*) "one by one" (*ekaiketi*) is intended here.

Furthermore, it is because the reading "trīṃstrīn" (three by three) cannot logically be treated as separate words; and because, having established the locus for the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*), it would contradict the context to then establish the locus of the voids (*śūnya-sthāna*) within those same six. [This is so] while omitting the pervasive elements (*vibhu*) among the nine, beginning with earth.

If it were said that "corporeality is to be known," corporeality would not be perceived as residing only in pervasive entities; for just as one should not say "girā gireti" (with the word *girā*, [saying] "gireti"), but rather "having made it *airaṃ*,

it should be sung," so too, if it were said that "empty things attain the status of being the locus of fire and so forth," there would follow the non-perception of the *repha* and other phonemes, just as there is no utterance of the word *girā*.

If it were stated by means of the locative case in "in the twelve [centers] beginning with Agni up to the End" (*agnyādidvādaśānteṣu*) that these very [centers] are the locus of the voids (*śūnya*), there would be a contradiction with the commentary on the phrase "three by three" (*trīṃstrīn*), because [the former] would stand in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it. This is because [the centers] would be the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) of the phrase "three by three."

Furthermore, there would be the necessity of supplying the words "hakārādīn" (beginning with the letter *ha*). Moreover, the mention of the abandonment of the three [groups] would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, if the word "traya" (three) were intended to refer to the group of six, it would entail an instance of extremely unestablished metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). If, however, the word "śūnyatraya" (the three voids) were to recur, that same fault of repetition would occur. [The phrase] "ekaśca ekaśca" (one and one)—

In that explanation, there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the rule *sarūpāṇām* (Pāṇini 1.2.64) for the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). Since the interpretation is consistent with the meaning of "separated by one each," it is all the more inappropriate to interpret the word *antara* as meaning "middle" and provide such an explanation. This is so even though, among the first five [consonants], each is situated between two others.

Furthermore, there is the impossibility of the sixth [letter] being situated between two letters. To that end, if it is stated that the twelve-word [mantra] culminates in the *mahābindu*, then— since the conclusion is that there is one *śūnya* between each pair among the sequence beginning with the letter *ra* and ending with the *mahābindu*— it results in [the *śūnya*] being located precisely at the *mahābindu* according to the sequence beginning with the vowel *ī* and the *bindu*.
By placing it in the sixth void, that same fault remains as before; if it is placed starting from the letter *ra*,
the first void remains as before because it lacks the encapsulation by any two of the enumerated twelve.

In that interpretation, where it is explained that the letter *ha* is the beginning of fire (*agni*), there is an absence of any other word such as "beginning" (*ādi*) in the sense of "starting point. Furthermore, if [the sequence] were to include the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*), it would become the thirteenth, which would contradict the statement of "twelve words. This is also the case when explaining [the phrase] as "at the end of the twelfth."
There is an absence of any other word ending in a term denoting the final limit;
furthermore, if only the letter *ha* and the *mahābindu* were taken, there would be a contradiction with the plural number.
Thus, [the expression] "from the three voids" (*śūnyatrayāt*) is used in the ablative case characterized by spatial relation (*digyoga*).
Let it suffice to say that the claim that the genitive case here signifies a "genitive of specification" (nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī) is likewise contrary to the grammatical rules (anuśāsana).
Now, he describes the meditation on the five states together with their characteristics, their expressive syllables, and their respective locations:
"Then, the meditation on the state of waking as being the cause of awakening."
O Goddess, the state of great wakefulness (mahājāgrat) occurs in the fire through the two pairs of sense organs. || 185 ||
Dream is the awakening to illusion by means of the internal organs alone;
deep sleep (suṣupti), at the region of the throat, is the perception of one's own self as it was previously dissolved. (186)
Through the dissolution of the functions of the internal organ and of the object, she who resides as the Bindu between the eyebrows [arises] by reversing the order of the preceding vowels. (187)
But for the sake of manifesting consciousness, there is no speaking of that which consists of sound;
rather, its form here is the fourth state (turya), comprising the half-verse and so forth.
O Dear One, the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is the abode of bliss, situated at the end of the Nāda and so forth;
at this very time of recitation, the wise man should contemplate the five states.

The meaning is that immediately after the explanation of the meditation on the six voids (*śūnya-ṣaṭka*), the meditation on the states (*avasthā-vibhāvana*) is now being described; however, this does not imply a temporal sequence between the two meditations,
for they are established as occurring simultaneously with the meditation on each respective syllable.
Because there is no dependence on another sequence;

by the two sets of organs— that is, by the ten [organs] consisting of the five pairs of each of the sense-organs (*jñānendriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*)— that which effects awakening is "awakening" (*prabodha*).

The activity of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) is their function, and that is also the activity of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). That is to say, it is the orientation of both toward their respective objects. The conceptualization of this [state] as "waking"—that is, its designation by the term "waking"—is common to both the learned and the ignorant.

The word "exists" (*asti*) is to be understood as the ellipsis for "worldly transaction" (*vyavahāra*). In the present context, however, that very waking state (*jāgrad-avasthā*)—which consists of the cessation of sleep at all times—is the "great" one to be contemplated; because it is the subject under discussion, it is to be understood within the third *repha* of the fire-mantra and meditated upon in its very location. As for the ancients, they [say] by means of the ten sense organs...
For the knower, awakening consists precisely in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). That alone is waking;
its instrument, that is, its cause, is Light (*prakāśa*). They explain that the effect, which is the manifestation of that [Light] as waking, resides in the letter *ra*.
[This occurs] by means of the internal instruments—that is, by the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—as indicated by the word "precisely" (*eva*).

The phrase "the cessation of the previously mentioned external sense organs" carries over as a qualification for the awakening agent (*prabodhakarana*). Since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) possesses the dual nature of both the cognitive and the active senses, there exists the conceptualization that the dream state consists of the two activities of awakening produced by the mind alone. And that [dream] is an awakening through illusion (*māyā*), to be understood by means of the third letter *A*.

Moreover, that state of dream should be considered as occurring precisely in the region of the throat. For the dissolution of all objects of the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) during the time of deep sleep is established in such scriptural passages as "everything is dissolved in the Sakala" and so forth. Therefore, the modifications themselves also dissolve precisely because they are their own objects.
When the functioning (vṛtti) has dissolved, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), although existing in a subtle form, is as good as dissolved.

When that qualification has dissolved, the Self characterized by it is likewise [dissolved]. Therefore, in the expression "previously dissolved" (līnapūrva), the word "previously" (pūrva) refers to the internal organ which serves as the qualification.

This is because of the metaphorical designation of "having been previously dissolved. Thus, the meaning is as follows: that which was previously dissolved—that is, one's own Self whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has melted away—the cognition of that [Self], which consists in its being the object of a nescient mental modification (*avidyāvṛtti*), is precisely what is called deep sleep (*suṣupti*). For in deep sleep...

For the author of the Vārttika has stated that there are three modifications of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) whose objects are precisely this triad: pleasure, ignorance, and "I. And since it is accepted that these [modifications] stand in a mutual relationship of the delimited and the delimiting (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*), [one says] "I am ignorant," "I..."

Those who know his intention maintain that the notion of "being happy" does not apply to the time of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Furthermore, although that state of deep sleep exists within the *bindu* through the relationship of denotative power (*vācakatā*) as defined by its own inherent denotability (*svaniṣṭhavācyatā*), it should be meditated upon specifically at the center of the eyebrows (*bhrūmadhya*). Thus, it is said to be "situated both at the center of the eyebrows and in the *bindu*."
Or another interpretation: in order to illuminate that the *bindu* resides precisely in the third peak (*kūṭa*), he says, "by the reversal of the preceding syllables.

The compound *pūrvārṇānām* is a *madhyamapadalopī* (elliptical) compound meaning "the syllables extracted previously" (*pūrva-mukha-uddhṛtā arṇāḥ*). The genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). For it is stated in the previous *Catuḥśatī*:

Only the third peak (kūṭa) of the Kādividyā has been extracted in reverse order. Therefore, the meaning is that she is established there, within the *bindu* among the previously extracted syllables, in their inverse sequence.
As for the earlier commentators: by the word "object" (*viṣaya*), which denotes the pervasion of the universe...

The third peak (kūṭa) is said to possess such pervasion (vyāpti). Regarding its bindu, those four syllables which precede it—meaning both in reverse order (viloma) and in direct order (anuloma)—are [to be understood];
for by stating that they are in reverse order again after having been extracted in reverse order, it implies that they are indeed in direct order.
Because of the finality [of this sequence]: by such a progressive order, the location of the third peak (kūṭa) is in the body at the tip of the uvula;
the location of the three imperishables (akṣara) is between the eyebrows;
and that of the *hṛllekhā* situated there is the point above it, which is the drop (*bindu*) located in the forehead.

They claim that "deep sleep" (suṣupti) is what should be cultivated; however, that [interpretation] is flawed, as it involves excessive textual interpolation and renders the term "between the eyebrows" (bhrūmadhya-pada) redundant. Furthermore, the notion that the word *viṣaya* is derived from the root *viṣḷ* (meaning "to pervade") is merely an error; rather, it is derived from the root *ṣiñ* (meaning "to bind") with the suffix *ac*.
When preceded by *vi*, *upa*, *pari*, *ni*, and *vi*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs according to the rule *sevasitasayetyādi*, thereby resulting in that form.

The state called the fourth stage (*turyāvasthā*) is the condition consisting of the contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of that *nāda* which is the cause for the manifestation of consciousness; it resides within the *bindu*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the obstructress (*rodhinī*), and the *nāda*.
It is to be meditated upon (*bhāvanīya*). "That which has a circle and a half-circle as its beginning" refers to the fourfold set;

"the collection of that" means the connection of that fourfold set, namely the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) and the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). [This applies] to the end of the resonance (*nādānta*) and so forth, as will be explained later.
According to the *Parāmarśa*, here [the *turyā*] is to be meditated upon in four parts. However, the earlier authorities (*prāñcaḥ*) say:

"The half-moon (*ardhacandra*) is half of a circle; one should meditate on the *turyā* in only the first three [parts] of that. That is not correct, because [the half-moon] differs from the circle both in duration and in form.

Otherwise, because the term *ardha* (half) would have to be placed first according to the rule for compounds where the two parts are of equal measure (*samāṃśa*), it would result in the undesirable form *ardhasama*. However, in the view that the word *bindu* connects only with the preceding part,
one must accept this [the placement of *ardha* first] at the outset, due to the lack of any other alternative, just as in the case of "half of Rodhinī" (*tadardhe rodhinyām*) and so forth.

The state beyond the fourth (turyātītadaśā) is abiding in the form of pure bliss alone, without even the pursuit of sound (nādānusaṃdhāna). That [state] is to be meditated upon as residing within the pentad beginning with the end of sound (nādānta), by way of being the signified and so forth. In this manner, it resides right here, in the third peak (tṛtīyakūṭa) itself.
The meaning is that one should contemplate the five states. || 185 || 186 || 187 || 188 || 189 ||
Now he describes the characteristics of the seven equinoxes (viṣuva):
"The union of breath, self, and mind is the equinox known as prāṇa;
having realized it as dissolved within the resonance (nāda) arisen from the foundation (ādhāra), one attains the nature of the Self. (190)
O Maheśvarī, through the conjunction and disjunction of the syllables of the mantra,
one should contemplate their nature as sound (nāda) from the unstruck (anāhata) center to the final support (ādhāra).
O Dear One, because of the contact with the nāda at the equinox (viṣuvat), it is called the nāḍī-viṣuva;
[this occurs] by the piercing of the twelve knots within the channel of the phonemes.
The word *viṣuva* ends both in the letter *t* and in the vowel *a*;
