for, under the heading of suffixes denoting possession (*matvarthīya*), the rule "it is seen after other [roots] as well" prescribes the optional application of the suffix *vap* and the suffix *matup* after the word *viṣu*. [This occurs] during a period of seven days and nights.

And from the *Āgneya Purāṇa*: "That is the equinox (*viṣuvat*). For the basis for the application of the word *viṣu* is the pervasion of the third [day] by both equal [halves]. Therefore, even in the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice, by means of the preceding and following fortnights (*pakṣas*), which consist of one hundred and eighty days...

The designation *viṣuvat* (equinox) applies to the day that is bisected; or, disregarding the sense of equality, the word *viṣuvat* may signify merely that which possesses pervasion (*vyāptimat*). In the present context as well, it is precisely because of possessing such a property that there is a relationship between two things of mutually equal magnitude.
The equinox of the vital breath (*prāṇaviṣuva*). Since it is well known, the heart alone is not mentioned as the location for all three;

for even in that very section on the equinox, it says, "one should contemplate the disciple [within] there. In both cases, the word "disciple" (*śiṣya*) refers simply to the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and its meaning is indeed "one's own self" (*svātman*). However, some...

Considering that there is a deficiency because the root of the locus of meditation (*bhāvanāsthāna*) has not been stated, some explain that the word *prāṇa* refers to the wind consisting of the letter *ka*. That is not correct;
for since the letter *ka* is threefold, it would result in a three-pronged dilemma regarding the locus of meditation. Of that...

And because there is an absence of the nature of air (vāyu). Nor should it be thought that its being such [as air] follows from the statement, "From the letter *ka* comes the wind," since it was established previously that the *ka* therein refers to the syllable *kāmakalā*. Nor indeed by the *kāmakalā* alone...

It must be stated that the destruction of the *sarā* (or *sara*) should be contemplated; for since it is fourfold, there arises the contingency of a four-pronged conceptualization (*catuṣkoṭika-vikalpa*). This is for the sake of establishing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the Self, which resides in the heart.

If it is argued that the realization of non-difference occurs through the *kāmakalā* residing in the second peak (*kūṭa*) alone, then the dawn has already occurred within the two peaks themselves; thus, the figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the term "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) [to the disciple] would be rendered useless. This concerns the passage beginning with "of the disciple’s self, vital breath, and mind" (*śiṣyātmaprāṇamanasām*).
Furthermore, the appearance of the word *śiṣya* (disciple) as applying to all three [states] contradicts its own inherent meaning.

In reality, however, the manifestation of that sound—which is well-known as *brahman* in the *mūlādhāra*—arises from the conjunction of the vital air (*vāyu*) and the *kuṇḍalinī*. That very sound, having reached as far as the navel...

She is joined with the vital breath (*pavana*) and the mind (*manas*). Having entered the heart, she is joined with the vital breath and the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, it is she alone who sequentially assumes the three names—*parā*, *paśyantī*, and *madhyamā*—in the three locations;
this very point has been described by us in the *Saubhāgyabhāskara*. And this indeed is...
It should be understood that the single contemplation (*bhāvanā*) consists of the convergence at the three locations of what is designated as the "equinox of the vital breath" (*prāṇaviṣuva*).

Therefore, the word "self" (*ātman*) here should be regarded as referring to the intellect (*buddhi*). The sound (*nāda*) arising from the *mūlādhāra* [pierces] the two pairs of knots existing on both sides of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*).

The established position is that [the sound] travels via the central path of the Suṣumṇā channel as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). That sound, being of the nature of the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, enters into the syllables of the second and third kūṭas and is indeed non-different from them. However, at the junction of the two syllables, it also becomes distinct from them.
Just as the consciousness (cittattva), when not entered into the succession of mental modifications (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti), shines as being of the very same form [as them],

whereas at the junction of two modifications it shines as distinct from them— this is the experience of the knowers of Brahman. Or, for example, just as the thread passing through the interior of a string of gems does not appear distinct within the gems themselves.
It shines; however, it shines distinctly within the junctions of the two jewels. This, then, is the distinction:
because the thread is entirely distinct from the jewels, it exists as something separate even while within them;
but the sound (nāda), while within the phonemes (akṣara), exists non-differently from them. And so too with the phonemes.
Because it consists of the transformation of sound (*nāda*), this very point is established by the statement "through the conjunction and disjunction of the letters of the mantra.
Here, by the word "mantra," the second and third *kūṭas* alone are intended by virtue of their suitability, not the first. However, the ancients [hold otherwise]:

They have explained that the term *saṃyoga* refers to the fourth seed-syllable (*turyabīja*) which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three peaks (*kūṭa*), while the term *viyoga* refers to the three seed-syllables (*bījatraya*) which are the individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*). This is clearly incorrect.
[One should contemplate] such a sound (*nāda*), beginning from the final position of the *vāgbhava* syllable up to its location in the heart.

Having visualized [the syllable] rising as far as the final letter of the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, one should contemplate the dissolution of one's own vital self (*jīvātman*) into it; then, having caused the sound (*nāda*)—which has swallowed that [vital self]—to ascend upward, one should contemplate it reaching as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). This is as follows:
The "equinox of the mind" (*mantaviṣuva*) is thus described. Here, the phrase "from the *anāhata* [cakra] to the end of the *ādhāras*" should be explained by resolving the compound as follows:
"having pervaded that which is the end—the final [point], the *brahmarandhra*—of the *ādhāras*, beginning with the *mūlādhāra* and ending with the *āśānta*.
This is to be understood through the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the prefix *ā-* (meaning "pervasion") in the word *ādhārāntam*.

According to another tantra, [the channel] from the heart to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) is designated as the "equinox" (viṣuva) mantra. Although one should have said "up to the end of the foundation" (ādhārāntāntam), the single word *anta* has been used twice by means of ellipsis (*tantra*), and is thus to be connected in two places.
The reading *prāyāmukti* is not to be accepted. Some say it is *viṣuvan-nāda*, while others maintain that the word division is *viṣuvat-takārānta*.
Now, regarding such a *nāda*, that which [occurs] preceded by the piercing of the twelve knots— (p. 382) ... this...

The entry into the *suṣumṇā* channel is itself called the "equinox of the channels" (*nāḍīviṣuva*). Regarding this, the ancient commentators have explained the word *varṇāt* as referring to the syllable of the *kāmakalā* situated at the peak of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*). However, it is more appropriate [to interpret it] as being from the letter *ī*, which is the final letter of the *vāgbhava* mantra; this is understood through the elision of the suffix *-lyap*.
The fifth [case]. The meaning is: "beginning with the letter *ī*. || 190 || 191 || 192 ||
The yoga of sound is peaceful; it is the sphere of those whose senses are pacified.
[One should contemplate] fire, māyā, time, consciousness, and the half-moon. (193)
One should contemplate the *rodhinī*, *nāda*, and *nādānta* as dissolved into Śakti; the equinox (*viṣuva*) is indeed named Śakti, and above that is the contemplation of *nāda*.
Beyond that, O Maheśvarī, is the temporal equinox (kālaviṣuva) extending to the end of Unmanā;
through eighteen lunar months [of breaths] and eight trutis, there is the perception of Nāda.
And the equinox, known as Tattva, is the cause for the manifestation of consciousness;
it is the supreme station, O Great Goddess, beautiful with innate bliss. (196)
Because the sound (*nāda*) connected to the channels (*nāḍī*) becomes tranquil and dissolved within the Power (*śakti*),
for that reason this is called the "tranquil equinox" (*praśāntaviṣuva*). Precisely because it is stated that the sound dissolves into the Power, one transcends the preceding *tatsvarṇa* (?).

Since it is already implied by the sense that [the breath] should be meditated upon until that limit without being dissolved, the author enumerates those locations together with that [limit] in order to indicate that another place must be contemplated between the fourth vowel (*turyasvara*) and the *bindu*— namely, "fire" (*vahnim*).

The letter *repha* is *vahni* (fire); the letter *ikāra* is *māyā*; and the letter *makāra* is *kāla*, which—despite the existence of a lexicon stating that *mahākāla* means *yama* or *antaka*—is to be understood here as referring merely to the phonetic sound of the letter *ma*, since only the word *kāla* is employed by omitting the term *mahā*.

The ancients, however, maintain that the word *kāla* refers to *kalā*. According to this view, a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) must be stated in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) after the word *kalā*. However, that [interpretation] contradicts the *Svacchanda-tantra*, because it states: "The letter *ma* is indeed the *bindu*. Furthermore, *anusvāra* is *cetana*, for the lexicon (*kośa*) states: "*Akrūra* is *cetana* and *nāda*."

The half-moon and so forth have already been explained; the word "these" implies that they do not follow this sequence. This, then, is the *praśāntaviṣuva* (the tranquil equinox), the range and object of those whose senses are tranquilized and restrained. The sense is that it is difficult to attain for those whose faculties are unsteady. [This occurs] at the term *gocara*.
The neuter form (*klība*) is used in accordance with the usage of the Ṛṣis. Now, just as one observes that a lamp or similar object,

while dissolving, becomes subtle and then returns to a gross state, so too, following that analogy, one contemplates the dissolution of the *nāda*— which had merged into the *śakti*— into the *samanā*, after it has been revived by its own power and has transcended the *vyāpikā*.
The Śakti-equality (śaktiviṣuva). Then, having been revived once more, its dissolution into Unmanā is the Time-equality (kālaviṣuva). (p.

383) "The Sound (nāda) situated in the center of Śakti flows forth as far as the end of Samanā; that is declared to be the Śakti-equality, while that which occurs in Unmanā is designated as Time. Thus it is said.

Because of its independence. Now, if this very *nāda* is uttered without interruption for a duration of three and a half *nimeṣas*, up to a period measured by three hundred and seventeen *truṭis*, then at its conclusion—
The manifestation of consciousness occurs; this is the *tattvaviṣuva* (equinox of the principles), because it effects the pervasion of the principles.
There are seven sages and one moon; thus, there are ten thousand eight hundred and seventeen *truṭis*. Three thousand *truṭis* constitute one *nimeṣa*.
As it has been said: "When a healthy man is sitting at ease, as long as his eye twinkles, the thirtieth part of that duration is proclaimed to be a *tatpara*."
"A hundredth part of that is called a *truṭi*.

Thus, the supreme state— which transcends the clamor of the twenty-six [categories], namely the nine wheels (*cakras*), the six voids (*śūnyas*), the five states (*avasthās*), and the seven equinoxes (*viṣuvants*)— is [the ultimate].
The meaning is that it is beautiful with innate bliss. || 193 || 194 || 195 || 196 ||
Although this reflection serves the purpose of the ritual, he also states that it serves the purpose of the person:
"O Pārvatī, for one who reflects in this manner at the time of recitation, all accomplishments (siddhis) are swiftly attained through your grace. (197)
This is clear. || 197 ||
Concluding the procedure for recitation (*japa*), he states several rules regarding its qualities:
"Having performed the recitation of the Goddess in this manner, one should offer it into her left hand;
by joining the ring finger and the thumb, one should satisfy the deities of the cakras. (198)
One should offer this to the goddess Mātaṅgī;
one should worship her together with heroes who are well-versed in the Kaula conduct. || 199 ||

The offering of the water while reciting the mantra preceded by the reflection on its meaning—"You are the guardian of the secret, even more secret than the secret"—is the presentation of the recitation (*japanivedana*). Following that is the rule for the locus (*adhikaraṇavidhi*) directed toward that [offering]. Next is the rule for the *tattvamudrā* directed toward the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Finally, there is [the rite] directed toward the presentation, performed with the verse of scrambled syllables (*vyākulākṣarapāda*).

The rule for the first three [stages] is the primary injunction; the other is the defining characteristic. Through the practice of the sandals (*pādukācāra*), the practice of the observances (*samayācāra*), and the practice of the supreme hero (*paravīrasāhitya*), there is the enumeration of those who have fallen away from the Kaula practice. 198–199.
Having thus prescribed the daily worship, he speaks of the occasional rites:
"O Supreme Goddess, [these are performed] daily, or on a day of Puṣya, or on a Saturday."
On the day of one's preceptor, on one's own birth star, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days. || 200 ||
One should especially perform the wheel-worship (cakrapūjā) for the Yoginīs, since there are sixty-four crores of Yoginīs of great splendor. (201)
O you who are praised by heroes, having taken refuge in this wheel, one should perform the eight groups of eight [offerings], free from stinginess regarding wealth. (202)
You alone, the enchantress of the universe, sport in their forms.

Although many occasional rites of worship (*naimittikārcanāni*) are prescribed in the *Kulārṇava*, nevertheless, among them, these few are absolutely essential: on the day of the Guru and on the birthday of the Lord (*nātha*).
And on a day of [planetary] conjunction; on one's own birth asterism;

and on the fourteenth and eighth days—due to the use of the plural, this refers to both fortnights—with particular emphasis on the daily worship through an abundance of offerings such as food, drink, and so forth, for the sake of the Yoginīs and Vīras.

The meaning is "or with a special substance. By this, it is indicated that even when special substances are unavailable during the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), one may proceed by means of a substitute. And it is stated in the *Kalpasūtra*: "Even in the absence of the five-fold [special] time, there is the performance of the daily rite. Regarding the number sixty-four: among the nine wheels (*cakras*).
The meaning is "each wheel" (*praticakram*). Taken together, there are five *arbudas*, sixty million, and six hundred thousand yoginīs.

The so-called "eight eights" (*aṣṭāṣṭakam*) is a specific ritual act consisting of the consumption of couples. These include Asitāṅgabhairava and others, as well as Maṅgalanātha and others—thus making eight.
From one of these two sets of eight, eight daughters were born from each pair;
from the other, however, males were born. Due to mutual disputes between them, eight pairs of offspring arose from each of those original pairs.

Together they constitute sixty-four. Their names are well-known in the *Sahasrākṣarī-mantra* and in the Tantras concerning their ritual placements (*nyāsa*) and so forth. These pairs are indeed of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, and they also constitute the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the host of the sixty-four million great Yoginīs.
Therefore, this mere act of eating must certainly be performed according to one's means;
the procedure for that meal is to be found in the *Naimittikapaṭala* of the *Kulārṇava*. By the word "but" (*tu*), [it is indicated that] those [details] mentioned in that very same [text]...
Of the rites beginning with the feeding of the fifty-one couples starting with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with the feeding of the three powers (icchā, jñāna,
and kriyā), as well as the rites such as the thousand-fold feeding and the three-hundred-fold feeding mentioned in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* and other texts.

And the lack of necessity has been implied. As for the claim that the worship of the sixty-four couples in the middle underground chamber (madhyamabhūgṛha) is called the "eight eights" (aṣṭāṣṭaka), this is merely an error of the ancients;
furthermore, it contradicts the inherent force of the phrase "free from stinginess regarding wealth. || 200 || 201 || 202 ||

(p. 385) Indicating by implication the conclusion of the treatise, he punishes the one who has not studied it: "But without knowing the conduct of the lineage, and without having worshipped the sandals of the Guru... (203)
"O lady of excellent hips, knowing this, you certainly afflict whoever engages in this scripture; therefore, one should always be devoted to the Kaula practice. (204)
Those who perceive the form of Śabala as belonging to us two should instead contemplate it as existing only within you, having the form of the expansion of your own renown.
One should meditate upon you as the Goddess, the embodiment of desire, appearing in the form of the Guru.
Having offered the remainder to the Guru, he should subsequently unite it with himself.

The conduct described in the *Kalpasūtra* in the passage beginning with "the customs of the region of practice" (*vyavahāradeśasātmya*) and ending with "and others instructed by the scriptures" (*pare ca śāstrānuśiṣṭāḥ*) constitutes family tradition (*kulācāra*). In the phrase "having worshipped the sandals of the Guru" (*gurupādukāmayaṣṭvā*),
there is no vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because the rule concerning a specific designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka-vidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
The meaning is that [the knowledge] was acquired through theft and other such means, even without the grace of the Guru.

Having concluded this incidental matter, he teaches the remainder of the procedure for worship: "Our form is variegated," meaning it consists of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti. Here, one foot [of the verse] contains disordered syllables.
Purity and attainment are achieved through the very word *śabala* (the variegated), because it is stated in the Tantra that the second [state] alone possesses the nature of Śiva.

One should contemplate within You alone those deities, such as Aṇimā and the rest, whose forms are the expansion of the manifestation of Your own glory (*tvat-prathā*). They have bodies consisting solely of the nature of light (*tejas*).

Having visualized that they have entered the body of the illustrious Mūladevī, one should contemplate her as follows: then one should contemplate you, Mūladevī, who have assumed a body by your own will, in the form of one's own Guru, transformed into the form of the Lord (Nātha) residing in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra). Then...

Having offered the substance remaining in the special arghya vessel to the Guru— either as manifest before him or as residing in the *brahmarandhra*— one should offer that remnant into one's own self.
O Great Goddess, one should offer the bali-oblation with the proper motive to the Yoginīs, to Vaṭuka who is of the nature of the Self, and to me, the Lord of the sacred fields (kṣetrapati). || 207 ||

In other tantras, offerings (bali) to Gaṇapati and others, such as Kurukullā, are mentioned; among these, the meaning is that the offerings to the Yoginīs, the Bāṭukas, and the Kṣetrapālas are essential. However, in the Kalpasūtra, only a single offering to all beings (sarvabhūtabali) is mentioned. By the word "with the reason" (hetunā), the preparation of the vessel for the offering is implied, as well as that of the special arghya.

Because it effects complete exhaustion. In reality, however, by overriding the order of the recitation (pāṭhakrama) through the order of the purpose (arthakrama), the offering of the bali-oblation comes first, followed by the disposal of the remnants of the oblation (haviḥśeṣapratipatti). By this, consistency with the Kalpasūtras is also achieved. || 207 ||
Whether one is subject to punishment or not, even if intent on acting according to one's own whims, one should wander happily, contemplating the identity of "I-ness" and "this-ness. (208)
The first quarter here contains scrambled syllables.
Even outside the time of formal worship, one should continue to move through worldly and Vedic activities while constantly contemplating the non-difference between oneself and the universe. By that—
Because he is not assailed by external torments, he remains in a state that is exclusively of the nature of bliss. || 208 ||

He concludes the latter half of the scripture by concealing it: "O lady of excellent vows, these three supreme divine conventions have been told to you; they must be guarded with effort, like one's own secret. (209)
O sinless one, you must not reveal this to a kisser nor to one greedy for knowledge;
O Maheśvarī, it must not be given to atheists by any unjust means.
"O Lord, I have been thus commanded by you, who are the embodiment of my own will;

[the command] to be kept secret from the disciples of others is the remainder [of the sense]. For it has been compared to a secret that must be concealed from other men alone. Yet, he mentions even among his own disciples a few exceptions—namely, the 'Cumbaka'."

One who is intent solely on the recitation of the root *Śrīvidyā*, yet remains unattached to the knowledge of its ritual procedures (*karma*), its *tāla* rhythms, and its secret lore (*rahasya*); one who is a mere "magnet" (a superficial practitioner) lacking devotion to its performance;
and one who, through a common knowledge of other scriptures, merely desires the scholarly erudition (*pāṇḍitya*) pertaining to this system—such a person is a pseudo-knower (*jñānin*).

Even if it were shown to those who are greedy for knowledge, it should not be said that "it must not be given. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, the injunction—"such a disciple who is greedy for knowledge may resort to another guru"—would suffer from invalidity characterized by non-implementation; for [this applies] in Kurukṣetra.

For even though the prohibition against accepting gifts and the injunction regarding giving there stand in mutual opposition, it is possible here as well to establish the authority of the injunctions for giving by taking the case of a Brāhmaṇa who acts in transgression of the prohibition; this applies likewise to the term "one greedy for knowledge" found there.

Or, because of the state of being a vessel for those greedy for both practice and knowledge; however, even for that good disciple who desires to practice and desires to know, [the teacher] should not— by an improper means—
transgress the sequence beginning with approaching the guru, initiation, the observance of restraints, and the preservation of the study of one's own Veda.
It should not be given by him; however, for those who possess intelligence, it should certainly not be given on the grounds that there is no other world—this is the meaning. || 209 || 210 ||

Having thus instructed the treatise, and wishing at the conclusion to avoid the faults of deficiency or excess, he remembers his own guru with the words: "In this way, by you... O Lord, O Sovereign, by you—who have assumed the form of my will and who are my teacher—I, your disciple, have been commanded.
The Lord’s feet (illuminate this very point):
"He who thoroughly understands the secret sign of the Yoginīs shall become beloved by them. (p. 387) || 211 ||
O Goddess, since the attainment of all desired fruits and the locus of all wished-for results are seen even from this [mantra], one should not entertain any doubt. (212)
By means of the path of knowing the three conventions, one becomes an object of compassion for the Yoginīs;
he alone attains all desired fruits, and he indeed becomes such [a person].
To indicate the completion of the treatise, the author repeats this very qualification, saying:

"the locus of all desired fruits. Having thus ascertained the essence of the supreme secret of this scripture, he states "from which also," summarizing in half a verse the meaning of the final sūtra of the Śaiva scriptures, which declares that "reunion shall once again take place. [The word] "yataḥ" means: because He is perceived everywhere by Himself.
One should not contemplate anything as distinct from oneself; this is the essence of worship. May all be auspicious! 211–212.
Thus ends the eighth rest in the commentary called Setubandha on the ocean of the Nityāṣoḍaśikā, composed by the illustrious Bhāskara.

Thus, the eighth chapter consists of two hundred and twelve verses. Summarizing [the previous chapters], there are four hundred and seventeen verses. By combining both sets of four hundred verses, the scripture contains eight hundred and thirteen and a half verses. Among these:

It is stated therein that the twelve verses beginning with "Gaṇeśagrahanakṣatre" constitute the auspicious preliminary rites (*maṅgalācāra*) and thus lie outside the Tantra itself; furthermore, because the final half-verse ending with "yato'pi" also lies outside,
the designation "Aṣṭaśatī" (The Eight Hundred) is justified.
Because the addition of a single verse constitutes only a minor difference; because we observe the conventional usage of "fifty letters" [despite the actual count being fifty-one];

and because the verse beginning with "sṛṣṭyā" occurs twice in the *Pūrvatantre* and *Uttaratantre* within that group of five verses on power (*tacchakti*), it may be intended that neither of those two [versions] is to be counted.
The justification for this should be noted:

there was in Kāśī a jewel among scholars named Gambhīrarāja, a descendant of the illustrious Viśvāmitra, devoted to the worship of Śiva, a follower of Bhāratī, and a drinker of Soma; his son was Bhāskara.

In the sacred field of Śrīsaptakoṭīśvarapura, on the night of Śivarātri in the Śaka year [of] Śarma-cāpa (1756), he constructed this bridge for the sake of reaching the further shore of the ocean of the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava. || 1 ||
Having thoroughly studied this Tantra, along with its secret portions and its oral tradition, from a teacher who was a fellow-student of the Elder (Jyeṣṭha),
and having also reflected upon other Tantras and their commentaries—
The noble Bhāskara composed this single work on the earth. || 2 ||
Although this commentary has been composed after churning and ascertaining the Śruti, Smṛti, Nyāya, Purāṇas, Tantras, Sūtras, Āgamas, and the tradition of the venerable Guru;
It must indeed be purified by the virtuous who possess love for me. || 3 ||
"Due to my dullness of intellect and laziness, negligence will certainly occur on my part,
given the inherent difficulty of fathoming even the principles of categories;
however, may the holy feet of the Lord, whose hearts are compassionate toward those within, [forgive this]."
Therefore, for me, there is truly no fear of the danger posed by wicked people. || 4 ||
Even today, there remains for the wise a great twofold doubt regarding him who is declared by the Śruti to be the Lord of the Universe: is he "seven" (sapta) or is he "attained" (apta)?
In this matter, what is clear for the sake of certain determination is that the first alternative alone—that he is the Lord—is the truth.
He became renowned by the name Paraśiva, the Lord of the seventy million [Śiva-mantras]. || 5 ||
The single syllable "ptā" denotes matted hair (*jaṭā*); one who is endowed with these is "sapta," meaning Śiva, who has attained (*āpta*) Hari.

Thus [ends the work] by the venerable [author], who is foremost among those who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the authoritative means of knowledge regarding words and sentences, and who is [the master of] all...

The *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava* was composed by Bhāskararāya, whose name is Bhāsurānandanātha Dīkṣita, the son of Śrīmadgambhīrarāja Dīkṣita, who was initiated into the lineage of the venerable and profound *Bharatī*.
The Setubandha, which consists of an exposition of the Ṛṇavaya,
is complete.
